WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
THURSDAY, JULY 14, 1921.
UNITED STATES SENATE,
COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION AND LABOR,
Washington, D. C.
The committee met, pursuant to the call of the chairman, at 10 o'clock a. m.,
in the committee room, Capitol, Senator Kenyon presiding.
Present: Senators Kenyon (chairman), Warren, Sterling, and McKellar.
Also present: Harry Olmsted, representing operators' association, William-
son field; Randolph Bias, Williamson, W. Va., appearing for certain mine
owners of the Williamson coal fields; Harry Scheer, Williamson, W. Va., ap-
pearing for certain mine owners; James Damron, Williamson, W. Va., appearing
for certain coal operators in the Williamson coal fields; Z. T. Vinson, Hunting-
ton, W. Va., appearing for the operators' association in the Williamson coal
fields; Neill Burkinshaw, 636 Munsey Building, Washington, D. C., appearing
for United Mine Workers of America; Samuel B. Montgomery, Kingwood, ap-
pearing for United Mine Workers' Association; E. L. Greever, appearing for
Williamson Coal Operators' Association; Capt. S. B. Avis, appearing for
Williamson Coal Operators' Association.
The committee had under consideration Senate resolution 80, directing the
Committee on Education and Labor to investigate the recent acts of violence
in the coal fields of West Virginia and adjacent territory and the causes which
led to the conditions which now exist in said territory.
(The resolution is here printed in full as follows:)
SENATE RESOLUTION 80.
Whereas there have been conditions of violence in the coal fields along the
border between West Virginia and Kentucky: Therefore be it
Resolved, That the Senate Committee on Education and Labor, or any sub-
committee thereof, to be appointed by it, is hereby authorized and directed to
make a thorough and complete investigation of the conditions existing in the
coal fields of West Virginia, in the territory adjacent to the border of West
Virginia and Kentucky; that said committee ascertain the causes of the recent
acts of violence upon said border and of the conditions which have existed and
do now exist in the said coal fields, and generally investigate thoroughly the
causes which have led to conditions which have obtained in the past, and which
now exist in said territory, and report its findings and conclusions thereon
to the Senate. The committee, or any subcommittee thereof, is authorized to sit
at such time and place as it may deem necessary; the expenses of said investi-
gation to be paid out of the contingent fund of the Senate.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, who represents the various sides to this controversy?
Mr. HOUSTON. Mr. Burkinshaw and Mr. Harold W. Houston, senior counsel for
the United Mine Workers, and with them associated Mr. Samuel D. Montgomery
and Mr. William West and Mr. Neil Burkinshaw.
The CHAIRMAN. And who represents the operators?
Mr. VINSON. I will state that Capt. S. B. Avis and Mr. E. L. Greever and
Mr. Z. T. Vinson represent the Williamson Coal Operators' Association, in con-
nection with Mr. Bias and Judge Damron and Mr. Scheer. These three gen-
tlemen represent the coal companies in that field. I will ask Mr. Bias to state
what coal companies he represents.

Mr. BIAS. I represent the Burning Creek Coal Co., the Standard Thacker Coal
Co., the Naugatuck Coal Co., the Red Jacket Coal & Coke Co., and the Red
Jacket, Jr., Coal Co.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, I think we would like to hear from each side and allow
each side to make a short statement.
Mr. DAMRON. I appear for the Lynn Coal & Coke Co. and the Borderland Coal
Corporation.
Mr. SCHEER. I appear for the Thacker Coal & Coke Co., the Crystal Block
Coal & Coke Co., and the Crystal Block Mining Co., and the Burnwell Coal
& Coke Co., the Smith-Pond Creek Coal Co., the New Howard Coal Co., the
Stone Mountain Coal Corporation, and the Allburn Coal Corporation.
Senator WARREN. Mr. Chairman, there are a great many witnesses present,
and, of course, many interests are to be represented. I hope that you will
impress upon those witnesses present to condense their arguments just as much
as they possibly can.
The CHAIRMAN. It is understood, Senator, that we have limited the number
of witnesses for this hearing to six on each side; that is, for this prelimi-
nary hearing. We would like to hear from each side and to receive from
each side a very short, brief statement of what this controversy is about and
just what Federal matters are involved in it. I think that you can do that
in 10 minutes, can you not?
Mr. VINSON. We can; yes, sir.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. We can do it in 10 minutes.
Mr. VINSON. We would be pleased, Mr. Chairman, if you will tell us some-
thing of the nature of the proceedings after the witnesses have been heard--
that is, the six on each side.
The CHAIRMAN. I think that will develop with the proceedings. It is im-
possible for this committee or for a subcommittee to leave here at this time,
so we have asked you to bring these six witnesses on each side to Washington
and to give us a picture of this situation and the essential things that we
should do.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. And what is the pleasure of the Chair regarding which
side shall open?
The CHAIRMAN. Suppose that the miners open.
Mr. VINSON. That is satisfactory to us.
The CHAIRMAN. And we hope that you will limit yourself to 10 minutes.
Mr. VINSON. I want to state, Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of the committee,
that the hearing of only six witnesses, so far as our side is concerned, would
give you but a very poor idea of the conditions down in that district and of
the issues involved. We have gone to a great deal of trouble and to a great
deal of expense to prepare for the hearing, and to reduce the number of wit-
nesses down to as few as possible.
The CHAIRMAN. Colonel, you do not understand that we have limited the
number of witnesses to six on each side for the entire investigation. The limi-
tation of six on each side is simply for the preliminary hearings, as I have
explained.
Mr. VINSON. I want to ask this question now, if it is the sense of the com-
mittee that we shall be permitted to introduce our evidence that is pertinent
and material and that bears upon the issues in this case, as defined by the
resolution which passed the Senate?
The CHAIRMAN. Of course, we have been instructed to investigate this matter
by the Senate, and we will investigate thoroughly pursuant to those instruc-
tions, because we are under the order of the Senate.
Mr. VINSON. So that we will not be cut off when we might call but a fraction
of the witnesses who will testify-material witnesses who will testify as to
the issues and that. we will be allowed to present witnesses-
The CHAIRMAN. Certainly, you may. That is the intention.
Mr. VINSON. That is all we want to know-that we will be heard.
The CHAIRMAN. You will be heard.
the resolution.

Mr. VINSON. Then, that is satisfactory.
The CHAIRMAN. Of course, we do not want to spend the whole summer on it.
You understand that. The original idea was for us to go down to West Vir-
ginia and to investigate it there, but we did not have the time to do so, and
we will have this preliminary hearing here.
Mr. VINSON. I will say that the heat of Washington is as oppressive to us
as it is, no doubt, to the Senators, and we will be just as short as we can.

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
5
OPENING STATEMENT OF MR. NEIL BURKINSHAW.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Mr. Chairman, I can only repeat what. the counsel has
said regarding the impossibility of stating this case with six witnesses. It is
my desire that we be allowed to put on at least 50 witnesses in order to make
a thorough investigation of the situation, and to make that investigation as
thoroughly as possible. The introduction of possibly 100 to 150 witnesses
would be helpful, but we are going to try to confine them to 50 each side. We
must have at least that many in order that we can make a thorough investi-
gation of this most deplorable situation.
This strike controversy had its origin in the dissatisfaction of the miners of
Tug River over a good many things, and over especially their inability to make
any economic progress without an organization of some sort. During the spring
of 1919 the United States Coal Commission awarded wage increases amounting
to generally throughout the country to 24 to 27 per cent. This did not apply to
the Mingo field. The miners down there became restless and disgruntled and
dissatisfied, and they were unable to keep up with the cost of living, and they
went to the employers and asked for an increase that they might be able to keep
their heads above water economically. Their request met with no response, and
their demands were ignored. Then the men met and they appointed a committee
and they sent representatives to Charleston to interview Mr. Frank Keeney,
president of the Mine Workers' Association of District 17, and they asked from
him a charter for the organization of the field. These men wished to join the
United Mine Workers.
Mr. Keeney sent them back to the mines, declaring that he would give them
no charter until they put the mines in operation, and there was what was called
a one-day strike. These men went back and put the mines in operation for the
purpose of getting the charter signed, returning to Charleston and asking
Keeney for a charter. This charter was granted, and the men flocked into the
United Mine organization in droves. In one place they went into a church
and gave out a notice that the church would be used for those men who wished
to join the United Mine Workers. That church was filled three times within
an hour and a half. They flocked in, and they flocked in willingly, and there
was no duress, no undue persuasion of any sort used.
When the organizers came I said to put these organizers on the stand, but
they were so busy receiving applications from men who wished to join that they
did not have time at any time. There was no persuasion of the men to go in.
As those men joined the United Mine Workers they were out of a job for taking
advantage of their rights as citizens to join any organization they saw fit;
they were fired, and not only fired but they were evicted from their homes.
These people were driven like cattle from their homes, and their goods were
thrown out into the roads, and some lived in tents and railroad stations and
temporary shelters, and others even were without shelter until the United Mine
Workers' organization at Charleston sent them tents, and to this day those
people are living in tents. They lived there during the winter. I was down
there last November and saw barefoot children, women with a single garment,
and men barefooted with nothing but overalls, living in that cold. It is a high
mountain country and it is very cold. They suffered tortures that I have never
seen before in this or any country.
These men held a convention on the 1st of July in Williamson to formulate
their demands.
The CHAIRMAN, Of what year?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. The 1st of July, 1920, formulated demands to serve on the
coal operators.
Senator STERLING. How many were there?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Four thousand men, roughly. These men met in Wil-
liamson and formulated their plans, and since that time they have never
had an opportunity to present those demands to the operators; they have
refused to let them present those demands.
Just a word about the character of these men.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Were these demands put in writing?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Yes; but no opportunity ever was had to use them, and
we will introduce them when Mr. Keeney takes the stand.
Senator STERLING. Are the men who were let out kept out or did they get
back into their work-any of them?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. After the strike order. The strike order was not issued
until July 1. At that time there were more than 2,700 miners and their


===== [扫描序号 14] =====
6
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
families, who had been locked out because of their taking out cards in the
United Mine Workers. That was talked of as a strike, but it is not a strike
but a lockout.
Senator STERLING. Are they still out?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Yes, sir; they are still out. There are about 2,900 of
them now, so the number is about the same.
The CHAIRMAN. How large a field does this cover. Give us a little picture
of that.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. It borders on the Tug River, about 50 miles wide. The
Tug River separates Kentucky from Mingo County, W. Va. The field is 50
miles long and 4 or 5 miles on each side of the stream.
Senator WARREN. You say they did not have an opportunity to present their
demands. Why was that?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. The men formulated their demands and selected a com-
mittee to serve these proposals on the representatives of the Williamson Coal
Operator's Association. That association refused to meet or receive this
committee. Efforts have been made since then to enlist the county authorities,
and the county authorities have endeavored to bring about a settlement. The
State authorities have endeavored to bring about a settlement, and even con-
ciliators from the Department of Labor were down there and tried to bring
about a settlement, but they were told that there was absolutely no possibility
of Williamson Coal Operators' Association dealing with them in any manner
whatever.
The CHAIRMAN. This field is under martial law?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Martial law was put into effect about a month or so ago-
I think about May 18.
The CHAIRMAN. Does that extend into Kentucky as well?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. No, sir; not into Kentucky, just West Virginia.
Senator WARREN. You say they refused to meet the committee. Did they
also refuse to talk to the men individually or jointly? I simply want to find
out the extent of the refusal.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. They simply refused to treat with the United Mine
Workers as an organization and refused to deal with men carrying the card.
The CHAIRMAN. Before July 1, 1920, how many miners were employed in
that region?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. About 4,000.
The CHAIRMAN. How many of them belonged to unions and how many
did not?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. There had been no organization in that field until the
men asked for a charter and asked for organizers to come down there and
enlist them in the United Mine Workers' Union. Before that time the field was
not organized.
The CHAIRMAN. Is that the fundamental trouble down there, the question of
unionizing the men-that is the issue?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Yes. The men wished to organize and the operators said
they would not be permitted to organize.
Senator WARREN. This was the United Mine Workers. Had the miners pre-
vious to that time been affiliated with other organizations of various labor
unions?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. The United Mine Workers of America, the international
organization, is affiliated with the American Federation of Labor.
Senator WARREN. I wanted to know if those men were connected with any
other union organizations.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. No; they were connected with no union.
The CHAIRMAN. What has been the decrease in the output of these mines?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. That is a matter of controversy that will be thrashed out
here. The operators have given out statements to the effect that the field is
putting out full capacity. We claim that their mines are operating only about
one-third or one-fourth-one-third or one-fourth are actually in operation.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you know what the capacity of the whole region is?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. I do not. The operators can probably tell you that.
Mr. Avis. That field is now putting out 96 per cent of its normal capacity,
doing more to-day than any field in the United States.
The CHAIRMAN. What is the normal capacity?
Mr. Avis. About 5,000,000 tons annually; approximately 450,000 tons a month.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. We shall introduce testimony to show that the larger
mines are not operating at this time.

Senator WARREN. Was there acts of violence following the affiliation of the
United Mine Workers?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. There was an act of considerable violence in Mattewan
on May 19, 1920. The operators sent a large number of armed guards-Bald-
win-Feltz detectives-who were sent for the purpose of evicting their men and
their families from their homes because they had joined the union. We shall
introduce testimony of miners to show the character of these men.
The CHAIRMAN. Since that time there has been practically a state of civil
war?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. There has been an absolute, complete breakdown of civil
government, and the breakdown we attribute-and we hope to prove is due to
the importation by the coal operators of Mingo County of armed guards, men
whose character we shall prove by the testimony of other witnesses.
The CHAIRMAN. What about the courts-were the courts open?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. The courts are open.
The CHAIRMAN. Are they open now?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. They are open now. But it is under martial law. I be-
lieve the circuit court is functioning down there, but the other civil processes
are subordinated to martial law, in the hands of Maj. Thomas Davis. A few
weeks ago, in the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, we got a deci-
sion to the effect that martial law was practically unenforceable because the
martial law was being enforced by the State police. A few days later the gov-
ernor drafted a new act which he promulgated in Williamson. At the present
time we have a habeas corpus proceeding coming up this morning in Charleston.
Senator STERLING. What were the acts of violence which did occur down
there?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. They consisted of the killing of 10 or 11 men at the cele-
brated Matewan battle. That was when the head of that force of armed de-
tectives shot down in cold blood the mayor of Matewan and precipitated the
general battle, in which six or seven of the armed guards were killed, and a
few innocent bystanders were killed also.
Senator STERLING. Were any of the mine workers themselves killed?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Yes; Joe Micklin, an elderly man who had been broken
down by long work, was running away and he was shot through the back.
I will try to state to you the character of these men in Mingo County. Re-
ports were sent out throughout the country by the operators' association indi-
cating that the mine workers in that country are largely foreign-born bolsheviks,
radicals of the worst hue, altogether untamable, altogether unmanageable. As
a matter of fact I do not believe that in any part of the United States you
will find a section containing so many of our so-called American stock as in
Mingo County. It runs 92 to 94 straight American stock. The names now
there are all British, Welch, Scotch, and Irish. They are descendants of pio-
neers, who came into Mingo County 150 to 200 years ago, emigrants of colonial
Virginia; they lived by trapping, hunting, and farming on a small scale.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. About what per cent?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. In the town of Matewan there are just two foreign
families.
Senator STERLING. What is the nationality of the foreign born?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. There are a few Italians in Matewan. The foreign ele-
ment in Mingo County is so slight-that is, it was so slight prior to July 1,
1920-as to be almost negligible. Mr. Montgomery informs me there are only
68,000 foreigners in the entire State of West Virginia, so, gentlemen, we are
dealing with Americans down there. It is not a foreign crowd which is being
led by radical agitators. Many of them served overseas in the war.
Senator STERLING. Have you been a mine worker yourself?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. No, sir.
Senator STERLING. What is your occupation?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. An attorney, sir.
Senator STERLING. At what place?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. At Washington, D. C.
Senator STERLING. Here in Washington?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Yes, sir. These men, I should say, are 92 per cent Ameri-
can stock.
Passing on from that phase, we tried everything possible we could do to settle
this controversy through mediation, conciliation, and arbitration. Even as late
as three days ago we appealed to the governor of West Virginia not to settle
the controversy but to put into effect a program that merely called for the en-

Senator STERLING. As an attorney, did you go down to the scene of these

Mr. Chairman, may we put on as our first witness-
The CHAIRMAN. We should like to hear a statement from the other side.

Mr. BURKINSHAW. The lockout went into effect during the early days of May,

OPENING STATEMENT OF COL. Z. T. VINSON.
Col. VINSON. I can not hope, Mr. Chairman, to follow and take up the various
statements made by counsel, made by the United Mine Workers. The evidence
will show that the statement is subject to challenge, and will be challenged and
overthrown.
Now that you may get a different idea in as few words as I can state it. I
should like to say that for 20 years or more, practically ever since that field
was opened up for coal-mining purposes, the operators, the employers, and the
employees have had no difficulty; they have had no trouble; they have lived in
peace and quiet and satisfaction during those twenty-odd years. And the wages
that were earned and are being earned to-day are as high, if not the highest,
wages paid any miners in the United States. A good miner down there in that
field earns and can earn from $400 to $700 a month, in that nonunion field.
We will show, and we will file statements of the earnings of the men who
work in the mines before we are through with this investigation.
There has been no question of wages or conditions surrounding the employ-
ment at all. There probably have been an occasional isolated case where some
fellow thought he could do better at another mine and would go to the other
mine. The miners are not, as a class, disposed to stay very long at one place,
That is quite an element; and then I would say that 10 per cent of them are
migratory; will work for a while in this field, then go to another field. This
condition prevailed here until the United Mine Workers' organization sought


===== [扫描序号 17] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
9
to organize it and take it into their organization. In that connection I want to
state that prior to 1912 the United Mine Workers' organization was a plain,
ordinary labor union. At its annual convention in 1912 it changed its policy
and its principles from that of a labor union into an organized band of robbers.
Now I know that is a strong statement, but they themselves admit I am speak-
ing words that come from their own mouths. Prior to that time their constitu-
tion declared they were entitled to an equitable part of the product of their
labor, and of course no one can reasonably complain of that position; but at
that meeting they declared that they were entitled to the full social value of
all the coal that they helped to produce, and they interpreted that word “social
value" themselves and said, "That means every cent of money that the coal
brings in the market, except such as is necessary to pay for the transportation."
They boldly claim, boldly announce that what they propose is to keep on making
demands for increases until they will finally take over all the mines in North
America, including Canada and the United States, take them over bodily and
own them by the organization, for which they will not pay and do not propose
to pay the present owners one solitary cent.
Now, that is the policy, that is the fundamental principle upon which this
organization has been built up. There will be no denial of that. We have
their own records here, and in this connection let me read just a line, if you
please. Senator Kenyon, you will remember that our great and good friend
Bishop Donohue was before your committee in the Paint Creek investigation,
where he had been appointed along with two other gentlemen to investigate the
Paint Creek conditions, and they did investigate them and did make a report.
Now, when he was testifying before this other committee, of which Senator
Kenyon was a member, Senator Kenyon asked Bishop Donohue these questions:
"Senator KENYON. Does what you say about the spirit prevailing there of
optimism among the miners, are they looking forward to other things; is there
a spirit of contentment or unrest?
"Bishop DONOHUE. I may perhaps best explain that out of the mouth of one
of the witnesses who appeared before us, the secretary of the United Mine
Workers.
"Mr. KNIGHT. You mean the vice president?
"Bishop DоноHUE. Yes; the vice president; that is true. He said they were
profoundly dissatisfied with conditions as they were there and that they in-
tended to increase their demands until at last they got possession of the mines.
"Senator KENYON. You mean to unionize the mines?
"Bishop DONOHUE. They wanted first to unionize the mines and then in-
crease their demands for their labor and keep on in a progressive increase until
at last it will not be worth while for anyone to own the mines, and then to take
possession of them themselves."
Now, that was a statement of the official of the United Mine Workers, the vice
president of the association.
I will not read now, I have not the time, but here is the record of your hear-
ing, Senator, in that Paint Creek investigation.
The CHAIRMAN. Has this any connection with Paint Creek?
Mr. VINSON. Absolutely; they are absolutely linked together as a chain.
The CHAIRMAN. Are the same companies involved?
Mr. VINSON. Not precisely the same named companies, but the same mine
workers' organization. It is the same people even in the mine workers' or-
ganization, to some extent.
The CHAIRMAN. There is some distance between them geographically?
Mr. VINSON. Well, 40 miles, I guess; 40 or 50 miles through the mountains.
The CHAIRMAN. Is the Paint and Cabin Creek district in this same district?
Mr. VINSON. It is in this same general district, not in this same association.
This association is over in the Tug River Valley and the Paint and Cabin Creek
are in the Canois, two rivers running parallel there.
Every single, solitary disturbance, every murder, every assassination that
has been committed in the coal industry in West Virginia is traceable directly
to this announced policy of this organization to unionize first and then to own
the property themselves. That was the policy that they announced back in
1898, when they entered into an arrangement with the operators in the north-
west to unionize West Virginia.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, Colonel, let us get that. Do you claim that is the
policy of these organizations in West Virginia, or the entire organization?
Mr. VINSON. The entire organization.
The CHAIRMAN. The national organization?

We will show by their own records, by the official statements of their own

And they brought this on with the idea that what the law would not permit
they would take by force of arms. And that is their method, and that is the
trouble and that is the whole cause of the trouble existing to-day in Mingo
County. It is the cause, the essential cause, of the trouble that existed in the

for the purpose of getting control of the mines and running them—and we will
show that, not by outside witnesses but by their own official records in this
case. Only a few days ago that you may get the full force of this-they en-
tered into a written contract with the operators in Indiana and Illinois and
western Pennsylvania to unionize West Virginia. In 1898 they attempted to do
that, and they have been attempting to carry out that arrangement ever since
and their primary purpose is the one that I spoke of a minute ago. Mr.
Mooney, the secretary and treasurer of the organization-I want to read the

biased. For this struggle in Mingo County is an economic one. In fact, it is
the continuance of a struggle begun in West Virginia 23 years ago and extend-
ing through this period."
About that there will be no question and no denial. Now, the issue, gentle-
men, is a very plain one and a very simple one. We omitted from our printed
statement, which I will file with the committee, our contention in that regard.
We had it prepared and through mistake it was omitted-this change of policy—
the statement was made that the change of policy that the demand of an
equitable share of the coal mines to a demand for a full total share. That is
the reason that I take this opportunity to make that statement. I say that this
issue is job robbery, pure and simple. That is the whole issue. You can not
avoid it. They are convicted by their own records, coming out of their own
mouths.
Now, the question comes squarely up to every coal operator that is running a
peaceful business and is on good terms with all of his employees. Now, then,
when this last crowd of men came in there and unionized these m'nes, it means
they are coming in there to adopt the methods and pursue the practices by which
they propose to take the mines away from the owners of the mines. They will
do it if they can. They will do it peacefully, by peaceful negotiation, if you
please, or conciliation-a word that has been more abused probably than any
other word in the English language-but they do not propose to follow these
methods. Whenever the owner of the nonunion mine says no, he will not per-
mit and the by-laws of the constitution will not permit any nonunion man to
work at the mines, then it comes down to whether or not I shall run my mine
nonunion or whether it shall be run as a union mine. It is not a question of
whether it is an open shop. It can not be an open shop. It is either one or
the other, union or nonunion. That is the primary question, whether this op-
erator running his mine-and most of these operators, gentlemen, are men that
have worked in the mines and have grown up and accumulated and have be-
some owners of the properties themselves. It is a question of whether or not
they can say how their own mines are going to be operated?
Now, what are you going to do? You have a well-known band of open and
defiant robbers-suppose you had such a band of robbers come to you Senators
and serve you notice that they were going to call and take possession of your

house, what are you going to do? Are you going to risist if the law can not

Mingo County, as well as their counsel, say that they have not only a lagal and

Mr. BURKINSHAW. We will now introduce as our first witness, Mr. Fred
Mooney, secretary-treasurer District No. 17, United Mine Workers of America.
STATEMENT OF FRED MOONEY, SECRETARY-TREASURER, DIS-
TRICT NO. 17, UNITED MINE WORKERS OF AMERICA.
The CHAIRMAN. Tell us what District No. 17 is.
Mr. MOONEY. That comprises the entire State of West Virginia, a section of
the Northern Panhandle, and the territory embracing the southern portion of
the State from Gauley Bridge, W. Va., to the Virginia line.
The CHAIRMAN. Go ahead and make any statement you want to, and we may
question you at times.
Mr. MOONEY. Do you want me to begin at the beginning of this controversy,
Mr. Chairman?
The CHAIRMAN. Yes.
Mr. MOONEY. As a preliminary statement, in order that I might not be ac-
cused of being a foreign agitator or something of that kind, I want to state
that I was born in Loudon district, in Kanawha County, W. Va., about three
miles and a half from the capital. I went to work in the mines when I was
16 years of age.
The CHAIRMAN. How old are you now?
Mr. MOONEY. I will be 33 next January, the 22d. I worked in the mines 16
years. The beginning of the controversy in Mingo County was along some time
in the month of May, 1920; but prior to that time there had been petitions and
committees and letters and requests as far back, as early as in 1919, for the
United Mine Workers to come into this field, but we refused. So, when the
award of the bituminous coal commission was made in 1920, just after that was
applied, a committee of men representing a couple of mines at Mattewan and
Sprigg, came to our office in the city of Charleston and at that time they stated
to us that there were about 400 men on strike and that they wanted to be
organized. I was in the conference held with the miners' officers at that time.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Where was that held?
Mr. MOONEY. In the city of Charleston in the mine workers' office, and the
committee wanted us to send representatives, or either commission a committee
to organize these men. We refused. We told them to go back and put the
mines in operation just like they had when they quit, and then after they did
that, if they wanted to be members of the United Mine Workers they were to
ask us and we would take them in. So they went back, and our information
has been all the way along that they did put the mines in operation. They
returned their committees, and two of these men on the committee were com-
missioned to organize the miners in Mingo County. Well, the first ones that
were organized, about when they began their work, they called us up over the
telephone and notified us that the men were being ordered to vacate the com-
pany premises immediately on becoming affiliated with the United Mine Work-
ers. Well, then, we proceeded to purchase tents-and we spent an enormous
sum of money for tents and paid so much for property to put them on-and
as fast as the strikers were thrown out of their homes-and I will say that
there were some of the operators that did not turn them out-there were some
that let their men stay in, while some of them did not. The men were placed
in tents just as fast as the tents could be procured; but some of them had their
furniture thrown out on the public highway in the vicinity of Mattewan, and
before we could get the tents to them their furniture was ruined.
So, by the end of the month of June there were about approximately 2,700
miners affiliated with the United Mine Workers and who had been discharged
and were on relief along with their families. The general average of families
in that territory, as near as we can get to it, and we have almost a complete
record, is about five children, a man, his wife, and five children to a family. So
they were placed in tents and the relief was being paid out all the way along,
and they flocked into the organization. Several times the charters and supplies
that were furnished them were delayed for weeks, because they were unable
to get the supplies in time and cut the seals, etc., as fast as we really needed
them.
So everything went along smooth until on the 19th of May some one called
the office from Mattewan-
Senator WARREN. Of what year?
Mr. MOONEY. May of 1920, and some one called the Mattewan office and said
that the Baldwin-Feltz detective agency were in there in force and were


===== [扫描序号 24] =====
16
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
throwing what few household goods the miners had out on the public highway.
We appealed to the governor of the State and he did not give us any satisfac-
tion whatever, and about 7 o'clock, probably 6.30 or 7 o'clock, on the evening
of 19th of May, 1920, some one called me from Mattewan and informed me at
my residence of the altercation that had come about between the city officials,
the officials of the municipality of Mattewan, and the Baldwin-Feltz detective
agency. There was no strike order issued until the 1st day of July, 1920, and
I don't think that at any time since that strike order was issued have we went
higher than 200 men on relief over and above what were on relief when the
strike order was issued.
The men met in convention, formulated their demands, and they did not
demand anything except what was being given to the miners in the entire State
of West Virginia, with the exception of Logan, Mingo, McDowell, Wyoming.
Mercer, and part of Raleigh, with the exception of a few little minor opera-
tions scattered about over the State. We never have yet been able to get those
demands before the operators, and we have made strenuous efforts on numerous
occasions to do so. The Department of Labor representatives came in there
on several occasions and tried to bring the opposing factions together, and they
failed to do so.
Then, we sent telegrams and letters. We secured a list of all the operators
in Mingo County, all the owners, and we sent telegrams asking them for a
conference, on different occasions. We never yet have been able to secure any
kind of a conference whatever. So the strike continued in effect.
The strike question has never been considered by us what you would call a
strike, because the men were all locked out and driven away from their em-
ployment because they had joined the organization, before any strike order was
issued; and when the men met in convention and formulated their demands, at
the same time they formulated the strike order and agreed to it and put it into
effect, just as a mere matter of formality.
The strike was continued. I have been in there on numerous occasions and
spent considerable time, and my impression of the whole situation is that the
principles laid down by the Constitution of the United States and the bill of
rights of the State of West Virginia have been absolutely denied, all the way
through.
Now, in the State of West Virginia the mining law gives the miner the right
to have his coal properly weighed. It gives him the right to have a check
weighman to see that the coal is properly weighed. The statutory law gives
him a right to belong to a labor union if he desires to do so.
Senator STERLING. Does that in express terms give that right, or simply do
you mean they are not denied?
Mr. MOONEY. It says there shall be no discrimination.
Senator STERLING. Your law says that?
Mr. MOONEY. Yes.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Have you a copy of that?
Mr. MOONEY. We will be pleased to furnish you one.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. I hope you will.
Mr. MOONEY. Not only that, but there is a law on the statute books that pro-
hibits the employment of armed guards or detectives in industrial controversies.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Have you a copy of that law which you can furnish us?
Mr. MOONEY. Yes, sir. In the counties that I have enumerated that are non-
union it is a well-known fact, admitted by the operators on different occasions,
and some of them have even boasted of their arsenal in the public press; that
they employ either the deputy sheriffs that are deputized by the sheriff of the
county and paid by the coal operators' association, or they employ private
detective agencies to keep the union out of that territory and put down any
expression of any words at any time relative to securing union conditions.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Do I understand you to say that the only counties that
do not have union shops in West Virginia are four or five?
Mr. MOONEY. They are Logan, Mingo, McDowell, Wyoming, Mercer, and part
of Raleigh Counties.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. All the rest of the counties of West Virginia have union
labor?
Mr. MOONEY. In regard to coal; yes, sir. In northern West Virginia, which
comprises 124 counties, with the exception of one little place known as Widen,
W. Va., operated by a man named Bradley, they have strictly union; and in
securing that organization in 1918 Mr. Clarence W. Watson invited the United
Mine Workers into that territory, and he laid down the bars and called us to a

been our experience that under an open-shop agreement that if any trouble arises

Senator SHORTRIDGE. Whoever is to blame if trouble arises?
Mr. MOONEY. Yes, sir; instead of the union men being responsible, it is the

Mr. MOONEY. Now, the situation involved in Mingo County to-day is exactly
of the same nature with the controversy in Cabin and Paint Creek in 1912 and

The CHAIRMAN. I. should like to ask if there has been any trouble in the
Cabin and Paint Creek districts since then?
Mr. MOONEY. There has not.
Senator McKELLAR. Is that a unionized district?
Mr. MOONEY. Yes, sir; solid union from one end to the other, and the oper-
ators of that territory are absolutely fair, every one of them, and they deal with
us in an equitable manner all the time.
The controversy has been continued in this territory. We will produce wit-
nesses here before the investigation is concluded. One of the speakers was
accused of importing guns. We emphatically deny that. However, we will in-
troduce witnesses to prove that immense quantities of high-power rifles and
ammunition and guns have been brought into that territory by the operators.
The same gunmen that came into the town of Mattewan to conduct the evictions
in 1920, which brought about the controversy on May 19, 1920, are the same
men that participated in the Cabin and Paint Creek strike of 1912 and 1913.
They are the same men that participated in the Colorado strike of 1913.
When this controversy came about the State had no militia; the militia was
sent into the Regular Army when war was declared. They organized what they
called a State police, or the public safety department. The State police were
sent into this territory; have been sent in on numerous occasions. The first
time or two the State police were in there they were very fair; I have to say
that; they did not intimidate anybody, with the exception of a few occasions,
where it was reported they would get hold of some of that mountain dew, they
call it up there; then one would get out of the way sometimes; but then came the
gubernatorial election, and the new governor has taken his seat and has in-
creased the State constabulary as best he could by securing volunteers, and just
recently has issued a declaration of martial law, and under that declaration of
martial law they arrested a number of men and put them in jail. But in the
declaration of martial law it was specifically stated that the civil courts were
not suspended, and the right of habeas corpus would be in full force and effect.
We took habeas corpus proceedings, or had our lawyer do so, to secure the
release of these men. They were released, and the supreme court in its deci-
sion, in its opinion, said that the proclamation of martial law was illegal
because of the fact that a proclamation of martial law was incident to occupa-
tion, and, the State having no military force, that the proclamation of martial
law was illegal.
Since that time the governor has reissued another proclamation of martial
law, and in that proclamation directed the county clerk of Mingo County to
furnish a list of names to the adjutant general, and instructed the adjutant
general to draft a proper number of citizens into the military service of the
State to keep order, so called, in the county of Mingo. In that force there are
many coal operators, some ex-Baldwin detectives, men that participated in the
Cabin and Paint Creek strike in 1913, several of them men under indictment,
men under bond, men on parole from the penitentiary, and ex-convicts, and all
that kind of rabble are in this force that is now assuming to keep order in
Mingo County.
Senator WARREN. Are they keeping order?
Mr. MOONEY. No; they are not; from all indications they are making a com-
plete failure of it.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. They are under the command of whom?
Mr. MOONEY. Maj. Thomas B. Davis is the man that conducted the original
drumhead court that they set up-military court in the Cabin and Paint Creek
strike, which was investigated by the committee from the United States Senate.
Senator STERLING. Has anybody been killed there recently?
Mr. MOONEY. Not since Flag Day, I believe.
Mr. BIAS. Yes; in June a State policeman was shot.

Mr. MOONEY. Yes, sir. We have offered a proposition to the operators of that
county through the governor of the State that there merely be no discrimina-
tion; that men may belong to a union if they want to, or not belong to the
union; that it will be optional with the individual, and we do not call for a
closed shop.
Senator WARREN. I was speaking of your mines in other places, and that is
usually closed shops?
Mr. MOONEY. Yes, sir.
Senator WARREN. It means a closed shop, either for or against?
Mr. MOONEY. Yes.
The CHAIRMAN. What constitutional rights-I suppose that is what this
committee should investigate, where it comes in-what constitutional rights
under the Federal Constitution do you feel you have been denied?
Mr. MOONEY. We are denied a republican form of government; we are denied
public assemblage; we are denied the right to belong to a labor union-that is
also the law of the State. The declaration of the War Labor Board has in
effect been a dead letter with us. It has not been put into effect on any occasion.

Mr. MOONEY. Sure. And in that process the operators agreed to practically

Senator SHORTRIDGE. Probably I do not understand you. In gold mines out
in California what we call two shifts-others run three shifts-meaning they
work eight hours. One group of boys go below at say, to illustrate, 4 o'clock
in the afternoon; they work eight hours. They come up; another shift goes
down, and thus have three shifts in the 24 hours. How is it in coal mines?
Mr. MOONEY. That seldom happens in the coal mines except in cases where
they are developing territory and driving entries on a double shift; then when
that happens they seldom have but two shifts. I have never known but a few
minor instances where some inspector condemned a territory and they wanted
to rush, but I have known but a few instances where they worked three shifts
in the 24 hours. Usually we can not get 8 hours work in 24 every day, much
less working shifts.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. That is by the hour?
Mr. MOONEY. Yes, day labor; and the miner by the tonnage rate. Now, the
scale rate, the highest scale rate we have in West Virginia for machined coal
is 70 cents a ton-that is for the weight work which produces the major
portion of the mining-and the nonunion fields do not weigh their coal in any
instance. I do not think there is a pair of scales in Mingo, Logan, McDowell,
or Mercer.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What method have they of adjusting wages, if not by
weight?

we will file with you, worked out by a public accountant, the car holds only
2 to 5 tons, and some of those cars were paid down as low as 60 to 65 cents,

to in the neighborhood of $3, maybe something over $3.

TESTIMONY OF FRANK INGHAM (COLORED).
(The witness having been first duly sworn, was examined and testified as
follows:)
The CHAIRMAN. You may proceed with you statement.
Mr. INGHAM. I have mined in Mingo County for 14 years. When I joined the
union I was discharged, and notice was served on me by the constable, William
Blair, of Mingo County, to vacate the company's premises, and the notice said
five days from date, and that was given to me on Friday, and it was two days
that had passed, and I only had three days in which to vacate the premises, in-
cluding Sunday. But, however, I moved out, trying to comply with the law.
I moved my furniture off of the company's premises and stored it. I went to
McVeigh, Ky., about 11 miles from Williamson, and went to work for the
Pond Creek Coal Co. I worked there for two weeks, when Mr. Hogan, the
manager, came to the mine at 3 o'clock in the evening and called me up and
says, "Frank, I have had a telephone message from the manager of the mine
that you left, and he says that you belonged to the union, and he advised us
to get rid of you."


===== [扫描序号 35] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
27
I says, "All right, Mr. Hogan," and I left there then and came to Alfex
under the electric collieries, and I only worked there five days before Mr.
Lecky discharged me for the same thing.
I came back to West Virginia and went to L. G. Brady, and I said, "I
have been blacklisted by the operators after serving about 30 years in the
mines, and I would like to get some work to do to make an honest living.
I want some kind of work if you will give it to me." He says, "Al
right, Frank; I have got some work being done in a new drift." He says, "I
want you to open that drift and timber it up and face it, and I will pay you
good wages," and he did. I went there and went to work, and my wife was
teaching school at the place I was discharged from at the time I joined the
union, and Mrs. B. Ingham told me that I had better not come out in that
district any more, not even to the schoolhouse, because if I did it would not be
good for me. I went to the superintendent of the Lee district board of educa-
tion and asked him to transfer my wife to some other place to teach, and I
explained the conditions surrounding the case to him, and he said, No; that
he could not transfer her; to let her go on teaching school." So I secured a
room for my wife to stay at and teach school there, and while I was working
on my job, Mr. Bray, this same gentleman that discharged me and served notice
on the other company that I got employed with to do the same, he sent for me
to come back to the office. I went up to his office, and he says, I want you
to come back and go to loading coal."
Senator STERLING. Who was this man?
66
Mr. INGHAM. Mr. H. D. Ingram, the manager of the Howard collieries.
Senator STERLING. He was the one who discharged you first?
Mr. INGHAM. Yes. He had told Mr. Donaldson that I was one of the

coal. I says, "I am now doing some work, and I would like to finish that job
up before I leave, and if it will be satisfactory to you I will come back the
first of the month and go to work." He said, "All right." So I went back the
first of the month, finished up the job and got my pay, and went to loading
coal again.

Mr. INGHAM. 1920. And then my furniture having been stored ever since, he

Mr. INGHAM. Mr. H. D. Ingram.

Mr. INGHAM. That was when he first discharged me and then I was dis-

denied the privilege of working in those mines, and since they have got well
established in there, many of them had found employment there. I did not want
them to make enemies of the white race by taking their places that they had
been discharged from, and when I intervened in the interests of myself and my
people he told me my tongue was too long, with an oath, and to get out and
stay out.

Mr. Avis. May 19, six evictions.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. You use the word "evictions." In ordinary language
lawyers know what it means, but it carries a different meaning as it is used
generally. Do you mean by legal process?
Mr. Avis. Yes, sir; if the Senator will permit me to explain, and I think for
the benefit of the lawyers of this committee it should be explained. Our courts
have repeatedly held that the relationship between an employer and an em-
ployee as to a house occupied by him on the premises, which house is used in
connection with mining, is not that of landlord and tenant, but of master and
servant, and they have the right to hold that house dependent upon contiued
employment in the mines. Now, our courts have further held that where that
right exists under the common law and in our States-it applies to both Vir-
ginia and West Virginia-evictions can be made forcibly without going into the
courts.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What do you want to show in regard. to that by this
witness?

TESTIMONY OF BLAINE MAYNARD.
(The witness, being duly sworn by the chairman, testified as follows:)
The CHAIRMAN. Mr. Witness, you have stated your name to the reporter,
have you?
Mr. MAYNARD. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Where do you live?
Mr. MAYNARD. Williamson.
The CHAIRMAN. What is your business?
Mr. MAYNARD. Mine foreman.
The CHAIRMAN. Are you mine foreman now?
Mr. MAYNARD. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. How long have you been mine foreman?
Mr. MAYNARD. I have worked at that fellow's mine here that he bought out
there about three years.
The CHAIRMAN. Were you a miner before that time?
Mr. MAYNARD. And I worked there as assistant mine foreman about five years
on Pond Creek.
The CHAIRMAN. Were you born in West Virginia?
Mr. MAYNARD. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Where were you born?
Mr. MAYNARD. In Kentucky.
The CHAIRMAN. What is your age?
Mr. MAYNARD. Thirty-six.
The CHAIRMAN. Are you a married man?
Mr. MAYNARD. Yes, sir.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. At any time down there in Williamson was an effort made.
so far as you know, to incriminate any officials or agents or representatives of
the United Mine Workers of any criminal acts?
Mr. MAYNARD. Yes, sir; a fellow by the name of Bob Satterfield, he is superin-
tendent, I think, of Goodman, or Goodlow, I won't be positive what, Bob on this
last September he tried to get me to take a little place over there, it was
shut down and run it, and I told him no, I wouldn't take it, it was awful low,
you had just to crawl in and out, the hill was so low, you know, I wouldn't take
it. I owned some property across at Leckydale, I bought a piece of property
down there, a house and lot. I told him no, I was going to sell out and leave
there, leave that part. He says, "If you want to make you a piece of money,"
he says,
you help me do a favor and I will get you a piece of money." I went
on and asked him what it was. He told me if I would help him get shut of this
Charley Workman, C. H. Workman, he would give me $1,000, Bob Satterfield.
The CHAIRMAN. What did you understand him to mean?

Senator SHORTRIDGE. What was your average wages?
Mr. MAYNARD. I got $185, and when I quit I was getting $200 a month.

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Mr. MAYNARD. The Government, I think, allowed us a raise some way. Well,
I didn't get any. Of course, I got two or three raises while I was there.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Tell the circumstances incident to your leaving the By-
Products Coal Co. What took place on that occasion?
Mr. MAYNARD. I moved down at my place then down there at Leckeydale-
I had a place there I went to loading coal. I loaded coal a few days. Bilaker,
the high sheriff, Sellman, Blackburn, Crete Bentley, I could name all the men.
They come down on local to Pond Creek. They got off and went to Athelax, and
when they come back they was pretty nearly all drunk; one or two in the
• crowd I knowed-Thornsby, I knowed, didn't drink. The high sheriff was
drunk. Sele Courtney walked up; I was standing up on the head house then
just above the road; he asked a fellow named Burke for a cigarette. They
lit it and shook hands, and Sele turned around to go his way, and this fellow
out with a gun and knocked him in the head. That was the 20th day of June.
Well, I didn't ever go back to work there any more, none of the union men,
they all belonged to the union there. They never called no strike nor nothing
else, but didn't go back after they come back and knocked them in the head.
Then he got killed there later.
Mr. VINSON. Which fellow got killed?
Mr. MAYNARD. Thornsby.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Where were you during the big May battle of this year?
Mr. MAYNARD. I was back home at Williamson.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Did you hear Bailey or any official of the county in-
struct the cit zens of Williamson to remain in readiness?
Mr. MAYNARD. This last May?
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Yes.
Mr. MAYNARD. Yes; Tony Ware told me to go out and hunt up some men
and get them there to the courthouse, that Judge Bailey said if they didn't
quit shooting the Kentucky side across there, he would send us up there to
maintain peace. I went out and gathered up, I expect, about 100 men and
brought them back to the courthouse door, colored fellows and white fellows
and all. They was setting all around there, then they got squabbling among
themselves and quit.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. When was that?
Mr. MAYNARD. In May.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Living in Williamson you have come in rather frequent
contact with the State police, have you not?
Mr. MAYNARD. Several of them.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. What type of man are they?
Mr. MAYNARD. They seemed rough to me.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Name them, please.
Mr. MAYNARD. I don't know the men, to say I know them. I just know
them by their clothes they have got on.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Did they wear uniforms?
Mr. MAYNARD. No. The man I do know, there is Ebb Whitt; he is a State
police.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. When you say they are rough, that word sometimes
does not express the facts. When you say that, what do you mean by that?
Mr. MAYNARD. Well, they treat fellows rough. Two or three would be
standing there talking, they would walk up and tell you to get to the hell out
there, get on away from here. On Sunday a fellow named Fry started to
catch a train there to go to Sprigg; the State police would not let him go, and
told him if he fooled with them he would bust his damn brains out. I thought
they had trouble before, the way I heard them talk.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Did you see any men arrested in Williamson for what
you considered minor offenses?
Mr. MAYNARD. I see them pick them up all around there.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Did you see them arrested for the offense of carrying
the Mine Workers' Journal?
Mr. MAYNARD. Yes, sir.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Who was it?
Mr. MAYNARD. Baumgartner.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Was that the only offense charged against him?
Mr. MAYNARD. That was all.
Mr. BURKINSHAW. Under the martial law proclamation it is forbidden for
anyone but the State police officials, the sheriff, or deputy sheriff, or men of
that character, constables, to bear arms.

UNITED STATES SENATE,

The Committee on Education and Labor of the United States Senate met, pur-
suant to the call of the chairman, at 10 o'clock a. m., at the committee room of
the Committee on Education and Labor, Capitol Building, Senator Kenyon pre-
siding.
Present: Senators Kenyon (chairman), Shortridge, Caraway, and Sterling.
Also present: Harry Olmsted, representing operators' association, William-
son field; Randolph Bias, Williamson, W. Va., appearing for certain mine owners

Burkinshaw, 636 Munsey Building, Washington, D. C., appearing for United

TESTIMONY OF W. E. HUTCHINSON.
The witness, having been first duly sworn by the chairman, testified as fol-
lows:
Mr. HOUSTON. Mr. Hutchinson, where do you reside at the present time?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. At Charleston.
Mr. HOUSTON. West Virginia?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. West Virginia.
Mr. HOUSTON. What is your age?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. My age is 30 years 5 months.
Mr. HOUSTON. And your occupation?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Miner.
Mr. HOUSTON. Did you ever live in Mingo County?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Yes, sir.
Mr. HOUSTON. Where were you born, Mr. Hutchinson?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Richmond, Va.
Mr. HOUSTON. How long have you been a coal miner?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. It will be six years in September.
Mr. HOUSTON. Where did you first engage in coal mining?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. At Alvin McCarr, Ky.
Mr. HOUSTON. Did you ever work at coal mining in the State of Virginia?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. No, sir.
Mr. HOUSTON. Did you ever mine any coal in Mingo County?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Yes, sir.
Mr. HOUSTON. How long did you work in Mingo County, and for whom did
you work?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. For five years in Mingo County for the Burnwell Coal &
Coke Co., for the Crystal Block Coal Co. No. 2, for the Allburn Coal & Coke
Co., and for Lecky Collier Co., Leckyville, Ky.
Mr. HOUSTON. Where is the Burnwell Coal & Coke Co. located?

Mr. HUTCHINSON. At Sprigg, W. Va.
Mr. HOUSTON. Where are the other coal companies you mentioned outside of
the Lecky Colliery Co.?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. One about 24 miles above Sprigg; Crystall mine No. 2,
No. 3, and the Allburn Coal & Coke Co. is a mile and a half above Mattewan
on the Kentucky side of the river, and the Lecky colliery is east of Williamson
on the Kentucky side.

Mr. HUTCHINSON. The Burnwell mine is on the Kentucky side and the city

Mr. HUTCHINSON. In April, 1920-April 16, 1920.
Mr. HOUSTON. And where did you join?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Charleston.
Mr. HOUSTON. State whether or not in the early spring of 1920 you were

who worked in the mines in those sections.
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Yes, sir.
Mr. HOUSTON. What can you say about the sentiment throughout that sec-
tion in the spring of 1920 for unionizing—for joining the United Mine Workers
of America?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Ninety per cent of the men was in favor of the organiza-
tion at that time.
Mr. HOUSTON. What percentage of the men in that section, in your opinion,
are native-born Americans?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Ninety per cent.
The CHAIRMAN. What is that date he fixed?
Mr. HOUSTON. The early part of the spring, 1920.
The CHAIRMAN. Up to that time was there any unionization in those par-
ticular mines?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. No, sir.
Mr. HOUSTON. I will ask you to state, if you know, what grievances, if any,
the men at the mines at which you were working, and in the same community,
had against the operators?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Only for the increase in wages which the Government had
granted them in the fall of 1919-1918.
Mr. HOUSTON. How was coal mined in that section-mined by the ton, car,
or any other manner?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. It was mined by the car.
Mr. HOUSTON. What was the capacity of the cars used by these companies
that you are acquainted with, speaking now of the spring of 1920 and im-
mediately prior thereto?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Of each company?
Mr. HOUSTON. Of the company with which you were working in particular?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. From 2 tons to 3 tons.
Mr. HOUSTON. Referring to the time I have spoken of how much did the
men receive for mining that coal?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. They received from 85 cents to $1.15 a car at Burnwell.
Senator STERLING. State that again, will you?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. From 85 cents to $1.15 at Burnwell.
Senator STERLING. A car?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. A car.
Senator STERLING. And the capacity of the cars was 2 to 3 tons?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. From 2 to 3.
Mr. HOUSTON. On the figures you have given for loading the car or mining
it, shooting it down?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. It is for mining it; shooting after the machine has cut it
and loading it into the car.
Mr. HOUSTON. And would the same parties that shot it down, would they also
load it?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. Yes, sir.

Mr. HOUSTON. In what way would a man be discriminated against?

Mr. HOUSTON. What did the bank boss do, what favoritism would he show

Mr. HUTCHINSON. He would give him a better place, a better position than the

Mr. HUTCHINSON. Yes; from 5 to 20 per cent.

Mr. HUTCHINSON. Each time, whenever the raise from the company came
the store would raise.
Senator CARAWAY. Whether it was a company store or not?
Mr. HUTCHINSON. The outside store would not raise; they might raise only

Mr. HOUSTON. If the committee will pardon me just a moment, I would like to
say that it has always been the contention of the operators that they had the
right to throw out a miner without any notice. Mr. Avis has stated here—not
only here but on numerous other occasions-that the courts of West Virginia
have held that no notice is necessary, because the relation is one of master and
servant and not of landlord and tenant. I take issue with him on that; there is
no court that I know of of any standing in West Virginia that has ever held any
such thing. Possibly some justice of the peace or some circuit judge may have
held that, but we have always contended that it is the relation of landlord and
tenant. The relation of master and servant exists where the servant occupies
the premises as an incident to his employment and where there is no specific
rental charge; but the decisions hold that where there is a specific rental fixed.
as in the case of the employees of the coal companies, then the relation becomes
that of landlord and tenant, and these gentlemen have relied, so far as I have
ever been able to learn, upon the statement of counsel of the coal operators-
The CHAIRMAN. That question has been settled by the courts?
Mr. HOUSTON. Not by the Supreme Court of West Virginia.
The CHAIRMAN. Is that conceded?
Mr. Avis. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Then give us the case.
Mr. Avis. There is no decision.
The CHAIRMAN. You agree to that, Mr. Houston?
Mr. HOUSTON, No.
The CHAIRMAN. I had hoped we could agree upon something. Do you both
agree that the supreme court has not settled the question?
Mr. HOUSTON. I have never found that.
Mr. Avis. The Circuit Court of Kanawha County, which is the county court
and the seat of the capital, has decided that question for years and years.
There never has been an appeal from that decision, and Mr. Houston has rep-
resented the United Mine Workers of America for years. In this very Mingo
strike controversy there was an appeal from a decision of a court on that very
question, and the supreme court in refusing a writ of error announced from
the bench that the relationship of master and servant existed and therefore he
refused the writ of error. In other words, this was plainly the decision of the
supreme court.
Mr. HOUSTON. As you know, the action of a court on a writ of error is not
a matter where an opinion is given; it is not a matter of record. They did not
make it a matter of record.
I have no knowledge as to what one of the judges may have stated; but they
have never passed on that question so far as I know, and I have represented
the United Mine Workers for years, and I have never known a single circuit
court to hold that the relationship was that of master and servant.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Your contention is that as between the worker and the
employers no relation exists of master and servant?
Mr. HOUSTON. Yes; that the relationship is that of landlord and tenant.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. But, as I understand you, whenever the occupancy of
a building is by a miner there is the relationship of landlord and tenant?
Mr. HOUSTON. That is correct, if there is a rental fixed by the company.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And I understand you to say that your supreme court
has never passed on that immediate question?
Mr. HOUSTON. Yes; it has never passed upon that.
Mr. Avis. In that connection I will say that the question has arisen many
times and Mr. Houston has had that question decided against him and he has
never yet secured an appeal on a writ of error. That very definitely indicates-
the action of the supreme court in refusing the writ of error-that the rela-
tionship of landlord and tenant did not exist, but that the relationship of master
and servant existed.
Senator STERLING. Was that direct question up before the court?

and Stanley goes down to the clubhouse. So when I got up there, as luck
would have it, to be shot at, four or five of the transportation people wanted
to go up to the mines because they had not seen a mine and it was something
new to them. They was already up to the mine when Garter and I approached.
He goes up into the mountain, and I goes up to the transportation people by
the mouth of the mine, and I was taking particular pains in explaining this
machinery to the newcomers. There was some women and children. Directly
a shot rang out and a limb fell out of a beech tree right over the motor
house, and I told them, "You get in behind this concrete wall," which was a
part of the building, the concrete being about 6 feet high and the woodwork
on the top of that. I said, "You people get in here and they can not shoot
you through this wall." They said that I had better get behind the wall, but
I said I did not care-
The CHAIRMAN. You were very brave?
Mr. KIRKPATRICK. Yes; but they did not know.
The CHAIRMAN. The people who were there looking at you did not know it
was a sham battle?
Mr. KIRKPATRICK. No. I had a .45 Smith and Wesson revolver, and I
pulled the trigger and shot 18 shots. It was empty and I did not have any
ammunition, so I went down to the clubhouse and got a .30-.30 high-power
rifle and came back up, and there was nobody around me, and I said, “I
have got something now that I can do the business with." By that time Henry
and these other fellows, Garter and Stanley, got down to where these other
people were and told them they had been put to flight. There was a little
girl by the name of Thomas that said she had seen men running over the hill,
five or six of them, and I believe she was honest in her opinion. I said that
I would have gotten them but my gun was not big enough.
Henry said, "Now, we will put up a pretty good story," and that was the
end of the thing, and we never was molested any more.
Mr. BIAS. They never molested you any more?
Mr. KIRKPATRICK. Well, them people got scared at that and went away until
evening, and we never bothered them any more.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. NO shots went astray.
Mr. KIRKPATRICK. NO.
The CHAIRMAN. That was all for the purpose of creating a condition that
would bring about martial law?
Mr. KIRKPATRICK. He said he wanted to have martial law and thought it
was a good thing. He asked me what I thought about it, and I said it
looked good to me.
The CHAIRMAN. How much were you paid for that heroic conduct?
"
Mr. KIRKPATRICK. I was paid by the month, $300 a month, with the under-
standing it would be permanent if I made good. They told me nobody could
operate that mine on account of their being in control. All the mine owners
had turned that proposition down. They said it had been threatened any
man that operated that mine would die with his shoes on. I said, It may
be so, but I am going to take a chance anyway. It looks good to me." I
hired to them on them conditions. Afterwards they made it more than that.
After they seen I meant business and could handle a mine they gave me
my board on the side, and my expenses, my miscellaneous expenses.
Mr. HOUSTON. How did Mr. Henry treat those employees he brought in there?
Mr. KIRKPATRICK. He treated some of them very badly. Men he liked he
treated pretty good, but people he didn't like he treated very badly.
Mr. Avis. Are you a brother of Jim Kirkpatrick?

TESTIMONY OF C. F. KEENEY.
(The witness, having been first duly sworn by the chairman, testified as
follows:)
Mr. HOUSTON. State your name.
Mr. KEENEY. C. F. Keeney.
Mr. HOUSTON. Where do you reside?
Mr. KEENEY. Charleston, W. Va.
Mr. HOUSTON. How much of a family have you?
Mr. KEENEY. Six children, wife, and mother.
Mr. HOUSTON. What is your present occupation?
Mr. KEENEY. President of the United Mine Workers for district 17.
Mr. HOUSTON. Have you ever been, and if so, for how long, engaged in the
coal mines?
Mr. KEENEY. I have been engaged in coal mining off and on for 23 years.
Mr. HOUSTON. At what age did you enter the mines?
Mr. KEENEY. At the age of 9 years.
Mr. HOUSTON. Were your parents native-born American?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes, sir.
Mr. HOUSTON. How long have you been president of district 17?
Mr. KEENEY. Four years the 1st of last January.
Mr. HOUSTON. What portion of West Virginia does district 17 cover.
Mr. KEENEY. We cover all the territory in the northern part of the State, con-
sisting of twelve and a half counties, with he exception of the panhandle sec-
tion, which is a part of subdistrict 5 and district 6, of Ohio. We control the
western part of the southern field, including a part of Fayette County.
Mr. HOUSTON. In what part of West Virginia are the principal nonunion coal
mines located?
Mr. KEENEY. Logan County, McDowell County, and Mercer County.
'Mr. HOUSTON. Mr. Keeney, I wish you would tell the committee how the
organization came to enter the Mingo coal field. I would like for you to give a
brief history of that, if you will.
Mr. KEENEY. Along about the 1st of May, 1920, there was a committee came
into Charleston, consisting of Mr. Hutchinson, Mr. Frazier, and Mr. Combs,
from Mingo County, and stated to me on that occasion that there were two
mines on strike at Sprigg and Mattewan, and they desired to become members
of the United Mine Workers. I stated to them that it was not the policy of the
United Mine Workers to accept members when they were on strike; that if
they would go back and put the mines in operation and be governed in accord-
ance with the policy of the mine workers, and then if Mingo County men wanted
to become members, if they would report back to me I would give them that
opportunity. They carried out my instructions and sent another committee
back. Mr. Frazier came back with that committee. I granted him a commis-
sion, at the solicitation of the two other gentlemen that were with him, author-
izing him to obligate those who desired to become members of the United
Mine Workers into the organization. The report showed that he and Mr.
Hutchinson and Mr. Combs succeeded in completing about two locals. if I
mistake not, one at Sprigg and one at Mattewan. Mr. Frazier, the man I gave
the commission to, was held under suspicion by the other men, and they had
taken out of his possession the papers that I gave him and $75 in money that
he had collected from members as initiation fees. They came to Charleston
and turned those back over to me, stating to me that Mr. Frazier had gone
over to the coal operators.
On that evening I received a telegram from Mr. Frazier, at Huntington,
requesting that I pay $5 expenses while in Huntington. I ignored the telegram,
and did not even answer. Mr. Fry was on that committee, the last one, that
came back with the papers-Ezra Fry, Mr. Hutchinson, and Mr. Combs. I com-
missioned Mr. Fry. Mr. Combs, being a minister, had told me Mr. Fry was in
good standing in the county and well thought of as a citizen in that county and
suggested I commission him. I commissioned him on that occasion to obligate
the men who desired to become members of the United Mine Worker of America
in Mingo County. They went back to Mingo-Fry sent one of our men who
had been elected in the miners' union that did not belong in that county, in that
field; there had been 22 locals established, 22 operations organized, and on about
the 16th of May, as well as I remember, if I mistake not, on the 16th of May
we had, as reported, 22 locals organized in that field. Well, at some time after
the 20th-I am not sure; some time after the 20th of May, on the 16th of May,

on the 15th of May, possibly; I am not sure about that; the records will show,
anyhow-I sent Mr. Workman, one of my board members, into Mingo County
to take care of the interests of district 17 and prevail upon the boys to carry out
our policies.
Sometime, then, after the 20th of May Mr. Hutchinson was given a commis-
sion also the gentleman who just testified a few moments ago-and he became
a local organizer of that county. On the 19th of May, on the evening of the
19th, I was in Huntington on my way to the northern part of the State, having
arranged with the Northern Coal Operators' Association a joint board meeting
to settle a question which had arisen at the Century mines. The owner of that
mine, Mr. Bissell, from Baltimore, he was to meet me there on that occasion;
and when I got to Fairmount the next morning I picked up a paper and saw
what had occurred in Williamson and got through by business up there as quick
as I could and returned back and went into Williamson the following week,
and from Williamson I went to Matewan, and we finally succeeded in com-
pleting the organization in that field, the operators discharging our men as fast
as they became members of the organization. At the time the strike took effect,
on July 1, there was something in the neighborhood of 2,700 or 2,800 men dis-
charged.
The CHAIRMAN. Was a formal strike order issued?
Mr. KEENEY. No, sir; up until the 1st of July there was not any strike order
issued whatever.
The CHAIRMAN. Was there then-the 1st of July?
Mr. KEENEY. We called the rest of the men out to protect the men who were
discharged; yes, sir. There had been about twenty-seven or twenty-eight hun-
dred men discharged and a great many of them evicted at that time.
The CHAIRMAN. That is what you call the commencement of the strike?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes. In the meantime Mr. Mooney-I had been in Williamson
on one occasion just prior to that. Mr. Houston here, our attorney, Mr. Mooney,
I don't remember the name, I can refer to the records and get it, they was into
Williamson and the operators was into a meeting, the Williamson Coal Oper-
ators' Association, and they proffered a proposition to them looking to a settle-
ment. On that particular occasion the operators answered with a very scur-
rilous letter, condemning us as wild-eyed agitators, and things of that sort.
Mr. Houston and myself and Mooney made a speech that evening at the court-
house, had quite a number. I read to that audience a proposition tendered by
Mr. Mooney and the answer from the coal operators. That was the first at-
tempt to arrive at a settlement, or negotiation of a settlement. Then I imme-
diately got in touch with the operators and wired them, and I received several
answers and several of them I did not hear from. They stated to me there
was not any difference between them and their employees and had not been
any demands made upon them.
Then on the 1st of July, about the 20th or 22d, I guess it was, of June, we
called a convention of the Williamson miners at Williamson. In that conven-
tion the miners of Mingo County mapped out the policy to be pursued in the
future. They stated in that policy that I was to make another effort to get the
coal operators into a conference for the purpose of settling that dispute, and
should not the operators agree to a conference then I was instructed by the
miners of Mingo to put into effect a strike order calling the rest of the men out
in protection of the men on strike. I done that, and I have copies of all those
things here that took place, and the operators again refused. We then called
a strike, calling the balance of the men out that had not been discharged.
I must say that we effected what you might say was a complete tie-up, and
it remained that way until the operators began to bring in transports. The
original group of men who became members of our organization, so far as I
have any knowledge of, we have not lost over 81 that returned back to work.
There has been some of them that has left the field. We had included in that
strike, or in that lockout and strike, part of Pike County, Border and Tug
River, Pike County, Ky. We also included what is known as Pond Creek in
Pike County. That made up approximately the way we had it figured, and the
membership we had to show up at that time was approximately 6,000 men.
By virtue of the activities of what we commonly call in that section of the
country the Baldwin-Felts agent, we was not able to hold our organization in
Pond Creek, or only had it about 80 per cent organized in the first place.
These are the reports I have from our field worker there. Since that time
there have been continuous lawlessness going on, and, as we charge-I charge,
rather, here that on all the lawlessness that has occurred in Mingo County
