I will read this [reading]:
Hon. E. F. MORGAN,
Governor of West Virginia,
Charleston, W. Va.
MY DEAR GOVERNOR: There has existed in the coal fields of Mingo County
for more than a year an industrial conflict of great magnitude. The coal miners
have engaged in this struggle to better their conditions of employment and to
secure those things guaranteed to them by the laws and constitution of West
Virginia, namely, the right to belong to a labor organization of their craft
without discrimination; to be paid semimonthly; the selection of a check-
weighman to insure the honest weighing of the'r coal, and to establish 2,000
pounds as a ton, and to be paid accordingly.
With the exception of wages, all of these fundamental rights are expressed
and protected in this State by positive law, yet the State has spent large sums
of money in policing the scene of this industrial conflict and in establishing
and maintaining martial law. The general public and the taxpayers of West
Virginia probably do not understand that the present situation has been caused
solely by miners insisting upon their lawful rights.
I presume that there is little question that the contending parties can con-
tinue this struggle indefinitely, but it is the desire and wish of all good citizens
to see it terminated. Again assuring you that the miners are desirous of in-
dustrial peace in all sections of this State and are willing to use all honorable
means to that end, I desire, upon behalf of the miners, to submit the following
as a basis of settlement.
That the Williamson Coal Operators' Association shall agree:
First. That all employees return to work, and that there shall be no dis-
crimination against any employee belonging to a labor union.
Second. The establishment of an 8-hour day, applicable to all classes in and
around the mines.
Third. The semimonthly pay day.
Fourth. That the employees have the right to trade where they please.
Fifth. That employees shall have the right to select check-weighman as pro-
vided by law, and that 2,000 pounds shall constitute a ton.
Sixth. That there shall be a joint commission consisting of five representa-
tives from each side, each side to choose its own representatives, for the pur-
pose of adjusting wages of all men working in and around the mines; determine
the mining prices and yardage, etc., and to endeavor to arrive at an equitable
competitive basis; and to provide rules and methods for the adjustment of
disputes between employers and employees. In order to avoid any failure to
agree, a board of arbitration, consisting of three members, shall be created, one
to be chosen by the operators and one by the employees, and these two to select
the third member, who shall be a nonresident of this State. The board of
arbitrators shall meet with the commission, and any question that the commis-
sion is unable to settle shall be submitted to and decided by the said board,
which decision shall be final. The findings of the commission shall date from
the time work is resumed, and shall continue until April 1, 1922.
Respectfully, yours,
C. F. KEENEY,
President District No. 17, United Mine Workers of America.

Mr. HOUSTON. I will ask you to state whether you made any effort through
the county authorities to obtain a conference with the coal operators?
Mr. KEENEY. I did.
Mr. HOUSTON. And what were those efforts and what were the results?
Mr. KEENEY. On the second occupation by the military authorities of Mingo
County with Federal troops I happened to be in Williamson the night before
they came in. Judge Bailey, judge of the circuit court, sent to the hotel for
me to come to his office.
Judge Bailey said that he wanted a conference. I got Mr. Fowler, who was
the financial agent at that time of the international union, and Mr. Frank Rum-
mage, who was the international organizer at that time from Indiana. We
went to courthouse office of the circuit judge. In that meeting representing
Mingo County was Judge Bailey, his assistant prosecuting attorney, or the
prosecuting attorney, I don't know which it is-I believe his name is the one
they had then-Mr. Bronson, and the sheriff of Mingo County now.
He was the incoming sheriff then. Judge Bailey stated to me that martial
law was about to be declared in Mingo County, and he said, "It is a thing none
of us desire and there is only one way that it can be avoided, and that is
through the cooperation of the operators, some of whom were there, and every-
body." I said to him, "I stand now where we have always stood, Judge; we
are ready to cooperate with you to the fullest extent in order that law and
order may prevail in Mingo County." I said to him, I said, "These men who
are working under our jurisdiction are here. They will help you. They are at
your command. If you command them to do something and they fail to do it
and you will notify me, I will withdraw them from the field." I further
stated, "I will even say, to settle up this in a happy condition here, if you will
arrange a meeting of the coal operators "-and there was a group of them
there then-" you gentlemen can sit and be the judges in the matter, and if I
do not make a case and make it out fully I will revoke every charter in Mingo
County and leave the field."
The judge said, "That sounds good, I will try it." He took it up with some
of the operators-I don't know who-and reported back to me that the operators
were not willing to meet us.
Then I made him another proposition. I said, "I request that you have both
sides in the matter of preserving law and order arrange for and attend a meet-
ing with the coal operators and not refer to the controversy, and we will agree
jointly to enforce whatever is agreed upon in order to enforce law and order in
this county."
He attempted to arrange that conference. The operators refused again on
that occasion. That was the last time when the martial law was about to be
declared.
Mr. AVIS. Would you give us the date of that talk?
Mr. KEENEY. We will file that, so that you can get hold of it.
Mr. Avis. Can't you give it to us now?
Mr. KEENEY. No; I can not. It was on the night before the last-on the night
before Mingo County was occupied the last time by the military troops.
Mr. Avis. Do you mean by the United States military troops?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes, sir. And since that time there was a good deal of lawless-

as is often done by nonunion operators, and the sheriff of the county had a con-

and I requested of him to get up a document and submit it to me, and if I
would be able to I would sign it on behalf of the United Mine Workers of
America to preserve law and order in that field and give him our cooperation,

and if you will permit me I would like to read the proposition as addressed by

Hon. A. C. PINSON,
Sheriff of Mingo County, Williamson, W. Va.
DEAR SIR: Realizing the seriousness to you as the sheriff of Mingo County
and to all the people in both Mingo County, W. Va., and Pike County, Ky., of
the disorders and violence which have prevailed in the coal field adjacent to
Tug River in both counties for some time past, and desiring to do whatever
can be done by the organization of which I am an officer, I submit to you the
following proposition:
First. For the United Mine Workers of America, I hereby agree that all
members of our organization will henceforth refrain from the violation of any
criminal law in either Mingo County, W. Va., or Pike County, Ky., and par-
ticularly will refrain from the unlawful use of firearms and from firing the
same at or into any coal-mining operation or camp or in any community where
employees in coal mines reside or are engaged at work at or about any coal-
mining operations.
Second. If any member of the United Mine Workers of America in either
Mingo or Pike Counties shall fail, omit, or refuse to abide by this agreement
made by me in behalf of all such members, I hereby agree that such member
shall forthwith be discharged from membership in the union and shall no
longer be recognized or treated as a member thereof.
Third. In case any member of our organization shall omit or fail in good
faith to live up to this agreement made by me in good faith, I pledge myself
that the officers of our organization and all members thereof, so far as they
can be induced so to do, will forthwith report to you as the sheriff of Mingo
County the name of any member so violating this agreement and the specific
offense of which such member is guilty, and that the organization of which I
am an officer and all officers and members thereof, in so far as we can induce
them to do so, will in good faith aid in apprehension and arresting such mem-
bers so violating the law.
Fourth. This agreement is made in good faith and will be kept in good faith,
and if I shall find for any reason that it is impossible to prevail on the members
of our organization in the two counties affected to abide by and continue to
live up to, I will notify you promptly, and in so far as the same affects Pike
County, Ky., will notify the sheriff of Pike County, Ky.
All of which is given under my hand for and on behalf of the United Mine
Workers of America.
President District No. 17, United Mine Workers of America.

Mr. A. C. PINSON,
Sheriff of Mingo County, Williamson, W. Va.
DEAR SIR: In answer to a written communication from you and to certain
features of our conversation this morning, in both of which you took up the
subject of the recent acts of lawlessness and violence in this district, and
which are charged to members of the United Mine Workers of America and
their sympathizers, I desire to make the following statement on behalf of that
organization and of its members involved in the present industrial dispute in
Mingo County.


===== [扫描序号 119] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
111
The striking miners may at times be guilty of some acts of violence, but
such acts, if any, are not the result of concerted effort nor of advice of the
miners' organization, although it is part of the propaganda of the operators
of nonunion mines to charge every disturbance and every act of violence to the
striking miners.
It is true that many of the striking miners keep and bear arms, but that is
a constitutional right which can not be infringed. We recognize, however,
that such a right, like all other rights, must always be exercised with due
regard for the rights of others, and must not be construed as a license to
menace the peace, quiet, or welfare of the community. And with these prin-
ciples constantly in view it has always been and now is the policy of our
organization to counsel and use peaceful methods to establish its claims.
Ours is just the age-old struggle, which, reduced to a few words, is the
expression of a desire for a higher standard of living. That hope, that long-
ing, is common to all, and is the impulse back of all advancement.
It is to be regretted-we regret-that the operators do not view these ques-
tions in a more liberal manner and realize that the worker has not only a
right to join a union but the right to work at his calling after joining the
union.
Assuring you of the earnest cooperation of our organization and of the
members thereof in observing and maintaining peace, order, and law, I am,
Very sincerely,
C. F. KEENEY.

matter-by telegram, letter, or otherwise to the coal operators or their rep-
resentatives?
Mr. KEENEY. I might say that before Gov. John J. Cornwell went out of office
I had a conference with him.

WILLIAMSON, W. Va., June 24, 1920.
To the Officers and Delegates of Subdistrict No. 2 of District No. 17, United
Mine Workers of America, in Convention Assembled:
We, your policy committee, to whom was referred the subject matter on policy,
beg leave to submit the following for your consideration:
First, we recommend that inasmuch as the officers of District No. 17, United
Mine Workers of America, have used every honorable means to bring about a
peaceable settlement between miners and operators of Mingo County, W. Va.,
and Pike County, Ky., bordering Tug River, and since the operators have not
even answered their letter of June 1, 1920, which reads in part as follows:
CHARLESTON, W. Va., June 1, 1920.
DEAR SIR: In answer to practically a unanimous demand from your em-
ployees, the United Mine Workers of America has consented to admit them into
our organization.
I assume that you are sufficiently acquainted with the principles of this union
to know that we at all times seek to promote a feeling of amity and good will
between employer and employee. Industrial strife is destructive, not alone in
the pecuniary interests of the parties, but to the spirit of harmony that should
at all times prevail in such an important industry as that of coal mining.
Believing that you share our views, and earnestly feeling that there is no real
obstacle to a peaceful settlement of such differences as may exist, I wish to re-
quest that you meet the representative of our organization in conference.
Assuring you of our good will and friendliest feeling, I am,
Most sincerely,
C. F. KEENEY,
President District No. 17.
Mr. Avis. I understand you received no reply to that, Mr. Keeney?
Mr. KEENEY. No, sir.
66
Therefore, we recommend that the officers be instructed to again invite the
operators to meet them in joint conference and endeavor to settle the differ-
ences between employer and employee to the end that industrial peace may
prevail throughout the mining industry in the above-mentioned sections of our
country. Failure on the part of the operators to meet the district officers and
the scale committee; we recommend in that event that the district officers be
authorized and are hereby instructed to call a strike of all miners bordering
Tug River, in Mingo County, W. Va., and Pike County, Ky., on July 1, 1920.
"Second. All local unions will permit a sufficient number of men to remain
at work to insure the proper care and protection of all mining property.
"Third. We recommend that a vigorous organizing campaign be carried on
in McDowell Countl, to the end that all miners may be given the opportunity
of joining the United Mine Workers of America.
"We further recommend that all men continue at work and that no strike
be called in McDowell County until authorized by the district officers.
Respectfully submitted.

harmful to our employees and making impossible the satisfactory performance

most harmonious relations between employers and employees have been main-

organization into our affairs. You are, therefore, in the position of having
created discord, which you now propose to mediate and harmonize by a surrender
of our properties to your control.

HATFIELD, MINGO COUNTY, W. Va.,
June 20, 1920.
President District 17, U. M. W. A., Charleston, W. Va.
DEAR SIR: The text of your wire requesting that we meet representatives of
your organization to negotiate a wage scale and arrive at an amicable settle-
ment of all differences between the miners and their employers reached me this
morning.
In view of the fact that the principles of your organization in all of the coal
fields under your domination-the "closed shop," the compulsory “check off,"
and other like practices are at variance with the constitution and laws of our
State and Nation and an infringement on the constitutional rights of both em-
ployer and employee, we must firmly and finally, but with all the courtesy the
situation will permit, decline to enter into any such negotiations with your
organization.
As to a wage scale: Our rates of wages are as high as any in force in either
union or nonunion fields when fair comparisons as to conditions and service
are made; we have always been ready to discuss directly with our employees
any matter pertaining to wages or conditions of employment; and up to the time
of your intrusion the relations existing between ourselves and our employees
were perfectly amicable and satisfactory to both of us. These prosperous, peace-
ful, and satisfactory conditions have prevailed for a number of years and have
been interrupted only by the dangerous and threatening attitude of your repre-
sentatives whom you sent into our midst to preach violence and stir up ill feel
ing and class hatred. Since your organization is responsible for any interrup-
tion of the peaceful relations existing in this district, it is unreasonable to
assume that we will turn over to you the control of our properties as the price
of your rectifying the conditions you have created.
That our position in declining your proposal is in the best interests of not
only ourselves but our employees and the public at large also is further evi-
denced by recalling the fact that your members are obligated to " cease work
whenever called upon to do so," and that last fall, when the whole country
was in urgent need of coal, your officials called a strike in all organized fields
and even after your Government had declared your action unwarrantable and
called on you to end the strike your members and certain of your officials
secretly supported it with their advice and with funds of the organization for
a considerable period of time thereafter, and a large portion of the country
was only saved from cold and suffering by the continuous production by this
and other fields over which you are now trying to get control.
Our position is further supported by the advocacy and support recently by a
large contingent of your delegates and the adoption by your parent organiza-
tion of the wild and dangerous proposition to "nationalize all industry," the
fallacy that has proved such a dismal and disastrous failure in several coun-
tries of the Old World.
With these reasons as the basis of our positions we feel that you can not fail
to comprehend that your duty to yourselves, your members, and your country
demands that you cease to create turmoil and strife in this field and turn your


===== [扫描序号 126] =====
118
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
attention to honest efforts to increase production rather than to hamper and
curtail it.
We have the honor to remain,
Sincerely, yours,
Mr. C. F. KENNEY,
CHATTAROY COAL CO. (INC..).
By J. C. BAKER, Gen. Mgr.
VIVIAN, W. Va., June 28, 1920.
President District 17, U. M. W. A., Charleston, W. Va.
DEAR SIR: I have before me a copy of a night telegram sent by you to the
Sycamore Coal Co., and received on the 27th instant, in which you ask for a
conference with representatives of your organization.
No good can ever come from a submission of the control and domination
of the coal industry in West Virginia to your irresponsible organization—no
good to the coal operators or their employees or to this section of the State
in particular, to the State at large, or to the country generally.
And we do not propose to aid in bringing about such harm, which would
include the destruction of some of the fundamental rights enjoyed under our
constitutional government.
Whatever of discord there may be has been brought about by men hired by
your organization for that purpose, and harmony and good will are clearly
far from being the objects you wish to attain.
We decline, therefore, to meet you in any conference.
Yours, truly,
S. W. PATTERSON,
President Sycamore Coal Co.

WILLIAMSON, W. VA., June 30, 1920.
President District 17, United Mine Workers of America,
Charleston, W. Va.
DEAR SIR: We have before us your telegram of the 25th instant requesting
us to meet the representatives of your organization in an effort to negotiate a
wage agreement for the Williamson field and to arrive at an amicable settle-
ment of all matters in difference between the miners and their employers.
Our position is, first, that the wages we pay our employees represent a higher
scale than are paid miners in the organized fields under your scale, and there-
fore to agree with you upon a scale of wages to be paid our employees would
mean a reduction in wages; second, the most amicable relation has hitherto
existed between this company and its employees, and most of our men who have
joined your union during the past two weeks have done so at the solicitation of
your agitators, the men not having been advised that the scale of wages and
working conditions prescribed by your organization will be destructive of indi-
vidual efforts and a reduction in wages; third, had this field been organized
last winter the country at large would have undergone untold suffering on
account of lack of production of coal occasioned by your strike.
In the interest of our employees and of the public generally we respectfully
decline to meet your representatives as requested in your telegram.
Very truly, yours,
POND CREEK BY-PRODUCTS COAL Co.,
By S. H. GoODLOE, Jr., President.

DAYTON, OHIO, June 28, 1920.
President, District No. 17, United Mine Workers of America,
Charleston, W. Va.
DEAR SIR: I am just in receipt of a telegram from you, asking for a con-
ference between the United Mine Workers and myself, and beg to advise that
we must respectfully decline to enter into any conferences or negotiations
with your organization or its representatives.
We are at all times ready to discuss any wage matters or other differences
with our employees, and we are at all times prepared to pay the highest scale
of wages possible. I am reliably informed that, all things considered, our
present wages are just as high, if not higher, than the wage scales of competing
districts. Our living conditions we believe to be a great deal cheaper.
Our company is not against collective bargaining as such, but we firmly
believe that it is against the interests not only of our stockholders but to our
employees as well to enter into any agreement with your organization, whose
performances in the past, in our opinion, have not made for the advancement
of the industry or the country at large.
Very truly, yours,
Mr. C. F. KEENEY,
THE WHITE STAR MINING CO.,
R. D. PATTERSON, President.
ROANOKE, VA., June 28, 1920.
President of District No. 17, United Mine Workers of America,
Charleston, W. Va.
DEAR SIR: We beg to acknowledge receipt of your telegram of the 25th instant,
requesting that we meet with the representatives of your organization for the
purpose of negotiating a wage agreement and arrive at an amicable settlement
of all differences between the miners and their employers.
We most respectfully decline to enter into any conference or negotiations
whatever with your organization or its representatives for the following reasons:
We have in the past always paid our men satisfactory wages; they were per-
fectly satisfied with their wages and working conditions until your organization
entered the field and forced them to organize. They were receiving a wage
scale equal to that paid by that of any of our competitors in other fields,
whether operating under union or nonunion arrangements.
A majority of our men would willingly go back to work to-morrow as non-
union men were they not afraid for their personal safety. They are being
intimidated by your representatives and are afraid to assert their rights as


===== [扫描序号 129] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
121
free American citizens. Were it not for the intrusion of your organization
the miners of Mingo County would be at work to-day with the same harmonious
relations existing between employers and employees as has been maintained in
this field during the past 20 years.
The owners of the Stone Mountain Coal Corporation are free American citi-
zens, and we claim the right to say whether or not we shall work union or non-
union employees. If any of our men are dissatisfied with working conditions
they have the right as free American citizens to leave their work and go where
they will. We have never forced any man to work for us against his will, but
we reserve the right to say who shall or shall not work for us.
We are always willing to adjust upon satisfactory terms with our employees
any differences, and our men have no complaint whatever of their treatment,
wages, or working conditions, so far as they are personally concerned. You
are, therefore, in the position of having created discord, which you now pro-
pose to mediate and harmonize by requiring a surrender of our properties
and all rights to operate our own plants, which we most respectfully decline
to do.
Yours, respectfully,
STONE MOUNTAIN COAL CORPORATION.
H. C. ELLIOTT, President.

NOLAN, W. Va., June 28, 1920.
President District 17, United Mine Workers of America,
Charleston, W. Va.
DEAR SIR: We beg to acknowledge receipt of your telegram of the 26th
requesting a conference between representatives of your organization and this
company for the purpose of negotiating a wage agreement and the settlement of
any differences between the miners and the operators.
We must respectfully decline to enter into any conference or negotiations
with your organization or its representatives. We have arrived at this decision
for the following reasons:
First. Our wage scale is now as high as that of any union field and our living
conditions are as good or better than in any coal field in the entire country.
Second. We have always been able to settle with our men, to the entire satis-
faction of all parties, wage scales and any differences which have arisen. And
until the intrusion of your organization into the field the relations between
ourselves and our employees have been of the most harmonious kind. Peace,
good will, and prosperity have reigned supreme.
Third. We are not in sympathy with a good many of the principles which
your organization stands for and advocates. Among these are the 6-hour day,
the nationalization of the coal industry, and the denial to any person the right
to work as a miner unless he affiliates himself with your organization.
It is impossible to produce sufficient coal to meet the demand even while
working 8 hours per day. To reduce the working day to 6 hours would be a
calamity to the entire country.


===== [扫描序号 131] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
123
The nationalization of the coal industry is contrary to the principles upon
which our Government is founded, and in our opinion would be in the long run
very detrimental to the miners, to the public, and to the country as a whole.
The principle of the closed shop, which your organization has adopted, vio-
lates the constitutional rights of freedom and liberty. Labor has a legal right
to organize, but we can not deal with any organization which denies any man
the right to work where and when he pleases without affiliating himself with a
labor organization contrary to his desires and wishes.
Fourth. We believe that the unionization of this field by the United Mine
Workers of America would be very injurious to the entire public. The entire
country would be at the mercy of your organization. Last fall, on the eve of
winter, your officials called a strike, asking, among other things, the 6-hour day
and a 60 per cent increase in wages. No thought was given to the interest of
the public or the country. And if it had not been for this nonunion field the
industry of the country would have been paralyzed and the suffering from the
lack of fuel would have been appalling. In a great many cases women and
little children would have perhaps frozen to death.
Fifth. The speeches of some of the official spokesmen of the United Mine
Workers are revolutionary in their character, and they have a tendency to
cause the violation of some of our most sacred institutions and the things
which to every true American are dearer than life itself.
For these reasons we must, with all politeness and courtesy, decline to enter
into any dealings with your organization.
Very respectfully,
WINIFREDE-THACKER COAL CO.
President and General Manager.
By H. G. VAN HOOSE,

You say wagon mines?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Just explain it briefly.
Mr. KEENEY. That is the place where they dump coal in chutes and haul it

got tipples or sidetracks into their particular operations.
Mr. Avis. Mr. Keeney, the wagon mine you referred to is only a temporary

the time being. Isn't that a fact?
Mr. KEENEY. I couldn't say that is true, Captain.
Mr. Avis. What do you mean by "wagon mine," if that is not true?
Mr. KEENEY. In the northern part of the State of West Virginia they have
been running wagon mines for a number of years, and are still doing the same.
Mr. Avis. They are small inconsequential sort of fellows that have an opening
there which in good times they operate and get out a few tons of coal?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes, sir. It is not in full swing like a tipple mine, does not
work so many men, works anywhere from 10 to 30 men.
Mr. Avis. Of the real coal operators only three signed that agreement?
Mr. KEENEY. Three tipple mines, large concerns.
Mr. AVIS. You mean the men you are fighting?

SEC. 2. In cases where a higher day wage rates are paid the price shall con-
tinue as long as the individual retains his present employment.
OUTSIDE DAY LABOR.
SEC. 3. The prices now paid for outside day labor shall continue, except
where the price paid is less than $5 per day. In that event an increase shall be
applied to establish a minimum of $5 per day.
EIGHT-HOUR DAY.
SEC. 4. That an 8-hour day means eight hours in the mine at usual working
places for all classes of inside day labor. This shall be exclusive of the time
required in reaching such working places in the morning and departing from
the same at night.
SEC. 5. Regarding drivers, they shall take their mules to and from the stables
and the time required in so doing shall not include any part of the day's labor,
their work beginning when they reach the change at. which they receive empty
cars, but in no case shall the driver's time be docked while he is waiting for
such cars at the point named; that when the men go into the mine in the
morning they shall be entitled to two hours' pay, whether or not the mine
works the full two hours. But after the first two hours the men shall be paid
for every hour thereafter by the hour, for each hour's work or fractional part
thereof. If for any reason the regular routine work can not be furnished the
inside labor for a portion of the first two hours, the operators may furnish
other than regular labor for the unexpired time. The prevailing custom for
drivers relative to harnessing and unharnessing their mules shall continue.
74020-21-VOL 1-9


===== [扫描序号 134] =====
126
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
SEC. 6. That all men in and around the mine shall be members of the United
Mine Workers of America, excepting mine foreman, mine foreman's assistant,
weighman, dock boss or trimmer, stable boss, electrician, and night watchmen.
We adopt the check-off system as a part of this agreement. This pertains
to regular dues and assessments of the United Mine Workers of America, not to
exceed $5 from each employee in any one month, the initiation fee to be in
addition to the above. In order to be honored the check-off list must be fur-
nished to the company not later than 24 hours after the expiration of each
half and the United Mine Workers of America of District No. 17 agrees to
protect the operators under this clause.
MACHINE WORK.
SEC. 7. The price paid in machine mining for loading coal in narrow work,
by the ton, shall be the same as in wide work, the excess price now paid for
loading to be on a yardage basis, according to the number of tons of coal pro-
duced in each yard of narrow work, at the option of the operator.
SEC. 8. Machine men will be required to cut coal level and close to bottom,
and all machine men leaving more bottom than 4 inches, except. in case of pots
or extreme variations, will be required to lift same or it shall be lifted at their
expense.
SEC. 9. In case sprags are left by machine men, they shall be notified by the
loader, and if they refuse to remove same the loader shall do so and be allowed
50 cents for so doing; the said 50 cents shall be charged to the machine men.
SEC. 10. All machine loaders shall be awarded two rooms, or equivalent of
three rooms in thin seams, for each two men, and they work "buddies," and
in that way load from one room at a time, so that it will give an opportunity
to cut the other room, and not lose any time to machine or loaders, and the
operator will provide such rooms for each two men at the earliest possible
moment, but in the event of territory becoming scarce from a squeeze or strik-
ing a horseback, or any other unavoidable obstacle, this shall not be construed
so as to diminish the output. of the mine.
CHECK WEIGHMAN.
SEC. 11. Checkweighman, selected as required by law from among the em-
ployees at that mine, may be placed on each tipple at the expense of the miners.
and their duties shall be only those prescribed by the laws of the State of West
Virginia, and all weigh scales may be tested by the miners at any reasonable
time. In case a suitable man can not be found at any mine, an outsider may be
employed by and with the mutual consent of the operator and his miners.
TRADE.
SEC. 12. Employees have the right to trade where they please.
RUN OF MINE-SCREENED BASIS.
SEC. 13. The mining rate per ton for splint or hard coal shall be fixed upon a
run-of-mine basis, but screened lump coal shall be according to the percentage
of screenings in producing screened lump as against mine-run coal..
HIRE AND DISCHARGE.
SEC. 14. The operator or his superintendent or mine foreman shall be respected
in the management of the mines and the direction of the working force. The
authority to hire and discharge shall be vested in the mine superintendent or
mine foreman, and nothing in this agreement shall be construed to abridge the
rights of the employer in either of these respects.
LOADING CARS OR BARGES.
SEC. 15. The operator shall at all times be at liberty to load any railroad cars
or barges whatsoever, regardless of their ownership, with coal, and sell and
deliver such coal in any market, and to any person, firm, or corporation that
he may desire.


===== [扫描序号 135] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
127
SEMIMONTHLY PAY.
SEC. 16. All labor shall be paid semimonthly. Semimonthly pay means that
the miners shall be paid twice a month, pay days to be determined locally, and
statements shall be available 24 hours prior to pay day.
MINING-WORKMANLIKE METHODS-TIMBERING.
SEC. 17. The miner shall be required to load his coal in every case free from
slate, bone, niggerhead, and other impurities.
SEC. 18. All coal mined, drilled, and blasted by the miners shall be done in a
practical and workmanlike manner and in accordance with the State mining
laws of West Virginia.
SEC. 19. In paying for coal before it is screened it is not intended to en-
courage unworkmanlike methods of mining and blasting coal or to decrease the
proportion of screened lump, and any miner will be subjected to discipline who,
from ignorance, carlessness, or any other cause, fails to properly mine, shoot,
and load the coal.
SEC. 20. The scale of prices agreed to for mining coal shall include the work
required to mine, shoot, clean, and load the coal, and properly timber the work-
ing places in the mines, and the operator shall be required to furnish the nec-
essary props and timber to properly timber all working places.
SEC. 21. If any miner shall fail to properly timber and care for his working
place, and such failure shall entail falls of slate, rock, and the like, or if, by
improper and reckless shooting of the coal in rooms or entry, the mine props
or other timbers shall be distributed, or unnecessary falls result, the miner,
whose fault is the occasion of such damage, shall repair the damage without
compensation, and if such miner fails to repair such damage, it shall be con-
sidered a dischargeable offense, and he may be dealt with at the discretion of
the superintendent.
SEC. 22. In any case where the mine foreman directs the placing of cross
bars to secure the roadway, then, and in such cases only, the miner shall be
paid prices for such cross bars as may be agreed upon between him and the
mine foreman. In case of miners shooting bottom, should any of the props be
loosened or displaced, thereby endangering the safety of the workman, the
miner agrees to reset same. The above does not contemplate any changes from
the ordinary method of timbering by the miner for his own safety.
DOCKS.
SEC. 23. In case any slate, bone, sulphur, or other impurities are sent out by
the miner, it shall be the duty of the trimmer of the car to call the attention of
the weighman and checkweighman, where one is employed, to the same, so as
to deduct weight of such impurities as estimated by the trimmer or dock boss
from the ascertained weight of such car; for the second offense he may be
suspended for one working day or fined 50 cents; for the third offense and
each subsequent offense occurring in any one calendar month, he may be
suspended, discharged, or fined $1 at the option of the superintendent; that in
malicious and aggravated cases the superintendent shall have the right to sus-.
pend or discharge for the first or subsequent offense.
SEC. 24. Any miner abusing or seeking to embarrass the trimmer for perform-
ing his duties shall be fined $3 or be discharged, at the option of the superin-
tendent.
SEC. 25. It is understood that if the checkweighman leaves his post to investi-
gate the amount of impurities thrown out, or for any other purpose, the run-
ning of coal over the tipple will not be suspended during his absence.
MINE COMMITTEE GRIEVANCES.
SEC. 26. The duties of the mine committee shall be confined to the adjustment
of disputes that the mine boss and miner or miners have tried to but are unable
to adjust. The mine committee shall have no other authority nor exercise any
other control, nor in any way interfere with the operation of the mine, and
for violation of this clause the committee or member thereof may be discharged.
SEC. 27-a. In case of any local trouble arising at any mine, the aggrieved
party shall first make an earnest effort to adjust the dispute with the mine
foreman. In case they are unable to agree, the matter shall be referred to the


===== [扫描序号 136] =====
128
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
•
mine committee and the local management of the mine, and if they fail to
agree, to the commissioner of the operators' association, and the miners' officials,
and if they fail to agree, to the district board of the two organizations, and
should they fail to agree, they shall select an umpire or referee, and the decision
of a majority of them shall constitute a final and binding award. In all such
cases all parties involved must continue at work pending the investigation and
adjustment as above set forth.
SEC. 27-b. If any employee for whom the scale is made refuses to work be-
cause of any grievance which has not been taken up in the manner provided
herein and such action shall seem likely to impede the operation of the
mines, such employee, or any of them, will subject themselves to dismissal with-
out recourse at the option of the company, and the mine committee shall im-
mediately furnish a man or men to take such place or places at the scale rate
in order that the mine shall continue at work; and it shall be the duty of any
member or members of the Mine Workers who may be called upon by the mine
boss or mine committee to immediately take the place or places assigned him or
them in pursuance hereof.
SEC. 27-c. The mine committee shall under no circumstances go around the
mine for any cause whatsoever unless called upon by the mine foreman or by
the miner or day man who may have a grievance that he can not settle with
the mine boss, and then only to investigate that grievance with the parties
involved.
SEC. 27-d. Members of the mine committee employed as daymen shall not
leave their places of duty during working hours except with the permission
of the mine foreman or in cases involving the stopping of the mine.
DISCIPLINE.
SEC. 27-e. No strike or stoppage of work shall occur at any mine until the
question in dispute shall have been considered and finally disposed of, as pro-
vided for in section 24-a.
(a) Should any officer or officers of the United Mine Workers of America, or
any member or members thereof employed at any mine, cause the mine or part
of the mine to shut down in violation of this rule, each member of the United
Mine Workers of America employed at said mine, except those who continue
at work, shall have deducted from his earnings the sum of $1 per day for each
day or part of a day they remain idle.
(b) Should any operator or his representative lock the men out for the pur-
pose of forcing a settlement of any grievance or cause the mine or part of the
mine to shut down in violation of this rule, he shall be fined $1 per employee
for each day or part of a day the mine is thus thrown idle.
(c) All money assessed against the employees under this rule shall be col-
lected from the pay for the half month in which the violation of the rule oc-
curs, or from the first money due thereafter. All moneys assessed against the
operator for violation of this rule shall be turned over to District No. 17,
United Mine Workers of America, and all moneys assessed against the miners
shall be turned over to the Red Cross or some other charitable institution.
All fines provided for in all agreements shall be automatically collected, and
any operator failing to collect and forward to proper parties such fine shall
pay a penalty of $2 for each employee subject to be fined, the same to be col-
lected and retained in the miner's district organization. And in no case shall
the fine be refunded except by mutual agreement of the accredited represen-
tatives of the operators and miners. It is further agreed that where any em-
ployee enters suit in civil courts to recover any time collected in accordance
herewith, the district organization shall reimburse the operator for expense
incurred on account of such suit.
SEC. 28. Under no circumstances will the operator recognize or treat with
any representative of the United Mine Workers of America during the sus-
pension of work contrary to this agreement.
WORKING IRREGULARLY.
SEC. 29. Should any employee absent himself from work for two days or
persist in working irregularly, unless through sickness or by first having noti-
fied the mine boss and obtained his consent, it shall be construed as a dis-
chargeable offense, and in case of sickness it is the duty of said employee to
notify the mine boss at once in order that arrangements may be made to fill
his place.


===== [扫描序号 137] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
129
TURN.
SEC. 30. The operator will see that an equal turn is offered each miner and
that he is given a fair chance to obtain same. The checkweighman, where one
is employed, shall keep a turn bulletin for the turn keeper's guidance. The
drivers shall be subject to whoever the mine boss shall designate as turn
keeper in pursuance hereof. This rule is not applicable and shall not be con-
sidered as preventing the operator from driving entries as rapidly as he may
desire.
DOUBLE-SHIFTING ENTRIES.
SEC. 31. Miners shall drive double-shift entries when called upon to do so
by the operator, and 283 cents per yard extra shall be paid for pick entry and
27 cents per yard for machine entry.
BURIAL FUND.
SEC. 32. A burial fund may be established by each mine or local, to which
fund each miner shall contribute 25 cents per month until a sum of not less
than $150 and not more than $500 shall have been created, when collections
shall cease until the fund is reduced by death, when a collection of 25 cents
per man per month shall again be made until the amount reaches the maximum
agreed upon, and so on, and the operator shall contribute in case of death of
miner, or any member of his family, an amount agreed upon by the operator
and the burial fund committee. In consideration of this contribution, it is
agreed and understood that the miners and day men will not cease work to
attend the funeral of either miner or member of the miner's family, except in
case the miner is killed outright while at work in the mine, in which event
the mine may be closed the day of his death, resuming work the following morn-
ing. This is not to be construed to mean that individual mine workers or rela-
tives of the deceased shall not attend the funeral if they desire so to do.
SEC. 33. There shall be a committee appointed, known as the funeral fund
committee, to take charge of these funds, and make all necessary funeral ar-
rangements in case of any death, and said necessary funeral arrangements in
case of any death, and said committee shall be paid for such duties as may be
agreed upon locally.
ENTRY GOB.
SEC. 34. Where there is not sufficient room to gob the dirt and draw slate
in entries with ordinary conditions, the loader or miner shall load it in bank
cars and the company shall unload it.
SEC. 35. It is understood that in the event of a disagreement between oper-
ators and mine workers, steam and electrical engineers, firemen, and pump
men are required to continue to perform such work as is in line with their
duties.
DEAD WORK-LOCAL CONDITIONS-INCREASE IN COST.
SEC. 36. For dead work where unusual conditions exist, the price to be paid
for same shall be a question of local adjustment.
SEC. 37. All discharge or suspension cases shall be taken up and disposed of
within five days, and should it be proven that the party discharged or suspended
has been unjustly dealt with, he shall be reinstated to his former employment,
and compensated for time lost. In any case not settled in five days, such em-
ployee shall be offered employment in some capacity until the case is dis-
posed of.
CONSTRUCTION AND REPAIR WORK DURING SUSPENSION.
SEC. 38. During any strike or suspension, it is hereby understood that all
men on all kinds of outside construction and repair work, together with all
kinds of work inside the mine that is not producing coal, must continue at
work; and it is further understood that such miners as are necessary are to
be permitted to mine coal for the boilers and domestic consumption on the
property; but this is not to be construed to mean to mine coal for shipment.


===== [扫描序号 138] =====
130
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
SEC. 39. When it has been determined a place is a wet place, the operator
shall pay 5 cents per ton in excess of the regular rate, 1 cent of which goes
to the cutter and 4 cents to the loader.
Places shall not be classified as wet when by ordinary methods of workman-
ship a mine worker can keep dry.
SEC. 40. The majority report of the bituminous coal commission regarding
the introduction of new machinery is adopted. The joint boards will agree
upon a commission for making any necessary tests.
SEC. 41. All local rules in violation of this contract shall be null and void,
and no local union or group of local unions shall pass any rules in violation;
neither shall any company enforce any rule in violation of this contract.

KEENEY EXHIBIT 8.
The WILLIAMSON COAL OPERATORS' ASSOCIATION.
GENTLEMEN: During the last few weeks trouble has existed between the
operators and miners of this district which has reached a stage wherein certain
coal mines have been closed down by a strike of the miners, efforts were made
to adjust the difficulties, but neither side would waive from their original stand
in order that the matter might be settled in a fair and equitable manner and
in the interest of the public.
The Government has data and information that serious trouble is probable,
constant agitation is on which might result in further loss of life and possible
damage to property. The coal situation is such that the Government demands
immediate settlement of this controversy in order to allow production to con-
tinue. The Government, desiring to always deal justly with problems of this
character, has given this matter fair consideration from the standpoint of both
employer and employee, therefore, as representatives of the Government, we
submit to you the following proposition:


===== [扫描序号 139] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
131
1. The Government is in favor of the policy of collective bargaining and advises
that the policy be put in effect.
There are two types of collective bargaining as thus defined; one in which the
employees act as a group through the trade or labor union. The other in which
a group of employees are represented by committees to confer with employers
regarding conditions of employment.
2. There shall be no discrimination against employees in the exercise of their
constitutional right to belong to any organization.
3. All employees evicted from homes shall be restored immediately and no dis-
crimination whatsoever as to eligibility to employment shall be made against
any one of said workmen on account of said strike or their participation therein.
4. We recommend the removal of the private agencies now employed and that
the regular constituted authority of county and State be invoked in the preserva-
tion of law and order in this district, provided such becomes necessary.
Subscribed and agreed to this
day of July, 1920.
Williamson Coal Operators Association.

EXHIBIT KELLEY 9.
CONSTITUTION OF DISTRICT NO. 17, UNITED MINE WORKERS OF AMERICA.
[Revision 1919.
Effective Jan. 1, 1920.]
MANUAL-OPENING.
The hour for the meeting having arrived, the president shall take the chair and
give one rap with the gavel, upon which all officers and members shall be seated.
If no regular doorkeeper has been appointed the president shall appoint one of
the brothers to see that none but members of the union are admitted.
PRESIDENT. The time for opening this meeting having arrived, I declare this
meeting duly convened and qualified to consider the best interests of this union
and the United Mine Workers of America. .
1. Roll call of officers.
2. Reading of minutes.
3. Correspondence.
ORDER OF BUSINESS.
4. Propositions for membership and initiation.
5. Finance.
6. Reports of committees.
7. Unfinished business.
8. New business.

10. Election of officers and installation.
PRESIDENT. The business of this meeting having been duly transacted, I
declare it adjourned until our next regular meeting, unless you are specially
called together, when I hope to see all members present.
NEW MEMBERS.
Any member of a local union can propose anyone who works in or around the
mine for membership in the organization. Propositions to be made to the secre-
tary, who shall announce the same to the union, under the head of order of
business No. 4.
PRESIDENT. Brothers, you have heard the name (or names) of the candidate
(or candidates) who desire to become members of this union. Are there any
objections?
NOTE.-Local unions having complete control over their own affairs shall
decide by what vote they will admit members to their body; if objections are
raised the president shall call for a vote in accordance with rule of this union.
If no objections are raised a vote is unnecessary, and the president shall say:
No objections having been raised, I declare the candidates entitled to take the
obligation and become members of this local union.

been accepted by this union?

elected to become members of this body.

The doorkeeper will admit the candidates and place them in line opposite the

PRESIDENT. Fellow workmen, the United Mine Workers of America requires
perfect freedom of inclination in every candidate for membership to its body.
An obligation of fidelity is required; let me assure you that in this obligation
there is nothing contrary to your civil or religious duties; with this under-
standing are you willing to take an obligation which binds you upon your honor
as a man to keep the same as long as life remains?
Each candidate answers: I am.
PRESIDENT. Raise your right hand.
"I do sincerely promise, of my own free will, to abide by the laws of this
union; to bear true allegiance to and keep inviolate the principles of the United
Mine Workers of America; never to discriminate against a fellow worker on
account of creed, color, or nationality; to defend freedom of thought, whether
expressed by tongue or pen, to defend on all occasions and to the extent of my
ability the members of our organization.
"That I will not reveal to any employer or boss the name of any one a mem-
ber of our unions. That I will assist all members of our organization to obtain
the highest wages possible for their work; that I will not accept a brother's
job who is idle for advancing the interests of the union or seeking better re-
muneration for his labor; and, as the mine workers of the entire country are
competitors in the labor world, I promise to cease work at any time I am
called upon by the organization to do so. And I further promise to help and
assist all brothers in adversity, and to have all mine workers join our union
that we may all be able to enjoy the fruits of our labor, that I will never know-
ingly wrong a brother or see him wronged if I can prevent it.
66
To all this I pledge my honor to observe and keep as long as life remains,
or until I am absolved by the United Mine Workers of America."
Answer: I promise.

PREAMBLE.
There is no fact more generally known or more widely believed than that
without coal there would not have been any such grand achievements, privileges,
and blessings as those which characterizes the twentieth century civilization,
and believing as we do that those whose lot is to daily toil in the recesses of
the earth, mining and putting out this coal which makes the blessings possible
are entitled to a fair and equitable share of the same; therefore, we have
formed "The United Mine Workers of America" for the purpose of the more
readily securing the objects sought by educating all mine workers in America
to realize the necessity of unity of action and purpose in demanding and se-
And we hereby declare
curing by lawful means the just fruits of our toil.
to the world that our objects are:
First. To secure an earning fully compatible with the dangers of our calling
and the labor performed.
Second. To establish as speedily as possible and forever our right to receive
pay for labor performed, in lawful money, and to rid ourselves of the iniquitous
system of spending our money wherever our employers see fit to designate.
Third. To secure the introduction of any and all well-defined and established
appliances for the preservation of life, health, and limbs of all mine employees.
Fourth. To reduce to the lowest possible minimum the awful catastrophes
which have been sweeping our fellow craftsmen to untimely graves by the thou-
sands by securing legislation looking to most perfect system of ventilation,
drainage, etc.
Fifth. To enforce existing laws; and, where none exist, enact and enforce
them; calling for a plentiful supply of suitable timber for supporting the roof,
pillars, etc., and to have all working places rendered as free from water and
impure air and poisonous gasses as possible.
Sixth. To uncompromisingly demand that six hours shall constitute a day's
work, and that not more than six hours shall be worked in any one day by
any mine worker. The very nature of our employment, shut out from the sun-
light, and pure air, working by aid of artificial light (in no instance to exceed
one candlepower) would in itself strongly indicate that, of all men, a coal
miner has the most righteous claim to a 6-hour day from bank to bank.
Seventh. To provide for the education of our children by lawfully prohibiting
their employment until they have attained a reasonably satisfactory education,
and in every case until they have attained 16 years of age.
Eighth. To abrogate all laws which enable coal operators to cheat the miners,
and to substitute laws which enable the miner, under the protection and majesty
of the State, to have his coal properly weighed or measured, as the case may be.
Ninth. To secure, by legislation, weekly payments in lawful money.
Tenth. To render it impossible by legislative enactment in every State for
coal operators or corporations to employ Pinkerton detectives or guards or
other forces (except the duly elected officers of each county) to take armed
possession of the mines in case of strikes or lockouts.
Eleventh. To use all honorable means to maintain peace between ourselves
and employers; adjusting all differences so far as possible by arbitration and
conciliation, that strikes may become unnecessary.
ARTICLE I.
SECTION 1. This organization shall be known as district No. 17, United Mine
Workers of America, and shall be composed of subdistricts and local unions in
West Virginia, except such sections as may be annexed to other d'stricts by the
national convention or the international board.
SEC. 2. The officers shall consist of a president, vice president, one secretary-
treasurer, one international board member, and three auditors, who shall be
elected by a majority of all legal votes cast in the referendum election.
SEC. 3. The officers of the subdistrict shall be composed of one president, one
vice president, one secretary-treasurer, and two board members, who shall be
elected from each subdistrict. The two board members of each subdistrict shall
constitute the district executive board of district No. 17, and they shall be
elected biennially. Three subdistrict auditors shall be elected in the next sub-


===== [扫描序号 142] =====
134
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
district election for each subdistrict. In case of death or resignation of presi-
dent of subdistricts the district president shall be empowered to appoint a
successor to fill vacancy that may occur in present electoral term with approval
of executive board.
ARTICLE II.
SECTION 1. Duties of president. The president shall preside at all district
coventions and all meetings of the district executive board. He shall sign all
bills and official documents when satisfied of their correctness. He shall fill by
appointment all vacancies occurring in any district office by and with the con-
sent of the district executive board. He shall in like manner remove from office
any district officer for a just and sufficient cause. He shall devote his time and
attention to the interests of the district, decide all questions of dispute concern-
ing the meaning of the constitution.
SEC. 2. When trouble of a local nature arises it shall be his duty to imme-
diately respond to a call from that subdistrict for his services, or send an officer
there without delay.
•
SEC. 3. Duties of vice president.-It shall be the duty of the vice president to
preside at all meetings and attend to all other duties in the absence of the presi-
dent. He shall succeed that officer in case of death, removal, or resignation.
SEC. 4. Secretary-treasurer.-The secretary-treasurer shall have charge of and
preserve all books and effects of the district office. He shall record the pro-
ceedings of all conventions and of meetings of the executive board and shall
keep copies of all important papers sent out by him. He shall prepare and
submit a quarterly statement showing the number of local unions in his dis-
trict, their financial standing and membership, and the amount of all moneys
received and disbursed by him; and what for. Any violation of this to be con-
sidered sufficient cause for impeachment. He shall perform such other duties
as shall be assigned to him; and shall give a bond of $2,500 and shall not keep
in his possession at any time more than $1,000. All other funds shall be de-
posited in a safe bank, subject to a majority of the executive board.
SEC. 5. Duties of the executive board.-The district executive board shall
constitute a board of arbitration and conciliation; shall execute the orders of
the district conventions and between the conventions shall have full power to
direct the working of the district. The board shall be reconvened at the request
of the president, secretary, or six members of the board.
SEC. 6. Duties of auditors.-It shall be the duty of the auditing committee
to examine the books of the district secretary and subdistrict secretaries quar-
terly, and report the result to each local union. They shall be elected by popu-
lar vote and remain in office two years.
SEC. 7. The auditors shall act as tellers and credentials committee, and they
shall meet 8 days prior to convention and examine all duplicate credentials
and report the same to the convention. The district secretary shall supply the
tellers with a list of all local unions in arrears.
SEC. 8. The legislative committee shall attend the regular session of the legis
lature and seek to have such bills introduced in the house and senate as have
been recommended by this organization. Work for them to be made laws and
work to prevent the enactment of any unjust legislation against our craft and
to report to the president the work done, with such other information pertaining
to legislative matters as they deem advantageous to the miners of this State,
who shall in turn report to the convention.
SEC. 9. If any district or local union officer or officers are seen in a state of
intoxication while holding such positions, he shall, upon conviction, be removed
from said office at once by the officers or union having proper jurisdiction over
the said officer or officers. This shall also apply to any organizer, delegate,
agent, or appointee in the employ or working for any branch of the organiza-
tion.
SEC. 10. Any officer knowing of another of the district being under the influ-
ence of intoxicating drink, and failing to report same, he shall be found guilty
of a misdemeanor and fined the sum of $5, the said fine to be paid into the dis-
trict treasury.
SEC. 11. It shall be the duty of any officer of this district knowing of any
international officer sent to this district being under the influence of intoxi-
cating drink to report same to the international office. Any officer failing to
do so shall be fined as hereinbefore provided.
SEC. 12. Any member of the organization in this district making false charges
against any of the above-mentioned officers in reference to being under the


===== [扫描序号 143] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
135
influence of drink shall be reprimanded for the first offense by the district
executive board, and for the second offense shall be expelled from membership
in the organization, and all local unions notified by circular letter, and adver-
tised in the United Mine Workers Journal.
SEC. 13. Any member guilty of slandering or circulating, or causing to be
circulated false statements about any member of, or any member circulating
or causing to be circulated any statement wrongfully condemning any decision
rendered by any officer of the organization, shall, upon conviction, be sus-
pended from membership for a period of six months and shall not be eligible
to hold office in any branch of the organization for two years thereafter. The
above shall be construed as applying to any local officer or member reading
such circulars to the members of a local union, or who in any way gives pub-
licity to such.
SEC. 14. The term of all elective officers shall be from April 1 to March 31
of each year.
ARTICLE III.
SECTION 1. Revenue.-The revenue of the district shall be derived from local
unions of the district, and at the rate of 15 cents per month per member; the
funds shall be used to pay the salaries of the officers and other necessary ex-
penses, and this tax shall be forwarded direct to the district secretary-treasurer.
The revenue of the subdistricts shall be derived from the local unions at the
rate of 10 cents per month per member, and this tax shall be forwarded direct
to the subdistrict secretary-treasurer. The district board shall have power to
levy an assessment whenever they consider such action absolutely necessary,
and no local union shall be entitled to representation when in arrears for
either dues or assessments three months. Any local union peristently refusing
to pay taxes or assessments authorized by the executive board, and not in con-
liet with the national constitution, shall be considered as refusing to pay their
lawful dues; any local union guilty of such conduct shall be suspended until
such time as they shall comply with the national constitution, Article XIV,
section 18.
SEC. 2. No local union shall be exempt from payment of per capita tax or
assessments unless they have been idle 30 days, and when they desire exonera-
tion from payment of same the request shall be signed by the local president,
secretary, and mine committee, with seal attached.
SEC. 3. All dues and assessments must be forwarded to the district secretary
and subdistrict secretaries on or before the 25th of each month for the tax and
assessments due for the preceding month.
ARTICLE IV.
SECTION 1. Regular conventions.—The regular district convention shall be held
biennially two weeks prior to the international convention in September, at such
place as shall be determined at the preceding convention.
SEC. 2. Representatives for the district convention shall be elected directly
from the local union they represent, and shall have one vote for every 50
members or less, and one vote for each 50 members or majority fraction thereof,
but no delegates shall be allowed more than five votes.
SEC. 3. Representation shall be based on the average membership of the
local union for the last three months upon which payment has been made
previous to the month in which convention is held.
SEC. 4. Any local union having 50 or more members in good standing must
be represented in convention or pay to the district a fine of $10 for each 50
members in good standing in the local union, unless exonerated by the district
executive board. This section shall not apply to local unions whose members
have been idle for one month or more prior to the convention on account of
strikes, suspensions, or lockouts.
SEC. 5. Local unions of less than 50 members may combine with similar
local unions within a reasonable radius of each other, but no delegates so
elected shall be entitled to more than five votes in the convention.
SEC. 6. No local union shall be entitled to representation that is in arrears for
per capita tax or assessment for two months preceding the month in which the
convention is held and which has not in every particular complied with the
district constitution.

SEC. 7. No person who is not a bona fide member of a local union, employed
in or around the mine or by the organization as a duly elected officer, shall be
eligible to act as delegate.
SEC. 8. Any member holding a position other than that of a United Mine
Worker shall not be eligible to act as a delegate to any district or subdistrict
convention or to represent the United Mine Workers in a central body or State
federation of labor convention while holding such position, but accepting a
position with the United Mine Workers or any other affiliated organization shall
not be construed as making a member ineligible to act as such.
SEC. 9. The secretary treasurer shall furnish each local union with credential
blanks, in duplicate, which must be attested as required on the blanks. The
duplicate shall be retained by the delegates and the original forwarded to the
secretary treasurer, and no credentials shall be accepted later than 12 days
prior to the date for the convening of the convention.
SEC. 10. The credential committee shall not transfer votes of any delegate
unless authorized by the local union to do so.
SEC. 11. Delegates to district convention shall be elected at an official meeting
of the local union after the call for the convention is received and has been read
to the local union. The local recording secretary or financial secretary shall post
notices signed by himself and the local president at the mine at least three
days prior to such meetings, stating that delegates are to be elected on a certain
date. Delegates must receive a majority vote from the members present at such
meeting, and no meeting other than the first one advertised and called in
accordance herewith shall be recognized as the official meeting for the election
of delegates. All delegates shall be elected by secret ballot.
SEC. 12. Local officers failing to read the call for the convention to their local
union and to post notices in accordance with section 11 of this article shall,
upon conviction, be removed from office and shall not thereafter be allowed
to hold office in the organization for two years.
SEC. 13. When any delegate's credential is to be contested notice of such con-
test shall be sent to the district secretary treasurer not later than 10 days prior
to the date for convening the convention; but any delegate whose credential is
contested may be unseated at any time during the convention.
SEC. 14. Any resolutions, grievances, or amendments not to be considered
unless sent in seven days prior to the convention, except by unanimous vote
of the convention.
SEC. 15. The district. convention shall not consider internal appeals or griev
ances unless they have been previously considered by the lower tribunals of
the organization.
SEC. 16. The district organization shall pay transportation of all delegates
entitled to a seat. in a regular or special convention.
SEC. 17. No district officer, other than the president and secretary-treasurer,
shall be allowed to attend any convention other than the regular or special
district convention, unless the local union employing said officers pays his
salary and expenses.
SEC. 18. No member shall be eligible to act as delegate to any convention
who is not a regular attendant of his local union the majority of meetings
six months prior to the election of delegate. This section shall not apply to
newly organized local unions.
ARTICLE V.
SECTION 1. Special conventions.-Special district and subdistrict conventions
shall be called by the president when so instructed by the district executive
board, or upon the request of a majority of local unions, after a petition and
statement of grievance has been submitted for a vote to all local unions in good
standing and received a majority of all votes cast in favor of holding such
special convention. He shall call and convene such convention, subject to the
provisions of Article IV. It is further provided that if a petition for a special
convention is submitted to a vote of the local unions of district and defeated,
the petition can not again be presented to the district executive board until
four months have elapsed from the time of the presentation of the first petition.
SEC. 2. The president shall, in the event that a special convention is called.
issue to all local unions within 10 days after receipt of proper petition, notice
of such call, and the time set. for such special convention, and this shall not
be less than 15 days nor more than 30 days after such calls are issued.

137
SEC. 3. Representation and transportation to and from special conventions
shall be upon the same basis as governs regular conventions.
SEC. 4. Delegates to regular or special conventions making false reports
relative to the action of such conventions which might cause a strike or shut-
down of any mine shall forfeit his membership for a period of not less than
two nor more than five years. This applies to all conventions attended by dele-
gates from the United Mine Workers of America.
ARTICLE VI.
SECTION 1. When trouble of a local character arises between the locals and
their employers the officers of said local shall endeavor to effect an amicable
adjustment, and failing in this shall immediately notify the subdistrict officers,
and the miners and mine laborers so involved shall in no case stop work unless
so ordered by the subdistrict officers.
SEC. 2. Any local union, committee, or member, acting in violation of section
1 of this article, shall be liable to expulsion or fine, subject to the discretion of
the district executive board.
ARTICLE VII.
SECTION 1. Nominations and elections.-The officers of this organization shall
be chosen by popular vote of the members; except as hereinbefore provided;
and the candidates receiving the highest number of votes to be declared elected.
Each local union shall designate, at a regular meeting of the local, where its
election shall be held and the place so designated shall be the official voting
place of such local union, and under no circumstances shall the votes of any
local be tabulated in any place other than the place designated by the local
union. The election shall be held on the same day that the international elec-
tion is held.
SEC. 2. The district secretary-treasurer shall prepare nomination blanks and
send them out from his office so the local secretaries shall receive them the 1st
of October of each alternate year. The local secretary shall fill in the names
of the persons nominated for the various positions and return same to the dis-
trict secretary-treasurer before October 15 of each alternate year.
SEC. 3. The secretary-treasurer shall within 10 days after nominations close
notify all members who have been nominated, and ask if they are candidates;
and get their written consent with certificate, showing them to be in good
standing for two years. Said certificate must be in the hands of the district
secretary by November 7, and if the certificate of any candidate is received after
that time, his name shall not go on the ballot. All certificates must be signed
by the president and secretary with the seal of the local attached. After re-
ceiving same the secretary shall place their names on the ballot, together with
their addresses. All candidates shall be placed upon the ballot in accord with
the nominations received.
SEC. 4. He shall have the election sheet so prepared and in the hands of the
local secretary by December 1 of each alternate year; each local shall receive
two election return sheets and two tally sheets and the vote of the local shall
be recorded on each election return sheet, and must be signed by the president
and secretary and the seal of the local attached, otherwise the vote will not be
counted by the tellers in convention. All members in good standing on Decem-
ber 1 will be entitled to vote.
SEC. 5. The secretary-treasurer shall prepare a tally sheet upon which the
tellers shall record the election, giving the local's number, the names of the
candidate, and the amount of votes each candidate receives from each local.
Said tally sheet shall be open for inspection and comparison to all the delegates.
SEC. 6. No candidate's name shall appear on the ballot unless he has received
the nomination from three or more locals.
SEC. 7. Any candidate for office in district No. 17 who shall be found guilty
of electioneering shall not be allowed to hold office in this district. And any
local union found guilty of sending out circular letters, or making slates in
favor of any candidates for office in this district shall be fined $25 and their
vote shall not be counted by the tellers when they are canvassing the election
returns.
SEC. 8. Any member in good standing in the organization shall be eligi-
ble to hold office in this district that does not hold a national office and if he
is a member of a local union and a resident of this district two years prior to

the election, but no person shall be eligible to hold office who is not a miner
or mine worker or employed by the organization and is a bona fide member
of a local union is good standing. The term "miner " or "mine worker" in-
cludes any one working in or around the mines and a member of a local union.
Article VII shall govern all subdistricts.
ARTICLE VIII.
SECTION 1. The salary of the president shall be $250 per month. The vice
president shall receive a salary of $225 per month. The secretary-treasurer
shall receive a salary of $235 per month. The district board members, auditing
committee, and tellers shall receive the sum of $8 per day while on actual duty.
SEC. 2. All officers shall be entitled to all legitimate expenses actually incurred
while in performance of duty.
SEC. 3. Officers will be paid on the 1st and 15th of each month, and they shall
submit an itemized account of such salary and expenses as provided for in the
preceding sections to the district and subdistrict secretary-treasurers, which
must have the approval of the district president. The district secretary shall
cause to be printed a statement of the salary and expenses paid out by him to
each officer and sent quarterly to each local union.
SEC. 4. The salary provided for in section 1 of this article is based upon and
shall be increased or decreased in proportion on a percentage basis as may be
established for the next joint agreement.
ARTICLE IX.
SECTION 1. Membership.-Local unions shall be composed of miners and mine-
laborers and all other workmen who work in and around the mines, except
those otherwise provided for by our agreement.
SEC. 2. Members' sons under 17 years of age, and old men who do not receive
the actual scale of wages, shall be known as half members, and admitted free
into the organization. The initiation of boys who are not members' sons to be
left to the discretion of the local.
SEC. 3. When a member through indifference or carelessness allows himself to
become three months in arrears he can only become a member again by initia-
tion as a new member, unless the local union, upon investigation, is convinced
that members have allowed their membership to lapse to evade payment of
levies or assessments. The local union may, at its option, demand the payment
of all back dues, levies, and assessments before said member can be eligible for
reinstatement.
SEC. 4. All local treasurers and such secretaries as handle the finances of the
organization shall furnish sufficient security for the faithful performance of
their duties, the amount of said security to be determined by the local union.
All local officers entrusted with the funds of local unions shall procure a bond
from a reputable surety company through the district secretary treasurer when
such surety company and contract therewith is approved by the district execu-
tive board.
SEC. 5. The financial secretary of a local union shall keep a systematic record
of all finances received by him and what for. He shall use standard books,
such as are supplied by the international union. The treasurer of a local union
shall give a receipt for all finances received by him and shall deposit the same in
the name of the local union subject to check only when signed by president,
recording secretary, and treasurer, with seal attached after order has been
drawn by local union in regular or special session. Any violation of the above
rules will be considered sufficient cause for impeachment, and anyone found
guilty will be held responsible for the amount of funds involved and not allowed
to hold office in the organization for a period of two years.
SEC. 6. Unless a dispensation has been granted, in accordance with section
11 of Article IX, international constitution, the initiation fee for miners and top
and inside day men shall be $10 where application is made for membership,
but no applicant shall be eligible for initiation until he has started to work at
a mine under the jurisdiction of the local union where application for member-
ship is made up.
SEC. 7. Any member going to work in a nonunion mine shall forfeit his mem-
bership and can not be reinstated only by paying his initiation fee and a $15
fine, unless such work is done with the consent of the district president of
the district where the nonunion mine is located.
