The CHAIRMAN. Go ahead and state what you can say.
Mr. KEENEY. I have the letter of the Central Labor Agency-
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Labor agencies wrote these letters to different com-
panies. Is that the fact?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. What did the company do?
Mr. KEENEY. They shipped transportation men in, both colored and white,
and of different nationalities. I think our records will show that we paid out
in the neighborhood of $14,000, paying the way of these men back to their
respective homes, and that we were not able to intercept all of them.
The CHAIRMAN. When you found men coming in you intercepted them and
tried to get them to go back, and furnished them transportation?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes. We would state to them that there was an industrial con-
flict going on in Mingo County, and we asked them not to take our places.
The CHAIRMAN. You spent $14,000 on that within what period of time?
Mr. KEENEY. From the time that the strike took place in July until December
of the same year.
Mr. HOUSTON. Did you have any talks with these men?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes; at my office at Charleston. I was not out in the field.
When they would come to Charleston-there would be a number that sometimes
would come to Charleston-we would pay their transportation to their homes.
We have paid their transportation to New York and we have paid their trans-
portation to Cincinnati and we have paid their transportation to Louisville.
Mr. HOUSTON. What would these parties say had been reported to them as to
the conditions in the field, where there was any industrial trouble in that field?
Mr. KEENEY. They were told that there was no trouble in the field whatever,
that the mines were being worked to full capacity.
Mr. HOUSTON. Did these people tell you what representations were made
to them?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes.
Mr. HOUSTON. And they reported there was no industrial trouble in that
field?
Mr. KEENEY. Absolutely.
Mr. HOUSTON. And they had been told that in order to get them to enter the
field?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. You mean, before they started to go to the field?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes, sir; in order to get them to go to the field they told them
that there was no trouble in Mingo County, and even some who came to my
office made the statement that the agencies had told they they were dealing
with an organization that was unionized.
Mr. HOUSTON. When these men learned that there was an industrial con-
troversy what did they do?
Mr. KEENEY. A great many of them were seeking some way to get out, and
did get out. Some of them left their belongings. I have in my office now 22
suit cases that belong to men that were transported, that were held back when
they came out, and some of them were prevented from receiving their clothes.
We finally got possession of them. I think they are from some men at William-
son and at Sprigg.
Mr. HOUSTON. Mr. Keeney, did any of the coal companies of the Mingo field
raise the wages of their men after the union entered the field?
Mr. KEENEY. They did.
Mr. HOUSTON. I will ask you to state whether you have a copy of the raise.
Mr. KEENEY. I have a copy of the letter and the raise, both; the letter that
was sent out to each member of their association.

CENTRAL LABOR AGENCY,

KEENEY EXHIBIT 18.
STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA, County of Mingo, to wit:
James Williams, being duly sworn upon his oath, says that he is a resident of
the Lick Creek tent colony and that he was there on the 14th day of June.
1921, when the same was raided by State police and their confederates and
deputy sheriff, and when Alex Breedlove was murdered; that he was about
30 feet from Breedlove when he was shot and saw James Bowles, State
policeman, shoot him; Bowles was about 6 or 7 feet from Breedlove, and
Breedlove had his hands up above his head at the time he was shot; Bowles
said to Breedlove, Hold up your hands, God damn you, and if you have got
anything to say, say it fast," and Breedlove said, Lord, have mercy," and
instantly the gun fired and Breedlove fell. They were standing facing each
other and Breedlove just above him on the hill.
..
66
At the same time Victor Blackburn, a special State police, was shooting at
Garfield Moore, who was behind a tree, the same tree that Breedlove had
just been behind, and after Bowles had called Breedlove to come out from
behind the tree and put up his hands and come to him and he had done so
and then was shot, Bowles immediately turned his gun on Garfield Moore,
but did not have time to fire until he was shot in the back by another State
police who was lying flat down on the ground straight down the hill below
Policeman Bowles; that at the crack of his rifle a half dozen or more women
who were there screamed out, "Look out, man, you are shooting your own
men," and ask him to get away from there; that he would get them all killed.
Affiant thereupon said to the man who had shot Bowles, "Yes; you done
shot this man up here now," and at that he said to affiant, You are a damn
liar, you damn black
you get away from there." And thereupon the
said police who had shot Police Bowles fainted and was carried off the

remained under this bridge 30 or 40 minutes, with a lot of union miners who
had taken shelter under said bridge.

KEENEY EXHIBIT 19.
STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA, County of Mingo, to wit:
William H. Ball, being duly sworn upon his oath, says that he is a resident of
Lick Creek tent colony and that he was present on the 14th day of May, 1921,
when the said colony was raided by the State police and deputy sheriffs; that he
was under the bridge across Lick Creek with the following-named other persons,
to wit, James Williams, J. H. Reed, Frank Mullett, and divers other persons,
including at least three women, to wit, Mrs. J. H. Reed and two colored women,
Ida Cargile and another, when the deputy State policeman who shot Policeman
Bowles was carried under said bridge; that he seen said policeman lay down
flat near the public road and fire several shots directly toward where affiant had
last seen Policeman Bowles; that affiant then heard a woman scream out,
"Look out, man, you are killing your own men," and instantly Bowles hollowed
"Lord, have mercy, I am shot." In just a minute I seen them bringing in the
man who had shot him; the party who shot him having fainted. He was carried
under the bridge across Lick Creek, where we were all huddled together for pro-
tection, and they kept him under there until he revived, or about 25 or 30 min-
utes. The women begin begging them not to bring him under there lest they get
them all killed, and to them the following language was used by Capt. Brockus:
"If you do not hush I will knock your God damn brains out with my gun."
Then Brockus gave orders to take the miners out from under the bridge and line
them up in the county road, and all the miners and the women and all were
ordered out and required to come out from under the bridge and line up together,
and then orders were given by Brockus to break into the tent, and to break
locks if necessary, and go in and search the tents, and thereupon his orders were
carried out. They broke into tents where they had doors and were locked and
where no doors existed they cut their way in. They then proceeded to cut the
tents all to pieces; break up the furniture; break up dishes, trunks, rifle drawers,
and destroy feed and clothing. They rounded up 56 of us, and after they had
destroyed everything we had they drove us at the point of their rifles down
through the city of Williamson and put us in the city lockup.
This was a room about 20 by 40 feet with a concrete floor, without chairs or
beds, and only one open window not more than 28 by 32 inches in size, and one
door which opens from the hall. The sink was stopped up and running over;
there were five commodes, and four of these were stopped up and standing full of
human excrement; the floor was covered with water about half shoe sole deep
and all kind of filth lying around on the floor in this water. Fifty-six of us were
put in this place and a guard placed at the door and we were denied the privi-
lege of speaking to our attorney or any other person, and held in this room from
about 3.30 Tuesday evening until about 9 o'clock Thursday night, when we were
taken out and taken to the jury room in the courthouse and there detained until
Saturday evening, and all released except Garfield Moore, Rochard Combs, Sam
Muncy, and Floyd Chaney, none of whom are guilty of any crime any more than
the rest of us were, which was not guilty at all.
Affiant further says that he served 18 months in France in the World War and
possessed a Victory medal and an American Legion badge and a Moose button
and a regulation uniform in his tent; that they entered his tent and cut his tent
all to pieces; cut up his uniform and a $65 suit was missing, and no trace of it
could be found except a stack of ashes in the stove, which indicated that they had
been put in the stove and burned; the Victory medal was never found and the
American Legion badge was never found, Moose receipts gone, and a $12 set of
knives and forks gone; coal oil poured into my flour, and groceries thrown away;
all the dishes broken, trunk torn all to pieces, and all the damage done that could
be done.
I also heard Capt. Brockus and Bill St. Clair, the deputy mine inspector, who
was a volunteer State police, say that all the "God dam
ought all be
burned"; that the women ought to all be piled up and the tents put on top
of them and burned. I also heard Dr. Lawson, a volunteer State police, say
to a woman "he would knock a kid out of her big enough to walk," and used
such language toward others, and all of this was done in the presence of Capt.
Brockus. They also tore down our American flag and stamped it in the dirt in
the presence of us all.
WILLIAM H. BALL.
Subscribed and sworn to before me this the 20th day of June, 1921.
THOMAS WEST, Notary Public.
My commission expires the 6th day of December, 1930.

Mr. BURKINSHAW. The subject was considered last evening.
Mr. KEENEY. The only thing I could say in connection with the Logan County
march is this: I was in northern West Virginia at the time that it occurred,
meeting with the Northern Coal Operators' Association, and Mr. Mooney called
me over long-distance phone and asked me to return to Charleston.
Mr. Mooney called me up over the long-distance phone and asked me to
return to Charleston. He also wired me and Gov. Cornwell did the same.
I arrived the next day, just as quick as I could get in. I arrived on the 4th
of September, as well as I can remember-I won't be positive about that—I
think it was about the 4th. There was said to be a group of men mobolized
at what is known as Linn Creek, about 10 miles east of Charleston.
When I arrived in Charleston the governor asked me to come to his office,
and I did. He told me that the men were mobilizing and attempting an in-
vasion of Logan County. He asked me to use my influence to stop them. I
promised him that I would do everything I could.
I went out and took a car and went to Linn Creek, and the temperament at
that time was running pretty high; the sentiment was running pretty high. I
did not succeed the first time, nor the second time, and I returned back to the
governor and told him of the success that I had. He requested that I go back
and prevail upon the men to return to their homes, and to tell them that he
would make an investigation into the condition of affiairs of Logan County.
He told me that if I was unable to persuade the men to return that I could
call him and that he would come up to Linn Creek and address the men.
I went back and saw the men and conveyed to them the settlement made by
the governor to me, and they told me frankly that they were going to go through
with the march.
Mr. Mooney was with me on the ground, and I sent Mr. Mooney to Marment
and he called the governor over the phone and had him come to Linn Creek,
and he came up with his wife in one car and his private secretary and his
wife in another machine. They had two machines. The governor delivered
an address to the men and told them that if they would return to their homes
he would make an investigation of the conditions complained of, and if they
found any men, women, or children being killed or murdered or wrongfully
treated that he would right it.
They didn't tell him-one man in the crowd did tell him; he said, "Governor,
you made a good speech but you have lost." This particular man came from
overseas. He had been overseas.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. In order that I may know, where was that?
Mr. KEENEY. That was at Linn Creek, Kanawha County.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And how far from Charleston was that?
Mr. KEENEY. It was 10 miles east of Charleston and three-quarters of a mile
from the creek where they were mobilized. The statement of the gentleman
was, "Governor, you have made a good speech, and one that would be all
right provided it was carried out. There is a group of men in this audience
who have been overseas fighting to save the world for democracy, but we
found "I will use his words-" we find the conditions here more hellish than
they ever were over there."
The governor tried to select him out, but he couldn't do it. I tried to select
him out, and I couldn't do it. It was dark-
Senator SHORTRIDGE. You say it was dark?
Mr. KEENEY. It was dark and the moon was shining and the camp fires were
there, and there were there in that crowd about 5,000 rifles. It looked more
like Dante's Inferno than anything I can think of, with the moonlight shining
on the rifles. The governor got into the machine, and there were several shots
fired in the air. That was in the way of a salute to the governor.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. A salute to the governor?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. The governor might not appreciate that particular
salute.
Mr. KEENEY. He seemed to enjoy it very much. He told me he took it as a
salute. He went on to Charleston and we kept prevailing on the men to return
back and thought they were in the notion of returning, outside of what this gen
tleman has said; but they did not, and they made their minds to go on.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And what was their destination from that point?
Mr. KEENEY. Do you mean the place where they were going?
Senator SHORTRIDGE. I mean the place where they were headed for.
Mr. KEENEY. I guess it must have been in the neighborhood of 65 miles.


===== [扫描序号 178] =====

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And was it a mountainous country?
Mr. KEENEY. It was mountainous; yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. How far had they come?
Mr. KEENEY. They had come from Cabin Creek and Pond Creek and Ka
nawha River, and assembled there.
The CHAIRMAN. Oh, that was the point of assembly.
Mr. KEENEY. Yes; this was the point of assembly. They started to march
on the fifth morning-the fifth or sixth; I do not recall just which-over the
mountains, and a number of them did turn back when they arrived at Dan-
ville, Boone County, about a 31-mile march, or 32 over the mountains. There
were 1,500 in the party that pitched camp that laid down that night. The gov-
ernor insisted on me going again. This is what he did: He called me back to
his office he was very much worried-and insisted that I go and stop these
men. By this time I was getting word from all parts of the field that men
were mobilizing everywhere, and the report came to us that 1,900 men were mov-
ing, and it also came to the governor.
The governor called me back in his office the next morning and told me
he wanted me to intercept those men; that he was going to delegate me as
his personal representative to stop those men. After he did that, I requested
him to send three men to Logan County, to send them on No. 3, on the C. & O.,
to go to Logantown and cross the mountains and report to me the conditions
in that field. We formed a collusion that they would report everything, and we
would help turn these men back.
Mr. Petrie, the vice president of district No. 17, and Mr. Stafford, and I
don't remember the name of the other one, but the governor gave credentials
to three of them to go to Logantown and cross the mountain. George Barrett
was the other.
They went to Logantown, took an automobile, and went across the mountain
to a place called Blair. They told the men there that were mobilizing that
nobody was being harmed, and that the conditions were not what had been
reported; that there hadn't been anybody killed, and asked them to stop. I
was in Dr. Carter's office in Danville, and they wired and told me what they
found, or called me up on the phone.
I insisted upon the men returning back, which I had done on previous
occasions, and I finally got them to agree that if these conditions were true
that I reported to them as coming from these men that they would return
back to their homes. That was about 12 o'clock in the day. The governor
called me to his office from Dr. Carter's office at Danville, and stated to me
that he understood they were mobilizing at the head of the river, and requested
that I take a car and go there immediately. I did that, and there was a
mobilization of men there. I don't know what the number was, but I ad-
dressed those men. They tried to pass resolutions and I wouldn't let them
pass any. They wanted to pass a resolution giving the governor a certain
number of days to make this investigation, and I would not permit them to
do that. We finally got them to agree to go back, and they did go back to
their homes. The governor admits that I averted a tragedy in that section
of the country. It has been claimed by some that I was responsible for that
march. I knew nothing of it; had nothing to do with it. It is not the policy
of our union. I was over 160 miles away from Charleston when it occurred.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What reports had come out from that country which
caused that uprising?
Mr. KEENEY. There had been 14 men produced to the governor from Logan
County with their heads beaten up. One of them had been shot through the
head. These 14 men had been produced to the governor in the condition they
were when they were beaten up, after they were beaten up, while their
wounds were being healed. Reports coming out from that field were that men
and women and children were being killed, and it was narrated throughout the
section, and then these men took it upon themselves to parade through that
section of the country. They told the governor when he was addressing them
that they were going to rehabilitate the constitution and bill of rights of
that State. That is the statement they made to him.
The CHAIRMAN. How many people have been killed down there in these
troubles?
Mr. KEENEY. That would be hard for a man to state accurately.
The CHAIRMAN. What is your estimate?
Mr. KEENEY. Something over 100.
The CHAIRMAN. Over 100?

UNITED STATES SENATE,
COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION AND LABOR,
Washington, D. C.
The Committee on Education and Labor of the United States Senate met,
pursuant to adjournment, at 10 o'clock a m., at the committee room of the
Committee on Education and Labor, Capitol Building, Senator Kenyon pre-
siding.
Present: Senators Kenyon (chairman), Shortridge, Caraway, and Sterling.

The CHAIRMAN. We will go ahead now, gentlemen.
TESTIMONY OF MR. C. F. KEENEY-Resumed.
(The witness, having been previously duly sworn, resumed the stand for
further examination and testified as follows:)
Mr. Avis. Mr. Keeney, did I understand you to say that the bulk of the
striking miners in Mingo County were living in tents?
Mr. KEENEY. You understood me to say that the bulk of the United Mine
Workers were living in tents in Mingo County.
Mr. Avis. How many tent colonies are there in Mingo County?
Mr. KEENEY. I believe there are six.
Mr. Avis. And how many tents are there?
Mr. KEENEY. I could not give you the exact number.
Mr. Avis. State to the committee about how many tents there are.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, gentlemen, let us see if we can not get down to some-
thing that you will agree to. I do not see, for the purposes of this investiga-
tion, that it make any difference whether there are 100 or 200 tents. Col.
Vinson states very frankly, as far as the operators are concerned, what seems
to be the issue, that they do not propose to employ union men in this region,
and they propose to discharge them, as they claim they have a right to do,
if they belong to the union. You propose, Mr. Keeney, to be equally frank,
that you are going to unionize these mines, if you can?
Mr. KEENEY. Yes, sir.

We walked around on Capital Street facing the Kanawha National Bank
Building, in which Mr. Houston's office is, and I stepped down in the street.
Mr. Burkinshaw and Mr. Huddy were talking as they were going along, and
possibly I said something a time or two. I don't remember just what I said.

National Bank Building, Mr. Burkinshaw said to Mr. Huddy, "Mr. Huddy,

I turned to Mr. Huddy and said, Mr. Huddy, I gave you credit for being

and I taken the gun and I knew I wasn't going to get the gun; I knew Mr.
Phelps-mostly I knew-he had got the gun; so I traded this gun off for another

go into this trouble until I get there with a special train with help." So
I waited 15 or 20 minutes and the shooting kept on; so I saw a great number
of State police going up the railroad and thought they had gone into it, so I
went down town and got hold of the chief of police and said, "Let's go up
there." That was Jerry Ringer. The shooting at that time had ceased.
We went on up to the bridge that crossed to the Kentucky side. I met three
men there with high-powered rifles, so I asked if the State police had went
on over. They said they hadn't saw them. I asked these three men where
the shooting started from. One said it started like the west side of the
tipple; another said a shot was fired at the east side; so I asked these men
if they fired any. An old man with an oath said, "It don't matter if I shot
any or not." One of the young men, that I knew personally, said he "had fired a
shot." So the old man asked who gave him the right to carry high-powered
rifles on the West Virginia side. He said Capt. Linsey; he is general manager -
of the Allburn Coal Co. I said to the sheriff, "Let's go over." He said, "No;.

Senator MCKELLAR. Let me see if I understand you. You say that on this

Senator MCKELLAR. Thirteen men?
Mr. HATFIELD. Yes, sir.
Senator MCKELLAR. And the mayor had directed you to arrest them for
what? What were they doing?
Mr. HATFIELD. We had an ordinance for nobody to have no gun unless he is
an officer.
Senator MCKELLAR. And these 13 men were there with guns?
Mr. HATFIELD. Yes, sir.
Senator MCKELLAR. And in that way they were violating the town ordinance?
Mr. HATFIELD. Yes, sir.
Senator MCKELLAR. Now, let me ask you, how did it happen that the mayor
instructed you to arrest them?
Mr. HATFIELD. I asked him for a warrant.

[Memorandum.]
MAY 13, 1920.
Make arrangements with a party at Matewan and employ him at a salary
of from two to three hundred dollars per month. I think you can make
arrangements for $200. Whatever arrangement you make must be under
cover and have this understood with Hatfield. If you make a deal with him,
I think you should suggest some means of bringing about a controversy or
misunderstanding of some sort which will result in a split between him and
the bunch which would look plausible and give him an opportunity of turning
against them and telling them where to head in, because that is what we will
expect if we make a deal.
Now, I do not want him to be neutral except during the interval before this
misunderstanding and complications are brought about and after that we will
expect him to stand squarely behind us in all matters which may come up and
let everybody know that he has become disgusted with the bunch and wants
nothing more to do with them and brand them as crooked and declare himself
with the other side when it comes to a show-down. However, I want to im-
press upon him the importance of not letting anyone know there is any ar-
rangement between us. His pay will be given to him in person by yourself or
one of our confidential men and no one should be taken into his confidence
about this.
I would also suggest that you show Ance Hatfield a little attention and let
him know that we appreciate the attitude which he has taken in these matters.
Please do not forget our conversation on the subject of Chambers; however, I
would suggest that you have a further talk with Mr. Bausewine before you
approach him and have a thorough understanding with the committee, because
there is no use of going into this matter at all unless you know where you are.
At our conference in Cincinnati a few days ago, it was suggested that we
keep after Blankenship, as they seem to think he might be worked yet; how-
ever, I am of the opinion the other parties have him under their control.
Also discuss with Mr. Bausewine about his talk with me on the subject of
Tony Webb; also the newspaper at Williamson; and in this connection I want
to emphasize the importance of getting a square deal from the press in con-
nection with news which is published in connection with this situation and in
this connection, it would not be a bad idea to see Ganner yourself.
I do not think it would be a bad idea to have an article written setting
forth the views of the operators in connection with these evictions, etc.,
and the precedent which has been established and go on and analyze it and
show that they had to take this action because these fellows would hold the
houses indefinitely and occupy them for the purpose of annoying the com-
pany and preventing their mining coal; that the houses were part of their
mining equipment, etc. Furthermore, that if this is not done, the public is
going to get a wrong conception of what has been done and the object in
doing it, because these things are being talked throughout the country, on the
trains, and in public places, etc.
Arrange for Cunningham to discontinue the room at Williamson.
[Memorandum-A. C. F.]
MAY 17, 1920.
On your next trip to Williamson, I want you to discuss with Mr. Bausewine
the question of getting Testermen right and see what he thinks about it.
Referring to the attached newspaper clippings, it seems to me that some
of these statements about the use of machine guns down there and all that
sort of stuff should be corrected.

Mr. GEORGE BAUSEWINE, Jr.,
BLUEFIELD, W. Va., May 17, 1920.
Secretary Operators' Association of Williamson Field,
Williamson, W. Va.
DEAR SIR: For your information I quote you below report received from S. S..
Operative No. 9, dated Williamson, May 16:
"On Friday night I attended a meeting held in the courthouse at this place,.
but there was nothing done of a secret nature, except to obligate about 12 men.
One hundred and five men from the Williamson Coal & Coke Co. joined during
the day, being obligated in a negro joint located at the east end of Main Street.
It was reported that 35 miners from the West Virginia By-Product Operation
had joined, and later it was said that this operation was solid.
"I accompanied Fry and Loyd Castel to the station, and upon our arrival:
there Fry introduced me to a deputy sheriff from Naugatuck named Blair.
During the conversation which followed Fry gave Blair a copy of the consti-
tution and told him to obligate every man whom he could induce to take it. Fry
stated that 178 miners had already joined at Naugatuck, and that another meet-
ing was scheduled to be held there on Tuesday night.
"On Saturday, the 15th, I overheard a man by the name of M. W. Collins, who
is employed by the Pond Creek Coal Co. at McVeigh, Ky., make the statement
that he had been discharged for agitating, but in some manner had been success-
ful in getting his job back with the company. This party said he was going to
get all the men he could from Pond Creek to attend the union meetings in
Williamson next Tuesday night, and that he thought he would be able to bring
as many as 30 men. Collins further stated that if he could induce as many as
30 men to go to Williamson and join they would be able to secure a charter and
could inaugurate a local right on the creek. He remarked that No. 6 would be
an ideal place to start, as there is some privately owned property located very
near the mine. Collins is described as being a short man, weight about 130
pounds, dark complexion, and wears a cap.
"To-day having a parade through the town, consisting of from 150 to 250-
miners. Fry made a speech in the courthouse yard, in which he stated that it
was his intention to organize the N. & W. field from Kenova to Bluefield. At
this speaking it was arranged to have a meeting in Williamson Tuesday night
and one at Matewan on Friday night.
"There was a young fellow in town to-day from Aflex, Ky., who stated that he
intended to join the union himself and would then return to Aflex and do what
he could to get all the men employed at that operation to sign up. I did not
learn this party's name, but it will be an easy matter to pick him from the
following description:
"He is a man about 21 or 22 years of age; height, about 5 feet 8 inches;
weight, about 150 pounds; and has four gold upper front teeth. He is employed
on the tipple at Aflex, Ky."
Yours, very truly,
T. L. FELTS.

tried and who can be relied on. I believe you know all of them with the
exception of E. O. Powell. We sent this man to Saltville in 1917, where he
has been working under F. R. Bailey. Mr. Bailey says he is one of the best
men he has ever worked. Reliable and conscientious. As you know, G. B.
Hildebrand has never had any officer experience, but he should make a good
watchman and can be used in throwing out the packages.
R. L. Casebolt, from Williamson, is an experienced officer and was used
during the Cabin Creek trouble, and you will no doubt remember him.
We have now a call for the following men: Two additional men to the
Lynn Coal & Coke Co., two men for the Thacker Coal Mining Co. at Rose Siding,
two men for the Pond Creek By-Products Coal Corporation, six men to report
to W. A. Wilson for use at Thacker No. 2 mine.
After you get through with the men at Matewan you can arrange to send
Casebolt, Powell, Hildebrand, Ferguson, and Capt. G. W. Anderson to Mr.
W. A. Wilson at Thacker, or distribute them at the other place named above.
Higgins can only be gone a few days and will have to return to his home.
J. R. Anderson will also have to return, as will Oscar Bennett. Of course,
McDowell and Houchins will be compelled to return to their regular work.
As Casebolt lives in Williamson, I told him we would try and place him at the
Pond Creek By-Products Coal Corporation plant. I have another good man com-
ing in to-morrow and have a line on several others, whom I may possibly get,
and will fill the vacancies just as fast as I can.
In this connection, I want you to try and get a line on some good men
whom we can employ in that county. Please see what you can do in regard to
this.
Yours, very truly,
T. L. F.

Mr. GEORGE BAUSEWINE, jr.,
BLUEFIELD, W. Va., May 17, 1920.
Secretary, Operators Association of Williamson Field,
Williamson, W. Va.
DEAR SIR: I quote you below, report received from operative No. 24, dated
Matewan, May 14:
"There was a mass meeting of the miners here to-night, which was at-
tended by about 500 men. The speaking was done in the open between the
railroad depot and the street. Mother Jones did not arrive, neither were there
any district or national men present, Preacher Combs, who is well known
and who has been signing up the men, was the first speaker, following by
a Negro preacher named Johnson. The meeting was opened with song and
prayer, after which Combs made a radical talk, in which he said that the
operators bitterly opposed the union and had managed to keep most of the
poor miners in ignorance of the benefits derived from the union by telling
them that the union was composed of loafers and men who did not want to
earn a living by work. He said, 'I am here to say that we do not want to
work but we want to earn,' that the operators wanted the miners to load coal
by the ton, and 2,000 pounds to the ton. He said that the operators were telling
the men that they were now paying them more than the union scale, and
that if this was true, why didn't the operators sign up with the union and
take it off of the men, that the men did not want to take it off the operators;
that all they wanted was the union scale and recognition.
"Combs said the operators accused the miners of criminal acts and that
they would burn the tipples and blow up the mines, but that this statement
was not true; that there was not a miner in Mingo County who would be
guilty of such an act, and that the companies need not nail up the drift
mouths and bring in a carload of men to guard the tipples; that the miners
only wanted fair treatment and that they were going to have it.
"He said all business men were organized and that if the laborers did not
organize that they would always be in bondage-to do the bidding of the
capitalist. He said the superintendents were going to all the miners with
a paper to be signed, which was an agreement that the miner would sign his
birthright away for five years house rent. Combs said that no man would
sign it; that those who did sign it were not as good as a yellow dog.
"He stated that the superintendent or operator who would ask his fellow
man to sign such a paper did not have a heart, that he carried a gizzard
around in a heart's place. He said he hoped the men would all go home and
tell their wives that they had decided to make a change; to tell her that
they were going to recognize the miners as human beings, and that they
intended to give them their just dues-a part of what they earn. He said the
Negroes were once in bondage and Abraham Lincoln gave them their freedom,
and now the miners, both black and white, were in bondage and that the
United Mine Workers were going to give them their liberty. He said the
sheriff was one man who had lived up to his promises when he was a candi-
date for office, and that if he continued to do so, he would be elected to any
office in the county that he asked for.
"The Negro speaker was comical and caused much laughter by his speaking.
One of his remarks was that if he wouldn't be a union man, he would go
home and ask his wife to chain him in the yard with the dog.
"After the speaking, some new miners signed up. I do not know how many,
but I saw about 200 go into the hall.
"I did not hear any expressions from the business men of Matewan and
do not know how they feel toward the union. There were some miners at
the speaking from Glen Alum. I noticed two Italians and one American
man at the speaking, and all left on No. 2 Saturday morning for Glen Alum.
"Judge Evans came to Matewan on train No. 2 Saturday morning. I was
informed that he had been employed by the union as their attorney.
"George Allen, a merchant from Thacker, was present at the speaking.
After the speakers had finished, he took the soap box and informed the men
that he had been a miner 11 years, but was now engaged in the merchandise
business in Thacker, and that some of the miners of Thacker mines wanted a
place to meet and organize. He said that his place of business was at their
disposal and that they could hold their meetings there, and if there wasn't
enough room in his place they could get a house on the Kentucky side of
the river."
Yours, very truly,
T. L. FELTS.

Mr. Avis. Mr. Hatfield, you spoke about Mr. Felts shooting the mayor. How

dence against the rest of us, and he was a cousin to Judge Damron, or he was
his uncle, and they taken him out and got him to swear to anything against the
rest of us, and he swore that, just like Mr. Avis swore to the affidavit up there.

(The letter so offered is here printed into the record in full, as follows:)
Mr. JAMES DAMRON,
Williamson, W. Va.
WILLIAMSON, W. Va., December 23, 1920.
MY DEAR JUDGE DAMRON: I am in receipt of your letter of the 15th instant,
and also the one of the 20th ultimo, relative to employment in the murder cases
growing out of the Matewan tragedy May 19 last. My failure to reply to your
letter of November 20 was on account of the thought that the matter of your
employment in these cases would be definitely arranged through Mr. Olmstead,
and therefore no reply was necessary.
I wish first to state that whatever I said to you about becoming associated
with counsel in these cases was, in my opinion, in your taking the employment,
nor was the same done for any other reason than to secure your services as a
lawyer.
You will recall that some time prior to your resignation and at your home here
in the city you mentioned the fact to Judge Sanders, who was present, and my-
self, of your having decided to resign as judge, and it was fully agreed that there
was no impropriety in such a course by you or the acceptance of employment in
any matters then pending in your court, for after your eight years on the bench
no one who knew you could impugn any dishonest or sinister motive to your
resignation unless he deliberately and maliciously did so, seeking to injure you.
I think it was shortly after that time that I met T. L. Felts and mentioned to
him the fact that you would possibly resign from the bench before your term of


===== [扫描序号 229] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
221
office expired, and he stated to me that he would like to secure your services in
these cases and asked me to approach you on the subject, but at the same time
stated that as to your fee for services I should take the matter up with Mr.
Harry Olmstead, of the Coal Operators' Asssociation, if it was really your inten-
tion to resign and the employment agreeable to you, my understanding at that
time being that the Coal Operators' Association was to pay all costs attending
the trial of these men, inasmuch as they were at Matewan under the direct.on
of the Coal Operators' Association.
If I am not mistaken, I did not mention the subject until after you told me
that your resignation was then in the hands of the governor, or would be in the
next few days, and I then stated to you that Mr. Felts would like to have you
in the cases, and your reply was that you would be glad to accept the employ-
ment, and I thereupon asked you what your fee would be, and you replied the
same fee that was paid to Judge Sanders, Capt. Avis, and myself. I told you at
the time what that was as I then recollected, but sent you a copy of the letter
setting out the amount of fee and scope of the employment, so that there could
be no misunderstand ng, and immediately wrote a letter to Mr. T. L. Felts stat-
ing our interview, and also called upon Mr. Olmstead and advised him that you
would take the employment and the amount of fee you would expect, asking him
to see you and definitely arrange for your employment. I felt then I had done
all I had been asked to do.
At a conference held at Bluefield between Judge Sanders, Capt. Avis, and
myself I asked the question whether or no the matter of your employment had
been definitely settled, and Judge Sanders stated that he had spoken to Mr. Felts
about it and advised that the matter should be definitely settled. Later, wh le
in Bluefield, Mr. Felts asked me to again see Mr. Olmstead in the matter, and
immediately on my return to Williamson I called on him and asked whether the
matter had been settled. He thereupon told me that he would go to Bluefield
on, I think, Tuesday, the 14th instant, and see Mr. Felts. Later I saw him in
Williamson, and he stated that he had gone to Bluefield, found Mr. Felts out of
town, and would be all during the week.
The statement in your letter wherein you say you met me in the courtroom
and I told you that I had authorized a check to be sent to you is at variance with
my recollection of our conversation. Before seeing Mr. Olmstead, at the request
of Mr. Felts, I asked whether you had received a check on account of this matter,
and you stated that you had not, and I thereupon replied that you ought to see
Mr. Olmstead; to which you replied that you did not think it was proper that
you should approach him in the matter, meaning, 'as I took it, that he should
approach you in the matter.
I am sending a copy of this letter to Hon. Joseph M. Sanders, T. L. Felts, and
Mr. Harry Olmstead.
Very truly, yours,
S. D. STOKES.

July 18, 1921, at 2 o'clock p. m.)

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
MONDAY, JULY 18, 1921.
UNITED STATES SENATE,
COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION AND LABOR,
Washington, D. C.
The Committee on Education and Labor of the United States Senate met, pur-
suant to the call of the chairman, at 2 o'clock p. m. at the committee room of
the Committee on Education and Labor, Capitol Building, Senator Kenyon pre-
siding.
Present: Senators Kenyon (chairman), Warren, Sterling, and McKellar.
Also present: Harry Olmsted, representing Operators' Association, William-
son field; Randolph Bias, Williamson, W. Va., appearing for certain mine
owners of the Williamson coal fields; Harry Scheer, Williamson, W. Va., ap-
pearing for certain mine owners; James Damron, Williamson, W. Va., appear-
ing for certain coal operators in the Williamson coal fields; Z. T. Vinson, Hunt-
ington, W. Va., appearing for the Operators' Association in the Williamson coal
fields; Neill Burkinshaw, 636 Munsey Building, Washington, D. C., appearing
for the United Mine Workers of America; Samuel B. Montgomery, Kingswood,
appearing for United Mine Workers' Association; E. L. Greever, appearing for
Williamson Coal Operators' Association; Capt. S. B. Avis, appearing for Wil-
liamson Coal Operators' Association.
TESTIMONY OF MR. HARRY OLMSTED.
(The witness, having been first duly sworn, was examined and testified as
follows:)
Mr. Avis. What is your name?
Mr. OLMSTED. Harry Olmsted.
Mr. Avis. What position or connection have you had with the Operators' As-
sociation of the Williamson field and the industrial troubles existing in that
field last June?
The CHAIRMAN. I think it would be well to state for the record just what
the association is.
Mr. Avis. If the chairman please, that will appear in the testimony.
Mr. OLMSTED. I occupy the position of chairman of the labor committee of
the Operators' Association of the Williamson field. I assumed this position
during the month of June, 1920, shortly prior to the calling of the strike by
the United Mine Workers of America. I have held that position ever since
and have been conversant from day to day and from time to time with the
progress of the strike, its collapse, and the resumption of work at the mines,
which is now and has been, since the first of this year, proceeding at normal
and with a full equipment of workmen.
Mr. Avis. What is this labor committee of which you speak?
Mr. OLMSTEAD. The labor committee is a creature of the executive commit-
tee of the Operators' Association provided for under the general terms of
authority given the executive committee under article 6 of the constitution.
The objects of the Operators' Association of Williamson field are specifically
set out in article 3 of the constitution, and are as follows:
"The objects of this association are:
"First. To promote the general business welfare of its members and of their
employees-
"(a) Through the collection and dissemination amongst its members of all
available information with respect to markets and labor conditions.

EXHIBIT 1.
CONSTITUTION OF OPERATORS' ASSOCIATION OF WILLIAMSON FIELD.
ARTICLE I.
The coal operators of the Williamson field hereby adopt the following con-
stitution to be known as the Constitution of the Operator's Association of
Williamson Field.
ARTICLE II.
This association shall be composed of all companies, firms, and individuals
operating coal mines on the Norfolk & Western Railway, between Kermit and
Panther, including all the branch lines and subsidiary lines of the Norfolk &
Western, between said points, who shall ratify this constitution or who shall
hereafter be elected to membership in the said association by a majority present
at any meeting of this association.
ARTICLE III.
The objects of the association are:
First. To promote the general business welfare of its members and of their
employees-
(a) Through the collection and dissemination amongst its members of all
available information with respect to markets and labor conditions.
(b) By discussion of mining methods and problems.
(c) By the promotion of better and more uniform methods of collierly ac-
counting.
(d) By keeping its members advised of new and proposed legislation and of
important court decisions affecting the industry.
Second. To consider and act upon any matter of common interest per-
taining to the production or transportation of coal.
Third. Anything pertaining to the protection of life, limb, or property and the
conservation of natural resources.
ARTICLE IV.
The annual meeting of the association shall be held on the third Thursday of
June, at which time the association shall elect its officers and executive com
mittee, who shall take office as of the 1st of July following and serve for one
year or until their successors are elected and qualified. Should any executive
membership become vacant by reason of death, resignation, or otherwise,
within its term, a successor may be selected by a majority vote of the executive
committee remaining, to serve through the unexpired term.


===== [扫描序号 233] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
225
ARTICLE V.
The officers of the association shall be a president, vice president, and treas-
urer, who shall be elected by a majority vote of the members of the associa-
tion present at the annual meeting and voting, and these officers, by virtue of
of their office, shall be members of the executive committee.
ARTICLE VI.
The executive committee of this association shall be composed of seven mem-
bers, of which number the president, vice president, and treasurer of the asso-
ciation shall constitute three.
It shall be the duty of the executive committee, and they are hereby au-
thorized, in their discretion, to take such action as may be necessary for carry-
ing out the purposes of this association or for the safeguarding of its interests.
ARTICLE VII.
In any ballot at general meeting of this association, the basis of voting shall
be one vote for each member of the association, unless a tonnage vote is called
for, in which event each member shall have one vote and in addition thereto
an additional vote for each 100,000 tons of coal, or major fractional part
thereof, mined by said member during the preceding calendar year. In ballot
by the executive committee each member shall have one vote.
ARTICLE VIII.
A quorum of the association shall consist of membership representing a ma-
jority of the tonnage of the association, whether or not the majority of the
actual membership is present.
A quorum of the executive committee shall have a majority of the members of
said committee, and likewise a quorum of any subcommittee shall have a ma-
jority of the members of any such subcommittee.
ARTICLE IX.
There shall be regular quarterly meetings of the members of this association.
A special meeting may be called at any time by the president, or, in his
absence, by the vice president or by any two members of the executive com-
mittee. A reasonable notice of any proposed special meeting shall be given all
members by the person or persons calling same.
The executive committee shall meet at least once each month at a time and
place to be fixed by the executive committee.

EXHIBIT 2.
BY-LAWS OF OPERATORS' ASSOCIATION OF WILLIAMSON FIELD.
SECTION 1. Each member of this association shall designate in writing to the
secretary of the association the name or names of their representative or repre-
sentatives who are authorized to attend meetings of this association and act
for and on behalf of said member, and no other person shall attend meetings of
this association without an invitation by the president of the association or by
a member of the executive committee.
In case it is necessary for any member of the association or any member of
the executive committee to be absent from any meeting, he may designate by
written proxy some one to act and vote in his stead.
SEC. 2. The executive committee shall appoint and fix the salary of a sec-
retary, who shall be secretary of this association.

Mr. Avis. Please state what is and has been the policy of the labor committee
to which you have referred.
Mr. OLMSTED. A survey of conditions in the field made at the time of my
arrival and shortly thereafter, convinced me that the progress of the proposed
strike would depend almost entirely upon law enforcement throughout the
field. It was disclosed, at any early stage of the game, that law was not being
enforced and that there was little prospect of its enforcement in Mingo County
by local law oflicers. This fact was evidenced by the attitude of the sheriff
of the county and some of his deputies at the time.
In view of this condition and responsive to the necessities of the case the
labor committee found itself committed to the task of assisting with all of its
power toward the enforcement of the law, and doing whatever it might be
able to do toward informing the people from time to time of the correct status
of conditions within the field.
The Senate committee is obliged to be convinced after having fully investi-
gated the trend of affairs in Mingo County that the law was being sacrificed
to the advantage of the organization that was endeavoring to unionize the field.
As a contrast to conditions in Mingo County where the strike did actually gain
some momentum because of resort to lawlessness, attention is called to the fact
that at no time was the strike effective, nor did the operation of the mines,
at any time cease, in Pike County, Ky., divided from Mingo County. W. Va.,
by a stream not more than 100 feet wide, where the law officers devoted their
attention to the enforcement of law and where the criminals and offenders
were taken into custody, tried, and convicted. An exception of the Pike County
part of the field is to be made as to mines operated along Tug River that were
exposed to assault by the strikers from the West Virginia mountains.
It was necessary from the very start of the strike for the labor committtee
of the Operators' Association to keep constantly in touch with all of the mines
and report disorders as they occurred, to the officers of the law, and to give
such other aid as was possible toward procuring the apprehension of persons
responsible therefor, who were committing murders, burning and dynamiting
property, and who were carrying on an incessant rifle assault upon employees
going to and from work and while at work at the mines. As a means toward
securing law enforcement and suppressing lawlessness and disorder, it became
necessary to invoke the aid of the governor of the State, who, conscious of the
unwillingness of the Mingo County authorities to police the county, kept in
service within the county at all times, as many of the State police force as were
available for duty in that county. The State police force at best was inade-
quate to the task of restoring order and protecting life and property within
the county. At times there was not at the disposal of the governor more than
20 to 30 such police officers to cover a range of practically 50 miles from one
border of the county to another along the State border. The numerical strength
of the regular State police force has at no time exceeded 100.
The siege being carried on against the workmen became so violent during
the latter part of August, 1920, that Gov. Cornwell applied to the Federal War
Department for a force of United States troops to be sent to the county to
restore order and make safe the lives and property of citizens which had been
rendered unsafe by conditions prevailing since the beginning of the strike on
July 1. The department responded on August 29, 1920, by sending a battalion
of infantry consisting of about 500 men from Camp Sherman at Chillicothe,


===== [扫描序号 235] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
227
Ohio, under the command of Col. Samuel Burkhart, jr. The troops established
a camp near the mouth of Sycamore Creek, adjacent to Williamson. Their
equipment included rifles, machine guns, and a 1-pound cannon, five motor
trucks, and several motor cycles. After conference held between Col. Burk-
hart and Maj. Thomas B. Davis, acting adjutant general of West Virginia,
who was here as representative of Gov. Cornwell, it was decided that the troops
would be stationed in detachments of 10 or more at the various mining opera-
tions from Kermit on the west to Dellorme on the east, covering a distance of
about 35 miles.
A statement was given out by Gov. Cornwell in an interview Saturday night,
August 28, in which he said that one of the causes for calling on the Federal
authorities for troops was the large number of letters of a threatening nature
that had been received by various people in Mingo County, who for some rea-
son or other had incurred the ill will of the writers. It should be remembered
in this connection that Ansie Hatfield, who was shot in the back at Matewan
a fortnight previous, had received such a letter, and the fact that the threat
that it contained proved a forewarning of what actually happened to him, had
the effect of making their recipients nervous, and drew the attention of the
governor to the gravity of the situation.
The governor also mentioned in his statement one man, the principal of the
high school at Matewan, named George Gunnoe, who had received one of these
letters and on account of fear had left the county with his family and located
in another county.
Mr. Avis. Right there, have you had copies made of a number of these threat-
ening letters to which you refer?
Mr. OLMSTED. A partial list.
Mr. Avis. Are you able to produce the letters of which you have a partial list
of the copies?
Mr. OLMSTED. We are.
Mr. Avis. I understand that some of those letters are now on file with the
Post Office Department?
Mr. OLMSTED. Yes.
Mr. Avis. And those would have to be obtained from that department?
Mr. OLMSTED. Some of the letters mentioned in that statement there.
Mr. Avis. We do not desire to encumber the record, but we have copies of a
number of letters which we would like to file for the inspection of the com-
mittee, and I would ask that these be marked copies of threatening letters re-
ceived by miners, operators, and others, volumes 1 and 2, respectively.
The CHAIRMAN (addressing the reporter). Do not copy them into the record.
Mr. HOUSTON. I do not see the pertinency of those letters.
The CHAIRMAN. The committee will have the opportunity of inspecting them.
Mr. Avis. A number of the men who received them have been killed since.
There are two volumes.
Now, will you please proceed with your statement.
Mr. OLMSTED. Gov. Cornwell was loath to go to the extreme of providing martial
law for the territory, holding to the hope that the mere presence of the soldiers
here would have the effect of quieting the situation and putting an end to the
lawlessness that had prevailed. With the coming of the troops all members of
the State police, who had been on duty here since the Matewan assassinations,
left the county. The troops remained in Mingo County until November 4, when
they were ordered withdrawn by the War Department.
On account of the steadily increasing disorders in the county and the inability
of the State police to control the situation, Gov. Cornwell was again compelled to
ask the assistance of Federal troops, and on Sunday, November 28, in response
to recommendation of certain local officials, a force of from 450 to 500 United
States soldiers were brought back into the county. Shortly after their arrival
strong detachments were sent to Matewan, Borderland, and other places in the
county.
With the second coming of the troops Gov. Cornwell deemed it advisable to put
the county of Mingo under martial law and requested the President to issue such
an order. Notwithstanding his urgent appeal to the President, the order was
not forthcoming. The governor was on record with the statement, made when
the soldiers were withdrawn from the county on November 4, that if it became
necessary to recall them that "they will be vested with full power to suppress
lawlessness and preserve order."
The soldiers brought into the county on the second call comprised a portion of
the Nineteenth Infantry Regiment organized into a tactical battalion.


===== [扫描序号 236] =====
228
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
The troops were in charge of Col. Herman Hall, of the Nineteenth Infantry, as
the commanding officer. Col. Hall established headquarters in the courthouse.
Upon their second visitation Gov. Edwin P. Morrow, of Kentucky, honored a
request of Gov. Cornwell to permit the troops to police both sides of the State
border. The importance of such an arrangement was quickly appreciated, be-
cause hundreds of shots had been fired during the past from the Kentucky side
of Tug River into the mining properties located on the West Virginia side, and
vice versa by the lawless element of the strikers who availed themselves of the
easy access from one State to the other.
Mr. Avis. Mr. Olmsted, do you know whether or not Col. Hall, in command of
the United States forces, issued a proclamation?
Mr. OLMSTED. He did, sir.
Mr. Avis. I take it the committee will not want us to read these various
proclamations, but that it will be sufficient to file with the testimony of Mr.
Olmsted the proclamation of Col. Hall, inviting particuar attention to the fact
that by the proclamation the civil officials of the county were for the time being
made an agency of the military authorities. Under the second proclamation
Gov. Cornwell declared a state of insurrection existed. That proclamation was
dated November 27. Now, under that second call, the proclamation of the gov
ernor, how long were the troops held?
Mr. OLMSTED. They were held until the 16th day of February, 1921.
Mr. Avis. Now, taking up the history of this trouble at that point, please
tell what followed after that-after the troops were withdrawn.
Mr. OLMSTED. At a later date, about the middle of May, 1921, and during
the progress of, or at about the time of the three days' battle carried on at
Merrimac, Sprigg, McCarr, and elsewhere, Gov. Morgan was solicited by county
officials and citizens generally to place the county under martial law and to
secure the return of Federal troops into the territory to carry out such a proc-
lamation. The county officials of Pike County, likewise, asked Gov. Morrow,
of Kentucky, to place Pike County under martial law and procure its enforce-
men by Federal troops. Application was made by Govs. Morgan and Morrow
to the War Department at Washington for a return of the troops, and the
matter of securing a proclamation of martial law was put up to the President
of the United States. New rulings in effect in the War Department requiring
that before troops could be detailed for such purposes it must be evident that
the afflicted communities had done their utmost to restore order and command
peace defeated the effort to obtain martial law and secure troops.
Mr. Avis. Right at that point. Gov. Cornwell was succeeded by Gov. Morgan
on the 4th of March?
Mr. OLMSTED. Yes.
Mr. Avis. In several places I note that you refer to the fact that the county
officials, or some of them, had not performed their duties. You were referring,
I understand, to the then county officials in 1920?
Mr. OLMSTED. Yes, sir.
Mr. Avis. The new county officials and the new judges of circuit court were
elected and went into office on the 1st day of January, 1921?
Mr. OLMSTED. Yes, sir.
Mr. Avis. You may go ahead with your statement or history.
Mr. OLMSTED. After the troops left the field, in the middle of February, con-
ditions grew worse, in that the number of outrages were increased and the acts
of violence became more numerous. The local officers of the law were unable
to apprehend, arrest, and punish those committing these acts of violence. This
violence culminated in what is locally known as the three days' battle, which
occurred on May 12, 13, and 14. The firing along the State border during this
three days' battle resulted in the effort to again obtain the Federal troops, as
above mentioned.
The CHAIRMAN. How many were killed in that battle?
Mr. OLMSTED. We have a record, I think, of about four. Our record is not
complete.
Senator MCKELLER. On which side were those who were killed?
Mr. OLMSTED. All the men we know about were nonunion men or citizens not
affiliated with the union.
The CHAIRMAN. Were any women or children hurt?
Mr. OLMSTED. Not to my knowledge.
Senator MCKELLER. Were those who were killed fighting with the operators
or with the men?
Mr. OLMSTED. One of the men that were killed was neutral. He was a prohi-
bition officer of the town of Sprigg, W. Va.

Senator MCKELLAR. How did he happen to be killed?
Mr. OLMSTED. He came out of his house and was shot during the firing, and

what was going on and what he could do to stop the trouble or disturbance,
and was shot at that time.
Senator MCKELLAR. The other three were whom?
Mr. OLMSTED. Mr. Goosner in the town of McCarr.
Senator MCKELLAR. Was he an employee of the operators?
Mr. OLMSTED. He was a nonunion miner, as I understand it.
Senator MCKELLAR. A nonunion miner?
Mr. OLMSTED. Yes, sir.
Senator MCKELLAR. What were the circumstances under which he was
killed?
Mr. OLMSTED. I believe he was running to catch a train while this firing
was going on, and was shot as he was crossing from Kentucky to West Virginia.
Senator MCKELLAR. He was trying to get out of the way?
Mr. OLMSTED. He was trying to catch a train coming from McCarr, was
crossing that bridge, and was shot on the bridge.
Senator MCKELLAR. What about the other two?
Mr. BIAS. Whitt was a nonunion man, was he not?
Mr. OLMSTED. I am not able to tell you about Whitt.
Senator MCKELLAR. What about the fourth one?
Mr. OLMSTED. We have a record of the fourth one that we have never been
able to get the details about, and I am not able to give them to you.
Mr. Avis. We at this point desire to invite the attention of the committee to
subdivision 6 of section 13 of chapter 12 of the Acts of the Legislature of
West Virginia at the extraordinary session of 1919. This section provides for
the calling in of officers, and so forth to assist the State constabulary and the
use of all citizens. That accounts for the number of volunteer State police
you have heard so much about.
The CHAIRMAN. Will you put that subdivision of the statute in the record?
Mr. Avis. I will be glad to do so. The section I referred to reads as follows:
"The members of the department of public safety and each of them when
called by the sheriff of any county, or when the governor by proclamation so
directs, shall have full power and authority within said county, or within the
territory defined by the governor, to direct and command absolutely the
assistance of any sheriff, deputy sheriff, constable, chief of police, policeman,
town marshall, game and fish warden, deputy prohibition officer, and any and
every peace officer of the State, or of any county or municipality therein or of any
able-bodied citizen of the United States to assist and aid in accomplishing the
purposes expressed in this act. When so called, any officer or person shall,
during the time his assistance is required, be, and be considered to be, for all
purposes, a member of the department of public safety force, and subject to
all the provision of this act"
We will say in this connection that these men, outraged at what had occurred
in that county, volunteered, and we will furnish a list of these men and their
occupations.
Senator MCKELLAR. How many of these volunteers were there?
Mr. Avis. Seven hundred and eighty.
Senator MCKELLAR. Were they from that county
Mr. Avis. From that county, including preachers, lawyers, doctors, dentists,

GILBERT, W. VA.

Mr. Avis. On what date did Gov. Morgan issue his first proclamation of
martial law?
Mr. OLMSTED. May 19, 1921.
Mr. Avis. We will file that proclamation later, but I desire to call to the
attention of the committee at this time and read into the record a paragraph
or two of that proclamation.
"Whereas the judge of the circuit court, the sheriff, and prosecuting attorney
of said county have declared their inability to put down or control such in-
surrection and riot and have been, and are now, powerless to enforce the
laws of the State within said Mingo County, and have called me as governor
of the State of West Virginia and as such governor ex-officio commander in
chief of the military forces of the State."
Senator MCKELLAR. What date is that?
Mr. Avis. May 19, 1921. That was before the time of the military occupa-
tion.
In that connection it sets forth all rules provided by the governor of West
Virginia for the government of the civil population of that territory, and it
is expressly provided in here as a part of the proclamation—well, I will read
you the entire paragraph:
I do hereby further deciare and proclaim that said territory is, and shall
remain, under martial law until the necessity therefor ceases to exist and my
further order: Provided, however, That the civil courts of said Mingo County
shall continue to have jurisdiction of, and try, all crimes, misdemeanors and
offenses against the civil law."
Senator McKELLAR. Is that still in force?
Mr. Avis. That is still in force, and has been supplemented by an additional
proclamation.
Mr. HOUSTON. The Supreme Court has practically nullified that proclama-
tion in one of its decisions.
Mr. Avis. They upheld the proclamation as being absolutely legal, but at
that time the governor had no military forces except the acting adjutant gen-


===== [扫描序号 245] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
237
eral of West Virginia, who constituted the military force of the State. He tried
to enforce the orders of the governor through the State constabulary. The
Supreme Court took the position that to enforce the orders of the commander
in chief there must be military occupation and they must be enforced by mili-
tary forces.
The CHAIRMAN. What is the condition down there now?
Mr. Avis. Since then the governor issued a second proclamation, reaffirming
the original proclamation, and the matter was decided by the courts last
Thursday as being legal and valid. In fact, the military forces were established
under an old statute of West Virginia.
Mr. HOUSTON. Have you the opinion of the court?
Mr. Avis. I do not have it here. I have a newspaper clipping of it. I
will say I have wired for the opinion of the Supreme Court and will have it
here to file, and the Supreme Court in that opinion passes upon questions of
fact.
Senator MCKELLAR. Was there any bloodshed in 1921?
Mr. Avis. Yes, sir.
Senator MCKELLAR. Who has been killed?*
Mr. Avis. Could not tell. It is impossible for me to remember all. In regard
to this Breedlove shooting you have heard so much about, we are going to have
some eyewitnesses. One State policeman was killed and one wounded; another
shot in the back and killed. We will also file the second proclamation of the
governor.
The CHAIRMAN. What is the date of that?
Mr. Avis. June 27. That proclamation was not only a proclamation but the
order of the governor of the State providing the method for securing the
safety of the force occupying that territory, and the whole thing has been
upheld by this decision, of which we will file a copy by to morrow.
Senator MCKELLAR. Under that proclamation how many soldiers were sent
into that territory?
Mr. Avis. They enrolled in that county two companies of 65 men each, each
single man of whom volunteered.
The CHAIRMAN. Were they sent in from outside counties?
Mr. Avis. No; from that county.
The CHAIRMAN. A force of 130?
Mr. Avis. One hundred and thirty men in the two counties.
The CHAIRMAN. And that is still the force?
Mr. Avis. That is still the force; and in that proclamation, it might appear
in the record so the committee can see just how the governor organized that
force in order to have a military occupation.
The CHAIRMAN. Is there any disorder there now?
Mr. Avis. We have been away from there since last Thursday; this decision
was just rendered last Thursday.
Senator MCKELLAR. I think you had all better stay away on both sides.
Mr. Avis. I do not mean to say on account of our absence, but on account
of our absence we have not heard.
The CHAIRMAN. Let us go ahead.
Mr. Avis. Please state to the committee your knowledge of the resumption of
work at mines in the field.
Mr. OLMSTED. It was my duty, as chairman of the labor committee, to en-
courage in every legal way the resumption of the mines after the strike order
became effective in Mingo County on July 1, 1920; to secure protection to men
about the mines who wanted to work and to provide additional men to operate
the mines.
66
Not many workmen were brought into the field on transportation" the total
number of each to accept work in the strike-affected portion of the district will
probably not exceed 350. All others who came were either turned back by the
strikers immediately upon their arrival or were affected by the threats of the
strikers and left for other parts.
66
The attention of the committee is called to the extent of the improvement in
production from the 1st of August, 1920, on, also to the steady acquisition of men
to work in the mines during that period. Since but a small proportion of the
men employed were brought into the county on transportation" or came volun-
tarily, the Senate committee wil be bound to conclude (which is the fact) that
practically all of the men now on the payrolls of the different companies were
former workmen who returned to work, disregarding the threats, menaces, and
intimidations of the strikers.

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
During the month of July, 1920, there were on the payrolls of the mines
affected by the strikes 658 men; the production report of that month showed an
output of 16,566 tons.
Mr. Avis. The portion affected by the strike, that was Mingo County, was it
not?
Mr. OLMSTED. Mingo County; yes.
It is proper to say that all of that tonnage was not produced during July, but
part of it was in fact coal mined in June but not weighed until July. It is proper
also to explain that the number of men on the payrolls, namely, 658, was the
record for the last day in July and does not represent the average number of
men employed throughout the month. During the first few days of July several
of the larger mines operated with a full quota of men. The operation continued
for only a few days, so that on the 15th of July there were only 107 men listed on
all of the payrolls in the mines of Mingo County. Toward the latter part of the
month several of the mines that had been idle previously resumed operation
and from that time on there was a steady increase in production as well as a
steady increase of the number of men returning to work. The total number of
men on all the pay rolls in Willianison field for July, 1920, was 2,673, and the
production amounted to 208,256 tons.
Mr. Avis. Right there, for the benefit of some of the committee who might not
have caught that, this strike order was effected as of July 21, 1920; that is cor-
rect, is it not?
Mr. OLMSTED. Yes. For the month of August, in the mines affected by the
strike, there were 638 men on the pay rolls and the production amounted to
33,007 tons. That is the Mingo County mines. For the entire field there were
during August 2,806 men on the pay rolls and the production amounted to
234,437 tons.
For the month of September in the strike-affected district the number of men
on the pay rolls grew to 977 and the production to 67,721 tons. For the entire
field there were 3,227 men on the pay rolls and the production increased to
263,021 tons.
For the month of October there were 1.337 men on the pay rolls in the strike-
affected district and the production was 105,627 tons. For the entire district
there were 3,913 men on the pay rolls and the production was 325,177 tons.
For the month of November the men on the pay rolls in the mines affected by
the strike were 1,703 and the production was 125,085 tons. For the entire field
the number of men on the pay rolls was 4,457 and the production was 347,215
tons.
For the month of December in the mines affected by the strike the number of
men on the pay rolls was 5,318 and the production amounted to 396,320 tons.
For the month of January, 1921, the number of men on the pay rolls in the
strike-affected district was 3,225 and the production increased to 185,514 tons.
For the entire district the number of men on the pay rolls was 5,961 and the
production amounted to 347,114 tons.
For the month of February, 1921, in the strike-affected district, there were
3,121 men on the pay rolls and the production amounted to 143,511 tons. For
the entire field there were 5,089 on the pay rolls and the production was
242,866 tons.
This decrease is accounted for by the slump in the market. The market went
to pieces in January and all to pieces in February.
Mr. Avis. You had fewer men enrolled in February than January?
Mr. OLMSTED. A few less; yes. It will be noted that this is the first month
during the entire progress of the strike when there has not been an increase
both of the number of men upon the pay rolls and the number of tons pro-
duced. The decrease of the number of men employed and of the tonnage pro-
duced was due wholly to the drop in the market, a situation that was expe-
rienced by every coal field in the United States. For the month of March,
1921, in the strike-affected district, there were 2.989 men on the pay rolls and
the production amounted to 158,895 tons. For the entire field the number of
men on the pay rolls was 5,164 and the production was 306,240 tons.
For the month of April, 1921, in the strike-affected district, there was a per-
ceptible increase in tonnage and a consequent increase in the number of men
employed, the number of men on the pay rolls being 3,016 and the production
183,129 tons. For the entire field the number of men employed was 5,360, pro-
duction 371,759 tons.
For the month of May, 1921, in the strike-affected district there were 3,105
men on the pay rolls and the production was 212,564 tons. In the entire
field there were 5,644 men on the pay roll and the production was 435,549 tons.

in the Kanawha fields of West Virginia, and in the three instances where
negotiations were entered into between mine owners in this field and the

miners' organization as a basis for such negotiation.
The mine owners of this field have all the while contended that the workmen
here can earn, and do earn, as much or more than the workers in the union
fields. As is observed elsewhere in this statement, workmen in this field are
paid in accordance with their skill and the energy applied by the worker,

field in net cash after all deductions, after the deduction had been made-the
store, rent, smithing, doctor, and miscellaneous charges-the average was
$240.89. He drew that money in cash, or averages that in cash, while in the
union field he drew $156.73.
Mr. Avis. Do you mean average?
Mr. OLMSTED. Yes, sir.

The CHAIRMAN. Are the prices in the company's stores higher?
Mr. OLMSTED. We have a comparison here which we will submit to the com-
mittee. The charge is so frequently made by organizers and agitators for the
United Mine Workers that store prices of living commodities at the company
stores are so high that they amount to robbery of the employees that we have
undertaken to furnish a comparison which will show the committee otherwise.
In this comparative statement of retail prices 18 articles of home food necessities
were named and prices obtained from two independent stores operating in the
city of Williamson and seven company stores selected within the field. The
two independent stores selected in the city of Williamson are the leading
grocery stores of the city. The plant stores selected were put upon the list
without any previous investigation and were chosen as typical of the stores
throughout the field.
The committee will observe that the difference in charges for the commodities
named are but very slight in any instance. In some instances they run along
practically the same. In some instances the company prices are lower than
those named by the independent stores in Williamson.
If the committee will take the pains to further investigate this subject it will
learn that in the company stores the very highest grade of products are han-
dled. This because the men working in the mines and their families demand
the best of food that is to be had.
The committee will further find upon investigation that there is not the slight-
est truth to the charge frequently made by and in behalf of the United Mine
Workers' organization that workmen are required to buy from the company
stores. Their dealings with the company stores are purely voluntary. Because
of the demands of mine workers and their families, the company stores are re-
quired by the necessities of their trade to carry the very highest grade of all
merchandise.
The comparative statement made up as of June 27, 1921, is as shown on the
following sheet-

Mr. Avis. What is the attitude of the employers of those constituting the
Williamson Coal Operators' Association as expressed by petition addressed to
this committee?
Mr. OLMSTED. There have been presented to the committee petitions carrying
4.931 names of workmen in the Williamson coal field, out of a total of about
5,200 men on the pay rolls June 30, 1921. These petitions set out that the
workmen are entirely satisfied with their terms of employment; that they
do not wish to become members of the United Mine Workers of America or
to be interfered with in their employment by this organization, and that they
wish that your committee shall make no finding that well render probable
any disturbance of their present relations with their employers.
These petitions, while originating with the labor committee of the operators'
association, were all calculated, generally, by the men themselves, and the
signatures were purely voluntary, the men signed them not only freely but
eagerly. In some cases, workmen learning that such petitions were in exist-
ence, presented themselves to the office of the company for which they worked
and inquired about them and asked permission to sign them. Instances of
this sort are not isolated and can be shown to have existed in large numbers
and at various places. At one colliery the impression got out that the peti-
tion was for the purpose of soliciting and obtaining members for the United
Mine Workers of America; with this understanding the men refused to sign.
After it had been explained to them-the exact nature of the petition-the
men signed en masse.
In a large number of instances the petitions were
signed by 100 per cent of the employees. No workman approached declined
to sign the petitions. The employees who failed to sign did so because of lack
of opportunity only.
It is worth while again, at this juncture, to call attention of the committee to
the fact that the large number of men employed in the mines in Mingo County
are workmen who have been here for years and many of whom, at the outset
joined the United Mine Workers' organization, but later repudiated it and re-
turned to their jobs.
Mr. Avis. These petitions, I take it, the committee do not desire to have in-
corporated in the record; but I would like to read the prayer of one of these
petitions and have it appear in the record:

"THE UNITED STATES COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION AND LABOR.
