Mr. Avis. There has been a statement here by witnesses for the other side
that in some instances this was a strike and in some other instances it was a
lockout. Will you explain whether it is a strike or a lockout?
Mr. OLMSTED. At no time since the first of the present year can it be properly
contended by any one that there has existed in this field either a "strike
or


===== [扫描序号 258] =====
250
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
a "lockout." From that time forward there has been employed in the mines
a full complement of men and the tonnage has approached or exceeded the
average normal production of the field. This fact demonstrates that there is
now nor has there been for many months a "strike." The fact that the men
who were previously employed, with the exception of a small number, returned
to their former places of employment demonstrates that there is no such thing,
nor has there been such a thing, as a "lockout" of the men,
There is now and has been for a great number of months a warfare conducted
on the workmen by a small number of men representing the United Mine
Workers of America, part of whom are strikers and part imported into the
territory for the purpose of making the warfare.
Full credit should be given by the Senate committee, as it has been by the
mine owners, to the large number of workmen who returned to the mines
and resumed their work for the showing made in the production records in
the field. They have pursued their work from day to day almost continuously
in the face of gun firing, under insults, and in defiance of the assaults,
threats, and intimidations of the organizers of the United Mine Workers of
America. A large number of them appealed, by petition, to the circuit court
of the county for protection, stating that they wanted to work and did not
want to be hindered from working and invoked the power of the law to protect
them.
In all cases the men employed at the mines have taken their place along with
the officers of the law, the regular State police, and the volunteer State police,
aiding in the suppression of violence and to put down rioting and warfare when
waged against them, their homes, and the property of the companies.
It is not denied by the association or its spokesman that the mine owners
of the county have from time to time bought ammunition and guns to be
used for the protection of themselves-number of mines involved. Will
you please file this statement as a part of your testimony, to be marked
as Exhibit No. 10"?

Mr. Avis. Please go ahead with your statement.
Mr. OLMSTED. The reputation of the United Mine Workers' organization for
breaking its contracts and halting or suspending the operation of mines for
weeks at a time without just reason or excuse has become notorious in the
history of the industry. The record of the operations of the United Mine
Workers' organization in the State of Kansas show that for 45 months, ending
December 31, 1919, there were 705 separate strikes at individual mines in the
State of Kansas, involving a loss to the men in wages, figures at the scale rate
per day per man, of $3,866,780.34. The strikes averaged 15 per month. For
the observation of the committee a detailed statement of the strikes, giving
their duration, the cause assigned, and gains and losses to the miners, issued
by the Southwestern Interstate Coal Operators' Association is respectfully
submitted herewith.
Mr. Avis. Will you file that as part of your testimony marked "Exhibit
No. 11."
Mr. OLMSTED. I do.
(The pamphlet referred to was marked "Exhibit No. 11," and is filed with
the committee.)

Mr. OLMSTED. This is the contract.

"If the president of the district and the commissioner of the operators'
association or their representatives fail to agree, they must either make other
disposition of the case for final adjustment or refer it and the records in
connection therewith, together with a brief in the case, to the district joint
board of miners and operators for settlement, whose duty it shall be to adjust
all grievances referred to said board, and their authority in the matter of
adjusting grievances shall not be questioned. Pending a final settlement of
any dispute the mine shall continue in operation and all miners, mine laborers,
and parties involved shall remain at work, except discharged employees."
In the face of that there was 703 strikes in that period.

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
WASHINGTON, D. C., July 31, 1920.
To the members of the United Mine Workers of America.
GENTLEMEN: It is with a feeling of profound regret and horror that I have
learned that many of the members of your organization, particularly in the
State of Illinois, have engaged in a strike in violation of the terms of the award
of the Bituminous Coal Commission and your agreement with the Government
that the findings of the commission would be accepted by you as final and
binding.
I am distressed not only because your action in refusing to mine coal upon the
terms which you had accepted may result in great suffering in many households
during the coming winter and interfere with the continuation of industrial and
agricultural activity, which is the basis of the prosperity which you in common
with the balance of our people have been enjoying, but also, and what is of far
more importance to you, because the violation of the terms of your solemn obli-
gation impairs your own good name, destroys the confidence, which is the very
basis of all mutual agreements, and threatens the very foundation of fair in-
dustrial relations. No government, no employer, no person having any reputa-
tion to protect can afford to enter into contractual relations with any organiza-
tion that repeatedly or systematically violates its contracts. The United Mine
Workers of America is the largest single labor organization in the United
States, if not in the world, but no organization can long endure that sets up
its own strength as being superior to its plighted faith or its duty to society
at large. It has in the past built up an enviable reputation for abiding by its
contracts, which has been one of its most valuable assets in making wage
agreements. It may now make temporary gains by taking advantage of the
dire necessities of the balance of the people through the violation of these
contracts, but what of the future? How can it expect wage contracts with the
employers to be continued in the face of such violations when normal conditions
have been restored and the country is free from the fear of immediate shortage
of coal? How will it be able to resist. the claims of the operators in the future
who take advantage of the precedent which the miners have established and
decrease wage rates in the middle of a wage contract under the plea that they
are unable to sell the coal at the then existing cost of production? A mere
statement of these questions ought to be sufficient to awaken the mine workers
to the dangerous course they are pursuing and the injuries they are inflicting
upon themselves and the country at large by the adoption of these unwarranted
strike policies.
In the consideration of the nation-wide wage scale, involving many different
classes of labor, by the bituminous coal commission in the limited time at its
disposal, some inequalities may have developed in the award that ought to be
corrected. I can not, however, recommend any consideration of such inequali-
ties as long as the mine workers continue on strike in violation of the terms of
the award which they had accepted as their wage agreement for a definite
length of time. I must, therefore, insist that the striking mine workers return
to work, thereby demonstrating their good faith in keeping their contract.
When I have learned that they have thus returned to work I will invite the
scale committees of the operators and miners to reconvene for the purpose of
adjusting any such inequalities as they may naturally agree should be adjusted.
WOODROW WILSON.
Mr. AVIS. What reasons have you for opposing the organization in the Wil-
liamson field?
The CHAIRMAN. You opposed them before that letter, did you not?
Mr. OLMSTEAD. Yes, sir; this is before the strike was called; theretofore we
were not opposing them; they had not called a strike.
The CHAIRMAN. You do not want us, then, to take Mr. Wilson's letter as the
reason?
Mr. OLMSTEAD. That is just one of the reasons, Mr. Chairman.
In addition, the mine owners of this field oppose the United Mine Workers
because of the conspiracy entered into between that organization and the opera-
tors of the four competitive States, Indiana, Illinois, Ohio, and western Penn-
sylvania, wherein it was proposed that the output from this State should not be
permitted to grow but should be suppressed, by means of unionizing the State,
in order that the market might be retained by the competitors of the four
States. Evidence of facts relating to this conspiracy will be offered in proof
during the progress of this investigation and will be of such substantial nature
as to admit of no controversy.

Mr. OLMSTED. Further, the mine owners of this field opposed the organization
of their mines by the United Mine Workers because of the acknowledged and
proclaimed aims and purposes of the organization, as set out by the program
adopted by them in their national convention in Cleveland, Ohio, and from
September 9 to the 23d, 1919, which demanded :
A six-hour day and a five-day week.
A substantial increase for all classes of mine labor.
Nationalization of coal mines through congressional action.
Cooperation instead of competition in the coal trade.
The free and unrestricted right to unionize under Government control.
The right to bargain with the Government.
Senator STERLING. Right there, have you the original documents? You are
stating it in a general way, as I understand it.
Mr. Avis. I think we have the proceedings of the convention.
Senator STERLING. You have the proceedings?
Mr. Avis. There is a Government document prepared by the National Bitum-
inous Coal Commission that sets forth those proceedings, showing the trouble
and the strike of November 1, 1919. Those are all set forth in that report,
which is dated March 10, 1920, and which is a public document.
Mr. OLMSTED. Further, our opposition is because of the general attitude of the
officers of the United Mine Workers to the effect that the workers, through their
organization shall direct the policy of the mines and shall have full partner-
ship in their operation.
The mine owners, also oppose the organization of their mines by the United
Mine Workers of America because with the organization of this and adjacent
fields, the United Mine Workers of America would be placed in a position of con-
trolling the entire bituminous coal output of the country and would have and
exercise at will the power to curtail or suspend operations by strike at any time
that they might desire to do so.
With such a grasp upon the industry this organization would have the power
to stop at any time the operation of the railroads, thereby suspending all com-
merce and industry throughout the length and breadth of the land. It was
their aim to do this with the strike of November and December, 1919, which
was called to enforce a demand for 60 per cent increae in wages along with the
other demands of the Cleveland convention as recited above. It was because
the coal fields of southern West Virginia and eastern Kentucky were not subject
to the dictation of the United Mine Workers, our Navy secured necessary fuel,
the industries of the country were able to proceed, the railroads were able to
move their trains, domestic consumers were supplied with fuel and all sorts of
industry and traffic so necessary to our civilization were allowed to continue.
During the progress of the 1919 strike the Williamson and neighboring non-
union fields of West Virginia and Kentucky gave to the country practically all
of the supply of coal that was had and averted general disaster among the
railroads and the industries of the country, and saved the people from incon-
venience, if not disaster. The nonunion fields in this section, including the
Logan field, Pocahontas field, Tug River field, Williamson field, Winding Gulf
field, Big Sandy field, Harlan field, and Hazard field have a production capacity
of about 67,000,000 tons per year. The yield from these fields is sufficient to
continue the operations of the railroads and to supply coal to the people for
domestic purpose in time of stress. The mine owners of the Williamson field
do not propose to yield to the United Mine Workers of America any such ad-
vantage over the people. They do not propose to surrender the relations that
have heretofore existed between themselves and their workmen, which have
at all times been amicable, and so satisfactorily adjusted as to prevent any sort
of trouble or disorder or the suspension of work within this field.

Mr. AVIS. That is a résumé of the figures from which the 67,000,000 came.

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Mr. HOUSTON. That was an unlawful process.
Mr. OLMSTED. Your committee can be shown' by proof during the progress of
this investigation a large number of instances where strikers, or organizers,
or gunmen acting for the United Mine Workers and in behalf of their alleged
strike have fired upon, killed, and wounded soldiers and police officers, showing
not only contempt for the machinery of the law but murderous design against
those charged with the enforcement of law.
Another and most important reason why the operators of the field oppose the
organization of the United Mine Workers is because the restrictions imposed by
this organization upon its members tends to decrease production, lower effi-
ciency, and destroy initiative. The present wage of the miner in this field, as
in all nonunion fields, is based upon the quality and quantity of work per-
formed, his remuneration is commensurate with the skill he is able to attain,
and the energy he is willing to expend. Your committee will be furnished
statistics which will conclusively prove that it is within the power of the
miner to earn a materially higher wage in this field than in the organzed fields,
and in addition to the possibility for larger earnings he has also the opportunity
to rise from the most poorly paid occupation connected with mining to the
highest position within the gift of the industry. The existence of this oppor-
tunity is demonstrated by the fact that many of the operators and owners
of this field rose from the ranks of the miners to their present positions, and
we believe that your committee can not but concur in our contention that it
is by the virtue of the individual contract between workmen and employer,
wherein shirking and inefficiency are discouraged by penalization and ambition
and energy stimulated by the proper reward of merit and ability, that our
country has been able to attain to its present high standard of living and en-
viable status of prosperity.
When the right of private contract between employee and employer is re-
placed by a contract with the United Mine Workers a flat wage scale is made
applicable alike to the honest workman and to the inefficient shirker, with
the inevitable result that the poorest workman becomes the pace setter for
the entire force. The earnings of the pieceworker are restricted by the fact
that the most skilled miner must take "turn" of mine cars with the slowest
worker in the mine.
In this connection it is proper to point out that this is one of the few large
nonunion coal fields of the United States. The native population affords only
a small percentage of the number of workmen necessary to properly operate
the mines, as a consequence the majority of workmen in this field, "which has
always enjoyed a virtually full labor supply," has come here from other
States.
Mr. HOUSTON. What fields?
Mr. OLMSTED. This nonunion field-Williamson.
A large percentage of them have at one time or another worked in organized
fields and come here for the express purpose of escaping the restricted earnings
and petty tyrannies incident to union contract.
Mr. AVIS. Right here, will you kindly explain to the committee what this
means, that the most skilful miner must take "turn" of mine cars with the
slowest worker in the mine?
Mr. OLMSTED. What is called the "turn" in the mine is the delivery of the
cars to be loaded by the miners. A driver will have a certain number of
miners on a certain territory in the mine. He drives from those miners the
cars that have been loaded and comes back with his empties which are placed
where the men are working. He returns with those loads to the tipple and
takes the additional empties back, and if those cars are not all loaded, that is
if one or two men have not loaded their cars because of the fact that they are
not as ambitious and efficient or not as good workmen as the others, he has
to wait for that car to be loaded, or if he does go back with that load and
leaves that car-if that car remains at that place, he has to furnish that man
with an additional car and that militates against the man and against the
work. The best one is the one who loads his car in a short time, so that the
other men won't have to wait for him.
The fact that most of the workers here did come from other States demon-
strates the mobility of labor in the coal mining industry and it will be readily
seen by your committee that if the wages paid, living conditions and treatment
accorded in this field did not compare favorably with that of organized fields
it would have been impossible for our mines to have retained a supply of
labor in the face of the keen competition for mine workmen which has existed
throughout the United States for the past six years.


===== [扫描序号 267] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
259
Your committee may properly take cognizance of the geographical position
of the Williamson coal field, relative to the other nonunion coal fields of West
Virginia and Kentucky. You will appreciate that, once organized, this field
would furnish an ideal and centrally located base from which the organization
of the remaining nonunion fields could be successfully affected, thus placing
virtually the entire coal-producing industry of the United States under the
control of the United Mine Workers of America. Evidence of the performances
of this organization in union fields will be submitted to your committee and
from which performances you may be enabled to forecast their probable future
actions once the production of coal (the basis of American industry and an
indispensable household necessity) is definitely within their control, and when
fairly considered we believe that you will have no difficulty in conceiving that
in contesting the organization of this field by the United Mine Workers we
are fighting to preserve the American principle of competition in the coal
mining industry and rendering a service of incalculable value to the public
interest of the American people as a whole.
Mr. Avis. What do you know of the secrecy of the operations of the United
Mine Workers of America, particularly in the Williamson field?
Mr. OLMSTED. As a general thing, extreme difficulty has been encountered in
obtaining evidence against persons committing crimes and depredations in
Mingo County during the period of the strike. As has been pointed out be-
fore, some of the constituted law officers of the county, prior to January 1,
1921, were apparently without inclination to secure arrests or to suppress
crime. At least one instance will be shown where Sheriff Blankenship was
summoned over the 'phone to go to the protection of workmen who were
being held up and mistreated in the lobby of the Hotel Vaughan at William-
son, less than a city block away from his office, and his answer to the sum-
mons was that he did not have time and would not have time that day. Your
witness can state and further proof can be offered in substantiation that in
practically every instance where offenses and crimes were reported to the office
of this sheriff no attention or perfunctory attention was given.
In five instances at least confessions have been secured from persons connected
with shooting and assaults done in behalf of the United Mine Workers of
America. In four of these, namely, Nelson Fields, William Howard McCoy,
Grady Sailer, and Columbus Price, confess ons have been made that the crimes
in which they participated originated at meetings of the United Mine Workers'
locals. In the fifth, that of Floyd Chaney, caught while making an effort to
blow up the conveyor lines of the Borderland Coal Corporation, the confession
involved a conspiracy with another man to do the act. Both of them were
members of the United Mine Workers of America, but it did not appear that
the conspiracy was concocted at any meeting of the organization. It did appear,
however, from the confess on that the conspiracy was hatched and the act
attempted in furtherance of the strike, and with the avowed purpose of put-
ting the Borderland Coal Corporation out of business, with the expectation
that a suspension of operations would force them to sign up with the union.
Because of the confessions of William Howard McCoy and Nelson Fields, they
were not prosecuted in Pike County court, but others connected with the same
crime were prosecuted, convicted, and sentenced to the Kentucky penitentiary.
Mr. Avis. I should like an opportunity to file those to-morrow.
Mr. BIAS. We will produce the witnesses, not to-morrow, but we will produce
them.
Mr. Avis. Mr. Olmsted, what do you know of the interference of workmen
coming into this field of work?
Mr. OLMSTED. During the progress of the strike, particularly during its
early days, it became necessary for some of the coal companies operating in
the field to solicit workmen from outside the territory and to transport them
to the mines within the field to augment the numbers of men within the field
who were gradually returning to work. For the purpose of hindering, obstruct-
ing, and defeating this moving picketing parties from among the strikers and
organizers were made up to meet the passenger trains coming into the city of
Williamson and other places in the county. Scouts were usually kept aboard
the trains, so that notice might be given that workmen were aboard.
Always upon the arrival of train carrying workmen into the field the rail-
way station at Williamson was jammed with crowds of strikers, organizers,
and agitators. Banners were paraded declaring the existence of the strike.
Upon alighting the men would be surrounded by dozens and perhaps hundreds

of the strikers, who would seek first to induce them to refuse to go further
and to accept transportation back. Should this mnranner of persuasion fail,
it was followed by a system of abuse, scathing denunciation, villification,
threats, and in frequent cases assaults. At times there appeared among the
strikers assisting in this enterprise men who were officers of the law in
Mingo County, who let it be known that there were officers of the law and

STATEMENT OF HARRY OLMSTED-Resumed.
Mr. Avis. Mr. Olmsted, when we adjourned yesterday afternoon, you were
stating instances of interferences with workmen coming into the field, but had
not quite completed your statement. Will you please start where you left off
and tell of that situation.
Mr. OLMSTED. Usually the men were met at the station also by the employers
or their representatives, who, realizing the state of terror into which the men
would be placed, came to give them courage to proceed. These men, residents
of Mingo County, West Virginia, and Pike County, Kentucky, were subjected
to abuse and threats, in some instances by the officers of the law. Frequently
the incoming workmen would be taken bodily from those accompanying them,
and under the pressure of force would be required to go to the headquarters
of the United Mine Workers and accept transportation away from the field.
Witnesses will testify to the committee of numbers of these outrages.
Mr. Avis. Mr. Olmsted, once or twice you referred to the officers of the law.
Please state to the committee what particular officers of the law you referred to.
Mr. OLMSTED. Well, State policemen, by the name of Deerfield, is one; William
Blair, deputy sheriff is another.
Mr. Avis. That is the deputy sheriff under Mr. Blankenship, the man de-
scribed as the friendly sheriff.
Mr. OLMSTED. Yes, sir.
Mr. HOUSTON. Who was it that described him as the friendly sheriff?
Mr. Avis. One of your witnesses on the first day that he spoke of this-
Mr. HOUSTON. But you would characterize him as an unfriendly sheriff?
Mr. AVIS. Well, we will speak of him as the friendly sheriff.
Mr. OLMSTED. It will be shown by proof that in some instances the men arriv-
ing here for the purpose of accepting employment were members of one union
or another in other crafts than that of coal mining. It will be shown by proof
that upon one occasion about two dozen such workmen on their way to Pond
Creek, Kentucky, were brought to the headquarters of the Williamson Field
Coal Operators' Association for safety; that while there a city policeman sought
to interview them for the purpose of persuading them. It will be shown that
261


===== [扫描序号 270] =====
262
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
in the presence of the city policeman the men were asked to vote as to whether
they wanted to continue on their way to the mines or accept the offer of the
representative of the United Mine Workers and return home. It will be shown
that the men thereupon voted almost unanimously in favor of proceeding to
the mines, whereupon the city policeman said that he would secure assistance
and guard the men safely through the town and to the Kentucky border, but
that he did not return and refused and neglected to give the assistance that
was promised.
The violence attending the picketing, as it called, became so great on this
and other occasions, that it was necessary to summon the reserves from the
United States Federal troops stationed here to give the men safety while passing
through. It became necessary likewise for the judge of the Circuit Court of
Mingo County to take cognizance of conditions and to issue a letter directed
to the then sheriff and his deputies requiring them to suppress the disorder
and protect the men coming into the field for the purpose of accepting
employment.
There are records of scores of assaults upon recruited workmen at the mines
throughout the country, which will be testified to by witnesses.
Despite any strike orders that may have been issued, despite the reluctance
with which the strikers viewed the resumption of the operation of mines, the
mine owners had the right to continue operation, and men willing to work therein
had the right to do so.
Witnesses will be presented who will tell their stories. A large number of
men coming into the fields to accept employment were destined to mines on
Pond Creek, in Pike County, Ky., all of which were practically in full operation.
There had been no obedience to the strike order at any of the mines on Pond
Creek, except one or two of the smaller operations near the mouth of the
creek. It is undeniable that some of the workmen employed by the Pond
Creek mines, either voluntarily or through inducement, when in Williamson
joined the union. But they left their places of work, moved out, and at no
time was there any serious effort to extend the organization of the United
Mine Workers of America into the Pond Creek part of the field. It was for the
purpose of filling up the gaps made by the departure of men from the Pond
Creek section that men were being brought into the field, and by far the
larger percentage of those coming here were destined for the Pond Creek
operations.
So offensive did the mine workers, hangers-on about the Norfolk & Western
station became, that it was necessary for the passenger agent of the railway
company to protest againt their presence and to demand their retirement.
However, no attention was paid to the demand until military orders established a
line beyond which the strikers were not allowed to come. J. B. Saunders,
freight and passenger agent at Williamson, will testify as to his experiences.
Mr. AVIS. Now, Mr. Olmstead, I wish you would tell the committee any
instances of interference that almost amounted to a riot that came under your
personal observation.
Mr. OLMSTED. About 18 or 17; between 17 and 19. There were 27 men, some
with their families and children, that got off at the station and were sur-
rounded.
Mr. Avis. At what place?
Mr. OLMSTED. At Williamson, and finally they worked their way through
and were brought into the headquarters of the association. After their arrival,
a city policeman by the name of Deerfield came in to interview them. He started
out to tell them there was a strike at Pond Creek and that it was dangerous
to go up there, and was advising them not to go, when I came out into the
office where these men were located and where he was speaking to them, and
I asked him if he came there to discourage these men or if he came there
in the interest of the United Mine Workers, and I said, "If you come down here
for that purpose you can get out. These men want to be taken through the
town and be guaranteed their safe conduct through the town."
Then I asked these men, "You came here knowing there was a strike, did
you?" They all held up their hands; the majority of them; I do not think
there were over one or two that did not hold up their hands. I said. "Do
you want to go to Pond Creek to work; did you come for that purpose? And
they all held up their hands. I said Do you want safe conduct through the
town?" and most of them held up their hands. I think not over two or three
did not.

Mr. Avis. I wish you would state to the committee what your committee has
done toward giving publicity to this industrial trouble in Mingo County.
Mr. OLMSTED. The Operators' Association has maintained throughout the
strike the bureau of publicity. The purpose of this bureau has been to keep
the people correctly advised as to conditions within the field, as to the objections
to its organization by the United Mine Workers of America, and as to the
progress being made from time to time in opposing the organization of the field.
In furtherance of these objects the association contracted and paid for space
in the local newspapers and in newspapers reaching this territory from other
points. All such advertising matter was prepared by the publicity representa-
tive, and was printed over the signature of the operators' association of Wil-
liamson fields. It was never disguised in the form of news, but took its space
in the newspapers as regularly paid for advertising matter. These advertise-
ments consisted largely of arguments in opposition to organization, and were
constructed in such way as to appeal to the judgment and sense of the news-
pa per readers. Statements were issued periodically in this advertising space
showing the extent to which mine operations was being resumed in the field,
the number of men employed at certain periods, and the monthly report of ton-

along the Atlantic coast, in New York State, in Pennsylvania, in Maryland, in

Mr. AVIS. It has been stated here by witnsses that the mine owners in the
Williamson field had maintained a guard system, and have employed a number
of Baldwin-Felts men as mine guards. What have you to say about that?
Mr. OLMSTED. The mine owners of the Williamson field do not, nor have they
ever, maintained what is popularly known as the “guard system" for the mines.
The complaint has been made by the United Mine Workers' organizers and their
newspapers and in their public statements, to the effect that the "guard system"
was maintained here, and as a consequence the miners were being enslaved and
held in peonage and that the territory was not accessible to them or to any
visitors not favorable to the coal companies is absolutely without foundation.
The Senate committee will have opportunity during the progress of this investi-
gation to learn that it is a part of the method and policy of the United Mine
Workers, when attempting to organize a coal field, to make an ado about the
presence and the oppression of the mine guards. This is done for the purpose
of exciting public favor in their behalf and public prejudice against the mine
owners. Lurid tales are published to the effect that the "brutal mine guards "
have been guilty of assaulting men, women, and children, and generally an
invasion is planned from some neighboring unionized field for the purpose of
suppressing the alleged outrages. The Senate committee will not dispute the
right of property owners to guard their property if they should see fit, or if it
should become necessary.
The oft-repeated charge that these mine owners have employed thugs and
gunmen to guard the mine property, to terrorize and abuse and hold in slavery
the mine workers and their families is wholly false and can not be supported by
any proof whatever.
Mr. Avis. Mr. Olmsted, have you at any time during this strike employed any

WILLIAMSON, W. Va., May 18, 1921.
DEAR SIR: Confirming conversation had with you, I write to further assure

promises and agrees to continue to exert every possible effort toward restoring

possible and proper aid toward the apprehension and punishment of all persons
guilty of violating the criminal law.

that any employee of his mine is guilty of the violation of any criminal
law that he will forthwith discharge such employee and report to you the
name of such employee and the specific offense of which he is guilty, and, if
requested so to do, aid in his apprehension and arrest.
Yours, very truly,
HARRY OLMSTED,

PROCLAMATION OF COLONEL COMMANDING, ISSUED TO THE CITIZENS OF THE COUNTY
OF MINGO, STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA, HEADQUARTERS UNITED STATES TROOPS, WIL-
LIAMSON, W. VA., NOVEMBER 28, 1920.
1. The governor of the State of Virginia, having called upon the commanding
general of the Fifth Corps Area of Federal troops for the protection of life and
property and the maintenance of public order in Mingo County, State of West
Virginia, the commanding general of the Fifth Corps Area, in compliance with
this request, and acting under general instructions of the President and laws
of the United States, has directed me to assume military control of Mingo
County, State of West Virginia, which county I hereby declare to be until
further orders under military control.
2. It is the purpose and the desire of the military authorities to conduct the
affairs of Mingo County to the greatest extent possible through the civil officials
of the said county, who will for the time being act as an agency for the military
authorities.
3. The following rules and regulations are hereby promulgated and declared
to be in force and effect and as controlling the civil population of Mingo County
until further orders:
(a) No public assemblages or meetings other than those held in organized
churches will be permitted in city, town, or village, or in any inclosure, or
other than open-air place within the county, except by special authority of the
officer commanding troops in that locality.
(b) All processions and parades are prohibited, as well as demonstrations
against the authorities.
(c) No persons except the constituted municipal, State, and Federal authori-
ties, troops, police, and other officers of the law are permitted to carry arms
or weapons of any description, or equipment, explosives, or munitions of war.
(d) All rights of property of whatever kind will be held inviolate and will
not be disturbed, except as the exigencies of the public welfare may necessitate,
and then only by direct command of the commanding officer of the district.
(e) All shops, places of business and of amusement, except as hereinafter
provided, will be kept open as usual in times of peace, and all persons are
enjoined to continue their customary peaceful occupation.
4. All persons within Mingo County, are admonished to observe and carefully
comply with the letter and spirit of the foregoing instructions.
5. Any person or persons desiring to present any petition or complaint will
present same to the command'ng officer, commanding United States troops, on
duty in Mingo County for his consideration and action.
HERMAN HALL,
Colonel Nineteenth Infantry, Commanding.
The proclamation of Gov. Cornwell declaring the territory to be in a state of
insurrection is quoted as follows:
PROCLAMATION OF GOV. CORNWELL, STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA, EXECUTIVE CHAMBER,
CHARLESTON.
Whereas there are in the county of Mingo certain individuals who are resisting
the laws of the State and the United States and offering violence to peaceful
cit zens and property in said Mingo County; and
Whereas at divers times and places in said county various crimes, including
murder, have been committed in said county with the aid and under the direc-
tion of said vicious and lawless persons; and
Whereas by reason of such lawlessness, acts of violence, and disturbances the
civil authorities of this State are powerless and unable to cope with the situa-
tion: Now, therefore,
I, John J. Cornwell, governor of the State of West Virginia, by virtue of the
power and authority in me vested, do hereby proclaim the said county of
Mingo to be in a state of insurrection, and all citizens and inhabitants of the
county of Mingo are enjoined and commanded to disperse and retire peacefully
to their respective places of abode and submit themselves to the laws and con-
stituted authorities of the State and the United States.
To the end that the laws shall be respected and that disorders shall cease I
have called upon the Government of the United States for assistance, and until
further notice the county of Mingo will be under the direct charge of the com-
manding general of the Fifth Corps Area, who has full power and authority to

establish peace and order in said county by such means as he may deem to
the best interests of good government and the laws of the land.
In witness whereof I have hereunto set by hand and caused the great seal of
the State to be affixed at the capitol, in the city of Charleston, this the 27th day
of November, in the year of our Lord 1920 and of the State the fifty-eighth.
JOHN J. CORNWELL, Governor.
By the governor:
H. G. YOUNG,

On their second visitation the troops were held here until the 16th day of
February, 1921, when, under orders from the War Department, they were
withdrawn.
At a later date, about the middle of May, 1921, and during the progress of
or at about the time of the three days' battle carried on at Merrimac, Sprigg,
McCarr, and elsewhere, Gov, Morgan was solicited by county officials and citi-
zens generally to place the county under martial law and to secure the return of
Federal troops into the territory to carry out such a proclamation. The county
officials of Pike County likewise asked Gov. Morrrow, of Kentucky, to place
Pike County under martial law and procure its enforcement by Federal troops.
Application was made by Govs. Morgan and Morrow to the War Department at
Washington for a return of the troops, and the matter of securing a proclama-
tion of martial law was put up to the President of the United States. New
rulings in effect in the War Department, requiring that before troops could be
detailed for such purposes that it must be evident that the afflicted communities
had done their utmost to restore order and command peace, defeated the effort
to obtain martial law and secure troops.
After the troops left the field in the middle of February conditions grew
worse, in that the number of outrages were increased and the acts of violence
became more numerous. The local officers of the law were unable to appre-
hend, arrest, and punish those committing these acts of violence. This violence
culminated in what is locally known as the three days' battle, which occurred
on May 12, 13, and 14.
The firing along the State border during this three days' battle resulted in
the effort to again obtain the Federal troops, as above mentioned.
Failing to obtain the presence of the troops, it became necessary that some-
thing be done to curb and lessen the lawlessness. The sheriff of Mingo County,
with the approval of the judge of the circuit court of that county and the
advice of the prosecuting attorney of the county, issued his warrant directed
to the head of the department of public safety, commonly called the State
police department, calling upon that department to take charge of the enforce-
ment of the laws in the county. This warrant from the sheriff to the State
police department was issued under subdivision 6 of section 14 of chapter 12
of the acts of the Legislature of West Virginia of the extraordinary session
of 1919, which section reads as follows:
"The members of the department of public safety and each of them, when
called by the sheriff of any county or when the governor by proclamation so
directs, shall have full power and authority within said county, or within the
territory defined by the governor, to direct and command absolutely the assist-
ance of any sheriff, deputy sheriff, constable, chief of police, policeman, town
marshal, game and fish warden, deputy prohibition officer, and any and every
peace officer of the State, or of any county or municipality therein, or of any
able-bodied citizen of the United States to assist and aid in accomplishing the
purposes expressed in this act. When so called any officer or person shall,
during the time his assistance is required, be, and be considered to be, for all
purposes a member of the department of public safety force and subject to all
the provisions of this act."
The warrant of the sheriff itself was as follows:
The State of West Virginia to J. R. Brockus, captain of the West Virginia
State police:
Whereas it has been made to appear to the undersigned, A. C. Pinsen, sheriff
of Mingo County, that on account of labor troubles and disputes now existing
in the said county of Mingo numerous breaches of the peace have recently
been committed; murder by lying in wait and shooting from ambush has
become common; and that there is now imminent danger of riots and resist-


===== [扫描序号 282] =====
274
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
ance of law pending within said county of Mingo, which can not be sup-
pressed or effectually prevented by the ordinary posse, comitatus in my
said county, and that the force of the department of public safety of West
Virginia is necessary to aid the civil authorities in suppressing and con-
trolling the threatened danger above set out: Now, therefore,
In pursuance of the statute in such case made and provided, and in pursuance
of section 14 of chapter 12 of the acts of the Legislature of West Virginia,
extraordinary session, 1919, you are hereby called upon to direct and command
absolutely the assistance of any deputy sheriff, constable, chief of police, police-
man, town marshal, any and every peace officer of the county, or any munic-
pality therein, and of every able-bodied citizen residing in Mingo County or
found therein, to assist and aid in the prevention of any further breaches of

Immediately upon delivery of this warrant to Maj. Arnold, of the State police
force, he authorized and directed Capt. J. R. Brockus, in command of the State
policemen in the county, to comply with the provisions of the act of the legisla
ture above set out.
This was done, and from that time until the proclamation of martial law and
the occupation of said Mingo County by the military forces of the State, the
said department was in charge of the enforcement of the laws of said county.
In addition to the sheriff and his deputies, and the policemen, constables, and
other civil officers of the county, Capt. Brockus enrolled approximately 780 vol-
unteer State policemen. About 200 of these men live in the city of Williamson
and are of the highest types of citizens there. The others are located at various
places in the county and are men of the very best character and habits. A list
of these men will be furnished to the Senate committee.
About the same time that this volunteer State police force was recruited Gov.
Morgan, at the instance and request of all the local officials of Mingo County,
issued a proclamation declaring a state of insurrection and war to exist in the
county and placing the same under martial law, and issuing rules or order to
govern and control the people of the county under such order.
This proclamation so issued by the governor is as follows:
STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA—A PROCLAMATION BY THE GOVERNOR.
Whereas a state of war, insurrection, and riot is and has been for some time
in existence in the county of Mingo, State of West Virginia; and
Whereas large bodies of armed men have assembled in the mountains of Mingo
County and fired into and shot up public and other buildings, and fired into
passenger trains while passing over the Norfolk & Western Railway in said
County; and
Whereas many lives and much property have been destroyed as a result thereof,
and riot and bloodshed is still rampant and pending; and
Whereas the judge of the circuit court, the sheriff and prosecuting attorney of
said county have declared their inability to put down or control such insur-
rection and riot, and have been, and are now, powerless to enforce the laws
of the State within said Mingo County, and have called upon me as governor
of the State of West Virginia, and as such governor ex officio commander in
chief of the military forces of the State; and
Whereas there is necessity therefor: Therefore
I, Ephriam F. Morgan, governor of the State of West Virginia, and as such
governor ex officio commander in chief of the military forces of the State, in
view of the foregoing, and in order to execute the laws and to protect the public
peace, lives, and property of quiet, orderly citizens, by virtue of the constitution
and laws of the State of West Virginia, do hereby declare and proclaim a state
of war, insurrection, and riot to exist in the said county of Mingo, State of West
Virginia.
And I do hereby further declare and proclaim that said territory is, and
shall remain, under martial law until the necessity therefor ceases to exist and

275
my further order: Provided, however, That the civil courts of said Mingo County
shall continue to have jurisdiction of, and try all cr.mes, misdemeanors and
offenses against the civil law.
The following rules and orders are hereby promulgated and declared to be
in force and effect and as controlling the civil populat on of said Mingo County
until further orders:
1. No person or persons shall compose or take part in, or encourage, aid, abet
or assist in any riot, rout, tumult, mob or lawless combination or assemblage,
or violate, or encourage, aid, abet or assist in the violation of any of the civ.l
laws of the State of West Virginia.
2. No public assemblages or meetings will be permitted in any city, town or
village, or in any inclosure or open air place within the county, except by special
authority.
3. All processions and parades, except by special authority, are prohibited, as
well as demonstrations against the authorities and officers.
4. No persons, except the constituted munic pal, State and Federal authorities,
militia, troops, police, and others officers of the law, are permitted to carry or
have arms or weapons of any character or description, or equipment, explosives,
ammunition or munitions of war in their possession, or at any place, except at
their own homes or places of business.
5. All military and other officers shall have the right of way in any street or
highway through which they may pass.
6. Any person or persons entering or remaining in said Mingo County for the
purposes of interfering in any manner whatever with the rights of citizens or
property of said Mingo County shall be arrested, detained and imprisoned.
7. All persons are admonished to observe and carefully and rigidly comply
with the civil laws of the State of West Virginia and with the letter and spirit
of this proclamation and these rules and orders; and any person or persons
violating the same in said Mingo County shall be arrested, disarmed, detained,
and imprisoned.
8. Any person or persons, except the constituted municipal, State and Federal
authorities, militia, troops, police, and other officers of the law, carrying or in
possession of arms or weapons of any character or description, or equipment,
explosives, ammunition or munitions of war, at any place other than at their
own homes or places of business, shall be arrested, disarmed, detained and im-
prisoned.
9. No publication, either newspaper, pamphlet, handbill, or otherwise, reflect-
ing in any way upon the United States or the State of West Virginia or their
officers, or tending to influence the public mind against the United States or
the State of West Virginia or their officers, may be published, distributed, dis-
played, or circulated in said Mingo County; and the publication, distribution,
displaying, or circulation of any such publication above specified is prohibited,
and any person or persons violating this paragraph shall be arrested, detained,
and imprisoned.
Maj. Thomas B. Davis, acting adjutant general of the State of West Vir-
ginia, is hereby designated and appointed and commissioned commanding officer
of the militia of, and my agent in, said Mingo County, with full power and
authority in the premises to execute, enforce, and carry out this proclamation
and said rules and orders in letter in spirit, and as such officer and agent he
shall have full and complete authority and power in the premises; and each
and all the officers and members of the department of public safety, the sheriff
of said Mingo County and his deputies, and all other deputy sheriffs, police
officers, State officers, and any and every peace officer of the State or of said
Mingo County or municipality therein are hereby required, directed, authorized,
and empowered to assist said acting adjutant general and agent in executing
the laws of the State of West Virginia and this proclamation and said rules
and orders in said Mingo County; and any such officer who shall willfully fail,
neglect, or refuse to execute or enforce the same shall in the fifty-eighth year of
the State.
In witness whereof I have hereunto set my hand and caused the great seal
of the State to be affixed.
Done at the capitol, in the city of Charleston, this the 19th day of May, in
the year of our Lord 1921, and in the fifty-eighth year of the State.
[SEAL].

Under the proclamation of martial law, Maj. Davis, employing the State
police force, and the sheriff of the county and his deputies, arrested a number of
people for violation of the rules and orders so proclaimed and for violations of
certain of the civil laws.
The validity and legality of the proclamation of martial law was assailed by
the United Mine Workers of America and their attorneys, the attack being made
in a habeas corpus proceeding brought directly in the supreme court of appeals
of the State, the action being styled Lavender v. Hatfield; the petitioner, Lav-
ender, having been arrested in the martial zone and at the time of the action
being detained by Sheriff Hatfield, of McDowell County. As the result of these
proceedings, the supreme court of appeals, a majority of the judges thereof
concurring in the opinion, released the petitioner, and in substance held that
the proclamation of martial law could only be enforced by the occupancy of
the zone covered by military force, and held that the force so occupying the
zone was not a military force. The decision of the court was oral, and no
written opinion has been delivered up to this time. The opinion did not hold
invalid the proclamation of martial law itself, but apparently merely questioned
the method of its enforcement.
Thereafter, and again at the instance of the law officers and civil authorities
of Mingo County, Gov. Morgan, under the provisions of the statute law of West
Virginia, directed the enrollment of the unorganized militia of Mingo County,
to the end and for the purpose of making available the necessary military force
with which to occupy the county covered by his proclamation of martial law
and comply with the apparent requirements of the decision of the supreme
court.
The second proclamation of the governor is as follows:
STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA—A PROCLAMATION BY THE GOVERNOR.
Whereas by my proclamation dated the 19th of May, in the year of our Lord
one thousand nine hundred and twenty-one, I, Ephraim F. Morgan, governor
of the State of West Virginda, and as such governor ex officio commander
in chief of the military forces of the State, did declare and proclaim a state
of war, insurrection, and riot to exist in the county of Mingo and State of
West Virginia; and
Whereas by my said proclamation I did further declare that said county is and
shall remain under martial law until necessity therefor ceases to exist and
my further order; and
Whereas said state of war, insurrection, and riot has continued to exist and
still exists in said county, and it is necessary that said county should remain
under martial law until necessity therefor ceases to exist; and
Whereas the judge of the circuit court and the sheriff and prosecuting attorney
of said Mingo County have again declared to me their inability to put down
or control such insurrection and riot, and have further represented to me that
there is grave and imminent danger and greater and more serious touble in
said county; and
Whereas the State is without adequate organized militia to execute and enforce
the laws of West Virginia and said proclamation in said county, and the act
of the Legislature of West Virginia passed April 28, 1921 (chap. 117 of the
Acts of the Legislature of West Virginia, Regular Session, 1921), is not yet
in force and effect; and
Whereas, in view of the premises, it is necessary to enroll the persons liable
to military duty in said county of Mingo, and when such enrollment is com-
pleted to call out a portion of the enrolled militia of the said county of
Mingo for active duty to execute and enforce the laws of West Virginia, said
proclamation, and this proclamation: Therefore
I, Ephraim F. Morgan, governor of the State of West Virginia, and as such
governor ex officio commander in chief of the military forces of the State, in
view of the foregoing and in order to execute and enforce the laws of West
Virginia, to protect the public peace, lives, and property of the citizens, by
virtue of the constitution and the laws of the State of West Virginia, do hereby
declare and proclaim a state of war, insurrection, and riot has continued to
exist and still exists in the said county of Mingo.
And I do hereby further declare and proclaim that said county is and shall
continue to remain under martial law until necessity therefor ceases to exist
and my further order; and do hereby declare and proclaim that it is necessary

TESTIMONY OF ERNEST L. BAILEY.
(The witness, having been duly sworn by the chairman, testified as follows:)
Mr. VINSON. State your full name.
Mr. BAILEY. Ernest L. Bailey.
Mr. VINSON. What is your age?
Mr. BAILEY. Thirty-three years.
Mr. VINSON. What is your occupation?
Mr. BAILEY. I am superintendent for the Portsmouth Solvay Coke Co. at
their Freeburn mine.
Mr. VINSON. What business are you engaged in?
Mr. BAILEY. The mining of coal.
Mr. VINSON. Where is the Freeburn mine; what is its location?
Mr. BAILEY. It is located in Pike County, Ky., opposite Delorme, W. Va.
Mr. VINSON. Have you a little rough sketch showing the relative location
of the Freeburn mine to the river and the hills adjacent thereto?
Mr. BAILEY. I have.

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Mr. VINSON. I would like for you to come over here and explain this little
map to the committee, so that they will have an idea of the location. Just
point out the Freeburn mine on that big map first.
(The witness proceeded to point out the location of the said mine to the
committee.)
Mr. VINSON. Your plants are located on the Kentucky side of the Tug River?
Mr. BAILEY. They are.
Mr. VINSON. How far is it from your main v llage over to the West Virginia
side of the river in feet?
Mr. BAILEY. About 200 feet.
Senator STERLING. When you speak of the main village, what do you mean?
Mr. VINSON. They have two villages, one on Peter Creek about a mile away
from the main village.
Senator STERLING. Are those villages occupied by miners?
Mr. VINSON. Yes. I will bring that out.
These villages are occupied by the men in your employment, that work at the
mines?
Mr. BAILEY. They are.
Mr. VINSON. Built for that purpose?
Mr: BAILEY. Built for that purpose.
Mr. VINSON. The Norfolk & Western Railroad serves your mining operations?
Mr. BAILEY. The Norfolk & Western Railroad serves our mining operations.
Mr. VINSON. With a switch running across the river to load the cars on?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. How far in the air line would it be from the top of the West
Virginia hills over to where your mine opening is in the Kentucky hills? I
mean about the distance in feet?
Mr. BAILEY. Approximately one-half mile.
Mr. VINSON. The hills are very steep and precipitous?
Mr. BAILEY. The hills are very steep and precipitous.
Mr. VINSON. And covered by forest?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes. The hills on the West Virginia side are very densely
wooded; the hills on the Kentucky side have been mostly cleared.
Mr. VINSON. That is where your No. 1 tipple is?
Mr. BAILEY. That is where our No. 1 tipple is; yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. Your No. 2 tipple or No. 2 mine on Peter Creek is how far from
your main tipple or No. 1?
Mr. BAILEY. About three-quarters of a mile.
Mr. VINSON. On the north side of Peter Creek are the mountains there just
the same as across the Tug River on the West Virgin'a side?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes. There are mountains on either side of Peter Creek, with the
exception that the valley of the creek is narrower than the Tug River Valley.
There is practically no valley.
Mr. VINSON. Are the mountains along Peter Creek wooded the same as on
the West Virginia side?
Mr. BAILEY. They are wooded on both sides.
Mr. VINSON. How far is it from the river up to your mine opening in your
main tipple? I mean how many feet?
Mr. BAILEY. It is an altitude of about 500 feet.
Mr. VINSON. How do you get the cars down from that mine opening?
Mr. BAILEY. By an inclined plane built up the mountain side, on which the
cars are let down by cable and a drum.
Mr. VINSON. How are those cables controlled, at the bottom or top of the
hill?
Mr. BAILEY. They are controlled at the top, at what we term in mining lan-
guage our "head house."
Mr. VINSON. Then your coal is mined, taken out of the mine and put on cars,
and when the cars come to the head of that incline they are let down by the
steel cables?
Mr. BAILEY. They are let down by the steel cable to the tipple at the bottom
and dumped on to the railroad cars.
Mr. VINSON. And the empty car is taken back up to the mine again?
Mr. BAILEY. The empty car is taken back up to the mine again. It is a
gravity system, the load coming down pulling the empty up.
Mr. VINSON. How is that operation regulated? At what point is it regulated?


===== [扫描序号 287] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
279
Mr. BAILEY. It is regulated at the top of the hill, at the head house, by a
drum which has a brake arrangement whereby the drum runner controls the
speed and the movement of the car.
Mr. VINSON. Your men going to work in the morning go up in these empty
cars?
Mr. BAILEY. They do.
Mr. VINSON. They go up to the mine in that way?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. They are hauled up in that way?
Mr. BAILEY. They are hauled up in that way.
Mr. VINSON. How many miners-how many people had you employed about
your mine in May of last year.
Mr. BAILEY. Approximately 400. Our pay roll for the first half of July showed
416 men.
Mr. VINSON. July, 1920?
Mr. BAILEY. July, 1920.
Senator STERLING. Were these all on the Kentucky side?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes, sir; they were all on the Kentucky side, Senator.
Mr. VINSON. When the strike call was issued how many men left your em-
ployment?
Mr. BAILEY. Four left when the strike call was issued, although only two
of them stated their intention of affiliating with the union. Two others told
me they were afraid to work; but I learned afterwards that they did join the
union. I might add, however, that before the strike call was issued some six
or eight persons had left our employment due to union affiliation.
Mr. VINSON. They had formerly been members of the union?
Mr. BAILEY. Well, either because they felt there would be industrial trouble
or because they wanted to join the union they left our employment.
Mr. VINSON. That was the sum total of all the men that quit your employment
and went into the union during the trouble?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. Was your mine shot up at any time?
Mr. BAILEY. It was.
Mr. VINSON. What date was the first time?
Mr. BAILEY. Well, there had been at night during the early part of July, on
several occasions, pistol shots fired opposite the camp.
Mr. VINSON. Do you mean on the West Virginia side?
Mr. BAILEY. On the West Virginia side. We never knew whether they were
fired into the camp or not; but on the morning of July 23, just as the men were
starting to work, going up the inclined plane which I have described-
Mr. VINSON (interrupting). That is, they were on these empty cars?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes, sir. That was the first car, with eight men on it. A rifle
flare from two points on the West Virginia side was directed at these men and
the head house. It was estimated that some 2,000 shots were fired into the head
house, and some shots were fired into the camp.
Senator STERLING. By the "camp" do you mean the village?
Mr. BAILEY. The village.
The CHAIRMAN. Did the shots come from across the river?
Mr BAILEY. The shots came from across the river on the West Virginia side.
The CHAIRMAN. In the woods?
Mr. BAILEY. In the woods.
A VOICE. About a half mile away?
Mr. BAILEY. About half a mile away.
Working in conjunction with the men firing on the West Virginia side our
tipple No. 2, which is about a mile in Kentucky on Peter Creek, was fired at
from the mountains on the Kentucky side, possibly 300 shots being fired.
The CHAIRMAN. Was anybody hurt?
Mr. BAILEY. Two men were wounded at our No. 1 mine, wounded from the
West Virginia side. One of them was Roland Coleman, who was a tipple em-
ployee, operating the drum. I might add that Coleman, although rather
severly wounded, still held to the brake that controlled the drum until he landed
the men on top of the incline.
Mr. VINSON. Please state what would have happened to the men going up
if the man controlling the drum had been completely disabled.
Mr. BAILEY. It is entirely probable that not only the 8 men riding on the
inclined plane would have been killed or injured, but that the loaded car
coming down when the control of the speed was lost would have torn up the
tipple and killed some 8 or 10 men at the bottom.

The CHAIRMAN. Were these men at the drum in open view from the West
Virginia side?
Mr. BAILEY. He was in open view from the West Virginia side.
The CHAIRMAN. Did any firing start on that side before the car started up
with the men?
Mr. BAILEY. No, sir. The firing started when the car was about halfway up
the inclined plane.
The CHAIRMAN. How long did it take the car to make that trip?
Mr. BAILEY. About three minutes.
The CHAIRMAN. Did the firing come from the West Virginia side and also
from that point you speak of on the Kentucky side?
Mr. BAILEY. Firing came from the West Virginia side first. After the firing,
had begun on the West Virginia side the firing commenced on the Kentucky
side.
The CHAIRMAN. Did that firing seem to be directed at the men at the drum
or the men coming up?
Mr. BAILEY. The men on the Kentucky side were not in the full view of our
tipple because of the woods and the fog which lent certain protection of the
tipple. From confessions and evidence which I heard at the trial of fellows
who were charged with that shooting it was said that the firing was directed
as best they could at the men going up the hill. However, none of these shots
were effective, as they were firing from long range.
The CHAIRMAN. As one car went up another car was coming down loaded with
coal?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes, sir. The loaded car coming down pulled the empty car
back to the mine.
Mr. VINSON. Regulated by the drum?
Mr. BAILEY. Regulated by the drum.
Mr. VINSON. You say two men were wounded?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. How long did the firing continue?
Mr. BAILEY. Possibly 15 minutes.
Mr. VINSON. Have you any idea how many shots were fired?
Mr. BAILEY. Well, personally I have very little idea how many shots were
fired, but it was estimated by fellows who were possibly less excited than I
was that there was 2,000 shots fired.
Mr. VINSON. Did any of your people return that fire after they had been
fired upon?
Mr. BAILEY. They did. Our people, of course, were completely surprised.
Very few of them were out at that time. But after the shooting had continued
for possibly 10 minutes several of the employees got what firearms they could-
rifles, pistols, and I understood there were shotguns in the bunch-and did
return the fire to the West Virginia side, with the effect that the shooting
soon stopped on the West Virginia side, although they need not have been
afraid because they didn't have anything they could have hurt them with at
that long range.
Senator STERLING Did that firing come in volleys as though there were firing
together?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes; it did. Shortly after it commenced it sounded almost
like machine-gun fire. Later it seemed that after the first volleys some of the
men evidently dropped out, and the firing became less severe, until at times it
seemed there were about two or three guns in action.
Mr. VINSON. Did you visit the place on the West Virginia side where this
firing came from later?
Mr. BAILEY. I did.
Mr. VINSON. State to the committee what you found there in the way of
a barricade or breastworks.
Mr. BAILEY. The firing had been done from the mountain top. The mountains
there come to a very narrow ridge and there are large bowlders there and loose
rocks. In two places on the ridge they had built up breastworks of these
loose rocks, which the ground showed they had laid down behind; it formed
an almost impenetrable barricade, even if we had gotten their range in our
return fire. Behind those barricades we found a great many shells from
high-powered rifles.
Mr. VINSON. You mean the empty shells?
Mr. BAILEY. Empty shells from high-powered rifles.

Mr. BAILEY. The confessions were to the effect that on the Wednesday night

was not progressing satisfactorily and that he wanted to speak to a large

Mr. VINSON. That is your mine?

100 from Lynn, others from Matewan, and others from Flacker-
Mr. VINSON. All in Mingo County?

men from the Kentucky side-
Mr. VINSON. What did he tell these men at the time about what would be

man truck started up the hill; and when they heard the firing on the West
Virginia side then they were to begin firing in the direction of our tipple No. 2.
Senator CARAWAY. How many men on the Kentucky side participated in the

Mr. BAILEY. Eleven.
Senator STERLING. Who was this man who made this speech, who gave this

Mr. BAILEY. Doc Wolfert by name.
Senator STERLING. Where does he belong?
Mr. BAILEY. He is a native of Kentucky. He is now in the United States

lough as his ship is undergoing repairs at Hampton Roads.
Senator STERLING. Why was he not prosecuted?
Mr. BAILEY. He was prosecuted, but he was not an actual participant in the

Mr. VINSON. State how long had the firing been going on from the West

Mr. VINSON. Well, approximately.
Mr. BAILEY. Approximately five minutes, I would say. Maybe not that long.
I understood from one of the boys who confessed that they did not fire imme-

the truck would start up the tipple at No. 2 mine.

Mr. BAILEY. There is a relationship there, I am unable to say just what.

Senator CARAWAY. What did you do after the shooting toward preparing
your people for defense?
Mr. BAILEY. After the shooting was over, had subsided, it is hardly possible
for me to describe the state of excitement that existed in the village.
Mr. VINSON. Among the women and children?
Mr. BAILEY. Among the women and the children and the men. The men, of
course, were excited and perturbed, but many of the women were hysterical;
their screams could be heard long after the shooting was over. The children
were crying, and it is well-nigh impossible to conceive the excitement that
occurred. of the state of terror and fright that was there. The men came to
me, I don't know how many, but it seemed to me everybody I saw, there was
a large crowd of them, and they said, "Well, what are we going to do?" And I
said, "What will we do, what are you fellows willing to do?" They said,
"We are willing to run." They meant operate the mines. "To prove we are
willing to operate we will operate it to day." And we did, we ran eight cars
of coal that day, which was not our normal tonnage, but they further said,
"We are not going to have anything to do with this bunch of outlaws, but we
can't stay here unless we have some protection. If you will buy us guns to
protect ourselves we will stay here and operate the mine," and I did. I imme-
diately dispatched-
Mr. VINSON. How many guns did you buy?
Mr. BAILEY. I bought, I think, 120 high-power rifles; I bought a Browning
machine gun-two bloodhounds.
Senator STERLING. Where did you get these guns?
Mr. BAILEY. They were gotten from different hardware stores, one was the
Sterling Hardware Co., in Bluefield.
Senator STERLING. It must have been high powered?
Mr. BAILEY. It is a very good hardware store, Senator, and I think some were
bought from another hardware store in Bluefield. I am unable to say just where
they did come from, but we did not get them all from the same store. I dis-
tributed those guns and shells-ammunition to the employees there on the
job. endeavoring to see that every man of that 416 employees had some kind of
a gun. Some of them had guns before and some of them bought revolvers, and
I distributed these 120 high-power rifles I bought.
I want to add right there that so far as I know not one single one of those
men did join the union, or, to my knowledge, have to this day joined the union,
and I might point out the fact that had those men been in favor of organiza-
tion I placed in their hands the means by which they could have absolutely
enforced their organization had they cared to do so. I realized that when I
did it, but had absolute confidence in the fact that they were going to remain
loyal to the company.
Mr. VINSON. What became of the women and children there at the camp, Mr.
Bailey?
Mr. BAILEY. Many of the men who could conveniently do so sent their families
away for a period of two or three months, keeping them at their homes or
their wive's home, but many of them did not have places where they could
conveniently send them and their wives and families stayed there.
Mr. VINSON. And what became of your men? How many of them are with
you now?

Mr. BAILEY. Our operations at our mines were suspended January 15, because
of no market.
Mr. VINSON. Please explain to the committee whether or not the coal you
mine is a by-product coal, such as is used in the manufacture of coke for steel
mills and for other purposes of that kind?
Mr. BAILEY. We mine two seams, and one is a small production and is a
fuel coal, a coal that is used normally for railroad fuel. Our principal pro-
duction is a by-product coal and goes into the manufacture of coke, and the by-
products have been located at Portsmouth, Ohio, and when the steel business
went to pieces along in the early part of January there was no further de
mand for coke, and we had no other alternative but to close down the mine.
and we closed it down and it is still closed down.
Senator STERLING. What became of them?
Mr. BAILEY. About 65 of the men are still with us, some of them working
at neighboring mines which are being operated and some work of other mines
in the field, and they kept their families there and come there when they can.
We do not charge the families anything for coal or light or rent or water.
Mr. VINSON. Your mine is shut down solely for a lack of a market for by-
products coal is it not?
Mr. BAILEY. Our mine is shut down solely for a market for by-products
coal. During the entire period of the strike we ran virtually our normal
tonnage.
Mr. VINSON. Well, now, when were you next shot up or fired on?
Mr. BAILEY. We were fired on July 23. That was the shooting I have de-
scribed.
Mr. VINSON. And when was the next time?
Mr. BAILEY. Now, the Kentucky State governor, Gov. Morrow, of Kentucky,
sent troops into Freeburn. Those troops arrived the latter part of July; I do
not just recall the date. Along about the 3d of August, on Thursday, I think
it was, the militiamen accompanied the deputy sheriff of Pike County to arrest
fellows for whom we had warrants out for this shooting on the Kentucky side
and against whom we had evidence. While they were making these arrests,
it is my information they were fired on from the West Virginia side and one
of the deputy sheriff's horses was shot through the neck and one of the na-
tional guardsmen was shot through his hat-through the crown of his hat
just above his head. They made the arrests, however, and brought the men
first into Freeburn and took them later to Pikeville, the county seat. On the
Saturday following this, about 7.30 or 8 o'clock in the evening, the headquar-
ters of the National Guard were fired on from the West Virginia mountains
from virtually the same position as I have described before.
Mr. VINSON. And where were the headquarters of the West Virginia guards-
men-of the National Guard. I should say?
Mr. BAILEY. The headquarters of the National Guard were in my residence.
Mr. VINSON. Were you present at that time?
Mr. BAILEY. I was. The first shot was evidently directed at myself and
the captain commanding the company.
Mr. VINSON. How close did it come to you?
Mr. BAILEY. Well, it sounded pretty close. It cut a limb from the branch
of a tree hanging down about 4 feet over our heads, so it was not dangerously
close.
Mr. VINSON. And how many shots were fired, if you can recall?
Mr. BAILEY. I don't know.
Mr. VINSON. What did the National Guard do?
Mr. BAILEY. They had fired possibly a half dozen shots when it was replied
to by the National Guard. However, I had no means of knowing how many
shots were fired from the West Virginia side. When the militiamen ceased
firing there were no other shots from the West Virginia side. It did not last
more than three or four minutes.
Mr. VINSON. Well, now, were you shot up at any other time?
Mr. BAILEY. On the following Sunday we had a baseball game there and the
diamond was down on Peter Creek, which is off of Tug River. Nearly the whole
village came out to the baseball game. We go to church down there on Sunday
morning and to a baseball game in the afternoon. Some sentinel who had been
left at headquarters came to the ball game and informed the captain that he had
noticed, through some glasses, some high-power glasses, that a bunch of men
were collecting on the ridge opposite on the West Virginia side, near the place
where the previous shootings had occurred. He said there seemed to be 40 or 50

Mr. VINSON. NOW, I wish you would explain or rather state to the committee
about the employment of peace officers at these mines, and more particularly
at your own mine, which were really police officers and appointed by the sheriff
of the county among your own people. Please explain that system and how
it has come about and the necessity for it.
Mr. BAILEY. It was entirely impossible, due to the large district for which he
is elected, and due to the topography of the country as well, for the regularly
elected peace officer to maintain order over his entire district. I might add
there that we are distant some 35 miles across country from the county seat,
where the sheriff stays, with hardly no roads and it takes about 14 hours on
horseback, and to go there on the train it takes about the same time. In other
words, to go to the county seat and return requires three days' time.
The CHAIRMAN. There is no railroad?
Mr. BAILEY. There is a railroad there, but it takes a day to go on the train,
and the schedule is so arranged that if you spend any time in the county seat
you lose your connection and you have to go back the following day.
The CHAIRMAN. For what distance?
Mr. BAILEY. Only 200 miles.

The CHAIRMAN. What is it across country?
Mr. BAILEY. About 35 miles, but it is just one series of mountains. So, being

Mr. VINSON. The statement was made here yesterday, or filed by Mr. Olmsted,

some a few days in the week. State the facts about that.
Mr. BAILEY. We work on an 8-hour basis. All day wageworkers, of course,
work eight hours. Pieceworkers are not restricted as to their time, except
as to the length of time. They, of course, can not work after the company
day wage workers go off; but they can go out at any time they want, and
they frequently go out at 12 and 1 and 2 o'clock.
Mr. VINSON. That is, they do not have to get there at any particular time?

Mr. VINSON. Those who work most continuously, say, for 26 days in a month,

Mr. BAILEY. Naturally so.
Mr. VINSON. The others could do so if they cared to work as long as the
ones who get these large sums?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes. Their earning capacity is limited, of course, by their
physical capacity as well as their inclination to work.

dependent stores.
Mr. VINSON. How far away from your mine are those five stores?
