TESTIMONY OF ERNEST L. BAILEY-Resumed.
The CHAIRMAN. You may go ahead, gentlemen, if you are ready.
Mr. HOUSTON. Mr. Bailey, I believe you have spoken of three shootings that oc-
curred at your place; is that correct?
Mr. BAILEY. That is correct.
Mr. HOUSTON. Will you give the dates those shootings occurred on?
Mr. BAILEY. The first one occurred on July 23, 1920. I am unable to give the
exact dates of the other two shootings, Mr. Houston, but it was about two weeks
afterward, one Saturday evening and one Sunday afternoon.
Mr. HOUSTON. What was the date of the third one, do you remember the
month?
Mr. BAILEY. August, between the 5th and 10th.
Mr. HOUSTON. They were all pretty close together?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes.
Mr. HOUSTON. Mr. Bailey, do you know anything about a shooting that oc-
curred on or about the 12th day of May, 1921?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes; I know there was considerable shooting through our section
at that time.
Mr. HOUSTON. Were you at your works at that time?
Mr. BAILEY. No; I was in Williamson on the day that the shooting started. I
went back to my work, the plant of which I have charge, on train No. 16 that
afternoon. We could hear the rifle firing as we went through that afternoon.
Mr. HOUSTON. Where is Blackberry City relative to your works?
Mr. BAILEY. About 6 miles below our works.
Mr. HOUSTON. And you did not see any of that shooting there at all?
Mr. BAILEY. NO; but there was terrific firing as No. 16 passed through that
afternoon-machine-gun and rifle fire.
Mr. HOUSTON. I believe you stated your operations are about 35 miles from
Pikesville, Ky., the county seat of Pike County; is that correct?
Mr. BAILEY. That is approximately correct.
Mr. HOUSTON. And you have very poor roads from your works over to Pike
County?
Mr. BAILEY. That is correct.
Mr. HOUSTON. Your works are located on a branch of Pond Creek?
Mr. BAILEY. No; at the mouth of Peters Creek.
Mr. HOUSTON. But that is within the Pond Creek coal field?
Mr. BAILEY. No, sir; not within the Pond Creek coal field.
Mr. HOUSTON. Is Pond Creek separate and apart from what is known as
Williamson coal field?
Mr. BAILEY. No; it is a part of Williamson field. The Pond Creek coal field
embraces the mines on Pond Creek. Our mines are about 20 miles east of the
mouth of Pond Creek. Pond Creek empties into Tug River at Williamson.
Mr. HOUSTON. Who owns the surface of the lands and the houses at your
works?
Mr. BAILEY. The surface is owned in fee by the coal company that the village
is built on.
Mr. HOUSTON. Any free property owned by individuals around there?
Mr. BAILEY. We have only about 70 acres in fee. There is one 400-acre farm
adjoining the village on one side and other farms adjoining the village on the
other side.
Mr. HOUSTON. What percentage of your employees live in company houses?
Mr. BAILEY. About 70 per cent.
Mr. HOUSTON. Are there any independent stores in the immediate neighbor-
hood?


===== [扫描序号 300] =====
292
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Mr. BAILEY. There are five.
Mr. HOUSTON. What is the population of that village-about?
Mr. BAILEY. About 1,500.
Mr. HOUSTON. Is there any other industry around there giving employment
to the men aside from coal mining?
Mr. BAILEY. No; no other industry besides coal mining. There are a few
small sawmills, but they employ only a very few people.
Mr. HOUSTON. You do not have anything to do with determining the labor
policy of the company you work for, do you?
Mr. BAILEY. Just how do you mean by that?
Mr. HOUSTON. Well, the question whether or not you shall employ union or
nonunion men?
Mr. BAILEY. Why, it is left to my own discretion largely as to whom I
employ, Mr. Houston. As to that particular question, though, I will say I do
not have anything to do with it.
Mr. HOUSTON. And you receive specifle instructions from your company not
to employ anybody belonging to a labor union, that is true, is it not, or at
least that is understood?
Mr. BAILEY. No; that is not true the way you state it there. I have specific
instructions not to employ a member of the United Mine Workers of America
unless he renounces his affiliation with the union. We do not object to some
of the other labor unions quite so strenuously.
Mr. HOUSTON. Whenever a prospective employee applies for employment
you interrogate him as to that matter?
Mr. BAILEY. No; it has never been my practice to interrogate a prospective
employee as to whether he belonged to a union or did not belong to a union.
Mr. HOUSTON. Do you ever make any inquiry at all of persons?
Mr. BAILEY. No; because during the strike now there if anyone asked for
work I naturally assumed he did not belong to the union, or at least he was
not a very loyal union man, so, if I had a place for him, I gave him work.
Mr. HOUSTON. Did you ever work in a union field?
Mr. BAILEY. I never did.
Mr. HOUSTON. You never had any experience in a union field?
Mr. BAILEY. No personal experience; no.
Mr. HOUSTON. How many deputy sheriffs are employed around the works?
Mr. BAILEY. Do you mean employed as deputy sheriffs, or how many em
ployees who are commissioned as deputy sheriffs?
Mr. HOUSTON. How many deputy sheriffs of Pike County were paid by
your company that you know of or by the operators' association?
Mr. BAILEY. I don't know of any that were paid by the operators' association.
During the summer we commissioned a number of employees as deputy
sheriffs-I don't know the exact number, possibly 20-most of whom performed
their regular line of work at the mine. Since January 15, when we closed
down mining operations, we have only had four deputy sheriffs, and they were
used as night watchmen to prevent property destruction.
Mr. HOUSTON. Were these deputies, that worked in the mine, paid for their
services as deputies and also for their services in the mine?
Mr. BAILEY. No; they received no compensation for their services as depu
ties. They simply got what they earned in the mines at their regular jobs.
Mr. HOUSTON. Did you give these deputies any instructions as to what
their duties were or what was exepected of them as guards?
Mr. BAILEY. Just what do you mean by guards, Mr. Houston?
Mr. HOUSTON. Whether they should attempt to ferret out anyone that may be
a member of the labor union.
Mr. BAILEY. I do give them instructions.
Mr. HOUSTON. What instructions do you give them?
Mr. BAILEY. I give them instructions to absolutely let any employee on the job
absolutely alone, regardless of what comes to their attention. As far as he is
concerned, they have nothing to do with this. I am over the employees myself.
Their only duty is to prevent disorder from outside sources or protect the camp
in case of disorder occurring from outside sources.
Mr. HOUSTON. Mr. Bailey, what machinery do you have, if any, for handling
the grievances of the employees?
Mr. BAILEY. My office door is always open to every employee. When he has
a grievance, real or fancied, he comes to see me. We sit down together and talk
it over, and I don't recall a single instance where I ever failed to adjust them
satisfactorily to the employee.


===== [扫描序号 301] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
293
Mr. HOUSTON. You have no committee of the men of any kind?
Mr. BAILEY. Every man is his own committee, Mr. Houston. I maintain the
closest personal relations with our employees. That is a practice which I have
always followed.
Mr. HOUSTON. But in the final analysis every question and every grievance is
ultimately determined by you, is it not?
Mr. BAILEY. No; it is not ultimately determined by me; it is determined at
a conference between the employee and myself.
Mr. HOUSTON. But if there is a difference between you and the employee as to
what would be a just settlement of a specific grievance
Mr. BAILEY (interrupting). It is usually settled in the employee's favor. We
more or less work on the theory that the employee is always right. That is, if he
is going away, if he is leaving our employ because of a real or fancied griev
ance, if he imagines there is something wrong, we try to remove that grievance,
regardless of whether he goes away or not, so that he will go away feeling that
he has gotten a fair deal; and when he looks for work again, which they usually
do after awhile, he will come back to us.
Mr. HOUSTON. And you have always maintained harmonious relations there?
Mr. BAILEY. We have always maintained harmonious relations.
Mr. HOUSTON. You have no trouble with your men at all?
Mr. BAILEY. We have no trouble with the men at all, except in a few instances
which I mentioned this morning.
Mr. HOUSTON. What is the object of keeping four deputy sheriffs on the
premises if you have no trouble?
Mr. BAILEY. Our object in keeping four deputy sheriffs on the premises is as
night watchmen. They are stationed at the tipples. We have two tipples there,
one on the bottom and one on top, another one at the bottom and one at the
top. Our reason for keeping those men there is to prevent men who would have
a real interest in dynamiting that property and putting our operation out of
business from having an opportunity.
Mr. HOUSTON. You had those deputy sheriffs there for a considerable period
of time prior to the trouble?
Mr. BAILEY. Before the strike commenced there we only had one deputy
sheriff, who was a special deputy acting as police officer.
Mr. HOUSTON. You are pretty well acquainted with the conditions that have
obtained on Pond Creek?
Mr. BAILEY. I am acquainted with conditions that obtained on Pond Creek up
until April, 1920.
Mr. HOUSTON. What time in 1920?
Mr. BAILEY. I left in April, 1920. I have forgotten the exact date. It was
the latter part of the month.
Mr. HOUSTON. So you know nothing about the conditions obtaining there since
that time?
Mr. BAILEY. Yes; I have been back there since that time, and I have kept in
reasonably close touch with some of my old employees there as well as a num-
ber of personal friends over there. I think I am fairly well acquainted with con-
ditions on Pond Creek right now.
Mr. HOUSTON. Mr. Bailey, as a matter of fact, is it not true that it is unsafe
for a man to be on Pond Creek and let it be known that he is a member of
the United Mine Workers?
Mr. BAILEY. As a matter of fact, Mr. Houston, I do not think it is true.
The last time I was on Pond Creek I met a man, a Dr. Smith, who I believe
is a very prominent member of your organization, and he did not seem to be
at all perturbed about being there or in any serious fear of his life.
Mr. HOUSTON. You have not heard, Mr. Bailey, of the large number of
assaults made upon members of the United Mine Workers of those suspected
of having union affiliations on Pond Creek?
Mr. BAILEY. No, sir; I have not. Mr. Houston; I do not know that I ever
heard of a single assault being made on anyone suspected of union affiliations
on Pond Creek. I did hear that some tents were burned on Pond Creek on
one occasion, but I have no information as to who burned them.
Mr. HOUSTON. Mr. Bailey, do you know anything about the Williamson Coal
Operators' Association or any of the operators affiliated with it buying a news-
paper in the city of Williamson for publicity purposes?
Mr BAILEY. No, Mr. Houston; not directly. I know that they advertised
to a large extent in the Williamson newspapers, but I do not know anything
of their buying one.

STATE OF KENTUCKY, County of Pike:
The affiant William Howard McCoy, being duly sworn, deposes and says
that he is the son of Columbus McCoy, deceased, and Jennie McCoy, his wife,
since married to Elliott Duty; that he is married and lives on Peter Fork
of Blackberry Creek, Pike County, Ky.
He further deposes and says that on Wednesday night, July 21. 1920, a meet-
ing of the United Mine Workers of America at Alma Thacker Camp was ad-
dressed by Dock Wolford, who at the close of the meeting said he wanted to
see a larger part of the membership after the meeting was over. Dock se-
lected a number of men, among whom were Garfield Yound, John Sanson,
George Sutherland, George Hall, Bill Greer, Elias Hagar, Jordon Hagar,
Willie Fields, Burlan Fields, Nelse Fields, Rose Mathews, and others. Dock
Wolford told this audience that if the union allowed Freeburn to continue run-
ning, other operations would soon start and the strike would be lost. He im-
pressed strongly upon his audience the necessity of shutting down the Free-
burn plant. He stated to them that he had a crowd at Grapevine ready to
shoot up the Freeburn plant from the West Virginia side Friday morning,
July 23, 1920, and he desired to organize a squad to shoot up tipple No. 2 of
the Freeburn plant from the Peter Creek side. There were a number of volun-
teers who were instructed to meet him at Pound Mill Gap the following night,
and the following men gathered there before 10 o'clock p. m. Thursday night:
George Sullivan, Nelse Fields, Denby Sloan, Arson Hatfield, Crawford Mosely.
James Ogle, Rose Mathews, Roy Walden, John Sanson. Dock Wolford ap-
peared about 11 o'clock with another man unknown to affiant and instructed
affiant and the foregoing parties to go back on the mountain between Black-
berry Creek and Peter Creek where they could get a plain view of Freeburn
No. 2 tipple at Freeburn. He stated that the Grapevine squad on the West
Virginia side would fire when the man truck started up the No. 1 incline, and
that the first shot fired would be the signal for them to start firing. Dock
Wolford and the person who had come with him then returned toward Grape-
vine and the affiant and parties before mentioned started toward the ridge
opposite tipple No. 2, at which time affiant and John Sanson decided to take no
part in the shooting and started to return home, whereupon James Ogle stated
that if any man started back he would shoot his damned brains out. They
therefore went on with the party, being afraid not to do so.
Having arrived at the site selected, they waited for the signal shot from the
Grapevine squad and then opened fire. Shooting continued for perhaps 20
minutes, and approximately 100 shots were fired. The men then returned down
the ridge between Blackberry Creek and Peter Fork. James Ogle was armed
with an Army rifle, five cartridges to the clip. Nelse had a 30-30 rifle, and
Denby Sloan also had a high-power rifle. John Sanson had a 22-caliber Win-
chester. Rose Mathews had a 38 Special pistol and Will Hall a 32-20 pistol.
Further the deponent sayeth not.
(Signed)
HOWARD McCoy.
Subscribed and sworn to before me, a notary public in the county and State
aforesaid, by Wiliam Howard McCoy, this the 4th day of August, 1920.
My commission expires July 5, 1921.

Mr. Avis. Before we start with the examination of another witness, I would
like to say that I wired to the supreme court for copies of opinions in martial-
law cases, and I am in receipt of a letter from the clerk of the court saying
that an opinion had not been prepared, but the announcement of the court from
the bench was sent me.
The CHAIRMAN. What opinion are you speaking of?
Mr. AVIS. The official opinion, which is to be published, has not yet been pre-
pared, and will not be handed down until November, but this is what the court
said from the bench; and the court made some findings of fact. These are the
martial-law cases referred to. Among the questions of fact determined by the
court the court announced from the bench as follows:
"An examination of the record in these cases discloses that for some time
bands of armed men have terrorized not only the citizens of Mingo County, but
the local civil officers as well. They have barricaded themselves in the moun-
tains and by shooting into groups of workmen have not only driven them from
their work but have in some instances killed and severely wounded them and
the local civil officers have been unable, on account of the strength of the armed
groups, to ever effect the arrest of any of the guilty parties, much less punish
them for their transgressions. Employees and passengers on railroad trains
passing through the county have been compelled to lie down upon the floor of
the cars to escape injury from the missiles discharged from rifles and machine
guns in the hands of these armed groups. On one occasion, quite recently, a
detachment of State police who were sent to quell disorder were surrounded
and actually detained as prisoners until released by some of their associates.
The record is full of other outrages and acts of violence which have resulted in
the killing and wounding of a number of persons and the wanton destruction
of property of large value.
"The judge of the circuit court, the sheriff of the county, and the prosecut-
ing attorney, the three officers who are especially charged with executing and
administering the law, all join in an address to the governor advising that they
are powerless to suppress the disturbances, to prevent like outrages in the
future, or to punish the guilty parties. Whether the parties perpetrating these
acts are union miners we do not know and do not care, but we do say that a
condition existed that authorized the executive to see that the law was re-
spected. The means to be used to this end was for his determination. We find
a case demanding the exercise of his discretion, and this is the limit of our
power. The contention that because the circuit court is sitting in the county
and trying cases, there can be no suppression of civil authority, is satisfac-
torily disposed of by the opinions in the Nance and Mays case and the Jones
case, and it is unnecessary to do more than cite those authorities. It is also
insisted that the petitioners are being detained without any formal charges
being made against them, that no complaints have been filed, no warrants
issued and no trials had. It must be borne in mind that when the civil au-
thority has been overthrown and the military arm of the Government called
upon to restore such authority to their proper functions, the will of the mili-
tary commander becomes supreme for the time being. He must determine what
is necessary to reduce the insurrection and restore orderly administration. He
may within the military zone arrest and detain persons who are guilty of con-
duct, which in his opinion is an obstacle to the restoration of peace, whether
their conduct amounts to a violation of any civil law or not.
"The detention is not a punishment for any offense committed; it is for
the purpose of removing an obstacle to the performance of the duty charged
upon him. If such parties are guilty of offenses against the civil law they
may be prosecuted and punished therefor by the courts when the civil authori-
ties are restored to their orderly functions. The fact of their imprisonment
by the military authority in no way discharges them from liability to punish-
74020-21-VOL 1--20


===== [扫描序号 310] =====
302
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
ment by the civil authorities. The law is not dead. The agencies created
for its execution and administration are simply overthrown, but through it
all the law of the land lives and breathes, and those violating it must be
called to account by its ministers when they are restored to power by the
military authority. That the military commander considers the conduct of
a part to be an obstacle to the restoration of a condition of peace is sufficient -
justification for his arrest and detention until the lawful authorities are
restored to power, when he will be discharged, or, if his conduct amounts to
a violation of law, turned over to such restored authorities for trial.
"Nor is the fact that no military commissions have been created for the
trial of offenders material. Such commissions are simply agencies of the
military power created for the purpose of advising the military commander
as to conditions in particular instances in which he may not have satisfactory
information. If, in his judgment, he is sufficiently advised to act without
the assistance of such commissions, they need not be created. The necessity
or expediency of their creation is for the military authority to the same
extent that that authority must determine the number and disposition of its
forces.
"Another contention is that section 54, of chapter 18 of the code, prescribes
the limit of the military power and that the executive can only use the militia
as therein indicated. That section prescribes one of the uses that may be
made of the militią. It does not treat at all of its use in quelling an insur-
rection or rebellion by a proclamation of martial law, such as we have here,
but only of its use as an aid to the local civil authorities in the execution of
their duties. Undoubtedly the militia may be used in the manner prescribed
by that section, but it does not limit the executive to that use.
66
'Much as we deplore the condition that makes it necessary for the execu
tive, in his opinion, to resort to the military arm for the restoration of peaceful
and orderly conditions in Mingo County, we find no justification in the record
in these cases for interfering with his efforts in that direction, and the peti-
tioners will be remanded to the custody of the military authorities."
That is the finding of fact in those cases, and I have also a letter from the
clerk of the court, accompanying it, which I do not think it is necessary to
place in the record.

Chapter 24 of the Laws of West Virginia, 1919, as passed by the Legislature
of the State of West Virginia, reads as follows:
"Chapter 24.-An act to foster the ideals, institutions, and government of West Virginia
and of the United States, and to prohibit the teaching of doctrines and display of flags
antagonistic to the form or spirit of their constitutions and laws.
"Be it enacted by the Legislature of West Virginia:
“SECTION 1. It shall be unlawful for any person to speak, print, publish, or
communicate, by language, sign, picture, or otherwise, any teachings, doctrines,
or counsels in sympathy or favor of ideals, institutions, or forms of government
hostile, inimical, or antagonistic to those now or hereafter existing under
the constitution and laws of this State or the United States or in sympathy or
favor of the propriety, duty, or necessity of crime, violence, or other unlawful
methods of terrorism as a means of accomplishing economic or political reform,

or in sympathy or favor of the overthrow of organized society, the unlawful de-

"SEC. 2. It shall be unlawful for any person to have in his possession or to

sign of any nature whatever indicating sympathy or support of ideals, insti-
tutions, or forms of government hostile, inimical, or antagonistic to the form or

"SEC. 3. Any person violating any of the provisions of this act shall, for the

Mr. BIAS. The next witness, Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of the committee,

Before he does that, however, I think it not improper for me to say that this
tent colony, which is located at the mouth of Lick Creek, a small stream 3
miles south of the business center of Williamson and 1 mile south of the
southern limits of the city of Williamson, is on a stream 4 miles long which
empties into the Tug River. This tent colony, comprising approximately 100
tents, is at the mouth of this creek, some of the tents being on one side of the
public road and some on the other. Sycamore Creek, which will be referred to
by the witness, is a creek which is 1 mile west or north of Lick Creek and
constitutes the southern extremity of the city of Williamson. It is another
stream of approximately the same size as Lick Creek, emptying into Tug
River.
This tent colony has been there since the early days of the strike, and there
have been repeated outrages perpetrated by the inhabitants of that tent colony.
I myself, as assistant to the prosecuting attorney of the county, prosecuted in
the circuit court two colored men who had beaten up a white man who was a
carpenter working at a mine about a mile farther from Williamson in a most
brutal way, calling him all sorts of vile epithets-

guards have flashed them so as to destroy the only abode that these poor
people have; their scanty furniture has been smashed and their little house-

unloaded Capt. Brockus had a number of men, perhaps 25 or 30, loaded in
cars and sent back around the road to the mouth of Lick Creek in order to
prevent anyone escaping down that way.

WEDNESDAY, JULY 20, 1921.
UNITED STATES SENATE,
COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION AND LABOR,
Washington, D. C.
The Committee on Education and Labor of the United States Senate met,
pursuant to adjournment, at 10 o'clock a. m. at the committee room of the
Committee on Education and Labor, Capitol Building, Senator Kenyon presiding.
Present: Senators Kenyon (chairman), Warren, Sterling, and McKellar.
Also present: Harry Olmsted, representing Operators' Association, Williamson
fields; Randolph Bias, Williamson, W. Va., appearing for certain mine owners of
the Williamson coal fields; Harry Scherr, Williamson, W. Va., appearing for cer-
tain mine owners; James Damron, Williamson, W. Va., appearing for certain coal
operators in the Williamson coal fields; Z. T. Vinson, Huntington, W. Va.,
appearing for the Operators' Association in the Williamson coal fields; Neil
Burkinshaw, 636 Munsey Building, Washington, D. C., appearing for United
Mine Workers of America; Samuel B. Montgomery, Kingwood, appearing for
United Mine Workers' Association; B. L. Greever, appearing for Williamson
Coal Operators' Association; Capt. S. B. Avis, appearing for Williamson Coal
Operators' Association.
Mr. SCHERR. I will ask you to swear Capt. Brockus.
STATEMENT OF CAPT. J. R. BROCKUS.
The witness, having been first duly sworn by the chairman, testified as
follows:
Mr. SCHERR. Captain, give the reporter your name, age, and place of residence.
Capt. BROCKUS. J. R. Brockus; age, 45; present residence, Williamson, W. Va.
Mr. SCHERR. What position do you hold at this time, Captain?
Capt. BROCKUS. I am a captain in the West Virginia State police.
Mr. SCHERR. How long have you held that position?
Capt. BROCKUS. Since September 1, 1920.
Mr. SCHERR. What previous military experience, if any, did you have?
Capt. BROCKUS. I enlisted in the United States Army when I was between
17 and 18 years of age, and I served almost continuously, up until May 13,
1920, when I was retired from the Regular Army. During that time I held
the grades from private to major. I was discharged at the expiration of the
war, or I was mustered out at Camp Taylor, Ky., on the 12th day of July, 1919,
as a major. I reenlisted as an enlisted man, finished up my 30 years' service,
and retired at Fort George Wright, Wash., on May 13, 1920. I hold a commis-
sion as lieutenant colonel in the Infantry section, Army Reserve Corps.
Mr. SCHERR. Did you see service overseas during the late war?
Capt. BROCKUS. I did. I served seven years in the Philippine Islands.
took part in the China relief expedition in 1900, and I served one year in
France during the late war, and commanded a battalion during that time.
Mr. SCHERR. Are you a native of West Virginia, Captain?
Capt. BROCKUS. No, sir; I was born in Tennessee.
I
Mr. SCHERR. Under what circumstances, Captain, did you come to West
Virginia and enter the service of the department of public safety of that
State?

Capt. BROCKUS. Well, Capt. Norton, who had been serving with me overseas,
had gotten into the department. He and I were pretty good friends, and,
through correspondence, I came to West Virginia after I was retired, and I
applied in Charlestown for a position, and was sworn in as a lieutenant on the
10th day of August, 1920.
Mr. SCHERR. Who is Capt. Norton, and where is he at this time?
Capt. BROCKUs. He is a captain in the State police. His residence is Wheeling,
W. Va. He is now at Red Star, Fayette County, organizing one of the new
companies.
Mr. SCHERR. For what period of time have you been in the Williamson
field?
Capt. BROCKUS. I have been in it continuously since about August 20, except
the time when the Federal troops occupied the county.
Mr. SCHERR. You went there on August 20, 1920, and have been there ever
since in the service, with the exception of the period that the Federal troops
occupied that territory, is that true?
Capt. BROCKUS. Yes, sir.
Mr. SCHERR. How many State police have been in the service in the William-
son field during the period you have mentioned?
Capt. BROCKUS. Well, it ranged at different figures. When I came down there
last August, they only had about 30 men in the field. It has been at different
strengths. When we came in in January, when the troops were moving out, we
came in with a force of about 45. Since that time it was increased until we
had approximately 100 but now, I believe, there are about 80 or 85.
Mr. SCHERR. You are speaking now of the regular State police?
Capt. BROCKUS. Of the regular State police.
Mr. SCHERR. Tell the committee how these regular State police are selected
or enlisted, and something of their character and the type of men they are?
Capt. BROCKUS. We confine our enlistments entirely to ex-service men, and
the majority are overseas men, men discharged from the Army, with excellent
character. They have to come up to certain physical requirements. They
have to be a certain height, and a certain age, of course, able to ride a horse,
and physically fit for that kind of service.
Mr. SCHERR. What requirements or regulations do you have with reference
to their moral character?
Capt. BROCKUS. Well, we go mainly on their discharge certificate and the
recommendations furnished from their last employer. That covers the period
from the time they left the service up to the present time, or the time they
enlist.
Mr. SCHERR. Then, after they are enlisted in the service of the department of
public safety, do you keep tab on them as to their performances, morally and
otherwise?
Capt. BROCKUS. Yes, sir; very carefully. It has been necessary in my com-
pany to discharge approximately 35 men on account of misconduct. The slight-
est show of intoxication, or abuse of authority, or keeping company with women
of questionable character, results in their immediate discharge.
Mr. SCHERR. Reference has been made in this record to the fact that three
State policemen have been killed and at least one wounded during the indus-
trial trouble in the Williamson field. Please tell the committee with reference
to that.
Capt. BROCKUS. That is correct. We have had
out of my company-four men shot, three killed.
of my company. All shot in the back.

Mr. SCHERR. Something has been said in this record as to the killing of Ansie
Hatfield, at Matewan, who was a witness in the Sid Hatfield case.
know whether Ripley was a witness also in that case?
Capt. BROCKUS. He was. Ripley was on duty at the time at. Packer Station,
which is about 3 miles east of Matewan, and he had come down in a motor
car with some family who were afraid to come into Matewan without some pro-
tection. He arrived at Matewan only a few minutes after the shot was fired
that killed Hatfield, and the party that he came down with saw the excitement
in Matewan and were very anxious to get out, so they loaded in the car and
drove just outside the town, and Ripley had the car stopped and got out and
went back to make a little investigation of his own. On the railroad track
about 30 yards from the front of the hotel where this man was killed he found
a man named Burgaff, standing on the track with a high-power rifle in his hand
in the position of what we call "ready;" had it down in a position ready to
bring it up and fire. He placed the party under arrest and he was searched
and a .38 Smith & Wesson pistol taken out of his pocket. He was later taken to
Williamson, tried for carrying concealed weapons by a jury, and found not
guilty.
Mr. SCHERR. Who was this man Fred Burgaff?
Capt. BROCKUS. He is a man, a resident of Matewan, under indictment for
the murder of a Baldwin-Felts detective on the 19th day of May, 1920. This
happened, I believe, in July following the murders on May 19.
Mr. SCHERR. Do you know whether he is a member of the United Mine
Workers of America?
Capt. BROCKUS. Well, I would say that he is, although I don't know that defi-
nitely. He is a very active man around Matewan and has been for some time.
Mr. VINSON. Referring to Burgaff?
Capt. BROCKUS. Yes, sir.
Mr. SCHERR. You made an investigation of the killing of Pvt. Ripley, and you
also attended the trial of the State against Cole for his murder?
Capt. BROCKUS. Yes, sir.
Mr. SCHERR. Please relate the circumstances surrounding that murder of
Ripley.
Capt. BROCKUS. The killing actually took place in view of the section men
working on the Norfolk & Western Railway repairing a broken rail or putting
in a rail, and the train was due in a very short time and they were pressed for
time, but the witnesses stated-and practically all of them told the same
story-that the first thing they saw was Ripley coming down the track


===== [扫描序号 334] =====

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Mr. HOUSTON. I would like to make an objection at this time to this testi-
mony. It is purely hearsay testimony, and I object to it.
Mr. VINSON. He heard the evidence on the trial.
The CHAIRMAN. Of course, that is true. We were supposed to follow that
rule when we started the testimony, but we have admitted hearsay evidence.
But he has investigated the matter, and he heard the testimony in the court,
and he can give us his understanding of it.
Capt. BROCKUS. I heard the trial from beginning to end, with the exception of
possibly an hour or so during the trial.
The CHAIRMAN. Tell us what the evidence in the trial showed.
Capt. BROCKUS. All of the witnesses stated on oath that they saw the three
men coming down the truck, Taylor Cole, Bill Hatfield, and Private Ripley, and
that Ripley had his hand over his head and he was walking with Cole on one
side with a drawn pistol and Hatfield on the other. The next thing they
observed was a pistol shot fired by Bill Hatfield at Ripley. Well, before that
they said they heard, apparently, Hatfield say, "Put up your hands," and Ripley
replied, "I have them up." Hatfield said, "Put them up higher," and after that
the shot was fired, and Ripley jumped back and pulled his pistol-he had two
pistols and emptied them at Hatfield and killed him on the spot. Cole in the
meantime had dropped slightly in the rear of Ripley and fired two or three
shots at Ripley, firing from the right rear. One shot entered the back just
back of the shoulder and came out and entered the neck and had no exit. The
other shot struck the right of the spine and came out there [indicating] near
the center of the body in front. Cole slid over the bank and got out of sight
and Ripley fell and died a few minutes after. That is briefly the substance of
the evidence brought out in the trial.
Mr. SCHERR. Tell us about the next policeman who was killed.
Capt. BROCKUS. The next police that was killed was Private Kackley, of
Company A, State police. He was killed near Big Flint west-about 5 miles,
I should say-west of Williamson.
The circumstances leading up to that were about as follows:
Some shooting had taken place on the Kentucky side early in the evening,
about dark. Private Kackley was in charge of the station at Big Flint, and he
walked down to Nolan, which is only about a mile, and reported it to the
Kentucky National Guards which was stationed across the river, and asked
them for assistance to come up and help investigate the firing. Lieut. See, who
was in charge of the station there, brought five or six men over into West
Virginia, and they started down the track to make an investigation, intending
to cross over where they could opposite the point where the shooting had been
heard. On the way down it had got dark and in the meantime they met a man
on the track, or two men on the track, and on meeting them one of them was
heard to say, "This damn place ought to be blown up." So they stopped or
halted them and started to search them, and when they were searching the first
man other men in the dark opened fire, killing Kackley, shooting him in the
back of the head with apparently high-powered rifle, tearing the whole top of
his head off-he could not be recognized-and also killing a private of the
Kentucky National Guard. I do not remember his name.
Mr. SCHERR. Pvt. Vaughn?

The CHAIRMAN. How many were held for that?
Capt. BROCKUS. I should say there were four, possibly five, and a couple got
away that they have not been able to apprehend yet.
The next man killed was Pvt. William L. McMillan, of my company. That
killing took place, as well as I remember, on the 28th day of June. The cir-
cumstances leading up to that killing were about as follows:
A man named Pennington, who lived at Lynn, W. Va., about 2 miles east of
Matewan, reported to the sergeant of police at the station at Matewan that
he had been assaulted by the United Mine Workers at Lynn. The sergeant sent
a patrol of four men to make an investigation, all members of the State police.
On arriving at Lynn they found the men they wanted had come to Matewan
in a motor car. After waiting there a few minutes they decided to return to
Matewan, coming down the county road. When they had reached a point
about 400 yards east of the tent colony known as Blackberry City they were
suddenly fired upon from the hillside, and Pvt. McMillan was shot in the back,
the bullet entering about 1 inch to the right of the spine just above the backbone,
passed through his cartridge belt and exploded a .45-pistol cartridge and tore
a hole in his body about the size of a hen egg, the bullet remaining in his body.
He was later brought to Williamson and died at 8 o'clock that night.
The news reached Williamson about 3 o'clock. I got a party of about 25
State police together, secured a special train from the Norfolk & Western
Railroad Co. and went up to McCarr, which was the nearest point. In
the meantime the sergeant had telephoned Freeburn, Ky., for bloodhounds.
They came down on train 29, which arrived there about 4.46. A few minutes
after we arrived the bloodhounds arrived, and we went up to the point where
the police indicated that the firing had come from.
On the ground we found tracks, cigarette butts and several empty cartridge
shells, .30 high-power shells. The dogs were put on the scent and they fol-
lowed the trail up the mountain side possibly 100 yards, then across over the
ridge down a deep hollow into the little tent colony known as Horseshoe Bend
of the Blackberry City tent colony. The dogs passed several tents and went to
the door of one tent and stopped.
In that tent we found two men named Lehman. When they were brought out
the guard took them over to the county road about 30 feet away, and the
dogs tried to break loose from the leash, barked like they were after rabbits,
and simply tried to eat the men up. If they had been turned loose I believe they
would have bit them.
They were brought to Williamson and placed in jail, where I believe they
still remain. I understand it is being investigated by the grand jury.
Mr. SCHERR. What did the investigation show as to these men by the name of
Lehman that you brought to Williamson, that you got there in that tent, as to
whether they were members of the United Mine Workers of America or not?
Capt. BROCKUS. One of them was a member of the United Mine Workers of
America, and I am not so sure about the other. He claimed he was a resident
of Columbus, Ohio, and was only visiting his brother. I can not say whether he
was a member of the United Mine Workers of America or not.
Mr. SCHERR. This tent colony in which you found these two men is the tent
colony of the United Mine Workers of America, is it?
Capt. BROCKUS. It is. That little colony comprised only about 10 tents, and
is about 200 yards east of the main tent colony of Blackberry City.

of the house, indicated that the shots came from the vicinity of Dave Phillips's

May 12: At McCarr on the same day, which is a place about one mile east

"The situation is serious, and unless steps are taken to disarm all persons
on both sides of the river officers will be ambushed, houses shot up, and murder
committed by the wholesale. Arms and ammunition are being purchased daily
from the local merchants and shipped in by express. Under the present condi-
tions we have no authority to take a rifle from a man whom we might meet on
the public road with a load of ammunition going direct to the firing."
May 14: Firing continued at McCarr. The situation was such that as soon
as a man exposed himself he was fired at. At other points in the firing zone
covering the days of May 12, 13, and 14, extending along Tug River for a dis-
tance of about 10 miles, the firing was intermittent.
On that day in my report to headquarters in part it read as follows:
"It is useless to try to enforce law and maintain order in this county if every
man is permitted to go freely with a high-power rifle swung across his back and
sack full of ammunition. Rifles are being purchased freely wherever they are
offered for sale, and ammunition is coming in by the thousand rounds. Had we
the authority to disarm every man caught with a rifle the situation would soon
improve, it is believed."
Mr. SCHERR. Captain, right at that point. What steps were taken, if any, by

legitimate business, although the Pershinger Hardware Co., which is the largest
wholesale house in Williamson, did comply with our request and refused to sell
arms and ammunition.
Mr. SCHERR. And those who did not refuse to sell were the retail merchants?
Capt. BROCKUS. Those retailers continued to sell right along as many arms
and ammunition that they had a market for.
May 15: State police picked up on the Norfolk & Western Railway tracks

On the south side of the track there, there are a few families of union miners
who live possibly 50 yards from the railroad. These rifles were all take-down
rifles, and the ammunition and rifles were packed in suit cases. The suit cases -
had been thrown off from the train, because the suit cases were all torn to
pieces. They were of very cheap material, and when they hit the ground they
simply busted open, and the ammunition spilled out and the guns spilled out,
and two of them were slightly broken. One of them was an automatic rifle. I
believe it was a Stevens. All of them were high-power rifles.
The police were up early looking over the ground there, and they found these
arms and ammunition and, of course, they were confiscated. No claim was ever
made for them.

June 4. Pvt. Roy Walker, of the State police. and Raymond Marks, vol-
unteer State police, fired upon from the Lick Creek tent colony, as their

June 7. Approximately 300 shots were fired from ambush at a detachment

Eagle Coal Corporation, that was shortly before that destroyed by dynamite

June 13. Maj. Welch, superintendent of the White Star Coal Co., together

June 14. Maj. Thomas B. Davis, acting adjutant general of the State of
West Virginia, Sheriff A. C. Pinson, myself, Pvt. Bowles, of the State police
Sergt. Taylor, of the State police, and Pvt. Ball were fired upon as we were
getting out of the car at Lick Creek to investigate that shooting that had
taken place the evening before. This man that was supposed to have done the
shooting was standing on the front porch of his house firing a pistol directly
at that car as it passed around the curve on the public road. It was re-
ported to police headquarters in Williamson. Maj. Davis, who is the governor's
personal representative down in Mingo County, went out to bring that man
in for investigation. I think his name was Collins.
As we were getting out of the car on the hillside on the public road a shot
was fired. It sounded so close I thought a man getting out of the car had
accidentally discharged his gun. I looked around and asked him what he was
shooting at. About that time several other shots rang out. We discovered
then we were being fired at from a point in the brush up on the hill. We
-discussed the matter there a little, and finally the major ordered Sergt. Taylor,
who was carrying one of these machine guns, to sprinkle the hillside. He was
rather slow doing it and he told him a second time. These guns fire a clip of
20. He opened fire and fired about half that number and stopped. Another
shot or two was fired from the hill, and he finished the clip, firing 20 shots
altogether, and the firing ceased.
We discussed the possibility then of going down and getting Collins, and I
suggested we go down and get him. The major thought it was rather risky,
as we would have to pass over open ground for a bout 100 yards, and he sug-
gested that we go back to Williamson and get some assistance and come out
and clean out these riflemen hidden in the woods.
We went back to Williamson and had our signal sounded, which is four
blasts of the fire whistle repeated three times, and in about 10 minutes approxi-
mately 70 men responded with rifles and ammunition which had previously
been issued to them. They were loaded in cars, about 15 or 20 cars, and drove
out Sycamore Creek, which is a creek which runs in the same direction of
Lick Creek, but there is a mountain between. We unloaded, and I picked out
the men that I thought were not able to climb this mountain, about 15 of them,

and sent them around to the west approach of the public road and instructed
the sergeant in charge to hold them there and let nobody escape coming
toward Williamson. I previously had received instructions from Maj. Davis
to clean out those hills and everything from Lick Creek for the investigation.
We went up to the top of the mountain and formed our men in line, in what
we call a skirmish line, and sent Pvt. Bowles with 10 or 15 men across the
Lick Creek Hollow and to come down and comb that hillside. We did not
suspect anybody being on that side of the hill, and we took the main force
and formed a line and struck down that rough, rugged country-a line a mile
long, approximately a mile long. We came right down through the colony,
and before that I had instructed some men to come down to Rawl, just east
of the tent colony, to prevent them from coming out to the east. The whole
idea was to force them into the camp and then bring them on into Willianrson.
When we had gotten down within, I would say, 100 yards of the fence we were
fired upon up on the left of the line, the east end of the line, and it was rather hot
for a time, and I should say there was between 50 and 75 shots fired. We
marched down to the county road and then went over to the bridge-a little
concrete bridge that crosses to Mingo County-and about the time I got to the
bridge somebody called from the hillside, and he called me by name, and I
answered, "What is the matter?"
He answered, "It is Bowles; I am shot; come and help me."
I sent a mran up and had him brought out, and I met him at the edge of the
brush about 50 yards from the creek itself. I found him shot, as I have de-
scribed before, I think, shot in the back of the shoulder and the bullet came
out in the upper part of the chest, passing through the right lung and severing
or breaking one rib and paralyzing his right arm. He is now in the hospital
at Williamson. His right arm is still paralyzed. At that point they stated
that a man had been killed up there. We did not have any particular time
right then to hunt up the dead, so we proceeded to gather up what men were
in camp.
I formed all the volunteer and regular police on the county road
and instructed them to go to the tent colony and bring in all men who assembled
there and assemble them on the county road and leave a detachment under
the sheriff to take charge of them. I personally took about 20 men and went
to the tent between the county road and the railroad, which is the colony
between the railroad track and the river. Sergt. Peterson took about 12
regular and volunteer police and went to the tents north of the county road.
These men were instructed to absolutely destroy no property, to take no fire-
arms, and to do nothing with any of the property, but only to get the men.
I will say that while there one man picked up a stick and made an effort as
though he was going to break a lock on a tent, and I immediately instructed
him to desist and to hunt up the man that owned the lock and have him
open it.
Now, on that round-up I think we got 47 men and formed them on the road

Mr. SCHERR. Tell the Senators how the body of Breedlove was taken to

Capt. BROCKUs. Well, after we had finished our work of rounding up all

just a piece of loose canvas; then the question came up as to how we would
get him into Williamson; and a man named Maynard said he had a small

Mr. SCHERR. You referred a while ago to the three-day battle, so-called, and
In that spoke of the shooting at Auburn and Blackberry City on May 12, 13, and
14. James Kirkpatrick, testifying before this committee a few days ago, made
the statement that in that shooting 10 State policemen and 2 deputy sheriffs
lined up with the striking miners for protection and carried on the battle
against the Auburn Coal Corporation and its employees. Tell us whether or not
that is true.
Capt. BROCKUS. I was not there, of course, and I had to rely on the reports
made by Sergt. Jennings, who was in charge of the State police at Matewan.
He had about 15 men there, and he told me the State police took absolutely no
part in the shooting except one day they made a patrol up on a point of the
ridge, which is only a few hundred yards from Matewan and at least three-
quarters of a mile from where the bulk of the shooting took place, and they
were fired upon by a sniper from the Kentucky side of the river, and they
lined up and fired two or three volleys into this particular point or clump of
trees, and that is the only shooting they took part in during that three-day
fight.

Mr. SCHERR. About the time of this three-day battle, or shortly thereafter,

Capt. BROCKUS. Well, I saw one fairly well-constructed trench; it would ac-

that that they had made by piling these flat rocks one on top of another,
affording shelter for possibly 15 men. That was up near the top of this point
facing the Allburn Co.
Mr. SCHERR. The Allburn Coal Co., I believe, is across Tug River from Black-

Capt. BROCKUs. It is in Kentucky. From the point where these barricades

Capt. BROCKUS. No; they were back of the tents in the edge of the wood.

Mr. SCHERR. Capt. Brockus, I want you to tell the committee why the State
police was organized and when it was organized.
Capt. BROCKUS. It was organized along about the 18th day of May, 1921,
shortly after this three-day battle, they term it. The governor had requested
Federal troops to come in and place the county under martial law on the rec-
ommendation of the prosecuting attorney, the judge, the sheriff, and other citi-
zens of Williamson, Mingo County, and they had gone so far as to load their
´equipment at Camp Sherman, and we had been advised that a detachment of the
Nineteenth Infantry had been selected to come down to Mingo County. I do
not know just what took place; at any rate the troops failed to come and the
sheriff called upon me, issued a written warrant requesting that I take charge
of the affairs in Mingo County; that they were beyond his control; and under
the act of the legislature that created our department, when called upon by the
sheriff or when by a proclamation the governor so directs, every State police
has the authority to command absolutely the assistance of every peace officer
in the State and every able-bodied citizen in the State to assist in quelling
any uprising or insurrection. On the basis of that law and the failure of the
officials to obtain Federal troops, I called for the volunteer State police, and
they responded. This was discussed at an open meeting at the courthouse
presided over by the assistant prosecuting attorney, Mr. Priest. We outlined
the work, what was expected of them, and they all volunteered to serve without
pay. The lists last year were circulated around there; it was put to a vote-
all those who wanted to enlist indefinitely in this police force were required to
take an oath, the same as we take, to stand up, and I think every man in the
court room stood up. Then following that up we circulated-well, I could not
say just how the names came in, but at any rate they were submitted to our
office there in the courthouse and they were gone over very carefully and the
men selected and a certain time set for them to report. It was published in
the Williamson daily paper when they should report to be sworn in, and in
that way the volunteer police were organized and sworn in. They were given
rifles and 80 rounds or 60 rounds of ball cartridges per man. The rifles had
been shipped down on my request from Charleston-Regular Army rifles.
Mr. SCHERR. Was this meeting you speak of in the courthouse an open meet-
ing; was it open to the public?
Capt. BROCKUS. An open meeting; it was talked around the streets and in
the office a public discussion-that we would have a meeting in the court-
house of all persons believing in law and order.
Senator McKELLAR. How many were there?
Capt. BROCKUS. The courthouse was filled; I should say 200-reasonably
filled there might have been a few seats, but ordinarily you would speak of
the courthouse being full-I should say 200 or more.

Mr. SCHERR. After that meeting was not a committee of citizens chosen or au-

Capt. BROCKUS. Well, I could not say it happened on that night. I was not

on then was the recommendations of the sheriff and the prosecuting attorney;

submitted and to cross off those they were not absolutely sure of; that is,
that they could be relied upon to be issued a rifle and ammunition and go out
in the interest of law and order.
Mr. SCHERR. This committee was not official, but merely advisory to you?
Capt. BROCKUS. No; it was not official, although I believe I suggested it

Mr. SCHERR. For your advice and guidance, you not being acquainted with

Capt. BROCKUS. That was the purpose of it-to put no man on who we did not

to appear for their oath of office and their identification card.
Mr. SCHERR. And every man to whom was administered the oath of office and
to whom was given a card was a volunteer; is that true?
Capt. BROCKUS. A volunteer. That applies only to Williamson. In the out-
side districts we had to rely solely on the recommendations of the officials of
these mining companies. We had no other way of determining who was re-
sponsible, but to take the recommendation of the mine superintendents or some
official there that knew the men working around the mines. The idea was to
appoint a certain number at each operation for the purpose of repelling an
attack and giving them some show of authority in guarding their property at
night and, in case of necessity, to make arrests.
Mr. SCHERR. I wish you would tell the committee. Capt. Brockus, what you
know of the sentiment and feeling of the people of Williamson and the sur-
rounding territory when they found that the Federal Government would not
send troops into the Mingo field in May, 1921, at the time or just before this
volunteer police force was inaugurated?
Capt. BROCKUS. Well, the better citizens, what we call the better citizens,
the men in business there and who have property were clamoring for protection.
They wanted some sort of protection, and I told them very plainly that they had
Federal troops in there before this was in an open meeting in the courthouse—
that they could not expect to clear up the situation in Mingo County unless they
showed some interest or took a hand in it themselves, and several speeches
were made along that line by different citizens, and the response to the call for
volunteer police was, I thought, mighty good. We got 207, I think, in two days,
and just as fast as we could fill out the papers and swear them in.
Mr. SCHERR. Was there not a very general feeling or sentiment that some-
thing would have to be done and done very quickly in order to protect life and
property?
Capt. BROCKUS. It was. That was the general sentiment of what we term
the better class of citizens in Mingo County-not in Williamson, but through-
out the county.
Mr. SCHERR. Referring to these volunteer State policemen, or State police-
men selected who live outside of Williamson, tell the committee if they are
men at work now and were at work at that time.


===== [扫描序号 348] =====

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Capt. BROCKUS. In the majority of cases they are at work and they receive
no pay. They are simply given this authority to protect the property of the
particular location and enforce the law, if necessary.
Now, we have at the greater number of these plants at least two regular
State police, and they are in charge of the volunteers at that particular opera-
tions. In other words, they work under the direction of the regular State
police.
Mr. SCHERR. These volunteer State police around the coal camps are men
who are working every day in and about the mines, are they not?
Capt. BROCKUS. They are.
Mr. HOUSTON. Now, do you know that, Captain?
Capt. BROCKUS. What is that?
Mr. HOUSTON. Do you know that?
Capt. BROCKUS. Well, I could not say that every one is working, but that is
what was the idea of the instructions sent out, that men that were employed
at the operations, that were reliable, and could be trusted with a gun, if neces-
sary, would be commissioned as volunteer policemen for their own protection
as well as for the protection of property at that particular operation.
Mr. SCHERR. And these volunteers are all under the direct supervision and
control of the regular police stationed at these plants.
Capt. BROCKUS. They are. Further along that line, I have instructed the
regular police that if they see any misconduct on the part of these volunteer
police, to immediately take up their authority, and that has been done in quite
a number of cases outside of Williamson. I think we have probably 30 that
have been canceled, and a note made on the back of the card as to why they
were called in. For instance, if a man is seen drunk or flashing a pistol
around in public, the police seize that immediately, take up his card and turn
it in, with a note why it was turned in, and that is filed away in the office
and his name is ruled off the list of police.
Mr. SCHERR. Capt. Brockus, you spoke a while ago to the effect that this
Lick Creek tent colony was a mile or so east of Williamson. Tell the com-
mittee if that Lick Creek tent colony is not located on the main highway lead-
ing east from Williamson, and that that highway constitutes about the best
driveway leading out of Williamson.
Capt. BROCKUS. It is. I should say it is 2 miles east of Williamson.
Mr. SCHERR. And is it not a further fact that now and for weeks past, on
account of the Lick Creek tent colony, citizens generally do not use that road
because of the fear that they and the occupants of their cars will be fired upon
by these men living in and about these tents?
Capt. BROCKUS. Yes; that is true. The people in Williamson feel unsafe pass-
ing on the public road, and the tents are very close to the road on both sides.
Mr. SCHERR. That is the general feeling, is it?
Capt. BROCKUS. That is the general feeling-that they are unsafe passing
along this road.

himself this way [indicating] and dancing around the floor and said it was the

In fact, I didn't want to have anything to do toward doing any organizing or

Mr. DAMRON. I wish you would tell the committee what information you got
and when you got it, whether it was in advance of the shooting or afterwards?
Mr. LIVELY. Well, the first information that I got that it was going to be
was the night before.
Mr. DAMRON. From whom did you get that information?
Mr. LIVELY. Henry Haywood and Frank Smith.
Mr. DAMRON. Now, tell the committee who Henry Haywood and Frank
Smith are?
Mr. LIVELY. They are both members of the United Mine Workers.
Mr. DAMRON. And where were they stationed at that time?
Mr. LIVELY. Matewan.
Mr. DAMRON. Now, go ahead and tell the committee about it.
Mr. LIVELY. They came into my place, both having rifles. Henry Haywood
had a .32 Winchester rifle. Frank Smith had one of the old makes of Spring-
field rifles, a single-shot rifle, and they had a quantity of red pepper that they
were to use to keep the hounds from tracking them, and they told me that they
were going up and join some of the other boys, and that they were going
to shoot up Freeburn the next morning, and they left my place with those
rifles, and that was the last I saw of them until the next day some time.
Mr. DAMRON. What conveyance did they use in going to Freeburn, if any?
Mr. LIVELY. Walked, I think.
Mr. DAMRON. How far is Freeburn from Matewan?
Mr. LIVELY. I think about 6 miles.
Mr. DAMRON. Tell the committee when you reported the fact that Freeburn
was to be shot up?
Mr. LIVELY. When I reported the fact?
Mr. DAMRON. Yes.
Mr. LIVELY. I mailed it. I think I got that off the next morning on No. 4,
and mailed it to Bluefield.
Mr. DAMRON. Was that before the shooting actually happened the next morn-
ing?
Mr. LIVELY. Well, it would have been; yes; from the time these boys told
me. They came back when they had done the shooting, and it would have been
before.
Mr. DAMRON. Did you have any information after the shooting at Freeburn
as to what took place there?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir. They told me they were going on the West Virginia
side, and had some stuff on the other side, on the Kentucky side of the river,
and it was very foggy. They had a time set for it and had a man down under
the hill to give a signal. He was to give this signal, and at that time they
were to start shooting. He was to shoot the signal-first a signal shot. They
said he done so, before the fog lifted, and they couldn't see so very well. They
got more of them, and when they say them, they opened fire on the head house,
it being about the time the men started to work.
Mr. DAMRON. Is the Freeburn mine the mine where the cars are let down
by conveyors?
Mr. LIVELY. Monitors, I think.
Mr. DAMRON. Tell the committee whether or not they told you anyone was
hurt.
Mr. LIVELY. They told me they thought they got the drum runner and an-
other fellow on the tipple.
Mr. DAMRON. How many did they say were in the crowd?
Mr. LIVELY. I don't remember hearing them say just how many was in the
crowd.
Mr. DAMRON. Did they give you the names of any that participated in the
shooting?

Mr. DAMRON. Is that the way in which you were to furnish information?
Mr. LIVELY. By mail?
Mr. DAMRON. Yes.
Mr. LIVELY. Yes.
Mr. DAMRON. Why didn't you use the telegraph or telephone?
Mr. LIVELY. I would just as well have told everybody who I was, in my
opinion, as to have told the telegraph operator who I was. Anyway, it would
have been dangerous and would have revealed my identity, which would have
meant my death. Also the same with the telephone, if anyone was to get next
to it. I have often heard of those fellows talk about getting to the telephone
and tapping the wires so they could get a message going over them. In either
event it would have been dangerous to have done it.
Mr. DAMRON. Now, in addition to that, were you instructed by your superior
not to use the telephone or the telegraph?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir; I was.
Mr. DAMRON. Now, Mr. Lively, in your work there did you have anything to

Mr. DAMRON. Did they get any rifles?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir; they got two that I saw.

Mr. DAMRON. Is that in Matewan?

Mr. DAMRON. What became of the other 16?
Mr. LIVELY. Those were distributed to the various different members of the
union.
Mr. DAMRON. For what purpose was these guns purchased?
Mr. LIVELY. They said it was to prevent Thacker and Red Jacket from work-

Mr. DAMRON. They told you the purpose was to prevent Thacker and Red

Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. From employing nonunion miners?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. What particular work or thing did Mr. Workman have to do
with the storing of these guns, if anything?
Mr. LIVELY. They were put up there and left in that room with no way to
lock them. He gave me instructions to go to the hardware store and get some
locks and get a man to put them on the door. It is in a room with part of the
partition gone. It was an inside room and had a skylight over it. I dont' know
what you would call it, but it was like going over a transom where you could
go from one room to another. He had me get locks to put on each of those
doors, and turn the bills for the locks and the carpenter for putting them on
into him, and he reimbursed me for it.
Mr. DAMRON. That was Mr. Workman of the United Mine Workers?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir.

Mr. LIVELY. I knew Jim Payne and Jack Payne.
Mr. DAMRON. Were they ever at your place?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir; several times.
Mr. DAMRON. When did you first see them at Matewan?
Mr. LIVELY. It must have been about the last of July or first of August, 1920.
Mr. DAMRON. What was their business there?
Mr. LIVELY. Well, they came to my place and introduced themselves to me,
told me who they were, and that they were up there to conduct guerrilla war-
fare there, said they were sent there by Mr. Mooney and that Mr. Mooney
told them they could see me, that they could rely on me to help them out any
way I could. So they came in to see me and told me their business and said
that the Mohawk was running plenty of coal and was doing most as good as
before the strike, and that there had to be something done; that the spirit
of those men up there were broken and they was going to get ready and shoot
it up, and said he was going to Williamson to confer with the officials down
there, and left there that evening-the two of them.
Mr. DAMRON. Did they tell you at that time they wanted to meet anyone
else?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. Who?
Mr. LIVELY. They told me they wanted me to introduce them to Sid Hatfield.
Mr. DAMRON. Did you introduce them to Sid Hatfield?
Mr. LIVELY. I did.
Mr. DAMRON. Did you hear any conversation between them and Sid Hatfield
as to what their business there was?
Mr. LIVELY. Well, I heard two or three different conversations between him
and Sid in which Sid pledged himself to assist him in any way he could in
getting men to agree to go up there to help shoot up the population.
Mr. DAMRON. Tell the committee whether or not those two men were going
under assumed names, or had aliases?
Mr. LIVELY. They was.
Mr. DAMRON. What names were they going under?
Mr. LIVELY. Going under the name of Jum Allen and Jack Dickinson.
Mr. DAMRON. Where were they from?
Mr. LIVELY. From Cabin Creek, Kanawha County.
Mr. DAMRON. Did they belong there in Mingo County?
Mr. LIVELY. No, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. How long did they saay there?
Mr. LIVELY. They left shortly after this operation was shot up, I think on
the 21st day of August, 1920; this operation was shot up along that time.
Senator MCKELLAR. Did they kill anybody there?
Mr. LIVELY. No, sir.
Senator McKELLAR. No one was hurt?
Mr. DAMRON. One was wounded.
Mr. LIVELY. One was wounded.
Senator MCKELLAR. And none killed. Let me ask you further. You said
something about their coming to you for guns. Did you ever give out any of
these guns?
Mr. LIVELY. Me?
Senator MCKELLAR. Yes, sir.
Mr. LIVELY. No.
Senator MCKELLAR. Why, if you never had given out any before and had
never given out at all, why do you suppose they came to you for guns?
Mr. LIVELY. Came to me for guns?
Senator MCKELLAR. Yes; you said they came to you for guns.
Mr. LIVELY. Because they thought if there was any there I would know about
it, being on the place. In other words, I looked after Mr. Workman's and

Roob's affairs a great deal in their absence, and looked after paying their
bills-any bills they had to pay, I paid for them out of my own personal money

Senator MCKELLAR. What did you do with the gun given you?
Mr. LIVELY. What did I do with it?
Senator MCKELLAR. Yes.
Mr. LIVELY. Wes Holbrook afterward came after it; he demanded it to send

Senator MCKELLAR. Did you give it to him for that purpose?
Mr. LIVELY. No, sir; I didn't give it to him. I told Holbrook I didn't want

because of creating suspicion on my part, and I told him the gun was at my

colored fellows and got them to leave them upstairs for a while, and in order to
save this man's life I got the two rifles in the clear where he couldn't get them.
Senator MCKELLAR, Where are they now?
Mr. LIVELY. They are available in Bluefields.
Senator MCKELLAR. You have them yet?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir. In order to get them away I put them in a trunk. I
didn't want them to think my wife was going east, I made them think my wife
was going to her home in Charleston, where she was raised; had them sent
to Williamson, carried through on the train to Bluefields and checked that
trunk and got them away that way.
Mr. DAMRON. Tell the committee whether or not since that time Wesley Hol-
brook had a search warrant issued for your restaurant and described these two
particular guns by number.
Mr. LIVELY. My restaurant and house-search warrant was issued for them-
and they searched for the guns by numbers, so my wife informs me. I wasn't
at home when my place was searched.
Mr. DAMRON. Tell the committee where these two colored men were from.
Mr. LIVELY. They were from Vulcan.
Mr. DAMBON. What were their names.
Mr. LIVELY. Mel Spicer and Hobart Saunders.
Mr. DAMRON. And where are they now?
Mr. LIVELY. The last information I had of them they were over about
Bowers-that is, up near Wheeling, W. Va.-up in that district somewhere.
Mr. DAMRON. You spoke of these two Payne men coming from Cabin Creek
and telling you what their business was there. Did they ever bring any guns
to your place?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir; to my house, they would stay all night with me when
they came and bring suit cases with guns and ammunition with them.
Senator MCKELLAR. What became of the men that did the shooting you have
described?
Mr. DAMRON. I was just going to reach that, Senator.
Senator MCKELLAR. All right.
Mr. DAMRON. How long had these two men been there before the shooting
occurred at Mohawk?
Mr. LIVELY. Since I had first met them about-oh, I can't say just how long-
possibly anywhere from two to four weeks.
Mr. DAMRON. Tell the committee the names of anyone who was to assist,
and did assist, according to the information you got from them, in shooting up
that particular mine?
Mr. LIVELY. There was Claude Brewer, John Collins, Joe Collins, Walter
Asbury, Steve Collins-them I know of going from Matewan up there—and
then there was John Buchanan and Dave Saunders at War Eagle.
Mr. DAMRON. When did they go up to this place to do this shooting?
Mr. LIVELY. The night of the 20th, I think it was.
Mr. DAMRON. Did you know, prior to the date of the shooting, when it was to
come off?
Mr. LIVELY. I did.
Mr. DAMRON. Did you notify your superior officers, or the office at Bluefield,
of the fact that the shooting had been staged and when it was to come off?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir; giving him the time and the details and the insignia
they was to wear in order that they would know each other from the officers
who might want them.

Mr. DAMRON. Who did you give this information to as to the insignia they
were to wear, and the signals to be given, and how the shooting was to be done?
Mr. LIVELY. Jim Payne, going under the name of Joe Allen.
Mr. DAMRON. What did he tell you?
Mr. LIVELY. He told me they were going to wear one of those large cheap red
handkerchiefs, each man around his neck, to identify each other by them.
Mr. DAMRON. What were they going to do at the mines?
Mr. LIVELY. The way he had it, said he was to place some dynamite, or have
some dynamite so he could explode it right under the truck as the first lot of
men went up, just blow that truck into the river, and get them, and then open
fire on the watchman that was at the head house, kill him, rush on him, and
set the head house afire, and then rush the bottom and not leave anything
alive there.
Mr. DAMRON. Did they carry out their plans?
Mr. LIVELY. No, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. Did they attempt to carry out their plans?
Mr. LIVELY. They did.
Mr. DAMRON. Tell the committee what they did.
Mr. LIVELY. According to the confession I got from them, conversations
with them themselves, they got up there and got down right close to the head
house and Collins and Jim Payne was together, and it was for Collins to fire
the first shot, but before they got ready to start this one of the officers that
the sheriff had there heard him and said, "There they are now." It being a
foggy morning, and just then Collins said he put his gun to his shoulder and
fired at this watchman and the watchman fired at him almost at the same time,
or just afterwards and hit the rock right in front of his face. Well, they
exchanged a few shots there; they said they opened a machine gun on them,
and they ran and one of their men was wounded as he was going away, a
colored man by the name of Dave Saunders.
Mr. DAMRON. Did you see these two Allens, Paynes, I mean, after the
shooting?
Mr. LIVELY. One of them.
Mr. DAMRON. Which one?
Mr. LIVELY. Jim.
Mr. DAMRON. Where did you see him?
Mr. LIVELY. I saw him in Williamson along-it must have been in February.
Mr. DAMRON. Where did they go after this shooting occurred?
Mr. LIVELY. I don't know; he told me when he was preparing for this he
was going back to Cabin Creek, then he thought he would drop back and put
some dynamite under a train up there and wreck some of the cars in the rear
and then get away and write the trainmen letters that if they didn't quit that
scabbing coal-that is, what they term coal mined by nonunion men "scab
coal," that he was goin to blow the real train up.
Mr. DAMRON. Now, the information that you got you say you furnished to the
officials in advance of the time that the shooting occurred?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. In order that they might be prepared to meet it?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. Were they prepared?
Mr. LIVELY. I think they were.
Mr. DAMRON. And from the information you furnished and the confessions
you got, did it lead to indictments against these men?
Mr. LIVELY. There were several of them arrested, and was under bond, being
held for the grand jury, and the grand jury was in session last week.
Mr. DAMRON. Last week?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. What became of Jack Payne? Was he arrested?
Mr. LIVELY. He was arrested at Williamson and taken to Welch, and gave
bond.
Mr. DAMRON. Who was with him when he was arrested?
Mr. LIVELY. I never saw him when he was arrested. From what informa-
tion I had, Mr. Keeney was in company with him when he was arrested.
Mr. DAMRON. Do you know whether he was placed under bond or not?
Mr. LIVELY. He was.
Mr. DAMRON. Do you know whether or not he forfeited his bond?
Mr. LIVELY. I was told by the justice of the peace that bonded him that he
did, and he never showed up any more.

Mr. DAMRON. Now, Mr. Lively, while you were at Matewan and doing that

assassination of John Yates, mine superintendent at Gates?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir; to a certain extent.
Mr. DAMRON. Do you know when he was killed and under what circumstances?
Mr. LIVELY. He was killed, as well as I remember, about the last part of
October. I don't remember what date, but I would say about the last part
of October, 1920.
Mr. DAMRON. Tell the committee where you got your information, and
whether it was before or afterwards or both.
Mr. LIVELY. Shortly before he was killed John Obell was at Matewan-was
inquiring of me where he could get some guns.
Mr. DAMRON. Who was John Obell?
Mr. LIVELY. I think he was president of the local union at Gate at that
time. I told him I had no guns, and asked him what was up. He said that
John Yates was getting Gates mine down there too well started; that he got
Ralls started and they were getting coal, and now he was coming in and
starting up Gates, and he shouldn't do it. I told him I had no rifles; and
said he would go over and see Sid Hatfield-he said “Sid," meaning Sid Hat-
field-and see if he could get some from him. He told me he would come back
and let me know; but he never did come back.
Mr. DAMRON. How long after that was it that Mr. Yates was killed?
Mr. LIVELY. Well, about the next day or possibly the next-just a day or two.
Mr. DAMRON. Do you know from what point he was shot; whether it was
from ambush or not?
Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. Do you know whether or not he was shot in the back?
Mr. LIVELY. That is my information; yes, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. Did you have any talk to anyone afterwards as to who had
done the shooting?
Mr. LIVELY. John Ogle told me that he did. He said they planned for some
men to go on the hill and get shooting at Yates and draw his fire, and that he
was hidden over there about the end of the bridge, and when Yates got shoot-
ing at them follows on the hill-they were shooting at Yates-that he shot
Yates.
Mr. DAMRON. Do you know whether Mr. Yates was still in front of his office
or going home from his office?
Mr. LIVELY. He was killed right there near his office; yes, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. Did you have a talk with him, or did Mr. C. H. Workman have
a talk with you afterwards as to the killing?
Mr. LIVELY. Just shortly afterwards; yes, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. What did he tell you?
Mr. LIVELY. He said it was the men from below done it.
Mr. DAMRON. Did he tell you who it was?
Mr. LIVELY. No, sir.
Mr. DAMRON. Did you tell him that Mr. Ogle told you that he had done it?
Mr. LIVELY. I did.
Mr. DAMRON. What did he say?
Mr. LIVELY. "I am afraid he is talking too much." He said "I know you
are all right, but if he talks that way he might talk to somebody who is not
all right."
Mr. DAMRON. In your work did you have information, or did you know

Mr. LIVELY. Yes, sir.
In one case Sid Hatfield came to me and said they

66
Felts said yes; he had consulted an attorney and that he was, and if he
thought he was not to call the prosecuting attorney, if he wanted to, and

Mr. DAMRON. By "these men," whom do you mean?

He said he was walking down laughing and talking; he swore and spoke to

said he ran around there and done some more shooting; said he just decided
to go 50-50 with every one he saw. He said in the meantime he had his hat shot
off his head.

rifle. He said he had a good .38, and said he knew that if they didn't get
through they took six bullets away with them.
Then he spoke of Ferguson being killed away down the alley. I asked him,
"Did he die game?" He said no; he held up his hands and begged for his life
and used very rough language. I had better not use it. here. He said he begged
for his life and he went ahead and told how he cursed him and killed him.
He said, "I told him he had gone too far; you have got to die," and shot him.
Mr. DAMRON. Tell the committee how many gunshot wounds Ferguson re-

Mr. LIVELY. They said he was just. shot all to pieces. I don't remember just

Mr. Avis. There were six. He was shot about 900 yards from this scene.

for a fixed period of time. The reason for the desire to have that interstate
joint meeting was that the coal industry of the United States was paralyzed.
Operators everywhere were going into bankruptcy and miners were on the
verge of starvation.
The section just read in the agreement that was finally reached was inserted
because of the belief of the operators who were anxious to do something
to stabilize the industry that whatever the terms of the contract might be,
if it was too high to meet the market conditions, it was necessary to protect
them from the competition of other States that might not have wage agreements
between employers and employees.
