Mr. BELCHER. I desire to read from the convention of 1901 a statement made
by you, Mr. Lewis:
"I think this conference is coming to that point where we should strip every
question clean of every sentiment. I believe when we do that we are coming
to a point where we can discuss these questions as they affect our interests
generally, and from that point of view I, for one, would like to know the
purposes and why we inaugurated what is known as the joint movement in
the four States represented."
Mr. HOUSTON. What page is that?
Mr. LEWIS. It is page 2355.
66
In asking that question I am going to answer the question as I understand
the purposes why we met. And in doing so, I am willing to assume as broad a
position and stand on as broad a platform as any man in this hall, it matters
not to me who represents the operators or miners.
"In the first place, as I understand it, we had something of a guerilla fight
in the mining industry-every operator was seeking to enter the market and
sell a ton of coal against his competitors at whatever cost. In order for them
to do that, it was necessary for them to reduce the wages of the miners step
by step, until it became a question with the miners of the country whether
it was not as well to starve being idle as to starve working. I am free to admit
that under these conditions many of the operators went into bankruptcy. If
this be true, and I do not think it can be questioned, then it was necessary
not only for the miners, but for the operators as well, to assume certain
responsibilities to give stability to the mining industry. Realizing this, we met
in joint convention. We agreed on a certain scale for mining, and every man,
whether he was in the organization or out of the organization, on our side of
the compact was expecting to adhere strictly to every term embodied in that
contract. We know, and every man in the hall knows, when the first compact
was made that the miners of this competitive field were not as well organized
as you and we would both like to have seen them in order that there would be
no friction between us in the year following that agreement. We have accepted
to the best of our ability to adhere strictly to every agreement that we have
entered into. It is true that we have asked-you may put it in the form of a
favor if you please-and in some cases we have insisted that the operators
would not only recognize the United States Mine Workers as a business in-
stitution, but that they would go one step farther and help us compel the
rebellious of our own ranks to be parties to this compact-for the benefit of the
miners and operators, jointly. Now, let us see how much farther this movement
must go to be successful.
"As I understand it, it is for the purpose of wiping out competition between
us as miners first, viewing it from our side of the question; next, for the
purpose of wiping out competition as between the operators in these four
States.
When we have succeeded in that and we have perfected an organization
on both sides of the question, then, if I understand the real purpose of this
movement, it is that we will jointly declare war on every man outside of this
competitive field who will do anything in any way endangering the peace that
exists between us. What is necessary to do this? Organize our forces in the
competing fields so far as the United Mine Workers are concerned. Go into
these outside competing fields and tell your competitors that they have to join
this movement whether they like it or not, and give stability to the coal
business of the United States."
That represented the policy of this organization at that time, didn't it, Mr.
Lewis?

Mr. BELCHER. Then, it is the policy and practice of the United Mine Workers

Mr. LEWIS. That is true.

Mr. LEWIS. After 1898, as the check-off system became effective in different
coal-producing States where the operators and the miners negotiated joint

INDIANAPOLIS, IND., January 28, 1902.
Officers and members of the Thirteenth Annual Convention, United Mine Work-

Gentlemen, we, your special committee, appointed to formulate a policy
which would culminate in a complete organization of all the competitive fields,
are fully convinced that the two Virginias have been a menace to the perfec-

Therefore we recommend that the national executive board pursue the most
aggressive policy that they in conjunction with the several district presidents
can pursue to bring about organization in the different districts, not only in
Virginia but in all other districts.
We also recommend that the national executive board be empowered to em-

in this work.

66
For several years efforts have been made to organize the miners of Virginia
and West Virginia, with the hope of securing for them the same conditions of
employment as obtain in the districts covered by the interstate agreement.
These efforts have not met with that degree of success for which we hoped,
although a larger number of local unions has been established during the past
year than at any other time in the history of mining in those States and
wages have been increased as a result of the persistent work of our organizers
there.
"In the early spring a convention was held at Huntington, at which a scale
for West Virginia was drafted and the officers of the district directed to in-
augurate a strike at the most opportune time should they fail in efforts which
they were authorized to make to have the scale signed without resorting to
a suspension of work. Pursuant to these instructions every possible effort was
made by both the national and district organizations to induce the operators
to meet our representatives in joint conference for the purpose of determining
the wages which should be paid and the conditions of employment that should
obtain.
66
My own time was so thoroughly consumed with affairs in the East that
I was unable to personally superintend the movement in West Virginia; how-
ever, I stationed our most experienced board members and organizers in that
field, giving them such advice and direction as I deemed necessary for the suc-
cessful prosecution of the work.
"In the early part of May it became evident that we should be forced to
inaugurate a strike or the organization which it had taken so many years to
build would disintegrate, consequently a conference of the national and district
officers stationed in District 16 was convened, and with only a few dissenting
votes it was decided to inaugurate a strike, to take effect on June 7. In the
interim a large force of organizers was stationed in District 17, and a vigorous
campaign was entered upon. On June 7 the strike began. Telegrams dated
from June 8 to 11, received from our representatives, informed me that fully
80 per cent of the miners had suspended work, and the prospects of a com-
plete tie-up were encouraging
** * *
"The strike in the New River field is still in progress and is being supported
by the national organization.
"The strike in West Virginia, while not by any means a complete success,
nevertheless resulted in an improvement in the conditions of employment, an
increase of 10 per cent in wages having been granted in the Fairmont district
and on the Norfolk & Western Railroad, taking effect January 1 of this year.
These advances were unquestionably brought about through the agitation of our
organization.

named were members of what was the central competitive field joint movement
from time to time, except when it was dissolved. At the present time I will
say it is dissolved.

rival national unions of miners, known as the National Progressive Union of
Mine Workers, and N. T. A. 135 of the Knights of Labor, which was the miners'
branch of the Knights of Labor.

were different methods of producing coal, varying costs of mining, different

"In order to correct these most harmful conditions a joint convention of

the solicitation of the miners' officials, was called to meet at Chicago in Jan-
uary, 1898. At this convention an interstate joint agreement was established.
After a long session of deliberation and negotiation, continuing over a period
of about three weeks, the basing price for mining in Ohio and Pennsylvania
was increased from 56 to 66 cents per ton, an advance of practically 18 per
cent, and both the existing price and method of screening and weighing of coal
was made uniform throughout the entire territory covered by the terms of the

66
As a result of the Chicago convention a representative meeting was sub-

"The granting of the 8-hour day by the operators, after making these
numerous other important concessions, was with the distinct understanding and
explicit promise of the miners to give to the operators of the four contracting
States adequate protection against the competition of the unorganized fields.
From year to year they have been called upon to fulfill that promise.
66
The operators, parties to that agreement, at the time of its execution felt
that it was absolutely necessary to the safety of their investments that they
be protected from the encroachments on them by their competitors of the un-
organized field. The tonnage of the nonunion fields entering into the com-
petitive market, particularly of West Virginia and Kentucky, at that time was
not so large as it was aggressive and threatening, the total tonnage entering
directly into competition from those fields being approximately 600,000 tons.
Since, however, coal from this unorganized territory coming into direct com-
petition with Ohio and Pennsylvania has so increased that a fair estimate
places this competitive tonnage at 8,000,000 tons, which does not include the
tonnage from nonunion fields adjacent to the Pittsburgh district. The markets
in western and northern Ohio, eastern Indiana, and Michigan, from year to
year have been encroached upon by coal from the unorganized districts until at
the present time nearly 50 per cent of the coal consumed in these markets is
supplied from fields operated with nonunion labor. To find a market for the
union tonnage displaced in the territory named, the mine owners of Ohio and
Pennsylvania within the past five years have made heavy investments and built
and equipped large coal docks to secure markets at the upper lake ports; but
these operators now find nonunion coal rapidly commanding a heavy percentage
of this market, when, at the time of the Chicago agreement, the nonunion fields
had but a small fraction of this trade. And unless these conditions are cor-
rected the markets so secured will soon be replaced by the tonnage from West
Virginia and Kentucky."

46
Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Lewis, will you state to the committee just what was meant,
if you know, by the term industrial organization," referred to by Delegate
Savage, whose statement I have just read?
Mr. LEWIS. Mr. Chairman, an industrial organization, as I understand it,
and as every representative of organized labor understands it, is an organiza-
tion made up of all the employees in an industry. The distinction between an
industrial organization and a craft or trade-union is that a union may be
made up of bricklayers, for instance, and that is a trade-union; a union mav
be made up of machinists, and that is a trade-union; and a union may be made
up of carpenters, and that is a carpenters' union. You have the miners, of
course, and we have engineers working in the mines, machine runners, day
men, drivers, tracklayers and timbermen. We have on the outside tipplemen,
such as dumpers and trimmers, because they are all employed in the production
of coal, and they are organized in one union, and that is an industrial union.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Made up of the different crafts?
Mr. LEWIS. Made up of the different crafts within the same industry.
Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Lewis, I hand you a report of the proceedings of the con-
vention of 1911, and I will ask you to state to this committee how much money
th's organization expended in West Virginia for the purpose of organizing the
mines, from the year 1899, when the contract was made between the operators

66 RESOLUTION NO. 74.
"To the officers and delegates of the Twenty-third Annual Convention :
'Whereas we believe that the emancipation of the workers can only be accom-
plished through the action of the workers as a class; and
"Whereas in the class struggle between the capitalist class and the working
class, the workers should avail themselves of every weapon at their com-
mand; and
"Whereas the ballot is one of the most powerful weapons in the hands of the
working class; and,
"Whereas the workers should work in union and harmony on both the industrial
and political fields; and,
"Whereas the Socialist Party has always and everywhere proved itself the
champion of the working class: Therefore be it
"Resolved, That we, the mine workers of the entire country, adopt and
indorse the Socialist Party as the political party of the working class, and urge
all workers to rally under the banner of universal brotherhood: And be it
further
"Resolved, That we request the officers and delegates of said convention of the
United Mine Workers of America to adopt these or similar resolutions.
"DAVID MCKEE, Secretary Local 1771.
"ANTON TROTTER.

"Delegate GERMER, District No. 12..* * ** Whenever we criticize or try to

many delegates-and a majority of them—who do not agree with me politically,

the Socialist Party wants the workers united. They want the workers united on

"As I have gone into the discussion so far I will go a little farther. It is

made them you have nothing more to do with it. For 20 years union officials
have gone to Washington to lobby for laws in favor of the workers, and the
twenty-first time they sent the same men back to make the laws and followed
them like cheap curs to beg for what belonged to them. If you would send
Socialists to make the laws, and if it was for your betterment, you would have
the referendum. If the Socialists send people to represent them they have what
they call the 'hook' to bring them back-the recall. Some of your Democrats
and Republicans are coming to the initiative, the referendum, and the recall.
Socialism, in my opinion, must come as sure as the rising of the sun.
"Gentlemen of the convention, it is your duty to study the question, to size

that must come to stop the oppression of the people, a revolution in thought or a
revolution in blood-which the Socialists are trying to keep down-and it is
your duty to help it along."

Delegate Germer says:
'There are men in the labor movement to-day who contend that the present
share that the workers receive is an equitable share, and they do all in their
power to perpetuate the system that only permits the worker to get one-fifth
of what his labor creates. The amendment to the committee's report is only
in keeping with the resolution adopted here in the convention of 1909, which
provided that we believed in the collective ownership of all means of produc-
tion and distribution, and that the workers shall receive the full social value of
what their labor creates. After the convention adopting that resolution three
years ago, we will be perfectly consistent if we embody the language of that
resolution in the preamble of our constitution.
"I realize that inserting that language in our constitution would not neces-
sarily give us the full social value of what our labor creates, but this is only a
declaration of principle, and it is a question as to whether or not we are
going to declare that we are entitled to the full social value of what our labor
creates or whether we will continue to say we shall continue to receive an
equitable share,' which can be constructed in a dozen different ways. I believe
the amendment should be adopted. It is consistent with our former action, and
I believe it is consistent and in harmony with the ideas of the great majority
of the delegates of the convention. I am entitled to all my labor creates ;
you are entitled to all your labor creates, and if that philosophy is right,
then why have any hesitancy in inserting that in our preamble? It is a decla-
ration of our sentiment."

are there any of their constituents at home, that do not want the full product

sources how the employers are treated in localities where the union is strong.

as we may.' They see reports of meetings of this kind, and of the miners'
demands. They read of the continual strikes and disputes and turmoils and
violations of contracts in districts that are unionized, and they conclude it is
cheaper to remain nonunion; that it is more profitable after paying all of their .
expenses than it is to unionize.

Mr. VINSON. No, sir; it has not. The acquittal took place March 19; this

(The act referred to is as follows:)
CHAPTER 69.
(Senate bill No. 14-Mr. Sander.)
An act to amend and reenact section 21 of chapter 116 of the Code of West
Virginia, relating to juries, and to when and how juries may be summoned
from another county in criminal cases.
Passed March 23, 1921. In effect from passage. Approved by the governor
March 29, 1921.
SEC. 21. Juries.-Special jury in civil cases, upon motion of all parties; how
drawn; when drawn panel exhausted; in criminal cases when may be drawn
from other county; order for; how venire facias issued; per diem and mileage
of jurors.
Be it enacted by the Legislature of West Virginia, That section 21 of chapter
116, of the Code of West Virginia, relating to juries, and to when and how
juries may be summoned from another county in criminal cases, be amended and
reenacted so as to read as follows:
SEC. 21. Any court may allow a special jury in any civil case, upon motion of
all the parties thereto, to be formed in the following manner, viz.: The court
shall direct a panel of twenty jurors to be drawn by the clerk, in the presence of
the court, from the box mentioned in section 5 of this chapter, who shall be
summoned by the sheriff to attend on the day named in the order, and from
which number sixteen shall be chosen by lot; and the parties thereupon, begin-


===== [扫描序号 446] =====
438
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
ning with the plaintiff's attorney, shall alternately strike off one until the num
ber be reduced to twelve; which number shall complete the jury for the trial of
the case.
The court may also allow a special jury in any civil case when the
panel of drawn jurors is exhausted, upon the motion of either of the parties, to
be summoned by the sheriff so far as may be required from the body of the
county; but no such special jury shall be allowed in any case unless the court
certifies of record that the interests of the parties so asking such jury, will be
promoted by the allowance of such special jury.
And in any criminal case in any court, if, in the opinion of the court, or the
judge thereof in vacation, qualified jurors, not exempt from serving, can not be
conveniently found in the county in which the trial is to, the court, or the judge
thereof in vacation, shall enter an order of record to such effect, and may cause
so many of such jurors as may be necessary to be summoned from any other
county. In said order the court, of the judges thereof in vacation, shall fix a
day on which such jurors shall be required to attend, and in such order shall
be indicated the county from which such jurors shall be drawn, and the number
of such jurors to be drawn. An attested copy of such order shall be certified to
the circuit court of the county designated, or the judge thereof in vacation, and
thereupon such circuit court or the judge thereof in vacation, shall, by order,
direct that a jury be drawn in the manner provided by law for the drawing of
petit jurors in his county, and proceedings respecting the drawing of such jurors,
including the names of the jurors so drawn, shall be certified by the clerk of the
circuit court of the county designated to the clerk of the court wherein the trial
is to be. Thereupon, writ of venire facias shall be issued by the clerk of the
court wherein the trial is to be, directed to the sheriff of the county wherein
such jurors have been drawn, commanding him to summon the jurors so drawn
to attend for jury service in the county wherein the trial is to be upon the day
named in the writ. Said jurors shall attend for the purpose of the trial, and the
jury shall be selected in the manner provided by law. For their service, the
jurors so drawn shall be paid the per diem and mileage out of the same funds
that the jurors of the county wherein the trial is to be are paid.

RESOLUTION 23.
LANSFORD, PA., December 11, 1913.
To the officers and delegates of the Twenty-fourth Consecutive and First Bien-
nial Convention of the U. M. W. of A.:
At the regular meeting of Local Union No. 1738, United Mine Workers of
America, held on the above date, the following resolution was adopted and the
secretary instructed to forward same to Secretary Green for action by the
international convention:
Whereas events are so shaping themselves in this country and Canada that
the solidarity of the workers is necessary to cope with the arrogant methods
of capitalism, which is organized and well solidified; and
Whereas in past years, on account of the unorganized condition of numerous
coal-producing States, it was impossible to demonstrate our solidarity in any
general movement looking for the amelioration of the conditions of the
workers in the mines; and
Whereas believing that a general movement of the coal miners of this country
is practical, under certain conditions: Therefore, be it
439


===== [扫描序号 448] =====
440
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Resolved by the United Mine Workers of America, in convention assembled,
That the agitation and organizing of the unorganized States of this country
and Canada be continued, and, if possible, increased, so that in 1916, upon the
expiration of the contracts between the miners and operators of this country,
the mine workers will be in a position to make one general stand in this coun-
try and Canada and by paralyzing the wheels of industry on the eve of the
Presidential election make great headway along the line of political and eco-
nomic action; and be it further
Resolved, That the national executive board be empowered to take this mat-
ter up with organizations having some bearing on the mining industry, such
as railroad organizations, in order to arrive at some understanding with those
organizations whereby they will cooperate with us if general action is taken.
ANDREW FORGAY, President.
DENNIS SHOVELIN, Secretary.
THOMAS KENNEDY,
DANIEL NIKENS,

Delegates.
CASTLE SHANNON, PA., January 2, 1914.
TO THE OFFICERS AND DELEGATES OF THE TWENTY-FOURTH CONSECUTIVE AND
FIRST BIENNIAL CONVENTION OF THE U. M. W. OF A.:
Whereas the administration of John P. White and his colleagues in office has
seen a phenominal growth in the membership of the organization, having
greatly increased the membership in the three anthracite districts, firmly
established it in West Virginia, and made wonderful progress in other dis-
tricts; and
Whereas the progress has been made through the cooperation and assistance
of the international executive board and by an active and militant cam-
paign conducted by them which necessitated strikes and many sacrifices to
gain a foothold in the unorganized portions of the country: Therefore, be it
Resolved, That we indorse the policy of the international executive board
for prosecuting an aggressive campaign in the unorganized districts and advise
that the campaigns be continued until all the miners of the country are en-
rolled in the membership of the United Mine Workers of America.
JOHN MCCARTHEY,
DAVID ADAMSON,
FRANK KARKALLA,

(The contract so introduced in evidence appears printed in full, as follows:)
Washington, D. C., October 6, 1917.
The joint conference was called to order at 10 o'clock a. m., Saturday, October
6, Mr. John P. White in the chair.
Secretary Green read the following report of subcommittee to joint conference:
"The following agreement, supplemental to the existing interstate and district
agreements, is entered into with the hope and belief that the advance in wages
will result in an increased production of coal and the abolition of local strikes:
"It is agreed-
"First. That the mining prices for mining mine-run coal, pick and machine,
in the present contract be advanced 10 cents per ton.
"In the block coal fields of Indiana, the screen coal price to be advanced 124
cents per ton.
"Second. That all day labor and monthly men except trappers and other
boys be advanced $1.40 per day, trappers to be advanced 75 cents per day.
Boys now being paid more than $1.90 per day and less than men's wages shall be
advanced $1 per day.
"Third. That all yardage, dead work, and room turning be advanced 15
per cent.
"Fourth. Subject to the next biennial convention of the United Mine Workers
of America, the Mine Workers' representatives agree that the present contract
be extended during the continuation of the war, and not to exceed two years
from April 1, 1918.
"Whereas stoppage of work in violation of the agreement has become so
serious as to menace the success and perpetuity of the United Mine Workers
of America and our joint relations, this conference instructs the respective
district executive boards to meet the operators in their various districts for
the purpose of agreeing on a penalty clause where none now exists, and if
necessary meet to amend and strengthen existing clauses so as to make
the penalty more effective in preventing strikes and violations of agreements.
"All fines provided for in all agreements shall be automatically collected,
and any operator failing to collect and forward to properties such fine shall
pay a penalty of $2 for each employee subject to be fined, the same to be
collected and retained in the miners' district organization, and in no case shall
any fine be refunded except by mutual agreement of the accredited representa-
tives of the operators and miners.
"It is furthr agreed that where any employee enters suit in the civil courts
to recover any fine collected in accordance herewith the district organization
shall reimburse the operator for expense incurred on account of such suit.
"This agreement is subject to and will become effective only on the condition
that the selling price of coal shall be advanced by the United States Govern-
ment sufficient to cover the increased cost in the different districts affected,

statements of the officers of the mine workers' organization and members of
that organization, appearing in the mine workers' journal for the year 1914,
as illustrative of the policy of the organization in not only condoning violence,
but in directly advocating it.
(The document referred is here printed in full as follows:)
[Statement of Thomas Scott, official of union. Jan. 22, 1914.]
FROM COLORADO-WILL FIGHT TO THE DEATH.
FLORENCE, COLO., January 16.
The mass meeting of the Fremont County miners, held at Rockvale, Colo.,
January 15, was one of the largest meetings that has been held in the county


===== [扫描序号 453] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
445
for some time and shows that the boys are going to fight to a finish. We had
a large parade led by the Coal Creek and Rockvale bands. There were between
twelve and fifteen hundred men in the meeting which showed that there will
be no compromise as some self-styled committee of men in Fremont County
would try and make people believe, as the miners of Fremont County will not go
back to work unless we get full recognition of the union, and, if necessary, we
will sell our lives dearly to win this great battle and will never go back until
we get full justice. Everything is going along fine and the men are in the best
of spirits.
There is no production of coal to amount to anything in this county and the
scabs that they are getting in can't produce the goods.
There are two guards to every scab and the companies can not stand that
long. We all feel grateful to our brothers in the East for the way they are
coming to our relief.
THOS. SCOTT,
Vice President, District 15.
GERNER STATEMENT.
The unrest is spreading throughout this Nation and abroad. The tyranny
exercised by the money-mad of the world is arousing labor from its slumber,
and the day is not far distant when the citadels of oppression and the oppressors
will fall and right will make right.
Mount Olive, Ill., March 28, 1914.
[Letter from miners. Apr. 16, 1914.]
ARKANSAS MINERS DETERMINED--DEMAND UNION CONDITIONS.
FORT SMITH, ARK., April 7.
Unionists to-day have frustrated an attempt of the officials of the Bache
Denman Coal Co.'s mine, at Midland, near here, to strangle their organization
and operate under an "open shop" policy. Previous to this decision 200 union
men had been employed.
The miners met about a mile from the Mammoth Vein mine, as the mine is
known, and held meetings. They were addressed by a number of speakers, in-
cluding Miss Freda Hogan, daughter of Daniel Hogan, a prominent Socialist.
Following the meetings the men formed in line and marched to the mine.
Several clashes marked the efforts of the unionists to persuade the men in
the mine to join them. Following a disturbance in which two guards were hurt,
the miners joined the unionists and left the pit. A United States flag was
then hoisted from a near-by pole and the crown departed.
open shop
The company has announced its determination to inaugurate the “
policy at its six other mines in western Arkansas and eastern Oklahoma next
fall. At present they are closed for the summer.
[Apr. 30, 1914.]
FIGHTING CONTINUES WITH ASSAULT MADE ON CHANDLER-SEVEN PERSONS SAID
TO HAVE BEEN KILLED.
DENVER, COLO., April 26.
After an all-day battle between union and nonunion coal miners, the town of
Chandler was captured to-night by 1,100 strikers, according to messages reach-
ing the governor's office.
Seven men, including four mine guards, were said to have been killed in the
battle. The casualties in the strikers' ranks are unknown.

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
The cigarmakers' union of Denver voted money to send 500 armed men to
Trinidad and Ludlow to-morrow. These men will start at daybreak.
The Denver Federation of Labor this afternoon adopted a resolution to be
presented to the national organization, asking that each of the 2,000,000
union laborers in the United States be assessed 5 cents a month to provide
money and arms for the strikers.
RECRUITING OFFICE OPENED.
First of the Denver unions to answer the call was the cigarmakers' union,
which met last night and opened recruiting offices in the painters' hall. One
hundred and fifty men were present and 100 men expressed their willingness to
bear arms against the gunmen and in defense of the strikers in the southern
field.
[Statement by Harvey V. Deuell, staff correspondent of the Rocky Mountain News.]
With arms ready, both sides now await the coming of dawn, when, it is
forecast, the battle will be resumed with greater bloodshed than that which has
occurred. The militia, which yesterday drove the strikers from their tent
colony, and it is charged, fired it, involving thereby the greatest loss of life,
is preparing for a machine-gun sortie at daybreak from their position along
the Colorado & Southern Railroad tracks at each side of the Ludlow station.
On the surrounding hills, sheltered by rocks and bowlders, 400 strikers await
their coming, while their ranks are being swelled by grim-faced men who
tramped overland in the dark, carrying guns and ammunition from the neigh-
boring union camps. Italian, Greek, and Austrian miners have appealed to
their consular representatives for protection, and John McLennan, president
of the local union district, to-day wired the Red Cross in Denver to be prepared
to render aid.
On the outcome of the engagement to-morrow may depend the fate of the
strike. Both sides face it as a battle of death, with no thought of quarter
asked or received. A a late hour it was said here the battle could be averted
only by the arrival of reinforcements from Denver.
No train service through the war zone is permitted. Telephone communica-
tion has been reestablished. Maj. Hamrock is in command of the troops,
hemmed in on all sides by the striker lines, which extend back three miles.
Through this cordon only the dead wagon is allowed to pass.
EDITORIAL.
The workers of Colorado are now in arms.
They claim they have no State government to which they owe allegiance.
[News item. May 7, 1914.]
CHASE REFUSES TRUCE-NINE MILITIA KILLED,
WALSENBERG, April 29.
Nine militia gunmen were killed to-day by strikers after Gen. Chase had
refused to agree to a truce offered by leaders of the strikers.
Leaders, Peter Quinn and E. M. Snyder, in charge of the Walsenberg dis-
trict strikers, offered this morning to observe a truce until the United States
troops came if the gunmen militia would return to their tents. The militia com-
mander communicated with Gov. Ammons and Ammons with Gen. Chase about
the allowing of a truce. Chase and Ammons, anxious to do everything they
could for the operators before their gunmen militia should be deposed by the
Regulars, refused, and the gunmen militia tried to take the hogback, the
strikers' position, nine of the gunmen falling. Firing is heavy this afternoon.
Every mine in the Walsenberg district, with the exception of the Walsen
mine, the strongest fortified in the State, are in the hands of the strikers fol-


===== [扫描序号 455] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
447
lowing 30 hours of fighting after Jeff Farr and his gang of gunmen attacked
the strikers.
One hundred and fifty gunmen militia were brought here from Ludlow last
night and Gen. Chase instructed them to disarm the strikers and let the
gunmen retain their arms, which the strikers refused to allow.
[May 7, 1914.]
TWELVE DIE BEFORE UNITED STATES BROUGHT PEACE.
WALSENBERG, COLO., May 1.
Peace again reigned here and the 100 strikers who made it so hot for the
militia in a three-day battle that Gen. Chase sued for a truce over the phone
from Denver returned to their homes, taking their guns with them.
The total dead in the fighting was 10 gunmen, 1 militiaman, and 1 striker,
who was shot by his friends when he lost the identifying white handkerchief
they all wore on their arms.
[May 21, 1914.]
RIFLES SURRENDERED.
Three thousand rifles surrendered to soldiers.
[By United Press. ]
"TRINIDAD, COLO., May 14.
"More than 3,000 firearms and about 70,000 rounds of ammunition had been
surrendered to the Federal soldiers here at 5 p. m., Wednesday, when the time
for voluntary disarmament, according to Col. James Lockett's orders, expired.
"Army officers said they believed both sides had given up all available guns,
and a general search and seizure of arms was regarded as improbable.
"The striking miners gave up altogether 852 rifles, revolvers, and shotguns,
while the mine guards surrendered 5 machine guns and 840 rifles, revolvers,
and shotguns. Three hundred of the rifles turned in by the strikers were one ·
shipment from a New York manufacturer."
[Editorial from Machinists' Monthly Journal.]
"Industrial organization seems to be the only solution to the problem. Why
do the United Mine Workers of America and the Western Federation of
Miners insist that everyone employed in the mines shall belong to the miners'
union? Why do the brewery workers insist that all employed in connection
with that industry shall belong to the brewery workers? The answer is
simple. They must control the men in all branches in order to obtain justice
and fair play.
"We hope that the bills introduced by Congressman Evans and Senator
Martine will become the law and be enforced.
"If not, we will in the future have to protect ourselves by any means in our
power from being enslaved by armed hirelings of an extra government to which
we owe no allegiance.
"We realize that the tailor, the shoemaker, the miner, trained only in the
peaceful, useful pursuits of his calling, beneficial and necessary to all society,
is at a disadvantage when confronted by the trained mankillers.
64
But if organized society, the Government, will give us no protection from
these, if no restriction is placed on the equipment of private armies, hired by
and responsible only to the corporations who are willing to pay the price, we,
the workers, must organize a like force to meet this condition.
We
Against the trained fighters we shall have to bring trained fighters.
shall have to meet machine guns with machine guns. If we have to face force
we will face it with force.
"Which way, gentlemen ?"

Mr. BELCHER. The statement of Mr. Penna in proceedings of the Interstate
Joint Conference of the Coal Operators and Coal Miners at page 215, is as
follows:
"We are up against this competition, there is no use trying to get away from
it. In your nonunion fields your men work 10 hours a day as a minimum and
the maximum is unmentioned-anywhere from that to 25. For 10 hours, the day
men get about $1.50, and if they work 12 or 14 hours a day they may get a little
more. I don't know whether they do or not. The coal is weighed or measured.
and our experience has usually been that when coal is measured in coal cars
those cars seldom get any smaller. And you say you can not organize those
people and their products goes in direct competition with ours. One reason
you can not organize them is because they have certain methods to which they
resort to prevent organization."
The statement of Mr. Maurier on page 235 is as follows:
"Let organized labor announce to capital, to Wall Street, if you please, to
the great railroad corporations the operators of Ohio and Pennsylvania have
commenced to fight-that are independent, that are not controlled by the rail-
roads or anybody else. We are going to stand with them shoulder to shoulder,
and every time you invest a dollar in nonunion States we are going to help wrest
it away from you, we will help through the Government, we will help our
operators through our votes. When you commence that policy you will com-
mence to make that long productive line in West Virginia that has been growing
crumble and shrivel away.
"Now, gentlemen, this competition is here. It ought not to be a fight. I
don't like to hear men on that side of the house, with these conditions actually
staring them in the face, with that line indicated growing, and growing, and
growing. I don't like to hear them state, 'We are ready to strike for our
rights.' I want you to say, 'We are ready to strike for our rights,' and include
this side of the house. We are doing our duty, we are fighting to prevent West
Virginia increasing her tonnage; and if you treat some of your operators in
this field with the consideration they are entitled to you might get those same
operators to treat you with the same consideration when you come over to
West Virginia."
Mr. White, on page 245, says:
"We are anxious to establish the organization in the West Virginia fields
and the other nonunion fields as the gentlemen on the other side of the house
are to have us do so. But constantly holding that State up to ridicule will not
help us do it. I believe, on the contrary, it will militate against a final solution
of that problem. As has been pointed out times without number, West Vir-
ginia has no markets within the State, and if it were thoroughly organized of
necessity it would have to find markets outside the confines of is own com-
monwealth. Nature has favored the little mountain State with an inexhaustible
vein of coal, of high quality and good mining conditions; but the operators
there have been successful in defeating the aims and purposes of the United
Mine Workers to a large extent, although no one can deny that under the
various administrations of the organization every effort has been put forth to
try to break down the conditions that are complained of here by the other side."
Mr. Walker at page 256 states:
"Our desire is that every man who works in a mine in this country shall be
come a member of our organization, and before you make progress that will
have to come, before you gentlemen make the profit you wish that will have to
come."
The testimony of Mr. Chapman on page 274 is as follows:
"When we met in Chicago in 1898 and reestablished the interstate movement
the competition from nonunion fields was the element, gentlemen, that entered
into negotiations in the adoption of the scale that was made there. It was
agreed to by both sides, and the question also of the ability of the miner
to earn a fair day's wage for the labor he performed entered into it. At that
time the miners were receiving 56 cents per ton for producing coal. I made
motions in that convention that increased the day wage scale.
"It was understood in that convention, although it was not placed in the agree-
ment, that the miners of the competitive field of the four States were to
bring the nonunion fields up to the price paid for mining in those States, and
unless they secured the adoption of an 8-hour day at the next convention the
competitive field was to be relieved by these burdens. That was not in the
agreement. Unfortunately, gentlemen, the proceedings of that convention were

not published. If they were published it would be found that the president of
the United Mine Workers and the gentlemen who aided and assisted him in
bringing about the results there agreed that they should be relieved.
*
And the question of the prices of coal and the competition that existed were
the sole questions that entered into the discussion there. We were there for
weeks before we finally succeeded in accomplishing the results we did.
"Now, gentlemen, when you look at 1897 as compared with 1911 you will find
the nonunion States in competition with Ohio have increased their production.
The State from which the keenest competition comes has increased its produc-

that is the mother of the organization, the State whose operators have ever
been loyal to the organization, has increased barely 10 per cent a year. That
is the record for our State, while this one State has increased annually for
the 14 years, taking the average of 25 per cent, and more than double the
output of Ohio coal.
And the nonunion fields continue to increase as

union fields. And more are going, more are going."

Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Lewis, you say you were connected with the mine workers'
organization as an official for about 30 years?
Mr. LEWIS. Yes; that is, in different capacities.
Mr. BELCHER. What year did you leave this organization?
Mr. LEWIS. About 1914.
Mr. BELCHER. I will ask you whether in the year 1912 the mine workers'
organization furnished to its members arms and ammunition to be used in
strike troubles?
Mr. LEWIS. Not that I know of. I know the international didn't.
Mr. BELCHER. I will ask you whether at any time prior to 1912 the miners in
West Virginia, during these industrial disputes or strikes, armed themselves
with high-powered rifles and invaded districts where nonunion men were em-
ployed and used the same to force a recognition of their union?
Mr. LEWIS. I do not know, personally, that to be a fact, but according to a
conference I had with the governor of West Virginia, when he sent for me to
come down there to get some advice on the industrial situation, I learned there
was a military court holding sessions at Cabin Creek and those facts were
being brought out. I do not know who armed them.
Mr. BELCHER. During the whole time of your connection with the interna-
tional organization I will ask you whether or not the miners armed themselves,
banded together, and sought by force and use of arms to compel a recognition
of their organization?
Mr. LEWIS. I never knew that to take place any time I was connected with
the organization.
Mr. BELCHER. Prior to 1912?
Mr. LEWIS. Prior to 1912.
Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Lewis, I will ask you whether or not the relations between
the operators of the central competitive field and the officials of the mine
workers' organization in reference to the policy of West Virginia, or toward
West Virginia, exists to-day as it did in 1912 and for a number of years pre-
vious thereto.
Mr. LEWIS. I don't know as I just clearly understand your question. If you
have reference to the fact that their wage contracts in existence in the central
competitive field, there are closed-shop agreements, as there have been for sev-
eral years, and dues collected over the pay rolls, the dues and assessments of
the organization, as there has been for a number of years.
Mr. BELCHER. And the money and dues collected over the pay rolls of the
operators of the central competitive field is used to organize and has been used
to organize the nonunion mines of West Virginia, and is now being so used?
Mr. LEWIS. I presume that is true.
Mr. BELCHER. Is the attitude of the operators of the central competitive field
and the miners' representatives in reference to the competition of West Vir-
ginia coal the same now as it was in 1912 and for years previous thereto?
Mr. LEWIS. Well, I could not speak for the operators, because I have not dis-
cussed that matter with them. It is fair to assume that the operators in every
State are interested in the competition of coal from every other State.
Mr. BELCHER. Has the attitude of the miners' organization changed in any
respect to those matters?


===== [扫描序号 458] =====
450
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Mr. LEWIS. Well, the object of the miners' organization is to organize all
the nonunion miners of the country, which, of course, includes the organizing of.
the nonunion miners of West Virginia.
Mr. BELCHER. Was the contract entered into between the operators of the
central competitive field and the miners' representatives in 1917 violated?
Mr. LEWIS. In my opinion it was.
Mr. BELCHER. How was it violated?
Mr. LEWIS. It was violated by the demands made at the Cleveland special
convention in September, 1919; the contract in effect in 1917 was to run during
the period of the war, but not beyond April 1, 1920, and that was known as
the Garfield wage agreement; the Fuel Administrator was a party to it as
well as the miners and the operators, first in the central competitive field and
then in every coal-producing district in the country where wage agreements
were in effect. There are included in the demands of the Cleveland convention
three clauses that in my opinion recognize the existence of a contract. Those
sections are Nos. 3, 9, and 12.
Mr. BELCHER. I will ask you if ever at any time during the life of this
organization, since you have been familiar with its activities, it had abrogated a
contract in any convention before 1919?
Mr. LEWIS. It had not.
Mr. BELCHER. We now desire to introduce into the record in this case the
wage demands adopted by the Cleveland convention, submitted to the op-
erators at the Buffalo conference at Cleveland, Ohio, September 22, 1919.
(The wage demands above referred to are printed in full as follows:)
66 WAGE DEMANDS ADOPTED BY CLEVELAND CONVENTION; SUBMITTED TO OPERATORS
AT BUFFALO CONFERENCE.
66
'CLEVELAND, OHIO, September 22, 1919.
"To the Twenty-seventh Consecutive Constitutional and Fourth Biennial Con-
vention of the United Mine Workers of America-Greetings:
"We, your scale committee, to whom has been delegated the duty of drafting
a proposed wage scale, herewith submit for your consideration and acceptance
the following report:
"1. We recommend that this report be accepted as a substitute for all wage-
scale resolutions that have been presented to the convention.
"2. We recommend that this convention demand a 60 per cent increase to be
applicable to all classifications of day labor and to all tonnage, yardage, and
dead-work rates throughout the central competitive field.
"3. We recommend that this convention demand that all wage agreements
that are negotiated to replace existing agreements shall be based on a 6-hour
workday, from bank to bank, five days per week.
"4. That all day labor shall be paid time and a half for overtime and double
time for all work done on Sundays and legal holidays.
"5. That all agreements entered into by the United Mine Workers of America
shall have incorporated therein a provision providing for weekly pay days.
"6. That all double-shift work on the coal shall be abolished except as may
be necessary for development and ventilating purposes, and development for in-
creased tonnage shall not be regarded as being a reason for double-shift work;
it being understood that this rule shall not be applicable to new mines that
are in the process of development.
"7. That no automatic penalty clause shall be written into any agreement
entered into by the United Mine Workers of America.
"8. That all internal differences not covered by joint interstate agreement
shall be referred back to the respective district for adjustment.
"9. That all contracts in the bituminous field shall be declared as having
automatically expired November 1, 1919, and that no sectional settlement shall
be allowed and new contracts must run concurrently for a period of two years
in all bituminous districts under our jurisdiction.
"10. That agreements negotiated for outlying districts shall be retroactive
and become effective on the date upon which the agreement for the central
competitive field becomes effective.
"11. That no agreement for the central competitive fields shall be concluded
until after this convention has been reconvened and the agreement has been
ratified by the reconvened convention, which reconvened convention shall also
define a policy to be applicable to outlying districts, and that the reconvened


===== [扫描序号 459] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
451
convention shall be held in Indianapolis, Ind., on such date as may be desig-
nated by the resident international officers.
"12. We recommend that in event a satisfactory wage agreement is not se-
cured for the central competitive field before November 1, 1919, to replace the
one now in effect, that the international officials be authorized to and are hereby
instructed to call a general strike of all bituminous miners and mine workers
throughout the United States, the same to become effective November 1, 1919.
"13. That this convention go on record as favoring the ratification of the
wage demands made by the anthracite miners in their tristate convention, which
was held in Wilkes-Barre, Pa., from August 19 to 23, inclusive, and that we
pledge to the anthracite mine workers our power and influence in aiding them
to the fulfillment of their demands.
"Respectfully submitted,

District No. 7; C. J. Golden. District No. 9; Robert H. Harlin,
District No. 10; J. C. Lewis, District No. 13; Alex Howat.
District No. 74; George O. Johnson, District No. 15; Francis

Mr. BELCHER. Was there any further contract after the coal commission had

Mr. LEWIS. The award of the United States Bituminous Coal Commission be-
came a part of the wage agreement in the central competitive field and was rati-
fied by the miners' and operators' representatives, and then the advances were
applied to the other bituminous coal-producing districts throughout the country,
and in Illinois and Indiana, and a number of the day men became dissatisfied
with the terms of the contract and went on what they called "vacation strike,”
and then there was a meeting called of the operators and miners of the central
competitive field to see whether or not the contract provisions were going to be
complied with and these men ordered back to work. They failed to reach an
agreement. They failed to reach an agreement in the central competitive field
on the dissatisfaction existing in the minds of the day men who had, some of
them, been paid as much as $2 a day over and above the price named in the
award of the United States Bituminous Coal Commission. However, the matter
was settled by the Indiana operators and miners entering into a supplemental
agreement to pay the day men $1.50 a day more than the award, and that
stopped the strike in Indiana, Ohio, Illinois, and other fields.
Mr. BELCHER. In other words, the central competitive district adopted the
same contract as to the increase of the day wage?
Mr. LEWIS. By districts, but not as the central competitive field.

[From United Mine Workers Journal.]
CONVENTION INDORSES THE PLUMB RAILROAD PLAN AND VOTES FOR ALLIANCE WITH
RAILROAD WORKERS.
The Cleveland convention unanimously indorsed the Plumb plan for Govern-
ment ownership and management of railroads, and followed this action by in-
dorsing the idea of forming an alliance between the United Mine Workers of
America and the railroad workers. Indorsement of the Plumb plan followed a
speech by Glenn E. Plumb, of New York, author of the plan.
The proposition to call for an alliance between the miners and the railroad
workers came in a resolution from district 10, which was reported by the com-
mittee on resolutions.
An attempt by Delegate Harkness, of Illinois, to substitute a resolution to
call an all-industrial conference and commit the United Mine Workers to the
one big union idea was ruled out of order by Acting President Lewis. Harkness
appealed from the decision of the Chair, and the convention sustained the
decision of the Chair by a standing vote that was nearly unanimous. Only
half a dozen or so delegates voted in support of the one big union idea.
Immediately following the speech of Plumb, Robert H. Harlin, secretary of
the committee, offered the following resolution, which was unanimously adopted
by a standing vote:
"Resolved, That this convention of the United Mine Workers of America, after
listening with interest to the explanation of the Plumb plan for the nationaliza-
tion of the country's railroads, made by him, herewith gives its indorsement to

said plan and pledges the support of the United Mine Workers in the great
work undertaken by the railroad brotherhood to secure nationalization and
democratic management of railroads under the Plumb plan."
Secretary Harlin said a number of resolutions had been submitted to the
committee on resolutions favoring an effort to bring about an economic alliance
between the railroad brotherhoods and the United Mine Workers of America.
He said the committee wished to introduce the following resolution, which was
proposed from district 10:
SEATTLE, WASH., July 23, 1919.
To the officers and delegates of the twenty-seventh consecutive and fourth
biennial convention, United Mine Workers of America:
The World War has ended and the Central Powers have been compelled to
sign the terms of peace dictated by the victorious allied nations.
Labor in America was asked to support this war to a victorious conclusion
because it was a war against autocracy and was being waged for the purpose
of establishing throughout the world the principle of democracy. The workers
of America, like their fellow workers in the allied nations, responded to this
appeal, and the loyal and unstinted support of labor made possible the victory.
Millions of graves in Flanders and France attest the price paid by the men
of labor in the World War for victory and democracy.
Throughout the world the working people are now asking the fulfillment of
the promises that have been made to them, and a condition of world-wide
unrest prevails. This unrest is not the creation of bolshevists or anarchists,
but in the main it is the justifiable revolt of the workers against the evil
and well-nigh intolerable industrial conditions under which they have been
compelled to work. In every country the workers are striving to strengthen
their economic power, because they realize their ability to use with telling
force the power of their organizations will be a stronger safeguard in bringing
about better conditions of labor and life than war-time pledges that may
be conveniently forgotten now that the crisis has passed.
We note the wonderful progress that has been made by the miners of Great
Britain and the tremendous economic power that rests in the organization known
as the "triple alliance." This allegiance between the miners' union, the
railway men's union, and the transport workers' union wields the power to
paralyze the industrial life of Britain, and it is now being used to eradicate
from the industries over which it holds jurisdiction the evil conditions of
employment, the long hours, and the low wages under which the workers have
been compelled to work and live.
We deem the time has arrived when the workers of America should adopt
some forward-looking policy to strengthen their economic power, and realizing
as we do that any action that seeks to materially improve the conditions of
labor in America must be nation-wide in scope and not confined to any
particular section of the country, we ask the adoption of the following resolu-
tion by the international convention of the United Mine Workers of America:
"Resolved, That this convention instruct the resident officers and the inter-
national executive board to endeavor to bring about a conference with the
railway workers' organizations for the purpose of formulating an alliance
whereby the organized workers in these two great basic industries may act
jointly on all matters of mutual interest, such as the democratic administra-
tion of these industries, with the workers having equal representation in the
management under a system of nationalization, and on all other matters where
the interest of the workers in these industries may be advanced by joint
action: And be it further
"Resolved, That in the conference above suggested consideration be given to
further alliances between organizations of labor in the basic industries with
a view to strengthening the economic power of labor in the fight that is now
being waged and which is destined to continue until the working people of
America have been granted that measure of industrial democracy to which
they are so justly entitled."
On behalf of the district board.
Indorsed by local union 2970.
ROBERT H. HARLIN, President.
BEN FARRIMOND, Vice President.
ERNEST NEWSHAM, Secretary Treasurer.
The resolution was adopted by a unanimous rising vote.

The CHAIRMAN. Let me ask you what is your understanding of "nationali
zation of mines"?
Mr. LEWIS. The nationalization of mines?
The CHAIRMAN. Yes.
Mr. LEWIS. My understanding is, nationalization of mines means that the
Government shall take over the mines and operate them.
The CHAIRMAN. And do you understand that the United Mine Workers of
America believe in that?
Mr. LEWIS. Yes, sir. Well, I don't know, Mr. Chairman, whether it is fair
to say that the United Mine Workers of the country believe in that. The
proposition, I do not think, has been submitted to them on a referendum vote.
However, their representatives in convention assembled have ratified that
principle.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, that would be contrary to this doctrine of full social
value for their services?
Mr. LEWIS. Well, the argument used is that the sure way of getting the
full social value for their labor is for the Government to operate the mines.
That eliminates everybody except the Government and the employees.
The CHAIRMAN. And that is what you understand by nationalization of the
mines?
Mr. LEWIS. That is what I understand by nationalization of the mines, and
I think that is what everybody else will admit it means.
The CHAIRMAN. Have you heard that doctrine advocated by any of the leaders
of the United Mine Workers?
Mr. LEWIS. I have.
The CHAIRMAN. How were the mines to be paid for?
Mr. LEWIS. That phase of it has not come up; that is, so far as I know, Mr.
Chairman.

(The sections of the 1918 Code of West Virginia, so offered in evidence, are
here printed in full, as follows:)
"SEC. 34. Intimidation of workmen; lawful associations.-Nor shall any per-
son or persons, or combination of persons, by force, threats, menaces, or in-
timidation of any kind, prevent, or attempt to prevent, from working in or
about any m ne, any person or persons who have the lawful right to work in
or about the same, and who desire so to work; but this provision shall not
be so construed as to prevent any two or more persons from associating to-
gether under the name of knights of labor, or any other name they may
desire, for any lawful purpose, or for us ng moral suasion or lawful argument,
to induce anyone not to work in and about any mine. Any person or persons
who shall violate the provisions of this section shall, upon conviction, be fined
not less than $50 nor more than $500, or be imprisoned in the county jail not
less than 10 days nor more than 90 days, in the discretion of the court.
1887, ch. 50; 1890, ch. 9; 1907, ch. 78; 1915, ch. 10, sec. 42.)
(Acts
"SEC. 47. Weighing and measuring coal; appliances.-It shall be the duty of
every corporation, company, or person engaged in the business of mining and
selling coal by weight or measure, to procure and constantly keep on hand at
the proper place, the necessary scales and measures and whatever else may be
necessary, to correctly weigh and measure the coal as mined by such corpora-
tion, company or person. And it shall be the duty of the sealer of weights
and measures for every county in which coal is so mined and sold to visit each
coal mine operated therein, and, where such scales and measures are kept, at
least once in each year, and test the correctness of such scales and measures.
The owner or operator of such coal mine or any two or more of the miners
working therein, may in writing require his attendance at the place where such
scales and measures are kept, at other times, in order to test the correctness
thereof, and it shall be his duty to comply with such requests as soon as he
can after receiving such request. If his attendance is required by the owner or
operator of such mine, or if by the miners working therein, and the scales or
measures tested be found not to be correct, his fees shall be paid by the
owner or operator of such mine, and if his attendance be required by the miners
and the scales or measures tested be found to be correct his fees shall be paid
by them. If in any such county there be no sealer of weights and measures,
the duties herein required to be done and performed by such sealer shall be
done and performed by the inspector of mines for the district of which such
county forms a part. (Acts 1891, ch. 82, sec. 1.)
SEC. 48. Same; cars.-Each car used by any such corporation, company, or
person in removing coal from any coal mine, shall be numbered by consecutive
numbers plainly marked, and placed and kept thereon as long as such car is
so used. And if the coal from such mine is mined, and the miners are paid
according to the weight thereof for mining the same, every such car so used
shall be weighed upon such tested scales, and the weight thereof shall be
plainly marked and placed thereon as long as such car shall be used as afore-
said. If the coal at any such mine is mined, and the miners thereof are paid
for mining the same by measure, the number of bushels of coal such car will
hold when loaded to its capacity, shall also be plainly marked, and placed and
kept thereon as long as such car is so used as aforesaid. And no car shall be
used for the purpose aforesaid, after 90 days from the time this act takes effect,
until the provisions of this section are complied with. (Acts 1891, ch. 82,
sec. 2.)


===== [扫描序号 468] =====
460
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
"SEC. 49. Same; weighing in car before screening.-All coal so mined and
paid for by weight, shall be weighed in the car in which it is removed from the
mine before it is screened, and shall be paid for according to the weight so
ascertained, at such price per ton as may be agreed on by such owner or oper-
ator and the miners who mined the same. And coal mined and paid for by
measure, shall be paid for according to the number of bushels marked upon
each car in which it is removed from the mine, and before it is screened, and
the price paid for each bushel so ascertained shall be such as may be agreed
on as aforesaid. (Acts 1891, ch. 82, sec. 3.)
“SEC. 55. Weighing and measuring products where wages depend on produc-
tion; check weighman.-Where the amount of wages paid to any of the persons
employed in any manufacturing, mining, or otherwise public enterprise employ-
ing labor, depend upon the amount produced by weight or measure, the persons,
so employed may, at their own cost, station or appoint at each place appointed
for the weighing or measuring, of the products of their labor a check weighman
or measurer, who shall in all cases be appointed by a majority ballot of the
workmen employed at the works where he is appointed to act as such check
weighman or measurer. (Acts 1901, ch. 20, sec. 1.)"

Mr. VINSON. Your name is D. C. Kennedy?

America?
Mr. KENNEDY. I was.
The CHAIRMAN. For how long?
Mr. KENNEDY. About five years.
Mr. VINSON. Are you now a member of that organization?
Mr. KENNEDY. I am not.
Mr. VINSON. What position do you occupy now, Mr. Kennedy?
Mr. KENNEDY. I am secretary of the Kanawha Coal Operators' Association.
Mr. VINSON. And does the Kanawha Coal Operators' Association include mines
lying north of the Kanawha River as well as south?
Mr. KENNEDY. It does.
Mr. VINSON. And it includes the Paint and the Cabin Creek mines?
Mr. KENNEDY. It does.
Mr. VINSON. Are you the same D. C. Kennedy that gave testimony along the
lines of what Mr. Lewis has stated to this committee in the Paint and Cabin
Creek investigation?
Mr. KENNEDY. I am.
Mr. VINSON. You have heard Mr. Lewis's statement in regard to the breach
of contract between the United Mine Workers' organization and the New River
operators, where there was a general strike called-between the United Mine
Workers of America and the New River operators, of which association he is
the secretary. Were those same contracts or kindred contracts broken by the
United Mine Workers of America in your district?
Mr. KENNEDY. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. If I understand then, Mr. Kennedy, in the Kanawha Coal Oper-
ators' district there was a general strike called to take effect the 1st of November,
1919?
Mr. KENNEDY. There was.
Mr. VINSON. Who made that general call for that strike?
Mr. KENNEDY. I think that the international organization issued the call, and
later it was supplemented by the call from the different organizations.
Mr. VINSON. At that time, or prior to the calling of that strike, was there any
demand made by the organization or any of its representatives upon the oper-
ators to adjust any questions or difficulties that might be between them?
Mr. KENNEDY. There were not.
Mr. VINSON. All the operators knew was that this call came before you were
advised of it, and you were later advised of it, as I understand?
Mr. KENNEDY. That is right.
Mr. VINSON. How long were the mines closed?
Mr. KENNEDY. About six weeks.

Mr. KENNEDY. I so understand it.
Mr. VINSON. That is your understanding?
Mr. KENNEDY. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. And it is your understanding that each delegate has one vote?
Mr. KENNEDY. Yes, sir.

Mr. KENNEDY. The forces on the one side say "We have a right to organize."

The CHAIRMAN. What have you to say as to the question of maintaining a

Mr. KENNEDY. We think we have had that in West Virginia.
The CHAIRMAN. I do not mean the Republican Party; I mean the republican

Mr. KENNEDY. Well, the republican form of government.
The CHAIRMAN. You feel there is no infringement of the Constitution as to

Mr. KENNEDY. Senator, I am not familiar with everything that has gone on
in these outside districts. The great question down there, as I understand it,
is that one side says that they have a right to go into another plant, a nonunion
plant, and organize it. The operator in the nonunion plant says he has a right
to keep them out, both sides taking the same position.
The CHAIRMAN. Well, that is the solution of that? Is that the irresistible
force meeting the immovable object?
Mr. KENNEDY. My solution of that proposition, Mr. Senator, is this, that if the
men have a right to organize, by the same token the operator has a right not to
recognize him, if he wants to.

SUNDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1921.
UNITED STATES SENATE,
COMMITTEE OF EDUCATION AND LABOR,
Williamson, W. Va.
Senators Kenyon (chairman) and Shortridge of the Subcommittee of the
Committee on Education and Labor of the United States Senate left Washing-
ton at 3.15 p. m. Saturday, September 17, 1921, for Williamson, W. Va., arriv-
ing at Williamson at 12.15, Sunday, September 18.
During the afternoon of the 18th the committee visited the Lick Creek tent
colony, Williamson, at which time and place the following statements were
taken.
STATEMENT OF GEORGE ECHOLS (COLORED), ONE OF THE
STRIKERS.
The CHAIRMAN. What is your name?
Mr. ECHOLS. George Echols.
The CHAIRMAN. And you live in this tent here?
Mr. ECHOLS. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. How many are there around in these various tents?
Mr. ECHOLS. I suppose there is something like I could not tell you, and I
have not an estimate of our men here.
The CHAIRMAN. How long have you been here?
Mr. ECHOLS. I have been here about five months now.
The CHAIRMAN. Were you working in the mines?
Mr. ECHOLS. I used to; yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And all these people in these tents, did they use to work in
the mines?
Mr. ECHOLS. Yes, sir; all of these are miners from the camps here.
The CHAIRMAN. Where did you come from when you came to work here?
Mr. ECHOLS. I came here from Columbus, Ohio. I have been here four years,
very nearly five.
The CHAIRMAN. You have been here nearly five years?
Mr. ECHOLS. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And you were born in this country, were you?
Mr. ECHOLS. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Where were you born?
Mr. ECHOLS. I was born in eastern Virginia. I was born at Chatham, Va.
The CHAIRMAN. And what is the trouble down here anyway?
Mr. ECHOLS. I will tell you. The miners have asked the contractors or op-
erators to give them an opportunity to weigh the coal, and they announced that
they will not weigh it. They say that whenever we load a load of coal, then
that is all that that amounts to, that it does not make any difference. We
may load 2 tons to a car and they may say it is a ton and a half or two tons.
The CHAIRMAN. Do they pay you by the ton?
Mr. ECHOLS. They promised to pay us by the ton but they don't do it. They
promised according to whatever the coal is to pay us by the ton, and we want
them to put it on the scales. All they do is to say that so and so much, and
we have to take it.
We feel we want to give and take, and we want them to
measure it for us, that is, weigh it, and we are paid for whatever they like
to pay us or feel like paying us, and they give it out at the office, they give
us the balance. We pay them for the lights and the fuel and then the supplies,
and whatever they say at the office they give us the balance. We always felt
that we ought to have the coal weighed. I have loaded coal when I got $1.25
a car, and if we had the scales there I would get as much as $4 a car.
The CHAIRMAN. Well, what seems to have been the trouble with you? Why
are you not working?
469


===== [扫描序号 478] =====
470
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Mr. ECHOLS. Well, I think it is because I signed up with the union.
The CHAIRMAN. In other words, you were a union man?
Mr. ECHOLS. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And why did you quit?
Mr. ECHOLS. I was discharged. I was vice president of the local, and many
excuses, but if I am sitting in a church I try to do the thing as near right as
I can according to the agreement. There is some things that we can not stand
for. I was raised a slave. My master and my mistress called me and I
answered, and I know the time when I was a slave, and I felt just like we feel
now. There have been several of the constabulary out this morning. There is a
car there now that went down and whirled against a tent [indicating a car being
whirled by another passing by the road]. You will notice it when you get
down there. You can see those tents down there now. You can see the tents
that are out, too.
The CHAIRMAN. Who cut your tents?
Mr. ECHOLS. These men who we call the State constabulary, those men
came out and they cut the tents. They came out here twice. They just rounded
up the men and they shot from over across the other side [indicating] and they
took this man here, and they dragged him into town.
The CHAIRMAN. When was that?
Mr. ECHOLS. That was in August or July. We have had quite a time trying
to live here. They come in here, and they round them up, and they put as
many as 67 men and turn them into town. They would come out here and
walk up and down and talk at us in any way they want to. You know our rights
under the Constitution, that no man should be condemned or jailed until we
have had a free and impartial trial. We claim to be citizens of the United
States and we ask for the rights of citizenship; we claim to be loyal to our
country, and we are loyal to our country, and all we ask is that we shall have
our rights. We claim that we are citizens of the United States of America,
according to the amendment to the Constitution. You know that that guaran-
tees us free and equal rights and that is all we ask.
The CHAIRMAN. Just what rights do you feel are getting away from you?
Mr. ECHOLS. We are denied the right of anything to protect ourselves with.
They will not let us have a gun. If we get together and are talking, we are
ordered to scatter, and to move out. If we go out for a walk, two by two, we
are ordered to scatter and to move out. If we go to town we have to go in
such a way that we have to tell our wives good-by, for we know that we might
not come back, and that we may be under lock and key. There has never been
such a thing as these 300 men that come out here, there has never been any-
thing like that, and when they came out here they would drive them like sheep,
as they did before the Constitution prohibited slavery.
The CHAIRMAN. Who do you mean did that?
Mr. ECHOLS. Some of these gunmen. If you will go into town you will find
them. They are called constabulary. In other words, when I first heard of
them they were called the Baldwins. I know that they are very officious, and
they take away from us our rights and privileges, and they would not allow me
to speak as I am speaking to you now. I do not believe that those men think
of citizenship at all. The United Workmen of America have privileges which
are guaranteed by the United States, and we have rights to protect us, both
the black and the white, but they do not regard those rights at all. They take
those privileges away from us. Now, we are asking you to give them back to
Let us be free men. Let us stand equal. I do not mean that there is any
prejudice against the colored people here.
us.
The CHAIRMAN. How many people are colored?
Mr. ECHOLS. There are not so many colored here. I don't suppose that there
are more than 150. I don't know. I have never taken an estimate of the men.
The CHAIRMAN. And how are all these people around here living? Does the
union support them?
Mr. ECHOLS. Yes; the union supports them. The union supports some of these
men that you see in tents and some others in houses.
The CHAIRMAN. How does it happen that this particular tent here [indicating]
is all slashed up and the other ones are not?
Mr. ECHOLS. That was slashed by those men.
them.
These men came here and cut
The CHAIRMAN. And what made them do that? What were you doing?
Mr. ECHOLS. Why, I don't know, except that they were mad. Nobody didn't
ask them to molest us. They just come in here and they slashed those tents.

The CHAIRMAN. What is the system as to the measuring of the work that is

STATEMENT OF MR. R. C. KIRK.
Mr. KIRK. There were some places around where they had nine hours and
some places where they had eight hours, and the most of the places, the place
where I was working, was working nine hours at the time I was called out.
The CHAIRMAN. You went out and went away; at the time you went to work,
how were the wages measured?
Mr. KIRK. It was by the car. The place where I was working was just across
the river at the mouth of Pond Creek, and I was working for the Pond Creek
By-Products Co. We had a car there that would hold something like 3 tons, and
we were getting, on the 15th day of March, we were getting 80 cents a car, and
on the 16th of March we got a raise of 10 cents a car, making 90 cents a car, and
on the 1st of April-
The CHAIRMAN (interrupting). That is this year?
Mr. KIRK. Last year.
And on the 1st day of April it was put back to 80
cents a car again. They raised the rate of the car to $1.25, and on another car
it was considerably bigger than the car that was a 3-ton car. They paid $1.25
for a while, and after they came out on the strike they raised the price of the
car again, and I don't know what they are doing now.
The CHAIRMAN. You don't know what they are doing now?
Mr. KIRK. No, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What did you call a full car? You filled it up level, did
you?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir.
Senator
SHORTRIDGE. Was there anybody there whose business it was to
measure it and see that it was full, or whether it was overcrowded?
Mr. KIRK. There was not any inspector or regulations, and they would not
allow it to come out light. If it came out light it was docked light.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What are they paying now?
Mr. KIRK. They are paying about $3 and something for day labor.
The CHAIRMAN. For eight hours?
Mr. KIRK. Eight hours. They call it 8 hours, but if you are working on the
tipple you have got to stay until you clean up if it is 11 hours or whatever it
may be, and it is called 8 hours. I know that. I have done that myself, and
lots of time I have put in 9 hours and 10 hours and 11 hours, and I have been
paid for 8 hours.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Don't they pay you by the ton or by the car?
Mr. KIRK. The men who are employed up on the tipple, doing work on the
tipple and dumping coal is employed by the day, and the miners are paid by
the car. That is piecework, paid by the car.
The CHAIRMAN. And how do you get it weighed?
Mr. KIRK. We had no way of getting at it and we never had any system in
that regard. The miner never knew how much that car held. Some say
that it is a ton and three-quarters a car, but it will measure something like 50
cubic feet. We never knew what the car would hold, the weight or the measure-
ment of it, and it would be because the majority of the miners in this country
have been educated enough to figure out what a car is-
Senator SHORTRIDGE (interrupting). The custom was to pay by the car, as I
understand you?
Mr. KIRK. Yes.
