Senator SHORTRIDGE. And has that been a custom for a good many years?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir; for a good many years, it has always been the custom
here.
The CHAIRMAN. And how is it at the union mines? What is the custom there?
Mr. KIRK. The union mines pay by weight or measurement; the coal is
weighed. You take a car, if they have not got a scale at the plant, they take
scales there and they take the coal out and they weigh it as it is loaded level
full. The contents of that car are weighed. They weigh maybe three or four
or five of those cars, and they average those cars, and bring it to an average ton-
nage basis on which to pay in that way.
The CHAIRMAN. And what would you average per day? What is your average
daily wage?
Mr. KIRK. When I was loading coal I would average about eight cars of coal.
The CHAIRMAN. And that would bring you how much?
Mr. KIRK. I was getting a dollar a car. My total earnings would be about $8
a day, but my net earnings would fall down to $3 a day and $3.50 a day.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. How is that?
Mr. KIRK. Well, you see I would have to pay for my dynamite, the paper,
the powder, and everything of that kind.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Well, when you would run out eight cars a day, when
you would load that many, it would be $8 a day, wouldn't it?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir; but there would be $3.50 or $4.50 a day of expenses to be
taken out of that.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. For what?
Mr. KIRK. I would pay for the paper and the dynamite and the monodel, the
paper, the fuse, the tools, and everything of that kind.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Do you mean by that that you would furnish your own
tools?
Mr. KIRK. I would furnish my own tools.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. NOW, which do you think is the better plan for pay-
ment, by the car or by the weight?
Mr. KIRK. Why, I think that the weight system would be more satisfactory,
because if we have a weight system and if we have a check weighman, and have a
man to look after our part of it, to look after our interests, then we would be
satisfied.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Was that uatter taken up by the boys with the manger
of the company and discussed as to which way would be the better plan?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir; it has been taken up time and again, and he has been
told, or the company has been told, that we wanted a check weighman through-
out this field.
Sentor SHORTRIDGE. And that is the same system of paying by the carload, is
it, throughout here?
Mr. ECHOLS. Yes, sir; that is the way they are paying.
The CHAIRMAN. And is that one of the causes which led up to the strike?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir; I guess that that is the chief thing.
The CHAIRMAN. And you thought that you were not being paid for all that
you did; is that it?
Mr. KIRK. Yes; I was satisfied that we were not getting paid for what we were
doing.
The CHAIRMAN. And what else was there that led to the strike? What else
was there that happened that led up to the strike?
Mr. KIRK. Well, this guard system was just about as strong and just about
as unsatisfactory as the use of the check weighman. The guard system around
here was very objectionable to the men, and another thing, that we did not
have the free right to trade in the independent stores.
The CHAIRMAN. Did not you not have the right to buy wherever you wished?
Mr. KIRK. No; we did not. I attempted to do so, and I traded at independent
stores a time or two, and I was discharged off of the job and I was unable to get
any details of why I was discharged, and I was satisfied that that was the cause
of my discharge.
The CHAIRMAN. That was the reason for your discharge, so you think?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. You wanted the free right to trade wherever you pleased?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, what about this mine-guard system?
Mr. KIRK. Well, those are the private officers, men who are carrying guns.
If a man, if anything should happen that a man would not be working on any.

The CHAIRMAN. Now, what else? What other complaints did you have?

The CHAIRMAN. Now, when you joined the union, were you discharged from
the mine?
Mr. KIRK. I was discharged the next day. I joined the union one night and
by next morning a notice was put up that all of the men that had joined the
un on or affiliated with the union in any way to come to the office and get their
money.
The CHAIRMAN. To come to the office and get their money?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. In other words, you were discharged?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And how many were you that were discharged?
Mr. KIRK. I think there were six discharged at the same time that I was dis-
charged.
The CHAIRMAN. And what company was that that you were with at that time?
Mr. KIRK. Pond Creek By-Products Co. I was working for them at that
time; but I think it is now the Norfolk & Western.
The CHAIRMAN. Does the Norfolk & Western run some of the mines around
here?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir; since the strike came on, on the border, on the Kentucky
side.
The CHAIRMAN. Has there been any shooting at these mine guards by the
miners?
Mr. KIRK. I have never seen any, but I heard it reported; but I have never
seen any of the miners doing any of the shooting at all.
The CHAIRMAN. And has there been any burning up of any of the mine
property?
Mr. KIRK. I have heard that reported, too, but I do not think that the
miners did that at all. It was done by other sources and the miners got the
credit for it.
The CHAIRMAN. And did the miners try to stop that?
Mr. KIRK. Yes, sir; in the first place, when we came out on a strike, the
organization offered to put a watchman at each operation, and asked the com-
pany to put a watchman there, and let the brotherhood put a watchman there at
their plant to assure them that there would not be any violence of the prop-
erty. They would not have a union man on the job at all, under any circum-
stances, so they said.
The CHAIRMAN. As I understand it, none of the mines in this country are
unionized.
Mr. KIRK. Some of the small operations have signed up; but I do not know
whether they are operating now or not. We had a mine at the mouth of Wil-
liamson Hollow, the Superior Thacker. That was signed up, and they were
working on the 1st of January, and it was supposed to be an open shop; but
they would not have a union man there.
The CHAIRMAN. And did the union men object to the nonunion men working
with them in those mines?
Mr. KIRK. No, sir; they did not object.
The CHAIRMAN. You do not claim that a man has not a right to earn his
living because he does not belong to the union?
Mr. KIRK. No, sir; all we are working for is for equal rights.
The CHAIRMAN. As I understand it, you desire to have the right to join
a union, if you want to, but you do not think that a man should be compelled
to join a union if he does not want to?

STATEMENT OF RICHARD COMBES.
The CHAIRMAN. You were born here, were you, Mr. Combes?
Mr. COMBES. I was born in North Carolina and raised in Virginia.
The CHAIRMAN. What is the matter here? Why are the people living in these
tents?
Mr. COMBES. Because they could not get nothing for their labor. I made from
$3 to $4 a day.
The CHAIRMAN. You made from $3 to $4 a day?
Mr. COMBES. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. You are not getting as much as that now, are you, to live on?
Mr. COMBES. No; but we are living better. Part of the time we had enough
to eat and part of the time we did not have enough to eat, and we worked every
day.
The CHAIRMAN. What are the things that you complain of?
Mr. COMBES. We were not getting enough for the coal that we were mining.
The CHAIRMAN. And do you complain that the coal that you were mining
was not weighed properly?
Mr. COMBES. It was not weighed at all. The coal was loaded, and they paid
you whatever they pleased.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, these men joining the union; what has that to do with
it? Has that something to do with it?
Mr. COMBES. It has had right smart to do with it. If they were union, if they
were union, if they belonged to the union, you could get the coal weighed, and
you could get paid for what you do.
The CHAIRMAN. Then the men feel that if they join the union they will have
the coal weighed properly, and they would get better pay; is that right?
Mr. COMBES. Yes, sir.

The CHAIRMAN. Now, will you tell us about the 14th of June?
Mr. KIRK. About 10 o'clock in the morning of the 14th of June there was two
automobiles drove up to the point out [indicating on the road] loaded with
so-called State police and deputy sheriffs, and Alexander Pinson and Maj. Davis
accompanied those fellows. A part of them, all of them, got out of the cars
there [indicating] and commenced shooting, but whether or not they were
shooting in our tents we do not know.
The CHAIRMAN. And were they near your tents?
Mr. KIRK. They were in front of the tent colony in the valley, but later from
the position that Pinson was standing I found a bullet in the trunk of a tree,
and Mr. P.nson must have been shooting toward the ground, and some of them
were shooting over the tops of the houses, and some over the tent colony.
Later in the day, something like four or five hundred men came up here and
lined the road around here and got in the woods, and we did not know what it
meant. We supposed that they were going up there shooting off in the air.
Some of us went over to the river bank; we were all fixing to go in bathing
when they came back the second time, and they lined up along this road [indi-
cating] and along that hillside [indicating] and on this hill and over in there
[indicating], and some of the fellows tried to get into the woods, you know,
and tried to get up into the hills out of the way. They gathered everybody up,
the women and the children, and all of the men that they could get hold of at
the time and got them down in there [indicating], and some of the fellows
went off in the hills in order to stay in the clear, and these fellows had auto-
matic rifles and pistols, and they had a machine gun, or a submachine gun, we
think, and this man Breedlove that was killed was on the hillside over there
[indicating].
The CHAIRMAN. Tell us how he was killed?
66
Mr. KIRK. He was on the hillside over there with a boy about 13 years old
with him. The boy said to him, 'Don't run off and leave me." Alec stopped
there then, and a fellow ran up there on the side of the hill where some of
them were shooting down here, and Alec threw up his hands and told him that
he surrendered, and then this one fellow walked up to him and said, so this
boy says, "that you have two minutes to live, and if you have anything to say,
say it now," and this boy says that Alec threw up his hands and he said, "Lord,
have mercy on me, and fell.
The CHAIRMAN. Who is this boy that was with him?
Mr. KIRK. It was Will Hodge, and he is at Huntington. The boy claims the
man said, "Lord, have mercy on me" and the man shot, fired the shot, and
he grabbed a little bush and sank over, and he said, "Lord, I am killed."
Another fellow was at the bottom of the hill shooting up, and the man saw
him shoot, and he was hurt, and he felt very bad that he had shot one of his
own men.
The CHAIRMAN. When was that?
Mr. KIRK. On the 14th of June of this year.
The CHAIRMAN. What had this man been doing who had been shot-this man
Breedlove?
Mr. KIRK. He had not been doing anything. He was trying to get out of the

[indicating], and they took all of us fellows and they bunched us around with
guns and put us in the city hall down in town, and we were there around 3.20
o'clock on the 14th of June.
In that city hall where they put us there was not a chair or a bench or a box
or anything that we would sit on but the floor. There was not anything, and
there was a bunch there of 46 men. There was not anything in there to drink
out of. We all had to drink out of a spigot, and every time that we drank the
water would be wasted on the floor. The water had accumulated something

STATEMENT OF BUD FRANCIS.
Mr. FRANCIS. On the 1st day of June, which was on Saturday, two State
police got some men, and the State police and men looked into the camps, and
they went into Mr. Kid Davis's house and they knocked the bed springs out
from under his wife's head, and then on Sunday they came back here and got
52 boys, and they sent me to Welch, and as we went along the train got over
here; the State police arrested me and a fellow by the name of Emery Parsley,
and the State police had us handcuffed and they said, Go in and 'shoot these
tents to hell." I said, "My wife is in the tent, and please go in and notify my
wife to get out." They said they would.
On the 14th of June they came up here and were shooting, and we were get-
ting breakfast and we did not know anything about it until then, and my wife
grabbed the baby and she took his clothes and started to the tent, and some
of the State police and deputy sheriffs they says, "Where are you going?
She said, "I am going to town." He said, "No; you are not going; get to hell
back up the road."
They drove her back and she went up to Uncle Bud Maynard's. There she
met another man and they said, "Where are you going?" She said. "Up the
creek." They said, “No; you are not. Get back down out of the hill." She
says. "Well, I don't know where to go." They abused her and left her up
there and they poured out all of her groceries and poured kerosene in the baby's
milk, and they busted up her rocking chair and broke up pretty nearly all of
the furniture in the tent. She had to do without anything to eat from that
morning until along at night when she went to town, and the United Mine
Workers of America took her to a hotel and got her her supper, and they had
me in jail at that time.

man. He said, “Are you a union man?" I said, "Yes, sir."
He said, "We know you."
I said "These men ought to know me, for you have arrested me here three
times for nothing."
He said You are going over the hill this time." I laughed. He put me in
jail and he carried me to Welch and kept me there for 48 days, and they
would not give me train fare to come back now with to get me away from
there.
The CHAIRMAN. Had you been fighting at all?
Mr. REED. No, sir; I hadn't done a thing in the world.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. How old are you?
Mr. REED. Twenty-seven,
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And were you born in this country?
Mr. REED. I was born in Alabama. I came into this country when I was
16 years old-just a boy.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Is there any provision made for the colored children
here to go to school?
Mr. REED. No.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. How about the other white school?
Mr. REED. That was started; we started there last Monday morning.
A VOICE. Some of the colored children are going to town.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. You men understand that what we want is the truth
here.
Mr. REED. That is what we want. I can show you scars on my head which
were put in there by the Baldwin-Felts men in 1917. There was four of them
that jumped on me until they thought me dead, but I didn't die. They kicked
two or three ribs loose-two or three of them-on Cabin Creek. I hadn't
done a thing on earth. The way it was I was going up the road, and there
was some fellow that got full, and he was a friend of mine-that is, he was
not a friend, but I just knew him-and he stayed down there, and I walked
up, and he was full, and I took some of his clothes from him in order that
he wouldn't lose them.

It got kind of chilly, and I slipped it on me, and I walked on up the road.

slipped on his coat, and I wore it up the road and they walked out and said,
What are you doing prowling around up here?" I told them that I was not-

He said "Don't give me none of your head." Then he hit me with the
gun, and he cut a place in the back of my head, and he told me to go on up the
road and never come back any more. That is the trouble with this country
to-day-that it is ruled by gunmen.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. In some of the States, in some of the districts, some of

Mr. REED. I suppose they would. If the men would not join the union-

Coal Co., and when they granted the 27-cent raise to the miners I was getting

Well, the men who loaded the cars were raised, and it cost the 27 cents on

18 inches deep.

Mr. REED. Yes, sir.

STATEMENT OF WILLIAM H. BALL.

STATEMENT OF N. H. ROBERTS.
The CHAIRMAN. We would be very glad to have your experience.
Mr. ROBERTS. I was arrested in Williamson. I was in town when I heard
about the shooting up here, and I came to see about my family, and they cut
my tent right here [indicating on a tent], and down to here [indicating], and
that side they took it up and cut it [indicating]. I had a box of fruit jars
sitting out there, and this man Lawson came in and he took his gun and he
jabbed it right down in the fruit jars, and old man Hatfield, who kept a
little store out there, stood and watched him.
The CHAIRMAN. Old man Hatfield?
Mr. ROBERTS. John Hatfield. I started from town up here. I got down
yonder [indicating] and there was, I guess, 300 of them, they seemed to be
under every bush, and they halted me and Mr. Thompson and arrested us,
and they would not let us go any farther. They started up the hollow, and
at last we were taken around the county road, and at last we got away down
yonder [indicating], and they would not let us come back to the tents or go
down town, and they arrested us. They arrested me and took me before
Maj. Davis at the courthouse, and then they released me.
(The committee then returned to Williamson, and during the afternoon and
evening informal interviews were had with Prosecuting Attorney Stokes,
Sheriff Finson, and afterwards the committee adjourned until the following
morning.)
MONDAY, SEPTEMBER 19, 1921.
At 8.30 a. m. the committee visited the courthouse where a murder trial was
going on, and had an informal interview with Maj. Davis, who filed with the
committee certain papers, alleged confessions, etc., copies of which are attached
at the end of this hearing.
At 11 a. m. the committee visited the operations at Borderland, W. Va.,
where the following statements were given.
STATEMENT OF J. D. BLEVINS.
The CHAIRMAN. Is this a union place or a nonunion place?
Mr. BLEVINS. It is nonunion.
The CHAIRMAN. Is this one of the places where they have had trouble?
Mr. BLEVINS. Not very much. At the start we had some.
The CHAIRMAN. Was there shooting from both sides of the river?
Mr. BLEVINS. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. When was that?
Mr. BLEVINS. A year ago last July.

The CHAIRMAN. Are they running full capacity here now?

Senator SHORTRIDGE. How many men are there employed here?
Mr. BLEVINS. I do not know exactly. I could not tell you, somewhere be

STATEMENT OF M. S. LAMBERT, OF THE BORDERLAND COAL
CORPORATION.
The CHAIRMAN. Have you had any trouble around here, Mr. Lambert?
Mr. LAMBERT. No, sir. We have not had any trouble since the 14th of July,
last year, when we had some shooting.
The CHAIRMAN. What was that?
Mr. LAMBERT. They shot us up at that time and we shot back at them.
The CHAIRMAN. Did they attack from the Kentucky side?
Mr. LAMBERT. No, sir; from the West Virginia side.
The CHAIRMAN. Your plant is not unionized?
Mr. LAMBERT. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. What was the reason for their attacking you?
Mr. LAMBERT. Well, they were trying to stop us from working because we
would not recognize the union.
The CHAIRMAN. They made a demand on you to recognize the union, did
they?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. When was that demand made?
Mr. LAMBERT. Some time in June.
The CHAIRMAN. And was this attack in a concerted manner, or was it just
a few shots?
Mr. LAMBERT. On July 7 we had an attack made from this hill here [indicat-
ing], and on the 14th the other attack was made from this hill over here
[indicating].
The CHAIRMAN. Was there anybody hurt?
Mr. LAMBERT. No, s r.
The CHAIRMAN. How did you fire back, from this hill over here?
Mr. LAMBERT. From the Kentucky side and from the hill here [indicating].
The CHAIRMAN. And do your operations extend over into the Kentucky side?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. The mine proper is over in Kentucky-
Mr. LAMBERT. The mine proper is over in Kentucky and the coal company
cross on this tramway here [indicating].
The CHAIRMAN. How many men do you employ?
Mr. LAMBERT. Under normal conditions we employ about 150 men in our
mines.
The CHAIRMAN. Are you up to normal now?
Mr. LAMBERT. No; not qu'te. The coal business is a little dull all over the
country just at the present time.
The CHAIRMAN. You are not up to normal, you say, because of lack of orders?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. There is no trouble about cars?
Mr. LAMBERT. No; we have practically a full crew of men now.
The CHAIRMAN. There has been no trouble, then, since that time?
Mr. LAMBERT. On the 22d day of August our No. 2 power plant was blown
up, and on the 2d of September they tried to blow up the conveyor line.
The CHAIRMAN. Where is the No. 2 plant?
Mr. LAMBERT. You can see the headhouse right over there [indicating].
The CHAIRMAN. Completely blown up?
Mr. LAMBERT. No; we caught the fellow in the act.
The CHAIRMAN. What was done with him? Did you find out who put him
up to do it?
Mr. LAMBERT. It is generally understood that the union put him up to do it.
He was arrested and tried and found not guilty. Under the statutes of Ken-
tucky you can not convict a man l'ke that unless there are two or more of
them. He did not accomplish his act and he was acquitted.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What building was blown up?
Mr. LAMBERT. No. 2 power plant.
The CHAIRMAN. How large a power plant was that?
Mr. LAMBERT. It is the same size as this one here [indicat'ng], right out here.


===== [扫描序号 493] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
485
The CHAIRMAN. What was it blown up with?
Mr. LAMBERT. It was blown up with dynamite, or something like that. It
was the same size as th's [indicating]. The power plant was the same this
[indicating inside of the power plant]. Maybe it was just a little larger. The
charge of dynamite was placed on the outside of the wall right upon the
switchboard. When 't went off it blew the entire wall down and it blew the
entire ceiling out of the building.
The CHAIRMAN. Was that done in the day or in the night?
Mr. LAMBERT. It was done at 2.40 in the morning; Sunday morning, August
22, 1920. It was all destroyed .
The CHAIRMAN. Did you get the people who blew it up?
Mr. LAMBERT. No; we never did. We had two watchmen on duty that night.
They had just made the round and were standing out in front of the store,
and were just getting ready to come back when it was blown up.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, is your experience typical of what others have gone
through in this district?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Did you have any trouble here years ago, before the ques-
tion of unionizing came up?
Mr. LAMBERT. No, sir; I have been in this county, well, before it was Mingo
County, and when it was Logan County. I have been here since 1895, I guess,
with the exception of about two years at one time and three years at another.
I was in McDowell County two years.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, what do you attribute the trouble to?
Mr. LAMBERT. I attribute the troubles to this attempt to unionize the fields,
and the operators won't agree to it. That is my understanding of it. Natu-
rally, being connected with a coal company as I am. I am in favor of not having
it unionized. This country has always been peaceable between the mine owners
and the miners, and we have always gotten along decently together, and we
have settled our own complaints.
The CHAIRMAN. Have you complaints about the measuring and weighing
system?
Mr. LAMBERT. No, sir; we never have had.
The CHAIRMAN. How many men have you here; 150, do you say?
Mr. LAMBERT. Something like that.
The CHAIRMAN. What is your tonnage capacity here?
Mr. LAMBERT. Our tonnage capacity here at the present time would be about
800 a day.
The CHAIRMAN. And what are you getting out now?
Mr. LAMBERT. We are getting out at the present time about 7,000 tons a
month, running three days a week.
The CHAIRMAN. About a third of your capacity?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And is that typical of the other coal mines in this district?
Mr. LAMBERT. I think so, with a few exceptions. You take some of the
mines that are running on contract, why they are running regularly, but when
you depend upon the domestic market it is different.
The CHAIRMAN. A few years ago, in years gone by, at this time of the year,
have you been running at your capacity?
Mr. LAMBERT. No; this has been the dullest season that I have ever seen.
The CHAIRMAN. This has been the dullest season?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. What are you going to do about it this winter?
Mr. LAMBERT. Somebody is going to freeze to death this winter unless they
have got a good supply on hand.
The CHAIRMAN. At this time of the year ordinarily how are the orders?
Mr. LAMBERT. At this time of the year our orders are generally heavy. We
have always enjoyed an excellent trade at this time of the year.
The CHAIRMAN. How are the prices? Are the prices so high that the people
do not buy?
Mr. LAMBERT. I do not think so.
The CHAIRMAN. How do you account for the fact that they are not buying
coal this year?
Mr. LAMBERT. In the cities most all of the factories have slowed down, most
all of the factories of any magnitude, and the laborer has not got the money
to buy coal with. That is what they tell me. I do not go out or anything
like that, and I am on the job all the time.


===== [扫描序号 494] =====

The CHAIRMAN. And is your labor practically all white?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir; we have several colored people. I should say that
about 25 per cent are colored people.
The CHAIRMAN. And what do the miners make on an average?
Mr. LAMBERT. I have never tried to average it, but if you will look at the
pay rolls you will find that they are getting good money; the best money that
I have ever known miners to make. I have been around coal mines all my life,
and I am 38 years old. They make anywhere from $300 to $350 a month.
The CHAIRMAN. They are making that now?
Mr. LAMBERT. Well, we are not running full, but even now they are making
good money, considering the time that we have had and the trouble.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you employ these guards here-
Mr. LAMBERT. We have no Baldwin-Felts guards and never have had any.
We have our own watchmen here.
The CHAIRMAN. And are they deputy sheriffs?
Mr. LAMBERT. Some of them are. We have two on this side.
The CHAIRMAN. And do you pay them, or does the State pay them?
Mr. LAMBERT. They get something from the State, and we pay them, too.
The CHAIRMAN. Then they are paid by both of you?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And is that the general way of paying them?
Mr. LAMBERT. I do not know what the other companies do.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What company is this?
Mr. LAMBERT. It is the Borderland Coal Corporation.
Now, our watchmen that we have on at night, we pay them as we do any
other employees. They are not deputies.
The CHAIRMAN. What about the foreign element? Have you many for-
eigners working for you?
Mr. LAMBERT. No, sir; not very many. On No. 2 plant we have some Span-
iards, and we have got a few yet. Some of them have left, but we have got a
few of them left.
The CHAIRMAN. Are there many children?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. What about the schools?
Mr. LAMBERT. We have a school building right yonder [indicating]. You can
see that building.
The CHAIRMAN. That is a public school, is it?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. It is a State school?
Mr. LAMBERT. Yes, sir. We have not any school on this side.

The committee then proceeded to Merrimac, W. Va., and at the plant of the

STATEMENT OF C. N. JEFFRIES, MEMBER OF THE STATE POLICE.
The CHAIRMAN. What was the last trouble that you had here?
Mr. JEFFRIES. The last trouble that we had here was the Sunday that we re-
turned from Logan, on the 3d of the month.
The CHAIRMAN. What was that that happened on the 3rd of this month?
Mr. JEFFRIES. There was shooting that started on the 2nd, but the 3rd was the
last of it.
STATEMENT OF GEORGE H. PERKINS, SUPERINTENDENT WHITE
STAR MINING CO.
Mr. PERKINS. It started on Thursday night. Some gentlemen coming up here
about 11 o'clock Thursday night in a car were fired on, and they left the car
and they turned out the lights, and they stayed here, and the following morning
they started again, and they fired on them Saturday at 4 o'clock in the after-
noon-
74020-21-VOL 1- -32


===== [扫描序号 502] =====
494
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
The CHAIRMAN. Where did the shots come from?
Mr. PERKINS. From the Kentucky side.
The CHAIRMAN. Who was it that was doing the firing?
Mr. PERKINS. It was the residents over there, and some others that came in
during the night-Thursday night.
The CHAIRMAN. And did they keep the shooting up throughout the night?
Mr. PERKINS. No; they fired just about one volley of 15 or 18 shots, and they
fired on this car Thursday night, and early Thursday morning Maj. Davis sent
some of the militia out here. and they left here about 8 or 9 o'clock, and before
they got to Williamson they opened fire on us again. He sent some more men
out here then. It continued through Saturday and Sunday until about 4
o'clock.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, was the firing directed at anyone?
Mr. PERKINS. They were shooting at the houses, and every now and then they
would hit some. One man was in his house on the 12th of May and he was
shot through the hand. Another man in the store was shot through the arm, and
Harry Allen was shot the third of this month.
The CHAIRMAN. Where was this man Allen at the time he was shot?
Mr. PERKINS. He was right around between this and the camp.
The CHAIRMAN. How do you understand they start shooting of that kind?
Mr. PERKINS. Well, they have a big horn that they blow; they blow the horn,
and as soon as they hear the horn they start out. In May, I think it was, they
opened fire all along here from the lower drift mouth, throughout the camp,
to the upper end-
The CHAIRMAN. When was that?
Mr. PERKINS. That was on the 12th day of May.
The CHAIRMAN. Could you judge, in a general way, how many shots were
fired?
Mr. PERKINS. We estimated that there were several thousand. That lasted
four days.
The CHAIRMAN. Was it intermittent or how was it?
Mr. PERKINS. Most of the time it was going on pretty keen.
The CHAIRMAN. If they were shooting at the houses they must have hit some
of them.
Mr. PERKINS. There were 82 holes right in this house.
Mr. JEFFRIES. I have a handful of bullets that I picked up upstairs.
Mr. PERKINS. It cut it all up. The bullets were coming through the roof,
too, and a good many of the houses back in the camp had to put in new roofs
on them.
The CHAIRMAN. What was done to stop that firing?
Mr. PERKINS. We returned the fire from here.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you know whether you hit anybody over there?
Mr. PERKINS. We found out since that that they had strangers over in there.
The CHAIRMAN. Did they have machine guns?
Mr. PERKINS. I do not think that they had machine guns. They might have
had a Browning, but I do not think that they had anything any larger than
that.
The CHAIRMAN. What did the Kentucky authorities do over there?
Mr. PERKINS. They sent deputies on the 13th of May, but there were so
many more of these men in the hills than the deputies that it was no use; they
did get one man.
The CHAIRMAN. Was anybody hurt over there?
Mr. PERKINS. We do not know, positively. The Kentucky National Guard-
the governor sent some of them, and their commanding officer searched all
of these hills and claimed they found some new graves over there, but how
they died we never heard.
The CHAIRMAN. And does this firing go on in the night, too?
Mr. PERKINS. At times; yes, sir. We would have no lights in the camp; if
there were any lights, they would be fired at. We got in the habit of having
no lights. We had to have the lights on the tipples.
The CHAIRMAN. There was some testimony before us at some place I was
trying to remember where it was where a bucket was going up filled with
men and it was shot at. They shot at the man at the top.
Mr. PERKINS. No; we have had nothing of that kind. That was over about
4 miles above Matewan.
The CHAIRMAN. Your trouble seems to have run up to a very recent date.
Mr. PERKINS. I think that this was the first place that they commenced and
the last one where they quit. They fired on us, I think, the 13th day of last

August. They fired at the tipple at that time. We estimated that they fired
about 250 shots.
The CHAIRMAN. About 250 shots.
Mr. PERKINS. That is what we estimated. As we brought the coal out of the

and they told us the next time that they shot us, that if we had any guns we
should return it. Some of the State police on the 5th of April were sitting
around in front, and all of a sudden, about 6 o'clock in the evening, all of a
sudden a shot was fired and some one saw a little dust fly up. They sat there.
and another shot was fired, and some more dust flew up. They came up near
the side of the house and then they began to shoot generally. The man who
was in charge of the State police stationed here called Capt. Brockus by phone
and asked him what to do. He said to return the fire. They walked out of
the door and got about 4 feet and they fired a volley into them, and they ran
to cover, and they returned the fire.
That lasted about an hour and a half, and we called the sheriff, but it was
stopped before he got out there.
On that occasion the sheriff and Capt. Brockus drove up the road and they
fired on them. Having a light on their car they left it and they walked on.
The same night, later in the night, they fired on Burnwell, the next operation
above us.
The CHAIRMAN. Were there many shots fired at Burnwell?
Mr. PERKINS. I do not know just how many. We estimated something like
1,500 or 2,000 shots fired.

there were fired in the 3-day battle here lately?
Mr. PERKINS. Just the other day?
The CHAIRMAN. Yes.
Mr. PERKINS. I expect, Senator, from three to five thousand shots were fired

information we can get from the other side there must have been more than
a hundred men over across the river there. Those men were strangers. We
heard of one family over there that fed 53 strangers during that time, and of
another that fed 30, and we estimate that there were about a hundred strangers
over there.
The CHAIRMAN. Are there mines over there?
Mr. PERKINS. No; not until you get to Pond Creek.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, I am curious to know how, for instance, like this

Mr. PERKINS. We can not find out. That is what we have been trying to

The CHAIRMAN. Now, these men over there, are they men who have worked

Mr. PERKINS. Most of them are men who have worked for us.

The CHAIRMAN. Had you had any trouble up to-
Mr. PERKINS (interrupting). None whatever.

Mr. PERKINS. This company has owned this mine since in 1909, I believe.

Mr. PERKINS. Yes; it has been operating all of that time.
The CHAIRMAN. You say you had never had trouble there before?
Mr. PERKINS. They never had any trouble of any kind. Everybody was
satisfied.

in normal times in the mines of Mingo County?

The CHAIRMAN. Yes.
Mr. PERKINS. No, sir; I could not. I suppose that information can be gotten

that shows the coal-every coal operation on their lines.

The CHAIRMAN. And do you have company stores?
Mr. PERKINS. Yes, sir; this is a company store right here.
The CHAIRMAN. And are the men expected to buy at the company stores?
Mr. PERKINS. Well, we do everything that we can to secure their trade of
those who work here. We work for it just the same as any independent store
would.
The CHAIRMAN. And does your company discriminate against the men who
do not trade with your company stores?
Mr. PERKINS. No; there is no discrimination whatever. They can trade
wherever they please. We get out and hustle for business for our stores just
the same as anybody else would.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Then there is competition?
Mr. PERKINS. Yes; we have competition.
The CHAIRMAN. Is there any payment in script that is good in the stores?
Mr. PERKINS. Yes; they can get and trade scrip any time they want to do
it, to trade in the stores.
The CHAIRMAN. Are they compelled to do that?
Mr. PERKINS. No; we have had men make as high as $150 and $200 in two
weeks and never get a cent in scrip. They draw every cent of it in cash.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Is it optional with them to take the money or the scrip?
Mr. PERKINS. Well, they can use their own pleasure about that.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And they can trade wherever they please?
Mr. PERKINS. They can trade wherever they please.
The CHAIRMAN. Do very many of the men use the scrip?
Mr. PERKINS. Oh, yes; a large percentage of them do.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Now, at these other stores, is there scrip transferrable
at those other stores?
Mr. PERKIN. No; that scrip is only good here.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. At your store?
Mr. PERKINS. At our store.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. You spoke a few moments ago of some of the mines

union or nonunion mines?
Mr. PERKINS. They were nonunion mines. There are no union mines in this

Senator SHORTRIDGE. Will you give up some of the names of some of the mines

say-
The CHAIRMAN. And how do you account for the fact that they have had no

Mr. PERKINS. Well, these organizations did not get in there.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Some of them have been affected, I infer from your
answer, and some of them have not been affected.
Mr. PERKINS. Practically everything on the West Virginia side has been
affected.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. When you say "affected," what do you mean by that?
Mr. PERKINS. By the labor troubles.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What form did it take?
Mr. PERKINS. Practically all of these mines were closed down the 1st of last
July.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Why?
Mr. PERKINS. On account of the organizers attempting to organize the mines.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Well, did the men in the mines, that were then working,
go out?
Mr. PERKINS. Those that had not already gone out came out, yes, sir; except
those that would not have anything to do with the union.
The CHAIRMAN. Did they go out as the result of the closing down of the

Mr. PERKINS. A good many of them had gone out. They started the strike
as of July 1.
The CHAIRMAN. Did the operators agree among themselves to close down?
Mr. PERKINS. I think so.
The CHAIRMAN. They could have gone ahead with some workmen, could they?
Mr. PERKINS. We had a few workmen here, and did go ahead with them.
The CHAIRMAN. The purpose of closing them down was to break the strike,
I suppose?

Senator SHORTRIDGE. Now, the men, women, and children that occupy these

Mr. PERKINS. I think that there are some families living in the tents who

Senator SHORTRIDGE. What is the daily wage of those that you hire and pay

The CHAIRMAN. Where is your head house?
Mr. PERKINS. We have no head house. The upper seam that we used to use

Senator SHORTRIDGE. I do not understand coal mining.
Mr. PERKINS. I thought that you were an old miner.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. I know something about gold mining. Is this what you

Mr. PERKINS. No, sir; we have some water, but it is not a wet mine.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. How about your timbering?
Mr. PERKINS. We have a dry slate in there, and we have to timber, especially

gets started, then you have a lot of trouble.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What is the width of the seam you are working on now?
Mr. PERKINS. It will average about 4 feet.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Is it rather uniform or does it pinch out occasionally?
Mr. PERKINS. No; it does not-
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Have you any white horses in your mines?
Mr. PERKINS. No; we have some [the balance of the answer was unin-
telligible].
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What is that?
Mr. PERKINS. It is a slick piece of slate, and if you do not watch out it will
fall right on you.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. It is not a bucket mine, then?
Mr. PERKINS. Not exactly.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Have you any faults in the mine?
Mr. PERKINS. Yes; we strike faults occasionally.

Senator SHORTRIDGE. And do the seams run more or less uniform in quality
and in volume, or does the character of the coal change?
Mr. PERKINS. No; it remains practically the same. This is what is known
as the Pond Creek seam and it varies in different localities as to thickness,
and it is an open coal; that is, mixed in with a coal, and we cut that out
with the machine when getting it.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Have you such a thing as a hanging wall and a circle

Mr. PERKINS. No, sir; no, sir.

Mr. PERKINS. Well, the thing is I am not a practical miner. You might get

Mr. PERKINS. On the same elevation, do you mean?

Mr. PERKINS. You all stopped at the drift mouth where you got out.

Mr. PERKINS. Yes; but we have a little vary.

Mr. PERKINS. On a royalty basis, and the timbers are included in the lease-

Senator SHORTRIDGE. What is the sentiment of the people in these villages

Mr. PERKINS. Well, they do not like it much. They are just like I am.
They would rather that we did not have it. If a man gets in the habit of
dodging these bullets, he gets pretty good at it.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. How many people are gathered around about here, Mr.

Mr. PERKINS. I suppose there are about 150 here now-men, women, and

Senator SHORTRIDGE. Are there any other ways that they make their living-

Mr. PERKINS. No, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. They are all directly or indirectly connected with the

Mr. PERKINS. All directly or indirectly connected with the mining industry;
that is right.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. There was no loss of life here, was there? None lost
his life, did he? Were there any lives lost in these troubles right here in this
vicinity?
Mr. PERKINS. No; not right here. There have only been three, I believe
struck; one was shot in the hand and the other in the elbow and the other
in the hip.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you think that this shooting was for the purpose of
hitting people, or was it for the purpose of terrifying them?
Mr. PERKINS. I believe that at first it was to terrify them and to get them
to quit, to scare them, but the last two or three that we had, they were shoot-
ing too close to try to scare anybody.
The CHAIRMAN. With 15,000 shots it is a wonder that there were not more
hit.
Mr. PERKINS. It is very strange. We have all talked about it- -so many shots
fired and so few hits.

STATEMENT OF H. L. VAN TRUNK, BOOKKEEPER.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. How many men have you on the pay roll, Mr. Van
Trunk?
Mr. VAN TRUNK. We have 80; 25 per cent colored.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What have you to inform the committee in regard to
the mails, Mr. Perkins?
Mr. PERKINS. The mail was thrown off of 16 over there [indicating], and
we could not get at it to get it, and it remained there until the following even-
ing when darkness came on, and the mail the next day stayed there until we
got it under the cover of darkness. The mail trains would throw it off on this
side [indicating], and the men would have to get it before the train would
pass. On one occasion I climbed up on the crane, and they fired three
shots at me, and I heard all three of them slide by.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. When was that?
Mr. PERKINS. That was during the last shooting. I did not attempt to go
out and get the mail after that time.
On the morning of the 12th day of May I had quite a bunch of merchandise,
a good deal of perishable stuff-ice, strawberries, tomatoes, honey, flour,
sugar, and meal, and it stayed there for two days. It rained on it, and it
stayed out in the rain, and when I got it the second evening practically all of
it was gone.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Why didn't you go out and bring it in?
Mr. PERKINS. Every time that anybody showed up out here he had to com-
mence dodging the bullets.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Do you mean to say that when you would come out
it would invite the shots?
Mr. PERKINS. Yes, sir; we had a team of mules to haul a load of sand. They
fired onto the team and the man left the mules. The mules stayed there and
they crossed the track. Several of us attempted to get the mules away, but
the minute that we went out in the clearing they would fire at us. Finally the
mules pulled out of the railroad track and stopped and a couple of us started
out again to get them out of there, and they fired on us again. We heard the
balls sing by as they would fly by. We did not go to the mules.
Well, we stepped out to where this gate is and tried to get them. They stepped
over this way and that threw the wagon across the railroad track. They turned
around this way [indicating] and pulled back and got up on the railroad track,
and that was about noon, about time for No. 19, the passenger train. We made
another attempt to get the mules off, and just as soon as we appeared out here
they would fire at us, but before 15 came by those mules had gotten the wagon
loose and were at the tank, and they stayed there all afternoon. Two or three
times we tried to open the office door.
Finally No. 1 came out there; when it came and stopped a couple of boys went
out there with knives and released the mules. The wagon stayed there about a
week and hung up on top of that post [indicating].
(The committee then took the train for Huntington, W. Va., and arrived there
at about 9 o'clock p. m.)

TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 20, 1921.
The committee left Huntington, W. Va., at 6 o'clock a. m., and arrived at Logan
at 9.45 p. m.. and the following statements were taken at the sheriff's office:
STATEMENT OF ROBERT BLAND, JUDGE OF THE COURT AT LOGAN.
The CHAIRMAN. Can you tell us, Judge Bland, whether the mines are running
here at full capacity?
Judge BLAND. I say that they are, yes; but take into consideration the market
for coal. It is just about full capacity.
The CHAIRMAN. That is, you are able to fill all of the orders?
Judge BLAND. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And the orders are a trifle slight?
Judge BLAND. Yes. We could market much more coal than we are doing if the
market was good.
The CHAIRMAN. Is there any trouble in getting the men?
Judge BLAND. NO.
The CHAIRMAN. What are some of the large plants near here that we might
visit?
Judge BLAND. Well, there is the plant of the Island Creek Coal Co. at Holden,
about 4 miles distant from here.
The CHAIRMAN. And that would be a typical plant, would it?
Judge BLAND. That is one of the companies; yes, sir; the main Island Creek
Coal Co., which runs to the center of their operation and perhaps about 9 miles,
and on the way along, just as you cross the river here, just a few hundred
yards, all the way up to either of these mines, you will find coal-mining opera-
tions.
The CHAIRMAN. The mines of this country are open and are not unionized?
Judge BLAND. Not in the valley of the Guyan River.
The CHAIRMAN. Are parts of the county unionized?
Judge BLAND. There is a small section on the other side of the divide to the
north of here, which is in the valley of the Spruce Fork and Coal River,
which empties into the Oh'o, which is unionized. That is the section over which
these disturbers marched when they started across here.
The CHAIRMAN. Our reporter is taking down some of your answers; have you
any objection to that?
Judge BLAND. None in the world.
The CHAIRMAN. And what part of the area of the county would that cover?
Judge BLAND. The proportionate part?
The CHAIRMAN. Yes.
Judge BLAND. Oh, perhaps 10 per cent of the area. I do not know whether
that is accurate.
The CHAIRMAN. And on the mining property, based on that percentage-
Judge BLAND. Well, it is very small. I could not say. Perhaps the same
percentage would hold good that I spoke of in relation to the territory.
The CHAIRMAN. And how is this other county, Wayne County?
Judge BLAND. Wayne County is a farming community. It is a border county,
lying on the southwest. It just joins this county by corners.
The CHAIRMAN. There are no mines there?
Judge BLAND. A few.
The CHAIRMAN. It is not a mining county?
Judge BLAND. It is not a mining county; no, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. We are very much obliged to you.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And do the two counties form your district, Judge,
Wayne and Logan?
Judge BLAND. Wayne and Logan; yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What are the terms of the court here? Do you have
regular sessions?
Judge BLAND. Yes. In this county the regular terms are January, April,
July, and October.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And your court is one of general common-law juris-
diction?
Judge BLAND, General jurisdiction, criminal, and civil.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Law and equity.
Judge BLAND. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And what is the duration of the term here?

Judge BLAND. Why, we try to complete the work—

Senator SHORTRIDGE. What was the cause of the march?
Mr. WILEY. As near as I can figure, the cause of the march was this: The

touch with this all of the time. They had failed completely in Mingo County
to unionize there. The governor put in martial law and the supreme court
held that the circumstances under which he put in the general martial law
were invalid, and he changed it in some way, and the second time the martial
law was put in and it was held to be legal. That gave the nonunion people

The operators got the best of the publicity. The operators for the first

and they were feeling sore about it.
Nevertheless, it looked to me that the situation was all in the hands of
Gov. Morgan when this unfortunate thing of the killing of Hatfield took place.
The minute that that happened there was a fermentation started among
the men and there was a great deal of unrest. They were brought or they
were induced-to go to the meeting in Charleston, and I heard such stories
as that "so many people had been killed in Mingo County that they could
not bury them," and "what was the other union men going to do about that:"
"that they were killing off so many of them that they were piled up in the
streets and could not be buried," and that there was a great deal of unrest
succeeding Hatfield's death at Welch. From that, and from these meetings
which were held at Charleston, protesting against the governor's action, grew
this second march.

Mr. WILEY. In Marmet, and it ended at Danville.

Mr. WILEY. Again I would have to guess, and to form my judgment from

the sheriff of Kanawha County stated his inability to handle the situation

Keeney and those in charge of the union that it had to be stopped, and
I understand they said that they would stop it, and they went to Madison,
where the march was at that time, and they publicly asked these people to
return to their homes, but, as a matter of fact, what happened was that the
very night that the mob was supposed to have returned and that Gen. Band-

his visit, a train at Clothier was commandeered and taken down as far as
Ivy Branch, below Danville, and loaded with people from there to Madison

I should like to connect that story with another story which shows why

The CHAIRMAN. Yes; certainly.
Mr. WILEY. At that time they were talking about Hatfield. Hatfield was

about him. The State constabulary was talked about there in order for you
to understand it I had better tell you this-the mine worker does not want
any kind of a policeman except a policeman of his own making, and they talk
among themselves about how bad a policeman is. They objected to deputy
sheriffs being paid by the operators, and the State constabulary was formed
here with a view of being a State force to take the place of the deputy sheriffs,
but the minute the State constabulary is used, they talk about them in the
same way as they do of the deputies, and call them such names as would tend
to lessen the respect that the people should have for them.
That was done succeeding Hatfield's death very generally.
Five constabulary came into Sharpless on the afternoon of August 12.
Their conduct conveyed the idea to me that they were young and untried boys,
loose-mouthed, talked a lot, and bragged a good deal of what had occurred in
Mingo County.

They came to Sharpless, mounted, on a dead run. I was not there, but I
am told this. One of the five, going at a dead run across a railroad bridge
collided with a motor car and there was quite an accident; a horse was thrown
and hurt somewhat, and one of the men was quite badly hurt, scarred up about
his head and face and the car was damaged, but the best information that I
could get was that this was a pure accident.
Now, they talked to this man pretty roughly. They asked him if he was a
union or a union sympathizer, which was like shaking a red flag to a bull in
that particular locality, to men who were sympathizers of the union, and when
he left he went to his place of abode in Ottawa. Ottawa is in Boone County.
The CHAIRMAN. Where is Sharpless?
Mr. WILEY. It is in Logan County, and Ottawa is in Boone County, and it
is the place where the radical element assembles, and he carried the tale down
there that from 50 to 150 constabulary had been brought in; that they were
searching everybody's house, abusing women and children, doing away with
all arms and guns, and making themselves extremely offensive to the people.
About 8 o'clock that night, Embrey-I do not know his initials-but they call
him Kid Embrey, a very popular man, a man who is very generally liked by
all classes of people, and is the conductor of the local freight train, with head-
quarters at Clothier, started out with two little girls, his wife's sister and an-
other little girl who was a friend of his, sitting in the back seat of his jitney,
and a boy named Chambers in the front seat with him, to take a ride. Just
then Dr. Harless, a local physician, steppod out and asked him where he was
going. He said that he was just going to ride. Dr. Harless asked, “I have
got to pay a call half a mile out, and will you ride me up there?" He said,
"I would be glad to." Kid rode him up there and he went up the road about
a mile and turned around with his children to come back to pick Harless up
on his way coming back.
As he was going back through this village, Harless stepped out of the
patient's house, when a bunch of men that he estimated from 10 to 15, none
of whom he knew-and being the practicing physician there he knew most of
the people that lived in that immediate neighborhood-but as Embrey's car
came on down to pick him up, these men opened fire on Embrey's car. The
car was hit 12 to 15 times. One bullet went through one side of Embrey's
straw hat, and one bullet went through the other side, and the car was
shot up pretty well. Embrey put his foot on the accelerator and got out
of the trouble as fast as he could, and Harless went to the telephone at Clothier
and called up Sharpless for policemen. Two of the constabulary who had come
in that afternoon and two of the deputy sheriffs got in a car and went down
to see what the trouble was. When they got to Mifflin, a mile and a half this
side of Clothier, they were held up by a body of men variously estimated from
40 to 60, all with high-powered rifles, and they were disarmed and turned back;
whereupon the two constabulary went back to Sharpless and got the other two
that had not been hurt and came over to Logan, leaving the one that was in-
jured in the accident in the clubhouse or hotel, and leaving their horses and
accouterments there. From that time all roads were guarded with patrols of
from 5 to 10 men every 2 to 5 miles in that whole section, with the
evident purpose of preventing the State from resenting the slap in the face
that the constabulary had got, and for the purpose of preventing the county
resenting the slap that the deputies had got, and to prevent the serving of
warrants. Just at that time-I had better state to you first, so that you will
get a clear understanding of this-there was no trouble at all between any of
our men and my company. We tried to do business on a business basis, and
we give them exactly what is coming to them under the contract, and we refuse
to give them anything that is not in the contract, and by that means, to a con-
siderable extent, we have gotten their confidence, and our relations are of the
very pleasantest.

Mr. WILEY. I was just saying to you that the relations of my men with the
company are very pleasant. We have no trouble of any kind between them and
our company, and we felt that, having signed the union contract, and having
lived up to it as honestly as we had tried to do, we had a right to ask the
union for protection in order that we could continue to do our work. You can
readily understand that when the price of coal has slumped to the price that it
is to-day, a company like ours had to take up all that loss, and, because of our
contract, we can not pass it to the men, and the burden is very heavy, and when
there are interruptions to the work it not only costs a great deal of money,
but it costs a place that is closed in addition an amount to get ready, and the

the union contract, and I told this committee what it cost, their going to Charles-

to see that we were permitted to operate every day and to keep our costs down

Mr. WILEY. To back up on that, the contract provides that if the men do not

The CHAIRMAN. That is under the terms of the contract, is it?
Mr. WILEY. That is under the terms of the contract.
The CHAIRMAN. Did these miners pay the fine?

up of whether the men should pay the fine for the stoppage of the mine, and

The CHAIRMAN. And you did not impose it?
Mr. WILEY. No, sir.

The CHAIRMAN. Now, let us get back to that third march-you got diverted
from that.
Mr. WILEY. This patrolling of the road and this unrest was going on in our
immediate neighborhood at the time that march came from Marmet to Dan-

That is the third march, sir, and that is the reason I said it was a part of

any intention of the first march going to Logan.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you mean the 1919 march?
Mr. WILEY. Yes; and there was never any intention of the second march go-
ing to Logan, in my judgment. The United Mine Workers of America are the
greatest publicists in the world. They know best how to get things into the
newspapers on the front page. They have learned fairly the lesson that
Charles Dana used to teach. He used to say to the men who went to work
on his paper that he wanted them to get the news. He told them that if a
dog bites a man it is not news, but if a man bites a dog, then it is news. The
newspapers are hungry to get the news, and it was for that purpose that that
march was made, because the march would get to us and we would be in-
terested in whether it was going to happen-
The CHAIRMAN. Then, you were not badly frightened about it?
Mr. WILEY. No; I did not think that there was any danger of it at all;
and when the last trouble began in our immediate neighborhood, and these men

ties, that there lay the cause of a great deal of trouble, because all these men
had high-powered rifles and were carrying them, and the law was being
broken down. We had not a policeman in that neck of the woods, and the
only authority I saw was these committees who controlled these affairs as far
as they could. Now, things stayed in this condition until the Saturday after
these men turned back-
The CHAIRMAN. Do you mean to say that you have no protection by law of
your property over there in your country?
Mr. WILEY. I mean to say that we had not the slightest.
The CHAIRMAN. And who is to blame for that condition of affairs, Mr. Wiley?
Mr. WILEY. Why, these men were. They drove the officers out. They
threatened them with death if they stayed, and they could do nothing but go.
There were 6.000 men in that army.
The CHAIRMAN. Well, I had in mind what you said about your place not
having any protection. Did they get to your place?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir; we were right in the middle of it. On this night a
body of men-my ideas of this are very general-these gentlemen around here
can tell you more than I can-came down to Beach Creek. We have a mine
there, two mines, one at the head of Beach Creek and one, which is lower on
down, and Sharpless is located where Beach Creek runs into Spruce River.
The body of men increased, and I expected all this time that these warrants
one time would have to be served, and when they were served things were
going to crack, and it was going to be uncomfortable living around where I
was, but, nevertheless, all we could do was to wait for the service. This night
word came over my telephone line that 500 deputies and constabulary were
coming down Beach Creek, and I happened, at that time, to be seated on my
porch with my general superintendent, and I said "I don't believe it."
There were all kinds of rumors flying around at the time, all kinds of them,
and they were all wrong. "What makes you so certain that it is not true?
he said. I said that I thought, in the first place, they would not attempt to
serve the warrants at night; and the next thing that they would do would
be to cut the telephone lines to keep people from knowing what was going
on in advance of them. Therefore, I was certain that it was not anything
like that.
Soon after that we heard quite a volley of shots-quite a number.
One man was killed instantly; a miner's son was wounded badly and died
the next day; and two others were badly wounded. The constabulary and the
deputies did not come any farther that night.
The CHAIRMAN. What was the date of that, as near as you can give it?
Mr. WILEY. I have not my diary with me. It was the Saturday after the
Friday that those men turned back at Danville; the second day after that
Friday. It was on Saturday night.

Senator SHORTRIDGE. What time of night was it that the shots were fired?
Mr. WILEY. Well, I think that it was about 10 o'clock at night that the

Senator SHORTRIDGE. And how far was the shooting from where you were

Mr. WILEY. Oh, I should say about a mile and a half. One of my committeemen
came to me that night at 2.30 and said that things were very serious and that
the governor would not listen to him if he asked for troops, because he was on
the miners' side, nor would he listen to me, but that he would listen to both
of us. He said that if he and I would go together that we possibly could get
the troops, and he asked me would I go. I asked him, “Shall we start now?”
He said No; the roads are too bad and our lives would not be worth a cent.”
Then I said "Can we start to-morrow morning early enough to catch the
train leaving at 4.25?" He said "No; then it would be dark, and I would not
think of going. Somebody might halt us, and we might not hear them, and
we would get in trouble."
I said or asked him what means there were to get into Charleston after
daylight. He said that he did not know what the railroad had at that time,
that it had been commandeered, and that they had been operating the road.
At daylight he and I went in, and we could not get a train nor an engine.
but we got one of the gasoline motor cars that you see being used on the
track.
Mr. Keeney would not agree with me that this man should go with me to
the governor and ask for troops. On that day the Logan Operators' Association
passed a ringing resolution, which was telegraphed to the Charleston Chamber
of Commerce, who had a meeting, and a committee from the governor to
Washington to explain to Gen. Bandholtz just exactly what the situation was
and to put up to the Federal authorities the dire necessiy for troops.
To get back of my story a little bit, Senator, there was an entire difference
between the march from Marmet to Danville on these two former occasions
and the action which the miners took after this shooting on Beach Creek.
In order to get the miners to resist the serving of these warrants a syste-
matic propaganda had been carried on among the men, to the effect that the
deputy sheriffs of Logan County were terrible things, drinking a bucket of
blood before breakfast each morning and eating up the women and children
alive and shooting the towns up while the people were in bed, and if they
ever came across the hill the people would be killed by the thousands.
In answering some of the talk I pointed out to the men how foolish that was.
I told them that they had lived there for years before I came there, and I
had been there for three years, and nobody had been hurt on our side of the
hill there had been no depredations and nobody had been abused. and no
deputy sheriff ever came over there and acted in the least way offensive, and
if they did come to serve the warrants they would come in a dignified manner.
Well, I might just as well have talked to a fence. Whether it was right
to believe it or not did not make any difference. They did believe it. On the
third march these men did not congregate at Marmet and march to Danville.
They commandeered every automobile, and they came in automobiles, in cars,
and the roads were loaded with them, and they came by trainloads. To
illustrate the situation, the Coal River branch divides at Sproule, and one
branch runs up the Big Coal River to the neighborhood of Whitesville, Paint
Creek, Cabin Creek, and that county. The other comes up the Little Coal
River, where I live. They took the trains and loaded them up on the Big
Coal River branch from Cabin Creek and Whitesville and that country and
brought them around to this other branch, where they were mobilizing."
The CHAIRMAN. You say "they" took the trains; who do you mean?
Mr. WILEY. The miners.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you mean to say that they took possession of the trains?
Mr. WILEY. They took possession of the railroad. They commandeered the
trains and took complete control of the road above Sproul.
The CHAIRMAN. And how long a stretch is that, approximately?
Mr. WILEY. About 50 miles in one direction and about 45 miles in the other.
The CHAIRMAN. And did they operate the trains themselves?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Or were they operated by the regular engineers?
Mr. WILEY. They were operated by the regular engineers and crews; the
regular engineers and crews operated them, but they operated the trains under
the guns of the miners.
The CHAIRMAN. And how long did that keep up?

Mr. WILEY. That kept up for about a week. They brought in-I heard about

only thing that I saw on the streets were commissary provisions.

Mr. WILEY. I have been told that they had machine guns a number of times.

The CHAIRMAN. And what became of this army?
Mr. WILEY. They treated me with a great deal of decency. My men would
come to me and state that there was no trouble between them and me, and that
if I was going to run the business and give employment to them, that they
would protect our stores. They did.
The minute that this anarchy occurred, it gave the radical boys and irre-
sponsible kids the right to do all kinds of things that had never been done
before. They were armed with high-powered rifles, and all of them had two
pistols strapped on them, and they started searching the houses. I went to the
committee and I said that the women and children would not stand that and
that they must stop it. They stopped it. They came to my house with their
high-power guns and I went to the president and asked him to stop it, and they
did stop it.
They protected our stores and property because they had an interest in them.
These men came in on the trains, and some of them marched into our club-
house where our officers lived and at the point of a gun demanded that food
be cooked for them at most unusual hours. Colored people were not supposed
to go into the dining room, and they took them as they pleased and they refused
to pay for what they got.
At our stores they acted very decently and did not rob them except in one
instance, and in that instance they paid for it. Immediately on getting off the
train they went up into the woods and from there we could hear the shooting and
the riffraff of the mob, the strangers that we did not know were marching up
there all the time, and one can have no conception of the terrorism that existed.
I had none before that time. I had known before of the terrorism in France,
and I had heard from people in San Francisco of the terrorism there, telling
me of the terrorism that existed there after the earthquake, of the great ter-
rorism that existed, and how big executives, when troops marched down the
street, how tears ran down their faces, but I had no idea what terrorism could
be until that anarchy came there without anybody to check it.
The CHAIRMAN. And did there seem to be anybody at the head of it?
Mr. WILEY. Nobody. Every man did as he pleased, and he made good with
his high-powered rifles and his pistols, and with 6,000 men back of him, 6,000
men to back him up.
The CHAIRMAN. Is it your judgment that there were as many as 6,000 men?
Or are those stories that go out?
Mr. WILEY. My general superintendent and my three superintendents were con-
sulting with me constantly in conference throughout all of this trouble and they
had various estimates of the men in the hills at various times, and they figured
it out rather carefully, and when we got through the best estimate that we
could arrive at was that there was between 5,000 and 6,000 men.
I want to say this in this connection: That in every local union there are a
few agitators. I do not believe that 10 per cent of my men wanted to do this. I
am perfectly certain that 90 per cent of my men were forced to do this.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you mean that 90 per cent of your men were forced to
join the march?
Mr. WILEY. Ninety per cent of them were forced to join the march and carry
a gun.
The CHAIRMAN. And did most of them do that?
Mr. WILEY. It was a question of life or death with them. They all had to
do it.
The CHAIRMAN. Were there any of those men who did not go out themselves
and who afterwards lost their cards from their union?
Mr. WILEY. There was not any of my men that did not go out. The terrorism
was so strong in the air that they had to do it. A great many of them tried to
get out and leave on the train, but they were not permitted to do that. After a
while every man had to carry a gun or believe he would be killed.
The CHAIRMAN. Did they furnish each man with a gun?

Mr. WILEY. Senator, you have touched me on my hobby. I belong to the
National Association for Constitutional Government in Washington, the Na-
tional Security League in New York, and was one of the men who formed the
American Constitutional Association in Charleston for the purpose of teaching
the teachers in school the fundamental principles of American Government.
There is no systematic effort outside of this little association to do that.
It is doing well, sir. It is being well supported with money by the citizens. We
have gotten men before each of the institutes of the teachers here, and we have
had a good deal of writing about it and we published a little pamphlet. I
suppose I have given 250 copies of Elihu Root's speech on the benefits of govern-
ment, given them away.
The average American citizen-in Charleston I made the statement the other
day to a friend, that if you will take the first 10 men that you will meet, be
they lawyers, doctors, college graduates, or whatever they may be, and if you
ask those first 10 men wherein the Government of the United States is the
best in the world, and wherein the Government of the United States differs
from other Governments, you will find that they do not know the fundamental
principles of our Government. You can start out in the town of Logan and
you can take 50 people, take them as they come, and ask them if they know the
fundamental principles of the Government of the United States, and you will
find that they will not know anything about it and that they do not know any-
thing about the Constitution. The lawyers study the Constitution as a weapon
to use in a suit, but the great fundamental principles of our Government,
wherein they differ from those of any other government, they do not seem to
know anything about that.
The CHAIRMAN. We passed a bill through the Senate along that line, to

help to get it through the House of Representatives.
Mr. WILEY. There is nothing in this world that I would rather do than to

know how valuable it is.

were not substantiated. Then I said to my general superintendent, “I am
ready to answer the committee and to meet the committee." I told him to tell
them to have a meeting of the union on the next Sunday afternoon, and told
him to tell the superintendent that his specific business was to see that every
member of that union was present. We went down there, and when I came
in the president of the union he said, "Well, here he is; let us hear what you
have got to say to us now." Some of the radicals got up and they tore stars

mine guards and there was not a place on his body that was not scarred
from wounds from those mine guards. Another fellow got up and said that
he had to go down into the bowels of the earth to work, to leave his family on
the outside, to be away from his family, and that he would not know what
would happen to his family while he was down in the bowels of the earth.
They talked in that way and then I said, “Have you all finished?" They said,
"Yes." So I said, “Do you want to hear from me now?" They answered,
"Yes."
Now," I said, "the matter is very simple, and it doesn't take a very long
time to tell it. We are going to have a decent town. We are trying to make
it a place where your women, children, and your grandchildren will grow up
decently. We are trying to keep booze out of here, and this pistol shooting,

town will be satisfied. Now, those men who want to live in the other kind of
a town can go out and go somewhere else. I want a vote taken, and I want to
see which of the men stand for a decent community and which do not."
I got a unanimous vote, because the agitators did not vote.

Senator SHORTRIDGE. What is your system of weighing?
Mr. WILEY. We weigh the coal and they have a check weighman that stands
alongside of our weighman and they get the right weight. We lose about 2
per cent. When we are paid for our coal we are paid about 2 per cent less
than we pay the miners for the mining of the coal.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. So that the sum total of weights, as reported in the
mine, is some 2 per cent more than the weights when you sell the product?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Have not you some there to check it up, too?
Mr. WILEY. Oh, yes; I have a man, but I am giving you just about the net re-
sult. Unfortunately, we coal people suffer from a great many troubles, and one
of them is our coal is weighed by the railroad. When our stuff is shipped down
to Newport News, for instance, the railroad does not weigh it at the first
scales but weighs it at the boat. It has to be responsible to the boat for
the coal delivered to it. Therefore it does not weigh our coal; and if a car
sets for six months on a siding we get no report and we get no payments,
and when it is dumped into the boat, after the loss, we are credited with the
amount dumped in at that time, and not credited with the amount delivered
to the railroad when we turn the car over to it, and we lose a good deal by
that.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. AS I understand it, it is about 2 per cent less than is
pa'd the men; and that might be attributed to the railroad-
Mr. WILEY (interrupting). Oh, yes; I do not mean that it is illegitimate. It
is not illegitimate.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Then it is not a matter of intentional underweigh-
ing-
Mr. WILEY. No: I do not mean to say that at all.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Does coal lose in weight by standing on the side track?
Mr. WILEY. Not much; to a very slight degree is all.
There is one phase of this thing that I should like you gentlemen to get at,
and that is the coal in West Virginia is a very high grade, and the people who
have less high grade coals are very jealous of us and are taking a good deal
of business away from us in the West and Northwest, and it has made it very
hard for us to live in these bituminous-coal fields, by reason of the way that
we pay the men. We had 44 per cent a ton imposed on us to pay, as against
27 per cent imposed in the other fields.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Do you mean the other union fields?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir.
To take away from us some of our differentials and to put a burden upon
us which our competitors would not have, in what is known as the central
competitive field the miner is paid by the ton, but he is expected to do a con-
siderable amount of work in the loading of a ton of coal, which is not done in
West Virginia. Fearing that the rates would be imposed by the bituminous
coal commission upon us in a horizontal scale, and that they would not take
into account the unfairness which would result to us in this matter, we had
asked to have our special conditions considered, but they were not considered.
And when the award was made by the bituminous commission we found that
while in the central competitive field the cost of mining was increased 27 per
cent in the West Virginia field it was increased 44.4 per cent.
The United States as a Nation needs the good coal that is produced in
West Virginia; and these increased costs which are imposed upon us by the
commissions from the Federal Government only increase the cost to the con-
sumer of the high-grade West Virginia coal.
