Mr. WILEY. I do not suppose that you want me to read a lecture on this
subject. Some 15 or 20 years ago the doctrine was advanced by the unions


===== [扫描序号 537] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
529
and their sympathizers that wrongs or depredations to life and property which
occur in a strike or an industrial dispute should be condoned. This matter
has gone so far that, if my memory serves me, one of the Presidents of the
United States recently announced such a doctrine in a public utterance.
For 20 years the careful growth of this thought in the public mind has led the
strikers to believe that they will not be punished for any wrongs, either against
property or life, which occur in an industrial dispute. And by this means law
and order, which depend upon public sentiment, have been greatly broken
down.
A boy drives a motor car at 60 miles an hour, feeling no sense of responsi-
bility and having no knowledge of the brains required to produce a machine
capable of this feat; he prides himself upon the accomplishment of the car,
whereas all he did was to touch the button. The speed has gone to his head,
and he feels no sense of responsibility for the safety of others, nor any sense
of appreciation for the man who made such a machine possible.
In like manner the tremendous power of the union leaders has gone to their
heads, and they have never been made to feel a sense of responsibility in the use
of their power. Law and order depends upon public opinion; and so long as pub-
lic opinion responded to the propaganda so carefully spread abroad that the
wrongs committed in industrial disputes were to be condoned, to just such an
extent law and order broke down. Our Government has changed, not from a
government of law to a government of man, but from a government of law to
one of men. And men who sway public opinion of the country have so affected
our policies that all of the constitutional restrictions placed upon the majority
have been removed.
Troubles such as we have had in West Virginia are tried in the court of
public opinion. The business man is inarticulate. The union man is the
greatest publicist known, and the business man never gets his day in court.
The churches seeking popularity cater to socialist doctrines. The newspapers
seeking popularity cater to the class which will give it the most circulation, and
the politician seeking for the same popularity caters to that class from which
the most votes come. With the great forces of the church, the newspapers, and
the politicians compromising with principles on which law and order are based,
such principles have little weight.
When this trouble started on August 12 all of the telephone and telegraph
wires were cut, and no one has been punished. After a time they were repaired,
and they were cut a second time, and no one was punished. One branch of the
Chesapeake & Ohio Railroad was commandeered by the miners' union. No one
was punished. The officer who brought the proclamation of the President of
the United States and read it to the crowd came very near being captured, and
the proclamation might just as well have been read to the birds. Thirty-six
hours after the troops arrived the firing continued. Three times in contraven-
tion of the laws of West Virginia this body of men have marched across the
State, and on two occasions they returned as conquering heroes on special
trains waving their arms out of the windows. The last time, while they did
not have the arms to wave out of the windows, they went home feeling that
they had succeeded, because there was no punishment.
Chief Justice Taft said the other day that taxes are taken from the citizens
not to cheat them but to give them protection, and if the taxes so taken did not
give protection the citizens were cheated. This was an address made by Chief
Justice Taft at the Union College at Schenectady.
Montescue, whose teachings were the basis of our Federal Constitution,
announced the theory that in taxation the Government took from the people
the small amount of his property that the rest of it might be enjoyed in peace.
I submit that these people who are paying the horribly high taxes that we
are paying that they have got a right to ask of you that we have protection in
the operation of our business, because, by God, we can not exist unless we get it,
and I do not hesitate to say to you that the important mines in the Kanawha
field are going to be closed down unless we get protection.
The doctrines of Karl Marx have been taught to these people until they have
accepted them as a religion instead of the teachings of their mothers. Each
vies with the other to see how far they can go from everything that their
mothers taught them. They do not want policemen or deputy sheriffs in our
part of the country, and the church services in my country have been broken
up by the boys coming in and out in such a noisy way to show their disrespect
for the church that the services had to cease.
The first cure for this trouble as I see it is this: Make the States so strong
that they can produce law and order and protect the business of their communi-


===== [扫描序号 538] =====
530
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
ties. Let the workingman as well as the business man realize that they will be
protected in their life and property and that they will have the right to choose
what work they shall do and the conditions under which they shall do it. Let
everyone-workingman and business man-realize that they can not break laws,
cut telegraph wires, commandeer interstate trains, and tread on the President's
proclamation with disrespect and with impunity. If we do not teach them these
things, by whom will they be taught? If they are not taught to respect the law,
contempt and disrespect will go with each breach.
The CHAIRMAN. Let me call your attention to another thing. You can not
simply take these men and say that they are the only ones who apparently
have little respect for the laws. Take our prohibitory law of the United States
to-day, and whether a person believes in it or not, nevertheless it is our law.
Our rich people and the middle class, if they violate that law it seems to be
all right. There is universal violation of that law-
Mr. WILEY (interrupting). Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Then you have got others violating the laws-other than
the miners?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And above all else we need respect for the law.
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir. I think we have gone into a deep subject, Mr. Chair-
man, and I think that the law is something that the people should look up to.
These so-called ladies of our polite society and the men, their conduct has been
such that it does more to break down these household gods than anything else.
No country has even been greater than its women, and when our women begin
to go down some 15 or 20 years ago-
The CHAIRMAN (interposing). In other words, the whole problem is inter-
related.
Mr. WILEY. We have got in some way to bring to these men's mind that
there is some authority in the United States. Once they realize that they
can not go to Washington and tell their stories and make their misrepresenta-
tion to such an extent but they will invite the arm of the law, things will be
different, and they have said that they could make the soldiers do anything
they wanted to do in Washington. When they respect the law, then I think
we will have the thing settled.
I have been asked the question whether a union man from over there could
come over here and work. We have had a large number of men who have
worked over there, and they have come over here and worked, and if a man
wants to come here and work he may do so.
The CHAIRMAN. But if a nonunion man comes to a union field can he work?
Mr. WILEY. Not unless he joins the union. But if a man comes over there and
wishes to work, we will hire him, and there is an exchange of men in that way.
The CHAIRMAN. How do you get an exchange of men in that way, when yours
is a union field?
Mr. WILEY. Why, when I hear of a good man, and I want to get him, I go after
him, and if a man will come over there we will send a wagon and bring him
over. The man on one side ofthe hill has not the least trouble in getting work
on the other. I think that that is a very important point. Of course, when a
man comes over here he must join the union.

I saw a number of trains going by there, and in some instances counted the

Mr. BURNS. We took the place of the other men, probably a hundred men in

Dr. BRADSHAW. No; I do not know of any. I never heard of any.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What has been the general condition of the city-not
to be leading--but has it been boisterous and quarrelsome, or has it been a
peaceful community or otherwise, as the case may be?
Dr. BRADSHAW. I would call them a peaceful community. There have been
a good many crimes here and there, falling out between neighbors and things
of that kind.
The CHAIRMAN. Has there been anything in the nature of an insurrection?
Dr. BRADSHAW. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And the quarrels and troubles that you have in mind, what
are they?
Dr. BRADSHAW. They are simply individual affairs, and have no bearing what-
soever upon the relation of the operators and the miners. My impression has
been that the relations between the operators and the miners have been cor-
dial. It seems to me that has been the case. That has been the situation.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Has there been what we call or sometimes speak of as
economic labor troubles in the district?
Dr. BRADSHAW. No; nothing of that kind.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Have you formed any impressions, Doctor, from what
you have seen as to the causes of this approaching mass of men? Will you
kindly give us the benefit of your conclusions?
Dr. BRADSHAW. I am afraid that I am not competent to answer that very
satisfactorily. I have some impressions, but they are only my impressions, and
I can only give them as such. The impression that I got has been that those
who came from the organized field came for the purpose of probably placing
an organization here. Now that may not be just right, but that is the impres-
sion I personally have received.
Senator SHORTRIDGE, Have you ever talked with any of the miners here as to
their wishes in the premises?
Dr. BRADSHAW. No, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. As to whether they wished to become unionized or other-
wise?
Dr. BRADSHAW. I have had no conversations of that kind. I mingled with
them some, in town and out through the county, but I never talked about the
question of the relationship between the miners and the operators, so I have
no information directly of that sort.

537
Senator SHORTRIDGE. You have good schools here, Doctor, have you?
Dr. BRADSHAW. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And you have a number of denominational churches. I
suppose?
Dr. BRADSHAW. Yes, sir; we have six churches in town-five Protestant and
one Catholic--and out through the county there are meetings in practically
every mining camp, and these are sustained largely, financed largely, by the
mine owners and operators. In our own case we have a missionary who is
supported by our State board, and our church, our church pays about two-thirds
of his salary. In the last four or five years we had him over the field, but in a
good many cases there are many children that are attended to in the fields with
perhaps a few little groups of communities, and then preach to them. Those
men are supported nearly entirely by the mine owners. Perhaps there is some-
thing added to their salaries from the collections taken, but, of course, that
would come from the owners and the employees alike. Then as to the social
conditions, in a good many of these mining camps, so far as my knowledge goes,
practically the whole county is covered by social-settlement workers, women who
leave their homes to teach the women how to take care of their children and
how to keep house and how to keep well, and frequently do nursing in case of
sickness. Really I have been impressed with that kind of work that has been
done in the community.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And is that volunteer work?
Dr. BRADSHAW. It is on the part of the owners and the women. We have a
Red Cross organization which is general, but aside from this the mine owners
take care of the individual miners by appointing women to do work for them and
seeing that they have physicians and nurses and hospital treatment.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. NOW, will you please tell us, Doctor, whether you have
heard any complaints lodged against the constabulary or the State police?
Dr. BRADSHAW. I have heard no expressions in regard to that. I have not had
an opportunity to come in contact with anybody who was speaking of it, so I
have no direct information in regard to that.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And since the cessation of that big trouble, I will term it,
you have taken note of the conditions here in the city and round about, have
you not?
Dr. BRADSHAW. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And what have you found out in regard to that? How
has it been?
Dr. BRADSHAW. It has been quiet. Seemingly by the next day everything
dropped back to a normal condition. Of course, there was the work of getting
rid of the guns and the ammunition, but the mood of the people seemed to drop
back into ordinary conditions and community life.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Have you seen any disposition to make reprisal as against
those who caused the trouble?
Dr. BRADSHAW. I do not know of any.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. You have heard no threats, have you?
Dr. BRADSHAW. No, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Or any determination to get even or to make reprisal?
Dr. BRADSHAW, I have heard nothing of that kind; no, sir. The things I have
heard from those who talked have been questions of grievances to their friends
around in helping them out of a hard situation. In fact, there was a meeting
in the courthouse and the citizens were called together and a letter was pre-
pared to be forwarded to the other counties expressing the thanks of the people
for the help they gave in keeping out the invaders.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. From that we may assume this is a law-abiding com-
munity, and the great majority of the men and women of this community are
law-abiding people and believe in law and order.
Dr. BRADSHAW. I think that that is a just assumption.
STATEMENT OF W. R. THURMOND, PRESIDENT OF THE LOGAN
COAL OPERATORS' ASSOCIATION.
Mr. THURMOND. I am president of the Logan Coal Operators' Association,
operators of coal mines.
The CHAIRMAN. What is the local coal operators' association called?
Mr. THURMOND. The Logan Coal Operators' Association, and it is a voluntary
organization composed of the individual coal operators of the Logan coal
field—that is, all the mines in Logan County except the mines lying on the other
side of the watershed of the Guyan River.

Senator SHORTRIDGE. How many coal mines does it represent?
Mr. THURMOND. One hundred and thirty-four mines; there are 66 companies;
some of them have more than one mine.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Are those companies' stock owned largely here or are
they owned outside of the State?
Mr. THURMOND. It is owned very largely in the State, and quite a large
proportion of it in this county.
The CHAIRMAN. Are any of your large properties owned outside of the State?
Mr. THURMOND. I think there is some stock held outside the State, but I do
not know how much.
The CHAIRMAN. Your association have meetings and decide on courses of
action, do you not?
Mr. THURMOND. Well, the association has meetings, and as to such matters
relative to the-yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. But not the fixing of prices?
Mr. THURMOND. No, sir; they have never discussed that-we have no desire
to be put into the penitentiary.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Then the Sherman law is observed in this county?
Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Have you had any trouble in this field?
Mr. THURMOND. No, sir; this field has been in operation for 17 years, and
the first car of coal was shipped out of here in November, 1904. In 1905 there
were 127,300 tons of coal shipped out of this field, and that has increased each
and every year till 1918, when the figures reached 10,211,390 tons shipped out,
and they had employed between 8,000 and 9,000 men. During that time
there has never been anything but the most harmonious and peaceful relation-
ship between the employer and the employee.
The CHAIRMAN. Is there any reduction in the output of the last year or two?
Mr. THURMOND. There was a slight reduction in 1919, and then a recovery
in 1920, and in 1921, up to the present time, we are mining at a rate larger
than ever before.
The CHAIRMAN. And at such times how did the work compare with previous
years?
Mr. THURMOND. We are about 6 per cent ahead of 1919, the banner year, and
we are larger than that.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Your output this year will be your banner year?
Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. How many men are employed in this industry in this
county?
Mr. THURMOND. Between nine and ten thousand, I believe.
The CHAIRMAN. Can you give us a guess of how many are colored and how
many are white; can you give us an estimate of that?
Mr. THURMOND. No; I can not.
The CHAIRMAN. How many are foreign and how many are native Americans?
Mr. THURMOND. About 20 per cent of them are foreigners.
hTe CHAIRMAN. And what nationalities are those?
Mr. THURMOND. Well, various nationalities-Hungarians, Polish, Lithuanians,
a few Italians; those are the principal ones, and those other allied races.
The CHAIRMAN. I wish you would tell us about the schools in these districts.
There seems to be in these mining communities where we have visited nothing
of that kind at all-there has been no race suicide anyway.
Mr. THURMOND. We have quite splendid schools, starting with the growth
of the county. In 1910 this county had a population of 14,000; in 1920
it had a population of approximately 45,000. We kept pace with that increase
in population the best we could. We have built schools, and where the levy
was not sufficient to give enough money to build schools bond issues have been
resorted to, the first $40,000, and the second $400,000, making $440,000, and
that levy of $400,000 was only voted in May, and we have not yet reaped the
benefit of it.
The CHAIRMAN. Do the miners' children go to school?
Mr. THURMOND. The miners' children go to school. Where the county has
not been able to build the schools in nearly every instance they have been
built by the mine owners. They build the schoolhouses.
The CHAIRMAN. And pay the teachers?
Mr. THURMOND. In nearly every instance they supplement the teachers'
salary. The county fund is not sufficient to get the type of teachers that should
be gotten and those teachers' salaries are supplemented $25 or $50 a month each,

and in some instances the school has been extended from seven months to
nine months, the last two months being paid entirely by the coal operators.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, we have heard some complaint about the various
deputy sheriffs being paid by private corporataions. What is the situation
here in regard to that?
Mr. THURMOND. In this State we have 50 deputy sheriffs. I mean in this
County. These are recommended to the county court by the sheriff of the
County and appointed by the county court. They give a bond the same as
any other officer of the county. They are under the direction of the sheriff,
and are under his charge, both as to hiring and discharging. The amount of
money allowed by this county for police protection is inadequate, and the
coal operators are levied upon for the deficit, a sum of money which they
pay into the county.
The CHAIRMAN. And that is used to pay the deputy sheriffs?
Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir. That is used to pay the deputy sheriffs who are
the peace officers of the entire county, and not simply the guardians of the
mine owners.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. You say that this money is paid into the county?
Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And does it go into the treasury, into the hands of the
County treasurer?
Mr. THURMOND. It goes into the hands of the sheriff.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, how much did the mine owners contribute last year
to the payment of the salaries of the deputy sheriffs?
Mr. THURMOND. I could not tell you. I do not know that. I could get it

The CHAIRMAN. Can you give it for any previous years?
Mr. THURMOND. No, sir; I have only been president of the association

Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir.

Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir. I might say in connection with that that we have
54 police officers in this county-approximately 50-I think it is 54 and that
is not as many policemen per capita as the average city has, where we are
scattered over 424 square miles of territory.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you believe it is a good policy for private interests to
pay the officers?
Mr. THURMOND. I do when the county has not sufficient funds to do it.
You must have police officers in any community.
The CHAIRMAN. And that is one of the duties of government, isn't it, to
protect. property and to furnish police officers for that purpose?
Mr. THURMOND. I SO construe it; yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And that seems to be one of the complaints of the miners.
Do you know about other counties in this part of the State?
Mr. THURMOND. I do not know the practice in other counties, but I do not
think you have heard any complaints from Logan County in reference to that.
I do not think that you have heard any complaints from the people who have
been interested, but it is barely possible that you might have from people who
have no interest. Your complaints have been by noninterested parties.
The CHAIRMAN. As I understand it, you have never had any Baldwin-Felts
men here?
Mr. THURMOND. I think there were two or three employed about 12 years
ago, but not within the last 12 years. Every officer is a citizen of this county.
The CHAIRMAN. Outside of this strip of territory over near Boone County
the mines are nonunion mines?
Mr. THURMOND. They are in the owners' association.
The CHAIRMAN. And do you prevent a man from working if he belongs to
a union?
Mr. THURMOND. No; of course, we have no union here.
The CHAIRMAN. But suppose a union man comes here and asks for work, do
you prevent that man getting work because he belongs to the union?
Mr. THURMOND. Well, we do not inquire whether he is a union man or not.

The CHAIRMAN. If you find out that he is a union man, is he discharged?
Mr. THURMOND. No; not unless he is doing something that makes him
worthy of being discharged.
The CHAIRMAN. Suppose that he agitates?
Mr. THURMOND. If he agitates he is discharged, because he is a menace to
our business.
The CHAIRMAN. And in these union fields, do you know whether these non-
union men can work?
Mr. THURMOND. My understanding is that no nonunion man can receive em-
ployment in the union fields. But that is hearsay information. I never had
had anything to do with the union field.
The CHAIRMAN. The real controversy down here-this is the question-seems
to be that the operators of the district will not permit the employment of
union men, and the union men will not permit the employment. of nonunion
men, and the union wishes to organize. The union seems to be determined to
unionize.
Mr. THURMOND. They are determined to try it. They have been very jealous
of the cordial relationship between the mine owner and the employees ever
since we had a field here. They know that this is a field which is a large
producer, and that the employee is well treated, and that everything is cordial
between capital and labor, and just as long as that exists they can not. form
their organization here in these fields, because we have good representative
American citizens mining the coal, who will work and produce coal, and pro-
duce it rapidly, and furnish it to the country. If they get. the country organ-
ized they can tie up the wheels of industry.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you know or have you seen any indication of operators
in other fields, in Indiana, Ohio, and Illinois, attempting to unionize these
fields?
Mr. THURMOND. I have seen nothing more than what I have heard, and I
can tell what. my opinion is, personally. I have not seen it. There has been
a good deal of testimony submitted in relation to that in Washington. I think
it is reliable testimony, and that is a matter of record, and they took the
records of the meetings of the United Mine Workers of America first.
The CHAIRMAN. That was presented at very great length to the committee.
Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Have you any difficulty here now in getting labor?
Mr. THURMOND. No, sir. They have a plentiful supply of good, loyal labor;
and what I mean by loyal labor is that they are ready to work six days a week.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And did any of them join in protecting the county dur-
ing these recent troubles?
Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir; I know of one instance which will serve as an
illustration where there were 23 men that walked 10 miles from one mine to
offer their services, and they said that they felt like they wanted to join in
and help this county against an armed mob.
The CHAIRMAN. What do you think that mob was trying to do?
Mr. THURMOND. I think they were trying to march over here and undoubtedly
influence these miners in becoming organized and burning the tipples and stores
and dynamiting the houses and going to Mingo and committing like depredations
over there.
(At the conclusion of the above statement, the committee returned to Hunting-
ton, W. Va., arriving there at 7.30 p. m.)
WEDNESDAY, SEPTEMBER 21, 1921.
(The committee left Huntington at 7 a. m. for Charleston, W. Va., where it
arrived at 11.30 a. m. Informal unreported conferences were held with Gov.
Morgan and other State officials at the governor's mansion. At 3.30 in the
afternoon the committee had other conferences with John B. Floyd, Attorney
General England, and others, portions of which conferences were not reported,
the reported portions being as follows:)
STATEMENT OF JOHN B. FLOYD.
The CHAIRMAN. You said something a while ago about there being passed in
1913 a law prohibiting the appointment of deputy sheriffs as guards. Will you
tell us about that, please, Mr. Attorney General?
Attorney General ENGLAND. That law was passed in 1913, and it prohibited
the appointment of deputy sheriffs as guards. There was no penalty to that


===== [扫描序号 549] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
541
law, and the last session of the legislature, at the request of the parties, I
prepared a bill fixing the necessary penalties, and it was before the legislature,
but it never was passed.
Mr. FLOYD. But they knew that that law was in existence and it was per-
sistently violated. You have heard of the situation, of course. As I say, I
do not think that anyone would pretend to say that a union organizer would
be allowed in Logan County or Mingo County or McDowell County, and I have
no doubt that he would be run out inside of 10 hours, and if he was not run
out he would be killed. You might have a similar condition of affairs where
a nonunion miner would undertake to work in the union coal field.
The CHAIRMAN. Can a man, for instance, from the Logan field go over into
Boone County, a nonunion man, and work in the mines over there?
Mr. FLOYD. Being a union man, I presume that he could not.
The CHAIRMAN. Take a district-
Mr. FLOYD. In a district, I understand that the nonunion man, generally, is
not permitted to work in a mine which is unionized.
The CHAIRMAN. And a union miner going over to Logan is not permitted to
work in those mines?
Mr. FLOYD. Not unless he renounces his religion.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What justification, if any, did the political parties give
for not enacting the law that was contemplated by their platform?
Mr. FLOYD. I do not know. I was not here only just a little time during the
session of the legislature. I was out of the city. The fact of the matter is
I was in Washington and New York, and I did not hear why the law was not
enacted. Of course, a man has a right to have his property protected, but it
ought to be protected by the State.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Could the State protect the property. Did it have suffi-
c'ent force to do it; that is, the forces of the constabulary, the State police, and
the National Guard?
Mr. FLOYD. After the murder of Hatfield and Chambers in the courthouse in
McDowell County, I understand-
Senator SHORTRIDGE (interrupting). That was but recently?
Mr. FLOYD. That was but recently; and after that occurred, I say, I do not
think that the State had power enough, you understand, to stop this march;
but the fact of the matter is, I went to the governor and advised him to ask
for Federal troops, because I felt that the State could not stop the march. I
told him that it was utterly impossible, in my judgment, to delay the Federal
troops coming here, because I knew anything might happen. The only thing
that astonished me is that more did not happen than did. It is simply a
wonder to me, knowing the people as I do, and I do not see how they got off
without the loss being greater than it was.
The CHAIRMAN. You feel in your mind that this system of enforcing the law
with people paid by private parties is one of the main causes of these troubles?
Mr. FLOYD. There is no question about that in my mind at all. It would be
just like you going into court and the judge had his money in his pocket, his
pay, by a private individual.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What, in your opinion, is the issue around which this
Controversy revolves?
Mr. FLOYD. The issue around which this controversy revolves is the issue
of union or nonunion. It is whether the mines will be unionized or whether
they won't be unionized. That is the crux of the question, and it is an ex-
ceedingly serious question, too. It is more far-reaching than a person could
imagine. For instance, it not only affects the miners, but it also affects the
mine owners. If it is a nonunion field it affects the scale of wages, for they
are taking coal out for less money than they do in the union fields, and they
have the advantage in the market, and it is possible for them to put into
bankruptcy the people in the union field.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Do you think that the operators in the union fields are
endeavoring to force the unionizing of the other fields, for certain economic rea-
sons, and are trying to bring about and compel unionization?
Mr. FLOYD. I won't say that I think that. I do think that it will be the union
or nonunion, because there is no other alternative. If the wages begin to cut
in one field, if you have got 5 or 10 cents a ton additional to pay in a union
field, it means bankruptcy on the one side or riches on the other, or just eking
out a living. That is the thing that will have to be faced, and will be fought
out, and of course the coal operator wants it union or nonunion all over, so
that he may go into the market unhampered in the price of his product.

The CHAIRMAN. Do you think that the nonunion operators have an advantage
in the matter of labor?
Mr. FLOYD. They feel that the nonunion field can force labor to take less
money than if the labor is organized, and they feel that the nonunion workmen
can be forced to take less price and work under less favorable conditions than
they could in the union fields, where every man could walk out if they under-
took to cut the price.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Assuming that the nonunion operators have the power,
do you understand the fact to be that they have exercised it in the matter of
paying labor, that is, that they pay them less than they do in the union field?
Mr. FLOYD. I have not looked into that matter, and do not know, but that is
the milk in the cocoanut. Of course you can see at once that the mine owner
in a union field—I mean in a nonunion field--if he announces that the wages are
cut, why, naturally, there would be nobody except each individual to say he
would or would not accept the cut, because there is no organization, and of
course they will probably take the cut, and then the operator in the union field,
he is up against a 10 per cent deficit in his business. There is the situation
exactly. As I say, the fight will be and it has been to determine whether it will
be all union or all nonunion, and it will come in this State next spring.
The CHAIRMAN. It will come next spring?
Mr. FLOYD. It will come next spring, because the contracts in the union
fields all expire on the 31st of March.
The CHAIRMAN. And naturally they can not be half union and half nonunion?
Mr. FLOYD. No; it can not be half union and half nonunion, any more than
a man can be half slave and half free.
The CHAIRMAN. And if that applies to West Virginia, then it will apply all
over?
Mr. FLOYD. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And these are about the only remaining nonunion coal fields?
Mr. FLOYD. Yes, sir; these are about the only ones. Now, I think that the
employment of deputy sheriffs and the payment of deputy sheriffs from private
funds has embittered things a great deal more than they otherwise would have
been. If the deputy sheriffs had not considered that they belonged to a con-
siderable part, I do not think that we would have the same feeling that we
have. The people know that the organization of such people by individuals
or corporation, that such people feel that the corporation puts up its money for
them to do a particular job, and those people have got to do it, and do it
according to the ideas of the coal operators.
The CHAIRMAN. Suppose there had not been this system of deputy sheriffs
paid by private interests, but there had been deputy sheriffs appointed and
paid by the county or by the State, do you think that the trouble would not
have come?
Mr. FLOYD. I do not think it would have come in the way that it did, because
I do not think that the sheriffs would have picked up men who were prejudiced,
who were known to be in a particular line. I do not know who these deputy
sheriffs are, but I presume that a great many of them are men who have been
employed as mine guards and private detectives, like this detective agency
which spread all over this country, and who are bringing infamy to the mine
workers.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. I think that we have received information to the effect
that only citizens or residents of the several counties are appointed deputy
sheriffs.
Mr. FLOYD. They might be citizens and residents, but at the same time they
might be part and parcel of a detective agency, you see. I do not know, because
I have not been interested enough to investigate it.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Do you recall specific instances where they have
illegally and improperly exercised their power as against those supposed to be
agitators?
Mr. FLOYD. Well, Senator, personally I do not know, you understand, but-
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Or has there come to your knowledge specific cases
where they did what would be regarded as improper.
Mr. FLOYD. I have every reason from information that comes to me from
various sources to think that these deputy sheriffs in the Logan field-for in-
stance, specifically, when they found that an organizer was in there or getting
in or was coming to a mine and began to talk organization they summarily
kicked him out or beat him out or did whatever was necessary to get him out.
I do not suppose there is any question about them doing that. I do not know

543
that of my own personal knowledge, but I do not suppose that there is any ques-
tion in the world about that being the truth.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. We get a good deal of information from both sides,
and, among other information which we have received, or as part of that
information that we have received from one side, it is to the effect that in
Logan County, for instance, they are getting along very peacefully and have
had no trouble in that county except a small portion of it-I believe 10 per

the citizens yesterday over at Logan.
Mr. FLOYD. Well, of course, as a matter of fact, the mine workers have not
been able to build up things there. There is not any question about that. Two

gone in there, and they were met at the train and put on the next train and
told to get or to lose their scalps. I have no doubt of that.
Attorney General ENGLAND. I know that that sort of thing has happened.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Mr. Attorney General, what do you think is the initial
cause of this?
Attorney General ENGLAND. It is unquestionable; as the colonel has said, the
mine guards.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What were the mine guards appointed for? What was
their intention in appointing them?
Attorney General ENGLAND. Their duty is to keep out organizations; not to
maintain law and order, but to keep out organization.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And how are they appointed?
Attorney General ENGLAND. They are appointed by the sheriff and approved

Senator SHORTRIDGE. And is it a fact that the companies are paying their

Attorney General ENGLAND. It is just as Col. Floyd says: They apportion

it. I know something about it, but I am not interested except to maintain law

Senator SHORTRIDGE. What is the system of State police or National Guard

Attorney General ENGLAND. Well, we have thought that the last legislature

Senator SHORTRIDGE. And there is no punishment, you say, fixed in that law?

STATEMENT OF COL. ARNOLD, SUPERINTENDENT DEPARTMENT
OF PUBLIC SAFETY.
The CHAIRMAN. Colonel, what is your position?
Col. ARNOLD. I am superintendent of the department of public safety.
The CHAIRMAN. And you are appointed by whom?
Col. ARNOLD, I am appointed by the governor and confirmed by the senate.
The CHAIRMAN. And generally speaking, what is the scope of your duties under
this law?
Col. ARNOLD. In a nutshell, our men are deputy sheriffs for the entire State,
except for civil purposes, but in the matter of criminal process we have juris-
diction throughout the State.
The CHAIRMAN. Under your law, how many are you authorized to name or to
appoint?
Col. ARNOLD. Under the present law, which became effective July 15, 1921,
including the office force and everything, we have a total of 290.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And where are they distributed?
Col. ARNOLD. They have been, more than half of them, up in Mingo County
to enforce martial law for the last eight months, and have been absolutely out
of my authority.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. Assuming that martial law terminated, who would have
authority in that case?
Col. ARNOLD. I have complete charge of them, except by the governor's procla-
mation he placed them in Mingo County, and they automatically come under
the authority of the adjutant general.
The CHAIRMAN. Who is he?
Col. ARNOLD. John H. Charnock.
The CHAIRMAN. The law, as amended, went into effect in July of this year?
Col. ARNOLD. July 15.
The CHAIRMAN. And that provides for a force of some 290, including all?
Col. ARNOLD. Yes, sir. When that law went into effect we only had 80 men.
We now have 200.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. How many are assigned down to Mingo County?
Col. ARNOLD. One hundred.

good many of those men-

Col. ARNOLD. Well, in Logan County, in Logan a great mass of men were

the mountains which divide Boone and Logan.
The CHAIRMAN. Where is Blair Mountain?
Col. ARNOAD. If you will recall, by the map, it is on the main pike going
from Charleston to Logan, and goes through Boone County, Madison, Sharp-
less, and so on. Blair Mountain is just beyond Blair, leading toward Logan
and near the town of Ethel.
The CHAIRMAN. Is it in Logan County?
Col. ARNOLD. Yes, sir. And these invaders, if you term them such, were in
Logan County.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. And they were passing through Boone?

The CHAIRMAN. And that was the battle of Blair Mountain?
Col. ARNOLD. Yes, sir. After it had been going on a few days a great many
of the attackers made a flank movement and the hardest fighting was probably
on the head of Crooked Creek, a continuation of Blair Mountain, but it was
not a battle. Every time they would see anyone move they would fire shots
into them.
The CHAIRMAN. How many were there there?
Col. ARNOLD. I do not know, sir. The defending party and the Logan people
as they were called-
Senator SHORTRIDGE (interrupting). They formed and went to the mountain

Col. ARNOLD. On Blair Mountain.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. On the Logan side?
Col. ARNOLD. Yes, sir.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. What were they doing?
Col. ARNOLD. They were simply up there on the mountain to stop anyone from

The CHAIRMAN. Was there any well-defined march over that mountain among

Col. ARNOLD. There is a regular road leading from Blair to Ethel, and it

ment was; up in the mountain were trails.
Senator SORTRIDGE. Was there anything in the way of a military formation?
Col. ARNOLD. A great deal, sir; and there were with them a great number of

Senator SHORTRIDGE. And they seemed to be in command, and were giving

Col. ARNOLD. I only know definitely as to two of them. They were gotten at

Senator SHORTRIDGE. And which side had the machine guns?
Col. ARNOLD. The attacking side; and they took them from the store.
Senator SHORTRIDGE. They commandeered them, did they?
Col. ARNOLD. They are said to have commandeered them.
The CHAIRMAN. They did not buy them?
Col. ARNOLD. They did not buy them, at least, not at that time; no, sir.
They would not buy them. They were owned by the coal companies them-
selves. A great many reports were coming in that merchants were being held

Senator SHORTRIDGE. And the telephone wires were cut?

hook an engine onto some cars and took them. But the armed men who were
gathering at Marmet and elsewhere rode on the regular passenger trains.

STATEMENT OF QUINN MARTIN, COAL OPERATOR.

The CHAIRMAN. You are in the union field?
Mr. MARTIN. We are in the union field with the exception of one mine in

is involved. We have been trying in every way possible to meet these people
and do business with them and to have dealings with them, but the United
Mine Workers of the district have become absolutely intolerable,and it seems
to me that the only solution, so far as we are concerned, is, first, of disposing
of the check-off, which you understand, I think.

union, the quiet men, men who have their families here in the vicinity, and
have you conversed with them personally in regard to their views?
Mr. MARTIN. Senator, for the last four or five years I have not been in close
touch with the operating end of the mines. Prior to that time I lived on
the job and knew every man, woman, and child on it, and my relationship with

Now, notwithstanding all of this marching that we have had around here,

be going on, and they push them on, while the leaders of them are in their

people. I do not believe there is any interest or force under God's heaven that
will get those fellows to meet with anybody else, or to make a contract or to
negotiate by them with the United Mine Workers of America.
The CHAIRMAN. In the nonunion fields?
Mr. MARTIN. That is my candid opinion. I think that the United Mine
Workers of America, by their own methods, injured themselves and their
chances of organizing furthermore by their arbitrary and arrogant methods in
the organized field than they have in anything else. I want to say something
in reference to that. When this army forced itself over there, we have a mine
right at the foot of the mountain, and I have a small interest there. There were
50 men that got up there and said, “ Give us guns; we are ready to go up in the
mountains and protect our county from invasion." We had 25 of them and they

Attorney General ENGLAND. The mining conditions in Logan County is not

order to get it we will have to reduce the wages. If you are willing to accept the
wages, I will take the business and get the work." That is the way they kept
at work where they did.
Mr. Lewis says that there will be no reduction in the miners' wages. Well,
mines have been idle while we have been working over there. We are not
working steadily now. The men are stirred up.

AFFIDAVITS FILED WITH THE COMMITTEE ON SUNDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, AT LICK
CREEK TENT COLONY, LICK CREEK, W. Va.
To whom it may concern:
We, the undersigned, whose residence is at the tent colony, do solemnly
swear that on the day that Elel Breedlove was stood up and killed that the
first shots were fired by Sheriff Vinson, Maj. Davis, and Capt. Brockus as they
came in view of the said camps from the county road. They came for the sole
and only purpose to brutally murder men, women, and helpless children, as
they shot up the place. Some of us, running helter and skelter in a frantic
effort to escape, was soon overtaken by Gov. Morgan's thugs and his honor Mr.
Vinson's gunmen. They threatened our women with rape, our camp with arson,
and men and boys with powder and lead if they should resort to any means
other than smiles. On the day Alexander Breedlove was forced to put up his
hand while a bunch of Mr. Morgan's West Virginia cossacks brutally shot him
to death another squad of 300 desperadoes, gunmen, and thugs were bursting
open and ransacking our homes, stealing such bounty as they wished to take to
their homes and breaking up the rest. I was in bed when I heard a gun fired.
got up, looked out in the road, and recognized Sheriff Vinson, Maj. Davis, and
Capt. Brockus. They had stopped the car in which they were riding and delib-
erately, without any provocation whatever, trained a machine gun on our help-
less home and began pouring in a deadly fire. We ran the best way we could,
but they had surrounded the colony and forced us to return to our home if
such a place could be called a home. I was standing on my porch when about
14 of the State gunmen came to my house. One of them said, "Oh, yes; you
have a damned old pistol you
I told them "No; but if I did have one
I would die before you could tear up my home." At this juncture Capt. Brockus
and some other men came up on the porch, the madam was at or near the door,
and he, Capt. Brockus, charged with his gun and knocked her down. They
then lined all of us men up and marched us down the railroad. They stood us
up beside the hill. Some said, "Just kill the
union

or break up
We was
said, "No; we will fill up every jail in the State with the
this union." They then marched us about 4 miles to jail for 56 hours.

us about five days. My mother, who is blind, and father, who is very feeble,
was overtaken and drove back home.
SAM MUNSEY.
Local Union 4807.
I was working in my garden when the two autos came up. The men in those
cars without being molested by anyone. They began to fire with machine gun,
high-powered rifles, and pistols. I ran home. By the time I was there about
50 State police, Mr. Ben Maynard, of Kentucky, and Mr. Boyd McCoy began
busting and breaking up everything. My little girl of 4 years old was
knocked down and ran over by Capt. Brockus. They then marched me out
with the other boy. I did not go fast enough. As I was about to get over the
fence Capt. Brokus knocked me over with his pistol. After they had us in jail
they told us if we did not keep quiet they would blow up the county jail.
ROY COMBS, 4803.
COMMUNICATION FROM AMERICAN CIVIL LIBERTIES UNION FILED WITH THE COM-
MITTEE BY ROGER N. BALDWIN, SUNDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1921.
AMERICAN CIVIL LIBERTIES UNION,
138 WEST THIRTEENTH STREET, NEW YORK CITY,
September 13, 1921.
To the Senate committee investigating the civil warfare in West Virginia.
GENTLEMEN: As American citizens interested in the maintenance of civil
rights as the only guarantee of orderly progress, we have followed the course
of the industrial conflict in West Virginia now under investigation by you. We,
74020-21-VOL 1-36


===== [扫描序号 566] =====
558
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
therefore, take the liberty of stating to you our views, and of sending to you in
West Virginia our director as our representative (Roger N. Baldwin). We
speak from a careful examination of the facts, both those published and those
we have obtained first-hand.
At the outset may we express our hope that the committee will proceed at
once to an inquiry into the underlying causes of the breakdown of civil govern-
ment and not concern itself with the more dramatic but far less important ef-
fects in terms of violence. So far as we can see, that violence will continue
indefinitely so long as the causes remain. The armed resistance of the
mountaineer miners to oppression is obviously too deeply rooted to be put
down permanently by force. While we are wholly opposed to all methods of
violence, the spirit behind the mountaineers' struggle for what they believe
to be their constitutional rights challenges the admiration of all who are
devoted to American traditions.
Wherever in West Virginia the miners have been oppressed by armed force
in the hands of their employers, there has been war. Wherever armed force
has been withdrawn by the employers and organization permitted, there has
been peace.
In our view the settlement of the warfare in Mingo County and its prevention
in the four unorganized counties where it will inevitably break out next, can be
achieved only by the authority of the Federal Government. The issue is at
bottom simply the free exercise of the rights guaranteed all citizens by the
Federal Constitution. This is the opinion expressed to us by all persons in
impartial positions, competent to judge.
Behind the local conflict in the State is a struggle between the greatest in-
dustrial interests of the Nation on the one side and the United States Mine
Workers on the other. This national aspect of the struggle makes it even more
imperative, in our judgment, that the Federal Government, through your find-
ings, devise means to reach a settlement that will restore peace and civil
government. If that could be done as it was so successfully during the war,
it can be done now. For the vindication of the rights we cherish as Americans,
we look to you to act.
Respectfully, yours,
Harry F. Ward, Norman H. Thomas, Albert De Silver, John Haynes
Holmes, Helen Phelps Stokes, Mary McDowell, Robert Morse
Lovett, Chicago; Henry R. Mussey, Washington; Henry R.
Linville, New York.

QUESTIONS BY FEDERATED CRAFTS OF HUNTINGTON, W. VA., FILED WITH THE COM-
MITTEE WITH THE ABOVE LETTER.
To whom it may concern:
We, the delegates of the Federated Crafts of the City of Huntington, repre-
senting 3,500 workingmen, desire to ask and know if owners of coal mines


===== [扫描序号 567] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
559
can organize a coal operators' association and the men who toil to dig the
coal can not organize a miners' organization?
Again we would like to know how C. F. Keeney and Fred Mooney, president
and secretary of the miners' organization, can be held without bond for a murder
which we understand was committed in another county while they were
attending the West Virginia State Federation of Labor meeting in the city of
Huntington, and the personal aides of the coal operators' association, who we
know did kill Sid Hateld and Ed Chambers, still run at large on a small bond?
If Keeney and Mooney are mudererers, why are not members of the coal
operators' association when their aides murder someone?
Does it look like the miners of Logan, Mingo, and McDowell have been
operating in peace for 15 years when the same public press that makes this
statement at the request of the operators has reported an average of at least
one murder a month, and we have good reason to believe that the half has
never yet been told?
We should like to ask if the law is being carried out which provides for
a weighman at the mines; also in regard to pay days?
The coal operators of Logan claim they pay more for coal than is paid
în union fields. In the same statement they say if their fields were organized
the price of coal would be so high the public could not buy. Please explain.
We should like to ask as to living and working conditions in these nonunion
fields. Does not the same dollar bill stay in the same place and pay off the year
around, made so by the company store and other compulsory methods of
trade?
We would like to ask if when a worker wants a little real money, will his
script bring as much as 90 cents on $1?
We would like to ask how it is the coal operators' association can buy arms
and ammunition by the thousands and a miners' organization or other organiza-
tions are to be prosecuted if they buy or attempt to buy?
We would like to ask, can not the railroad officials be prosecuted for hauling
guns and ammunition to a coal operators' association when they know they are
getting them with the intent to kill.

A. I was in Kentucky.

that I moved from Leckie colliery to Rawl and then from Rawl over to Leckie
colliery.
Q. Where do you claim your home, in West Virginia or Kentucky?-A. Well,
my home, where I claim my home is in Mingo County.
Q. When did you move into Mingo County?-A. About five years ago.

Q. You came over here to see about it?-A. I told them I had to have some-

Q. How many children have you?-A. Three; two living and one dead.
Q. Where have you been living ever since last fall?-A. Me and my family?
Q. Where have you been?-A. On Pigeon Creek.

Q. What have you been doing over there?-A. Working at a sawmill and

Q. Where were you when the shooting started; in the tent colony?—A. I was

Q. What did you do?-A. I just brought my baby up there to a big tree and
told my wife to get up there under this big tree, and we stayed there under the
tree until the shooting ceased.
Q. Did you see anybody?—A. Nobdy but the residents of the colony down there
washing.

Q. You heven't even got a pocket knife?—A. No, sir; I haven't.
Q. Did you see some cars come up there?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. What happened when they came up?-A. I saw the cars. I didn't see the

up in the road, and I saw one State constabulary laying down under the bank, and
then after a few minutes he got up and brushed the dirt off of himself and
got in the car.
Q. Did you hear any shooting before you saw this man lying there?-A. That
was after the shooting.
Q. How long before the shooting commenced was it you saw the man?—A.
The shooting had commenced and was over when I saw the man.
Q. That is all you saw?-A. Yes, sir; until that evening.
Q. What did you see that evening?-A. I saw the officers coming up there is
all.

By Mr. STOKES:
STATEMENT OF MILLARD HALLEY.
Q. Where were you born?-A. How is that?
Q. How old are you?-A. Twenty-eight the 5th day of July.
Q. Have you a family?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. What is it composed of?-A. My wife and two children.
Q. Where were you born?-A. I was born in Boyd County, Ky.
Q. Are you a miner?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. How long have you been a miner?-A. Well, I couldn't say just exactly;
somewhere like 12 or 13 years.
Q. Where were you working at the time the strike was called here in Mingo
County? A. At Sharondale, Ky.
Q. You claim Kentucky as your home? A. Yes, s'r.
Q. Did you ever work up in the Kanawha field?—A. Yes, sir; I worked up
there a short while.
Q. What year was it?-A. I couldn't tell you.
Q. Were you there during the strike?-A. No, sir.
Q. Are you a member of the union?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. When did you jo'n the union?-A. I believe it was in July.
Q. A year ago last July?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. When you joined the union what did you do?-A. Well, when I joined I
was asked to vacate the house.
Q. Then what did you do?-A. That is exactly what I done.
Q. You vacated, and where did you go to?-A. Moved to Lick Creek.
Q. Have you been living there ever since? A. Yes, sir.
Q. You haven't worked any since?—A. No, sir.
Q. You know pretty well everybody in the colony there, don't you?-A. There
is lots of people moved in there the last few days that I don't know.
Q. How many rifles are in the tent colony, would you say, owned by people
in there or controlled by them?-A. I don't know. I never did see but just a
few around there. I don't know anything about the upper camp, but there is
just a few rifles in the bottom.
Q. Did they keep them there in the tents or on the Kentucky side?—A. I
couldn't tell you about that, where they kept them.
Q. You couldn't tell where they keep them?-A. No, sir.
Q. Where were you the morning that the shooting took place; this last
shooting?-A. I was in the tent when the firing took place.
Q. Well, I wish you would describe what you first heard, so far as the firing
is concerned; how did it take place?-A. Well, I was in the tent and it seemed
like there was 30 or 40 shots fired, and I come on to the outside and was there
and got the old lady and kids over the river bank.
Q. You went over into Kentucky?--A. No, sir.
Q. You got them over there?-A. Got them over the river bank.
Q. When you came out did you see anybody out there, when you came out of
the tent?-A. I didn't see anybody, only I saw some of these constabulary.
saw three.
Q. Where were they?—A. They were by the side of the cars.
I
Q. Now, what were they doing?-A. They wasn't shooting when I came out.
I didn't see any shots fired at all; the shooting was ceased when I come out.
Q. You were in the tent and you heard a volley or 20 or 30 shots? A. Yes, sir.
Q. And you came out of the tent and saw the constabulary, but at that
time they were not shooting?-A. No, sir; they had ceased.
Q. How do you know?--A. I could hear if there had been any shooting done.
Q. You say they had ceased shooting? A. Yes, sir.
Q. How do you know they fired any shots?-A. I said somebody done the
shooting; I didn't say who done it.
Q. You say they had ceased firing?-A. I heard shots fired, but it was over
when I got out on the outside.
Q. You don't mean to say that they did the firing?-A. I didn't say who had
fired.
Q. You say they had ceased firing?-A. I said whoever it was had.
Q. Then what did you do after you took your wife and children over the
river bank?-A. I stayed around the tents there; I wasn't out of the tent
colony.
Q. Did you stay over the river bank with them? A. Yes, sir; I was over
the river bank down here.

STATEMENT OF AARON COPLEY.
Q. Where were you born, Mr. Copley?-A. I was born in Wayne County,
W. Va.
Q. Have you lived in West Virginia all the time?-A. Yes, sir; I have been
raised in West Virginia.
Q. When did you first come to Mingo County?-A. I have been in Mingo

Q. What have you been doing?-A. Mining.
Q. Where have you been working?—A. I have been working at Chattaroy

working over here at the mouth of Pond.
Q. For what company?-A. The Black Diamond Coal Co.
Q. Did you quit work then? A. Yes, sir; I quit work the 1st day of July.
Q. And you haven't worked at mining since then?-A. No, sir.
Q. Where did you go to after you left Black Diamond?-A. I moved to the
tents over here at the mouth of Pond Creek, on a fellow's place over there,
and he sold the place and then I moved to Lick Creek. and how come me to
move off of Pond Creek when they give me the notice to move they ordered
me off of the waters of Pond Creek.
Q. And you have been living in that tent colony ever since?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. You are a married man?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. How many in the family?-A. Just me and the wife.
Q. Have you any children?—No, sir.
Q. How long have you been in the Lick Creek colony?-A. I went there in
September, I believe it was.
Q. Who has charge of that colony; who is the head man there?-A. Well, I
don't just know who is the head man. There ain't no man who was the head
man over the whole camp. We have got two-we have got about three or four
presidents up there. You see each man looks after his own local affairs.
Q. When did you join the union?—A. I joined the union in June.
Q. Where were you when you joined?-A. At Black Diamond.
Q. Who got you to join; who came and got your membership?-A. Nobody
at all; I joined myself.
Q. You came down here and joined?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Who did you come to see when you came here?-A. A fellow by the name
of Ben Page.
Q. That nigger? A. Yes, sir.
Q. Who is the president of your local there?-A. Mr. Justice is president
of my local.
Q. Who is your secretary?-A. The recording secretary is John Hall.
Q. Who is he?-A. He is a fellow that stays up there in the camp.
Q. Who is your treasurer?-A. Martin holds the treasurer himself.

Q. Who was there with you?—A. George Newsom and Richard Kirk, and an

sitting there with me when they come down and lined us、 up.
Q. And they arrested you? A. Yes, sir.
STATEMENT OF SAM MUNCY.
Mr. MUNCY. Thirty-seven years old; moved to Lick Creek in March. Worked
last at Jack Goodloe's. He said he had no trouble with wife on Monday. I
had taken a few drinks Monday. Between 1.30 and 2 Monday I was at home.
I did not shoot at anybody in the road. I was not fighting with my wife-was
just carrying on. I stepped out the back door shooting at the sand bar. I
was standing when shooting. I saw Alex Breedlove Tuesday, June 14. I did
not see him any more that day. I was sitting on the bed and heard some shots
fired. I got my gun and went to the door. I don't know who were doing the
shooting. I don't know whether it was Lee Hatfield or not.

Q. Did you have any weapons at the time they arrested you?-A. I had

Q. You had been in that colony about how long, you say?-A. Well, some-

STATEMENT OF GEORGE TOLBERT.
Examination by Maj. Davis:
Q. About the time there was some shooting up there, about 9 o'clock, or 9.30,

kind of a gun, as I walked up, but I turned immediately back.
Q. When the first shooting began?-A. Yes, sir; that is all I know anything
about was that first.
Q. And so when the first shots were fired you didn't get up there until after it

and I could see some person, but I wasn't there in view enough to see what they
was doing or anything like that. I turned and put the women folks back over
the hill. My wife and girls was washing, and I put them back, and I walked
back up, and by that time it was all over.

any place?-A. No, sir; I wasn't out in the tent colony at all, but I was out
early in the garden to work.
Q. Did you see Martin Justice?-A. No, sir; I didn't see him.
Q. Were you around there Monday when Sam Muncy and his wife had a
little trouble?-A. I was at home.
Q. You didn't see anything of that trouble?-A. No, sir; I didn't see any of
that.
Q. You don't know anything about this shooting at all?-A. No, sir; I don't.
Q. Do you know a colored fellow they called Green? A. Yes, sir; I know
one that stayed there in the camp.
Q. What was his name?-A. Green is all I know about his name. I just know
his face when I see him. I wasn't acquainted with him.
By Capt. BROCKUS:
Q. Where did you live in the tent colony?-A. Down next to the river-in
the lower camp.
By Maj. DAVIS:
Q. Did you see anybody with rifles at all in that camp or guns?-A. During
that day?
Q. Yes; or at any time?-A. No, sir; I didn't.
Q. At any time?-A. Oh, I seen rifles there somtime ago.
Q. About how many rifles do you think are in that camp?-A. I think there
is four or five or something like that that I have seen.
Q. When they do guard duty do they use these rifles or did you ever do any
guard duty?-A. No, sir.
Q. Did you ever see anybody doing guard duty?-A. No, sir; I am paralyzed
and am never out only around camps there.
STATEMENT OF WATSON SLOAN.
Examination by Maj. DAVIS:
Q. How old are you?-A. I am 18 years old.
Q. Did you ever work in the mines?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. How long?-A. About a year.
Q. Before the strike?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Where were you when this trouble hanppened?-A. I was standing out
in the county road at Lick Creek.
Q. Tell us exactly what you saw of it around there?-A. Well, sir; I heard
the shooting, but I never saw anybody fire any shot.

Q. And when you heard this first shooting, where did it seem to be from?—A.
It seemed to be well, it was in the hills. The first shot was fired, and, then,
they begin to shoot and shot about-I couldn't make no estimate how many.
Q. Fifteen or tewnty?-A. Yes, sir; and they kind of ceased up and I was
standing there in the road when the shooting began, and a bullet struck in
about 2 feet of me and I went up the county road and went to a rock.
Q. You saw us there in the cars?-A. Well, I seen lots of them; but I don't
know who they was.
Q. But you could see us there?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Where were you in the county road?-A. When the shooting began I was
right there just before the shooting began I was right under the culvert. You
know where the culvert is, and that road comes down the hill, I was about the
second bend.
Q. The dirt road?-A. No; I was in the automobile road.
Q. Where the colored people live?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Clear at the bottom?-A. No; I was still up about 100 feet down from the
county road, that little dirt road, you know, that goes down there; it is the
county road, I reckon.
Q. It is the same road everybody uses?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. You were between us and the creek?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. How far were you away from the automobiles?--A. Something like 100
feet.
Q. You say a bullet struck close to you?-A. In about 2 feet of me. They were
falling in every direction and one struck close to me, the only one I noticed.
Q. That would have to come over the top of the automobiles?-A. Yes, sir; it
would have to come over the top of the automobiles.
Q. From out of the hill?—A. Yes, sir. When that shot struck close to me I
went to the cliffs or got at them rocks.
Q. You remember when we shot back, don't you?—A. I don't know that any-
body shot; I didn't see anybody.
Q. You heard something like an automatic?-A. Yes, sir; I heard all kinds of
shooting, but it was so fast I couldn't tell how it was.
Q. Leaving that shooting, you know there was a garden near there, do you?—
A. Yes, sir.
Q. That wasn't very far from you?-A. No, sir; just a short distance.
Q. Now, getting back a little to later on. What did you do between that and
the time that they brought you down here and arrested everybody. Where did
you go after the first shooting and before the time they arrested you?—A. I
went up there in the county road.
Q. That was two or three hours later. Did you stay there two or three
hours?-A. No, sir; by the time I got there I hadn't been there but 15 or 20
minutes when they come along and arrested me and sent me up to the spring
to get water. They kept me there in the county road maybe two hours and
brought me on. I was about the first one that was arrested.
Q. Do you know a colored fellow they call Green?-A. No sir; I don't know
none of them colored fellows up there.
Q. How long have you been there?-A. About two, three, or four months, but
I don't visit among the colored fellows.
Q. Where do you live in the camp?-A. My tent is back up on the hill, up in
that little hollow up the hill.
Q. Going the county road-you know where the colored fellows live?-A. Yes,
sir.
Q. You live up on that side of the road?-A. Yes, sir; back up in that hollow.
Q. Where were you when the shooting took place in the hills in the after-
noon?-A. Oh, I was over there in the county road.
Q. Did you see anybody shooting out of the tents down there?--A. No, sir; I
didn't see anybody shooting, but I heard some shooting.
Q. You were under arrest when the second shooting occurred? A. Yes, sir.

Q. John, what is the number of your local?-A. 4803.
Q. Is that the same local that Martin Justice is president of?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. He is also treasurer?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. How many members have you up there-A. Well, he is financial sec-

Q. And acting president?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Who was the president?--A. Didn't have any.
Q. About how many people do you have on the roll up there-I mean members
of the local?-A. Well, sir, I couldn't state just how many there is. I don't
know as I have noticed the roll lately. We have 28 on the issue, but we have
some several that is not on the issue.
Q. Twenty-eight on the issue? A. Yes, sir.
Q. And several that are not on?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Well, some fellow said there was about 40; that would make it about
right? A. I guess it would. I wouldn't make a permanent thing of that.
Q. Going back to Tuesday, when this trouble occurred; you know what time
I am talking about?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Where were you Tuesday morning?-A. I was at home.
Q. You heard the shooting? A. Yes, sir; I heard some shooting.
Q. Were you at home when the shooting occurred?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Had you been out that day?-A. No, sir; I never was on the railroad
that day until I was arrested and taken out.
Q. Now, when the shooting began, what did you do?-A. I was standing in
the store and I was waiting on some one. I don't remember who it was, but I
was waiting on some one.
Q. At the store at the willow tree?-A. No, sir; the store down in the
bottom. And I stepped to the window, and when the shooting began I looked
up in the road and I seen some fellows in the road shooting. I could hear the
shooting, but couldn't tell where it was, only I seen some one or two up there
shooting.
Q. In the road?-A. Well, one fellow was in the road and one was a little
below the road.
Q. How many times did they shoot?-A. I couldn't say, but some several
shots was fired.
Q. Where did the shooting seem to be coming from?-A. I couldn't tell
where it was; I was in the storehouse and didn't know.
Q. Are you sure that you saw more than one person shooting in the road?-
A. Yes, sir; I am pretty sure there was two.
Q. Sitting down, standing, kneeling, or what?-A. Well, one fellow was
standing up. Now, I will say it this way: There was, I think, two different
guns firing, from the reports, and I seen one fellow and the other one acted
like he was, on the back of the road, and I could see the smoke from the gun,
and it seemed like he was on the back of the road shooting, maybe kneeled
down and I couldn't see him well; probably he was over in the ditch. I
couldn't see him good. There was two fellows I could see, but I wouldn't say
positive they was both shooting, but I took it they were both shooting.
Q. John, how many guns do you reckon are in that camp?-A. I couldn't
tell you anything about it. I haven't seen very many guns. I have seen a few
old shotguns and things like that; as to pistols, I haven't seen any pistols.
Q. Did you ever see this gun that Alex. Breedlove had, that 30 Army
rifle? A. No, sir; I didn't know he had a gun.
Q. Did you ever see him with a gun?-A. No, sir.
Q. Did you ever see Martin Justice with a gun?-A. I saw Martin Justice
away long back last winter with a 25-20, but he sold that one.
Q. When was that?-A. Along back in the winter, but since that I haven't.
Q. What system do you all have up there for guarding your camp up there?-
A. None at all in our camp.
Q. You never place anybody on the lookout?-A. No, sir. We used to have a
regular guard system, but not lately, not for the last three months I will say.
Q. You haven't had any guard system for three months?--A. No regular.
Of course we have had reports that such things were going to happen several
times and probably we would pretty well all sit up and watch around in order
to take care of our families in case anything might happen, but the reports
never come true.
Q. There is a colored fellow named Green; do you know him?-A. No, sir;
I don't.
Q. He is not in this crowd?-A. I don't know him.
Q. Who brought the information up there that the State police or somebody
was going to clean up the camp?-A. I didn't hear anything about that state-
ment until after we was all arrested. I didn't hear anything of it. The fact
is I am never out any; I have a position there and, of course, I have to stay
in there mostly all the time. The business is not so big, but still I have to be
there.

STATEMENT OF GEORGE NEWSOM.
Examination by Maj. DAVIS:
Q. How long have you worked in the mines, George?-A. Well, I have been

Q. Where were you the day this shooting occurred?-A. I was up where that

up the hollow and don't fool around in the bottom.
Q. Were you in the woods at all the other day?-A. No, sir.
Q. Do you know a nigger named Green?—A. No; I don't know him.
STATEMENT OF DOCK CARGILM.
Examination by Maj. DAVIS:
Q. Where were you last Tuesday when this trouble happened; tell us what
happened about the shooting in the morning? A. I was sitting on this porch
in behind this Italian's store; I was sitting on that porch with my feet swing-
ing on the ground, at an apple tree.
Q. You heard the shooting? A. Yes, sir; I was sitting there when it hap
pened.
Q. Then what did you do?-A. I couldn't do a thing; I was sitting there.
Q. What did you see: did you look up to see where the shooting come
from?-A. You see where this little old box of a house was sitting, there is a
big store sitting facing it; a Dago has a store there.
Q. You couldn't see where the shooting was?-A. No; I couldn't say. I
heard it and I thought I would just as well sit where I was.
Q. You didn't walk around and look?—A. I just sat there.
Q. You don't know anything about the shooting?-A. Only heard the shoot-
ing.
Q. You don't know whether it was on the hill or in the road?—A. I don't
know where it was.
Q. Where were you when they arrested you?-A. Sitting right there.
Q. You were there all that time?--A. Stayed right there. I thought there
was no use to go anywhere and that I would stay there, and I just set there:
it was shady under that apple tree.
Q. Did you see any men with guns that day; did you see Alex Breedlove go
up with a gun?-A. No, sir; I never seen him.
Q. Now, as a matter of fact, he went that way; he is dead and can't be
prosecuted for it?--A. Yes; that is so, but I didn't see him.
Q. Did you hear anybody else say that he went up that way or that they
had seen him that day?-A. They didn't tell me they seen him.
Q. Did you hear them talking about it, that he had a gun that morning?—
A. I say nobody didn't tell me a thing about it.
Q. Was that the general talk?-A. That they were saying he had a gun?
Q. Yes?-A. No, sir.
Q. How about Martin Justice?-A. I don't know nothing about that. I
started to bathe and I thought I would go to the store and get a bar of soap,
and this thing all happened and I didn't see anything.

STATEMENT OF MRS. AFTON MCCOY TO MAJ. THOMAS B. DAVIS AND SHERIFF
PIMSON, AT WILLIAMSON, W. VA., SEPTEMBER 13, 1921.
The witness was first duly sworn before J. G. Nesbit, notary public in and
for Mingo County, W. Va.
Maj. DAVIS:
Q. Mrs. McCoy, you live at Stringtown?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Were you at Stringtown on September-about the 1st, 2d, 3d, 4th, and
5th? A. Yes, sir.
Q. About that time there was some shooting there?-A. Yes, sir; I was there.
Q. How long have you lived at Stringtown?-A. About four years altogether-
have been here about 13 years.
Q. Mrs. McCoy, I wish you would tell us from the beginning-you know what
we would like for you to tell us-all about what happened up there-I think
it commenced-the shooting-about Friday; what do you know about this
last shooting over there?-A. Do you want to know the names of the ones
that had the guns?
Q. I want to know something about the shooting; when did you first notice
that something was going on?-A. The first I noticed was that the men
would go out and stay out of the day.
Q. What day was that?-A. It commenced on the Saturday before the shoot-
ing began.

Q. A week before?-A. Yes, sir. And the next there was nine men came to
Mrs. McCoy's on Saturday a week before the shooting began.
Q. Where did they come from?-A. She said they came from Lick Creek.
Q. Do you know who these nine men are?-A. I do not know; they were
strange men that came in there.
Q. Was Wade Hampton there?-A. I do not know.
Q. You do not know anyone from Lick Creek?-A. I do not know anyone
except-I forget the name now.
Q. Did she tell you anyone?-A. She told me Alex Murphy's son-in-law-
I forget his name the one that commenced the shooting they said was a
Halley, who lived at Lick Creek. George Cunningham, from Lick Creek,
he was there; I knew him.
Q. When was the next that came in?-A. The next came in on Friday, the
following Friday.
Q. The following Friday some more came?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Where did they come from?-A. They said some came from Lick Creek.
some from Borderland, and some from Goodman, and some from Pond Creek.
Q. Did you know any of them?-A. No, sir; I did not know any of them;
they were all strangers to me.
Q. Where did they stay?-A. They stayed at Uriah McCoy's. Julius Me-
Coy's, Jim McCoy's, and Dan Thompson's and Henry McCoy's houses; also
Tom McCoy's and some at Boat Allen's.
Q. Did any stay at Scott's house?-A. No, sir; they stayed at Lunce Pat-
terson's.
Q. Any stay at Borem's house?-A. No, sir; they did not stay at Borem's
house.
Q. Where else did they stay?-A. Let me see-
Q. Did you keep any?-A. No, sir.
Q. Any stay with Lafe McCoy ?-A. Some stayed with Lafe McCoy.
Q. How about Phillips?-A. None stayed there.
Q. Do you know of anywhere else where they stayed?-A. No; I do not
know of anywhere else where they stayed.
Q. Then what happened-first shooting?-A. Well, the first I noticed of the
shooting, that there was going to be shooting, I heard Urias McCoy's wife,
she told me the night before she believed there was going to be shooting right
away.
Q. That was Friday night? A. Yes, sir; so we never went to bed until it
was 12 o'clock and men were still passing our house yet. We never got up
until 11 o'clock, and I just had breakfast and was on the porch when the
first shot was fired.
Q. Where did it seem to come from?-A. It seemed to come from off the
point above John Robinson's, on the Kentucky side. Urias McCoy told us
to get up the hollow, so we went up the hollow and stayed until about 3 o'clock
that evening-Saturday afternoon.
Q. Who did you see shooting?-A. I never saw anyone shoot at all.
Q. Who did you see with rifles?-A. I seen most everyone over there that
I know.
Q. Who that you know?-A. Henry McCoy, Dan Thompson, Floyd Roberts,
Garcy Roberts, Letcher McCoy, Willard McCoy, Jim McCoy, Uriah McCoy,
Julius McCoy, Kel McCoy, Lafe McCoy, John McCoy, Homer McCoy, George
Cunningham, and Millard Hally.
Q. Where did you see these men with their rifles?-A. They were along
the road Saturday night when we went up to Mr. Allens. We left out of one
hollow and went along another.
Q. Did you hear them state what they were going to do?-A. I never heard
them state just exactly what they were going to do, but I heard them state
after it was over what they said they did do.
Q. What did they say?-A. They said they shot up Merrimac; they said
they thought nearly everyone in Merrimac was killed.
Q. Who said that?-A. Letcher McCoy. There was a boy came over from
Pond Creek-Tom Roberts-and said they were looking for trouble over there,
and Letcher McCoy and Willard McCoy said to send them word and they would
be over there to-morrow night.
Q. Mrs. McCoy, did not they bring some one wounded to your house?-A.
Not to my house.
Q. Whose house was it?-A. J. P. Allen's.
Q. Did you see him?-A. Yes, sir.

Q. Who was it?-A. It was a boy from Lick Creek, just a young boy; I do

Q. How bad was he wounded?-A. Had his ankle broken.
Q. Shot?-A. No; he was not shot, but there was one from Lick Creek that

Q. Do you know of anyone else that was wounded?-A. No, sir.

back in the hill. Landon Bevins has one back in the hill and Grover McCoy.
Q. Do you know the kind of fortifications they have on this lower graveyard
point?-A. No, sir; I do not know.
Q. What is Tom McCoy and those boys doing at Van Lear?-A. They said
they went over there for Richard Beverly's trial; he has a trial next Monday.
Q. The man that was captured some time back-back in April?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Is that the case he is being tried for now?-A. Yes, sir. The trial will
begin Monday, and they left on Tuesday.
