STATEMENT OF W. W. WHITE.
Q. You are members of the United Mine Workers? A. Yes, sir.
Q. Drawing benefits? A. Yes, sir.
Q. Now on a strike?-A. Yes, sir.
On the last Sunday in August, will you please tell us what happened in
reference to a meeting being called near Lenore by some of the union offi-
cials? A. Well, there was a union fellow came up the road and told us there
would be a man at Lenore Sunday evening and to be there when the evening
train run, and a few of us went down.
Q. Who was this man?-A. I was told that this man's name was Dean.
Q. You do not know him?-A. I did not know him; I was told.
Q. Where was he from?-A. I could not tell you; I do not know.
Q. Did anyone else tell you where they thought he was from?—A. No, sir;
I never heard say.
Q. About how many of you went to the meeting?-A. Twenty-five or thirty.
Q. Were any of them armed, that you could see?-A. No, sir.
Q. Did you hold a meeting?-A. No, sir; the man who was to meet us failed
to come, and no meeting was held.
Q. What did you do then?-A. Went back home.
Q. Have you been to any meeting since? A. No, sir; or not for a month
before.
Q. How long before?-A. Well, since the martial law was declared the first
time.
Q. What was discussed at that meeting?—A. Nothing, but just common busi-
ness of the lodge.
Q. No talk of any armed march or anything?—A. No, sir.
Q. Who did you see at the last meeting, by name-that is, the meeting about
two weeks ago-the last Sunday in August?-A. Myself, three of my brothers-
John, Jim, and Ben White-Ples Chafin, son of Henry Chefins; Albert Clark;
Emanuel Rose; Jim Aldrich; Robert Lloyd; Oliver Meade; Jeff Meade; Naah
Rose; Russ Bryant; Jim Clark; Joe Blair; W. C. Brown; George Runyon;
A. B. Blankenship; Charles Boldin; Lee Brewer; Charles Ausbern; Tate
Durosett; Joe Evans; Rube Evans; Bobby Hall; Ed Hatcher; Jim Ward;
Henry York, and William York.
Q. What did you tell your father-in-law, Mr. White-W. W. White-with ref-
erence to your family as you were starting to this meeting?-A. I told my
father-in-law if I did not get back for a day or so to take care of my wife and
baby.
(Statement of Ben White is the same as W. W. White with the following
exception):
I did not hear who the man was that was going to hold a meeting, and am
not certain that I saw all the men mentioned by my brother, W. W. White,
who went to the so-called meeting at Lenore on the night in question.
Signed this 14th day of September, 1921, at Williamson, W. Va.
STATEMENT OF HERBERT PACK, MADE ON THE 4TH DAY OF SEPTEMBER, 1921, at
WILLIAMSON, W. Va.
(The witness, being first duly sworn, made the following statement:)
Examination by Mr. STOKES:
Q. Pack, we want you to make a statement of all you know about this mat-
ter; I want you to tell us all of it and want you to tell us the truth and, if


===== [扫描序号 605] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
597
है
you are willing to do that in the event you should be mixed up in this, we
will not prosecute you. Are you willing to do that?-A. You will not prose-
cute me?
Q. That is what I said; if you will tell us all the truth, everything you
know about it, we will not prosecute you.
Q. And you will turn me loose now?-A. I wouldn't say that, because we
want you possibly to get other information that would come up. I wouldn't
say we would turn you loose at this time, but we won't prosecute you in the
court. I don't know much about it. I will just tell you the truth about it. I
told them over there all I know about it.
Q. Tell us what you do know about it, how it started, and all about it.-A.
Well, I was at Kermit and belong to the Kermit local down there, and there
was a fellow come down there.
Q. Who was he?-A. I don't know the man. I will tell the truth about it.
He come down there and said they wanted us all at Lick Creek, wanted all the
union men at Lick Creek, and he fooled around there and told us we all had
to go and begged around until five of us-there was five of us come and went
to Lick Creek and we eat our breakfast. We went day before yesterday, I be-
lieve, and went ahead up to Lick Creek, and we was all laying around there
and a man come and took a bunch and went over there on the Pond Creek
side, on the Pond Creek side, and there was another bunch down there about
the river, I wasn't in that bunch, I was on the Pond Creek side there, and along
about-I don't know what time it was when I heard the shooting start, and
I was sitting back on the hill, and along about 1 or 2 o'clock, I guess, or may
be 12, there was a bunch of men come in from the Pond Creek side, and we
was sitting down there and they fired into us and I lit out running and they
was cutting bushes all over my head. I lit out and run and went around that
ridge there and come off down at the Burnwell Hollow and was aiming to go
and catch No. 3 and get out and these fellows, some of them, I don't know
how many there was, headed me off and arrested me. That is all I know
about it.
Q. How many came from Kermit?-A. Five, I think.
Q. Who were they?-A. I don't know their names.
Q. How did you get up from Kermit?-A. There was two Harmon boys.
Q. What are the Harmon boys' first names?-A. I don't know exactly their
names. I know their names, but I don't know the boys apart. I think they call
one Dan and the other one Ike, or something.
Q. Are they brothers?-A. And there was Sherman Keesee, and that is all I
know.
Q. They came up from Kermit? A. Yes, sir.
Q. Which way did you come from Kermit?-A. We come up to Naugatuck
and caught a train and come up.
Q. You came up on a freight train?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. How far did you come up on the freight train?-A. To the Williamson
yards up here.
Q. How many were with you?-A. Six with that man that took us.
Q. Where did he come from?-A. He was from Lick Creek. They called his
name, and I believe they called him Hammonds.
Q. You don't know his first name?—A. I think they called him Pete Ham-
monds.
Q. He took you on up through the railroad yards after you got up there?—
A. Yes, sir.
Q. Just which way did you go?-A. Went up to Lick Creek and eat and went
up the road.
Q. How many did you meet at Lick Creek?-A. Nobody there.
Q. How many men did you meet there at Lick Creek?-A. They had all gone
ahead to Stringtown. There was three or four there in the camps.
Q. Now, you went on from there on to Stringtown?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Did you go to this side of the river or the other side?--A. Went to this
side and went to the section house.
Q. And you crossed the river there? A. Yes, sir.
Q. And when you got over the river how many men were there?-A. I don't
know; I didn't count them.
Q. How many would you say?-A. I am afraid to guess. I just actually
couldn't tell. I guess maybe 100 or somewhere along there.
Q. When you all got together there, what was said about dividing them up?-
A. I don't know what was said. They stayed all night there that night and I


===== [扫描序号 606] =====
598
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
slept on a man's porch there, and the next morning they all ganged up and
bunched me up with them, and we went on top of the hill between there and
Pond Creek and was sitting up there.
Q. What did they say they were going to do when they got up there?—
A. They was aiming to hold them Pond Creek fellows off of the Stringtown
men down there if they got into a shooting match.
Q. They got up there before the Pond Creek men got up?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. What did they go up there for?-A. To keep them Pond Creek men back.
Q. What did they want to keep them back for?-A. I don't know. They was
fighting over there and didn't want them to come over there.
Q. And you got up there before any fighting was done?-A. I told you what
they said they was going up there for.
Q. For what?-A. To keep Pond Creek out of Stringtown there.
Q. Who told them Pond Creek was coming in there?-A. I don't know who
it was. There was so many men talking about it that I don't know. I was a
stranger among them all except what I told you.
Q. Were you armed?-A. I had a little old .32, but I throwed it away.
Q. A .32 rifle? A. Yes, sir.
Q. You threw it away?-A. It was one of these little cheap light-weights.
Q. Were the other men armed?-A. Yes; most of them. One or two wasn't,
I don't think.
Q. Who furnished the ammunition?-A. They already had it there.
Q. Did you have it or who gave you your ammunition?-A. Well, I got it at
Stringtown.
Q. Who gave it to you?-A. I don't exactly know who.
Q. What kind of looking man was he?-A. Dogged if I could tell you. There
was so many of them. Some of them fetched some from Kermit, a little dab,
but not much, though.
Q. When this man came down to Kermit to get you all what did he tell you
he wanted with you on Lick Creek?-A. He said 700 union men come through
that way and wanted to meet us at Lick Creek.
Q. That 700 men had come through from where?-A. Back through that way
from Cabin Creek or somewhere.
Q. And he wanted you all to meet them at Lick Creek?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. And what did he say they were going to do when they got over there?—A.
He never said, I don't reckon. He talked it to our men and our men told us
that we had to go to Lick Creek.
Q. How is that?-A. I say the head president of our local down there, he
talked it all to him. He didn't talk it to us, and he come around and told us
we had to go.
Q. Who is the president of your local?-A. Sherman Keesee.
Q. He came on up with you?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. What day did you go up to Lick Creek?-A. It was on Thursday, I believe.
Q. You got up there on Thursday?—A. I believe it was.
Q. And what time Thursday?-A. Thursday morning.
Q. And what did you do all the time until the shooting started?—A. I be-
lieve it was Friday morning we got there.
Q. What did you do all that day?-A. I just laid around there at String-
town.
Q. What was the general talk there as to what they were going to do?—A.
Well, them men there said they aimed to start something across the river.
Q. They aimed to start something across the river? A. Yes, sir; that is
what they said.
Q. Who said that?-A. I don't know. I don't know the man and I couldn't
tell you who did say it.
Q. Now, how many men do you recall as being over there that you knew?—A.
Well, just what I told you is about all I knowed.
Q. These are the men that came up from Kermit with you. But after you
got up there?-A. There was no man there-yes, there was another man there
at the time. Jake Coburn was with us. I think that is all I know. There was
so many I didn't pay attention. That is about all I noticed.
Q. You say they talked around there that they were going to shoot across
the river?-A. They said they would start something with them across the
river there, is the way I understood it, across the river, that they aimed to
start it with them.
Q. How did they say it?-A. They said across the river that they aimed to
start it with them.

Q. That the men were coming across the river?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. And come over on the West Virginia side?-A. I said that they said, the
way they talked it was like Merrimac, or some of them, was going to start
trouble with Stringtown.
Q. That Merrimac was going to start something with Stringtown. Where
were you when they commenced to shoot up there night before last, along
about 10, 11, or 12 o'clock?-A. They shot at something in the river; I don't
know what it was. Some of them said it was a haunt. It was a calf or some-
thing. but them people there said it was a haunt that lived there.
Q. They fired in on that, did they?-A. Yes; they shot some at it.
Q. Where were you at that time?-A. I was there on the river bank.
Q. Didn't you see an automobile come along the road about that time?-A.
I never saw it, but some of them said one passed.
Q. Did they shoot at that?-A. No, sir.
Q. You mean you didn't shoot at it?-A. No, sir; I never, and I never saw
anybody else.
Q. Where were you at that time; where on the river were you?-A. When
that automobile went by?
Q. Yes.-A. I think I was out on a man's porch asleep.
Q. What did you do-somebody woke you up? A. Yes, sir.
Q. Who woke you up?-A. I don't know who it was. It was dark, and I
went out there and sat down.
Q. What did he say to you when he woke you up?-A. He said some of
them started it and woke me up and I went and sat down a few minutes, and
then went back and laid down on the porch and went to sleep.
Q. Some of them started it. What did they mean?-A. Started a fight or
something, I don't know what they meant.
Q. Then what day was it they divided up into a bunch? A. Yesterday.
Q. What time? A. Yesterday morning some time, I don't know exactly
what time.
Q. What was said about dividing up the bunch?-A. I told you all I can
tell you.
Q. Who did the talking in the bunch?-A. I don't know.
Q. Who talked to you, how did you find it out?-A. Some of the men there
that I didn't know.
Q. What did they say?-A. They told some of us to go up the hill and some
to stay down there, and I went with them to the top of the hill.
Q. Which way did you go, up the hill or stay down there?-A. Up the hollow.
Q. How many went up the hollow with you?-A. I believe we counted 16
in all.
Q. Sixteen of you went up the hollow?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. How far did you go up?-A. Went up to the top of the hill.
Q. When you got up there what did you do?-A. Sat down.
Q. What were you going up there for, or what were you told you were going
up there for?-A. I told you a while ago.
Q. To keep the Pond Creek people off of you?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Was any shooting done up there by any men with you at that time?—A.
Yes, sir; some of them shot, but I never had very many cartridges, and when
they commenced shooting I went down the hollow and went around-
Q. Some of the men did some shooting? A. Yes, sir.
Q. And who were they shooting at?-A. They was shooting at them men that
was shooting at them, I reckon. I never saw a man shooting. I heard the
guns cracking, and some of them fellows out from me was shooting, too, but I
never saw a man.
Q. When the shooting started what did the bunch do that you were with?—
A. They all run when they commenced shooting at them.
Q. Which way did they run?-A. Around. the ridge and down the hill and
into the hollow and throwed their guns away and done everything, and I run
down there and taken the hill and went around the hill and went to catch my
train to go back home, and these fellows got me.
Q. What became of the other men after that that were in the bunch to-
gether, the men you were with?-A. I saw them all hiding, or trying to hide
in those houses and things as I was going up the hill, and these fellows across
the river was shooting at them.
Q. They hid in the houses?-A. And in the woods and the men across the
river was shooting at them.
Q. When you went with the 16 how many did you leave back down on the
river, do you think?-A. I don't know how many.


===== [扫描序号 608] =====
600
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Q. Did you see anything more of the bunch that you left down there on the
river after you threw your rifle away?-A. I saw them all running up a big
bench. I don't know whether it was all on the river or not. They all run into
the hollow there, and they quit fighting and throwed their guns away.
Q. What kind of guns did they have there, did you see any of these Brown-
ings? A. I don't know a Browning.
Q. One with two handles that you hold that way?-A. No; I didn't see any.
Q. Did you have any machine guns?-A. No, sir. These Pond Creek fellows
had machine guns.
Q. I am talking about your crowd.-A. No; I never saw none.
Q. The only kind of guns you saw-A. Was little old Winchesters.
Q. Now, you have given me the names of all the people you can recognize
as being there in the crowd?--A. That is all I know.
Q. Who fed you up there?-A. Well, I don't know the people.
Q. Were you fed there in Stringtown?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. And did they furnish you any ammunition there in Springtown?—A. I got
a little dab there. I didn't have very much of anything. I couldn't hit any-
body with what I had; it was a little old lightweight.
Q. You say you are a member of the union. Were you working over here
in West Virginia when this strike was called?--A. Yes, sir.
Q. Where were you working?-A. I was working-I reckon I was working-
when it was called I wasn't working any. I joined the union, and the last work
I did was at Goodman, and when the strike was called I quit and moved down
home where I told you I lived, and then I laid around and worked for the
Tug River Power people a while and went home, and they said they aimed
to organize the river, and it would cost a man a dollar to join if a man wanted
to work any more, and I went to Kermit and joined the local and went home
and tended to my business.
Q. How many from Goodman did you see in the crowd?-A. I don't know.
I don't know all them fellows down there.
Q. How many did you see up there in the crowd that you recognized that
were from Goodman?-A. They told me there was about 20 or 30 of the Good-
man men up there I don't know.
Q. What ones did you recognize?-A. I told you all I could recognize.
Q. Just Jack Coburn?-A. Yes; and there was some more of the boys I know
if I could see them I could tell, but I don't know their names.
Q. You ought to know more names than Jake Coburn?-A. From Goodman?
Q. Yes.-A. All the Goodman boys up there were from Chattaroy Hollow;
men I didn't know. I just knowed their faces. I wouldn't tell a lie about it.
I didn't know their given names or their last ones, neither.
Q. Where were you when you got this ammunition, or when it was dis-
tributed?-A. The men already had it on them. They never had any ammu-
nition that I saw only what they had in a little satchel on their side.
Q. Were you around that store any up there at Stringtown? A. Yes, sir; I
went down there and tried to get my supper that night. I stayed there.
Q. Were there any guns in the store at that time?-A. I never saw none. I
couldn't get any supper and a man taken me up to his house and give me supper.
Q. Who was that. man that give you supper?-A. I don't know. He lived
there, but I didn't ask his name.
Q. Were all the men that lived in Stringtown out in the hill and engaged
in this shooting?-A. I reckon they was.
Q. You say when you went to the mountain you divided into two parties?—
A. Yes, sir; they sent a few of us up on top of the hill. I wouldn't stay down
there where they aimed to have shooting.
Q. How many did they leave in the bottom around those houses?-A. I told
you how many went, and all the rest stayed back there somewhere; I don't
know where they were at.
Q. Were all those men that remained in the bottom armed-did they have
guns? A. Yes, sir; most of them, I think.
Q. Did you hear Harmon Phillips's name called down there?-A. No, sir; I
don't believe I did.
Q. Harmon Phillips is a little short fellow and wore blue overalls?-A. Har-
mon Phillips, I don't know him.
Q. Bill Terry, did you hear his name called?-A. I don't know; I don't re-
member if I did.
Q. You don't remember; did you hear Bill Fitch's name called?-A. No; I
don't think I did.

​Q. Or Wells Fitch?-A. No, sir; I am under oath and I want to tell the
straight of it if I can.
Q. Or Jack Summers?-A. I heard a fellow called Jack, but
the other name.

don't know
Q. He lives around Stringtown?-A. I heard a man called Jack, but I don't
know his other name.
Q. You know Noah Phillips-A. No, sir.
Q. Harmon Phillips is president of the local up there?-A. I don't know
who is president up there.
Q. You know that little Harmon Phillips; if you saw him you could recog-
nize him if you were to see him?—A. No, sir; I don't know him, I don't believe.
Q. If he was in the crowd you would more than likely have recognized him,
if you would see him?-A. No, sir; I didn't pay any attention to him and I
wouldn't know him.
Q. How many were from Matewan whose names you don't remember did you
see up there?-A. I don't know any of the men up there.
Q. You have been in the town of Matewan? A. Yes, sir; I have been in the
town, but I was in there and out. The only work I done for them people up
there was for the New Howard, in that hollow up there, and I just worked two
or three weeks.
Q. Didn't you recognize anybody whose names you can't recall as having
seen around Matewan in that crowd?-A. No, sir; I can't.

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
OCTOBER 24, 1921.
UNITED STATES SENATE,
COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION AND LABOR,
Washington D. C.
The Committee on Education and Labor of the United States Senate met,
pursuant to the call, at 10 o'clock a. m., in the committee room, Capitol, Sena-
tor Kenyon presiding.
Present: Senators Kenyon (chairman), Sterling, Warren, McKellar, Walsh,
and Caraway.
Also present: Harry Olmsted, representing Operators' Association, William-
son field; Z. T. Vinson, Huntington, W. Va., appearing for the Operators' Asso-
ciation of the Williamson coal fields; E. L. Greever, Tazewell, Va., appearing
for Williamson Coal Operators' Association; S. B. Avis, Charleston, W. Va.,
appearing for Williamson Coal Operators' Association; A. M. Belcher, Charles-
ton, W. Va., appearing for Williamson Coal Operators' Association; H. W.
Houston, appearing for United Mine Workers of America; Frank P. Walsh,
appearing for United Mine Workers of America; Roger Baldwin, of the Ameri-
can Civil Liberties Union, 138 West Thirteenth Street, New York City.
The CHAIRMAN. Let us go ahead, gentlemen. We have tried to get some time
for these hearings that would be agreeable to both sides. and we have had great
difficulty in doing so, but we intend to finish this matter up this week. The plan
is to give two days for the miners to give their side of the case, two days
for the operators, and the next two days the committee wants to use for witnesses
for themselves.
OPENING STATEMENT OF HON. FRANK P. WALSH ON BEHALF OF
UNITED MINE WORKERS OF AMERICA.

STATEMENT OF PHILIP MURRAY, VICE PRESIDENT, THE UNITED MINE WORKERS OF
AMERICA.
The section of the coal-producing area of West Virginia which you are investi-
gating is a festering, cankerous, sore upon that body politic which we take pride


===== [扫描序号 621] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
607
in proclaiming the healthiest, sanest, richest, and most civilized self-governing
nation in the world. That this sore exists is the worst indictment that can be
brought to-day against our free Government, its institutions, and the processes
by which it functions. That it should be permitted to continue to exist is
unthinkable. I take it, therefore, that the minds of all good citizens should be
directed to the questions: How can this sore be cured? How can we guard
against its breaking out again, and how can we protect against its malignant
infection those who have not as yet suffered from it? It is in the desire and
in the hope that we may demonstrate ourselves to be good citizens, deploring
existing conditions as greatly as any other part of our patriotic citizenship, that
we shall make our presentation to this committee.
We are essentially the complainants in the case, for we have begged, urged, and
demanded that this inquiry be made. However, we shall not confine ourselves
to a recital of the wrongs that have been done us, nor to the production of
evidence against those whom we believe guilty of those wrongs. We believe that
a crime has been committed, but we do not seek primarily the punishment of its
perpetrators. We believe that we have been fundamentally right in the course
we have pursued, but we are not clamoring for a verdict of vindication. We
seek first of all not retribution, but justice in the broadest sense of the term-
justice with peace, safety, and freedom.
We want this committee to know, and we challenge it to ascertain and publish
to the world the whole truth and the exact truth about the events that have
transpired, the situation, and the conditions in the Mingo, Logan, Mercer-
McDowell district of West Virginia. Indeed, it is upon the truths being made
known to the public that our hope for the future depends. To-day, the average
man knows little about the situation in West Virginia other than that there has
been prolonged conflict between the miners and the mine operators, that there
have been disorder, lawlessness, and loss of life and property, that conditions
approximating civil war have existed and that it has been necessary to send in
Federal troops to restore and to maintain order. Opinions as to which side is
right and which side is wrong have been based largely upon prejudice and upon
partial and misleading information. Public opinion, to be sound, intelligent, and
of the kind that will prevail, must be based upon the truth, and it is because we
court that kind of public opinion that we have sought this investigation.
Let the truth be known! Then, and only then, may we know who is right and
who is wrong in West Virginia. We believe we are right, and if we are not, then
we say to this committee that industrial peave wherever it prevails is based upon
false principles and upon pernicious practices. We may be wrong, but if we are
wrong then we say that this very Government of ours is founded upon a fallacy,
for in West Virginia we are fighting for fundamentals identical with those that
inspired the fathers of the Republic-freedom of speech, freedom of assemblage,
freedom of the press, freedom of person, administration of law without favor,
and the preeminence of human rights over property rights.
If the truth be made known we believe that the conditions and practices of
which we complain will be corrected and never again permitted. If the truth be
established, then the fight we have made shall have proved worth while, good
shall have come out of the evil, and suffering visited upon innocent women and
children, and the men shot down upon the mountain slopes of West Virginia
shall not have died in vain.
We appreciate that under a strict interpretation of its powers and juris-
diction, your committee is to investigate and ascertain the truth as to whether
factors exist which make for a constant breakdown of civil government in
Logan, McDowell, Mercer, and Mingo Counties and whether these conditions
also result in the impairment of specific activities which constitutionally must
be exercised by the Federal Government. We realize that the usual procedure
in matters such as these is that after proper inquiry, an analysis of the facts
is reported to the Senate with such recommendations as may seem desirable
to correct any evils which may have been discovered.
We wish frankly to state at the outset that, although this traditional practice
will ultimatley be of great benefit, and although we are heartily in favor of
its adoption by your cómmittee, pending its completion, we feel that some more
immediate and effective action is necessary in the present case. Conditions are
such that they will not probably wait upon the usual delays and obstacles of
remedial legislation. Moreover, it is doubtful, because of constitutional limita-
tions and unwarranted but clever objections which will probably be interposed,
whether really effective relief may be had by legislative enactment.

The only really effective method for restoring industrial cooperation and
peace and tranquility in these regions would consist of an agreement between
the mine operators and the representatives of their employees which would
adjust existing differences and constitute a rational basis of procedure. Our
belief that this was and is the only certain and complete remedy for the
deplorable conditions which exist has been so firmly grounded that we petitioned
the President some weeks ago to call a joint conference of operators and officials
of the United Mine Workers of America for the purpose of reaching a just
and reasonable arrangement. In reply, President Harding stated that he
would not interfere, as this committee had been created for inquiry and
constructive relief. We urgently request you, therefore, to supplement your
usual course of procedure by using your mediatory offices to compose the
existing situation and to provide a stable basis of production and local tran-
quility for the future. The President evidently anticipated and hopes for
such a policy. We believe, therefore, that you should not limit yourself to
the accumulation of evidence and the slow processes of legislative action, but,
under the solemn responsibility which rests upon you, you should go beyond the
immediate terms of the Senate resolution, and, through your prestige as
representatives of great commonwealths and of a large proportion of our ex-
pectant citizenship, you should make earnest and continued effort to secure the
adoption of an agreement or an arrangement which would immediately compose
this deplorable situation.
If I may venture to say it, we are also firmly convinced that if you permit
the scope of your activities to be limited by technical considerations, public
opinion will not only feel that you failed to take advantage of a great oppor-
tunity for real human service but will even condemn you as lacking in courage
or as evading a manifest duty by pleading technical limitations of authority.
Every consideration of elementary justice and human rights demands that this
matter be settled promptly and in a spirit of real, courageous, public-spirited
statesmanship. By an aggressive, fearless attitude you can immediately com-
pose all differences which exist and provide a peaceful and prosperous basis
of future procedure. The only practical way in which this can be done is to
bring about for these counties a working agreement under your auspices which
will safeguard properly the fundamental rights of mine workers and mine
operators, and which will provide a just and reasonable basis for working rela-
tions and conditions.
The safeguards which are essential to regularity of production and to peace
and tranquility are:
1. The guaranty of freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, and freedom of
movement.
2. The right of all workers to organize and bargain collectively through rep-
resentatives of their own choosing.
3. The protection of mine workers against discrimination because of member-
ship in the United Mine Workers of America or any other labor or other
organization.
4. The protection of unorganized workers against intimidation or coercion
by members of the United Mine Workers of America or any other labor organi-
zations.
The CHAIRMAN. Please read that again.
Mr. MURRAY (reading). “4. The protection of unorganized workers against
intimidation or coercion by members of the United Mine Workers of America
or any other labor organizations.”
5. The assurance that democratic institutions will not be subordinated to in-
dustrial control by the practice of the coal operators in paying and controlling
deputy sheriffs and constables or by employing private guards instead of using
the services of disinterested and conscientious public officers.
6. The assurance to those mine workers or strikers, if that term is preferred,
who were originally debarred fom employment because of membeship in the
United Mine Workers of America, that they will be restored to their former
occupations or to ones equally as good.
These are the simple fundamentals which will restore the normal conditions
of a self-governing republic in West Virginia. They are so elementary and
so obvious that their absence at present seems incredible. The assertion by
your committee that they must become effective will commend itself every-
where to the sound and right-thinking citizenship of our country.
With all the earnestness of which we are capable we urge your committee
to embody these fundamentals into an agreement, the conditions of which will

609
be made mandatory upon the relations between mine workers and mine opera-
tors in this territory. We are willing to sign such an agreement and abide
faithfully by its terms. The operators have stated that they will not meet
with the representatives of our organization. If they still persist in this un-
reasonable attitude we ask your committee to make every possible effort to
secure the approval of the coal operators to this agreement through the officers
of their county associations.
Under such conditions, the question at once arises how such an agreement
may be enforced and how grievances which may arise under its operation may
be adjusted. Your committee may easily provide penalties for both parties
for any infractions of the terms of the agreement. Fortunately, we already
have a noteworthy and successful precedent which affords a practical method
for adjusting grievances which may arise and for ensuring proper interpreta-
tion and practical application of such an agreement. A situation almost identi-
cal with the condition of affairs existing in the coal mines of this territory
arose in all the packing centers of the country in the year 1917. The packers
would not recognize the organizations of their employees and refused to enter
into an agreement with them. A Federal administrator, therefore, was ap-
pointed by the President to arrange working conditions and relations and to in-
terpret and apply those conditions and relations. Judge Samuel Alschuler, of
the United States Circuit Court was selected and since that time he has been
the arbitrator and administrator of conditions and relations in the large pack-
ing-house industry.
Practically similar conditions as now obtain here also prevailed in the an-
thracite coal field in 1902. President Roosevelt appointed a commission to in-
vestigate and to prepare an award or an agreement as to working relations and
conditions. A joint board of conciliation was also created to pass upon differ-
ences, and a final arbitrator or administrator to pass upon grievances when
the joint board could not agree. Dr. Charles P. Neill, formerly United States
Commissioner of Labor and now in charge of industrial relations for the rail-
roads of the South was named as arbitrator, and for almost 20 years this
agreement has been in force.
Senator WALSH. Was that board named at the request of both the miners and
operators, by President Roosevelt?
Senator WARREN. It was not named at the request of either side.
Mr. MURRAY. We earnestly request, therefore, that in addition to drawing up
an agreement containing the fundamentals involved and requiring both parties,
the United Mine Workers of America and the coal associations, to sign this
agreement through their representatives, your committee provide a means for
selecting an administrator who will interpret and apply the agreement and pass
upon grievances which may arise under its operation. We suggest that in order
that there may be no attack upon his disinterestedness, the Chief Justice of
the Supreme Court of the United States be requested by your committee to
name this impartial administrator of the agreement.
This is a practical constructive suggestion which we feel no impropriety in
urging your committee to adopt, because of the human and property rights
involved. There are more fundamental remedies such as actual governmental
ownership which might be applied. These require, however, careful delibera-
tion and most exhaustive study before they can be applied. Our suggestion,
on the contrary, will immediately relieve the situation. It is reasonable, con-
servative, and its practicableness has been proved by precedent and experience.
The West Virginia operators have memoralized the President of the United
States, stating with all emphasis that they can not and will not meet the United
Mine Workers of America in conference under any conditions. They have also
made the same statement to this committee. This is in effect an ultimatum
to the Government that the only settlement of this controversy to which they
will agree is one made on their own terms, which means that they will insist
upon the continuance of the policy that has caused all the trouble. Their
management of the coal industry in this State has resulted in a breakdown, but
nevertheless they purpose to make no change in their methods. They appealed
to the Government for aid, when the situation had got beyond their control
and when they feared their properties might be endangered, but having received
that aid they would bar the forces of the Government from any adjustment
of the controversy that might settle it for all time to come.
Their reason for this is that they see in the United Mine Workers a sinister
purpose to organize the entire mining industry with a view of obtaining control


===== [扫描序号 624] =====
610
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
of the industry-that we plan to freeze the public into acceptance of a radical
and revolutionary program for the future conduct of the industry.
This is too absurd to be dignified by serious consideration were it not put
forth seriously by the operators. We do seek to organize the entire coal in-
dustry, but our sole purpose is to secure uniformity of wages and working con-
ditions and regularity and continuity of employment, and to be able to bargain
collectively with the operators on terms approximating equality.
All the operators of the country, including those in the nonunion fields of
West Virginia, are organized in a single, compact national association, known as
the National Coal Association. In all fairness it should be possible for all the
miners of the country, including those in West Virginia, to be united in their
national organization, so that they may meet the maximum economic strength
of the operators with the maximum economic strength of the mine workers.
This is not radical; it is not revolutionary. There is nothing sinister or ulterior
about it.
The United Mine Workers of America have no desire to injure the operators,
for they realize that fundamentally the interests of the operators and of the
mine workers are identical. They respect the right of the operators to or-
ganize, but on the other hand they insist that the operators must respect the right
of the mine workers to organize without being subjected to discrimination.
64
We say to the operators, Come, let us reason together!" There is nothing
radical or revolutionary about that. We know that this controversy will never
be settled until it is approached in a spirit of common counsel, cooperation, and
good faith, and we are now, and always have been, willing to meet them half way
in that spirit. Progress in industrial relations is defined in terms of better-
ment to change from a given condition to a better condition. That has been
the keynote of the union labor movement from its very beginning. We have
progressed in the coal-mining industry until outside this West Virginia district;
it is 80 per cent organized. If our cause were not just; if our purpose were not
honorable; if what we do were not consistent with the public welfare, we would
never have been permitted to make the progress we have made.
We do not seek to control the coal industry, but we do demand a voice in its
control. Advocates of the open-shop movement have taken as their slogan:
"Those who pay shall have the say." That means going back to the dark
ages when might made right. To-day the whole world knows that might
does not make right, but that right makes might, and we believe that we
are fundamentally and eternally right. We say that the men who go down
into the bowels of the earth, hazard their lives and endure the hardships of
the miner "pay" just as much to make the coal industry what it is as do the
operators who sit in comfortable offices and risk nothing but their dollars,
and therefore we insist upon our right to have a part of the "say" as to the
conditions under which the industry shall be operated.
We come here not to tear down but to build up; we are not destructive but
we are constructive. If our proposal, our plan, is not good, we have no ulti-
matum to serve on the President of the United States, on this committee, or on
anyone else, but we challenge the operators to submit to this committee a better
plan!
Our organization stands for industrial peace, the judicial settlement of in-
dustrial disputes, the stabilizing of conditions of employment, and for the
continuity and acceleration of production.
The operators have nothing to offer except arbitrary action and industrial
autocracy. They constitute an autocratic, industrial oligarchy. The fruits of
their policy are industrial and civil warfare. If their policies were applied on a
more general scale they would be followed by industrial and political chaos.
Turning now from constructive proposals for the settlement of this deplorable
condition of affairs and referring to conditions which have actually developed.
as to which your committee is seeking concrete information, our position is as
follows:
1. It is our contention at the outset that the problem in West Virginia is not a
question of unionism versus nonunionism but is a question of the establishment,
acceptance, and observance of certain fundamental principles and practices
which are essential to peace and orderly progress in all industry.
2. We shall show that the miners of West Virginia have been denied the right
of collective bargaining, the right to organize in lawful trade-unions, the right
to engage in legitimate trade-union activities, the right of free speech, the right
of free assemblage, and the right to travel upon public highways when and
where they pleased.

3. We shall show that they have been intimidated, coerced, maltreated, and
shot down by armed guards and private detectives employed by the mine
operators.
4. We shall show that deputy sheriffs, presumed to be public officials employed
in the interest of the whole public, have in fact drawn their pay from mine
operators, a single association of operators having expended for this purpose
a sum in excess of $32,000 in one year.
5. We shall show that the relation of the miners to their employers has by
judicial decision or interpretation been established as that of servant to master,
and that under such decision miners and their families have been evicted from
their homes without notice and without any consideration of mercy or decency.
6. We shall show that the miners have been subjected to government by in-
junction in such a way and to such a degree that they can not hold union meet-
ings, that they can not discuss their union or attempt to persuade their fellow
workers to join the union, and that the officers of their union can not call a
strike or declare a strike to exist without rendering themselves liable to imprison-
ment or other punishment within the discretion of the courts.
7. We shall show that the operators control the law-making and the law-
enforcing machinery of the State, and that the laws are enforced for the op-
erators against the miners but never for the miners and against the operators
or impartially against both operators and miners.
8. We shall show that the operators are not merely the miner's employer; they
are his landlord, his merchant, the provider of his amusements, the sanitary
officer of his community, often the source of his police protection and the patron
of his physician, his minister, and his school-teacher.
9. We shall show that the miners throughout a large part of the nonunion
section of the State are coerced by the use of antiunion contracts, known as
"yellow dog contracts."
10. We shall show that officials and leaders of the miners' organization
did not incite or encourage the threatened or attempted armed invasions of
the antiunion section, but on the contrary, used their best efforts to prevent
such demonstrations, to persuade the miners to return to their homes and to
render effective the program of the Federal authorities.
11. We shall show that the operators are waging a bitter, last ditch fight
for the closed nonunion shop, whereas they represent falsely to the public that
they contend only for an open shop.
12. We shall show that this closed nonunion shop policy of the operators is
in harmony with and dictated by the policy of the United States Steel Corpora-
tion and closely affiliated great financial interests which control by far the
larger part of the unorganized coal fields of West Virginia, and that this is
a part of the so-called open shop movement on a nation-wide scale inauguarated
shortly after the armistice with Judge Elbert H. Gary, the head of the United
States Steel Corporation as its prophet and its leader.
13. We shall show that the only other sections of the United States in which
conditions in the coal mining industry have even approximated the conditions
in West Virginia are those in the Birmingham region of Alabama, where the
dominent factor is the Tennessee Coal & Iron Co., a subsidiary of the United
States Steel Corporation.
14. We shall also point out that the so-called open-shop movement on the
railroads has been aggressively prosecuted by Gen. W. W. Atterbury, vice presi-
dent of the Pennsylvania Railroad, and that the Pennsylvania Railroad through
its control of the Norfolk & Western Railroad is one of the dominant factors
also in the antiunion fight in the State of West Virginia.
Mr. VINSON. May I interrupt just a minute. Could we have a copy of your
statement?
Mr. MURRAY. Yes. When I complete the making of my statement to the com-

15. We shall show that the open shop or antiunion movement in West Vir-
ginia and Alabama is unjustified and unjustifiable because 80 per cent of the
bituminous coal industry in the United States as a whole is organized, with
recognition by the operators of the United Mine Workers of America, and that
the organized portion of the industry has progressed to the mutual advantage
and satisfaction of the operators and the miners and with due regard for the
public welfare.
16. In conclusion, we shall show, by pointing to failures in the past, that
the establishment for the time being of law and order under military authority
is not a solution of the West Virginia problem, and that to fix responsibility

Collective bargaining and the right to organize. The immediate cause of
the West Virginia trouble is the refusal by the operators to permit their ´
employees to join the United Mine Workers of America. This is a right
which is now so usually recognized that its denial seems almost incredible.
Indeed, aside from the West Virginia operators, the only conspicuous denial
of this right is by President Gary, of the United States Steel Corporation.
Moreover, there is reason to believe that the West Virginia attitude is inspired,
or greatly influenced, by the United States Steel Corporation. Absentee owner-
ship has always ben a source of trouble in all industries and countries. From
the records it appears that the West Virginia fields are largely controlled by
absentee owners, the control centering in the so-called Steel Corporation and
the Morgan financial group, which is known to be the power and the directing
force back of the present drive against the principle of collective bargaining
on a trade-union basis. In the present case this control has peculiarly vicious
tools to work with.
It is my judgment that the evil in West Virginia, which is a blot not only
upon that State but upon the United States, will be cured when and only when
the principle of genuine collective bargaining is recognized and practiced in
good faith by the operators and miners in the Mingo field. The best proof
of this lies in the fact that wherever and whenever the principle of genuine
collective bargaining is applied we never find a situation that even approxi-
mates the conditions that have obtained and still obtain in West Virginia.
This principle, which is now accepted as elementary in industrial relations,
means that the workers have a fundamental right to organize in trade-unions
or other associations of their own choosing and that employers shall not
discriminate against them on account of their membership in trade-unions
or other associations, or on account of legitimate trade-union activities.
It was upon the application and enforcement of this principle through the
National War Labor Board that it was made possible for this country to go
through the war without a single serious interruption of war industry. It
is through its application and enforcement that we may hope to prevent
chaos and tragedy such as prevail in the blood-stained coal fields of Mingo,
Logan, and McDowell Counties.
Denial of the right of workers to organize is ethically so unjust, economically
so unsound, and socially so dangerous that modern civilization no longer
tolerates it. However, it is not through flat, unqualified denials of this
right that trouble arises, but through the evasions and practices of unen-
lightened employers who, while affirming that they do not deny the right of
their employees to join unions, undertake to make it inadvisable or impossible
for the workers to be union members and hold their jobs. That is the sort
of thing we of the labor organizations are fighting against. It is the sort of
thing that those who have the welfare of our country at heart should guard
against.
"Labor organizations are not forced products," says Prof. Richard T. Ely,
Political Economy, pages 238-9. They have grown up almost spontaneously.
They have arisen naturally out of modern industrial conditions. Wherever
capital is a separate factor in production and is organized on a large scale
labor inevitably organizes sooner or later in order that it may stand on an
equal footing and make labor contracts advantageously. Let us suppose that
one capitalist employs a thousand men. If these men are not organized, each
man treats individually with all the capital in the establishment. All the
capital is represented by one man, but one wage earner represents buy one-
thousandth part of the labor force, and he is not in a position of equality.
The laborers, therefore, unite their labor, and, speaking through one repre-
sentative, place all the labor against all the capital."
No less emphatic indorsement of the principle of organization is to be found
in the utterances of our leading statesmen and publicists. Theodore Roosevelt,
while President of the United States in 1902, said (addresses and presidential
messages, 1902-1904, pp. 54-56):
"I believe emphatically in organized labor. I believe in organizations of
wage workers. Organization is one of the laws of our social and economic
development at this time."

Chief Justice William Howard Taft, before his election to the Presidency,
in his address before Cooper's Institute, New York City, January, 1908, said:
"What the capitalist, who is the employer of labor, must face is that the
organization of labor-the labor union-is a permanent condition in the indus-
trial world. It has come to stay. If the employer would consult his own in-
terest, he must admit this and act on it. Under existing conditions the blindest
course that an employer of labor can pursue is to decline to recognize labor
unions as the controlling force in the labor market and to insist upon dealing
only with his particular employees. Time and again one has heard the indig-
nant expression of a manager of some great industrial enterprise that he did
not propose to have the labor union run his business; that he would deal with
his own men and not with outsiders. The time has passed in which that
attitude can be assumed with any hope of successfully maintaining it."
While he was Chief Executive of the United States Mr. Taft, in an address
at Worcester, Mass., April 3, 1910, affirmed his belief in labor organizations,
and on May 26, 1915, in addressing the National Association of Manufacturers
in New York City, he said:
"I fully approve the principle of labor unions. I believe that they are
essential in creating a state of equality between employees and employers."
During the war emergency Mr. Taft served as joint chairman of the National
War Labor Board, and it is interesting to note that after his experience in that
work he said on August 9, 1919:
Labor unions have been necessary to secure to the individual working man
an opportunity to deal with his employer on an equality and free from the
duress of immediate want of a daily wage, to demand what he regards as an
adequate and just return for his labor or to withdraw from employment."
Charles Evans Hughes, now Secretary of State and former associate justice
of the Supreme Court of the United States and former candidate for the
presidency, in an address at Columbia University on November 30, 1918, said:
"I trust there will be no more struggles in futile opposition to the right of
collective bargaining on the part of employees. The recognition of the right
of representation and the prompt hearing of grievances provide the open door
to reasonable and just settlements. And in returning to peace conditions there
should be the utmost care to preserve every possible means which has been
found helpful during the war for the investigation of the complaints of labor
and for the adjustment of demands."
Far-sighted employers concede the right of the worker to organize whenever
and wherever they discuss the subject. Thus we find John D. Rockefeller, jr.,
saying (The Annals of the American Academy, January, 1919, p. 171):
"As regards the organization of labor, it is just as proper and advantageous
for labor to associate itself into organized groups for the advancement of its
legitimate interests as for capital to combine for the same objects."
J. N. Tittemore, a member of the employers' group in the President's first
industrial conference, October, 1919, said :
"So far as I am concerned, I am committed in my mind and in my very soul
to unionism as it is expressed by the administrative faculty of the American
Federation of Labor; and in saying that, my friends, I do not sanction ultra-
radicalism."
Harry A. Wheeler, another member of the employers' group, said:
We freely accord the place of the trade and labor unions in those organi-
zations which the men have a right to join."
The Chamber of Commerce of the United States in its Referendum No. 27,
on a report on principles of industrial relations declared :
“ 4. The right of workers to organize is as clearly recognized as that of any
other element or part of the community.
“5. Industrial harmony and prosperity will be most effectually promoted by
adequate representation of the parties in interest. Existing forms of represen-
tation should be carefully studied and availed of in so far as they may be
found to have merit and are adaptable to the peculiar conditions in the various
industries."
From the report of the Bureau of State Research, section 2, Volume VI,

industrial unrest.

615
However, it is in the principles and policies of the National War Labor Board
that we find the right to organize enunciated in detail. This declaration, worked
out in conference between representatives of employers and employees and
given the force of law for the war emergency by presidential proclamation, was
as follows:
"The right of workers to organize in trade-unions and to bargain collectively
through chosen representat ves is recognized an affirmed. This right shall not
be denied, abridged, or interfered with by the employers in any manner what-
soever.
"The right of employers to organize in associations or groups and to bargain
collectively through chosen representatives is recognized and affirmed. This
right shall not be denied, abridged, or interfered with by the workers in any
manner whatsoever.
Employers shall not discharge workers for membership in trade-unions,
nor for legit mate trade-union activities.
"The workers, in the exercise of their right to organize, should not use
coercive measures of any kind to induce persons to join their organ zations
nor to induce employers to bargain or deal therewith.
"In establishments where the union shop exists the same shall continue, and
the union standards as to wages, hours of labor, and other conditions of em-
ployment shall be maintained.
“In establishments where union and nonunion men and women now work
together and the employer meets only with employees or representatives en-
gaged in said establishments, the continuance of such conditions shall not be
deemed a grievance. This declaration, however, is not intended in any manner
to deny the right or discourage and practice of the formation of labor unions
or the joining of the same by the workers 'n said establishments, as guaranteed
in the preceding section, nor to prevent the War Labor Board from urging or
any umpire from granting, under the machinery herein provided, improvement
of their situation in the matter of wages, hours of labor, or other conditions as
shall be found des rable from time to time."
In the application of this principle the National War Labor Board had
occasion to re-state the broad general rule as to the right to organize in several
cases, but in far the greater number of cases the practice of discrimination
was involved-the discharge of workers for leg timate trade-union activities.
Invariably when the complainants proved their case the board ordered the rein-
statement of the discharged employees with compensation for all they had lost
in wages, senior ty rights, etc., by reason of their discharge.
One of the earliest cases handled by the board involved this principle and
established a precedent as to the extent to which the powers of the Government
could be invoked in backing up the decisions and awards of the board.
The Western Union Telegraph Co. made it a practice, if not a rule. to dis-
charge employees who joined the telegraphers' union. Upon complaint of the
union, in behalf of employees so discriminated against, the board ordered the
company to cease the practice and to reinstate the discharged workers. The
company denied the authority of the board in the matter and declined to obey
its order, whereupon the board laid the case before President Wilson, who
directer the Postmaster General to take over and operate the business of the
telegraph companies for the Government for the period of the war.
In connection with this case it should be noted that the defendant com-
pany permitted its employees to join an association composed solely of its own
employees. Thus it did not deny the right of the workers to organize, but in-
sisted upon exercising the prerogative of dictating the kind of organization
they might form or join. The company did not want its employees in any
organization that had any outside affiliations, and took the position that they
could exercise their right to organize only by joining the associations, which
is a kind of organization known to trade-unionists as a company union. No
one thing is more objectionable to trade-unionists than a company union, which
is simply and only a device created and controlled by the employer for the
primary purpose of preventing the unionization of his employees.
The National War Labor Board did not pass upon the company union ques-
tion in the Western Union case, but it arose in other cases, and the board held
that (1) the countenancing of a company union by an employer was not a
sufficient recognition of the workers' right to organize; (2), the employer could
not compel its employees to join a beneficial organization conducted by the
company; and (3) the employees must be permitted to become members of any
legitimate labor organization without interference on the part of the employer.
As the board said in the case of the New York Consolidated Railroad:


===== [扫描序号 630] =====
616
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
"The right of the workers of this company freely to organize in trade-
unions, or to join the same, and to bargain collectively, is affirmed, and dis-
charges for legitimate trade-union activities, interrogation of workers by offi-
cials as to their union affiliations, espionate by agents or representatives of
the company, visits by officials of the company to the neighborhood of the
meeting place of the organization for the purpose of observing the men who
belong to such unions, to their detriment as employees of the company, and
like actions, the intent of which is to discharge and prevent men from exercis-
ing this right of organization, must be deemed an interference with their rights
as laid down in the principles of the board.”
In efforts to conceal discriminatory practices employers caused their records
to show that the employees were discharged for incompetency, when in reality
the cause was membership in a trade-union or trade-union activity. When this
was called to the attention of the board it laid down the broad rule that the
fact that a worker had been employed by a company must be accepted as proof
of his general competency, and that, accordingly, a statement of specific in-
competency must be given a dismissed employee upon demand by himself or by
his representative.
In other decisions and awards the board held that peaceful participation in
a strike should not be a bar to reemployment, referred to the War Department
evidence that employers had misused the selective draft law in an effort to
punish union men; held that employees, upon giving proper notice, must be
permitted to absent themselves without pay to attend union conventions; for-
bade the blacklisting of union men; and ruled that under ordinary circum-
stances an employer can not object to the wearing of a union button by an em-
ployee even while he is on duty, unless the wearing of the button actually
causes a lack of cooperation between the union and nonunion employees, in
which event the employer may forbid the use of such a symbol during working
hours.
The board was called upon to pass upon the individual contract system or
question in several instances, and it held that the employer should not make
with or require of their employees individual contracts which deter the em-
ployees from joining unions. It was in one of these cases that further evidence
was afforded as to the extent to which the Government would go in enforcing
the board's decrees. It was shown that the Smith & Wesson Co. required as a
prerequisite to employment that the worker sign an agreement not to join a
trade-union while he remained in the company's service and to give due notice
of his intention so to do should he at any time decide to identify himself with a
union. The board held that this contract was a violation of the rights of the
workers, and ordered the reinstatement of men who had been discharged for
failure to keep the individual contract agreement. The company declined to
comply with this ruling, whereupon the Secretary of War, at the direction of
the President, took over the plant of the company and operated it until it was
decided that the war emergency was over.
