Mr. MURRAY. Surely the testimony I have adduced in support of the right of
workers to organize in trade unions is overwhelming and conclusive. No one
will contend that the miners in the four counties of West Virginia where all
this trouble is centered have been accorded this right and protected in the
enjoyment thereof. I do not presume to instruct this committee as to whether
legislation can be framed and enacted to correct this wrong and to prevent its
recurrence. I am not a lawmaker. However, I have great faith in the power
of enlightened public opinion, and I believe that the committee can accomplish
much merely by ascertaining and publishing to the Nation the whole truth
about Mingo, McDowell, and Logan Counties.
I know that thousands of miners there have been denied their fundamental
human and economic rights, and I know that they and their families have been
subjected to privations unspeakable and almost unendurable. I know that we
have never had such conditions in the coal fields where the operators deal with
the miners through their chosen organization, the United Mine Workers of
America.
From the opinions elsewhere quoted, it is evident that the right of employees
to bargain collectively and to affiliate in trade-unions is recognized as an ele-
mentary principle by leaders in all fields of modern thought and activity.
Granting this, the question may still arise in the minds of members of this
committee as to just what sort of an organization is the mine workers' union.
Is it a lawless band of thieves and blackguards, such as it is represented to be
by this small group of West Virginia operators? Or is it a lawful and proper
organization with reputable principles and worthy ambitions? My answer is
that, not only is it a lawful and proper organization, but also that it is construc-
tive in its aims and its existence has been a benefit not only to the mine workers
but to the coal industry itself and to the development of democratic principles
and ideals in our self-governing Republic.
There are at present some 700,000 coal-mine employees in the United States
and Canada. Approximately 80 per cent of this number are members of the
United Mine Workers of America. The nonunion miners and mines are almost
entirely limited to the southern part of West Virginia, Kentucky, and Alabama,
and I may make a correction there of the southern part of Pennsylvania.
Practically all of the remaining coal districts of the country are organized—–
that is to say, the mine workers are members of the United Mine Workers of
America, and the operators deal directly with representatives of that organiza-
tion in the fixing of wage rates and working conditions.
The fact that the number of mine workers in the disturbed section of West
Virginia is such a small proportion of the total mine workers in the country
would in itself indicate that the troubles existing must be due to local condi-
tions, and not to any vic'ous qualities or peculiarities on the part of the mine
workers. The coal miners are just ordinary human beings. The fact that a
vast majority of them can live and work in cooperation with the operators in
such great. coal States as Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, and Pennsylvania, and
even in large areas of West Virginia, when, on the other hand, a small number
of them can not do so in a certain section of West Virginia would, in itself,


===== [扫描序号 632] =====
618
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
be presumptive evidence that something must be wrong with the operators
or with the local conditions in this small section of West Virginia.
Large organizations of individuals, sufficiently strong to persist and grow
in the face of strong opposition, are seldom, if ever, the creation of any one
man or group of men. Rather they are the slow outgrowths of conditions.
Such is the case with the United Mine Workers of America. It has a history
of small beginnings and slow extension, and its roots sink deep into the very
vitals of the coal industry. Its principles and purposes, its significance to the
economic life of the country, can not be understood except in relation to the
conditions which gave it birth and have made it strong.
Furthermore, except in the light of its industrial background, it is not
possible fairly to weigh the social value of the United Mine Workers' organi-
zation. By the critical student it can not be judged merely by the preamble
of its constitution any more than the success of American democracy can be
judged by the gracious words in the preamble of its Declaration of Inde-
pendence. On the other hand, it can not fairly be condemned by the character
of individual members of isolated groups of members any more than the
Christian church can fairly be condemned by the action of individual members
or even of isolated congregations.
66
I can not undertake at this time to review the history of the Mine Workers'
organization, as would have to be done if its purposes and accomplishments
are to be fully understood. I urge most strongly, however, that the record of
the organization be examined as presented in such comprehensive studies of
the subject as Conciliation and arbitration in the coal industry of America,"
by Prof. A. E. Suffern; and "The coal mine worker," by Frank J. Warne,
Ph. D. These histories were written by impartial students approaching the
subject in an entirely nonpartisan academic manner. Neither of them fails to
criticize the mine workers or their organizations, and I do not agree with many
of the things they say. The significant fact, however, is that both of them see
in the Mine Workers' organization a necessary and beneficial instrument in
social and industrial progress. I am submitting copies of these books for the
information of the committee.
If these histories be read, and if the records and activities of the United
Mine Workers as developed in other studies and investigations be carefully
studied, two points will stand out clearly.
One point is that the United Mine Workers of America has never been a
lawless organization or a supporter of lawlessness. In certain rare instances,
where the administration of civil law and justice has broken down, its mem-
bers may have been compelled to meet force with force. Such occasions arise
in the history of every country and every group of people. But from its very
nature and purposes the union can not tolerate lawlessness or violence as a
policy. Its one flaming principle is the principle of collective bargaining.
This means conference and agreement between employers and employees, and
those can not thrive save in an atmosphere of peace and good will.
A second and still more important point which appears from a study of its
history is that the United Mine Workers' organization has always been a sta-
biliz ng force, beneficial not only to the employee but to the employer and to
the public. Without it, it is not too much to say that there would not be gen-
eral chaos in the bituminous coal industry, just as chaos was an almost con-
tinuous condition in the central coal fields prior to the firm establishment of the
interstate conferences between operators and mine workers.
The bituminous coal industry is highly competitive, due primarily to the fact
that too many mines have been developed. The potential supply is always,
except under extraordinary conditions such as existed during the war, very
much in excess of the demand. Thus, according to the report of the United
States Bituminous Coal Comm'ssion of 1920, page 26, the country, under normal
conditions, now requires less than 500,000,000 tons a year, while the capacity
of the mines in operation is over 700,000,000 tons. In the past this overpro-
duction led to competition of the bitterest character and on the lowest plane.
Not only were wages pressed down to the barest subsistence min mum but every
operator sought to keep on hand a much larger force of men than could ordi-
narily be used in order to take advantage of possible rush periods. This led to
short-time work with consequent unemployment and suffering among the em-
ployees. It also led to constant irritations, disturbances, and strikes.
Mr. A. E. Suffern, in the book mentioned above, summarizes these vicious
effects as follows, pages 1 and 2:


===== [扫描序号 633] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
619
..
In periods of prosperity many mines were opened. During years of depres-
sion, instead of restricting production to meet the demand, the operators ex-
tended production to a point where the sale of the product brought a meager
amount for capital and barely enabled labor to subsist. The underlying motive
for such a procedure was the desire of the operators to make even small profits or
to escape the necessity of closing their mines altogether with consequent dete-
rioration in the properties. Their inability to withdraw their fixed capital from
the coal industry and employ it in some other way gave a further impetus to
such a policy."
This condition led to a barbarous and ruinous competition among operators.
Labor was exploited. In the words of Mr. Suffern, pages 2 and 3:
"With continued overproduction on a falling market, capital insisted on what
it regarded as legitimate returns on its investment. If any sacrifice was to be
inade, labor was the first to feel it in the form of reduced wages."
Labor was peculiarly helpless because of its isolation.
"The immobility of labor, due to the isolated environment of the mining in-
dustry and the difficulty of moving to a new place, encouraged labor to remain
in its old haunts during a period of depression."
The more honest operators were helpless. Coal mining became a competition
in beating down labor costs, and this in turn led to despicable trade practices.
Thus, to quote Mr. Herman Justi, a representative of the operators, before the
Industrial Commission of 1901 (Vol. XII, p. 678):
"Under the old system (i. e., prior to the institution of the interstate agree-
ments in the central field) the more powerful operators could, and the less
scrupulous operators would, take advantage not only of the miners, but also of
of their more scrupulous rivals. That system not only encouraged unfair prac-
tices and threw into idleness tens of thousands of working men, but it bank-
rupted many honest coal operators."
The first serious attempt to bring the operators and miners together on the
basis of a joint working agreement was made in October, 1885, when a confer-
ence of the two sides was held in Chicago. This conference was preliminary
in nature, but paved the way for a conference later in the year out of which
grew the first working agreement and general wage scale of 1886. The condi-
tions which made such an agreement desirable are nowhere better summarized
than in the joint circular issued by the preliminary conference and signed by
representatives of both operators and mine workers. The following extracts
from this circular are of particular interest. (Reproduced from Evans' History
of the United Mine Workers of America, vol. 1, p. 147):
Senator STERLING. What was the date of the organization of the United Mine
Workers of America?
Mr. MURRAY. Well, its origin came in the year 1898. Prior to the year 1898
we had various organizations of mine workers, some known as The National
Association of Federation of Mine Workers.
Senator STERLING. It was not organized at the time of the two conferences?
Mr. MURRAY. The United Mine Workers of America, as it is now known, was
not then in existence until the agreement of 1886 was made in Chicago. The
United Mine Workers of America was the outgrowth of that organization which
was commonly known, I believe, as the National Association of Mine Workers.
Senator STERLING. The working agreement was reached between the opera-
tors and mines in the Chicago Conference?
Mr. MURRAY. Yes; in 1886.
"The history and experience of the past make it apparent to every intelli-
gent and thoughtful mind that strikes and lockouts are false agencies and
brutal resorts for the adjustment of the disputes and controversies arising
between employing capital and employed labor. They have become evils of the
gravest magnitude, not only to those immediately concerned in them, but also
to general society, being fruitful sources of public disturbance, riot, and blood-
shed. Sad illustrations of this truth are now being witnessed in certain of our
large cities and in several of the mining and manufacturing centers of the
country. These industrial conflicts generally involve waste of capital on the
one hand and the impoverishment of labor on the other. They engender bitter
feelings of prejudice and enmity and enkindle the destructive passions of hate
and revenge, bearing in their train the curses of widespread misery and wretch-
edness. They are contrary to the true spirit of American institutions, and
violate every principle of human justice and of Christian charity.
"The question of what the one should pay and the other receive in com-
pensation can be best determined by friendly conferences, where intelligence


===== [扫描序号 634] =====
620
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
and arbitration will take the place of the usual irrational and cruel methods of
the past. It is evident that the general standard of reward for labor has sunk
too low by reason of the reductions that have taken place during the past few
years and that miners generally are receiving inadequate compensation in an
employment full of toil and danger.
"It is also equally true that the widespread depression of business, the over-
production of coal, and the consequent severe competition have caused the
capital invested in mines to yield little or no profitable returns. The constant
reduction of wages that have lately taken place have afforded no relief to
capital, and, indeed, have but tended to increase its embarrassments. Any
reduction in labor in any coal field usually necessitates and generates a corre-
sponding reduction in every other competitive coal field."
The interstate agreement of 1886 applied to the so-called central competitive
field-namely, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Illinois, and Indiana. The withdrawal of
two of these States caused the disruption of the agreement in 1889. Then fol-
lowed a period, lasting almost 10 years, of intense disorganization and suffering
to both mine workers and operators. The condition of labor during this period
is thus described by Mr. Suffern (p. 41):
"The mining prices in the Pittsburgh district in the beginning of 1893 had
ranged from 65 cents per ton in the thick vein to 79 cents in the thin vein,
but by 1897 they had sunk to between 28 cents and 30 cents in the thick vein
and between 47 cents and 54 cents in the thin vein. When it is known that a
man can mine but 3 to 5 tons a day, and, added to this, could obtain but about
190 days' work a year, the low level to which the standard of living must have
fallen is obvious. The testimony before a special legislative committee of
Pennsylvania revealed the fact that in some localities 80 per cent of the miners
had no knowledge of the English language and lived like sheep in shambles.'
In Indiana and Ohio mining prices had fallen from 75 cents and 70 cents,
respectively, to 51 cents, with a contemplated cut to 45 cents in Ohio. Ia
Ohio the yearly earnings for 1896 ranged from $213.20 to $319.62. Illinois
wages had been on a par with the other States, and for five months previous
to the strike averaged about $12 per month. President Ratchford, of the
United Mine Workers, characterized the strike of 1897 as a spontaneous
uprising of an enslaved people,' but pointed out that the conditions of the
industry could not be laid at the doors of the great majority of employers.
The situation, he held, depended for the most part on the actions of a few
operators who cut prices far below the demands of the market.'”
Nor was the condition of the operators much better than that of their
employees. To quote Mr. Suffern again (p. 42):
"The average selling price of coal at the mine had fallen in the previous
six years (i. e., prior to 1897) in Illinois, 11 per cent; in Indiana, 18 per cent;
in Ohio, 16 per cent; in Pennsylvania, 18 per cent; and in West Virginia. 28
per cent. The full significance of persistent overproduction and the exploita-
tion of unorganized labor by uncontrolled fields is demonstrated by the fact
that, in the face of the beggerly condition of the miners and the low earnings
of capital in their own States. West Virginia and Illinois operators were
increasing their tonnage by 2,000,000 tons each, while the production of the
other States was falling behind their usual output. All the evils of the com-
pany store, abuse of screen system, dockage, etc., were rampant. The New
York & Cleveland Gas Coal Co.. which utilized all these methods, make its
men work under an iron contract,' and got its coal mined for 10 cents a ton
less than any other company in the Pittsburgh district, gave testimony under
oath that it was making only $800 profit on an investment of $1,000,000.”
The conditions in the coal industry were indeed curiously like those in the
clothing trade before the abolition of sweatshop competition-a competition
of low wages, bad working conditions, unfair practices against rivals, and an
absence of reputable trade standards.
The present organization of the mine employees-the United Mine Workers
of America-was established in 1890. It represented the culmination of the
efforts toward organization, which had manifested itself for a long series of
years under different names and with varying degrees of success. At first
it grew slowly, having in 1897 a membership of only about 10,000, but so strong
was its influence and so deplorable was the lot of the mineworkers at this time,
that when a strike was called in 1897, some 150.000 men, or practically all the
central field, responded. Out of this strike grew the joint conference and
agreement of 1898. This was the beginning of the long series of conferences
and agreements, which, with few interruptions, have brought conditions of


===== [扫描序号 635] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
621
industrial peace and stability to the central coal field which it could never
have hoped to experience under the old order of things. The agreements in
the earlier years were limited to the so-called central competitive field, but later
the same policies were extended to other fields, such as the southwest and
northwest fields.
HOW AGREEMENTS HAVE OPERATED.
Let us now see how these agreements have worked out and how the union
has established itself as a constructive factor in the industry.
Before the Industrial Commission of 1901 many coal operators appeared and
answered inquiries of the commission regarding the operation of trade agree-
ments and the good or evil effects of the mine workers' organization. This
testimony was of particular significance, because at that time-1901-the
memory of the days prior to the agreements was still fresh in men's minds.
One of the witnesses was Mr. George W. Schulderberg, coal operator of Pitts-
burgh, employing about 20,000 miners. He said (Vol. XII):
Trade unions, in my early experience, which was some 30 years ago, were
very overbearing and caused a great deal of embarrassment; but in later
years, since there has been a closer coming together between the laboring men
and employers, our dealings in the Pittsburgh district with the organization
known as the United Mine Workers have been very satisfactory. In the early
days of the mining industry, things were in rather a crude state. We have
learned much, both operator and miner, in coming together in our annual er
interstate meetings. We have worked in a harmonious way on lines of concili-
ation and arbitration; have never had to resort to arbitration but have always
arrived at results by merely consulting, becoming acquainted with one another's
conditions, and agreeing upon terms. That is my experience in the Pittsburgh
district; and as far as labor unions are concerned, the only drawback to those
who recognize them in a manner is that they are not strong enough or able to
enforce conditions in competitive districts, and thereby we labor under more or
less disadvantage for the reason that we agree and are in a manner bound to
do certain things, following out certain lines that others in surrounding districts
and surrounding States are not called upon to do, and at times it makes it a
hardship to operate on the lines that we do (p. 74).
"The organization of miners has brought about yearly, State and interstate
conventions at which miners and operators have met, become acquainted with
one another, learned their wants, and become acquainted with the faults of one
another; have consulted together, so that we know one another better. We, as
operators, are a little more liberal and fairer; so are the miners in the same
measure. There is more intelligence on both sides." (p. 76).
Before the commission in 1901, Mr. Hermann Justi, commissioner, Illinois
Coal Operators' Association, testified as follows (vol. XII, pp. 677–678.
"You gentlemen perhaps well know that the interstate movement was in-
augurated at Chicago in January, 1898. It was a direct result of the long and
bitter strike in the coal industry that prevailed throughout Pennsylvania, Indi-
ana. Ohio, and Illinois during 1897. Prior to the interstate joint movement,
chaos prevailed in the bituminous coal fields. The condition all through was
demoralized. Labor was dissatisfied. Strikes or lockouts occurred always in
one of two ways: There being no uniformity in wages or conditions, the
miners of one mine or a set of mines would strike because they were getting
less pay than the miners at some other mine or set of mines. Then, on the
other hand, certain operators who were paying a higher mining scale than their
competitors would often shut down the mines until their rates were reduced.
As a consequence, there was always a strike or lockout somewhere and such a
thing as industrial peace in the bituminous coal fields was unknown.
..
· Under the old system the more powerful operators could, and the less scru-
pulous would, take advantage not only of the miners but also of their more
scrupulous rivals. That system not only encouraged unfair practices and
threw into idleness tens of thousands of workers but it bankrupted many
honest coal operators.
"Severe as we find competition to-day in the bituminous fields it has its limi-
tations which it did not have before. The reason for this is plain. Relatively
speaking, every operator in the bituminous field pays the same scale of wages
and is governed by the same mining conditions. As the miner pays no rebates,
each operator knows substantially what it costs his rival to produce coal, and
hence the selling price is more nearly uniform.


===== [扫描序号 636] =====

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
"Then, again, prior to the interstate movement there was no reliable standard
of justice by which the miners were to be guided. The interstate joint move-
ment has had a tendency to impress on the men the sacredness of a contract,
thus making the task of the miners' officials less difficult in the carrying out of
the agreements into which they entered on behalf of the men. This is not pos-
sible always as yet, but there is at least a steady and gratifying improvement,
Notably is this true in Illinois, where the operators and miners have strong and
thoroughly equipped organizations." (Pp. 677, 678.)
To the same effect was the testimony of Mr. Walter J. Millins, coal operator
of Wooster, Ohio, before the same commission in 1901 (Vol. XII):
"My experience or observation has been that they (i. e., trade unions) have
been rather beneficial both to the employees and to the mine owners, for this
reason: With an organization that is managed by conservative and able men,
as has been the case with the miners' organization for some years past, we
have been able to form a fair basis of prices. It has made our industry more
stable and has given a certain security to our operations that we could not have
had if we were troubled by local disturbances, as was the case before the union
was formed and made as solid as it is now." (P. 166.)
*
*
*
"I think the general opinion is that an annual agreement is a very beneficial
arrangement, because it enables the mine owner and operator to figure intelli-
gently on his yearly contracts with some guaranty that prices will be main-
tained throughout the season of his contract, and it insures him regular work
unless there is some local difference at the mine. I have always been in favor
of that system of settling the wage question." (P. 173.)
In 1913 the Industrial Relations Commission, similar in most respects to the
Industrial Commission of 1901, took up again the subject of trade unions and
trade agreements. Among the very few coal operators testifying before this
commission was Mr. Francis S. Peabody, one of the most prominent and influen-
tial of the operators in the bituminous coal fields. I may say, in my judgment.
that Mr. Peabody is the largest independent coal producer in America. Mr.
Peabody found occasion to criticize several features of the existing agreements,
but he strongly approved the principle involved. He said in part (Vol. 1, p.
429):
My experience in the operation of mines and in dealing with organized labor
began in 1899. Prior to that time I operated nonorganized or nonunion mines.
In 1899 the mines which I had at that time been operating were organized, and
since that time I have been operating entirely with organized labor.
*
In my opinion trade agreements are wise. I think that the method of arriving
at them is as satisfactory a method as can be arrived at.”
A little later, after pointing out certain features of the existing agreements
to which he strongly objected, he reiterated his approval of agreements and
organization:
"I do not want the commission to understand that I do not fully believe in
trade agreements and that I do not fully believe in the employees uniting to
negotiate with the employers, because I do.
"
Writing in 1914, Prof. A. E. Suffern thus summarizes some of the benefits re-
sulting from organization and agreements in the coal industry (pp. XIX, XX,
348, 349):
**
"The employers and employees have both learned the advantage of cooper-
ation and organization and at the same time have gained a new tolerance
each for the other. They have transferred the settlement of the wage con-
troversy from scenes of force and violence to the conference hall, where reason
and intellect are working out something bigger than mere trade agreements.
** Membership in the local group and striving together for group in-
terests have given the parties a concept of the meaning of membership in a
larger national group and greater appreciation of efforts looking to the public
welfare. This is demonstrated by increasing deference to public opinion and
a recognition of the necessity of fair treatment to all concerned. Both sides
realize that their actions are of national importance, as well as local, and that,
if they are to wear the badge of desirable citizens, individual and group selfish-
ness must be subordinated.” (P. XIX.)
"If the conciliation movement in settling labor disputes had contributed
nothing more than men of the kind it has brought forward on both sides, it
would be worth all the efforts expended in building it up." (P. XX.)
"In conclusion we should recall the economic and industrial conditions which
brought about the rise and extension of the system of conciliation and arbi-


===== [扫描序号 637] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
623
tration in the bituminous field. The elaborate machinery of the interstate
joint conference, States conferences, and the agreements for settling disputes
that arise under agreements are only made possible by the effective organization
of the United Mine Workers and the operators' associations." (P. 348.)
"It is evident that the methods utilized in the bituminous fields have reached
a very high stage of development. When it was once recognized that the old
order had changed and that labor had the right of representation in adjust-
ing its affairs, the parties were ready for collective bargaining. But we have
seen that a realization of this came only after much strife and bitterness of
feeling. As an industry develops to a stage where it is possible by ill-adjusted
production and exploitation to reduce the level of wages and profits to a
bare subsistence for labor and small earnings for capital, the rise of a workers'
organization to better these conditions must be expected." (P. 348. )
Moreover, we have seen that collective bargaining softens class antagonism
and encourages friendly relations between employers and workers, while, at
the same time, each party becomes aware of the difficulties with which the
other has to contend. The employers have shown a willingness to democratize
their industry, and the workers, as their power has increased have demonstrated
a sense of larger responsibility to the public." (P. 349.)
"Those who are afraid that they will surrender some of their prerogatives
and, because of their fear, fail to see the opportunity for utilizing the cooper-
ative force of rising intelligence are in reality a hindrance to themselves and
to society. Rising intelligence and increasing efficiency, properly directed,
should bring greater prosperity to wage worker and to capitalist alike. It goes
without saying that at least approximate justice must be granted in order to
bring cooperation and good feeling." (P. 349.)
From these citations of opinions by impartial students and by operators
themselves, few and brief as such citations must necessarily be at this time
and place, it appears that the union has played a most important part in
stabilizing the bituminous-coal industry. The union has never opposed compe-
tition, but it has fought and is still fighting to raise competition to a higher
plane, to make it a competition of efficiency in mine operation, and not a com-
petition in the exploitation of labor. This is a desirable thing and beneficial
to the public interest. It is also beneficial to the operators, and intelligent and
far-seeing operators (and these are in a vast majority) see the matter in this
light.
Unionization has brought to a disturbed and diseased industry the stabilizing
force of equitable wage rates and fair working conditions. This has permitted
both employees and employers to devote their attention to their primary job of
producing coal without the loss of time, energy, and efficiency incident to con-
tinuous bickerings over wage rates and working conditions. The employee,
moreover, because of the union, becomes a more intelligent, a more self-respect-
ing, and a more efficient worker.
The union does not claim for a moment that all these good effects have been
attained in their fullness as yet. The trade agreement is a piece of social
machinery which requires experience and training to operate at its most
complete success. There are necessarily many difficulties and many misunder-
standings.
Over most of the bituminous fields, however, great progress has been made.
Here and there on the outskirts certain operators, such as those of Logan
and Mingo Counties, strive to block the path of progress. They can not ulti-
mately succeed, but they can cause great temporary damage and needless suffer-
ing. In the long run the principle of collective bargaining and the trade agree-
ment will win out, because it is the only practicable way to insure peace and
progress in industry. It is not only the best way to these desired ends, but it
is the only practicable way to avoid on the one hand the autocracy of em-
ployers, and on the other hand the autocracy of bolshevism.

The CHAIRMAN. You may resume, Mr. Murray.
Mr. MURRAY. The next feature I wish to discuss is the recognition of the
United Mine Workers of America by the Federal Government during the war.
The importance and dignified standing of the United Mine Workers' organi-
zation is also evident from the attitude of the Federal Government toward the
organization during the war. Not only did the Government, at that time,
invoke the assistance of the United Mine Workers and their officials; it
recognized the organization as the representative of labor in the coal-mining
industry, and the Labor Bureau of the Fuel Administration, to which all mat-
ters relating to labor controversies were referred for settlement, had as one
of its joint heads Mr. John P. White, formerly president of the United Mine
Workers of America, the other being Mr. Rembrandt Peale, the well-known
coal operator. The importance attached to this action is indicated by the fol-
lowing statement issued by the Fuel Administration under date of July 24,
1918:
"At a recent conference held in the city of Washington, D. C., between the
United States Fuel Administrator, Harry A. Garfield, and the international
officials of the United Mine Workers of America, a complete understanding was
reached wherein all questions pertaining to labor in the coal-mining industry
will remain under the jurisdiction of the Unted States Fuel Admnistrator. This
is in accordance with an understanding previously reached between the Secre-
tary of Labor and the United States Fuel Administrator.
"In order that this arrangement may be made effective, the United States
Fuel Administration has created a Bureau of Labor, to which all matters relat-
ing to labor controversies will be referred for settlement. The United States
Fuel Administrator has appointed Mr. John P. White, formerly president of
the United Mine Workers of America, and Mr. Rembrandt Peale, coal operator
for central Pennsylvania, joint heads of this bureau, with power as his deputies
to consider and dispose of all matters concerning labor in the coal-mining
industry properly coming before the Fuel Administration and subject to the
procedure prescribed in existing joint agreements.
"The following statement of principles was made by Mr. H. A. Garfield,
United States Fuel Administrator, at conferences at which were present Mr.
Frank J. Hayes, president, Mr. John L. Lewis, vice president, Mr. William
Green, secretary, Mr. Rembrandt Peale, representing the Fuel Adminstration,
all of whom acquiesced in the statement as expressing their understanding of
the principles followed by the United States Fuel Administration and by the
International Union of Mine Workers in settling questions relating to labor in
the coal-mining industry, it being understood that wherever the Federal Gov-
ernment is called upon to intervene or of its own motion intervenes in the
settlement of such questions, whether in organized or unorganized fields juris-
diction shall remain for the present and until otherwise arranged in the hands
of the United States Fuel Administrator."
Then follows a list of the principles promulgated. I will not take the time
to read these, but would like to point out as of particular pertinence to the
present difficulties in West Virginia that one of these principles which the
United States Fuel Administration accepted and laid down for guidance in the
settlement of disputes was as follows:
"(b) That employers will be required to relinquish the right to discharge
employees because of affiliation with labor unions."
As a result of this close association between the Government and the United
Mine Workers during the war there was practically no interruption because
of strikes or labor disturbances and the production of coal was enormously
stimulated. I believe this statement will be supported by all those officials of
the Fuel Administration and of other branches of the Government who were
in a position to observe conditions in the coal industry. In October, 1917, the
wages of bituminous coal miners were fixed by an agreement between the coal
operators and the United Mine Workers. In spite of the pressure of in-
creased living costs and the dissatisfaction caused thereby among the mine
workers, the United Mine Workers strictly observed the terms of that agree-
ment during the whole period of hostilities and for a year thereafter. This
was done in the face of conditions, imposed by Dr. Garfield's interpretation of
the 1917 agreement, so unfair and so obnoxious to the mine workers that Dr.


===== [扫描序号 639] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
625
Garfield's advisers in the Fuel Administration urged him, without success, to
modify his attitude. Thus in the report of the directors of the labor bureau, of
which Mr. Rembrandt Peale, an operator, was a member and signed the report,
the situation is clearly outlined in the following words (Report dated Jan.
6. 1919):
"The position of your advisers was that on account of the splendid showing
that the miners had made in all sections of the country and the abnormal cost
of living and because the operators themselves in many bituminous fields had
acknowledged their willingness and ability to pay an increase, the patriotic
thing to do was to grant to all the mine workers some increase in wages, and
to those districts south of the Ohio River and the anthracite districts further
consideration could be given. We felt that it was a mistake to separate the
demands of the anthracite and bituminous miners. You thought otherwise.
Your decision was adhered to by us, and we have endeavored to carry it out
in every detail.
"The miners have not yet given up the idea that they are entitled to the
claims they were making. President Hayes, Vice President Lewis, and Secre-
tary Green, however, displayed splendid judgment in these matters, keeping at
all times in mind the welfare of our Nation in its great crisis."
In another section of this same report tribute is paid to the war services of
the United Mine Workers as to the operators in the following language:
"The international officials of the United Mine Workers of America, to-
gether with their various district and local officials everywhere, are entitled to
a great deal of credit for the manner and way in which they responded to
every appeal made by the Government to supply the enormous tonnage so
badly needed to prosecute the war. The most serious difficulty, in the early
fall of 1917 and during the early part of 1918, was the shortage of railroad
cars, which materially retarded coal production. However, the miners rec-
ognized the inadequacy of the car service and cooperated very splendidly to
see that all cars that were supplied to the mines were loaded as promptly as
possible. Acting upon the advice of their officials on numerous occas'ons the
miners suspended many of their organic rules in order to meet the extraor
dinary exigencies.
"The United Mine Workers of America, with its vast constituency, sensed
its duties in the war just as keenly and as loyally as did any other group of
citizens and the coal-mine operators are entitled to their full share of credit
for their cooperation in all matters that pertained to coal production.”
UNFAIR PRACTICES OF WEST VIRGINIA OPERATORS,
The above brief survey of the history and place of trade-unionism in the coal
industry throws valuable light upon the present situation in West Virginia.
This history shows clearly that the industry itself can not prosper save through
stability in the relations of operators and mine workers and that such sta-
bility can be secured only through the establishment of fair labor standards
on the basis of trade agreements, periodically revised to suit changing condi-
tions.
This history also shows that the success of these agreements depends, in
large degree, upon their covering a determining portion of the industry within
the competitive territory concerned. If any considerable number of operators
refuse to become parties to the agreements, the functioning of the agreements
is naturally rendered more difficult, especially in times of industrial depression.
When business is very active the menace is slight, as the demand for labor
will force the nonunion operator to meet union standards, and perhaps even
to improve on them. But when business is slack and labor plentiful the union
operator may be put at a serious disadvantage by a competitor which observes
no rules or standards.
Reduced to its simplest terms, what is the real objection of this group of
West Virginia operators to the extension of unionism or union standards to
their mines? Their objection is simply that the acceptance of union standards
would place them on a parity with their competitors. They do not oppose
unionism for the other fellow. On the contrary they are keenly in favor of
having all other fields organized. The more complete the organization outside
of their own field, the more favorable their own position. If their compet tors
are all bound by agreement to observe fair labor standards, even in time of
depression, so much the better for this group of nonunion operators. They
can take advantage of the situation to reduce wages and thereby undersell
their competitors.


===== [扫描序号 640] =====
626
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
It is obvious that such would be the result. It is like a baseball game or
other sporting contest, in which one of the teams is compelled, or through
motives of honor and sportsmanship feels itself compelled, to observe certain
rules, whereas the second team is freed from all restrictions. Under such cir-
cumstances the second team, which has no rules nor no scruples, will have a
distinct advantage over their more principled rival.
This is exactly the situation at present. The union operators, constituting
about 80 per cent of the coal industry, are working under agreements with
the United Mine Workers' organization, which will have until March, 1922,
to run. These agreements, it should be noted, were imposed by the decision
of a presidential tribunal-the Bituminous Comnrission of 1920-of which
Mr. Henry M. Robinson was chairman.
The nonunion operators have never observed the terms of this decision,
although, as I will establish later, they were under the same moral obligation
and, I believe, also under the same legal obligations, as were the operators in the
union fields. By not observing the terms of this decision these West Virginia
operators were naturally placed in an extremely favorable position in times
of depression and unemployment, such as the present, when they can take
advantage of the necessities of their employees to force down wages almost to
any extent, and thus undersell their competitors who are observing fair
standards.
This, indeed, is precisely the conditions described by Gov. Morgan in a
statement by him published in the Washington Star of September 13, 1921.
In this statement he said:
"The mines in these two counties (i. e., Logan and Mingo) are operated by
nonunion labor, and in order to secure employment the employees have accepted
voluntary reductions in wages, as have employees in many other trades when
they realized that war-time wages can not be continued.
"In the union mines of the State the officers of the United Mine Workers
have refused and declined to permit the employees to accept reduced wages
during the life of the contract which was made by the Government, and which
does not expire until April of next year. As a consequence the union mines are
idle much more than the nonunion mines, where the cost of production has
been lessened, consequently lessening the cost of coal to the consumer. Except
where physical conditions operate to their advantage, the union coal fields
can not compete in the present market with the nonunion coal fields, and the
officials of the United Mine Workers are familiar with this condition."
This is an extract taken from the Washington Star of September 13, 1921.
From the general tone of this statement it is clear that Gov. Morgan intends
to criticize the United Mine Workers for their position in seeking to carry
out the contract as fixed by the President's Bituminous Coal Commission in
1920 and in not joining with the nonunion miners of Logan and Mingo counties
in accepting drastic wage cuts.
This is, of course, an extraordinary position for the governor of West Vir-
ginia to assume. Further, his argument is for the reasons pointed out entirely
fallacious. For it should be carefully noted that the favored position of these
West Virginia nonunion operators is due solely to the fact that they constitute
but a small part of the industry, of which the vastly greater portion is observ-
ing the terms of the agreements of 1920. If to-morrow those agreements
should be abrogated and the union completely dissolved, this group of West
Virginia operators would cease to enjoy their present position. Other fields
would begin the wage-cutting and price-cutting policies which marked the
earlier days of the industry. In the resulting chaos of competition the mine
workers and the operators would both lose.
The public would gain nothing, as any reduction in price would be obtained at
too high a cost in suffering, in industrial losses, and in labor dissatisfaction and
strikes. This has been demontrated over and over again in the history of the
industry. No one gains from the cut-throat competition to which the bitu-
minous coal industry so readily gravitates when no agreements whatever exist.
In view of these facts, is it any wonder that the attitude of this group of non-
union operators is resented by the operators and mine workers in the organized
fields? The latter, after long struggle. have come to a working agreement under
which warfare and unfair trade practices are supplanted by conciliation and
fair standards, and they now see their interests endangered and the stability
of the industry threatened by a small group of what may be termed "outlaw'
operators, who refuse to abide by any standards and are willing to sacrifice
everything and everybody to their own selfish ends. And yet, such is the irony


===== [扫描序号 641] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
627
of things, it is this group who are now clamoring for protection against what,
with amazing effrontery, they claim to be a conspiracy to drive them out of
business. They are the real conspirators. They are engaged in a selfish and
vicious conspiracy to destroy standards of work and compenation which have
been promulgated by a disinterested governmental commission and to disrupt
the lawful organization of the United Mine Workers of America.
These West Virginia nonunion operators claim they are within the law in
fixing whatever wage rates and working conditions they see fit to fix.
In my
opinion, such an attitude, even in normal circumstances, would be socially
wrong, injurious to the industry, and harmful to the public interest. Under
existing circumstances I believe such an attitude to be infinitely worse, for it is
only by a technicality and the inactivity of the Government that these nonunion
operators have been able to escape the obligations of fair wages and fair work-
ing conditions imposed by the terms of the decision of the Bituminous Coal
Commission.
That this decision was binding upon all operators, nonunion as well as union.
is evident when the circumstances are recalled under which this decision was
rendered. On November 1, 1919, the United Mine Workers inaugurated a strike
to obtain what they believed to be necessary wage increases and improvements
in working conditions, efforts to obtain which through conferences with the
operators having failed. It is unnecessary to discuss at this place the merits of
the situation. The mine workers believed, and still believe, that they were justi-
fied in their demands, and that no contracts were violated by their action in as
much as their contracts had been for the duration of the war, which to all prac-
tical purposes was terminated. The Government took another view, holding that
the war, in a legal sense, was still on.
As a result of the strike work ceased in all the organized coal mines, but a con-
siderable number of nonunion miners went on working.
At this juncture President Wilson intervened. In a statement issued October
25, 1919 (p. 8 of Report of Butuminous Coal Commission), he stated that if
the mine workers would immediately return to work he would appoint a tri-
bunal to adjudicate all points in dispute. This offer was accepted by the parties
immediately concerned, and the tribunal was duly appointed. Under the cir-
cumstances of its appointment, however, this tribunal can not be regarded as
an ordinary arbitration body, voluntarily selected by the parties to a dispute. It
is true that the action of the President was in the form of an offer, later
approved by both parties. But in as much as the President, with all the power
of the Government, including the Army and Navy, back of him, had already
declared the strike to be "unlawful," and that he would appoint an investigating
tribunal at the request of "either or both sides," the offer was not without a
compulsory threat, and this undoubtedly had an important influence in securing
its acceptance. The section and attitude of President Wiylson, indeed, was
closely analogous to those of President Roosevelt in the appointment of the
Anthracite Cial Commission in 1902. In both cases the tribunals established
were essentially governmental tribunals.
I have laid stress upon this point as it is a very important one. If the
Bituminous Coal Commission had been an ordinary arbitration board, volun-
tarily decided upon and selected by the parties to a controversy, there would, of
course, be no doubt that its decision would have been binding only on the signa-
tory parties. On the other hand, if the Bituminous Coal Commission had been
solely of this character, its whole course of procedure would have been different,
and its award would have been very different from what it was. As a matter
of fact, there can be no doubt that the award of the commission was based
on the supposition that it was to be universally applicable and not merely limited
to the so-called organized mines. Even a casual reading of the commission's
report shows this to have been the case.
Thus take the sections of the report dealing with wages (pp. 35-38). The com-
mission finds for a 27 per cent increase over the wages in effect October 31,
1919. In reaching this conclusion it considers the industry as a whole, and all
its computations and deductions are made for the whole industry and not merely
for that part of it which was organized. And it assumes, moreover, that the
increase would be paid all mine workers and not merely the union miners. Thus
to read a paragraph of the report summarizing the results of the wage increases
granted (p. 37):
"On the basis of $1,300,000,000 as the annual value of bituminous coal, the
labor cost, which constitutes about 57 per cent of the total realization by the
operators, is about $741,000,000. Twenty-seven per cent of this amount is


===== [扫描序号 642] =====
628
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
approximately $200,000,000, which is the additional sum that will be paid to the
miners as the result of our award above what they were receiving on October 31,
1919. For it must be borne in mind that our award is based on the status prior
to the application of Dr. Garfield's 14 per cent. The 41 per cent itself involved a
cost of over $104,000,000, to which our award adds approximately another
$96,000,000.”
Can anything be more evidence then that the commission here was dealing.
just as Dr. Garfield had previously dealt, with the industry as a whole? All the
figures as to production and costs are for the whole industry, and the estimate
of the cost to the public of the 27 per cent increase in wages assumes that the
whole industry would be affected thereby.
Again, on page 39, the commission takes up the question of profits of coal
operators, and in discussing this subject deals with the whole industry, without
any regard whatsoever to the organized mines as a separate group. Thus to
quote merely the paragraph giving the basic figures as used by the commission:
"A table is shown below based on the returns made by coal operators to the
Bureau of Internal Revenue for the year 1918. In this table are included returns
from 1,551 operators, representing about one-third of the coal tonnage produced
in 1918. We have the assurance of the United States Geological Survey that
the relative figures would not be greatly different if all the operators were in-
cluded in the returns. Of the 1,551 companies, 337, or 22 per cent, reported net
losses in 1918, and 168 companies, or 11 per cent, reported net incomes of less
than 5 per cent on invested capital."
The commission here bases its conclusions regarding profits on the coal-mining
industry as a whole. If it had been concerned solely with the organized mine
workers and the organized mines it would have been absurd to have used the
figures which were used, as the profits of the latter group may have been very
different from those of all mines considered collectively. It is possible, for in-
stance, that all the highly profitable mines or all the no-profit mines may have
been those in which the union was not recognized.
Again, at the very beginning of its reports the commission declares as a
fundamental:
"It is essential that the miners shall have living wages." (P. 5.) Nor
has the passage of time in any way affected the force of the wage obligation.
The decision of the Bituminous Coal Commission is still effective, and will
remain effective at least until March 31, 1922. A decrease in the cost of liv-
ing would not in any way reduce its force, as Gov. Morgan evidently implies
in his statement previously quoted. Not only is such an attitude had in
both law and ethics, but it overlooks the fact that the Bituminous Coal Com-
mission fully recognized the possibility of a decline in the cost of living and
acted accordingly in fixing the wage rates granted. The commission's atti-
tude on this point was perfectly clear-cut.
“We hope," says the report of the commission, “that there will be a de-
cline in the cost of living in the next two years, but we realize that the miners
have borne an increase above their advance of wages and consider the possible
future decline in living costs as an offset for these losses."
A reading of the full report would show how practically every paragraph
must have been based upon the belief of the commission that it was dealing
with the whole bituminous-coal industry. Nowhere, however, is this point more
clearly evident than in the attitude of the President. From the statements of the
President during the whole period of controversy it is evident that he regarded
the whole trouble as one affecting the whole industry and not merely the
organized mines, and that the remedies must be of universal application. Thus
the duties which he places upon the commission are, not only to be the fixing of
wages, but also if necessary the fixing of profits and prices. Thus note the
language of his memorandum (p. 10, Bituminous Coal Commission report):
"Immediately upon a general resumption of operations, which shall be in
all districts, except as to wages upon the basis which obtained on October 31.
1919, the President will appoint a commission of three persons, one of whom
shall be a mine owner or operator in active business, which commission will
consider further questions of wages and working conditions, as well as profits
of operators and proper prices for coal, readjusting both wages and prices
if it shall so decide, including differentials and internal conditions within and
between districts."
And again the language of his letter creating the commission (p. 9 of the
Bituminous Coal Commission's report):

* If a readjustment of the prices of coal shall be found necessary,
I shall be pleased to transfer to the commission, subject to its unanimous
action, the powers heretofore vested in the Fuel Administrator for that pur-
pose.
"I am sure it is not necessary for me to call your attention to the tremendous
importance of the work of this commission or the great opportunity which it
presents for lasting service to the coal industry and to the country. If the

ing either the miners, the coal operators, or the general public, unless the find-
ings of this body are comprehensive in their character and embrace and guard
at every point the public interest."
Surely the President had in mind the clearing up of all the evil spots in the
industry to the extent of fixing not only minimum wages but also maximum
prices and profits. Clearly it would have been imposs ble even to consider
the fixing of profits and prices except for the whole industry. To have done so
for particular mines would have led to absurd results, and to have fixed profits
and prices for the whole industry, and to have while fixing wages for only a
portion thereof, would have been equally absurd.
In view of the above facts, I contend that according to all the usual standards
of right and justice the decision of the Bituminous Coal Commission was binding
upon nonunion as well as upon union operators and miners. Whether it created
a technical legal obligation upon the nonunion operator is not for me to say. I
am not versed in the technicalities of law. But in any case I do contend that
it created an obligation upon the Government to enforce the decision. For the
Government not to accept such an obligation is to do grave injustice to innocent
parties.
The first and greatest injustice would be to those operators who have dealt
amicably with the unions on the basis of trade agreement. As a result of the
strike of 1919, those operators were compelled (for presidential request at that
time meant virtual compulsion) to submit their difference to a Government
tribunal under the implied promise that justice would be done.
The decision of this tribunal required these operators to pay increased wages
and make other improvements in working conditions, and provided that these
should not be changed unt 1 March 30, 1922. A certain small but active group
of their nonunion competitors did not appear before this tribunal. The
tribunal, however, was supposed to deal and did deal with the problems of the
industry as a whole, and its report and decision is absolutely meaningless unless
construed as applying to the industry as a whole. Shall this small group of non-
union operators (whose existence was almost forgotten in the excitement of the
time) be permitted to d sregard without even a rebuke the terms of this de-
cision which the tribunal, the Government, and, I believe, the people as a whole
found to be fair and reasonable? Shall this small group of nonunion operators
be permitted, without even a rebuke, to "scab" on the industry? If so, then I
say that the whole procedure by which the Bituminous Coal Commission was
created and functioned was a flagrant miscarriage of justice.
If, on the other hand, the decision of that commission is to be accepted as a
fair and honest one, and the result of fair and honest intentions, then I say
that that dec sion must be interpreted as binding on the whole coal industry,
and that the Government was placed under obligation to enforce the decision.
During the period of the strike the Government did not hesitate to use its great
authority, under the war powers, against the United Mine Workers even to the
extent of placing its members in jail. Is there any reason why it should not
have used its authority, under the same war powers, to make the nonunion
operators observe the terms of a decision by a governmental tribunal?
Even aside from questions of legal obligations in this matter, it is clear that
a strong moral obligation rests upon the nonunion operators to observe the
terms of the Bituminous Coal Commission's report. Of course, I do not expect
such men to be influenced by moral considerations. But I do contend that, by
their action, these West Virginia operators-I refer now to the nonunion
operators have at least forfeited all rights to the good opinion of honest fair-
minded men. They are guilty of the grossest sham and hypocrisy in making
their unwarranted charges and attacks on our organization. Their own hands

are unclean, their patriotism is sullied, and they can not in their blindness

The West Virginia antiunion operators have claimed that unionization would
ruin them; that the union would impose terms which would make it impossible
for West Virginia to compete with Ohio, Pennsylvania, Indiana, and the ad-
jacent competitive States. They have even gone further and charged that the
United Mine Workers are in a conspiracy with the union operators in the
neighboring States to unionize West Virginia in order to suppress the competi-
tion of that State by increasing mining cost and decreasing output. Allegations
of this character were made before the Paint Creek investigation committee
of the Senate and similar allegations have since been made and will no doubt
be repeated at the present hearings.
Such charges, I believe, are absolutely refuted by the account I have just
presented regarding the history of concilliation and trade agreements in the
coal industry and of the unfair practices of the West Virginia nonunion opera-
tors. From that account, I believe it is clear just what are the animating
motives of the mine workers and of the operators. It is true that the United
Mine Workers desire to extend their organization into the unorganized terri-
tory of West Virginia. Indeed, it is a fundamental principle of the United
Mine Workers to extend its benefits to as many coal miners as possible. It
is also no doubt true that certain operators of union mines in Ohio, Illinois.
and Pennsylvania believe that the extension of the union to the unorganized
sections of West Virginia will be advantageous to the industry, by removing
the unfair competitive practices, such as low wages, long hours, etc., existing
in the unorganized mines. To that extent the desires of the mine workers'
organization and of certain operators in outside States may be identical. But
to deduce from this that there exists a conspiracy to monopolize interstate com-
merce and injure the West Virginia operators is absurd. It is absurd for
several reasons. In the first place, an unknown number of operators, who are
operating union mines outside West Virginia and nonunion mines within that
State, have strenuously opposed the unionization of their West Virginia proper-
ties. Thus, according to the report of the Senate committee investigating the
Paint Creek situation in 1913 on page 37, it says as follows:
"There is also evidence in the record that a number of coal operators
of Ohio were also engaged in the business in West Virginia and were opposed
to the unionizing of the miners in their employ in that State, thus tending to
controvert the charge that they were combining with others against the West
Virginia operators."
Furthermore, the possibility of a conspiracy such as that charged would be
opposed not only to the whole past policy of the organization but to the founda-
tion principles upon which it is built. The aim of the United Mine Workers is to
extend its organization as widely as possible. But at no time has it been blind
to the fact that the interests of the industry must always be considered.
Biuminous-coal mining is spread over many States, with many varying condi-
tions as to the ease of mining, character of product, and accessibility to mar-
kets. The organization has always recognized these facts and acted accord-
ingly. It has not insisted upon a uniform wage rate, but has freely varied
its wage rates to suit local conditions. Deliberately to have fixed in any section
wage rates or other conditions of labor which would interfere with the mar-
keting of coal would be to deprive the miners themselves of work. It would
be unthinkable that the organization could be guilty of such stupidity.
This is the answer to the arguments of the operators that fair competitive
conditions between West Virginia and the other States could not be estab-
lished in a joint conference embracing the so-called Central Competitive Coal
Field. This reasoning was well expressed in an official statement of the United
Mine Workers as long ago as 1912, wherein they say:
"We have made it clear to both sides (northern operators and West Virginia
operators) that it is not our intention to unionize these fields for the purpose
of strangling competition with the operators in the Northern States nor to
establish prohibitive wages and conditions, viewed from a competitive stand-
point, that will keep their product out of its most favorable market. It is
needless to say that if we adopted such a short-sighted policy it would act as
a boomerang and would hit our cause and the men we organize harder than
it would the operators, inasmuch as it would greatly limit the output of these
fields, deprive the men of work, and cause them more hardship than they are
now suffering. Such, of course, is not our intention, all reports and wild state-
ments to the contrary notwithstanding, and in the making of any wage scale

"Plans of the operators of other States against conditions prevailing here

From what I have just said it is clear that the charge that the United Mine
Workers and the operators in the central competitive field, namely, Illinois,
Indiana, Ohio, and western Pennsylvania, have conspired to deprive the West
Virginia operators of a profitable market is absurd on the face of it. No
possible motive can be advanced by any man of intelligence who is acquainted
with the situation that could actuate or in any way influence the mine workers
to work toward such end as this. There are in West Virginia many thousands
of good union men employed in the mines, led by capable, alert leaders who
are kept thoroughly informed concerning any agreements that may be arrived
at elsewhere and that could in any way affect their welfare. If an agreement
were made in the central competitive field that deprived the West Virginia
m.nes of a profitable market, of course the result would necessarily be an
immediate decline in production and this in turn would mean the closing of
the mines in whole or in part and the consequent loss of work of the mine
workers, both union and nonun on alike. Do you think for one moment that
the 50,000 union mine workers in the State of West Virginia, leaders or mem-
bership, would stand for such as tuat.on? There would straightway be such
an outery as would fill the front pages of the press of the entire country, and
the public.ty would force a modification of the agreement even before the
courts could start any act on,
Nor could the United Mine Workers, even if so disposed, afford to harm
the nonunion miners of West Virginia if it were possible to do so without at the

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
same time also harming the union miners. Our ultimate goal, to repeat, is to
unionize all the mines in the United States. extend the benefits of our organiza-
tion to all mine workers no matter where employed, improve living conditions,
obtain regular and humane hours, establish equitable working rules under as
safe and unburdensome conditions as are compatible with the exigencies of
the occupation. This goal we are constantly approaching, but our progress
would inevitably be stopped if the nonunion miners were to be persuaded that
the organization of the United Mine Workers was unfriendly or was conspiring
against their interests.
But entirely apart from the absurdity of the charge of conspiracy, the
statistics collected and published by the United States Geological Survey prove
conclusively that whatever might be the disposition and intent of the oper-
ators and mine workers in the central competitive field, there has resulted no
harm, no discrimination, no prostration to the mining industry in West Virginia.
On the contrary, the yearly production of coal in West Virginia has increased
faster than the production in the central competitive field and faster than the
country as a whole. From 1900 to 1918 the production in West Virginia was
quadrupled, while in the four States of the central competitive field it in-
creased to only two and one half times, and in the United States as a whole
to only two and three-quarters times its 1900 figure. And, furthermore, the
slump in production since the armistice was felt less in West Virginia, inasmuch
as its 1920 production was only 3 per cent under the high output of 1918, while
in the central competitive field it was 5 per cent under, and in the United States
as a whole it was 4 per cent under.
During 1921 also the West Virginia operators were more successful in market-
ing their product than were the operators elsewhere, as is shown by the reports
of the Geological Survey. During the first six months of the year there was
produced in West Virginia 38.8 per cent of the 12 months production of 1920,
while the central competitive field produced only 34.2 per cent, and the United
States as a whole 35.3 per cent.
It is perhaps interesting, and to me it is extremely significent, that this
increase in the production of coal in West Virginia as compared to the central
competitive field took place chiefly after the year 1908 or 1909. From 1900 to
1909 the increase in production in West Virginia was roughly the same as the
increase in the central competitive field, while after 1909 the production in
West Virginia increased at a rate 50 per cent faster than the rate of increase in
the central competitive field.
In other words, while the employees in the majority of the mines of West
Virginia were unorganized—that is, prior to 1909-the increase in the produc-
tion there was at about the same rate as in the organized central competitive
field, but during the period that organizations of the employees were forming
and thereafter, the production of West Virginia increased faster than the
production of the central competitive field. Surely there could be no more
striking proof of the benefits derived from the union organization, and of the
falsity of the charges of conspiracy.
Another way of showing the growing importance of the West Virginia fields
is by the ratio that the production there bears to the production elsewhere. In
1900 West Virginia produced 10 per cent of all the bituminous coal produced
in the United States. In 1909 it produced 13 per cent of the coal, and in the
first six months of 1921 produced 17 per cent with approximately two-thirds of
the entire number working with the miners, the United Mine Workers.
Similarly comparing the production of West Virginia with the production of
the four States of the central competitive field, the Geological Survey reports
show that in 1900 West Virginia produced 17 per cent as much coal as was
produced in those four States, in 1909 it produced 22 per cent as much, and
during the first six months of 1921 it produced 30 per cent as much.
All of these figures indicate clearly that there could have been no conspiracy
to reduce production in West Virginia. They also show conclusively that
unionization has not harmed the business of the operators.

Coal in West Virginia Compared with production in United States and in
Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, and Pennsylvania.
(The statement above referred to is inserted in the record at this point, as
follows:)
"The weakness of the argument that the extension of union wages and
working conditions to the nonunion mines would ruin, or even harm, the busi-
ness of those mines is further demonstrated by the fact that no such results

have occurred in those sections of West Virginia where the union has been

In Kanawha County, where the union was recognized in the year 1910, the

per cent. In Logan County and in McDowell County, both nonunion, it in-
creased in the same period of time only 54 per cent and 2 per cent respectively.
In Mingo County the results were better than in either Logan or McDowell, as

in daily hours of labor, and as these hours have been reduced more in the
unionized districts than they have in the nonunion districts the increase in the

“During the period of the European war (1915 to 1918) there was a drop

increased. This drop, however, was much greater in the nonunion districts

ployee per day decreased from 1915 to 1918 by 16 per cent. In McDowell
County it decreased by 22 per cent. In Kanawha County it decreased by only
8 per cent. All these figures are from the reports of the United States Geo-
logical Survey."
From what has been said above regarding the increased output of the West
Virginia mines, it is evident that the unionization of certain districts has not
placed any undue burden upon the operators therein. This would seem com-
pletely to substantiate our contention that any increase in wage rates incident
to the payment of the living wage contended for by the union would be more
than met by the increased efficiency of a stable, contented force of workmen.
But even if this were not true-if the operators in the West Virginia nonunion
counties have now such low working standards that the raising of them to the
union scale would actually increase the labor cost of production-still the
operators would be in an extraordinarily favorable position. For the West Vir-
ginia coal deposits are natually among the best in the country.
(According to the Senate committee investigating conditions in Paint Creek
coal fields in 1913, report, p. 23):
"The coal found in West Virginia is susceptible of being mined much cheaper
and is of a superior quality to that found in the other States (i. e., Ohio,
Illinois, Indiana, and western Pennsylvania).”
This being the case, the West. Virginia operators should be able to operate
under union standards and still mine coal more cheaply than almost any other
district in the country.
Nor can the operators take refuge in the charge that freight rates are un-
favorable to them. If they mean by unfavorable that the freight rates are
unfair it becomes a matter for the Interstate Commerce Commission to consider,
and the mine workers should certainly not be penalized for the errors of the
Interstate Commerce Commission. If, however, the operators mean by un-
favorable that their mines are so much farther from particular markets than
are other mines that the freight rates are, and in the judgment of the Interstate
Commerce Commission should be, higher, then the reply is that there is no
reason why the West Virginia operators should seek to compete in these mar-
kets unless their natural advantages are such that they can afford to pay the
freight rate differential. Surely no fair-minded man would contend that a mine
operator has a right to demand an unfairly low freight rate or to pay less than
a living wage to his employees in order that he may compete in a distant. mar-
ket with other coal operators who are more favorably situated.
The advantages which West Virginia has in quality of coal, ease of mining,
etc., are legitimate advantages, and no one could or would deny the operators
the fruits thereof. In addition, however, the nonunion operators of West Vir-
ginia want the additional advantages of better freight rates, lower wages, and
longer hours than those of other States. This is unfair competition and has
no moral or legal right to existence. No one State or field can ask for prefer-
ential freight rates and wage rates which would permit it to undersell all
other fields in all markets.
The statement will be made here by the operators that the miners in the
unorganized fields of West Virginia do not want to join the union; that they

I need but remind the committee that a similar argument was advanced by
the slave owners of the South when the abolition of human slavery in this
free country was proposed. Their black slaves did not want freedom; they
were satisfied and would be happy and contented if they were not stirred up
by the misleading promises of the abolitionists. But how many slaves refused
their freedom when their shackles were struck from them?
The unorganized miners of West Virginia are not satisfied. They are
silenced, intimidated, coerced into acceptance of conditions against which they
dare not protest lest they and their women and children starve. We know
this to be true, for we have sources of information far more accurate and far
more dependable than any of which the operators may boast. It has also been
established by an authoritative public inquiry made under ex-Gov. Cornwell in
1919.
However, it is not necessary to rely entirely upon our sources of informa-

"Everywhere one goes down in this country he hears the name of Don Chafin,

This testimony does not come from one who is prejudiced in favor of the
union, and it is not published in a newspaper which we regard as especially

weight to which it is entitled.
The mine operators will claim, of course, that they do not say to their
workers, “You can not belong to the union," but the hard fact remains that
that is what their practice amounts to, for they do say, "You can not work in
these fields if you do belong to the union." Moreover, they have gone into
the courts and secured injunctions restraining officials and organizers of the
United Mine Workers from going into certain counties to appeal to the workers
to join the union, and restraining them in another instance "from advertising,
representing, stating by word, by posted notices, or by placards displayed at
any point in the State of West Virginia or elsewhere, that a strike exists in
the Pond Creek field, or at plaintiff's mines, and from warning or notifying
persons to remain away from said Pond Creek field or from plaintiff's mines;
from assembling together or causing others to assemble together, or to assem-
ble with others, in and about the railroad depot at Williamson, or in the city of
Williamson, in such numbers and under such circumstances as to make a show
or appearance of force or opposition to the free passage of the plaintiff's agents,
representatives and employees to and from said mines."
No incident in the West Virginia struggle shows more clearly the weakness
of the operators' position than the charge made by them that the United Mine
Workers constitution advocates the destruction of property rights and that
therefore the United Mine Workers organization is revolutionary in its aims.
The charge is baseless. The United Mine Workers do believe in the na-
tionalization of the coal mines to be accomplished in a perfectly legal and
proper way with proper safeguards to the public interest and with adequate
guarantees to the capital invested in the industry. This belief is held by a
large and growing number of our citizens as the only permanent solution of
the coal problem. I believe the chairman of this committee advocated such a
policy in the report in the Cabin Creek investigation of 1913. But this is a far
cry from the forcible expropriation of private property, which the operators
charge is one of the objects of the United Mine Workers' organization. As a


===== [扫描序号 649] =====

matter of fact, the operators, in pretending to each read such an object into
a certain phrase of the Mine Workers' constitution are guilty of a deliberate
effort to misrepresent and deceive. The charge is so absurd as hardly to merit
reply, but inasmuch as it has been spread quite widely, and very few persons
are in a position to examine the facts, it seems desirable to make here a truth-
ful exposition of the real facts.

An examination of the wording of this preamble in relation to the body of
