A study of the proceedings of the 1921 convention of the United Mine Workers
of America, in which the new constitution was adopted, also brings out clearly
the lack of significance attaching to the insertion in the preamble of the clause
regarding the value of the product.
At this convention, as at practically all of the conventions of the United
Mine Workers, a certain group of members was of distinctly socialistic affilia-
tions. This group constituted but a relatively small minority of the members
of the organization and of the members of the convention, but they were very
active during the whole course of the discussion involving the revised constitu-
tion, and were constantly making motions to insert clauses of a socialistic tend-
ency. On all important points these suggestions were voted down, usually by
an overwhelming majority. In the case of the preamble to the constitution,
however, the clause now being discussed was permitted to be inserted under the
general belief of the conservative majority that the matter was unimportant.
This appears from the record of the convention. (Pp. 432-434.) Delegate
Bittner, secretary of the committee on constitution, reported and moved the
adoption of the preamble as drawn up by the committee, as follows:
"Believing that those whose lot it is to toil in the earth's recesses, surrounded
by peculiar dangers, and deprived of sunlight and pure air, producing the
commodity which makes possible the world's progress, are entitled to protec-
tion and equitable share of the fruits of their labor, we have formed 'The
United Mines Workers of America' for the purpose of establishing, by lawful
means, the principles embraced in the body of this constitution."
Delegate Williams, a member of the socialistic group, moved the amendment
to the committee's report, striking out the phrase “an equitable share of the
fruits of their labor," and inserting the words "the full social value of our
product." Discussion was very brief. Delegate Germer made the chief argu-
ment for adoption of the substitute. His argument was that the use of the
words "equitable share" was susceptible to misinterpretation, as it permitted
the enemies of improvement to argue that the amount they now received was
entirely equitable. Neither in his speech nor in the speech of Delegate
Hefferly, who made the only other speech in support of the substitution, was
there any suggestion that the term social value" shall be construed as mean-
ing any more than that the worker was entitled to the full product of his
labor. Delegate Bittner, who was representing the committee on constitution,
answered that it was merely a matter of English and that all the United Mine
Workers were asking for was "that which is just and right." Following Mr.
Bittner's statement, the substitute was carried without further comment and
without later discussion. I am submitting the full report of the proceedings on
this point for the information of the committee.

LOW WAGES AND LONG HOURS IN NONUNION MINES.
It is impossible for anyone to ascertain accurately whether wage rates and
earnings are higher in the union or in the nonunion counties of West Virginia.
The wage rates of those employees who are paid in accordance with the
amount of coal handled are based on two factors. In union mines the men are
paid by actual weight, each car of coal being weighed as it comes out of the
mine by representatives of the operators and of the mine workers, so the


===== [扫描序号 651] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
637
66
27
miners and loaders are assured of receiving no more and no less than their
just dues. In the nonunion mines, on the contrary, payment is made by the
car, regardless of the weight of coal that it contains. These cars are different
dimensions in different mines, and even vary considerably in the same mine.
Also a car that is old and battered will hold a different weight from the same
car when new. These cars are not loaded level with the top, but a topping'
is always required; that is, the coal must be heaped to a specified height. That
is the general practice. The result is a complete uncertainty on the part of
the miner as to wether he is receiving all that his labor should entitle him to,
and there is always present a certain temptation to the miner to try to
"best" the system by methods of piling the coal and to the mine foreman
to dock the miner unfairly for alleged shortage.
Last year Mr. Keeney, the president of district 17 of the United Mine
Workers, obtained the dimensions of several of the mine cars in Mingo
County, with the rate paid per car for different classes of work. The data
was turned over to Mr. Winthrop D. Lane, a journalist, who was making a
study of conditions in West Virginia for the New York Evening Post, and he
in turn submitted them to a certified public accountant in Charleston to make
the necessary calculations. It was found that for machine loading in rooms, a
very important occupation, the average rate paid in 13 mines in Mingo County
was 45 cents per ton, one mine paying as low as 31 cents. The union scale for
this class of work in Kanawha County under similar conditions is 69.3 cents
per ton. Other classes of work showed almost the same variations.
When it comes to actual earnings the situation is still more complicated. The
miners at the nonunion mines work much longer hours than in the union m´nes
and can therefore produce more coal, and it is also true that in Logan and
McDowell Counties the coal in general comes in comparatively thick veins
which are easy to cut out, and is free, usually, from impurities.
The conclusion arrived at by Mr. Lane was that a miner benefits financially
when he joins the union. This conclusion was reached, not by studying mines
in different districts where the conditions were dissimilar but by taking figures
from the books of several companies that had just recognized the union so that
it was possible to compare earnings of the same men on the same properties
under both union and nonunion conditions.
One of the chief benefits accruing to the mine workers from their membership
in the union lies in the certainty of the wage rate established by contract agree-
ment. This very point is also one of the chief objections that unfair nonunion
operators have to the union. These nonunion operators desire to possess auto-
cratic control over the wage rate and to vary it at wll so that the workers and
not the owner is forced to shoulder all the risks of the investment. During
period of prosperity, when the market is able to absorb all the coal that can be
produced, it may very well be true that not only earnings but also wage rates
in nonunion districts can be shown to be as high in some instances, or even
higher, than in union districts. But when a slight depression strikes the indus-
try it is the nonunion worker who immediately suffers.
An elaboration of this point of view was recently published in the Washington
Star of September 13, 1921, as coming from Ephraim F. Morgan, the governor
of West Virginia, wherein Gov. Morgan said in part:
"The mines in these two counties (i. e., Logan and Mingo) are operated by
nonunion labor, and in order to secure employment the employees have accepted
voluntary reductions in wages, as have employees in many other trades when
they realized that war-time wages can not be continued.
"In the union mines of the State the officers of the United States Mine Work-
ers have refused and declined to permit the employees to accept reduced wages
during the life of the contract which was made by the Government, and which
dos not expire until April of next year. As a consequence, the union mines are
idle much more than the nonunion mines where the cost of production has been
lessened, consequently lessening the cost of coal to the consumer. Except where
physical conditions operate to their advantage, the union coal fields can not
compete in the present market with the nonunion coal fields, and the officials
of the United Mine Workers are familiar with this condition."
This is no more than saying that respectable manufacturing establishments
operating under decent conditions are unable to compete with sweated indus-
tries, where the workers are paid a starvation wage and are forced to work
12 hours a day or longer in order to obtain it. Of course, wherever the power to
reduce wages is arbitrarily lodged in the hands of a few operators, they are
going to exercise this power in order to protect their own profits; and equally,


===== [扫描序号 652] =====
638
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
of course, a mine that is able to thus cut its cost of production is bound to
create havoc in the industry and adversely affect its competitors who are living
up to the contract rates established by the United States governmental com-
mission. If it were possible for a district further to cut its wage rate so that
the employees were working for nothing, it is clearly apparent that such a
district would be able to undersell all other districts and quickly obtain a mo-
nopoly of the entire business of the country.
But industry in general can not exist under such cutthroat methods. Sweating
is universally condemned, from humanitarian standpoints, through a wise
understanding of what is best for the industry in the long run, and from public
policy. The views thus expressed by the governor of West Virginia are archaic
rennants of exploded economic fallacies, and for the sake of humanity and of
industry as well they must not be allowed to prevail.
THE VICIOUS PRACTICE OF ARMED GUARDS AND SPIES.
The system of mine guards or private police stands out as one of the ugliest
features of the West Virginia situation, and certainly the one which more than
any other has been responsible for such acts of violence as have occurred. I
need not dwell upon the existence of such guards or the character of their
activities. The memory of the tragedy of Mattewan is still fresh in men's
minds. Aside from any technical question of who fired the first shot, it is evi-
dent that this and similar tragedies would never have occurred if it had not
been for the presence of private detectives and guards.
The committee is also familiar with the illuminating testimony of C. E. Lively,
a Baldwin-Felts operative, as made before it on July 20. Furthermore, certain
members of the committee have made a first-hand study of the fields where the
trouble has been most acute and undoubtedly gained thereby an insight into the
effects of the mine-guard and private-detective system as practiced by the
notorious Baldwin-Felts agency. The committee has been requested to summon
Mr. Tom Felts. the head of the Baldwin-Felts agency, and also Sheriff Don
Chafin, of Logan. These two men can testify probably better than any other as
to the inner workings of the mine-guard and private-detective system as prac-
ticed in these troubled counties of West Virginia.
The lamentable industrial situation now precipitated in West Virginia by
the system of armed guards and spies is not a new one either there or elsewhere.
In 1912 there were serious industrial disturbances in the Paint Creek and
Cabin Creek regions of West Virginia. The disorder reached such a point that
Federal investigation was called for and made.
6.
At the hearing held before the Senate committee, making the investigation
the fact was brought out that West Virginia operators employed private agencies,
who brought in strong-arm" men from outside States. (Hearings before the
subcommittee of the Committee on Education and Labor of the United States
Senate, 63d Cong., 1st sess., S. R. 37, pt. 1, p. 85, Washington, 1913.)
*
*
In Senator Swanson's summary report of the Federal investigation, he de-
clares that "Among the contributing causes of the violence and disorder of
1912" was "the employment by the operators of the mine guards, many of
whom were aggressive and arbitrary; mine guards in the employment of the
operators acting as deputy sheriffs and clothed with the authority of law
(S. Rept. No. 321, 63d Cong., 2d sess.; on Investigation of the
Paint Creek Coal Fields of West Virgina: also Report of Senator Swanson,
Virginia, chairman of the Committee on Education and Labor, Mar. 9, 1914, p. 5.)
Senator Kenyon, a member of the same committee, refers, among other con-
dit ons responsible for the trouble, to " the employment of mine guards
acting as deputy sheriffs" and declares that "the conditions found by the
committee as existing on Cabin and Paint Creeks-the employment of mine
guards and arming them to go out and shoot and kill the employees, the arm-
ing of employees likew.se to go out and shoot and kill their employers-is a
condition that can not continue to exist in a free Republic." (Senate Report
No. 321, 63d Cong., 2d sess., on Investigation of the Paint Creek coal fields of
West Virginia; also report of Senator Swanson, West Virginia, chairman of
the Committee on Education and Labor, Mar. 9, 1914, p. 5.)
* *

while the union men were "arranging a march to sweep down on Cabin Creek

Another authoritative account of the West Virginia coal strike of 1912 has
been given by Mr. Lawrence R. Lynch, writing in the Political Science Quar-
terly, published by the Academy of Political Science, New York (December,
1914). Mr. Lynch states that "in order to guard their property, to protect
those who continued at work, and to make possible the operation of the mines
through imported labor, the operators contracted with the Baldwin-Felts De-
tective Agency for men to act as mine watchmen or guards.
Some
were secured who were unfit to serve in that capacity. Their bravery can not
be denied or can their loyalty and efficiency in serving their employers' interests
be questioned, but the fact remains that their presence was the direct cause of
much of the violence which followed. A few of the guards had criminal records,
and there was occasionally one who was able to boast that he had killed his
man.'
** * Not until after their arrival was any violence committed. But
for their presence it is probable that the subsequent acts of violence would have
been less serious than they were."
*
**
Mr. Lynch further points out "the injustice of permitting mine guards in the
employ of the operators to act as deputy sheriffs, enabling them to serve one
master while clothed with the authority of a second." This injustice was recog-
nized by the legislature of 1912-13, which amended the former law so as to
make unlawful the appointment of "any deputy or deputies to act as or perform
any duties in the capacity of guards or watchmen for any private individual,
firm, or corporation." This law has never been enforced by the State govern-
ment.
The West Virginia coal operators themselves admit that they have made use
of detectives or secret-service men. Mr. Harry Olmstead, chairman of the
labor committee of the operators' association of the Williamson field, at Wil-
liamson, W. Va., so admitted in a telegram to President Harding last month.
In the same telegram he declared that " the operators of this field do not employ
private detectives to guard their property." However, Gov. Cornwell's commis-
sion to investigate conditions in Logan County “found that the treasurer of
the Guyan Coal Operators' Association, Mr. C. W. Jones, paid to the sheriff of
that county $32,700 a year for the salaries of deputy sheriffs."

This vicious mine guard and industrial spy system has no defenders.
Wherever it has developed it has been condemned, not only by the workers but
by all disinterested observers and by all employers who believe in democratic
rather than czaristic industrial relations. The armed guard is the tool of an
industrial autocracy. He begets fear-and fear begets violence. The labor
spy is the unfailing cause of distrust and suspicion-a suspicion just as
likely to be directed toward the innocent as the guilty.

LABOR POLICIES DICTATED BY THE UNITED STATES STEEL CORPORATION AND THE
PENNSYLVANIA RAILROAD.
One of the most significant facts in the maintenance of an active antiunion
policy in the coal fields of the southern part of West Virginia is the owner-
ship and control of immense coal-producing areas by a few powerful corpora-
tions whose directors are allied, through intercorporate relations, with the
United States Steel Corporation and Pennsylvania Railroad interests. Both
the United States Steel Corporation and the Pennsylvania Railroad have
for a number of years been notorious for their unrelenting opposition to organ-
ized labor. This policy has been relentlessly pursued in the State of West
Virginia as in other States.
The extensive control of these interests over the West Virginia coal fields
is not a recent development, but is the outgrowth of a policy begun as early
as 1901. For the past 10 years those interests have extended their acquisition
of coal lands around and in Mingo and Logan Counties, until to-day their
holdings are vast and their control is powerful.
As to the close association of these corporations the records are clear. The
Pennsylvania Railroad financial interests have for years been allied with the
Girard Trust Co., of Philadelphia, and this banking house is one of the princi-
pal connecting links with a group of New York financial institutions closely
associated with Morgan & Co. The financial control of the Steel Corporation
has for many years centered in Morgan & Co. These facts were clearly and
undisputably established as far back as 1913 by the Pujo report on the
money-trust investigation.
The formation of the United States Steel Corporation was based on a policy
of extending its influence and control through interlocking directorates. This is
clearly developed in the following quotation from the report of the special com-
mittee of the House of Representatives on the investigation of the United States
Steel Corporation, July, 1912, page 209:
"A corporation speaks and acts through its officers, and the character and
scope of its influence are to a great extent determined by the personnel of its
directorate.

In 1901 the United States Steel Corporation began acquiring coal land holdings
in the Pocahontas region. In that year a syndicate managed by three men,
Messrs. E. H. Gary, Williams Edenborn, and Isaac T. Mann, bought up 300,000
acres of coal land, or about four-fifths of the Pocahontas field, and turned it over
to the Norfolk & Western Railroad, a subsidiary of the Pennsylvania Railroad.
In this syndicate Messrs. Gary and Edenborn represented the Steel Corporation.
One-sixth of this tract, or 50,000 acres, was acquired by the Steel Corporation
under a lease which is still in effect. This deal is thus described in the following
excerpt from the Preliminary Report of the Board of Directors to the stock-
holders of the United States Steel Corporation submitted at meeting of stock-
holders February 17, 1920:
66
Subsidiary companies of the corporation have secured a lease of 50 000
acres of the best Pocahontas coking and fuel property, on a royalty basis, and
on favorable terms for production and transportation: Plans for the prompt
development of this property on a large scale are under consideration, and it
is expected that in the near future there will be received from this field a large
supply of coke and fuel coal. With this acquisition it is estimated that there
is now controlled by subsidiary companies a sufficient quantity of the best and
cheapest coking coal to provide, on the basis of the present consumption, for
all the necessities of the furnaces of the companies during the next 60 years.
The corporation has guaranteed the performance of this lease on the part of
the lessees."
At that time the Steel Corporation estimated that its controlled coal lands
were sufficient to provide for its necessities for the next 60 years. Since then,
however, it has extended its holdings in the adjacent territory to a size several
times that acreage.

"Of the hundreds of disputes brought before this board probably less than

of this class on this road desired and had authorized this organization to

decisions must obey the mandate of Congress. If the carrier refuses, it is an
attack not so much on this board as on Congress. It is nothing more or less

expressed by Congress."
The antilabor policy of the United States Steel Corporation was early and
clearly stated, as appears in the following extract from the report of the spe-
cial committee of the House of Representatives on the investigation of the
United States Steel Corporation, July, 1912 (p. 128):
"The attitude of the United States Steel Corporation toward organized
labor was early determined. On June 17, 1901, six weeks after the Steel Cor-
poration was organized and began operations, a meeting of the executive com-
mittee was held in New York City. At this meeting Mr. Charles Steele, then a
member of the firm of J. P. Morgan & Co., and also a member of the executive
committee of the Steel Corporation, was present. The question of the attitude
of the corporation toward organized labor was extensively discussed at this
meeting. As a final result of the deliberations of the executive committee. Mr.
Steele brought forward the following proposition, which the records show was
finally voted upon and the president of the Steel Corporation instructed to
convey it to the presidents of the subsidiary companies, to-wit:
"That we are unalterably opposed to any extension of union labor and ad-
vise subsidiary companies to take firm position when these questions come up
and say that they are not going to recognize it; that is, any extension of
unions in mills where they do not now exist; that great care should be used to
prevent trouble, and that they promptly report and confer with this corpora-
tion.'"
Absentee ownership is always bad. It is particularly bad in the present case
because of the vicious and benighted character of these absentee owners as
regards all matters affecting labor. The powerful interests controlling these
fields have always denied the right of collective bargaining to their employees.
Even though this policy may be found to be within the strict letter of the law.
in actual practice the evils of its application through the zealous activities of
private detectives, of armed guards, of civil officers who are also in the pay of
the operators, and through other insidious and invidious practices, amount to
a denial of such elementary fundamental rights as freedom of speech, freedom
of assembly, and freedom of movement to any miner who is a member of a
labor union. The application of such policy means that the mine workers must

One of the significant facts in the maintenance of an active antiunion policy
in the coal fields of the southern part of West Virginia is the ownership and
control of immense coal-producing areas by a few powerful corporations whose
directors are allied, through intercorporate relat.ons with the United States

The extensive control of these interests over the West Virginia coal fields is
not a recent development, but is the outgrowth of a policy begun as early as
1901. For the past 20 years these interests have extended their acquisition of
coal lands around and in Mingo and Logan counties, until to-day their holdings
are so vast and the control so powerful as to entail serious social consequences
for the Nation. The United States Steel Corporation has carried with its con-
trol of land its labor policy of unalterable opposition " to any extension of union
labor," and under the relentless prosecution of this policy, the local government
itself is overshadowed and democratic institutions have become subservient to
private interests.

associated with Morgan & Co. The financial control of the Steel Corporation
has for years centered in Morgan & Co. These facts were clearly and undis-
putably established as far back as 1913 by the Pujo report of the Money Trust
investigation.
Here is a situation where absentee landlords owning, and in some cases oper-
ating, vast tracts of coal lands in and adjacent to the counties of Mingo and
Logan are centered largely in an association of interests.
The formation of the United States Steel Corporation was based on a policy
of extending its influence and control through interlocking directorates. The
following is a quotation from the report of special committee of House of

The corporation has guaranteed the performance of this lease on the part of

Some years after the acquisition of the large tract in the Pocahontas field,
referred to above, in 1917 and in 1918, the Steel Corporation extended its in-
terests into Mingo County and into the Kentucky coal fields in the region south
of Mingo County. In this Kentucky district the Steel Corporation has recently
built a coal-mining plant, which is probably one of the largest in the world,

NORFOLK & WESTERN RAILWAY CO.
As to the Norfolk & Western Railway Co., we desire to report that prior to
the year 1901 there were 300,000 acres, more, or less, of coal lands in what is
known as the Pocahontas Flat Top coal field, in the States of Virginia and
West Virginia, along the lines of the Norfolk & Western Railway, which were
owned by the Flat Top Coal Land Association.
In the year 1901 the Flat Top Coal Land Association gave an option thereon
to certain persons, to wit, Messrs. E. H. Gary, William Mienborn, and Isaac T.
Mann, known as syndicate managers. Some time thereafter the Pocahontas
Coal & Coke Co. was incorporated, under the laws of the State of New Jersey,
for the purpose of acquiring the lands aforesaid from the Flat Top Coal Land
Association, and this company did acquire said lands. The capital stock of
the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. is $1,000,000.
The above-mentioned syndicate managers on the 11th day of October, 1901,
made a written proposition to the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. to sell to it
the lands and property, including mineral rights, timber and timber rights,
railroad and railroad franchises of the Flat Top Coal Land Association, which
lands are stated in the proposition as comprising 300,000 acres more or less
of what is known as Pocahontas coal. In consideration of the conveyance by
the syndicate managers of the lands aforesaid to the Pocahontas Coal & Coke
Co., and of the payment by the syndicate managers to the said company of
about $4,500,000 in cash, the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. was to issue to the
syndicate managers certain securities.
As a result of this transaction the lands aforesaid were conveyed to the
Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co., but by agreement dated the 31st day of December,
1901, the proposition of the syndicate managers to the Pocahontas Coal & Coke
Co. was modified in some particulars and a new agreement was entered into
between the syndicate managers, the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. and the
Norfolk & Western Railway Co., whereby it was agreed that $1.000,000 of the
capital stock of the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co., full paid and nonassessable,
and being all the stock of said company, should be turned over to the Norfolk


===== [扫描序号 662] =====
648
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
& Western Railway Co., and that the Norfolk & Western Railway Co. jointly
with the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. should execute and deliver to the
syndicate managers "the bonds of the railway.company and of the Pocahontas
Coal & Coke Co." for "the aggregate principal sum of $20,000,000."
. This contract will be found on page 2404 of the record and sets forth very fully
the history of the transaction.
It would appear from this agreement that the syndicate managers were to
pay to the vendor of the several properties to the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co.
the sum of $13,500,000, and for this same property the Pocahontas Coal & Coke
Co. paid $20,000,000 in the joint bonds of the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co.
and the Norfolk & Western Railway Co., secured by first mortgage of the
Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. on the lands aforesaid, and that there was further
turned over to the syndicate managers $1,000,000 of the stock of the Pocahontas
Coal & Coke Co., full paid and nonassessable, which was all of the stock of
said company outstanding, and by said agreement this entire issue of stock
was turned over by the syndicate managers to and is now held by the Norfolk
& Western Railway Co. In addition to this the Pennsylvania Co. and the
Pittsburgh, Cincinnati, Chicago & St. Louis Railway Co. jointly guaranteed the
payment of the interest on the $20,000,000 of bonds aforesaid.
It further appears that it was originally contemplated by the syndicate
managers, after the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. was organized, that said
company should issue a very much larger amount of securities, which were
to be used in purchasing other lands or properties in the coal territory afore-
said, but when the Norfolk & Western Railroad Co. bought the stock of the
Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. and thus acquired control of the coal properties
this plan of purchasing additional territory was abandoned, and no securities
were issued by the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. except the $1,000,000 of capital
stock and the $20,000,000 of first-mortgage bonds, except $500,000 of bonds,
which are held by some one whose identity does not appear.
So at present the situation is that the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. owns
the fee simple title or mineral rights upon about 300,000 acres of Pocahontas
coal in the States of Virginia and West Virgin'a, and the securities of that
company are outstanding as follows:
First. Its entire capital stock of $1,000,000, held by the Norfolk & Western
Railway Co.
Second. Twenty million dollars of joint bonds of the Pocahontas Coal &
Coke Co. and the Norfolk & Western Railway Co. outstanding, secured by first
mortgage on the lands of the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co., the interest upon
which is guaranteed by the Pennsylvania Co. and the Pittsburgh, Cincinnati,
Chicago & St. Lou's Railway Co., and $500,000 additional bonds secured as
aforesaid.
The Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. gets its revenue from royalties on coal and
coke produced on its lands by lessees, who pay 10 cents per ton royalty on all
coal and 15 cents per ton on all coke produced. And the revenues from the
lands of the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. have never been sufficient to meet
its expenses and pay the interest on its bonded indebtedness, the deficit having
been paid by the Norfolk & Western Railway Co., the Pennsylvania Co., the
Pittsburgh, Cincinnat', Chicago & St. Louis Railway Co.
The Norfolk & Western Railway Co. purchased the entire stock of the
Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co., and thus acquired control of the coal lands
aforesaid, with the idea that the acquisition of these coal lans by any other
person or corporation than itself would be detrimental to the interests of that
company, and in the sale of the coal lands aforesaid to the Pocahontas Coal
& Coke Co. it was arranged, through Mr. E. H. Gary, one of the syndicate
managers, who was connected with the United States Steel Corporation, that
said corporation would have a lease upon 50,000 acres of sail land for the
purpose of furnishing it with a fuel supply.
The Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. does not own any coal mines in the sense
that it is an operator engaged in mining coal (pp. 2396-2397). It is a land-
holding company, and leases part of its lands to other persons who are engaged
in min ng coal, and the Norfolk & Western Railway Co. does no mining itself,
nor does it own any coal mines other than through the stock ownership in the
Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co., and the charter of the Pocahontas Coal & Coke
Co. prohibits that company from engaging in the buying and sell ng of coal
and coke.

The lease for the benefit of the United States Steel Corporation is operated
under the name of the United States Coal & Coke Co., which is a subsidiary
company of the Steel Corporation. The Norfolk & Western Railway Co. is
not interested in any other coal lands or coal properties by stock ownership or
otherwise than 'ts interest by reason of the ownership of the stock of the
Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co.
About 70 per cent of the coal tariffs of the Norfolk & Western Railway Co.
originates in what is known as the Pocahontas field, and a large amount above
one-half of the tonnage from the Pocahontas coal field is mined upon lands
owned by the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co., and other lands upon which coal
is raised in that territory being owned by the Croser Coal Land Association and
James H. Browning, and recently a new and large operation has been opened
in said field on lands owned by the Berwind-White Coal Mining Co.
As will be seen above, the Norfolk & Western Railway Co. has an interest
in a large amount of coal carried by it, by means of its ownership of the entire
cap tal stock of the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co., and while it may be prop-
erly said that the Norfolk & Western Railway does not own the coal after it is
mined, still it undoubtedly has an interets therein by reason of its ownership
of the landlord company, and the fact that all of the coal mined upon the lands
of said company must pay a royalty in which the Norfolk & Western Railway
Co. is interested by means of its stock ownership.
The Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co. is closely allied to the Pennsylvania Rail-
road both through the Norfolk & Western Railroad Co. and its own directorate.
Three directors and one vice president of the Pennsylvania Railroad are di-
rectors of the Norfolk & Western and three of the same men are directors of
the coal company. The Norfolk & Western Railway Co. is closely allied with
the Pennsylvania Railroad and the Pennsylvania Co., having four directors in
common. The Girard Trust Co. of Philadelphia-one of the Morgan & Co. group
of banks-and the Pennsylvania Railroad Co. have five directors in common.
Both the United States Steel Corporation and the Pennsylvania Railroad Co.
are dominated by Morgan & Co.
The Norfolk & Western Railway, while already owning the large Pocahontas
Coal & Coke Co. tract in the Pocahontas field we have previously described, in
1917 extended its interests into Mingo County and Pike County, Ky., as shown
by the following extract from its annual report of December 31, 1917 (p. 14):
46 FUEL COAL.
Owing to the high price of fuel coal, your company decided to acquire lease-
hold interests in coal-mining properties in order to mine a substantial portion
of its supply. Accordingly, leasehold interests in mines in Mingo County,
W. Va., and Pike County, Ky., known as the Howard and Vulcan operations,
have been acquired. These operations include about 3,800 acres, and it is
estimated that they will furnish one-sixth of your company's present fuel-coal
requirements."
The Steel Corporation's subsidiary company in the Pocahontas field, the
United States Coal & Coke Co., is the largest producer in the State of West
Virginia, putting out in 1918 nearly 5,000,000 tons, or more than one-fourth of
the aggregate of the seven companies producing above a million tons per an-
num. (Annual report Director of Mines, West Virginia, 1918). This company
in 1918 operated 11 plants at different points in McDowell County and employed
3,888 men, or nearly twice as many as the next largest company in that field.
The second largest producer in the Pocahontas field is the Pocahontas Fuel
Co., producing in 1918 nearly 3,000,000 tons and employing over 2,000 men. The
president of this company, Mr. Isaac T. Mann, who was associated with Messrs.
Gary and Edenborn, of the United States Steel Corporation, in the syndicate
purchase in 1901 of the largest portion of the Pocahontas field, to which we
have previously referred.
As well as controlling a group of local banks in this section, Mr. Mann also
controls the Red Jacket Consolidated Coal & Coke Co. located in Mingo County
and the largest producing company in that county and employing the largest
number of men. (Annual report Director of Mines West Virginia, 1918).

As will be shown later, the control of the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co., which
company is referred to above, is Pennsylvania Railroad interests. Both the
United States Steel Corporation and the Pennsylvania Railroad are conspicuous
for their fight against trade-unions and the denial to their employees of the
right of collective bargaining.
The labor policy of the Pennsylvania Railroad is well known.
Relative to the Pennsylvania Railroad's denying the right of certain em-
ployees to join the labor unions, the following excerpt from report of L. A.
Brown, special investigator, United States Commission on Industrial Relations,
dated April 20, 1914, states:
* *
The evidence shows that the company's attitude toward organized
labor is well defined and well understood, which amounts to drastic and even
fanatic despotism in opposition."
Only within the past few months has this railroad refused to comply with a
decision of the United States Railway Labor Board relative to the rights of the
railroad's employees in selecting representatives of their own choosing to repre-
sent them in negotiations with the railroad. The Pennsylvania Railroad now
stands in defiance of that board. With reference to the railroad's attitude,
the following is quoted from the board's order of September 16, 1921, in re
Docket 404, relating to petition of the Pennsylvania system requesting the
Labor Board to vacate and set aside decision No. 218, entitled "Railway
Employees' Department, American Federation of Labor. (Federated Shop
Crafts v. Pennsylvania System), pages 13 and 14:
..
The carrier also asserts the right to limit the representatives to be selected
by the employees to persons who are in the actual employment of the carrier.
The transportation act does not prescribe any such limitation. We know of
no law in this country which prevents or limits a man in selecting his own rep-
resentative, and this board has certainly no power to prescribe a 1 mitation
which the law does not and has no disposition to do so.
"As has been repeatedly pointed out, when the transportation act was passed,
Congress knew of and obviously had directly in view the labor conditions exist-
ing on the transportation lines and the previous history of labor troubles.
"It knew of the labor union and organizations, their history, growth, pur-
pose, and nature. It knew that negotiations as to rules and working condi-
tions and as to disputes had in the past been largely conducted on behalf of the
employees by these organizations, and that their officials, committees, agents,
and employees were peculiarly fitted and qualified to conduct these negotiations;
that it would be difficult and unsatisfactory for individual employees or even
small groups of employees in the face of these conditions to conduct negotia-
tions and settle disputes; and that an attempt to do so and to ignore such


===== [扫描序号 665] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
651
organizations and the acquired and vested rights of the members thereof
might lead to industrial war. No one can doubt that these matters were
known to and considered by Congress, and with these matters before Congress,
it is to be noted as most significant that Congress provided only three methods,
or only three classes who were authorized to bring disputes before the board:
(a) The chief executive of any carrier; (b) the chief executive of any organi-
zation of employees or subordinate officials; and (c) 100 or more unorganized
employees.
The organizations are repeatedly and expressly recognized in the act and
shown to have the right to represent the employees in these matters.
"Of the hundreds of disputes brought before this board probably less than
five have been brought by and for unorganized employees. It seems useless and
even stupid to argue and discuss this phase. But we want to make it plain
that Congress contemplated that the organizations would largely represent the
employees, and made it the imperative duty of the board to hear them.
"This presents the real crux of the controversy in this case. Here was an
organization to which many, if not a majority, of the employees in the shop
craft class of this company belonged. It is strongly insisted that a majority
of this class on this road desired and had authorized this organization to rep-
resent them in the conference and negotiations to be held. For reasons and
motives that are immaterial to this board, it is evident that the management
was not willing, if it could be avoided, that this organization, its officials,
agents, and committees should represent these men, and it evidently formed
its plans to prevent this if it could. Anyway, it was unwilling to agree, or
d'd not agree, with this organization on a plan to fairly ascertain the wishes
of this class of employees on the road. Both of the contending parties adopted
and carried out their own separate plans, both of which were held by this
board to be faulty and unfair. The board endeavored to prescribe a plan and
method that would fairly obtain and accurately express the wishes of the
majority of the employees of this class. This decision the carrier rejects
and refuses to abide by, and arrogates to itself the sole function and power to
decide these matters. If a majority of this class of employees on this road has
an absolute right under the law to select their own representatives-and this
is the clearly expressed will of Congress-this board, in its proceedings and
decisions, must obey the mandate of Congress. If the carrier refuses, it is an
attack not so much on this board as on Congress. It is nothing more or less
than a denial and repudiation of the sovereign will of the United States as
expressed by Congress."
The following quotation sets forth the early and definitely expressed labor
policy of the Steel Corporation :
[Extract from report of Special Committee of House of Representatives on investigation
of United States Steel Corporation, July, 1912, p. 128]
LABOR UNIONS.
The attitude of the United States Steel Corporation toward organized labor
was early determired. On June 17, 1921, six weeks after the Steel Corporation
was organized and began operations, a meeting of the executive committee
was held in New York City. At this meeting Mr. Charles Steele, then a member
of the firm of J. P. Morgan & Co. and also a member of the executive com-
mittee of the Steel Corporation, was present. The question of the attitude of
the corporation toward organized labor was extensively discussed at this meet-
ing. As a final result of the deliberations of the executive committee, Mr.
Steele brought forward the following proposition, which the records show was
finally voted upon and the president of the Steel Corporation instructed to
convey it to the presidents of the subsidiary companies, to wit:
"That we are unalterably opposed to any extension of union labor, and advise
subsidiary companies to take firm position when these questions come up and
say that they are not going to recognize it-that is, any extension of unions
in mills where they do not now exist-that great care should be used to prevent
trouble, and that they promptly report and confer with this corporation."
The powerful interests controlling these fields have always denied the right
of collective bargaining to their employees. These operators are themselves

652

members of associations whose object is a unified labor policy which has
always denied the rights of collective bargaining to the miners. In their pro-
claimed theory this benighted policy is within the law. In actual practice the
evils of the application of this policy through the zealous activities of private
detectives, of armed guards, of civil officers, who are also in the pay of the
operators, and through other insidious and invidious practices amount to a
denial of such elementary fundamental rights as freedom of speech, freedom
of assembly, and freedom of movement to any miner who is a member of a
labor union. The actual application of this policy could have no other pur-
pose than the stamping out of labor unions. It practically says the mine
workers must not have the right to bargain collectively with an association of
the most powerful interests in this country, but must deal with this giant
as an individual, and woe be unto him should he not acquiesce in its most
arbitrary dictation.

In conclusion, I wish to emphasize as strongly as I can that the fundamental
cause of the present trouble, as of a long series of similar troubles in the past,
is the den al to the miners of certain basic rights to which they are entitled
as American citizens. At this point it is well to make perfectly clear what the
mine workers hold to be the basic rights, and to emphasize the fact that they
do not demand union recognition as such a right. They believe in unionism,
believe that it is for the best interests of the worker, and in the long run of the
operator and of the public. But they concede that the extension of union rec-


===== [扫描序号 669] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
655
ognition should come through reasoning, argument, discussion, conference, and
strike. They demand the right to strike peaceably, just as they concede the
right of the employer peaceably to "lock out " his employees. These are both
crude measures, but, in the absence of better measures, seem inevitable at
times.
The essential demand of the mine workers is therefore, not for union recog-
nition but for freedom-freedom in disseminating ideas in speech and in as-
sembly, and freedom for the worker to join the union if he so desires.
These we claim are fundamental rights to which the miners are not only
entitled by the laws and the Constitution of both the United States and the
State of West Virginia, but are rights in the exercise of which the State should
in every way protect them. It is here that the State of West Virginia has
failed lamentably. Not only has there been no effort to protect the miners,
but at times it would appear that the governmental authorities have been in col-
lusion with the operators to forcibly deny the mine workers their simplest rights
as citizens. Thus the State has placed legal sanction upon the nefarious mine
guard system by permitting the deputy sheriffs to be paid by private indi-
viduals.
It is this lack of freedom which most galls the worker in these fields, as it
would gall any self-respecting American. It is not always a matter of earn-
ings-although earnings are low-but the fact that the worker is utterly without
a voice in ordering his life. It is because of this condition that the union makes
its appeal, for the union takes the individual and puts him in a position where
he can deal in man fashion with his employer.
Otherwise, there is no course for the individual mine worker except slavish
submission. For paternalism exists in these counties, in a manner never ap-
proached since the time of the feudal barons. The coal owners and the rep-
resentatives of absentee owners control the whole section in a way that can
hardly be appreciated by an outsider.
This power of the operators to control is based primarily upon their owner-
ship of property. They own the land around the mines, including the town or
camp sites, and sometimes they own even the roads. The houses are practically
all company houses. The stores and the amusement places are also company-
owned. Frequently the companies build the churches and school houses and
supplement or pay in full the salaries of the preachers and teachers. The
Y. M. C. A. buildings are built and owned by the company and the secretary
is usually one of its employees. All the meeting halls and places of assembly
are owned by the company.
Whether conditions in a particular camp or town are good or bad depends,
not upon the inhabitants but upon the company. Some companies are reason-
ably good to their employees, and supply fairly comfortable houses, clean
streets, and such essentials as sewage systems. This is found to be good
policy sometimes in fighting the unions. Other companies are less humane or
less far seeing. The houses are wretched hovels, the streets are filthy, there
is no pure water or sewage disposal of any kind.
In any case, however, the character of the towns-the generosity or lack of
generosity of the operators-is not the fundamental point. The fundamental
point is that this whole territory, with thousands of inhabitants, is absolutely
under the control of the operators. The individual is helpless. He may not
even receive visitors from the outside if the company disapproves, for the com-
pany owns the roads and neighboring land. If he falls under the displeasure of
h's company he may be evicted from his home at a moment's notice and will
not be able to obtain another habitation in that community and perhaps in none
of the adjoining communities. This explains the reasons why a mine worker
will often put up with the greatest indignities and refuse openly to affiliate
with the unions with which he is in complete sympathy.
No matter how benevolent the employer in the matter of welfare work may be,
such conditions are vicious and un-American. It is not the environment that
develops self-respecting and responsible citizens. Because of the isolated char-
acter of the country, some of the evils can not be immediately eliminated, such
as the necessity of the operators building houses and running company stores.
But the major evils can be and must be stopped. For instance, the police must
cease to be controlled by the operators. Such a condition is absolutely opposed
to the very principle of democracy. Again, the roads and streets must be public
highways, so that workers and outsiders may at least go and come freely. It is
almost unthinkable that there are towns where a man can not get to his own
home without passing over company property and thus being guilty of trespass


===== [扫描序号 670] =====
656
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
and so subject to arrest. Moreover, this power has been actually used by West
Virginia operators as was instanced in the Paint Creek troubles of 1913.
These kinds of remedies are for the State, Federal, or local government to ap-
ply. In addition, however, the situation is one where the union has a particu-
larly valuable function to perform. The union can not play the whole part of the
State, but it can and does bring into the strongholds of feudalism some of the
elements of democracy, and offers to the coal miners therein the only practical
means of protect ng themselves against oppression. Through organization, the
workers become strong enough to meet the operators face to face and work out
their mutual problems as man dealing with man and not as a servant petitioning
his master.
There can never be more than an armed truce until the autocracy of the op-
erators is broken, and, in the light of history, it would seem that the union is
the most logical and will be the most effective leader in this fight. In the mean-
time, there will be some violence. Throughout history where a people or a group
have been arbitrarily deprived of rights which they conceived to be theirs reac-
tion has been unavoidable. Violence can be prevented only by removing the
causes of violence. Industrial peace can rest only upon industrial justice.
This is the explanation of the struggle that has been going on in West Virginia
for more than 20 years. It is a struggle as old as civilization itself; in fact,
it is the struggle that has evolved modern civilization and all that it means
politically, economically, and industrially. It was through such a struggle that
this Republic was born-the fruition of men's ideals of political democracy—and
it is through such a struggle that we have progressed so far toward a realiza-
tion of men's ideals of industrial democracy.
The miners of West Virginia have been and are struggling for the funda-
mentals of industrial democracy. They want to live and work in circum-
stances and under conditions such as surround miners in other States and dis-
tricts, and such as surround workers in other industries. It is intolerable
that they should be denied rights and privileges which are enjoyed by other
miners and by workers in other industries, and it is the lesson of every page
of human history that whenever any considerable number of men find them-
selves subjected to conditions which they regard as intolerable they will rebel
and continue to rebel until those conditions are righted.
Thus it is that the state of affairs in West Virginia may be characterized
as a rebellion, but it must be clearly understood that it is not a rebellion
against State or Federal law and authority, or against our civil and political
institutions. It is a rebellion against an industrial autocracy or feudalism
which at its worst is cunning, cruel, and relentless, and which at its best is
indifferent, unintelligent, and selfish.
Such an autocracy can not endure, because it provokes, aggravates, and per-
petuates the conditions that eventually will destroy it, and we are serene
in the faith that when this committee has published the truth about West
Virginia to the country the whole American people will join us in a protest
that will end for all time an industrial tyranny which is the worst enemy
of modern civilized society. Do not mistake what I say or what I mean.
I do not say and I do not mean that capitalism or industrialism as such
is to be attacked and destroyed and I do not speak of and I do not mean a
movement that is a resort to arms, with resultant bloodshed and destruction
of property. It is not industrialism, but industrial autocracy and tyranny
against which we rebel, and the revolt in which we have faith is an awakening
of the public mind and a quickening of the public heart, against which no
autocracy and no tyranny ever has prevailed.
Our only fear is that the great mass of the American people may not be
made to understand and to believe the truth as to conditions in West Virginia.
Living as they do normal lives under normal conditions in normal communities,
it will be difficult for them to realize that the miners we represent are denied
almost everything which they enjoy and accept as a matter of course.
This, Mr. Chairman, completes my statement to your committee, and I may
say that I will be compelled to leave the city to-morrow morning at 4.30 for
the purpose of taking depositions in connection with certain suits which have
been entered against the United Mine Workers of America in the Federal
courts in the city of Indianapolis on Friday of this week.

The miners, in compliance with their request, returned home, and on or
about the 25th or 24th day of August-the 25th, I think-the State authorities,
in performance of its civil duties and its lawful duties, proceeded then to make
arrests, as I understand it, and proceeded to arrest a number of the leaders
of this movement who had participated in the original march of August 20,
and for some reason or other the time selected for arresting those whom it was
alleged were guilty of participating in the march was at midnight on the 27th
day of August; and some deputy sheriffs, some members of the State con-
stabulary, visited the small mining village of Sharpless, and it is alleged by
inhabitants who reside in that community and who were there on the evening
of the shooting that when the State constabulary came into the town of
Sharpless that evening they were shooting.
Some three miners, as I am told, living in close proximity to where the shoot-
ing was being done, came to their doors. The shooting was apparently directed
at their homes. They took their guns and they went to the door. They were
going to shoot, as they thought, in defense of their homes and their wives and
children who were sleeping in bed, and before they were given an opportunity
to do any shooting two of the three coal miners were killed, in the vicinity of
the`r own homes in the town of Sharpless at midnight of August 27 by members
of the State constabulary and by deputy sheriffs, as we understand it, under the
control of John Chafpin, of Logan County.
The news spread like wildfire among the men, who had just returned to their
homes under the plea of the president of district No. 17. The news spread
that they had returned to their homes and they had disarmed, and they had
went home peacefully, they had committed no crime, but that the State
constabulary the minute they had disarmed proceeded to the town of Sharpless
and there had killed two men of the United Mine Workers of America.
This resulted in a general remobilization of the old force that had assembled
at Marmet, and in addition to that there came hundreds of other men from
practically every corner of the State. Pleas in the meantime had been put
up to the governor asking the governor of the State of West Virginia to in
vestigate, and if it was found to be true that members of the State constabulary
had brutally murdered some innocent people who had committed no crime
that these men should be punished-prosecuted; but the governor, as I under-
stand it, lent an unwilling ear to the plea of the mine workers or their
friends, and this resulted in a general remobilization of the old forces, and
in addition to that there came new ones-not of the mine workers-but the
general opinion prevailed throughout the country that it was a mine workers'
uprising, and I say to you, Mr. Chairman, I say it now, just as truthfully
as I can, that it was a general-community uprising through every section of
the State, rising in open revolt at the wanton manner in which the members
of the State constabulary and deputy sheriffs were murdering innocent people
guilty of committing no offenses.
The responsibility of it would not and could not be placed to the United
Mine Workers of America as an organization.

Mr. MURRAY. I do not think so.

Mr. MURRAY. My thought is this, to make it plain, that a working man—a coal
miner, for example-is exercising, in my judgment, a God-given and a constitu-
tional right as a citizen of this great country to hold membership in an organi-
zation without the employer being privileged to exercise discrimination, such as
discharging him because of his union affiliations. I do not think that the em-
ployer has any right to do that.
The CHAIRMAN. By "any right" you mean a constitutional right or a moral
right?
Mr. MURRAY. Any moral right or any constitutional right, in my humble judg-
ment, without professing to have any knowledge of the law whatsoever.
Senator CARAWAY. Conceding he had no constitutional right to discharge a
man because he belonged to a union, would your organization have a constitu-
tional right to object to nonunion work in a mine?
Mr. MURRAY. None whatever.

Mr. MURRAY. We do that in many organized fields.

TESTIMONY OF MR. H. W. HOUSTON.
The witness having been first duly sworn by the chairman, testified as follows:
Mr. WALSH. What is your name?
Mr. HOUSTON. H. W. Houston.
Mr. WALSH. Where do you reside?
Mr. HOUSTON. Charleston, W. Va.

Mr. HOUSTON. I am an attorney at law.
Mr. WALSH. How long have you been practicing in West Virginia?
Mr. HOUSTON. Since 1901.
Mr. WALSH. You are a native of what State?
Mr. HOUSTON. Ohio.
Mr. WALSH. And how long have you lived in West Virginia?
Mr. HOUSTON. For about 47 years.
Mr. WALSH. Have you held any professional relations with the United Mine
Workers of America, or with any of the parties concerned in this controversy?
Mr. HOUSTON. In 1912 Mr. Belcher and I were attorneys for the United Mine
Workers of America for about one year, and Belcher continued for several years
more with them, and I became counsel for district No. 17 about five or six years
ago and have been their counsel up to the present time.
Mr. WALSH. And will you sketch in a general way for the committee what
the character of the decisions have been in cases in which you were engaged,
not quoting the title of each case, but what sort of case, etc.?
Mr. HOUSTON. Well, we not only handled civil cases and criminal cases, but
had general charge of the litigation for district 17 of the United Mine Workers.
We have had quite a number of criminal cases.

Mr. HOUSTON. That is the rule.

Mr. HOUSTON. That is the general rule.

Mr. HOUSTON. The counties are divided into magisterial districts. I believe

Mr. WALSH. Most of the camps are not incorporated?
Mr. HOUSTON. No; so they do not constitute political units in themselves.
Mr. WALSH. But they are a part of the county?
Mr. HOUSTON. They are a part of the county government.
Mr. WALSH. The office of high sheriff has been mentioned here. Do all of

Mr. HOUSTON. They have the right; yes, sir.
Senator STERLING. Do they have any municipal government?
Mr. HOUSTON. Very few; some of the larger ones are incorporated.
Senator STERLING. So they do not elect a mayor and aldermen or a board of

Mr. HOUSTON. Most of them have no local government whatever; very few
have mayors.
Mr. WALSH. And as local government is understood, whatever local govern-
ment there is in those places is taken over by the company, is it, or adminis-
tered by the company?
Mr. HOUSTON. The company practically administers the local government, and
McDowell County and Mingo County and Logan County, and all that territory
in its entirety is generally under the domination of the coal operators.

===== [扫描序号 713] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
699
Mr. UNTERMYER. Yes; I am still continuing the Lockwood investigation in
that State.
Mr. WALSH. And did you have some connection with the Pujo committee?
Mr. UNTERMYER. I was the counsel for the congressional committee here that
conducted the Money Trust investigation that had to do with this entire
situation.
Mr. WALSH. And for the Lockwood committee did the question of industrial
relations and the attitude generally of the Steel Co. toward industrial relations
come into issue?
Mr. UNTERMYER. Yes; that was a very prominent issue. It may be safer to
state what that is. We are conducting a housing investigation in the State
of New York, and I am representing the joint legislative committee on housing.
One of the difficulties about the construction of houses in New York was the
steel situation, with respect to structural steel, and I have that evidence here
that was taken in that connection. It appears that the Steel Co. felt that it
was necessary to intrude into the State of New York in the building situation
for the purpose of carrying out its campaign for what it called the open shop-
what I call the nonunion shop. They wanted, apparently, to extend their field
and strengthen their hands in the so-called open-shop fight. Up to that time,
which was in 1919, a builder could get structural steel delivered f. o. b. at
New York and could erect it either by union labor or nonunion labor, as he saw
fit. It had necessarily to be erected by union labor, because all the building
trades are unionized. In 1919 the Steel Co., or the steel companies which had
theretofore been members of an association called the National Iron Erectors'
League, organized a local league in New York as a subsidiary to the National
Iron Erectors' Association, and they called it the Iron League, and the steel
companies, most of them, became parties to it.
The CHAIRMAN. I do not wish to interrupt, but I do not just get the connec-
tion between this New York situation and the Steel Co.'s connection in West
Virginia.
Mr. UNTERMYER. Now, I am endeavoring to show you what their methods are
of enforcing the nonunion shop. If it is not considered of sufficient importance
or interest, I am not at all anxious to tell it.
The CHAIRMAN. Your theory, then, is that they use the same method in West
Virginia, is it?
Mr. UNTERMYER. Yes; that there is no such thing as an open shop. Our proof
showed this. As I said, the steel companies organized themselves into the
Iron League. The United States Steel Co. is never a member of any of these
constituent organizations; its independent power is so great that it simply
dominates the organizations from outside. It is not necessary for it to become
a member of any association to limit production or competition, or anything of
that kind; it simply operates with these people alongside of them. So they
organized an Iron League, and from that time on the builders did not get any
structural steel f. o. b. New York.
The great builders like Thompson-Sterrett and George H. Fuller & Co., who
had a hundred million or two-hundred million a year business, and had their
equipment and machinery for constructing steel buildings, simply had to take it
away; and this intermediate profit was shoved in between them, and they had,
in order to get their steel, to buy it erected in place and erected by what is
called open-shop labor, which was nonunion labor. That led to conflict that
gave this man Brindell his opportunity. I do not know whether you have
heard of him. We have convicted him in New York. He was the labor leader
of the building trade. "You are erecting your steel by nonunion labor," and he
would blackmail them in order to have this erection go on, and that very greatly
emphasized the difficulty in the labor situation there, and the only way that
builders in New York and Philadelphia, because they extended to Philadelphia,
were able to get steel for structural purposes was to get it through a member of
the Iron League, which had his nonunion foreman, nonunion organization.
We put a dozen or more witnesses on the stand, and their testimony is here,
and in the course of that investigation we brought laborers from Pittsburgh who
went upon the stand and testified one by one, some of them that they had their
pockets rifled and the union card taken, and others that they had been refused
work in the Pittsburgh district because they belonged to the union, our purpose
being to show, as they did show, that this was not an open-shop question at all.
but it was a crusade against organized labor. Now, that has been the attitude
of the Steel Co.

That is the issue, I say; I think it is a great enemy to industrial peace in
this country. If an open shop were a possible thing I would be in favor of an
open shop, because I believe it is more consistent with the American notion
of personal liberty; but there is no such thing. There is no such thing in any
great industry. The shop is either a union shop or a nonunion shop. In times
of depression, when labor is plentiful and there is an oversupply of labor, the
employer seeks to get better control of his own business, and he therefore
naturally drifts toward nonunion labor in place of union labor. In times of
great business activity organized labor seeks to drive out nonunion labor; in
all kinds of business activity organized labor seeks to drive out nonunion
labor, and so we face an economic situation in this country with the alternative
of a union shop or a nonunion shop. That is the real alternative, as between
a union shop and a nonunion shop.
I think it must be generally agreed that the peace and happiness and comfort
and welfare of the community would require that organized labor should be
recognized and encouraged, rather than the.nonunion shop, where that labor
does not have a fair chance in any way against organized capital, as it is at
the mercy of concentrated capital.

TESTIMONY OF E. T. ENGLAND, ATTORNEY GENERAL OF WEST
VIRGINIA.
The witness, having been first duly sworn, was examined by the chairman and
testified as follows:
The CHAIRMAN. State your name to the reporter, General.
Mr. ENGLAND. E. T. England.
The CHAIRMAN. You are the attorney general of West Virginia?
Mr. ENGLAND. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And how long have you been attorney general?
Mr. ENGLAND. Five years the 4th of next March. I am serving my second
term.
The CHAIRMAN. What is your home town, General?
Mr. ENGLAND. Logan.
The CHAIRMAN. That is the county seat of Logan County?
Mr. ENGLAND. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Of necessity you have come into pretty close contact with
this industrial situation in West Virginia?
Mr. ENGLAND. Well, I have, especially in Logan County. I can not say that
I have so much out of Logan, except in a very general way.
The CHAIRMAN. We are trying, General, as a committee, to find out the
reasons for the trouble, the causes of the trouble in West Virginia, and see if
there are any remedies that can be found. We are more concerned about that
than just the question of who shot somebody down there. We would be glad
if you could give to the committee your idea, in your own way, of the reasons
for this condition down there, and what could be done to stop it.
Mr. ENGLAND. Well, I don't know, Senator, whether I could do that very
accurately or not. There might be several reasons attribute:1 to the industrial
conditions down there, and it is a matter about which men might have, of
course, different views.


===== [扫描序号 734] =====
720
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Now, so far as Logan County is concerned, I feel that the mine guard
system, as maintained there, is one, if not the greatest, source of trouble in
that particular county. That is on account more of possibly the excesses they
commit.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, just what do you mean by the mine guard system as
practiced in that county?
Mr. ENGLAND. What I mean by the mine guard system is this-I could go
back, if you would wish, and give you the entire history from its inception to
the present time.
The CHAIRMAN. Is that a very long one?
Mr. ENGLAND. No.
The CHAIRMAN. All right; I wish you would.
Mr. ENGLAND. This is a rather young coal field. The road, I believe, was
completed in that county about 1904, and possibly a year or two after that
began to ship coal in some of the sections. The first I remember of the system
was under a sheriff there by the name of Chambers, who was elected in 1904--
oh, maybe he was elected in 1908, I believe it was 1908, and they had then the
Baldwin guards, the Baldwin-Felts detectives. In 1912 Mr. Chafin was elected
sheriff, and he promised the people to discontinue Baldwin-Felts detectives,
which he did. They did not operate any longer in the county, but he inaugu-
rated a system of his own. Now, these detectives, or rather mine guards, as
they are known, are appointed as deputy sheriffs, and then-
The CHAIRMAN. Are they paid by the coal companies?
Mr. ENGLAND (continuing). Who directs the activities of these deputies.
But I understand that possibly the entire fund-while I am not entirely ad-
vised, fully through the sheriff, but really the deputy sheriffs are paid by the
coal companies.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you know how many of those there are in Logan County?
Mr. ENGLAND. No; I could not tell you. There is quite a number. I could
not say how many. Especially at the present time. I have only been there
just occasionally in the last four or five years. But I have not the number.
There are quite a good many, however.
The CHAIRMAN, Does that system arouse a good deal of feeling and trouble,
do you think?
Mr. ENGLAND. Well, there is a good deal of feeling over it, a good deal of
feeling; yes.
The CHAIRMAN. Is there among the people of Logan County outside of the
miners?
Mr. ENGLAND. Yes; it affects the ones that are not engaged in mining as
much as it does the ones that are actually engaged in the mining industry.
The CHAIRMAN. Now the argument as to that, General, that we have had is
this: A man has the right to protect his property. The State should protect
it. If the State does not protect it, what is he going to do? He has got to get
officers, get men and make officers of them.
Mr. ENGLAND. No one, I take it, would question the right of the owner of
property having it sufficiently protected. There has never been any feeling
along that line, and no question of that. That is the right that he should
have; his property rights should be protected. But that is not what they
complain about. It is the things that these deputy sheriffs do as officials act-
ing as mine guards. Nobody complains about them protecting the coal property.
They ought to do that, and they are entitled to have it protected under all con-
ditions.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, it has been said here that the county could not afford to
employ a sufficient force to protect them. What do you say as to that?
Mr. ENGLAND. Well, I could not agree with that statement, Senator. That is a
very rich county.
The CHAIRMAN. I was going to ask you about that. Tell us about that.
Mr. ENGLAND. In the first place, that is true. In the second place, to main-
ta'n order a thing every good citizen is interested in-it would not be neces
sary to have a very large force. That is not what they are kept there for.
The CHAIRMAN. What are they kept there for, in your judgment?
Mr. ENGLAND. The main thing is to prevent organization, as I understand it.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you say that from your observation of it?

the trial, so he had a change of venue, so that we all had to appear there, of
course, but I don't guess they were going to try the case. So we were there in

Kirkpatrick, the deputy sheriff, made the remark: "There is Mr. Lively," he

Mr. Hatfield got up off the bed and looked out through the window, and we didn't

Mrs. CHAMBERS. Well, as we went up the first flight of steps, just as we landed

of Sid Hatfield's witnesses, were coming up the other flights of steps on the

at them, and at that time the first shot was fired about three steps up the
second flight of steps that led into the courthouse.
Mr. WALSH. Who fired the shot?
Mrs. CHAMBERS. Well, one of the detectives.
Mr. WALSH. How many of them were there?
Mrs. CHAMBERS. Well, I wouldn't say how many were there; there looked like
there might have been 100 or maybe 200 there that day, and there were about
6 or 8 right on these steps shooting, while there were more at the top of the
steps standing on the lawn.
Mr. WALSH. Did they take aim at your husband and Mr. Hatfield?
Mrs. CHAMBERS. They did. Lively put his arm across the front of me and shot
my husband in the neck; right there was the first shot. I don't mean that that
was the first shot that was fired, but that was the first time my husband was shot.
Sid was shot first-Sid Hatfield.
Mr. WALSH. How many times was your husband shot?
Mrs. CHAMBERS. About 11 or 12 times.
Mr. WALSH. And about how many times was Mr. Hatfield shot; how many
shots entered his body?
Mrs. CHAMBERS. I am unable to say; some said he had 9 and some said 11; so
I am not sure how many.
Mr. WALSH. You say Lively reached around your neck and fired a shot?
Mr. CHAMBERS. No; he was up on the step in front of me and kind of on
this side, you see, and my husband was on this side of me [indicating], and
kind of reached his arm across in front and shot my husband that way, you
see, in the neck. My husband, he rolled back down the steps and I looked
down this way and I seen him rolling down and blood gushing from his neck,
and I just went back down the steps after him, you see, and they kept on
shooting him, and when he fell he kind of fell on his side leaving his back
up, you know, toward the steps and they were shooting him in the back all
the time after he fell.
Mr. WALSH. How many shots entered his back?
Mrs. CHAMBERS. All the shots excepting these two; he was shot one time
in the neck and the last shot that was fired, C. E. Lively shot him right behind
the ear.
Mr. WALSH. Just describe that, what was the position of your husband's
body when Lively shot him behind the ear?
Mrs. CHAMBERS. He was lying down kind of on his side at the time that he
shot him the last time, and his head, of course, was turned up this way, kind
of lying on his side, and he just reached down and put his gun just about that
near his ear, and before he did that, though, I seen him coming down to do
that, I said, "Oh, please, Mr. Lively, don't shoot at him any more, you have
killed him now."

TESTIMONY OF DR. ARTHUR E. SUFFERN.
The witness, having been first duly sworn by the chairman, testified as
follows:
The CHAIRMAN. What is your business?
Dr. SUFFERN. I am an economist.
The CHAIRMAN. Connected with Columbia University?
Dr. SUFFERN. I prefer not to state my connections. I think it is irrelevant
to this. I am here simply to testify to writings I did eight years ago in con-
nection with a study I made in connection with the industrial relationships I
made in the coal industry, and I am only in position-in fact, you might say
right now-only in position to testify on the basis of these writings up to about
1913. I have only followed the West Virginia situation very generally since
that time.
The CHAIRMAN. Up to that time had you made a study of the West Virginia
situation?
Dr. SUFFERN. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And troubles that were going on in West Virginia then?
Dr. SUFFERN. Yes, sir. I think the Committee on Education and Labor was
carrying on investigations at that time-1912-13.
The CHAIRMAN. You have written a book on the general subject?
66
Dr. SUFFERN. Yes, sir; a book entitled Conciliation and Arbitration in the
Coal Industry of America."
The CHAIRMAN. We should like to have your ideas as to the causes of these
troubles and the remedies.
Dr. SUFFERN. Well, the reason that I included a consideration of the West
Virginia section in my book, and dealing with the coal situation in the large,
was because of the seeming strategic importance of that section of the bitu-
minous-coal districts.
The CHAIRMAN. You may go ahead, Dr. Suffern.
Dr. SUFFERN. In connection with the consideration of the developments of
industrial relationships in the coal industry, one could not go very far into that
without realizing that there were certain economic aspects in the industry in
connection with West Virginia, western Virginia, Maryland, southwestern
Pennsylvania, and central Pennsylvania that had a large bearing upon the eco-
nomic developments in the whole industry as well as upon the industrial rela-
tionships of the parties concerned. So that was the fundamental reason why
I gave consideration to West Virginia; and this region being the richest, per-
haps, in bituminous resources in the country, and having the resources there
relatively consolidated, as contrasted to the scattered distribution in the central
field and the southwestern field and elsewhere, one found that this factor in
the industry had to be considered as a matter of getting at certain complications
in industrial relationships.
