Senator MCKELLAR. Did you visit these fields personally ?
Dr. SUFFERN. No, sir; my writings on the West Virginia situation are based
primarily upon State reports. The report of the Interstate Commerce Com-
mission in 1906, that was investigated, and the investigation of this Committee
on Education and Labor and the evidence and data brought out by these sources.
This region as a region, it seems to me, is quite analogous to the anthracite
fields in the anthracite industry and is of such strategic importance because of
its richness, because of the general nature of the region, because of the nature
of the population, because of the way it is penetrated by certain railroads,
and because of the general developments of industrial progress through central
Pennsylvania, southwestern Maryland, and West Virginia that that aspect has
to be kept in mind as explaining, it seems to me, certain reasons, certain
motivations that lead over into industrial relationships, so it was with that in
mind that I attempted to go into the details to explain why West Virginia had
not made the progress in industrial relationships that were found in the other
coal districts. Do you wish me to go into further detail there?
The CHAIRMAN. No; well, in just what respect now has West Virginia not
made the progress you speak of with other industrial districts, and to what
did you attribute that?
Dr. SUFFERN. Well, under individual bargaining, as was the prevalent thing
through the West Virginia field, there were several important items besides
the natural resources in the industry that gave the owners and operators an
advantage over the operators and miners in the other fields-the matter of the
length of the day, the fact that coal was mined on the long-ton basis and sold
on the short-ton basis, the fact that the miners were not allowed check weighers,
the fact they were rewarded, as claimed, disproportionately to their work, the
fact that they were compelled to trade at company stores, the fact that they
were compelled to pay whatever rental was demanded for their houses, and
many things like that showed directly upon the relative advantage the owners
and operators in that field had over other fields aside from their natural
resources.
Then there was another factor that stood as a matter of investigation-that
the price per ton and the price per hour for the labor was as a rule lower, and
that could very well be from the standpoint of the laborer; he could with a
big vein take down more tons for the same amount of effort, and maybe his
daily wage and maybe his yearly wage under these circumstances might amount
to more than in the other fields where the resources were not so thick. Now,
these factors, aside from any other conditions, gave the region and those
operating a controlling and natural advantage, and this served as a very
disrupting factor in the matter of competition between the different coal fields.
and as far as I could get it from the general study of industrial relationships
they were greatly concerned in the central fields in having conditions near
enough on an equality so that West Virginia coal would not be driving them
out of the markets, and of course not only the hourly wage or the wage per
ton, but the general living conditions, the general working conditions, what
was paid for dead work, and so on, would come into the economic factors
making severe and strenuous competition. So there was a natural economic
incentive, both from the standpoint of the operators and the miners in the
other fields to establish relationships with that section and differentials in con-
nection with the increasing development of West Virginia, so that other fields
less favorably situated could stay in business, and naturally the operators used
this in the central fields upon the miners when they asked for increased wages
and better conditions. They constantly told the miners that before they could
meet them on those conditions West Virginia would have to be brought up
closer on a parity with them and that it was up to them to organize West
Virginia.
Then, it stands as a matter of record, I think, from the investigation of this
committee in the investigation had in 1912, that some of the operators in the
central fields had ownership in West Virginia as well as ownership in the
central fields, and they were very strenuous in connection with negotiations and
telling them to organize, but when it came to getting the good returns out of
West Virginia they were naturally not there interested in having the organi-
zation.. So this thing was played back and forth as an important factor in
the industrial relations in the other fields, and by both parties on industrial
relations. in West Virginia.
The CHAIRMAN. Did you go into the question at all of the operators in the
central fields desiring to unionize the fields of West Virginia?

Dr. SUFFERN. The operators of the central fields?
The CHAIRMAN. Well, in Indiana and Ohio.
Dr. SUFFERN. Yes; that was frequently mentioned in the joint conferences
between the miners and the operators and given by the operators as a reason
why they could not meet certain demands unless West Virginia was brought
on a nearer competitive basis.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you understand the attempt was being made on the part
of the operators to assist in unionizing the West Virginia fields?
Dr. SUFFERN. I do not think they ever put up any money on it. I think they
simply used that as a basis of argument with the miners, and the miners, of
course, were up against whatever conditions they found there, as has been
developed here in this hearing and other hearings, and the relative ease and
influence which they met when they did attempt to organize.
The CHAIRMAN. Have you given any study, Professor, to methods of adjust-
ing these difficulties, such as have taken place in West Virginia?
Dr. SUFFERN. Yes; I have made quite a considerable study of labor problems,
and I have given some study to different methods of industrial relationships.
Of course, there is no one method that is a panacea for all conditions or all
industries, but an interesting thing about the evolution in industrial relation-
ships in nearly all industries where there has been any great amount of de-
velopment is that to the extent that you have industrial harmony in the industry
new ways and means are invented to bring out better cooperation and better
understanding.
The CHAIRMAN. What have you to suggest as the result of your thought and
study as to any method of settling these industrial troubles?
Dr. SUFFERN. Well, one of the first things that should stand as a matter of
principle, I think, in industry is that both parties, there is no question about
the capitalist, as a rule, because he has ownership, but both parties should have
representation in dealing with conditions which really affect their lives and
work. If that principle is not admitted on the basis that enables the workers
to cope with the relative strength of capital in industry, it does not matter
what industry it is, labor is at a great disadvantage. The laborer can really
oppose organization only with organization; that is as far as getting a hearing
and receiving consideration of the actual conditions under which he lives, and
for that matter meeting economic competition with his own fellow workers. It
stands as a matter of record in industrial relationships that the only bottom
to the decree of a competition that may be carried on is that which will be sub-
mitted to by those in the worst status in industry, that is those who are the
weakest, those who are working too cheaply, as a rule, because of their necessity
they must have a job, they will work under cut wages, they will put up with
conditions in industry, so that the only way that these fundamentals can be lifted
to the level, if it can be lifted, is through organization and the control that es-
tablishes universality, establishes uniformity, something of a uniformity, those
things as they develop in industry on both sides in the matter of competition
more within the range of fair competition rather than cut-throat competition.
Senator MCKELLAR. You do not think it would be effective where the employer
just deals with his employees?
Dr. SUFFERN. There has been considerable development along that line.
A good many of the developments have a very favorable prospect, I think; but
it will be mostly dependent, I think, on the attitude of the employer in each
instance as to how far he is willing to go with it after he starts it, because the
employees under such circumstances as a rule do not have an extent of organi-
zation-I think Mr. Untermyer this morning spoke of that-the fact that work-
ers in a particular plant, dealing with a corporation owning many plants, are
not in a position to deal collectively with the owners unless the extent of the
organization or representation is on an industrial basis, but there are promising
aspects about that movement in dealing with their own employees, and I think
some of the most promising aspects about it are these:
In the first place, the right of representation is admitted, the right of organi-
zation is admitted, and the men in connection with this organization and rep-
resentation, even though it may be subjected to considerable dictation and mold-
ing on the part of the capitalists, there are many instances--considerable room
has been left for evolution and development toward better understanding and
better cooperation. Now, from that point on it seems to be a matter of choice on
the part of the employer how far he will go toward taking the employees into his
cooperation and giving information showing the actual conditions in the indus-
try; what his particular plant or the industry at large can bear in the way of


===== [扫描序号 758] =====
744
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
charges upon it, wages, and overhead cost, and so on; in fact, I think that is
going to be one of the most significant developments in many industries, par-
ticularly in a period such as we have on our hands now, in a time of depression
like the present, where some industries are favorably situated and have orders
and are doing business and making money, and some wageworkers making
high wages and some people making good profits, and others making no profits
but making losses, and some wages very low, or else the men out of employment
entirely. In striking a new balance one of the most fundamental things met
with is what is a fair return and what is a fair means, and what will the
industry as an industry, the economic condition of the industry, as it is spoken
of, what will it bear as a charge and a wage upon it?
There is an interesting thing in connection with industry there in the appli-
cation of that principle. In the coal fields where the veins are thin and expense
of production is high, or where in some instances they have run into condi-
tions where it is questionable whether the operators could pay a price per ton
that would give a living wage and still exploit the coal, particularly since the
more favorably situated regions had thick veins, better resources, lower costs
of production, and for many reasons were able to go into the market and put
prices to a point which would make it very difficult or may be impossible to
produce in the less-favored region. Then we have it as a matter of record that
in many instances where the vein is thin and expenses of production are high
the wageworkers have borne part of the burden of exploiting these resources
when it is really an unkindly period for them to carry it on; that they have
had their homes, their associations, and wanted to continue to work, and in
establishing differentials they have had to accept lower prices per ton, have had
to accept lower day or weekly or yearly wages than in other industries where
they perhaps with lower prices per ton have made bigger weekly, monthly, or
yearly wages. And there has been a development in the industry at large that is
naturally to be expected considering the way coal has been owned and bought
and exploited under the system as it has naturally grown up from the earliest
times of our history, when we first began to use coal. The only way it could
have been worked on a different basis would have been to exploit the richest
regions first and then your less wealthy sections later on a basis of a universal
and fairly scientific survey, and in beginning the exploitation make your invest-
ments there and take out what you need, and then as your coal resources are
exploited work toward the less favored regions.

Dr. SUFFERN. Up to the time I was consulted about describing it I was very

Mr. Chafin, and after making several trips he was denied permission to see the
parties confined in the jail. But I believed he did learn from some one-the
clerk of the court-the names of the men who were confined at that time, but
so far Mr. Hanley has never been able to interview these men.
As has been shown here by Mr. England, Logan County is dominated by Don
Chafin. The judge of the circuit court of that county having jurisdiction of
criminal matters is Judge Bland. My information is that a few years ago he
was a partner of a wealthy coal owner and a partner of John Chafin, who has
been prosecuting attorney for the preceding four years. Mr. John Chafin and
Mr. Bland were partners up to the 21st of January, 1921. Judge Bland goes on
the circuit bench and John Chafin is prosecuting attorney and Don Chafin is
sheriff of that county.
The CHAIRMAN. Are they brothers?
Mr. HOUSTON. They are cousins, in my information; whether first or second
cousins I do not recall.
A large number of indictments have been returned by the grand jury of that
county against a large number of men. I presume the big majority of them, so
far as my information goes, are members or have been members of the United
Mine Workers, growing out of this trouble in this march.
I took up with the prosecuting attorney over the telephone the question of
admitting these parties to bail. They are charged with various offenses. It
would be utterly impossible for us to expect a fair and impartial trial in Logan
County. Judge Bland knows that as well as anybody in Logan County, that it
would simply mean conviction to be tried there, whether the man was guilty
or not, in my opinion, and I believe that is the opinion of other people familiar
with the situation.
The prosecuting attorney notified me that he would use every means in his
power to prevent us getting a change of venue. I took it up with Judge Bland
and he very courteously told me "I won't consider that until it is presented to
me; then I will see what kind of case you make.”
I say I do not go into Logan County personally and have not for some time,
because the officials who employ me object to my going there, and I do not desire
to go there because of the threats made against me, so I send other counsel.
I
We will have to go in there and make application for a change of venue.
sent Mr. Van Fleet. I prepared a petition myself rather fully reciting the
industrial disturbance that had been created, and it was informally taken up
with the judge, and he would not agree to it at that time. We did not file, but
it was informally discussed with him, and we have to present that later.
Representing the United Mine Workers at that place, there has come to my
knowledge a large number of instances of the most wanton cruelty against
members and suspected members of our organization. Men are jailed there
without any charges being lodged against them. They are picked up on the
street under the merest suspicion, if they are strangers and have the appear-
ance of being workingmen, and put in jail and kept there indefinitely without
any charges against them. Often the sheriff, discovering they have no connec-
tion with the United Mine Workers of America, will let them go.
I do not want to take up the time of the committee dealing with the in-
stances of that, but there is a large number of them. I recall just a recent
instance. A young man named Gregg, living a few miles west of Cleveland,
Ohio, the son of a widow, who recently served 18 months in the recent war,
was out of work and went to Huntington, hearing he could get employment at
Logan. He had had nothing to eat for two days, and he boarded a freight


===== [扫描序号 764] =====
750
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
train and arrived at Huntington in the evening just at the time this trouble
was going on; went in a restaurant and got a drink of water; came out-a per-
fect stranger-he was approached by a couple of men and accused of being a
union man. He denied it, which is correct. He never belonged to a union.
And they jailed him and kept him for five days.
While he was there he saw a man shot down in the jail by Oscar White, the
son of W. E. White, the former justice of the peace and now deputy sheriff
and jailer of Logan County.
His statement is corroborated by at least three other witnesses. A young
man named Stanfield, from Atlanta, Ga., who arrived there on the same day
but on a different train was put in jail under the same circumstances and
in the same cell with Gregg, and they both tell the same story about the shoot-
ing down of this man, whose name, to the best of my information, was John
Komanskie.
I have seen numbers of men run out of Logan County with their heads tied
up in bandages. Being miners, they have come to the headquarters of the
United Mine Workers at Charleston and asked for help in some way and have
told us of all sorts of atrocities committed in that county.
This condition has gone on for a considerable period of time. It has created
an extremely bitter feeling among all union men, because they feel that these
acts are directed against the members of their organization, which is correct,
no doubt, and they resent it. And that situation had a great deal to do with
the recent industrial trouble in that county.
Just about one other matter I might refer to, and in making this statement I
want to confine myself strictly within the record of the case that I refer to.
I want to say in a general way that when we get a change of venue from
one of these counties to the other, the Baldwin & Felts guards or the coal opera-
ators' deputies follow us up. I have recently completed the trial of a case in
Greenbrier County, which is almost wholly an industrial county. It is a
garden spot of the State of West Virginia. Hot Springs is located there, and
the county seat 8 or 9 miles away; a beautiful paved road and a wonderful
country. The case in which Sid Hatfield was indicted and the case in which he
was going to Welch to be tried with the boys indicted with him was transferred
to Greenbrier County, and we tried that case about three weeks ago.
We had a large number of witnesses and the nearest way for them to have
gone would have been to take a train through McDowell County, but they
were afraid to go. They said they would not go. I went to the governor on
two or three occasions and asked for protection for these men. I have gone and
asked for protection for our men at different times, and I got an assurance of
protection but, in fact, got none. No; these men go down to Huntington, a
rather roundabout way, and under assurance from myself that there would be
no danger for them I got them as far as Charleston, and then, under persuasion,
got most of them the rest of the way, and nearly all of them stayed there during
the trial.
When this case came up John Collins was one of the parties indicted with
Mr. Hatfield-when this case came up before Judge Sharp, of the Green Briar
Circuit Court, this man Lively later came he was not there at first-Buster
Pence, one of the men indicted for the killing of Hatfield and Chambers, and
one Salters and several other men who have a bad reputation, whom I do not
know by name but know by sight, including the general manager of the Baldwin
& Felts Agency, Mr. Anderson, who I will say has always acted very courte-
ously to me, personally, and the other witnesses, as far as I know-but the
witnesses were afraid to stay around the courthouse. I appealed to Judge
Sharp, who is one of the best judges I think we have in West Virginia, and
tried to explain to him the situation. I think it was difficult for him to un-
derstand the situation these witnesses were in. I asked him to protect them.
He said he would see they were protected, but I saw no evidence of any pro-
tection of them except I believe the first day-I don't know whether for the
whole of the first day-parties entering the court room were searched for
guns. But that, of course, was no protection to the witnesses who were ex-
cluded from the court room and had to stay around the courthouse.
And Lively came in a little bit later and saw the defendants-most of them
had fled from Welsh when the shooting of Chamber and Hatfield occurred.
John Collins himself, who was to be put on trial first, fled and got on a Pull-
man train and was hiding in the ladies' toilet of one of the Pullman cars, and
the guards even entered the train and attempted to get the conductor to let
them have the key to take him out, evidently with the object of shooting him.

Some of the witnesses fled clear back to Charleston, a distance of approxi-

gone to Huntington, a dstance of 38 miles away, and spent part of the time
there.
As far as I know, not a single witness in one of those cases stayed in the

the defendants so badly that he went back to Charleston and the court has for-
feited a bond of $2.000, and the prosecuting attorney has notified us that he
will make a motion on that bond on the 26th of this month.
Senator MCKELLAR. Was any violence done?
Mr. HOUSTON. No; no violence was done, but it was that feeling of the wit-
nesses. They were afraid to testify openly and fully, afraid of this violence,
because of the experience they had had before.
Senator MCKELLAR. How many agents are there of this Baldwin-Felts Agency?
Mr. HOUSTON. It is extremely difficult to say. In our State we call them

Mr. HOUSTON. I have no record of that from which I can give their names.

Mr. HOUSTON. I would like to state to the committee, just in a general way, an
outline of some facts that were brought out in the trial of John Collins-undis-
puted facts, I am speaking of.
Mr. BELCHER. Which case was that?
Mr. HOUSTON. The John Collins case.
A number of the witnesses against Mr. Collins-and who would also have been
witnesses against Mr. Hatfield if he had not been killed- turned State's evi-
dence. Some of those witnesses, notably Lloyd Robertson-he was the principal
one testified in that trial that C. E. Lively organized the United Mine Workers'
local at Mohawk-that is where this trouble occurred-and at the same time
he organized the local of the United Mine Workers at War Eagle, over the line
of Mingo County; that he secured the election of Mr. Robertson as president of
the local at Mohawk.
The witnesses testified-Mr. Collins and his half brother and Lively did not
contradict these statements-that Mr. Lively got them in his restaurant and
proposed to them that they go up to Mohawk and shoot up the tipple and the
Baldwin-Felts guards; that Lively furnished the guns and the ammunition
with which to carry out that enterprise; that he got Robertson a number of men,
a number of these defendants and several others who turned State's evidence,
to go up there on a certain morning, around on the mountain top, and locate
themselves where they could shoot into the men being brought up on a conveyor.
In the meantime Lively had sent word to the Baldwin-Felts people-Mr.
Anderson, the general superintendent, admitted that-that the Mohawk tipple.
was to be shot up; and a number of Baldwin-Felts men and deputy sheriffs
from Welch went to Mohawk. Several of them stationed themselves in the head
house at Mohawk and at the foot of the tipple. They had Browning machine
guns and two bloodhounds in wait there to ambush these men that Lively had
induced to go up on the mountain and shoot into that conveyor line.
Those are the undisputed facts on that trial.
Senator MCKELLAR. Did these miners whom Lively sent there appear at the

Mr. HOUSTON. Quite a number of them testified they did.
Senator MCKELLAR. And they were killed?
Mr. HOUSTON. For some miraculous reason no one was struck, although a
number of shots were fired. Not a soul was hit on either side.
Senator McKELLAR. How did that trial arise?
Mr. HOUSTON. It arose through a prosecution of the coal operators for con-
spiracy to murder.
Senator MCKELLAR. Was Lively indicted for the conspiracy?
Mr. HOUSTON. No, sir; Lively was not indicted. All indictments were against
the miners.
Mr. WALSH. The men whom he had induced to do that?

The trouble started over in the Pocahontas coal fields last spring, and Mother
Jones was advertised to speak at the town of Princeton, the county seat of
Mercer County, on Sunday at a ball park, and, having no one to go with her,
I went, as a vacation more than anything else, and found a large number of
pople there, and I made a few opening remarks. I had spoken but a little while
when some one started a free fight, and they ordered me off the box. There
were a number of Baldwin-Felts people there who probably came to break
it up.
Following that the coal operators started two chancery injunction suits to
enjoin the organization of the Pocahontas coal fields. One of them was started
in McDowell County and the other one in Mercer County, and Judge Herndon
refused to grant the temporary restraining order in both cases on the ground
there was not sufficient evidence, and counsel for the coal operators-one of
them, Judge Sanders, whom I have referred to this morning-appealed to the
supreme court and got a temporary restraining order and ultimately got a
permanent injunction restraining the United Mine Workers of America doing a
variety of things.
The coal operators, when they thought there was going to be an organization
of that field through the Pocahontas association, had a large number, probably
thousands of these yellow-dog contracts sent out through the field and asked
the men to sign them.
Mr. WALSH. What is the yellow-dog contract; is there one in evidence?
Mr. HOUSTON. I think probably there is one in evidence. It is the contract
by which the men agreed they will not join the United Mine Workers of America
or the I. W. W., or any similar organization.
Mr. WALSH. Did you ever make any investigations into the question of
whether or not large numbers of these miners understood that? Perhaps it
might be well to give your experience.
Mr. HOUSTON. I did cause an investigation and talked to quite a number of
them. Depositions-rather voluminous depositions-were taken at Bluefield
in the office of Judge Sanders, and in cross-examining these witnesses I found
out that almost without exception the men who signed these contracts had no
ideas of unionism; most of them did not know a thing about the United Mine
Workers of America, and one of them, as I recall, testified, when I asked him
about the I. W. W., that he thought it was some kind of a religious organiza-
tion; and most of these men were North Carolina darkies that did not know
how to read or write.
Mr. WALSH. That is the free expression of a contract?
Mr. HOUSTON. That is the free expression of a contract.

EXHIBIT ORDER OF INJUNCTION," FILED WITH INTERVENING PETITION.
In the District Court of the United States for the southern district of West
Virginia, at Bluefield. Red Jacket Consolidated Coal and Coke Co., a Corpora-
tion, plaintiff, v. John L. Lewis, president of the United Mine Workers of
America, et al., defendants.
The original bill in this cause having been filed in the clerk's office of this
court at. Huntington on the 30th day of September, 1920, and summons on said
bill having been duly executed on the following-named defendants, C. F. Keeney,
president of District No. 17 of the United Mine Workers of America; Fred
Mooney, secretary-treasurer of District No. 17 of the United Mine Workers of
America; Harold W. Houston, attorney for District No. 17 of the United Mine
Workers of America; J. A. Bumgardner, C. L. McShan, James Spencer, Charles
Kiser, C. H. Workman, Ezra Frye, Arbie Meade, Sidney Hatfield, J. L. Work-
man, Warren Hutchinson, K. D. Koonce, Harry Chaffin, Adon Brown, George
Sullivan, Tom Dick Murphy, William Clay, Joe Browning, Troy Parley, Henry
Hatfield, Gordon Dean, Lee Gillespie, Ben Kiser, Fred Burgraff, Fred Webb,
John Williams, Henry Wright, John Entry, Newt. Watkins, Oscar Cole, Wilson
Cole, Isaac Cole, Jim Bolton, Clarence Van House, B. R. Page, Dave Phillips,
Walter Edwards, Roy Rose, Maston Varney, Van Clay, Evans Justus, Red Bill
Sizemore, Mann Wolford, Bass Keeton, and Clarence Stevens, and notice that an
application for injunction in accordance with said notice and the prayer of the
bill would be made on the 11th day of October, 1920, at 10 o'clock a. m., in the
courtroom of this court, in the Federal Building at Huntington, W. Va., having
been duly served upon the above-named defendants, and the court not being
so situated on the 11th day of October, 1920, as to hear said application or said
injunction, said application was, by agreement of the parties, continued to the
20th day of October, 1920, to be heard by the court in the courtroom in the
Federal Building in Bluefield, W. Va.; and now, on this the 20th day of October.
1920, said plaintiff again made application for said injunctions, and in support
thereof filed the affidavits of the following-named persons: William N. Cum-
mins (1), Oscar Leffler, R. H. Leffler (1), R R. Leffler (2), J. W. Varney.
Joseph Sipple, Richard Caines, Albert Ball, C. L. McKinnen, John Moore (1),
J. W. Bowling, Ira McGlothin, George Fletcher, Mason Varney, Jerry Brown,
John Moore (2), Richard Harris, June Wilson, H. W. McGinnis, William N.
Cummins (2), and Joe A. Sloan.
Thereupon the defendants, C. F. Keeney, president of district No. 17 of the
United Mine Workers of America; Fred Mooney, secretary-treasurer of district
No. 17 of the United Mine Wookers of America; and Harold W. Houston,
attorney for district No. 17 of the United Mine Workers of America, filed
their joint and several answers, together with certain affidavits in support
thereof, as is shown by another order entered herein on this date.
Upon consideration of the bill, answers and affidavits filed in support
thereof, the court is of the opinion that it sufficiently appears, to require the
granting of the preliminary injunction hereinafter awarded and set out, that
the plaintiff is operating certain coal mines in Mingo County, W. Va., as
nonunion or unorganized mines, and has entered into contracts with each one
of its employees, whereby each of said employees has agreed that so long


===== [扫描序号 769] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
755
as the relation of employer and employee exists between him and said plaintiff
he will not become a member of the United Mine Workers of America, or
affiliate therewith, and the plaintiff has agreed that it will not knowingly per-
mit any member of the United Mine Workers of America to work in or about
its said mines; that, notwithstanding their knowledge of the existence of
said contracts, the defendants and those associated with them have sought
and are seeking to procure plaintiff's employees to join said United Mine
Workers of America, and have succeeded in procuring some of them to do so,
and said defendants and those associated with them, have, by persuasion,
threats, intimidation, abuse, and violence of different kinds prevented or at-
tempted to prevent plaintiff's employees from continuing in its service, and
have, by persuasion, threats, intimidations, abuse, and violence of different
kinds prevented or attempted to prevent others who have desired and en-
deavored to become employees of plaintiff from so doing, and will continue
the use of the same methods and to do the same acts unless enjoined from so
doing; and further, that unless said injunction is awarded the plaintiff will
suffer irreparable injury to its property and property rights.
For the foregoing reasons and until further order of the court, it is adjudged,
ordered, and decreed that the above-named defendants, their officers, agents,
servants, employees, and attorneys, and those in active concert or participa-
tion with them be, and they are hereby, enjoined and restrained:
(1) From interefering or attempting to interfere with plaintiff's employees
for the purpose of unionizing plaintiff's mines, without its consent, by repre-
senting or causing to be represented to any of plaintiff's employees, or to
any person who might become an employee of plaintiff, that such person
will suffer or is likely to suffer some loss or trouble in continuing in, or in
entering the employment of plaintiff, by reason of plaintiff not recognizing
the United Mine Workers of America, or because plaintiff runs nonunion mines.
(2) From interfering or attempting to interfere with plaintiff's employees,
for the purpose of unionizing plaintiff's mines, without its consent, and, in aid
of such purpose, knowingly or willfully bringing about the breaking by plain-
tiff's employees of contracts of service. known to them at the time to exist
with plaintiff's present and future employees.
(3) From knowingly and willfully inducing plaintiff's employees, present or
future, to leave plaintiff's service, on the ground that plaintiff does not recog-
nize the United Mine Workers of America, that plaintiff runs nonunion mines,
or that the interests of the United Mine Worekrs of America require that
plaintiff shall not be permitted to run nonunion mines, or that the interests of
the union will be best promoted thereby.
(4) From interfering or attempting to interfere with plaintiff's employees,
so as knowingly and willfully to bring about the breaking by plaintiff's employees,
present and future, of their contracts of service, known to the defendants to
exist, and especially from knowingly and willfully inducing such employees,
present or future, to leave plaintiff's service without plaintiff's consent.
(5) From tresspassing on, or entering upon the grounds and premises of
plaintiff, or its mines, for the purpose of interfering with or hindering or ob-
structing its business, or with the purpose of compelling or inducing, by threats,
intimidation, violence, or abusive language, or persuation, any of plaintiff's
employees to refuse or fail to perform their duties as such; and
(6) From compelling or inducing, or attempting to compel of induce, by
persuasion, threats, intimidation, or abusive or violent language, any of plain-
tiff's employees to leave its service or fail or refuse to perform their duties as
such employees under their contract of employment, or from compelling or
attempting to compel by false representations, threats, intimidations, or abusive
or violent language, or other unlawful means, any person desiring to seek em-
ployment in plaintiff's mines and works from so accepting employment therein.
This injunctoin shall not become effective until the said plaintiff or some one
for it execute a bond as required by law, with surety in the sum of $20,000, con-
ditioned upon the payment of such costs and damages as may be incurred or
suffered by any party who may be found to have been wrongfully enjoined or
restrained thereby.
November 3, 1920.
EDMUND WADDILL, Jr.,
United States District Judge.
Indorsed: District Court U. S. So. Dist. W. Va. Filed this 27th day of
January, 1921.
ALBERT V. FITZWATER, Clerk.

WEST VIRGINIA:
At a circuit court, continued and held for the county of Mercer, at the court-
house thereof, on Tuesday, the 16th day of August, 1921.
Present: Hon. Isaiah C. Herndon, judge. Algonquin Coal Co. et al., plaintiff
in chancery, v. John L. Lewis president of the United Mine Workers of America
et al., defendants.
This cause came on again this day to be further heard upon all of the plead-
ings and papers heretofore filed herein and decrees and orders hereinbefore
entered, and upon the depositions of witnesses duly taken and filed herein in
behalf of the plaintiff, and was argued by counsel.
And the court, after maturely considering the demurrer of the defendants
interposed to the plaintiffs' bill, doth overrule the same; and the court being
of op nion that the plaintiffs are entitled to the relief prayed for in their
bill, it is therefore adjudged, ordered, and decreed that the temporary injunc-
tion awarded herein on the 16th day of September, 1920, by W. N. Miller,
G. W. Lunch, and Harold A. Ritz, judges of the Supreme Court of Appeals of
this State, be, and the same is hereby, made perpetual, and that each and all
of the defendants herein, their agents, employees, servants, and attorneys, ex-
cept the defendants John L. Lewis, president of the United Mine Workers of
America, and William Green, secretary and treasurer of the Un ted Mine
Workers of America, be, and they are hereby, perpetually enjoined, restrained,
and inhibited from in anywise molesting or interfering with or attempting to
molest or interfere with the employees of the plaintiffs in the performance and
fulfillment of their contracts of service with the plaintiffs; and from com-
pelling or inducing, by violence, threats, intimidation, abusive or violent lan-
guage or persuasion, the employees of the plaintiff, or either of them, to break
their contracts of service with the plaintiff; and from in anywise interfering
with the employees of the plaintiffs, or either of them, in the full performance
of their contracts of service with the plaintiff; and from inducing or attempt-
ing to induce, by persuasion, threats, intimidation, or abusive or violent lan-
guage, the employees of the plaintiff, or either of them, so long as they are
under contract of employment with the plaintiffs, to join the United Mine
Workers of America; and from entering upon the grounds and premises of the
plaintiffs, or their mines, for the purpose of interfering with the employees of
the plaintiffs, in the performance of their said contracts of service with the
plaint ffs, or in an attempt to persuade or coerce the said employees to breach
their contracts of service with the plaintiffs, or to persuade them to join the
United Mine Workers of America, in violation of their contracts with the
plaintiffs.
And it is further adjudged, ordered, and decreed that the plaintiffs do recover
of and from each and all of the defendents herein, except John L. Lewis, presi-
dent of the United Mine Workers of America, and William Green, secretary and
treasurer of the United Mine Workers of America, their costs in and about the
prosecution of their suit in that behalf expended, including an attorney's fee
of $20.

This is a suit of civil nature in equity, and is between citizens of different
States and the amount in controversy herein exceeds the sum of $3,000, ex-
clusive of interest and costs; and arises around the Constitution anl laws of
the United States in this, to wit, this suit necessarily presents for decision the
proper construction and application of certain provisions of the act of Congress
commonly known as the Sherman antitrust law, and of the act of Congress
approved October 15, 1914, and commonly known as the Clayton Act.
The plaintiff says that it brings this suit for and on behalf of itself and on
behalf of 62 coal mining companies and operations having their mining plants
located in what is known as the Thacker or Williamson district on the Norfolk
& Western Railroad in Mingo County, W. Va., and Pike County, Ky.; that the
interests of all of said 62 companies in this suit is identical with that of the
plaintiff, and the questions involved in this proceeding are all of common and
general interest with the plaintiff and these 62 companies, and they constitute
a class so numerous that it is impracticable to bring them all before the court,
and therefore the plaintiff sues for all of them; that the interest of all the
defendants in this suit is the same and is identical with the interest of all the
coal mining companies operating mines in the State of Indiana, and the actions
and conduct of all of said companies are precisely the same as hereinafter
complained of the defendant companies, and the relief sought against the last-
named companies is the same as will be asked against each of all the othe
companies; and the questions involved in this proceeding are of common and
general interest to all of said companies, which constitute a class so numerous
as to make it impracticable to bring them all before the court.
That the defendants, John L. Lewis, president, and William Green, secretary-
treasurer of the international organization of the United Mine Workers of
America, as such have charge and control of all the said districts and of all
the mine workers belonging to said association in the United States and
Canada, including those men who work at the mines of the defendant com-
panies hereinabove referred to, and that there are about 6,000 workers at the
mines of the said defendant companies, who are members of said association and
subject to its rules and control, and that the questions involved in this pro-
ceeding against said organization and its officials are the same and identical in
interest with the interests of each of said 6,000 workers, and they constitute a
class so sumerous as to make it impracticable to bring them all before the
court; and that the actions and conduct of said workers and the remedies
sought against all and each of said workers are the same.

I.
(1) That said corporation was at the time of institution of this suit, and
still is, a corporation duly chartered, organized, and doing business under and
by virtue of the laws of the State of Virginia, and is a resident and citizen of
said State; that the defendants are nonresidents and citizens of the State
of Virginia, but are citizens of the State of Indiana, residing at Indianapolis
in said State, and of States other than the State of Virginia.
(2) That while said plaintiff is chartered, organized, and doing business
under the laws of the State of Virginia, and is a citizen of that State, it is
duly licensed to do business in the States of West Virginia and Kentucky; that
the plaintiff, Borderland Coal Corporation, is the owner of a certain leasehold
on a large boundary of coal lands, approximately 1,900 acres, situate in Pike
County, Ky., just across Tug River, which is the State line. from Mingo
County, W. Va., and is engaged in the mining of coal from said land, which
coal is taken across said Tug River to the Norfolk & Western Railroad in
Mingo County, W. Va., and there loaded in the railroad cars, and is further
engaged in the shipping of said coal from said lands in interstate commerce
to different States of the Union other than Kentucky and West Virginia, and
to Canada; that said company has been engaged in the said business of mining
coal and in the said business of shipping coal in interstate commerce as afore-
said for a number of years prior to the institution of this suit and prior to the
labor difficulties hereinafter more specifically set out, and has conducted its
said business continuously from the time of the beginning thereof, and that it
annually produces a large tonnage of coal, shipped in interstate commerce
as aforesaid, and is now engaged in said business.
(3) That practically the entire output of the mine of said plaintiff has
always been sold, shipped, and delivered to points outside of the States of West
Virginia and Kentucky, and the larger part of it to points in Illinois, Indiana,
Ohio, Michigan, and the Northwest, and in the territory generally known as
central competitive field, and in Canada.
(4) That the plaintiff has expended a large sum of money in the construc-
tion of its mining plant and equipping the same as was necessary in order to
mine and ship its coal as aforesaid.
(5) That prior to the labor difficulties hereinafter mentioned and set forth
the said plaintiff had entered into various contracts with customers residing in
said States above mentioned and in Canada for the delivery to them of speci-
fied amounts of coal, which said contracts said plaintiff was engaged in filling
at the time said labor difficulties occurred; that the plaintiff, Borderland Coal
Corporation, is still engaged in filling said contracts.
(6) That the United Mine Workers of America is an unincorporated asso-
ciation of mine workers engaged in and about the work of mining and ship-
ping coal in and from different mines throughout the United States, its head-
quarters being located in the city of Indianapolis, in the State of Indiana;
that the said association is subdivided into about 30 districts and subdistricts
and numerous local unions are located therein, each district having jurisdiction
over the local unions within its territory; that each member of each local
union is a member of the United Mine Workers of America and subject to
the orders of said international association and subject to the rules laid down
in its constitution and by-laws as well as to the constitution and by-laws of
the various districts, subdistricts, and local unions having jurisdiction over
them respectively; that each of the district branches or local unions which
are parts of the international organization of the United Mine Workers of
America is created by said United Mine Workers of America to carry out the
objects, purposes, and business of said international organization, and more
particularly to act with, for, and under said international organization in
carrying out the unlawful acts hereinafter set forth; that the United Mine
Workers of America, District 17, is one of the said district branches of the
United Mine Workers of America, and has jurisdiction over all union mines
and union miners in the counties of Mercer, McDowell, Mingo, Wayne, Boone,
Logan, and Kanawha, as well as the Fairmont section in West Virginia, and
that District 29 of said United Mine Workers of America has jurisdiction over
all of the union mines and union miners in the remainder of West Virginia;
that the United Mine Workers of America divides all coal mines in the several
States of the United States into two classes, one class being called "union
or "organized" mines, because they are operated under agreements with the
United Mine Workers of America, or one of its district branches, to employ

(7) That the plaintiff has always operated its mine as a nonunion mine;
that is to say, it has never in any manner recognized said United Mine Workers
of America or contracted or dealt with it in any manner whatsoever, but on the
contrary has always employed only such men as were not members of, or affili-
ated with, said United Mine Workers of America, and has entered into individ-
ual contracts with its said employees as to wages, working conditions, and
terms of employment generally with full knowledge upon the part of said em-
ployees that only nonunion men were employed in and about its mine by the
plaintiff, and that whenever any employee joined or became affiliated with said
United Mine Workers of America his employment was thereby terminated, to
all of which all of the employees of said plaintiff have at all times fully agreed;
that this policy of the plaintiff to employ in and about its mines only men who
were not members of said United Mine Workers of America was adopted by
reason of the firm conviction that said policy operates to the best interests of
both the employer and the employees, and the experience by the plaintiff in so
operating its mines has fully justified the correctness and soundness of this
policy, in that it has resulted in continuous and productive work on the part of
the employees and in entire satisfaction on the part of the employees as to
wages, housing, working conditions, and other things affecting their interests,
and neither the plaintiff on the one hand nor its employees on the other have
been disturbed and annoyed or subjected to loss of production or of time by
strikes or labor troubles of any kind; that during the whole of the time this
plaintiff has been operating its mine and shipping coal, as above stated, there
has been no interruption of work and no dissatisfaction on the part of its em-
ployees until the United Mine Workers of America undertook to compel the
plaintiff to unionize its mine and to compel its employees to join said union;
that during the whole of the period aforesaid the employees of this plaintiff
have been able to earn and have earned more money per day and per month
than miners s'milarly employed in what is known as union fields have been
able to earn.
(8) That plaintiff's said mine is located in what is known as the Thacker or
Williamson coal field, and all of the other coal mines in that field are also oper-
ated as nonunion m´nes, just as in the mine of the plaintiff; that there are also
in the State of West Virginia other nonunion fields, which are what is known
as the Logan coal fields, Pocahontas coal field, Tug River coal field, and the

of West Virgin a along the Norfolk & Western Railroad, in the North and North-
west, and in said central competitive field, are union or organized mines.
(9) That is and the other coal-mining companies in said Thacker or William-
son coal field have repeatedly and consistently refused to have anything to do
with the United Mine Workers of America, or any organizers or representatives
of sa'd organization, and have made known to them and to each of them that
they and each of them have always operated their mines as nonunion and
intend to continue to so operate their mines, as they have the right to do, and

ference by said United Mine Workers of America, its subordinate organizations,

service and to prevent others from working for the plaintiff, all with the pro-

bination and conspiracy formed in the year 1898, and now existing between the
United Mine Workers of America and the coal operators of said central com-
petitive field, which will be hereinafter more fully set out.

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
II.
Plaintiff further says that it is advised and so believes and charges:
(1) That in order to properly understand and appreciate the reasons for and
the effect of the conspiracy above mentioned it is necessary to set forth some
facts in the history of the said United Mine Workers of America, as follows:
The United Mine Workers of America was organized about 1890 and was
apparently intended to be a trade organization, but its membership was small
at that time and did not increase materially for a number of years; that in the
year 1890 and for some years thereafter the coal industry in West Virginia
was in its infancy, and the coal produced in said State, by reason of the com-
paratively small amount thereof, did not seriously interfere with the sale of
coal produced in said central competitive field, but from the year 1890 to the
year 1898 the production of coal in West Virginia steadily and rapidly in-
creased; that this West Virginia coal was shipped and sold in the markets in
the United States and Canada in interstate commerce, and a large portion
thereof was sold in competition with the coals produced in said central com-
petitive field; said competition became year by year more and more sharp and
more and more serious to the coal operators in the said central competitive
field, by reason of the fact that the West Virginia coal was produced under
more favorable mining conditions and that the production thereof was more
regular, because it had not been disturbed by any labor conflicts, troubles,
or agitations; that by reason of said increase in production of West Virginia
coal under conditions above set forth it began to supplant and did supplant to
some extent the coals produced in said central competitive field in their common
markets.
(2) That under these competitive conditions a joint conference was held in
1918 between the officials and representatives of the United Mine Workers of
America, on the one part, and the coal operators of said central competitive
field, on the other part, in the city of Chicago, at which time and place the ef-
fect of said West Virginia competition was fully discussed; and in order to
destroy said competition and to bar West Virginia coal from said central com-
petitive field an unlawful combination and conspiracy was entered into be-
tween the United Mine Workers of America and the said coal operators of
said central competitive field, by the terms of which it was intended, under-
stood, and agreed, among other things, that the said coal operators of said
central competitive field would grant, and did grant, to said United Mine
Workers of America certain demands made by that organization, while on
the other hand said United Mine Workers of America agreed to unionize or
organize the West Virginia coal fields for the purpose of thereby controlling the
production of coal and the employment of labor in the coal mines in West
Virginia, and especially to increase the cost of production of coal in West Vir-
ginia to such an extent that it could no longer compete with the coal produced
in said central competitive field; that pursuant to the terms of said conspiracy
and to make the same effective the said coal operators of said central com-
petitive field agreed to employ in and about their mines no one not a member
of said United Mine Workers of America, and further agreed to collect from
their employees members of that organization, through and on their pay rolls,
all dues and assessments, known as the "check off," levied or imposed by the
officials of said United Mine Workers of America upon its members.
(3) That since the year 1898 it has been the primary and avowed purpose
of the said United Mine Workers of America to secure the control of and to
operate a monopoly of all labor in and about the coal mines by compelling all
persons working in and about said mines in the United States and Canada to
become members of that organization and to abide by its rules and regulations
and become obedient to it in all matters affecting mine labor and the terms
and conditions of the employment of the coal industry in the United States
and the Dominion of Canada; that inasmuch as the labor cost in the coal
industry is from 75 to 90 per cent of the production cost of coal, the United'
Mine Workers of America, in the event it succeeds in carrying out its objects,

(4) That the objects and aims of the United Mine Workers of America
appear from its constitution and by-laws and the oath which its members
are required to take; that the constitution and by-laws provide:
"First. To unite in one organization, regardless of creed, color, or nationality,
all workmen eligible for membership employed in or around coal mines, coal
washers, and coke ovens in the American Continent.
"Second. To increase the wages and improve the conditions of employment
of our members by legislation, conciliation, and joint agreements or strikes.
* * *
"Eighth. To increase by legislative enactment laws protecting the limbs and
lives of our members, establishing their rights to organize, prohibiting the
use of deception to secure strike breakers, preventing the employment of pri-
vately armed guards during labor disputes, and such other legislation as will
be beneficial to the members of our craft.
"ARTICLE III.
"1. All district, subdistrict, and local unions must be chartered by and shall
be under the jurisdiction of and subject to the laws and rulings of the inter-
national union.
"2. In all questions of dispute, appeals, and grievances affecting their mem-
bers (unless restricted by joint agreement) the decision of the international
executive board shall be final and binding until reversed by the international
convention.
"ARTICLE VI.
"SEC. 3. If, in the judgment of the officers of the international district or
subdistrict union, any local union has taken any action opposed to the interest
of the United Mine Workers or the International Union, or the district or
subdistrict union having jurisdiction over the local union, they shall have the
right to reverse the action of the local union."
The oath which its members are required to take is as follows:
"I do sincerely promise, of my own free will, to abide by the laws of this
union; to bear true allegiance to, and keep inviolate, the principles of the
United Mine Workers of America; never to discriminate against a fellow
workman on account of creed, color, or nationality; to defend freedom of
thought, whether expressed by tongue or pen; to defend on all occasions, and
to the extent of my ability, the members of our organization.
"That I will not reveal to any employer or boss the name of anyone
member of our union; that I will assist all members of our organization to ob-
tain the highest wages possible for their work; that I will not accept a
brother's job who is idle for advancing the interests of the union; and as the
mine workers of the entire country are competitors in the labor world, I
promise to cease work at any time I am called upon by the organization to do so.
"And I further promise to help and assist all brothers in adversity, and to
have all mine workers join our union, that we may all be able to enjoy the
fruits of our labor; that I will never knowingly wrong a brother, or see him
wronged, if I can prevent it.
"To all this I pledge my honor to observe and keep as long as life remains,
or until I am absolved by the United Mine Workers of America."

At the joint conference held between said operators and said officials of the
United Mine Workers, held in the city of Pittsburgh, Pa., January 17-24, 1899,
the following statements were made:
Mr. Mitchell, president of the National Association of the United Mine Work-
ers of America, said:
"I know of no breach of faith of the miners since the last convention ad-
journed in West Virginia. It is true that our organization has not made as
much progress as we might desire, but I want to say to the operators that an
effort has been made during the past year to curtail the production of West
Virginia coal by attempting to prevent its sale on the market."
Further, in reply to Mr. Robbins, Mr. Mitchell denied the proposition that
there were on more than 350 members in the miners' union in West Virginia.
Mr. G. N. Trear, of Illinois, speaking for the operators in the joint conference,
said:
"The West Virginia coal, gentlemen, is really the whole question, and is the
key to everything that must be considered by this convention. It affects the
States unequally, it is true, but it affects them all. West Virginia coal goes
by lake to the Northeast and meets us there; and it is increasing in the markets
into which we go, and have gone, every day in the week, every week in the
month, and every month in the year. The next president of the miners' organi-
zation has asked us to accept his statement that, through a boycott of the West
Virginia coal, they have made, or are making, some progress toward the cor-
rection of that condition. Gentlemen, I live in Chicago, where the West Virginia
coal reaches us by lake and by rail. It has not been more than one or two years
since we were accustomed to seeing long lines of loaded wagons with Indiana
block coal, Hocking or Jackson coal, or southern coal passing through our
streets to the dwellings which use coal for fuel. Within the last year these
wagons are carrying signs of the West Virginia coal-Pocahontas, New River
smokeless, and all the other smokeless coals that are mined in the mountains of
West Virginia; and to-day you will see three or four, or more than four, wagons
of West Virginia coal to every one of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois put together, on
the streets of Chicago."
Mr. Ratchford, whose office of president of the mine workers' organization had
just expired, said:
"Mr. Chairman, in our agreement of one year ago we promised to the opera-
tors who met with us that we would afford them all possible protection against the
competition of unorganized fields. From the remarks of some of the delegates
to-day and yesterday, I take it that the operators are of the opinion that such
protection was not given, and, in fact, that no effort was made to give it. To
disprove those assertions, I can give you no better illustration than this, that
when we met you one year ago we had 5 States represented; when we meet
you to-day we have 13 represented:
"Furthermore, a great deal of importance has been attached to the condition
of West Virginia. I want to make a proposition here--that the interests of the
West Virginia miners, by reason of the efforts of our organization, have been
hampered and injured more within the past year than in any year since they
have been operating in the State of West Virginia. It is true, gentlemen, that
we did not follow the old line of trying to organize miners during the summer,
for the reason that we saw it was useless expenditure, and, in fact, a waste of
money."
Mr. L. H. Chapman, operator from Ohio, said:
"What were the conditions last year when we were entering into the agree-
ment at Chicago, and what were the inducements that led the operators
of the four competitive States to enter into that agreement? What promises
and pledges were made on behalf of you gentlemen who are on my right
and your representatives? It was as much a part of that agreement that
was made at Chicago, although not incorporated in the written instrument

to be put upon a competitive basis with that field. When it was suggested
in the convention that that should be incorporated into the agreement the

To the above statement of Mr. Chapman, Mr. Ratchford replied:

Gentlemen, this is not correct. The money referred to by our friend, I

Again, Mr. Robbins, of Pennsylvania, in the course of his remarks said:

for wage scales for these four States."

At another of said joint conferences, held in the city of Cincinnati in 1910,
Mr. Maurer, coal operator from Ohio, said:
“The chief evil was the fact that districts which did not recognize United
Mine Workers and had no agreements with them, produced coal much more
cheaply than those districts which sustained contractual relations with that
organization.
"In order to correct these most harmful conditions, a joint convention of
operators and miners of western Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, at
the solicitation of the miners' officials, was called to meet at Chicago, 1898.
At this convention an interstate joint agreement was established. The granting
of the eight-hour day by the operators, after making these numerous other im-
portant concessions, was with distinct understanding and explicit promise of
the miners to give to the operators of the four contracting States adequate pro-
tection against the competition of the unorganized fields. From year to year
they have been called upon to fulfill that promise. The operators, parties to
that agreement, at the time of its execution, felt that it was absolutely neces-
sary to the safety of their investments that they be protected from the encroach-
ments upon them by the competition of the unorganized fields.
"It is evident to any candid observer that such unfair conditions should not
be imposed upon the operators and miners of the unionized territory. That the
interests of operators and miners are mutual in every respect does not admit
of controversy. Each is equally concerned in rescuing this business from its
present peril.
"Finally we ask for the fulfillment of the pledge of 1898, upon which we
made to the miners so many important and costly concessions. Though that
promise has not been kept, we have continued for 12 years to make additional
concessions by increasing the mining price from 66 cents agreed upon at that
time to 90 cents, and in other respects conceding demands without any compen-
sating concessions upon the part of the miners, until we now find ourselves at
the limit of financial safety. The operators can make no further concessions.
It is now, in our view, not only to the interest of the miners, but their duty as
well, to do their share to meet these conditions.
"It has been set forth as the controlling reason for an increased price for
mining that the cost of living has increased during the past few years. Is it
now fair, equitable, or reasonable to believe that by making conditions in all
competing districts equal, the districts which are parties to this agreement will
benefit by a larger number of days' employment, and thus the earning capacity
of the miners of our district be largely increased?
"We believe this to be a true statement of facts, and therefore call upon
you to relieve us as well as yourselves from the unfortunate situation in which
we now find ourselves, due to the failure of the miners' organization to keep the
faith pledged at Chicago in 1898.
"We therefore insist that your organization place the districts, parties to
this agreement, on the same relative basis as the unorganized districts with which
we are compelled to compete."
Mr. Green, an official of the United Mine Workers' organization, replied
thereto, as follows:
"Our friend, Mr. Maurer, in the well prepared statement he has submitted
to this conversation, referred to an obligation he claims was assumed by the
United Mine Workers of America in the meeting at Chicago, 1898. Mr. Chair-

At another such joint conference, held at Cleveland, Ohio, in the year 1912,
Mr. Chapman, Ohio operator said:
"When we met at Chicago in 1898, and reestablished the interstate move-
ment, the competition from nonunion fields was the element, gentlemen, that
entered into negotiations in the adoption of the scale that was made there. It
was agreed to by both sides, and the question also of the ability of the miner
to earn a fair day's wage for the labor he performed entered into it. At that
time the miners were receiving 56 cents per ton for producing coal. I made
motions in that convention that increased the day wage scale.
*
*
"It was understood in that convention, although it was not placed in the
agreement, that the miners of the competitive field of the four States were to
bring the nonunion fields up to the price paid for mining in those States, and
unless they secured the adoption of an 8-hour day at the next convention the
competitive field was to be relieved of these burdens. That was not in the
agreement. Unfortunately, gentlemen, the proceedings of that convention were
not published. If they were published, it would be found that the president of
the United Mine Workers and the gentlemen who aided and assisted him
in bringing about the results there agreed that they should be relieved.
** And the question of the prices of coal and the competition that
existed were the sole questions that entered into the discussion there.
The State from which the keenest competition comes has increased its produc-
tion 35 per cent, or 25 per cent annually for the 14 years; and Ohio, the State
that is the mother of the organization, the State whose operators have ever
been loyal to the organization, has increased barely 10 per cent a year. This
is the record of our State, while this one State (West Virginia) has increased
annually for the 14 years, taking the average, 25 per cent, and more than double
the output of Ohio coal,
and if the nonunion fields continue to in-
crease as they have been doing, there will be no coal interests remaining in
Ohio. In some districts of Ohio half the miners have left and gone to the
nonunion fields, and more are going. More are going."

At the same meeting the president of the United Mine Workers, Mr. White,
said:
"We are as anxious to establish the organization in West Virginia fields and
the other nonunion fields as the gentlemen on the other side of the house are
to have us do so. As has been pointed out times without number, West Vir-
ginia has no markets within the State, and if it were thoroughly organized of
necessity it would have to find markets outside of the confines of its own
Commonwealth. Nature has favored the little mountain State with an inex-
haustible vein of coal of high quality and good mining conditions; but the
operators there have been successful in defeating the aims and purposes of the
United Mine Workers to a large extent, although no one can deny that under
the various administrations of the organization every effort has been put forth
to try to break down the conditions, competitive conditions, that are complained
of here by the other side."

CHICAGO, January 28.
Contract between the operators of the central competitive field and the United
Mine Workers of America.
The following agreements, made and entered into in joint interstate con-
vention in this city (Chicago, Ill.), January 26, 1898, by and between the
operators and miners of Illinois, Indiana. Ohio, and western Pennsylvania,
known as the Pittsburgh thin-vein district, witnesseth:
First. That an equal price for mining screened lump coal shall hereafter
form a base in all the districts above named, excepting the State of Illinois
and the black-coal district of Indiana, to pay 10 cents per ton over that of
Hocking Valley, western Pennsylvania, and Indiana bituminous districts, and
that the price of pick run-of-mine coal in Hocking Valley and western Penn-
sylvania shall be determined by the actual percentage of screenings passing
through such screen as is hereinafter provided, it being understood and agreed
that screened or run-of-mine coal be mined and paid for on the above
basis at the option of the operators, according to market requirements, and
the operators of Indiana bituminous shall also have like option of mining and
paying for run-of-mine and screened coal.
Second. That the screen hereby adopted for the State of Ohio, western
Pennsylvania, and the bituminous district of Indiana shall be uniform in
size, 6 feet wide by 12 fet long, built of flat or Akron-shaped bars of not
less than five eighths of an inch surface, with 1-1.4 inches between bars, free


===== [扫描序号 785] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
771
from obstruction, and that such screen shall rest upon a sufficient number
bearings to hold the bars in proper position.
Third. That the block-coal district of Indiana may continue the use of the
diamond screens of present size and pattern with the privilege of run-of-mine
coal, the mining price of which shall be determined by the actual screenings;
and that the State of Illinois shall be absolutely upon a run-of-mine system
and shall be paid for on that basis.
Fourth. That an advance of 10 cents per ton of 2,000 pounds for pick-mined
screened coal shall take effect in western Pennsylvania, Hocking Valley, and
the Indiana bituminous district of Indiana on April 1, 1898; and that Grape
Creek, Ill., and the bituminous district of Indiana shall pay 40 cents per ton
run-of-mine coal from and after same date, based upon 66 cents per ton screened
coal in Ohio, wetsern Pennsylvania, and the Indiana bituminous district, the
same to continue in force until the expiration of this contract.
Fifth. That on and after April 1, 1898, the eight-hour work day with eight
hours pay, consisting of six days per week, shall be in effect in all of the dis-

in any of the States or districts, both as to prices or conditions, shall be re-
ferred to the State or districts affected for adjustment.
Sixth. That the same relative prices and conditions between machine and

Seventh. That present prices for pick and machine mining and all classes of
day labor shall be maintained in the competitive States and districts until
April 1, 1898.

tract, do hereby further agree to afford all possible protection to the trade and
to the other parties hereto against any unfair competition resulting from the
failure to maintain scale rates.
Ninth. That this contract shall remain in full force and effect from April 1,
1898, to April 1, 1899, and that our next annual interstate convention shall con-
vene in the city of Pittsburgh on the third Tuesday of January, 1899.

constabulary of West Virginia into said district.
That said constabulary was not sufficiently strong to maintain peace and

ers' organization continued to become so serious that the governor of said State
was compelled to call on two occasions in 1920 for Federal soldiers, who were
first sent to the said district on August 29, 1920, to preserve order, life, and
property, where they remained for a considerable space of time, until the 4th

said strike so declared there were employed about the coal mines of said dis-
trict about 2,500 employees, nearly all of whom, by means of the unlawful acts
aforesaid, for a time ceased work; that a majority of said employees who thus
remained away from work did so because of fear, caused by said unlawful acts
of violence; and that as soon as the soldiers of the United States Army took
charge of said district the former employees of said companies began to resume
their former employment, and within a short time thereafter there were working

these facts, well known to him and the other officials of the United Mine Work-
