FROM BARNES CODE OF WEST VIRGINIA, 1918.
SEC. 34 (p. 183). Intimidation of workmen; lawful associations.-Nor shall
any person or persons, or combination of persons, by force, threats, menaces, or
intimidation of any kind, prevent or attempt to prevent from working in or
about any mine, any person or person who have the lawful right to work in or
about the same, and who desire so to work; but this provision shall not be so
construed as to prevent any two or more persons from associating together
under the name of knights of labor, or any other name they may desire, for any
lawful purpose, or for using moral suation or lawful argument to induce any one
not to work in and about any mine. Any person or persons who shall violate
the provisions of this section shall, upon conviction, be fined not less than fifty
nor more than five hundred dollars, or be imprisoned in the county jail not less
than ten nor more than ninety days, in the discretion of the court. (Acts 1887,
c. 50; 1890, c. 9; 1907, c. 78; 1915, c. 10, sec. 42.)
SEC. 11 (p. 113c). Deputies; appointment; oath; powers, watchmen.-The
clerk of any court may, with the consent of such court, or the clerk of the supreme
court of appeals or of a circuit, may, with the consent of the judge or judges
thereof in vacation, appoint any person his deputy. And the clerk of the county
court of any county, in which now exists a tribunal for police and fiscal pur-
poses, established under the thirty-fourth section of the eighth article of the con-
stitution of this State, may appoint any person his deputy. A sheriff, surveyor of
lands, or assessor, may, with the consent of the county court, appoint any person
his deputy. Such consent shall, in every case, be entered of record, and such ap-
pointment by the clerk of the county court in a county where now exists such tri-
bunal as aforesaid, shall be entered of record. Every deputy so appointed shall
take the same oath his principal is required to take, and may during his continu-
ance in office discharge and perform any of the official duties of his principal, and
any default or misfeasance in office of such deputy shall be deemed a breach
of the conditions of the official bond of his principal. And when in the opinion
of the circuit court the public interest require it, a sheriff may, with the consent
of the said circuit court, appoint any person his deputy.
It shall not be lawful for any of the aforesaid officers of this State to appoint
any deputy or deputies to act as, or perform any duties in the capacity of guards
or watchmen for any private individual, firm, or corporation, nor shall the
above-named officers be authorized to appoint any person or persons as deputy
or deputies to act for or to represent, in any capacity, as officers of the law.
any individual person, firm, or corporation. (Acts 1865, pp. 16, 156; 1864;
p. 7; 1872-73, c. 185; 1882, c. 42; 1885, c. 18; 1913, c. 29.)
SEC. 78 (p. 197). Same; sales of goods to employees. From and after the
passage of this act it shall be unlawful for any person, firm, company, corpora-
tion, or association engaged in mining or manufacturing, either or both as afore-
said, and who shall likewise be interested directly or indirectly in merchandising,
as owner or otherwise, in any money, per cent profit, or commission arising from
the sale of any such merchandise, their clerks, servants, officers, or agents, to
knowingly and willfully sell or cause to be sold to any employee any goods, mer-
chandise, or supplies whatsoever for a greater per cent of profit than mer-
chandise or supplies of like character, kind, quality, and quantity are so sold to
other customers buying for cash and not employed by them, and shall any
person or member of any firm, company, corporation, or association, his or their
clerk, agent, or servant, violate this section, then and in that case such person,
firm, company, corporation, or association shall collect for such merchandise and


===== [扫描序号 797] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
783
supplies only the price for which like merchandise and supplies are sold by them
to such other customers as aforesaid buying for cash; and, moreover, shall be
guilty of a misdemeanor, and on conviction thereof shall be fined not exceeding
$100 nor less than $25. (Acts 1887, c. 63, sec. 4.)
SEC. 58 (p. 193). Same; when check-weighman unnecessary; offenses.-Where
the weighman is mutually selected by the consent of a majority of the miners
working in any mine and the operator or agent of such company, it shall not be
considered necessary to employ said check-weighman, but at any time that either
of the said said parties to said agreement should become dissatisfied with said
weighman they may dismiss him on 10 days' notice or the miners may employ a
check-weighman. Any corporation, company, or person violating any of the
provisions of this act shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and upon conviction
thereof shall be fined for each and every offense not less than ten nor more than
two hundred dollars. It shall be the duty of every court in each county in which
any such coal mine is operated and in which a grand jury is impaneled, to give
this act in charge of the grand jury. (Acts 1901, c. 20, sec. 4.)
SEC. 50 (p. 193). Same; weighman.-Every such corporation, company, or
person shall employ a weighman, and the miners working in any such coal mine
may employ another such weighman, and the two so employed shall supervise
the weighing of each car while empty and the weighing of the same when loaded
with coal so paid for by weight, and the measuring of the number of bushels
therein, when necessary, so paid for by measure. But if the miners fail to
employ such weighman, then the person so employed by such corporation, com-
pany, or person shall perform that duty. Each of the persons so employed,
before entering upon the discharge of the duties of his employment, shall take
and subscribe an oath or affirmation that he will honestly and impartially do and
perform the duties of his employment and do equal and exact justice between
the employers and employees interested in the matter of his employment, to the
best of his judgment, skill, and ability. (Acts 1891, c. 82, sec. 4.)
SEC. 53 (p. 192). Same; maines subject to act.-This act shall not apply to
any corporation, company, or person owning or operating a coal mine in which
less than 10 miners are employed. (Acts 1891, ch. 82, sec. 7.)
SEC. 49 (p. 191). Same; weighing in car before screening.--All coal so mined
and paid for by weight shall be weighed in the car in which it is removed from
the mine before it is screened, and shall be paid for according to the weight so
ascertained, at such price per ton as may be agreed upon by such owner or oper-
ator and the miners who mined the same. And coal mined and paid for by
measure shall be paid for according to the number of bushels marked upon each
car in which it is removed from the mine, and before it is screened and the price
paid for each bushel so ascertained shall be such as may be agreed on a afore-
said. (Acts 1891, ch. 82, sec. 3.)
SEC. 34. Intimidation of workmen; lawful associations.-Nor shall any person
or persons or combination of persons, by force, threats, menaces, or intimidation
of any kind, prevent or attempt to prevent from working in or about any mine,
any person or persons who have the lawful right to work in or about the same,
and who desires so to work; but this provision shall not be so construed as to
prevent any two or more persons from associations together under the name of
Knights of Labor, or any other name they mad desire, for any lawful purpose,
or for using moral suasion or lawful argument to induce anyone not to work
in and about the mine. Any person or persons who shall violate the provisions of
this section shall, upon conviction, be fined not less than $50 nor mone than
$500, or to be imprisoned in the county jail not less than 10 days nor more than
90 days, in the discretion of the court. (Acts 1887, ch. 50; 1890, ch. 9; 1907, ch.
78; 1915, ch. 10, sec. 42.)
SEC. 48. Same; cars.-Each car used by any such corporation, company, or
person in removing coal from any coal mine shall be numbered by consecutive
numbers plainly marked, and placed and kept thereon so long as such car is so
used, and if the coal from such mine is mined and the miners are paid accord-
ing to the weight thereof for mining the same, every such car so used shall be
weighed upon such tested scales, and the weight thereof shall be plainly marked
and placed thereon as long as such car shall be used as aforesaid. If the coal
at any such mine is mined, and the miners thereof are paid for mining the same
by measure, the number of bushels of coal such car will hold when loaded to its
capacity, shall also be plainly marked and placed and kept thereon as long as
such car is so used as aforesaid, and no car shall be used for the purposes afore-
said after 90 days from the time this act takes effect until the provisions of this
section are complied with. (Acts 1891, ch. 82, sec. 2.)


===== [扫描序号 798] =====
784
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
SEC. 47 (p. 191). Weighing and measuring coal; appliances.-It shall be the
duty of every corporation, company, or person engaged in the business of mining
and selling coal by weight or measure, to procure and constantly keep on hand at
the proper place the necessary scales and measures and whatever else may be
necessary to correctly weigh and measure the coal as mined by such corporation,
company, or person.
SEC. 55 (p. 192). Weighing and measuring products where wages depend upon
production; checkweighman.-Where the amount of wages paid to any of the
persons employed in any manufacturing, mining, or otherwise public enterprise
employing labor depend upon the amount produced by weight or measure the
persons so employed may, at their own cost, station or appoint at each place
for the weighing or measuring of the products of their labor a checkweighman
or measurer, who shall in all cases be appointed by a majority ballot of the
workmen employed at the works where he is appointed to act as such check-
weighman or measurer. (Acts 1901, ch. 20, sec. 1.)

Mr. HOUSTON. I think that is all.

The CHAIRMAN. How much time do you want for cross-examination?

Mr. HOUSTON. Oh, I would estimate just roughly about 60 per cent of the
miners of the entire State belong to the union. About 53 000 in actual numbers.
Mr. BELCHER. I will ask you if it is not true that in the organized districts

Mr. HOUSTON. The closed shop does not obtain?
Mr. BELCHER. Does obtain, I say.
Mr. HOUSTON. Generally that is true. I don't know of any exceptions to it.
Mr. BELCHER. The check-off provision is in all contracts executed between
the mine workers' organization of district 17 and the operators of the organized
fields of West Virginia, isn't it?
Mr. HOUSTON. I think so. I would not say absolutely. I think so.
Mr. BELCHER. That check-off provision provides that all men who are eligible
to membership in the United Mine Workers' organization shall pay dues and

(The document referred to is here printed in full, as follows:)
SEPTEMBER 20, 1921.
To all local unions throughout District 17, U. M. W. of A., greetings:
I am submitting a few suggestions which, I think, the rank and file should
know, and hoping that you will give them due consideration and then take
action on same in the way which will tend to conserve the best interest of the
United Mine Workers of America, and our district in particular.
SUGGESTIONS.
It is significant that Mother Jones had a star-chamber session with Maj.
Davis, Capt. Brockus, Sheriff Vinson, and the entire official staff of Mingo
County just a few days before the indictments were returned against Keeney
and Mooney. It is significant that she had a dozen or more secret conferences
with Gov. Morgan before and after going into Mingo County. Why has she
spent most all of her time in West Virginia since 1917? There was never any
organization in West Virginia until the present administration was elected,
despite the 20 years spent in this State by Mother Jones; and when the secession
movement was on Mother Jones went into Cabin Creek and tried to get
Keeney, Dwyer, and their crowd to lay down, yet she boasts from the rostrum
that she cleaned up West Virginia. If she did clean up West Virginia, why is
she now conniving with the same crowd of coal operators that were forced out
of office in 1916 to frame Keeney, Mooney, Levinder, and Workman and send
them to the penitentiary?


===== [扫描序号 814] =====
800
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Mother Jones reported to Gov. Morgan that Keeney and Mooney prevented the
men from going home after she had secured a vote from them to return to their
homes. This was not the case. She also reported to Gov. Morgan that Keeney
and Mooney addressed the miners at Lens Creek after she left. This is abso-
lutely untrue. Neither of these men said anything to the miners about going to
their destination. Mother Jones reported to the international office that Keeney
and Mooney were responsible for the uprising and that the miners returned
from Logan County whipped and disheartened. Mother Jones in an interview
to the Charleston Gazette called Sid Hatfield and Ed Chambers dogs and said,
"Let the sleeping dogs lie." And we suppose when Keeney, Mooney, and their
associates are sent to their graves in the same manner that Hatfield and Cham-
bers were, she will again say, "Let the sleeping dogs lie," and boast again of how
she cleaned up West Virginia. Mother Jones has done her work in the labor
movement and the very men who are now in jeopardy because of the misrepre-
sentation of Mother Jones have stood up for her from the cradle up. She has
tutored those men from childhood, and it is to be regretted that some one who
was their enemy should have connived to frame them instead of Mother Jones,
but she has failed. The truth will come out, for truth crushed to earth will rise
again, and after the clouds of a great storm have passed away and the horizon
is again clear, we will see and know that the attempted betrayal of the miners'
union in West Virginia will, in the final analysis, revert to the discredit of
Mother Jones.
What a pity it is that one who has given a life of service to organized labor
should in her dotage fall for the flattery of a political pawn of the coal operators
like Gov. Morgan and, after falling on his neck, attempt to betray her own people
for a smile and a pat on the back. She accuses Keeney and Mooney of being
responsible for the uprising of the miners. Was Keeney and Mooney responsible
for the uprising in Cabin Creek in 1912-13? She boasts openly that she was
responsible for arousing the miners in Cabin and Paint Creek and causing
them to clean up the "thug system," and for two weeks prior to the last
uprising she criticized Keeney, Mooney, and everyone else around the office and
said that they were too tame, that they were reactionary, and that something
had to be started if she had to start it herself. She made the statement on
numerous occasions to miners congregated around the district office "that the
miners were cowardly curs and had a yellow streak up their back or they
would clean up on the Baldwin guards," and yet she attempts to saddle the
responsibility of her own misgivings upon the officials of the union by saying
"that they were responsible."
Time only will tell, and if the organization is injured because of the attempted
frame up of the miners' union by Mother Jones it will only prove conclusively
that one drawing a salary from the miners' union was compelled to undertake
something that the coal operators and open-shop crowd were unable to do. The
miners' union has grown with too much rapidity in West Virgina to suit some
people. Every onslaught of the open shoppers have been met and we have be-
come solidified and glued together and now where are we at? One in whom we
had the utmost confidence has attempted to frame Keeney and Mooney into the
hands of the enemy. Let us girdle on the armor and fight for Keeney. Mooney,
Workman, Lavinder, and the others until the last ditch, and, when the horizon
is again clear, we may be seared, it is true, but we will win. Injustice never
prevailed but for a time and the truth will always out. No one was responsible
for the uprising of the miners but the damnable, brutal thug system throughout
the southern part of West Virginia, and if Gov. Morgan had called off his dogs
of war on the night Keeney and Mooney turned the men back at Madison, and
if he had not permitted Capt. Brockus and his detachment to murder the miners
at Sharples, there never would have been any invasion of Logan County, and
Mother Jones has pretended to fight the thug system for years, yet, during the
hearing before the Senate committee in Washington, she stood for several min-
utes with her arm around Harry Olmsted, of the Williamson Coal Operators'
Association, and afterwards said "he was a fine boy."
Mr. BELCHER. I believe that is all, Mr. Houston.
Mr. WALSH. That is all.
The CHAIRMAN. Have you any further witnesses? If not, we will adjourn
until 10 o'clock to-morrow morning.
(Whereupon, at 9.10 p. m., the committee adjourned to meet again on Wednes-
day, the 26th day of October, 1921, at 10 o'clock a. m.)

TESTIMONY OF MR. A. E. HESTER.
The witness, having been first duly sworn by the chairman, was examined
and testified as follows:
Mr. BELCHER. What is your name?
Mr. HESTER. A. E. Hester.
Mr. BELCHER. What is your age?
Mr. HESTER. Forty-nine.
Mr. BELCHER. Do you know Charles H. Workman, executive board member
of District 17 of the United Mine Workers?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. Do you know his brother, J. L. Workman?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir,
Mr. BELCHER. Do you know Frank Keeney, president of District 17, United
Mine Workers of America?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. Fred Mooney, its secretary?
Mr. HESTER. I do.
Mr. BELCHER. Do you know David Fowler, who represented the international
organization in Mingo County last year?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. Do you know one David Robb, also a representative of the in-
ternational organization?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. Were you in Williamson at any time during the strike in that
county?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir; I was there practically all of the time.
Mr. BELCHER. When did you first go to Williamson?
Mr. HESTER. I went there in April last year.
Mr. BELCHER. Why did you go to Williamson?
Mr. HESTER. I organized Hardy--or hoped to organize Hardy, rather-and
they ordered us out of the house. Mr. Workman told me they could use me
to good advantage at Williamson, and I went down there.
Mr. BELCHER. So Charley Workman told you they could use you to advantage
at Williamson?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. Did you go there to work for Mr. Workman?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. Did you work for him?
Mr. HESTER. I did.
Mr. BELCHER. Were you paid by Mr. Workman of the United Mine Workers'
organization for your work there?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.

Mr. BELCHER. About what amount of money were you paid a month for your
work for Mr. Workman?
Mr. HESTER. Well, at an average I got something all told, something near
$300 a month, I guess, to the best of my knowledge.
Mr. BELCHER. By whom was this money paid to you?
Mr. HESTER. J. L. Workman.
Mr. BELCHER. What relation is J. L. Workman to Charles Workman?
Mr. HESTER. Brothers.
Mr. BELCHER. Was J. L. Workman employed or acting for the United Mine
Workers' organization in Mingo County?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir; he was district officer, and he had to O. K. all the
relief funds that came into that district.
Mr. BELCHER. How did he O. K, the relief?
Mr. HESTER. By stamping his name with a rubber stamp on the bottom of
each check and scrip.
Mr. BELCHER. In other words, scrip was issued for what is known as relief?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. And all of those so issued were countersigned by J. L. Work-
man?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. Were you in Williamson at the time of or prior to the Matewan
massacre?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. Did you talk to Charles H. Workman, the district board mem-
ber of district 17, about the expected trouble there before it occurred?
Mr. HESTER. Yes; there was something said to that amount just before that-
it was the evening before, I believe it was.
Mr. BELCHER. Tell the committee just what Charles Workman said in refer-
ence to that matter.
Mr. HESTER. Well, now, it was-I am not right sure whether it was the
evening or the day before, but anyway it was an evening or so before this
trouble happened, he met me on the street and he says, "How are you fixed
up?" Well, I says, "I don't know how." He says, "There is likely to be some
trouble up the road" either to-morrow or day after to-morrow; I couldn't say
positively which. Anyhow, a day or so. He said, "They are going to try to
throw some of the boys out of the houses at Red Jacket." He says, "Whenever
they do there will be some trouble about it." He says, "Would you like to
go up?" I says, No; I have more business here to do than I can look at.."
Mr. BELCHER. What did you understand him to mean when he asked you
how you were fixed?
66
Mr. HESTER. Well, I just took it for granted he wanted to know whether I
had any arms or anything like that on me. I don't know, unless that was it.
I taken it for granted that was it.
Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Hester, what, if anything, do you know about the purchase
of guns for the miners of Mingo County during that strike, and how were they
so purchased, if they were purchased?
Mr. HESTER. Well, Mr. Workman came to me, or I met Mr. Workman--
Mr. BELCHER (interrupting). Which Workman do you mean?
Mr. HESTER. J. L. Workman. He met me on the street one evening, and there
were quite a number of union miners standing over on the other corner; and
he came to meet me, leaving this crowd, and he told me, he says, "Now, here,"
he says, "These boys have all got to have something to protect their homes
with, their tent colonies." I says, "Well, what are you going to do about it?"
“Well,” he says, “Mr. Fowler, or the international officers,” he says, 'won't let
nothing like that out; no money; they won't appropriate anything; they can't.
appropriate it." He says, "We have got to have it." I says, “Well, outline
to me how it is to be done." I says, "I'll help you all I can.” So he told me
then, he says, "Now," he says, "you meet me Tuesday following," on the next
Tuesday, and he says, we will outline a way of getting those guns." "All
right," I says.

So on Tuesday-that was the day they issued this relief fund, you see-
Mr. BELCHER. Yes.
Mr. HESTER. Well, always we had more relief to each and every local than
was some of the men would scatter off and there was some relief funds left
over to be torn up each and every Tuesday.
Mr. BELCHER. You mean scrip left to be torn up?

Mr. HESTER. Yes; so he told me this Tuesday, he says, 'Now, here is this

Mr. BELCHER. Kentucky?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. From whom did you order guns in Williamson?
Mr. HESTER. The Roache Hardware Co. there; they ordered some.
Mr. BELCHER. How many did you have them order a week?
Mr. HESTER. Well, I told them to order about 12 a week myself, and others
did, and there was a couple of other fellows with me when I made the

Mr. BELCHER. Who went with you to make the arrangements?
Mr. HESTER. There was a fellow by the name of Roy Chapman.
Mr. BELCHER. What, if any, connection did he have with the United Mine
Workers?
Mr. HESTER. He was secretary of a tent colony-local.
Mr. BELCHER. Who was the other man who went with you?
Mr. HESTER. I have forgotten his given name, but his name was Ellison. He
belonged to a local up in Williamson.
Mr. BELCHER. You made this arrangement with the Roache Hardware Co.,
of Williamson, to purchase as many as a dozen guns a week, did you?
Mr. HESTER. When I went there first and foremost to help these boys buy
the guns these same two I speak of-he only had two or three in stock. I
asked him if he could order some. He said. "I might get them in; it's pretty
tricky work." I said, "Mr. Workman told me the boys need some guns up at
the tent colonies. I want to know just what you can do." He says, "I will
do the best I can." So he ordered about a dozen a week. I don't know this.
you know.
Mr. BELCHER, What kind of guns were they?
Mr. HESTER. They were .30-30.
Mr. BELCHER. Is that a high-power gun?
Mr. HESTER. Yes.
Mr. BELCHER. Thirty-thirty what-Winchester?

Mr. HESTER. About the wind-up of that term of court when Hatfield was on
trial over there and the United States troops were expected to leave daily, he
was absent-Page was-from Williamson, and they sent me out-someone from
the court house over there. I happened to be passing along there; I was only

was-and asked me to go and see if I could find Page, and I started to find
Page, and I met Mr. Workman and inquired where Page was at. He kind of
laughed. He said, "Page will be in sometime." I says, "Well, he is not here in
town, then?" No," he says, "he went away," he says, "to do what you have
been doing and to get a few more guns." I says, "Where has he been?" He
says, "To Fairmont."
66
So in an hour, or such a matter, there were several fellows came to me and
wanted to know of me if Page was in town, and after Page arrived, I told them,
"Yes, Page was in town." They wanted to know if they could get to see Page.
I says, "No; he is in the courthouse, or either in jail now; I don't know which;
I can't get to see him. What do you want?" They said, "We have got the
promise of some guns from him." I says, "I don't know nothing about that."

they had arrangements made as soon as court was over, but they couldn't get

not let the guns out until the Federal troops left.

Mr. BELCHER. Do you know how these men traveled, and when they traveled

Mr. HESTER. Well, they would go mysteriously and come the same way. Most

Mr. BELCHER. Did you see those men frequently in the company of Workman?

get too hot after us." He says, "All three of us has got that in our pockets at all
times, but," he says, "whenever they get after us we have got money enough to
go on."
Mr. BELCHER. How long were they engaged in the organization in the manner

Mr. HESTER. I don't know that, because I would hardly ever see them; that is

was their plan to throw me in and hold me responsible for all this money
and also the purchase of guns and everything else so they could audit up the
books and give an account of what was missing.
Mr. BELCHER. Make you the goat?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. You did not use any of that money for your own purposes?
Mr. HESTER. I never used one dollar of it.

Mr. HESTER. Up to Pennsylvania and around out in those mining fields up
there; then came back to Ironton, Ohio.
Mr. BELCHER. What happened to you in Ironton, Ohio?
Mr. HESTER. The chief of police arrested me there.
Mr. BELCHER. On whose orders?
Mr. HESTER. He told me he thought I was due to be held for investigation.
I went up to the city hall and asked him what the charge was. He said I
was wanted in Mingo County in connection with the organization of the
United Mine Workers, and I asked him in what way, so he would not tell me,
nor did not tell me until two or three days later-five days later it was.
Senator McKELLAR. Did they keep you in jail?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir; I was in jail, and on the third day I was there I told

Mr. WALSH. Did you first go to work in a coal mine?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir; I worked a year or two in coal mines and then went
and worked a few years in the copper mines and back to the coal mines.
Mr. WALSH. What mine did you work in first?
Mr. HESTER. For the James Bros., of Chattanooga, on the top of Lookout
Mountain, what they call Pittsburg, Ga., 17 miles from Chattanooga.
Mr. WALSH. How long did you work in the mines in Tennessee?
Mr. HESTER. I worked there about three or four years; that I don't remember.
Mr. WALSH. And conditions were very harsh working in those mines at that
time in reference to pay and conditions, were they not?
Mr. HESTER. I thought then it was mighty good.
Mr. WALSH. Then they were not harsh? Just whatever you say about it?
Mr. HESTER. At that time the work, where I was started at; why, I wished
lots of times I could find conditions just as good as it was then.
Mr. WALSH. How many hours a day did you work?
Mr. HESTER. Why, like we do now, I just worked whatever I felt like holding
out to work; then come out; a coal digger don't have to stay in after he gets
ready to come out nohow; I would just work until I was tired enough to go
home; then go home.
Mr. WALSH. What hours did men on daywork work at that time?
Mr. HESTER. It was 10.
Mr. WALSH. When you went to work in the industry?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. WALSH. Do you know what the wage was that a day laborer got at that
time?
Mr. HESTER. Twenty cents an hour; 20 to 27 cents.
Mr. WALSH. Now, what was the first mine in which you worked in West
Virginia?
Mr. HESTER. Freeborn, I think it was.
Mr. WALSH. What county do you say that is?
Mr. HESTER. The mine is on the Kentucky side, in Pike County.
Mr. WALSH. Where did you work last as a miner; working underground?
Mr. HESTER. The last work that I did I was mine foreman at Hardy, Ky.
Mr. WALSH. At what mines did you work in the State of West Virginia?
Mr. HESTER. I worked at Freeborn; well, that mine is still in Kentucky; I

is the name of the post office and I have worked at Pocahontas, Balseville,
Marco, Tams, and-
Mr. WALSH. Where was the last place?
Mr. HESTER. Hardy was the last place I worked.
Senator STERLING. At what periods did you work in these several mines, or
from what time up to what time?
Mr. HESTER. I couldn't tell you that positively, because sometimes my stay
may be a year at a place, and sometimes two, and sometimes not a month, at
a place; you see it would be owing to the conditions whether I liked it or not
how long I would stay; but with the last two or three years I have been mine
foreman and file boss and such as that.
Mr. WALSH. Where?
Mr. HESTER. At Ukon, I was over there; and in Kentucky I was mine foreman
over there. The last few years I have not loaded any coal or done very much
hard labor in the mines.
Mr. WALSH. When did you first join the United Mine Workers?
Mr. HESTER. In 1894, in Alabama.
Mr. WALSH. Were you a member of the United Mine Workers when you came

Mr. HESTER. No, sir; I had been; as I was saying a minute ago, I had been
a mine foreman and assistant and one thing and another, like that, and I wasn't
allowed in the organization.
Mr. WALSH. When did you rejoin the United Mine Workers of America?
Mr. HESTER. To go down to the facts of the business I had not joined.
Mr. WALSH. You had not joined?
Mr. HESTER. No, sir; I just came in there as a union man and nobody ever
asked me to join; they never asked me if I had joined or anything else about
it, and I just went ahead and went to work and just went on that way.
Mr. WALSH. You stated you were not a Baldwin-Felts detective at any time,
not in the employment of any detective association?
Mr. HESTER. I was not.

Mr. WALSH. And those that were on the company's property, what became
of them?
Mr. HESTER. Those that was on the company's property they all left immedi-
ately and some went out of the country to go to work and others moved over
into the tent colony. I don't know how many was moved over there.
Senator STERLING. When you were ordered to leave were you on strike at that
time?
Mr. HESTER. No, sir; they had never called it yet.
Senator STERLING. Were you working in the mines right along?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir; working every day.
Mr. WALSH. Was there any public protest made about this, what did the
newspapers say about it that such a large section of the community should
simply be ordered away-did they say anything about it?
Mr. HESTER. Well, I never saw anything about it.
Mr. WALSH. When you left Hardy where did you go?
Mr. HESTER. I went to Williamson.
Mr. WALSH. You went immediately to Williamson, did you?
Mr. HESTER. Yes; sir; I went down there on the 6th of July.
Mr. WALSH. Williamson is in Mingo County?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. WALSH. Was there any strike in Mingo County at that time?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. WALSH. When had the strike been called in Mingo County?
Mr. HESTER. The strike had been called there on the 1st day of May and
this was in July, and then they made the second call on the 1st day of July.
Mr. WALSH. How many men were on strike in Mingo?
Mr. HESTER. At that time there was some six or seven thousand men, I just
disremember now how many there was there.
Mr. WALSH. As a matter of fact, after the strike got under way in Mingo
County there was some twelve or fifteen hundred people living in the tent
colony and at the time of these occurrences to which you have testified about-
the buying of arms-there was relief being extended to approximately 10,000
people, 10,000 men in Mingo County?
Mr. HESTER. I don't think there was ever 10,000 men on relief there in Mingo
County, according to my estimation.
Mr. WALSH. How many would you say were on relief; the relief was being
extended to men, women, and children to the number of eight or ten thousand?
Mr. HESTER. I don't think there was that many.
Mr. WALSH. What would you say the number was, Mr. Hester?
Mr. HESTER. Now, I taken a census myself several different times.
Mr. WALSH. Then you ought to be quite accurate about it; you ought to be
able to give us a very good idea?
Mr. HESTER. And at that time I really don't remember just now what it was
at the time I went there, but later on in the fall why I could only gather about
600 men.
Mr. WALSH. And how many people would that represent would you say?
Mr. HESTER. It would represent, let us see, we had-I don't remember now.
Mr. WALSH. You don't remember?
Mr. HESTER. No, sir.
Mr. WALSH. Were they largely men with families?
Mr. HESTER. I found that the majority was men that was boarding and
single men.
Mr. WALSH. They were not largely men with families. Your answer is no,
then; they were not largely men with families?
Mr. HESTER. No; the majority was single fellows.
Mr. WALSH. Single men; just boarding?
Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Mr. WALSH. And how many people was relief being extended to would you

Mr. HESTER. I believe 7,000; 7,000 was about the best that I-

Mr. HESTER. Yes, sir.
Senator STERLING. How long had it been on?
Mr. HESTER. From the 1st of May until July 6.
Senator STERLING. Had there been any agitation at Hardy for a strike be-

I went to my office and Mr. Hester came in.

Mr. MITCHELL. McDowell County.
Mr. Avis. What position did you hold in August of this year?
Mr. MITCHELL. Chief of police of the city of Welch.

Baldwin-Felts Detective Agency?
Mr. MITCHELL. I have not.
Mr. AVIS. Were you in the city when Sid Hatfield and Ed Chambers were
killed?
Mr. MITCHELL. I was.
Mr. Avis. Did you see or hear the shooting?
Mr. MITCHELL. I did.
Mr. Avis. Just tell the committee in a brief way what you saw, and particu-
larly what, if anything, you saw Sid Hatfield and Ed Chambers do.
Mr. MITCHELL. Well, I was directly across the street, probably a distance of
50 or 60 feet from the shooting. I was walking up the street; had started to
A. C. Hubbard's office-the justice of the peace of the district-and I heard a
shot. I looked up, and at the time I looked there was just a volley of shots.
I never did see Sid Hatfield until he fell on the first landing of the platform
of the entrance to the courthouse. I saw Ed Chambers standing on the left
of where Sid Hatfield was, shooting a .38 Smith & Wesson special pistol.
Mr. AVIS. You saw Ed Chambers shooting, did you?
Mr. MITCHELL. Yes, sir. I saw Lively, Pence, and a fellow by the name of
Salters at the head of the steps, shooting down at the other fellows.
Mr. AVIS. But at that time Chambers was also shooting?
Mr. MITCHELL. Yes, sir; Chambers emptied his gun.
Mr. AVIS. Did you go over toward where the shooting took place?
Mr. MITCHELL. As soon as the shooting was over I ran over. Three officers,
Lively, Salters, and Pence. were at the head of the steps, at what would be the
second landing of the steps entering the courthouse yard.
Mr. AVIS. You had to go up several flights of steps?
Mr. MITCHELL. Yes, sir. There are two side entrances. The steps are at
angle, rather, and as soon as the shooting was over I ran over. Hatfield fell
down on the first landing, from about the third or fourth step starting up to
the second landing, and then it seemed as though he turned over and fell down
the steps toward the first land—that is, toward the pavement or the entrance of
the first steps. He rested there with his head about three steps from the bot-
tom and his feet back up toward the first landing. I pulled him down onto the
concrete of the main entrance, and as soon as I did that I ran up to the top
of the steps, and Chambers was lying on the first landing. As I got there,
Pence stepped down from off the steps of the second landing and picked up
two guns, one lying on the side where Hatfield had fell and one lying by Cham-
bers. I never did see Hatfield have a gun. I didn't see the gun, but I told Pence
to give me the gun Chambers had. He handed t to me. Lively put that-
Mr. Avis. You did not see this pistol picked up by Sid Hatfield's body?
Mr. MITCHELL. No, sir; his body was just rolled over to the next step, and
the gun was lying where he fell.
Mr. Avis. Did you make any examination of Sid Hatfield's body to find out
whether he had any ammunition of any kind or another revolver about his
person?
Mr. MITCHELL. Well, as his feet were up and his head down, cartridges were
running from his left pants pocket.
Mr. AVIS. What kind of cartridges were there?
Mr. MITCHELL. Two kinds. .38 Smith & Wesson spec´al and a .38 short.
Mr. AVIS. How many cartridges were falling out of his pocket?
Mr. MITCHELL. Twenty-six in all, I believe.
Mr. Avis. This pistol that was picked up near him--what caliber was that?
Mr. MITCHELL. .38 Smith and Wesson special.

TESTIMONY OF MR. ERNEST M. MERRILL.
The witness, being first duly sworn by the chairman, testified as follows:
Mr. VINSON. Where do you live?
Mr. MERRILL. Charleston, W. Va.
Mr. VINSON. How long have you lived there?
Mr. MERRILL. One year.
Mr. VINSON. Where did you live before that time?
Mr. MERRILL. Beckley, W. Va.
Mr. VINSON. What is your business or profession, Mr. Merrill?
Mr. MERRILL. Civil and mining engineer.
Mr. VINSON. Are you interested in any coal mines?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. What?
Mr. MERRILL. I am interested in the Alpha Pocahontas Coal Co., the Monti-
cello Coal Co., the Boyer Smokeless Coal Co., the Citizens' Land Co., Wyoming-
Pocahontas Coal & Coke Co., the Mordue Collieries Co.
Mr. VINSON. You are one of the principal stockholders of the Mordue Col-
lieries Co.?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir; I am secretary and treasurer.
Mr. VINSON. How many of these mines are unionized, belonging to the
United Mine Workers?
Mr. MERRILL. The Mordue Collieries Co. is the only one.
Mr. VINSON. The others are nonunion?
Mr. MERRILL. The others are nonunion; yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. Mr. Merrill, has it been a part of your business as a mining
engineer to construct mining plants?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. You have had quite a lot of experience in that line, have you not?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir; I have been in that business for 19 years.
Mr. VINSON. Mr. Merrill, in constructing mining plants for the production of
coal do you make any difference or allowance in capacity for mines that are to
be run union and those that are to be run nonunion? I mean, in the equipment
and the general capacity of the mine?
Mr. MERRILL. Everything else being equal, we have to equip the union mines
with about 20 to 25 per cent more equipment than we do the nonunion mines to
secure the same production.
Mr. VINSON. In other words, if I understand you, if you are constructing a
mine and providing it with equipment, with a capacity of a thousand tons, non-
union, you would have to construct the base mine for a capacity of 1,250 tons
union?
Mr. MERKILL. Approximately so, every other condition being equal.

Mr. VINSON. I mean, all the conditions being equal. Why is that, Mr. Merrill?
Mr. MERRILL. Because we can not get the same result with union labor that we

Senator McKELLAR. In what respect?
Mr. MERRILL. We do not get the production per man, per unit of equipment,

Senator MCKELLAR. Why is that?
Mr. MERRILL. It is the difference between running your own property and
having somebody else running it for you, as far as I know. I know it is a condi-

Senator MCKELLAR. How does it evidence itself? Your statements are a con-

The CHAIRMAN, Does a nonunion man work longer than a union man?
Senator MCKELLAR. That is what I would like to know.
The CHAIRMAN. Or is he not as efficient; or what?
Mr. MERRILL. In the nonunion mine all of the different factors are controlled
from day to day by the management. In the union district they are controlled
through committees and through contracts. In the one case you can act in
accordance with the requirements of the occasion. In the other case you have

Senator MCKELLAR. In what respects? You just give us a conclusion. What

Mr. MERRILL. Well, sir, I might illustrate by some incident-
Mr. VINSON. Suppose you give those incidents.
Senator MCKELLAR. Yes; following the facts.
Mr. MERRILL (continuing). That are peculiar to the union condition. I could
give numerous incidents. I have in mind a condition at Mordue Collieries Co.
We have a hollow there 3 miles long. It is 34 miles from the mouth of the
hollow to the drift mouth in the head of the hollow. The hollow is very narrow,
and the building ground is restricted, and we have to build to what we call
Stringtown. There is only one place in the hollow where we can build as much
as a double row of houses. Almost all the way along it is a single row of houses.
Therefore our men are scattered from one end of the hollow to the other.
In order to get the men to report promptly in the morning for work we fur-
nish a motor service up and down the hollow. That motor car goes along in the
morning and picks them up and delivers them at the foot of the service plane
in time for them to be handled to the bottom of the hill and around the tram
road to the drift mouth. The service is for their convenience.
Last summer that truck with its trailers would stop almost anywhere along
the hollow to pick up men in groups, one or two or whatever was convenient
for the men, but as we came along to the winter season, in order to cut down the
time of travel and to secure efficiency in this thing we worked out a schedule of
stop for the truck so it would not have to make so many stops and would not
keep the men out there so long in the open going back and forth to their work.
At one group of houses-I think we have 12 or 13 houses-at the lower end is a
foot log across the creek. There were three or four men, perhaps five, who
usually came across that foot log from the lower end of the town, and they
would stop there and pick them up. There was a bridge across the creek about
halfway up this row of houses. So we cut out that foot log stop and stopped
at the bridge.
The first morning that the truck went up the hollow on the new schedule the
men who were accustomed to get on at the foot log were there. The truck did
not stop, but went up to the bridge, and they called back to these men and waved
to them to come on up to the truck to get on, and they refused. The truck
waited a reasonable time and then went on up the hollow and picked up its
load and came back.
Senator MCKELLAR. Was that a union mine?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir. The next morning they went up there and these same
men were out at the foot log and the truck refused to stop. The men had gath-
ered up to the bridge as soon as they saw the truck did not stop for those men at

the foot log. They turned around again and went back and word was passed up
the hollow ahead of the truck, and there was not a man turned out that day. It
was a walkout, and we had to take that up with the committee and go through
to the commissioners, and we were on strike for five days.
The CHAIRMAN. A walkout because the truck did not stop?
Mr. MERRILL. A walkout because the truck did not stop. Now, the distance
from the foot log to the bridge by actual measurement was 320 yards. They
shut us down for five days over there. Our overhead ran from $450 to $500 a
day, and that one strike cost us from $2,000 to $2,500, the lowest estimate we

Senator MCKELLAR. How long had the truck been stopping at the foot log?
Mr. MERRILL. It had been put on the previous spring and had operated through

We offered the men at the time, in order to settle, if they would take the
truck and operate it we would furnish the fuel and furnish a runner, and all
they had to do was to agree to deliver the men at the tramroad at the foot of
the incline in time for them to be taken around to their work. They refused

Mr. VINSON. What other equation enters into your estimate of 25 per cent

Mr. MERRILL. Another incident: The contract provides that the men shall take
30 minutes for their lunch and that they can select that 30 minutes. We have
there an inclined plane and a tipple. There is a yard in which the loaded trips
come in from the mine around to the tramroad, and then they are handled
from that loading yard down the plane and into the tipple. There are from 12
to 14 men who take the coal down the plane and load it into the cars. That is
called the tipple-to-plane crew. They selected 12 o'clock as their noon hour.
They took their 30 minutes at that time.
The main-line motor crew for hauling the loads around from the drift mouth
selected 12.30 as their noon hour. They would come around from the mine
with a trip of loads, 40 or 50 of them, to the sand house just before you come
into this yard. When they got to the sand house, regardless of whether the
men at the plane had loaded cars to work on and keep busy running down the
plane, they would stop there for their lunch and take their 30 minutes. It
would take them about five minutes to run down and deliver the loaded trip to
the plane. If they did not take those loads down, the tipple-to-plane crew would
shut down. That happened several times. We tried to get them to change
their hour. They refused. We undertook to fire the motor crew for not deliver-
ing the load to the tipple, and we were on strike three days on that proposition.
It is a continual performance of that kind. There is hardly a month goes by
that there are not incidents of that kind occurring around the union mines. It
disorganizes, and you do not get your results.
Senator MCKELLAR. Do you recall any others?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes. We had a condition up there we had a wet heading. A
little water would gather in the heading overnight. We wanted the place bailed
out, and it was not more than a 10 or 20 minutes' job to bail it out. We asked
the motor crew to take a bucket down with them and bail that place out. They
refused. We undertook to make them do so. They refused on the basis that
we had to send a water bailer back there to do that work. We had two or three
days' strike on that proposition.
Again, they insisted that we have a substation tender. We had a man down
at the drift mouth whose job it was to load the mine cars to go back into the
works and turn switches-a kind of a handy man around the drift mouth;
and among other things, when the circuit breaker would go out into the sub-
station, his job was to go in there and throw it back in again. They insisted
that we could not do that work; that we had to employ a special man at $6.70
a day whose job it was to go there and stand by and when that circuit breaker
went out to put it back in. We had a strike about that.
Mr. VINSON. Of all these strikes you have, each strike costs from $400 to
$500 a day, as I understand it, overhead charges?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. In order to make up the loss of tonnage that occurs by reason
of this suspension of the work it is necessary to have more houses and more
men than you actually need?
Mr. MERRILL. That is the point I make; yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. How many men would go out on these different strikes?
Mr. MERRILL. Everybody on the pay roll; anywhere from 200 to 250.

Mr. Allen, local manager, and myself, walked up the hollow to see this new

The secretary-treasurer of the local, Mr. Grade White, was one of the
fellows laid up at home. He was having trouble with his stomach-ulcers
on it and had been excused. We went around and got hold of him and
asked him if he would not go up and tell those men that they were not called
out and that they could stay on the job. He said, "Certainly," and went along
with us, and went up and took the foreman of the Italian crew and the fore-
man of the carpenter crew and told them that this was not their quarrel at
all; it was purely a union matter and that they could keep right on about
their work. He told these men that in my presence. Then he went up on
the hill with the men. There were some up above, and he told them the same
thing up there. I was not present when he made that statement up there.
The next day Mr. Allen and I undertook to go through the mine end and
went on up to the mines. Coming out we met the president of our local there,
Mr. Matthew Perry-Perry has been quite a satisfactory fellow to deal with.
more so than the previous president we had to deal with-and we stopped
him and asked him just what the situation was and what the men hoped to
accomplish by this move. He just refused to talk. I told him that they had
a serious contract with us and were doing us serious damage; that we had
been furnishing them work and had the work offered for them; that they were
shutting us down and our overhead was going on, which meant four or five
hundred dollars a day to us, and we thought that we had treated them fairly.
He said that we had and that the quarrel was not with us in any way. I
asked him whom the quarrel was with, and he said it was with the governor
and the State authorities; that they had gotten to the point where they could
not get justice. Their men could not get justice; that the governor had
their men imprisoned in Mingo County and would not let them out on bail,
and that they had to do something; that they had given up trying through
the courts, and they were, going across country now to release their men over
there and see if they could not change the conditions.
Mr. VINSON. This man was one of your employees?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir. He was president of the local at our mine.
Mr. VINSON. Excuse me for interrupting you.
Mr. MERRILL. We told him about the trouble down on the construction work
and asked him if he would not also, as president of the local, stop by and give
those fellows instructions. He said he would be glad to, and he did. I was
not present when he gave those instructions. At any rate, throughout the
disturbance that construction work was not interfered with or delayed in any
manner. In fact, it was speeded up.
The following day I went out, returning to Charleston, caught the train to
Whiteville, and the train from St. Albans up Coal River, and the train across
Cabin Creek, and the train from Cabin Creek coming back, and when I came
in there were 25 to 30 standing around the station until the train came in, and
the moment it came in and unloaded I was in the middle of about four or five
hundred of them, and I never saw any wilder crowd in my life. I simply
retired to the background, and was mighty thankful I had on my mine clothes.
Some of the incidents were a little bit laughable. One big red-headed fellow
hopped off the train and got up on the platform and waived his high-powered
rifle, and said: "The Coal River hell cats have arrived. Now watch us work!"
He called for "Detail No. 74." He got up on some high ground and kept
hollering for Detail No. 74, and there were about 20 men, all armed. They
had on the customary overalls and a belt of cartridges and a couple of big 44's
stuck in their belt, and high-powered rifles. He called those men in and called
the roll, and then they started off up Coal River, and word was being passed
around through the crowd.
Some of them evidently were just getting into the game, and they wanted
to know which way to go. We had had information the night before that the
men were breaking up and going home. We did not know until afterward
that they had started to make their march at 11 o'clock that night, but the
word was passed around in the crowd that I was in that the men had
started their march and that the way to go now was not to Marmet, but down
to Ravine. So that whole crowd piled on the Coal River train and went down
to Ravine.
Mr. VINSON. Ravine is down the river, is it not?
Mr. MERRILL. Ravine is down the River from Mordue; yes, sir.
That is my first knowledge that the men were not breaking up. In fact,
when I saw the trains coming in with so many men on them, I thought, of
course, the thing had been dispersed and was all off, and they were coming in;

but when I heard those instructions going around I realized that they must

The following day Gen. Bandholtz was called in-
Mr. VINSON. Just before you get away from that, Mr. Merrill, what did you

Mr. MERRILL. What did I understand?
Mr. VINSON. Yes. What did that mean?
Mr. MERRILL. The country was full of rumors and counterrumors, and I had

of men sent up there to see that these people did come out. I do not know

Mr. VINSON. Proceed, Mr. Merrill.
Mr. MERRILL. There is not much more to the story. I got back to Charleston,

protect the community.
Mr. VINSON. Mr. Merrill, what information have you to the effect that a

Mr. MERRILL. That is a matter of common knowledge up and down our

Senator MCKELLAR. That is another interesting circumstance.
Mr. MERRILL. The cook, Mattie, had four brothers-
Mr. VINSON. Was she a colored girl?
Mr. MERRILL. A colored girl, and quite famous for her praying ability. So
they had a prayer meeting just before the boys started out, and they prayed,
and finally her younger brother called on Mattie and said-
Mr. VINSON. Was he a member of the union?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir. He said, "Mattie, you have prayed for all of these
other niggers up and down the hollow. I want you to get down on your knees
now and pray for Leroy; and don't you pray for any other nigger, but just
Leroy-that's me."
So that was the attitude of Leroy; and the fellows generally, I will say, in
our hollow were pretty well frightened, and they went because they were more
afraid of what was waiting for them if they did not go.
Mr. VINSON. What threat had been nrade in regard to them if they refused to

Mr. MERRILL. The threat was that they had better not be there when they

Mr. MERRILL. If they did not go with them. That was passed all up and
down the hollow and all over the fields.

a union district you have to stick to your contract and go through your com-

directly with the men; and if the man's work is unsatisfactory, regardless of
whether he has violated some contract or another, you can dispose of him and

It is rather an abstract thing
Mr. VINSON. But it does increase the cost of coal?
Mr. MERRILL. Undoubtedly so.
Mr. VINSON. And that cost must either be paid by the operator or the

Mr. MERRILL. Well, in the matter of cost, your contract controls. You have
a stated wage fixed in all of the different departments. You have got to pay
each fellow running a machine, for instance-you have either got to pay him
a rate per ton or a rate per day, and you can not give the good man a little bit
more to encourage him than you give the poor man.
Mr. VINSON. And you can not get rid of the poor man?
Mr. MERRILL. And you can not get rid of the poor man unless he violates his
contract.
Mr. VINSON. Then that operates, Mr. Merrill, as a practical proposition, that
the good man does not work any more or any better than he simply has to to
hold his place? He is not rewarded for extraordinary work, is he-I mean as
far as wages are concerned?
Mr. MERRILL. On the day man I think that that is true to an appreciable
extent. Of course, on the coal loaders, who are contract men or piecework
men, why, that does not enter into the proposition so much, because they get
so much a ton, and one man will load 15 or 18 tons a day as against another
man's 10 tons.
Mr. VINSON. But on the others, outside of the loaders, that does apply?
Mr. MERRILL. Well, on the loader in our nonunion district it costs just about
so much to maintain a working plate. That is a fixed charge. Well, now, if
you get a man in there who is only going to run 5 or 6 tons a day and call
that a day's work and quit, you are not going to keep him very long, because
he is not making your end good. You want a fellow who will load to at
least the average of the mine. In the union district you can not dispose of
that fellow until he has violated his contract. In the nonunion district you can
say: "Now, bring your loading sheets up or get out; one or the other."
Mr. VINSON. That, of course, of itself, increases the cost per ton in the union
mines over what it would be in the nonunion mines.
Mr. MERRILL. Very materially. And, then again, the nonunion condition is
flexible to such a condition as we are in now. In the nonunion district they
are working now on the 1917 wage scale, and where we are shut down the
men have come and asked to go to work on the 1917 wage scale in order to
get work.
Mr. VINSON. You mean the nonunion men have done that?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. Has there been any offer or effort on the part of the union men
to reduce the scale?
Mr. MERRILL. No, sir; absolutely no response to this at all. That is the rea-
son the union district is down and the nonunion district is running up.
Mr. VINSON. In other words, the situation to-day in the coal fields of West

Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir.

Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir.

sulation you have got to make allowances for that, and you have got to instal

Mr. WALSH. Just describe what the larger unit is.
Mr. MERRILL. A larger unit consists of everything that goes into a mining
property.

union as compared to nonunion?
Mr. MERRILL. Well, on my basis, where you would get your production
out by five short-well mining machines in a union district, you could get it out
by four machines in the nonunion district.
Mr. WALSH. The same amount?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes.

Mr. MERRILL. I don't know that I can get down quite that close to it.

Mr. MERRILL. Take the machine conditions at Mordue collieries.
Mr. WALSH. Yes, sir.
Mr. MERRILL. For instance, we have four machines working over there, and
I think the best mine ever produced was 14,000 tons. Over at Monticello we
have one machine which has run along to capacity at about 10,000 tons.
Mr. WALSH. Are they the same sort of machines?
Mr. MERRILL. One a union and one a nonunion mine.
Mr. WALSH. Are they the same sort of machines?
Mr. MERRILL. No. There is another factor. We tried to put the same ma-
chine in at Mordue as we had at Monticello, and we found this, that the
machine we had in Monticello cost about twice as much money as the one at
Mordue, and would cut about twice as much coal as one of those machines.
However, at Mordue we had to pay the same price per ton for coal produced
with this machine.
Mr. WALSH, Yes.
Mr. MERRILL. That we had to pay per ton for the coal produced with the other
machine. Therefore, we got no benefit of putting in twice as much money
against that machine.
Mr. WALSH. And you did not intend the miner to get the benefit, who is a
part of this industry, for any added improvement which made for efficiency?
Mr. MERRILL. Why not? We would be very glad to give it to him. He could
cut twice as much coal with the machine as he could with the other machine.

The CHAIRMAN. Let us stay where we are.

Mr. MERRILL. We don't hear much about it; no, sir.

Mr. MERRILL. Measure them by the car.

high or not, and everything of that sort?
Mr. MERRILL. Part of your efficiency, sir.

Mr. MERRILL. We like to see our cars well loaded; yes, sir.

ing his coal weighed and having it watched, just like a consumer thinks-like a

districts about the car basis.
The CHAIRMAN. Does the miner get the worst of that?
Mr. MERRILL. I do not think so, sir; I never have seen that.
The CHAIRMAN. What is the objection to paying him according to the tons he
gets out?
Mr. MERRILL. It is a matter of contract. Why not just as well pay him by
quarts? What is the difference; why must it be in tons?
The CHAIRMAN. When you pay him by the car-this is what I am trying to
get at do you pay him according to the amount that is in the car?
Mr. MERRILL. No; we do not. We take the newcomer to the mine, show him
his working place, and show him the car and say, "Now, here is the car you
have got to fill with a good hump on it. We pay so much for doing that piece
of work. Do you want the job, or don't you?" If he wants the job he goes
ahead on that basis.
The CHAIRMAN. Is this hump the same relative hump for the different men,
or some higher and some lower?
Mr. MERRILL. No; we just want a carload. If you see a hundred cars along
the line it will be practically a straight line on top. It is just a case whether a
man wants to measure in quarts, pecks, bushels, tons, or cars. We prefer to
measure it in the car. That is all there is to that proposition.
Senator STERLING. How much does a car hold?
Mr. MERRILL. Different amounts.
Mr. VINSON. Your car?
Mr. MERRILL. Depending entirely on the working conditions. Take a 3-foot
vein of coal and you have got to use a low, flat car; take a 6-foot vein of coal
and you can take a car as high as you want to-short and high. It depends
entirely on working conditions and the service you want to put it in. If you
are going to put cars over a plain you build one sort of car; if you are going
to have a crossover, then there is a different arrangement of cars; if you are
going to have a cradle dump, then you have something else.
Senator STERLING. Speaking of Nordeau and Monticello, are the cars just
the same in each of the two mines?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir.
Senator STERLING. How much do those cars hold?
Mr. MERRILL. About 3 tons. At Mordue we limit the load on those cars to
6,500 pounds, because we will not put over 6,500 pounds on those cars because
they have to go down over a steep inclined plane, and if we load them higher
than that the coal spills off. The car, level full, is practically a 3-ton car.
Mr. WALSH. You say that one reason you want to have nonunion instead of
union men is that you can not dispose of a man; that means discharge him, of
course?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes, sir.
Mr. WALSH. Unless he violates his contract?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes.
Mr. WALSH. That is, if he is in the union?
Mr. MERRILL. Yes.

Mr. MERRILL. They cost somebody a lot of money.

are matters of irritation on one side and the other?
Mr. MERRILL. Matters of expense. We do not care about the irritation.
Mr. WALSH. You do not care how bad you feel if you get the money?
Mr. MERRILL. No.
Mr. WALSH. Well, take this one about the train running through String-
town. Why did you want to quit stopping the tram at this place, the log across
the creek?
Mr. MERRILL. Why, the men-that truck starts from the mouth of the hollow
and goes up to the foot of the inclined plane. No men are handled up on top,
and a motor truck is waiting for them to take them around to the drift
mouth. All right. They have got to be there at 7.30 in the morning. Now,
that means the truck has got to leave the mouth of the hollow at 6.30. Now,
if it has to make 10 stops going up the hollow, we will say-I don't know just
how many stops they make there-I have never been over there for that-but
it will consume a certain amount of time. If you double that number of
stops, it will consume double that time, won't it? The fellow at the mouth
of the hollow then has got to get up and get there that much earlier in the
morning. Then the time element. When you go into rough winter weather,
those cars are open; it is not an agreeable trip out in the open; those men
who are already on the car have got to sit out to the weather and they are
exposed that much longer. Now, then, so far as the operation of the car is
concerned, the grade is an extremely heavy grade. On a dry rail in open
summer weather there is no difficulty about starting and stopping that ma-
chine, but get a wet-track rail with sleet on it in the morning and it is a
different proposition.
Mr. WALSH. This is in the wintertime?
Mr. MERRILL. This was approaching winter; this was getting ready for
winter. Now, the service there, it does not amount to that much to us in
dollars; it was merely a case of getting that thing on the program, and we
were serving the men as well as ourselves. We were perfectly willing to turn
the machine over to the men to operate, and we wanted to deliver the men to
the foot of the plain on time, but we had to get them up there.
Mr. WALSH. Have you something else you want to say about this?

good while to accumulate and it is going to take a while to work it out, but
I think West Virginia can and will work the problem out for itself.
The CHAIRMAN. You do not think the public have any interest in it at all,
that it is just a question between the operators and the union?
Mr. MERRILL. No; I think the public is very much interested.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you not think the public of the United States has some
interest in it?
Mr. MERRILL. I think so. I want to correct an answer I made to a question.
My attention was called in the recess to this answer. I stated inadvertently
that under the open-shop condition we did not have a signed contract with the
miners. We did, have a contract, a signed contract with the miners that had
the open-shop clause in it. I must have misunderstood the question if I an-
swered it as I did. We did have the contract.
The CHAIRMAN. Is that all?
Mr. VINSON. Just one question which has been brought out. Mr. Merrill, in
your judgment would there have been any trouble in West Virginia if the law
and the governmental powers would protect the mine owner in his right to
run his mine according to the Constitution of the United States and the rights
that have been construed by the Supreme Court of the United States? In
other words if the law would protect you and your workmen against any un-
lawful interference from the outside at all, would you have any trouble in
running your mines?
Mr. MERRILL. None whatsoever, sir.
Mr. WALSH. And if you were allowed to club men out of the neighborhood
that wanted to go into lawful organization, such as you would take a gun your-
self to protect your right to do-
Mr. MERRILL. I concede the law would protect those men too, Mr. Walsh, the
same as they protect mine.
Mr. VINSON. Is it not a matter of proper enforcement of law, is not that the
whole trouble?
Mr. MERRILL. Unquestionably so.
Mr. WALSH. You are familiar with all the constitutional provisions and de-
cisions of the Supreme Court of the United States, I take it, involved in this
question?
Mr. MERRILL. No; I am not.
Mr. WALSH. You just answer yes, because that comes through your counsel?
Mr. MERRILL. No; it is a matter of opinion.
The CHAIRMAN. Let us stop with that.

TESTIMONY OF MR. W. R. THURMOND.
The witness, having been first duly sworn by the chairman, testified as

The CHAIRMAN. Mr. Thurmond, what is your position with the coal operators?
Mr. THURMOND. President of the Logan Coal Operators' Association.
The CHAIRMAN. What is that association?
Mr. THURMOND. The Logan Coal Operators' Association is a voluntary asso-
ciation composed of 66 operating companies, located in that part of Logan County
lying on the waters of the Vim River, and operating 134 mines.
The CHAIRMAN. What is the area that is owned by the members of the asso-
ciation, either owned or leased?
Mr. THURMOND. In acres?
The CHAIRMAN. Yes.
Mr. THURMOND. About 250,000.
The CHAIRMAN. All in Logan County?
Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir. No; I will qualify that; there are two small com-
panies in Lincoln County, but they are very small.
The CHAIRMAN. How many men are employed by the companies represented
in your association?
Mr. THURMOND. Between 9,000 and 10,000. The last record we undertook to
gather of them was approximately 9,650 men.
The CHAIRMAN. Are these properties what we call nonunion properties?
Mr. THURMOND. All of them.
The CHAIRMAN. What percentage of the miners of Logan County belong to
unions?
Mr. THURMOND. Only about 5 per cent, and none of them are in that part of
Logan County. I have a map here that I think will show.
Mr. Avis. He has a map here showing the location of every mine owner.

seat, and the dots indicate the location of the different mines.

dividing line between the waters of the Guyandol and the waters of Coal River.
The union mines are located on the part of the river indicated there, this being
Blair and this being Sharpless.
The CHAIRMAN. It is a small percentage of the county?
Mr. THURMOND. Yes; just that small portion.

46 SCHOOLS IN LOGAN COUNTY.
"The Logan District High School was organized 10 years ago as a third-
class school. Six years ago it was made a first-class school. It now has an
enrollment of 317 pupils, and employs 12 college-trained teachers. Courses are
offered in the following subjects: English, Latin, history, physics, chemistry,
biology, general science, sanitation, hygiene, cooking, sewing, home making,
typewriting, stenography, bookkeeping, commercial arithmetic, business Eng-
lish, manual training, mechanical drawing, algebra, plane and solid geometry,
French, and Spanish.
"Three years ago junior high schools were established at Omar, Holden,
Ethel, and Aracoma. The first three named being for white children, the one

each of these schools.
"At present there are 49 enrolled at Ethel, 29 at Omar, 14 at Holden, and
20 at Aracoma; 64.7 per cent of those enrolled at Logan come from the mining
towns in the Logan district.

tisement has to run four weeks. I am not positive about that, but I know it
has to run some time; I think four issues of the paper.

JACK DALTON VERSUS BILL BLIZZARD IN THESE TWO LEADERS ARE PERSONIFIED THE
CONFLICTING IDEALS THAT HAVE LED TO CIVIL WAR IN WEST VIRGINIA.
[By Boyden Sparkes.]
(EDITOR'S NOTE.-Mr. Sparkes, the author of this article, was sent down to
the scene of hostilities in West Virginia as the staff correspondent of a New
York newspaper. In the course of a thorough investigation of the conflict,
including interviews with the leaders on both sides, he exposed himself to rifle
fire and came away with bullet wounds in the leg and scalp. He insists, how-
ever, on a strict neutrality of attitude, since both sides shot at him.)
