In one of the old melodramas that toured the country before the movies came
along to provide daily thrillers the hero through clenched teeth would shout:
"Now, then, Jack Dalton, gimme them papers!"
Then came the awful struggle on the edge of the precipice. So it was some-
thing of a surprise to discover that Jack Dalton is still cast in the rôle of
villain in West Virginia's mine war, or at least that part of it which raged along
the Logan-Boone County line until the Federal troops forced a temporary sus-
pension of hostilities.
Jack Dalton is the principal owner of the largest nonunion coal operation in
West Virginia. He is president of the Maine Island Creek Coal Co., which is
operating about 27 mines on its 27,000 acres of Logan County coal land. It has
other property in other counties.
It was with the intention of forcing the unionization of those mines that a
red-badged army recently sought to invade Logan County from the neighboring
and unionized county of Boone. To that mob, or army, if you would have it so,
Jack Dalton represents "privilege" and "the interests" and "Wall Street,"
and yet he used to be a miner himself. His career, in fact, suggests one of
Horatio Alger's boy heroes and is complete justification for those who argue
that America offers every youth a chance to get to the top.
Bill Jones was the first man down there in the West Virginia hills to mention
Dalton to me. Jones is the general superintendent of the Maine Island Creek
Coal Co. I had gone with him to Omar, the center of their operations, to see
for myself how nonunion miners are treated by their employers. All shooting
had stopped two days before.
66
"You'll sleep in our president's house," said Jones, easing his six-shooter into
a fresh position on the front of his khaki breeches. He is in Huntington now,
but the house is open."
We mounted the steps of a large frame house with a pyramidal roof. On one
side were the railroad tracks. Across the muddy street was the rambling
Young Men's Civic Association, a clubhouse conducted by the company for
their employees. Unlocking the door, Jones led the way through a deserted
lower floor to a large bedroom upstairs. It was furnished in golden oak.
"Dalton's a great guy," said Jones. "He used to be a miner himself. Came
up here with $10,000 and opened up this field. We're getting out 40,000,000 tons
a year."
I went into the adjoining bathroom. It was as large as an ordinary apart-
ment house living room. The tub was enormous, and there was a wonderful
shower. Here was a miner's long-suppressed desire to be utterly clean and
free from coal grime finally expressed in several thousand dollars' worth of
plumbing. I used both baths and then crawled into the massive golden-
oak bed with an armful of newspapers. Reaching up a foot or so I found a
brass chain that controlled the lights. There was one light
* his job
was cutting weeds, and Dr. Henry D. Hatfield, former governor of West Vir-
ginia. These men are all vice presidents of Dalton's companies. Dalton and
Kelly also are operating several pretentious real estate developments and
possess some oil interests in Kentucky. I also learned that Dalton is single,
which may account for the golden-oak furniture.
* *
I met him the following day in Huntington, at the offices of the Maine
Island Creek Coal Co., which occupy an entire floor of one of Huntington's tall,
modern business buildings. He proved to be wide, stoop shouldered, clean
shaven, and dark. He is big, and when he shakes hands you feel the power
of muscles developed digging coal far back inside of a West Virginia mountain.
Dalton was in the room where his board of directors meet. This is furnished
in mahogany. Maps of his companies' properties hang on the wall. Half a
dozen of his executives were there. Each of them told me something about the
depredations of union miners. They whispered tragically of nationalization; of
the winter suffering of the Nation if ever the Guyan field is unionized and a
general strike is called. Dalton merely listened. He puffed steadily at a
black cigar, but sat impassive, sphinx-like.
One of his executives, when the boss was out of hearing, said: "He's a born
trader. He'd rather trade than eat."
But I think that the important thing is that he used to be a miner, a non-
union miner, and that he is determined that his miners shall continue to be
nonunion. When the unions are willing to use force to effect organization.
Jack Dalton is willing to use force to prevent it.


===== [扫描序号 892] =====
878
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
His weapon-and the weapon of the other coal operators in that field-is
Sheriff Don Chafin and his deputies. And whatever you may think of the sys-
tem, the coal operators pay their salaries, and the deputies make of Logan
County a region utterly unhealthy for union organizers and agitators. Be
sure, however, that Jack Dalton cares little what you think.
Chafin, whose mother was a Hatfield, a woman of the feudist clan, is called
the king of Logan County. Yet, if there were no Chafin I believe that Dalton
would have another king on the shrieval throne. Chafin is merely a convenient
instrument, ready forged and tempered with Hatfield blood.
So much for Logan County, where each miner deals independently with his
boss. Across the ridge in Boone County it is different. There collective
bargaining is the method of dealing between miners and operators; and, it
may be said, the operators there sing in a different key. Some of them openly
supported the miners' army when it mobilized there in the Coal River Valley.
If there is a king in Boone County I should say it was Bill Blizzard. At
least Blizzard was the dictator while the miners' army had a firing line that
extended the full length of the Logan-Boone County line. Blizzard is a sub-
district president of the United Mine Workers. His territory includes all of
Boone County, and would include Logan if that county was organized.
Blizzard arose from the ranks in the coal mines to the leadership of his
fellow miners. Ten years ago he worked in the mines of Cabin Creek and
played an important part during the strike of 1912 and 1913. His work was
recognized by the State Federation of Labor, and he was elected first assistant
to Secretary James Pauley, State secretary. Two years ago he was elected
president of subdistrict No. 1. I first saw him when the Federal troops entered
Madison. The miners' army-the red necks-then confronted along the ser-
rated top of Spruce Fork Ridge the hastily recruited defending army of Logan.
That defending force was neither a miners' nor an operators' army. It con-
tained miners, operators, bank clerks. school-teachers, grocers, haberdashers,
and any sort of man who could tote and fire a gun. A lot of them came from
other West Virginia counties. They came because West Virginia had no
National Guard nor any other force sufficient to cope with the miners' army,
but they were vastly outnumbered by their foes. That was why Gov. Morgan,
of West Virginia, appealed for Federal troops.
The Coal River division, a section of the Chesapeake & Ohio, about 60 miles
long, loading from St. Albans on the main line (15 miles west of Charleston,
W. Va.), south across Boone into Logan County, for two weeks had been oper-
ated as the miners dictated, except for one train a day, that carrying the
United States mails. Even on that the miners had exercised a strict super-
vision over the passengers. It had been the miners' main line of communica-
tion with the world outside the valley.
Up and down this valley foraging parties of armed miners had gone from
store to store in the small towns purchasing entire stocks of supplies with re-
ceipts promising payment from the United Mine Workers' organization. They
had even held drumhead court-martials.
Presumably as a sequel to one of these a Coal River Valley undertaker was
awakened at midnight one night by loud "hellos” and poundings on the front
of his house. When he looked out through a raised second-story window a
voice shouted: “Here's some work for you."
Something was dropped heavily on the undertaker's side porch. When he got
downstairs he found the body of a foreign-born miner. There was five bullet
holes in the jumper of the corpse. Later it was established that the man had
refused to serve in the overalled army.
That was the way Pancho Villa kept reluctant peons in the field. It has
been the way of military leaders since war began. It is the simple business of
making a soldier fear the firing line less than the firing squad. I do not know
that this was Blizzard's idea. But I do know that when Blizzard spoke, his
overalled soldiers hastened to obey.
Order in Coal River Valley had been kept by armed patrols in overalls, dis-
tinguished by red bandanna handkerchiefs knotted about their necks or bits
of red cloth tied to their sleeves. Seven moonshine stills were found hidden iu
the hollows of the hills and destroyed. Blizzard knew that he could keep his
men in hand only so long as he could keep them sober.
It was through this region that Capt. John J. Wilson's command of 150
picked Regulars traveled by night to the scene of hostilities. The engine of
the troop train pushed ahead of it three flat cars, two soldier lookouts riding at


===== [扫描序号 893] =====

879
the very front. Those extra cars were intended as a protection against ob-
structions on the track or explosive mines. The train ran along steadily at 20
miles an hour. Forty-five minutes ahead of it, although Capt. Wilson was
then unaware of it, there traveled a commandeered train loaded with miners
going to the front.
Two hours after the start from St. Albans the troop train entered Madison,
unionized seat of Boone County, and with a normal population of 700. This
night a number of its men were up on the Spruce Fork Ridge doing their best to
kill other men who dwelt in the seat of Logan County. It was civil war; no less.
As the train slowed down the assistant prosecutor of Boone County swung
aboard. His name was Hager, a lark, sharp-eyed little man, in a wrinkled
suit of light summer "store clothes. His knitted tie, almost thick enough to
deserve the title of muffler, flopped over his shoulder.
"We're glad you're here," he said to the first soldier he saw. "A com-
mandeered train went through here on the way to the fighting at Blair just
45 minutes ahead of you. Its been just terrible."
If Prosecutor Hager had been a woman, his state of mind might have been
diagnosed as hysteria. His breath came convulsively.
The bugler sounded "assembly."
"Packs and guns," shouted a sergeant, “fall in."
Buckling on their heavy packs, each rolled as neatly and smoothly as a
stove pipe, and running their fingers in a final pat over each stuffed pocket
of their cartridge belts. the Regulars dropped to the cinder-covered right of
way.
There they waited, immobile, while half their slender number was
selected for guard duty. Outposts with machine guns were sent up and down
the tracks. Sentries were stationed at 5-yard intervals 50 yards up the hill-
sides from the train. As the last of these took his post Blizzard appeared
and accosted Capt. Wilson.
"William M. Blizzard, subdistrict president of the United Mine Workers,”
he introduced himself. He was young, wiry, dark-eyed, cordial, and convincing.
He was short, almost undersized; Jack Dalton, physically, would make two
Blizzards. Yet when both men were merely coal miners with numbered brass
tags to identify them Blizzard probably loaded quite as much coal as Dalton.
The difference between them even then was mental. Where Dalton pos-
sessed the trading instinct, Blizzard was endowed--or accused, as you will-
with the spirit of the zealot. When Blizzard takes sides on any question I
can imagine that for him the other side is effaced.
Blizzard wore a weather-beaten, black-felt, narrow-brimmed hat, pulled low
over his eyes. He did not wear overalls, but his suit appeared to have been
slept in for a week. A necktie was knotted wrong side out against his soiled,
white collar.
"Are you the general of the miners' army," he was asked.
"What army?" countered Blizzard with a smile, and added: "I guess the
boys'll listen to me all right. I just told the captain here that if he'll send a
squad of his Regulars up the line with me I can get all our fellows out of the
hills by daylight."
Blizzard launched into an account of a bombing raid made on Blair that
day by what he described as a Baldwin-Felts airplane. With Blizzard all
missels launched by the defenders of Spruce Fork Ridge were from the guns
of Baldwin-Felts detectives. Yet he must have known that this was not true.
He must have known, too, that the men in that line facing his men had come
from all over West Virginia at a call from Gov. Morgan. Blizzard must have
known these things, because he had been moving at will between Charleston
and the miners' camps in the Coal River Valley. But, even so, he persisted
in speaking of his "foes" as "Baldwin-Felts thugs or “Don Chafin's dogs."
Blizzard, in fact, is an inveterate propagandist, with a propagandist's disregard
of facts.
Capt. Wilson searched Blizzard and discovered he was carrying a pistol-
"toting a short gun," as they express it in West Virginia.
The Army officer asked him if he had a permit. Blizzard produced one
signed by the sheriff of Kanawha County. Charleston is in Kanawha. Capt.
Wilson returned the gun.
"Does this mean you are going to allow only men with permits to keep their
guns?" asked Blizzard. Capt. Wilson said that those were his orders.
"The men on the other side of the ridge will keep theirs?"
If they have permits; yes.”

Blizzards's eyes flashed. For a moment he ceased to be the diplomat.
"Know what that means," he demanded. "Our boys'll be unarmed and those

He thought a moment. Then he spoke to a man standing near. This indi-

red badges had been snatched off. They were simly a swarm of stubbly-faced

could take them. But it was Blizzard who started them out.

(The telegram referred to above is printed in the record in full, as follows:)
BLUEFIELD, W. VA., May 28, 1920.
Gov. JOHN J. CORNWELL, Charleston, W. Va.
Senator WILLIAM S. KENYON, Washington, D. C.
On my return here from attending the funeral of my two brothers, who were
murdered in the Matewan tragedy on Wednesday, May 19, I was shown several
press dispatches from John L. Lewis, president of the United Mine Workers of
America, and other officials of his organization on the subject of this tragedy,
request ng the Government to make an investigation of this affair and events
leading up to it.
The statements made in these telegrams are an insult to the intelligent law-
abiding people of this State, and his purpose could only have been to influence
public opinion in behalf of those respons ble for this crime.
There were no disturbances in these coal fields until two months ago, when
Lewis's emissaries were sent into Mingo County and started their agitation in
effort to organize these fields.
The miners and their families, throughout the entire Norfolk & Western
fields, were living in peace and happiness and enjoying as great prosperity as
any coal fields in the United States; and it was the bolshevistic teachings of
these emissaries which resulted in our men being wantonly and maliciously
murdered through one of the foulest plots that ever disgracel a State.
Not being satisfied with murder, the helpless bodies of their victims were
shot, maltreated, and robbed as they lay on the ground. In their greed for
plunder they even stole the Masonic Shriner's pin from the lapel of my brother's
coat.
The attempt on the part of the United Mine Workers to organize these fields
was not unexpected, since it was demonstrated during the coal strike of last
winter that the nonunion fields were able to prevent the country from freezing
and made it ´mpossible for the mine workers' organization to place the people
of the entire nation at their mercy.
We resent the cowardly libel given to the press of the United States by the
sheriff of Mingo County and the Matewan police, in which charged that Albert
Felts, one of the murdered men, started the trouble by firing a shot through
his coat pocket into the body of Mayor Testerman.
Albert Felts's dead body, as well as the other men, were left lying in the
streets at Matewan within a stone's throw of the home of Sheriff Blankenship,
and if he had wanted the truth, an examination of Albert Felts's coat would

I have before me copy of a news item dated Charleston, W. Va., June 9,
purporting to be a copy of telegram from Fred Mooney, secretary-treasurer
of District 17 of United Mine Workers of America to Attorney General Palmer,
Gov. Morrow, of Kentucky, and Senator France, of Maryland, in which he
charges among other things that Baldwin-Feltz detectives are terrorizing the
miners in Pike County, Ky., and that on last Saturday they broke into the
house of a miner, beat him into insensibility and shot him.
This is a malicious and cowardly falsehood without one word or semblance
of truth and could have been invented for no other purpose than to slander
us, and take advantage of the press to dissimilate their libelous propaganda.
We do not even have a representative in Pike County, and Mr. Mooney well
knows that it is the county officers and the good citizens of Pike County who
object to his paid agitators and trouble makers coming into that county and
starting a reign of lawlessness, as they did in Mingo County.
They also prophesy another tragedy which will make the Matewan affair
look like 30 cents.
It is not hard to prophesy the result of a game when the cards are already
stacked. Mr. Mooney does not seem to be satisfied with the bloody orgy which
occurred at Matewan recently for which his organization stands condemned in
the eyes of the public, but he would heap insult upon this terrible injury by
slandering the organization with which the murdered men were connected.

BALDWIN-FELTS DETECTIVES (INC.),
Bluefield, W. Va., September 29, 1921.
DEAR SIR: Many of the newspapers of the country have, within the past 30
days, published numerous statements from radical leaders connected with the
United Mine Workers' organization, bearing on the attempted invasion of
Logan County, etc., by the army of bolshevists connected with their organiza-
tion. Among the many excuses they have given for their lawless acts, is the
statement that "their army proceeded to march to Logan, where a large num-
ber of Baldwin-Felts guards were stationed, for the purpose of cleaning them
out of the State. These are the exact words of Philip Murray, vice president
of the United Mine Workers of America, in some of his newspaper utterances
and also embodied in his annual report made to the recent convention of the
United Mine Workers of America, held at Indianoplis, as shown in a published
report of that meeting under date of September 20, 1921.
In answer to some of their public utterances, I issued a statement, which was
published in a number of the newspapers of the country, in which I declared
most emphatically that "not a single man connected with our organization has
been employed in either Mingo or Logan Counties, in the capacity of guards or
other like service, since the Mingo strike was called more than a year ago, and
to the further fact that we have not had a man doing service of any kind in
Logan County for a period of more than 10 years."
For your information, I am attaching hereto a copy of my statement, pub-
lished in the newspapers under date of September 2, 1921. There can scarcely
be a doubt but that my public statement through the press was read by the
mine workers' officials and, notwithstanding my denial, they continue to prate
about the Baldwin-Felts mine guards in Logan and Mingo Counties. It is, there-
fore, evident that they have an utter disregard for the truth of their public
utterances.

SEPTEMBER 2, 1921.
My attention has been directed to an Associated Press dispatch sent out from
Indianapolis, under date of August 29, quoting John L. Lewis's reply to Gov.
Morgan's criticism of him for his failure to control his army of armed miners,
who are members of the United Mine Workers' organization, for their unlawful
attempt to invade the nonunion coal fields of Logan County, etc.
In this public statement, Mr. Lewis takes another rap at the Baldwin-Felts
agency in suggesting to the governor "that he compel the surrender and dis-
armament of the Baldwin-Felts private army now operating in the coal fields in
that State," etc. It is with the greatest reluctance and with a sense of humilia-
tion that I am forced into, which the public might term a newspaper controversy
with a man who has such little regard for his public utterances. Mr. Lewis's
statements to the press in regard to a serious situation which is engaging the
attention of the whole country, and in which all good citizens of the State of
West Virginia are especially concerned, are deceptions of such magnitude that
the public should know the truth.
Mr. Lewis is either the worst informed man in the United States, or he is the
most ingenious at deception, because everyone acquainted with conditions in
Logan and Mingo Counties know that the Baldwin-Felts Agency has no part in
the Mingo labor controversy or the affairs of Logan County. The county authori
ties, as well as the citizens in the counties named, will attest to the fact that not
a single man connected with our organization has been employed in either county
in the capacity of guards or other like service since the Mingo strike was called
more than a year ago, and to the further fact that we have not had a man doing
service of any kind in Logan County for a period of more than 10 years. It is
deplorable that the citizens of the State of West Virginia, as well as all news-
paper readers, should be so grossly deceived by a man in Mr. Lewis's position,
and I submit that it is unfair for him to use his position as president of the
mine workers' organization to mislead the public by his utterances through the
press on a question of such great moment to the people of our entire country.
It ill behooves President Lewis to talk about the detectives and other officers
of the law, when he knows that his organization is directly responsible for the
thousands of armed marauders, who, at this moment, are marching under the
red flag, directed and led by his lieutenants, defying the laws of the State, as
well as of the United States, and committing almost every excess known to the
law.
Then, why all this camouflage on the part of Mr. Lewis? Why do they at-
tempt to make us the goat and try to justify themselves at the expense of the
Baldwin-Felts agency? There is but one reason, and that is because Mr. Lewis
well knows that if the truth of the matter should be made known as to the
real conditions and motives for the attempted invasion of Logan County by
their army of bolshevists, his organization would stand condemned in the eyes
of every law-abiding and patriotic American, no matter whether he belongs to
a labor union or not. The first excuse they offered for the unlawful march of
the army of insurrectionists from the Kanawha mining district was that "it
was a protest against Gov. Morgan's proclamation of martial law in Mingo
County," and this bold and defiant statement was heralded to the world through
the public press. The statement appeared in the newspapers of this State time
and again and can not be denied. Afterwards, Mr. Lewis sends a message from
Indianapolis to the President of the United States and also declared in a state-
ment given to the press, that the attempted invasion of Logan Couny on the
part of his armed miners was on account of the Baldwin-Felts guards, thugs,
and other favorite expressions of his, which are characteristic of his libelous
propaganda and long-range abuse which they are accustomed to sending out
through the press against our organization whenever a strike is called, although
we may be operating within 100 miles of the zone of trouble.

887
If they are after the Baldwin-Felts guards or detectives, why on earth do
they want to march into Logan or Mingo Counties, when they know they will
not find a single one of them within the borders of either county? The coal
miners of Logan County are not organized and they never have been; therefore,
it is only a logical conclusion that the attempted invasion of that county was
originated for the purpose, of shooting 'em up, to shoot up nonunion miners
who are at work, and to shoot up the State constabulary force and the sheriff'
and his force of deputies, who are trying to uphold the law and protect life
and property. There can be no doubt as to the real motive of the invading
hordes whom Lewis says are going after the Baldwin-Felts detectives or guards
where there are none and where none have been for more than 10 years. Looks
as if they are on a cold trail, don't it? The good people of West Virginia are
awakening to the truth, just as the citizens of Mingo have been aroused by the
horrible methods employed by the United Mine Workers to extend their organi-
zation into the nonunion fields of that county.
In their cry of wolf they have substituted the name of the Baldwin-Felts
agency for so long that the good people of the State are beginning to open their
eyes to its true meaning and to realize that they are only trying to use us as ·
a screen to hide the real motives and activities of their organization from the
eyes of the public. The United Mine Workers of America have but one motive,
but one purpose, and that is to extend their organization into the nonunion
fields of the State, no matter if they have to resort to violence and intimidation
by force of arms and bloodshed. Mr. Lewis had just as well stand behind his
guns. On his flying trip to Bluefield, W. Va., about 18 months ago, and only
about 2 months before they started their campaign of agitation and organizing
in Mingo County, he sent out. a dispatch from Bluefield through the press in
which he declared his intention to "organize the nonunion fields of the southern
part of West Virginia."
Their failure to win the nation-wide strike, which was called on the 1st of
November, 1919, and to freeze the people of the United States into submitting
to their terms, was due to the miles and miles of “black diamonds" which con-
tinued to pour out. in a steady stream from the nonunion fields in this section
of the State; and while the eyes of a gracious people were directed to the non-
union coal mines in the southern part of West Virginia, the mine workers'
officials were casting about and devising ways and means to secure a foothold
for their organization in these fields, so that they could shut down the mining
industry entirely in case of a future strike of nation-wide proportion.

President of the United States, Washington, D. C.:
My attention has been called to an Associated Press dispatch sent out from
Madison, W. Va., dated August 26, authorized by C. F. Keeney, president of
District 17, United Mine Workers of America, commenting on a telegram from
John L. Lewis, president of the United Mine Workers of America, from In-
dianapolis, same date, directed by you, referring to the industrial conflict in
Mingo County, the unlawful march of thousands of armed miners from Kanawha
County, etc., in which Keeney quoted President Lewis as saying to you, among
other things, that the march of miners in West Virginia was declared by Mr.
Lewis in his message to the President to be "a sense of outrage against the de-
tectives employed by the operators." "These detectives," the message asserted,
were men of the "lowest type and character" who "kill as a part of their daily
work." The Baldwin-Felts Detective Agency, of Roanoke, Va., was named
as the employer of the detectives who, it was averred, were practically in con-
trol of the county governments of Logan, Mingo, McDowell, and Mercer Counties,
W. Va."
66
I want to brand the above statement of President Lewis, as quoted by Keeney,
as absurdly and maliciously false in every regard. It is in keeping with the
pernicious and lying propaganda which their criminal organization has repeat-
edly sent out through the press of the country since the industrial troubles
started in Mingo more than a year ago.
Our organization has nothing whatever to do with the county government in
Logan, Mingo, McDowell, and Mercer Counties, W. Va. Its sole object and
purpose is the maintenance and preservation of law and order, and it has the
utmost reverence for the Constitution of the United States.

Mr. WALSH. During the time he was chief of police?

Mr. WALSH. Where is Galax; what county?
Mr. FELTS. It is in Virginia. Another one of the men who was down there

number of years-the United States Army. He served two or three years as
a captain in France; two years, I believe, and a fraction. He had been dis-
charged from Army service, of course, after the armistice. Walter Anderson
was another one of the men; his brother, Tim Anderson, who was a lieutenant
in the overseas service. He was in France about two years. He was another
one of the men. A man by the name of Boor, who was killed at Matewan, was
on the police force at Bristol for a number of years, a most excellent officer.
Mr. WALSH. Working for you or your firm while he was a policeman?
Mr. FELTS. Yes, sir; he came with as good a recommendation as any officer
that was ever appointed-

Mr. FELTS. Afterwards. I say he was working for the company at the time
he was killed.
There was a man by the name of Ferguson, chief of police at one time of
Princeton, in Mercer County. He was deputy sheriff there one time, and came
with splendid recommendations, recommended by all the county authorities
there. Ferguson was in my service. He was killed at Matewan.
There was a man by the name of Powell. I think Mr. Slemp recommended
Powell to me, perhaps. I know he was on the police force at Marion for years,
and he was a most excellent man. He came with the most excellent reputation.
He was one of the men who was killed there.
There was a man by the name of Cunningham. Cunningham had been in
my service for seven or eight years. He was born in Pennsylvania, I believe,
but he was living in Mercer County at that time. I employed him in the Cabin
and Paint Creek strike troubles many years ago. Cunningham had a great
deal of experience, both as secret service man and as an officer. He was con-
nected with the Government service during the war in connection with fur-
nishing protection to the munition plants. He was a very high-class man. He
was a thirty-second degree Mason and belonged to a number of fraternal or-
ganizations. Every one of those men-
Mr. DAVIS. How about Buchanan?
Mr. FELTS. Buchanan was an overseas man, an ex-service man. He won the
highest medal that was given to any soldier from West Virginia.
Mr. WALSH. Was he killed at Matewan?
Mr. FELTS. No, sir; he was there, but he made his escape.
Mr. WALSH. How many men in your organization were killed at Matewan?
Mr. FELTS. Seven.
Mr. WALSH. How many did you have there altogether?
Mr. FELTS. I think there were about 13 there that day. My two brothers
were killed. One of my brothers was a graduate of Milligan College, Tenn.,
and had his A. B. diploma and belonged to two or three fraternal organiza-
tions; a man of affairs, a high-toned Christian gentleman, connected with the
church.
My other brother was a thirty-second degree Mason and a Shriner, and
was our field superintendent--a man who was as honorable as any man you
will find anywhere. There was not any man down there connected with that
service that any man could say aught against, and they would compare with
the men of our organization, I suppose.
Mr. WALSH. Who had charge of the recruiting of the men for your organi-
zation?
Mr. FELTS. We do not have out recruits. They are employed in various ways.
We get applications from men all over the United States for a position.
Those applications--whenever we get a letter from a man making application
we have a blank that we send him which requires him to give his name, age,
names of his parents and their business, and his business, and all about
himself, and 15 or 20 references, the names of all his employers for the last
10 years, and we investigate that man. If he seems to be a suitable man for
our work, why, we investigate him.
Mr. WALSH. Approximately how many men did you have in your employ
all over the United States in May of 1920?
Mr. FELTS. Well, I could not tell you that offhand, sir.
Mr. WALSH. Does the force expand and contract from time to time with
reference to labor trouble-that is, if there is labor trouble at a place do you
put on more men?
Mr. FELTS. No, sir. I just want to say this to you in connection with the
labor proposition: Many years ago we used to furnish a good many men for
guard service. During the Cabin and Paint Creek strikes, Senator, the
troubles you investigated over there, I suppose we had a hundred guards over
there at that time protecting property. I used to think that it was an hon
orable and a legitimate and commendable work to furnish service to guard
property or protect property and life, no matter whether it was labor dis-
turbances or what the emergency was. I think so yet, as far as that is con-
cerned. But that sort of work causes a good deal of trouble. We have had
a good many of our men killed. We had a good many of our men assasinated
during the Cabin and Paint Creek strike, some of the very best men we ever
had in the service.
Mr. WALSH. What year was it, please, that the peak of the trouble was
reached in Cabin Creek?

receiving compensation from you and making reports to you daily, or as fre-
quently as your company demands?
Mr. FELTS. Absolutely not true; sir.
Mr. WALSH. Just tell how your under-cover men work.
Mr. FELTS. I want to answer that a little further.
Mr. WALSH. Certainly.
Mr. FELTS. I want to tell you if I have got a man in my service to-day that
even belongs to the United Mine Workers of America I don't know it, and I have
never had occasion in any other labor organization to put secret-service men for
any purpose. I have found it necessary in a good many instances in recent
years in investigation-criminal investigations-in sections where they had a
United Mine Workers' organization for those men to become members of the
mine workers' organization. It was necessary. In the first place, a man could
not secure employment in the union field unless he joined the union, but I do
not maintain any service for keeping up with the general activities of the
United Mine Workers of America.
But, as I said a moment ago, and I want to repeat, I never had a man to my
knowledge in my life that ever joined any other organization-labor organiza-
tion.
Mr. WALSH. Was Mr. Lively working for you when he was an officer of the
United Mine Workers?
Mr. FELTS. I never knew anything about his being an officer but the one
time, and I will have to, in answer to that, refer to Colorado.
The CHAIRMAN. If that is necessary to answer the question.
Mr. FELTS. Well, sir, there were five or six men murdered at La Veta, Colo.,
supposedly by members of the United Mine Workers of America. The attorney
general of Colorado wanted me to put a secret-service man down there to try
to get information. I sent Lively from the East out there. He went to La Veta,
Colo., and joined the union and ferreted out that crime, and in about three
months after he landed I think he was secretary of that local, and if he ever.
got any higher there or elsewhere, I know nothing about it.
Mr. WALSH. Was he also a member of the union in West Virginia at the time
of this trouble?
Mr. FELTS. The only time that he was ever a member of the union in West
Virginia during the time he has been connected with my organization, that I
recall, was when I sent him to Raleigh County to investigate what they called
the Glen-White shooting case. It was a union case. He went there and in-
vestigated those shooting cases, and it was necessary for him to join the
union over there. He stayed over there about a year, and was a member of
the union perhaps during that time, and his work over there showed the
necessity for his joining the union over there, because it resulted in the arrest
and conviction of nearly all the officers of District 29, many of whom were
sent to the penitentiary as a result of Lively's investigation over there.
Mr. WALSH. That was in West Virginia?
Mr. FELTS. That was in West Virginia, in Raleigh County.
Mr. WALSH. Did he act as an officer of the miners' union while employed
by you up until the time he testified in the Matewan case?
Mr. FELTS. So far as I know and understand, he never joined the union down
there. If he did, I did not know anything about it, until about the time these
troubles occurred; as I tell you, I sent him to Mingo County to investigate a
store robbery at Red Jacket, and afterwards sent him to investigate the burn-
ing of a tipple at Charleroi, and after these murders were committed at
Matewan, it was necessary to get a man in there to get up evidence against
those people for the purpose of prosecuting them, and of course, Lively was a
member of the union at that time.
Mr. WALSH. Was he a member of the union in Mingo County at the time
these men were sent to Sprig?

stance of people interested or of the Government. Is that correct?
Mr. FELTS. That is correct, sir. I started to detail a little introduction. I
would just like to read that and give it to you. The Baldwin-Felts Agency was
organized about 30 years ago. The business of this agency is that of general
detective work, the principal work being purely of a secret-service nature,
conducting both civil and criminal investigations.
We furnish service to corporations, individuals, State, county, municipal
authorities, and the Government, as well as cooperating with the Federal, State.
county, and municipal authorities in the suppression and investigation of
crimes of every sort and character in connection with violations of both the
Federal and State laws.
Our agency does not operate for awards nor accept employment contingent
on convictions. We do no spotting for public-service corporations or shadow-

ing. We do not take divorce cases of any kind, have not for 30 years since

pose of asking to come before the committee in connection with one matter, and
it was then that I was called away for the first time. On account of illness in
my family I had to leave.
A man by the name of Winthrop D. Lane, posing as a newspaper reporter,
came to Bluefield, and was introduced to me by a very reputable gentleman,
and a mighty good friend of mine, as a reliable newspaper reporter. He came
over to my office and I gave him about three hours of my time and took him to
lunch and treated him as courteously as I would any man whom I believed to
be a gentleman. He went away from there and he wrote up a story about con-
ditions over in West Virginia, which was afterwards published in a book. I
have not that book with me-I thought I had-entitled, "Civil War in West
Virginia." That book has been sent broadcast over the United States and
been handed around this desk, as I understand; been advertised pretty exten-
sively around Washington. And I got hold of that book.
Among the other lying statements-I want to say in the beginning that I
want to brand that publication as false from cover to cover, and there never
was an outrage as wrongful and as contemptible an outrage ever committed by
any man posing as a reputable newspaper man as that publication.
In that publication he had what purported to be letters found on the body
of my brother-one of my brothers who was murdered at Matewan, and those
letters-I don't know where he got them-got them at Mingo, I understand.

Mr. Avis. If you will excuse me, I think you might tell the committee about

the trouble and expense you went to.
Mr. FELTS. My brother had a warrant that day for Sid Hatfield. That war-
rant was issued by the justice of the peace, one of the most honorable men in
the county, a merchant named Stafford; I have known him 20 years. And
he issued that warrant for Sid Hatfield. They found out he was in Matewan
that day. The warrant called for Sid Hatfield and Ed Chambers and two or
three others for releasing prisoners.
It seems Dan Mooney, a mine worker, had come to Stacker and assaulted a
doctor there. He had been brought before Squire Stafford, who tried and sen-
tenced him to jail. A man named Hatfield was conveying him to prison. Going
through Matewan, Sid Hatfield, the chief of police, Ed Chambers, his lieutenant,
and some others of their gang, took this prisoner away from them by force
and liberated him and Hatfield went before Squire Stafford to get a warrant
for Sid Hatfield and others. Dr. Rutherford was present at the time. The
squire asked Hatfield if he was going to execute the warrant. No; he said he
would be afraid to do it. Dr. Rutherford says, "Albert Felts is down there to-
day. Direct the warrant to him."
Dr. Rutherford is now the superintendent of the miners' hospital at Welch.
So he directed the warrant to Albert Felts; sent it down there by an em-
ployee of the Norfolk & Western Railroad Co., to deliver to Albert at Matewan
that day.
Now, they wanted to get rid of that warrant, because as long as that war-
rant was in existence they had no excuse, of course they knew that--for these
murders. So they destroyed that warrant, evidently, and forced a bogus war-
rant made out-a bogus warrant—and panned it off as the warrant that Albert
Felts had.
So I saw that warrant, and during the trials down there we succeeded in
getting the handwriting of one Dan Chambers, the brother of one of the de-
fendants, and one of the principal witnesses down there. In fact, he was con-
nected with several of these defendants. At the time he forged this warrant,
Dan Chambers was clerk in the bank-bookkeeper-at Matewan.
So Dan Chambers had filled out this warrant. As soon as I saw Dan
Chambers's handwriting and-and so did my attorneys; they all recognized it
was the same handwriting as appeared in this warrant. Any amateur could
tell that. There was no attempt in the world to disguise the handwriting.
I submited a copy of that-I had it photographed his handwriting photo-
graphed and the warrant photographed, and I sent a copy here to Dr. Hill, an
expert, assistant to the Director of the Bureau of Engraving. I believe. I sent
another copy to an expert on handwriting in Pittsburgh by the name of Wood;
I sent another to a man by the name of Malone, at Baltimore; all of them of
national reputation. And each of them gave me a statement to the effect that
these handwritings were the same. Of course, anybody could tell that.
Well, I brought those people down there to testify in that case, and they
went on the stand, all three of them, and swore unqualifiedly that Dan Cham-
bers had filled out that forged warrant.

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
THURSDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1921.
UNITED STATES SENATE,
COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION AND LABOR,
Washington, D. C.
The committee met, pursuant to adjournment, at 10 o'clock a. m., in the
committee room, Capitol, Senator Kenyon presiding.
Present: Senators Kenyon (chairman), Sterling, McKellar, and Walsh.
TESTIMONY OF MR. WILLIAM H. COOLIDGE, CHAIRMAN OF THE
BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF THE ISLAND CREEK COAL CO.
Mr. VINSON. State your name to the committee.
Mr. COOLIDGE. My name is William H. Coolidge.
Mr. VINSON. State your residence and occupation.
Mr. COOLIDGE. I live in Manchester, Mass. My office is in Boston, Mass.
am a lawyer, and I am chairman of the board of directors of the Island Creek
Coal Co.; not the Main Island Creek Coal Co., but the Island Creek Coal Co.
Mr. VINSON. Those are two separate corporations?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Absolutely.
Mr. VINSON. Mr. Coolidge, when did you become interested in Logan County
coal?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I have been counsel for and a director of mining companies
and other companies in a great many different States of the Union.
Associated with me especially was Mr. Albert F. Holden, of Cleveland, who
was probably the most eminent mining engineer in this country, of all kinds.
At least, nobody was a better engineer. We examined, under his direction,
alleged coal mines and coal mines in various States--for instance, out in Iowa,
and finally there was brought to our attention by Mr. McManus, of Parkers-
burg, W. Va., and Mr. Vinson, of Huntington, an alleged coal property in
Logan County, W. Va. At that time there were no coal mines in West Virginia.
Mr. VINSON. In Logan County?
Mr. COOLIDGE. In Logan County. This property was 40 miles away from the
railroad-the Chesapeake & Ohio. It was across the mountains from the
Norfolk & Western. Mr. Holden and myself; Mr. H. S. Kimball, who is now
one of the vice presidents of the Emergency Fleet Corporation and who was
associated with us; and Mr. Edward A. Clark, of Boston, who was also asso-
ciated, came down and went over the mountain and saw this property. There
were, I think, no houses; at the most, one house. It had been timbered, and
there were a few coal openings on this property. The town of Logan was a
little apparently two or three hundred inhabitants town. We had the coal
investigated and examined, and as a result the Island Creek Coal Co. was
formed, having purchased in all about 30,000 acres of ground in which the
engineers have estimated there were something like 500,000,000 tons of coal.
We went ahead in 1902; we obtained everything that went into the property
out of the property, with the exception of machinery and hardware. The
bricks were made from clay found on the property. We had our own stone
quarries. We had our own sawmills. In other words, under Mr. Holden's
direction we built what we believed to be the best coal property of bituminous
coal anywhere. We got out our first coal in 1905, or the last part of 1904.
In building the property, knowing the advantage of having something that
would be attractive for everybody, we built our houses, as we believed, better
907

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
than anybody else's. We put in everything that tended to efficiency and low
cost of mining. We kept out liquor. We have done everything we knew how
to make it a first-class mining concern. And, among other things, having in the
West had experience with the Western Federation of Miners, we kept out and
have continued to keep out, and propose, if possible, and the laws still permit,
to keep out the United Mine Workers of America.
We are now producing at the rate of 3,000,000 tons per annum. This year
we shall produce about a million tons more than last year. We are paying
higher wages to our men, and they are earning more money, I believe, than
corresponding work is earning in any union mine in this country. We have not
reduced wages yet. If the price of coal permits, we should not reduce our
wages. We have not profiteered. We did not charge last year at any time
more than $5 per ton, which was an enormous price, although we were offered-
not asked-$15 per ton for thousands of tons of coal. We advised, as counsel
of the company, that the Lever Act did not apply, but we believed then and
we believe now that it was good business to sell the coal at a reasonable price.
The average price which we received last year was about $3.50 a ton. The aver-
age price we are receiving this year will be less than $3 per ton.
The wages which we are paying to-day are from two to three times the wages
that were being paid in 1915. We have beaten the union organizers to the price
of wages. We have been ahead of them and have raised our wages before any
authorities or anybody else suggested it.
We believe that we are doing the best thing that can be done for the produc-
tion of coal and for the benefit and advantage not only of ourselves but also of
the consumers.
As I understand it, this committee has asked the operators on the one side
and the laborers' unions on the other to discuss what you call fundamentals and
what the remedy for the trouble is.
The CHAIRMAN. We shall be glad to know.
Mr. COOLIDGE. To that end I am going just to talk to you for a few moments
and see if I can express the issue in this case.
Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, there is but one issue in this case: Shall the
United Mine Workers get possession of the remaining nonunion mines and thus,
like the United Mine Workers of Great Britain, be able to freeze and starve
the people of the United States; to stop all industry unless they can have their
way?
That is the only issue before this committee, and it is the only issue before the
Congress. All the other alleged issues are but red herring drawn across the
trail of the real issue.
It is the purpose of the United Mine Workers, first, to unionize the mines,
and then increase their demand for their labor, and keep on in a progressive
increase until at last it will not be worth while for anyone to own the mines,
and then take possession of them themselves.
That was the testimony of Bishop Donohue, given to this same committee
eight years ago, as the sworn statement of the vice president of the union.
That is the end and aim of this organization. It is the same aim that the
Amalgamated Garment Workers have in New York. It apparently is a good
deal the same aim as the Plumb idea in connection with the railroads.
The United Mine Workers' constitution which contained the claim that
they were entitled to an equitable share of the fruits of their labor was delib-
erately, after argument in convention, changed in 1912 to a demand that they
were entitled to the full social value of their labor. They stated what they
meant when they changed their constitution, just as any bill introduced by this
or any other committee and containing special words would be explained. They
said that they meant that the "man who employs us will receive no compensa-
tion for the money he has invested."
It is this organization which the nonunion operators of Logan decline to
discuss. We decline to deal. We decline to sit around a table with our feet
and their feet under the table to see if we can come to an arrangement.
Mr. Chairman, we just as much decline to talk with them, knowing what
they intend, as we would decline to sit down and talk with a robber or any
other man who told us that when he got the power he intended to take our
property away from us. There is no use in discussing with a man whose aim
and object is to take away your property when he can.
What they now want to do and what Mr. Lewis says they must win the fight
in Mingo on, is in some way, using all the power they have, to unionize the West
Virginia mines before the 1st of next April, at which time, if they can unionize

909
the West Virgin'a mines, they will have a hundred and ten million people of this
country by the throat.
It is simply to prevent that that we are using all our power and propose to
continue to use all our power. It was the 30 per cent of the bituminous coal
of this country that was not unionized that saved this country in November,
1919, when they staged their strike and, regardless of the people of this coun-
try, would have continued to strike; but we, the nonunion mines, prevented their
freezing the people then. We propose, with the help of this committee and
the help of every legislative body, to prevent their freezing this country next
spring, and to prevent their stopping industry. The railroad brotherhoods,
regardless of the interests of the public, are attempting to stage a strike to
stop business. If the people of this country knew that 30 per cent of the
engineers and 30 per cent of the firemen and 30 per cent of the conductors and
30 per cent of the brakemen on every road of this country would be protected,
and knew that they would not strike, they would not care much what the other
70 per cent would do.
It is to keep this 30 per cent protected so that it can prevent these gentlemen
from attempting, at least, to freeze and starve the people of the United States,
that we have remained and propose to remain nonunion.
We do not object to union men coming to our mines. We do not ask whether
or not they are union men. I am informed that several hundred out of the
2,500 of our miners are union men, and I speak only for the company of which
I happen to be the chairman of the board of directors. We do not ask them
whether they are union men; but if we find that they are agitating, then we
ask them to leave our employ and go to more congenial quarters. If our con-
ditions, if our opportunities are so deplorable as counsel for the other side call
them, God knows we do not want them to stay with us. We prefer they should
go to better conditions.

The CHAIRMAN. As you are getting right down to some interesting funda-

Mr. Chairman, it is not a problem of industrial democracy; it is a question
of industrial autocracy. It is a demand of the United Mine Workers, or.
rather, their leaders, to get control of a necessity of life. In a word, to
establish a soviet government. Lenin and Trotski demanded no more. Even
the American Federation of Labor, in their convention in 1919, passed a reso-

to get class control of the United States, and we are opposed to it. At a
time when the people of the United States are beginning to understand the
aim and object of the closed shop, there are some unions that apparently

the people, the 105,000,000, notify the 5,000,000 that no class in this country
can take possession of the United States.

We hear about peaceful assembly-the right of peaceful assembly. Why,
Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, there is no right of peaceful assembly in a
street without a permit. The street is for the people to pass and repass.
There is no right of these gentlemen to assemble on my property or in my house,
on your property or in your house. If you invite them, they come, but if you
invite them not to come you have the right to have them stay away. They
have no right of peaceful assembly per se. They have the right if they get
permission. They have the right of free speech, but they have no right of
free speech which aims at robbery, murder, arson, and insurrection. They
claim the right of collective bargaining. They mean by that that a few
leaders in Indianapolis of a few representatives shall get together on the one
side and make demands on the other. There is an equal right guaranteed
by the Constitution-a constitutional right-of individual contract; and the

Mr. COOLIDGE. As I said, they object to us having guards, mine guards, so

I have not any objection, Mr. Chairman, to Mr. Gompers having a paid police-
man to guard him. I do not object when the bank automobiles go around
with money to having a policeman ride on the bank wagon. I have not any
objection to having every hotel have a policeman.
Mr. VINSON. In that connection, Mr. Coolidge, have you an idea as to the
amount of money required by your company in its pay rolls to be paid to your
employees?
Mr. COOLIDGE. As I thought I stated, our paymasters pay out in money each
month about $300.000; that is, in cash. And unless we have some protection
we would be open to the attack of robbers or anybody else. We feel we have
a right to that protection, and if the State laws do not fix it so we can get it
we feel we have a right to have somebody with authority to be armed to pro-
tect us.
Now, they complain that these deputy sheriffs kept their organizers out of
the county. So everybody whose picture is in the rogues' gallery in New
York complains that they are not permitted down around lower Broadway, but
the rest of the people do not complain. And we keep out the organizers of the
United Mine Workers for exactly the same reason that those whose pictures
are in the rogues' gallery are kept out of lower New York. Not because we
know and not because they know why they are there, but because we know what
will happen if they stay there. And we claim the right to keep out those who
will, as the evidence has shown for years and years, will be the result of their
coming in.
The CHAIRMAN. When you say keep out" what do you mean-keep them

Mr. COOLIDGE. Out of our property primarily; and apparently the sheriff

just the same-
The CHAIRMAN (interposing). Now, wait a minute.
Mr. COOLIDGE (continuing). Just the same as any known breaker of the law

The CHAIRMAN. But if the sheriff thought that joining the Methodist Church

what always has happened-as it has in Alabama, Arkansas, all over the coun-

Our men receive, I have stated, higher wages; our men are paid for efficiency.
We pay day labor, some of it, $4.50; some of it $7 for an 8-hour day. We pay our
loaders by the car. The cars are not of the same size. They are paid different
prices. These loaders know how many shovel fuls it takes to fill a car. The
amount that is paid to those loaders, the evidence that has been heretofore intro-
duced, shows that they get more in a month than they can get from any of the
organized fields per month, although they are paid, as they have an impression,
at a higher rate per ton.
Our men have steadier employment. While the union fields, the Kanawha,
etc., are loafing a good share of the time, our men are working 26 days a month,
if they so desire.

Our company is obliged, as every other employer of labor is obliged, to report
to the internal revenue department those whose amounts received exceed $1,000.
In 1919, we reported 857 men.
The CHAIRMAN. Out of how many?
Mr. COOLIDGE. About 1,400 at that time, as I recollect it. Eight hundred and
fifty-seven men who received an average of $1,790 per annum. That does not
include the foremen and those above. Those are the names on the pay roll.
In 1920 we reported 1,031 men who received $1,770.
The CHAIRMAN. Out of how many men?
Mr. COOLIDGE. There were 1,800.
The average for the whole 1,800 was $1,476, and that is whether they were
there awhile or stayed the whole year, because this includes all the men. About
60 to 70 per cent of our men are steady and about 30 per cent are migratory,
going back and forth. The older men stay and the young men travel around.
Mr. VINSON. They work a few days at a time and then leave.
Mr. COOLIDGE. Some do; but in our case we believe that the opportunities
which they get make our employees more steady than in most fields.
Senator STERLING. They have no requirements as to hours of work a day?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Eight hours is the limit.
Senator STERLING. The limit?
Mr. COOLIDGE. That is the limit. It is an 8-hour day for day labor, and I don't
believe there is anybody ever works more than 8 hours where they are paid by
the ton or by the car. It is an 8-hour day.
This year of course, this year has not been made up, but this year, by reason
of adding mines and building railroads up Mud Fork, we had 2,503 men in all on
our pay roll, and they averaged, all of them, $141 per month.
The conditions down there are not deplorable. The rents are $2 per room.
They are the same now-
Senator STERLING. I did not get that statement.

ago. Houses that we were able to build for $400 or $500 15 years ago cost
us $1,600 last year. The rent is the same.

Mr. COOLIDGE. Some of the little bits of houses, two, and from that up to
four and six.

Senator STERLING. Per month?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Per month; and it is peculiar, but they burn it day and night

The men can trade in our stores or not, as they see fit; but they do trade in

in Logan, 5 miles away. To two of our stores come the people of Logan, be-
cause they can get better goods at lower prices. Our prices are less than they
are in Huntington or Charleston, when you consider the greater freight we

We believe in a living wage, but we do not believe in what apparently is the
general understanding of the living wage. The general understanding of a
living wage would seem to be that the world owes me a living.
Senator STERLING. You mean that is a general understanding?

Mr. COOLIDGE. I don't know whether I would or not. I know it happened in
my own case. When I was 15 years old my father, who was a wealthy man,
called me in and told me I could have my choice of two things: He would pay
for my college education if I wanted to go or he would get me an opportunity
to work in any kind of work that I wanted to go into; that when I was 21, if
I went to work, he would give me as much money as it would have cost to put
me through college; that outside of that he was going to look out for my
mother; that he had enough so he could do that for each of the boys, and that
when his will was read we would find that that had been provided, if he died
before I got through college, or if I had got through college the will would

charity.
And when the will was read-and the boys had all been through college-it

believe in it.
The CHAIRMAN. A pretty wise father.

There would have been no trouble and there would have been no movement in

Unless some of the leaders of the United Mine Workers of America return to

Mr. VINSON. What effect would it have on the other coal operations, not

than 25 cents a ton profit, what effect would it have on the other companies?
Mr. COOLIDGE, Why, it would bust most of them, but it would not hurt us

The CHAIRMAN. What dividends does that company pay?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Six dollars the share on the preferred and $7 the share on the
common.
The CHAIRMAN. And the stock is $100 par?
Mr. COOLIDGE. No; the stock is $1 par.
The CHAIRMAN. And that paid $6?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Yes; and let me explain that.
The CHAIRMAN. Six hundred per cent dividend?
Mr. COOLIDGE. No; 60,000 per cent. Let me explain that. I have always be-
lieved in and attempted to get the law fixed so there should be no par value to
stock. When this company was organized there was no law that permitted
that; we therefore divided our stock into $1 shares regardless of the par.
That was the lowest we could make it, and we provided that our preferred
shares should pay $6 a year, and in liquidation that the stock should be worth
$120. Our common stock pays whatever we can afford to divide among the
common stockholders. We have a few less than 50,000 preferred shares, on
which we have paid since 1910. Before that there were no dividends; the
first seven or eight years there were no dividends; we have paid the $6. The
common stock, par value $1, has paid an average of a little over $5 per year for
10 years.
Our invested capital, as I recollect it, the Government has found to
be something like $15,000,000.
Mr. WALSH. Of the Island Creek Coal Co.?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Yes, sir.
Mr. WALSH. Your production was less in 1920 than it was for any year

Mr. COOLIDGE. Yes.

ciations.
Mr. THURMOND. We have a State organization in West Virginia, and its
entire time is given up now and has been this year to handling freight dif-
ferentials. The coal operators of Ohio, in seeking to keep West Virginia coal
out of their territory-
Mr. VINSON. That includes Illnois and Indiana.
Mr. THURMOND. This particular case does not. It is known as the Ohio
case; but similar actions have been up. The Ohio operators have undertaken
to secure, through the Interstate Commerce Commission, a widening of freight
differentials as between West Virginia and Ohio for coal moving into Ohio
points. That would be very disastrous to us, and we do not feel that the long
established differential should be disturbed; and it has taken up a good deal
of our time. The State association has handled that matter, and that is one
of the principal objects of the State association, to protect the industry along
that line.
Mr. AVIS. I wish you would explain to the committee about the national
association; what it has to do, if anything, with wages or labor or anything
of that kind.
Mr. THURMOND. The national association has nothing whatsoever to do with
wages or labor conditions, rates of pay, or the price of coal. It devotes its
time to the study of coal economics, the relation of the coal industry to the
public, the relation of the Federal Government to the coal industry, to matters
of export, and general matters of interest to the coal industry.
Mr. Avis. Is it not a fact, Mr. Thurmond, that in the national association
are some of your biggest competitors both in labor and everything else?
Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir.
Mr. Avis. It has been charged here in this hearing that the competitive field,
composed of the States of Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, and western Pennsylvania,
were in conspiracy against the West Virginia fields. Are they in that
organization?
Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir.
Mr. Avis. Your own competitors. Is not that true?
Mr. THURMOND. Absolutely.
Mr. Avis. You have nothing to do with labor matters-the employment of
labor, union strikes, or anything of that kind?
Mr. THURMOND. Nothing.
Mr. Avis. Col. Coolidge was asked yesterday something about the dropping
off of production in 1920 in Logan County. Would you please explain why
that production dropped off in 1920?
Mr. THURMOND. In speaking of the output dropping off in 1920, that was
applicable, perhaps, to the Island Creek Coal Co.; but as to the Logan dis-
trict as a whole, it produced a higher tonnage in 1920 than it did in 1919; and
the only reason why it did not produce a better tonnage was due to the car sup-
ply the inability of the railroads to furnish sufficient cars.
Mr. Avis. What was the per cent of that?
Mr. THURMOND. Between 51 and 52 per cent of the rating was supplied to the
mines. That can be verified by the records of the railroads.
Mr. AVIS. As I understand you, Mr. Thurmond, in what Mr. Coolidge said
about the dropping off of production he was speaking for his individual com-
pany. What you say now speaks for the entire county as a whole?
Mr. THURMOND. Yes, sir. We produced a little more coal in 1920-490,000
tons more in 1920 than we produced in 1919.

STAND BY THE MINERS OF MINGO.
Fellow workers! Forty thousand miners in the Mingo region of West Virginia
have for months been struggling for the right to live.
They have been fighting valiently against greedy coal barons and hired thugs,
gunmen, and spies.
The workers want a union to help them in their struggle against inhuman
living conditions.
The capitalists and the corporation-owned county and State governments
are doing all in their power to crush the miners and prevent their forming a
union. This fight is a fight for the very right of existence. Driven on by the
fierce oppression of the capitalists and their gunmen, thugs, and deputies, the
nearby union members have arisen to the defense of their fellow workers of
the Mingo.
The march of the union men was a march against the bitter repression and a
defiance to all enemies of union sm.
Now, the Federal Government is rushing to the aid of the coal barons.
Troops, airplanes, bombs, machine guns, and all the hellish devices of capi-
talist warfare have been rushed into the Mingo.
These have supposedly been sent to save law and order, but they have actually
been sent to crush the workers.
Workingmen and working women! Miners and their families have been
eruelly evicted from their homes!
Miners have been murdered by the Baldwin-Felts detectives and gunmen in
the pay of the corporations!
The State constabulary and deputy sheriffs have beaten and clubbed workers
to death!
Strikers' leaders have been indicted, jailed, and murdered!
Their wives and children are being starved!
Fellow workers! You must come to the aid of your struggling brothers of
West Virginia!
You must stand by the miners of Mingo. Their fight is your fight!
They are fighting against the vicious United States Steel Trust that owns
the entire strike area,
They are fighting against a most tyrannical wage slavery.
Their defeat will be your disaster. It will mean the open shop-open slavery
for the whole country.


===== [扫描序号 953] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
939
Force the hands of your leaders! Force your union leaders into action.
Make Gompers, Lewis and Co., who have been too long shirking the struggle, toe
the mark or get out!
It is high time that they do something and stop betraying your interests.
You can not afford to delay. Force your leaders to compel the Federal Gov-
ernment to disarm the murderous bandits-the Baldwin-Felts detective thugs.
The gunmen must leave the strike area at once!
We must rise to the defense of our enslaved brothers.
We must everywhere organize meetings and demonstrations to help the Mingo
miners financially and morally.
Let every union local and labor body force the Federal Government to compel
the profit-hungry coal magnates to go into conference with the miners.
Our slogan must be, "Disarm the Baldwin-Felts spies, gunmen, and notorious
guards!
99
"Away with the deputy sheriffs and State constabulary hirelings of the greedy
corporations!" All murdering of miners must be stopped at once!
Fellow workers! Act before it is too late! A defeat at Mingo will go a long
way toward driving the whole American working class into lower wages, longer
hours, and endless drudgery.
Don't rely on the Federal and State Governments to help you!
They won't give you a square deal. They are only brutal agents of the
capitalist class.
The Federal, State, and county governments and their gunmen, thugs, spies,
and white guards are fighting the battle of your exploiters and oppressors the
capitalists.
This capitalist dictatorship has already too often shown its ugly head
for the workers to have any faith in it.
The miners' demand upon Harding for a conference has been met with bullets
and gas bombs.
Only organized, united, country-wide working class action can stop the Govern-
ments committing outrages against the toiling masses.
Remember how the workers were massacred at Ludlow, Calumet, Mesabe
Range, and McKees Rocks!
Workers! The Communist Party of America calls upon you to help your
struggling brothers in the mines of West Virginia !
To your task! All as one in the name of working class solidarity!
Stand by the miners of Mingo!
Down with the hired murderers!
From your unions, mines, mills, and factories rally to the defense of your
enslaved West Virginia brothers!
The miners must have their union!
Rally to their cause which is your cause!
The miners fight for a union must be made the fight of all organized labor
of all workers of America!
On with the struggle! On to victory!
Issued by the central executive committee.

TESTIMONY OF MR. WILLIAM MCKELL.
The witness, being first duly sworn by the chairman, testified as follows:
Mr. VINSON. I believe you are a mine operator and owner of mines situated
in Fayette County, W. Va.?

.
Mr. MCKELL. Yes, sir; and in Raleigh, also.
Mr. VINSON. How long have you been interested in the mines which you are
now in control of?
Mr. MCKELL. I have been interested in the property and been there—I made
my home there since 1893—for 28 years. I have not been interested in the active
operation of the mine except since 1900.
Mr. VINSON. In other words, you had 20 or 21 years' experience in the actual
operation of mines?
Mr. MCKELL. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. Mr. McKell, are you interested in the Willis Branch Coal Co.?
Mr. MCKELL. I am now. I bought an interest in that in November, 1920.
Mr. VINSON. Mr. McKell, have you had experience in dealing with the United
Mine Workers in regard to paving the check-off in contracts which they propose
as between the owners of the Willis Branch mine and the mine workers' organi-
zation?
Mr. McKELL. I have.
Mr. VINSON. Did the owners of the Willis Branch mine agree to sign a con-
tract providing that they should collect the check-off and turn it over to the
officers of the mine workers?
Mr. MCKELL. No; they did not.
Mr. VINSON. What was the immediate result of their failure to do that, Mr.
McKell, so far as any violence that was directed toward that mine was con-
cerned?
Mr. MCKELL, A strike was called at the mine on September 1, 1919, as well
at Willis Branch as at the other mine that I am interested in. I was not at
that time interested financially in the Willis Branch mine.
Mr. VINSON. But you are familiar with the circumstances surrounding it?
Mr. MCKELL. Yes, sir; I am familiar, because the other two owners of the
Willis Branch mine are personal and intimate associates of mine.
Mr. VINSON. Mr. McKell, what is the condition of the Willis Branch mine
to-day?
Mr. MCKELL. The Willis Branch mine to-day is absolutely put out of business.
Mr. VINSON. What put it out of business?
Mr. MCKELL. The attacks by the United Mine Workers of America.
Mr. VINSON. Do I understand, Mr. McKell, that the mine has been abandoned
by the owners-I mean, so far as its operation is concerned?
Mr. MCKELL. The operation has been abandoned; yes.
The CHAIRMAN. Where was this mine located?
Mr. VINSON. In Fayette County.
Mr. MCKELL. In Fayette County, very near the county line between Fayette
and Raleigh Counties.
The CHAIRMAN. Is that near Boone County?
Mr. VINSON. Fayette joins Boone.
Mr. AVIS. It joins Kanawha.
Mr. VINSON. Yes; and Kanawha.
This mine to-day has how many inhabitants in and around it that formerly
worked there in the mine?
Mr. MCKELL. None; not a single man.
Mr. VINSON. Why did they leave, Mr. McKell?
Mr. MCKELL. Because they were run away; because the plant was dynamited;
because their houses were shot up. They were actually run away by the mob
of United Mine Workers.
Mr. VINSON. How close to this mining plant is the nearest union mine?
Mr. MCKELL. It is just across the railroad track.
Mr. VINSON. What is the name of that mine, Mr. McKell?
Mr. MCKELL. Weirwood mine, operated by the New River & Pocahontas Con-
solidated Coal Co., which is known as the Berwyn-White operation.
Mr. VINSON. Mr. McKell, was a memorandum kept by the secretary of the

Mr. MCKELL. I have.

Mr. MCKELL. I will.

Mr. MCKELL. I do.

Workers of America, who are actively engaged in trying to unionize them. And
I think the serious trouble is probably summed up in the statement that you

neutralizing force.
The CHAIRMAN. On account of the discussions and outbreaks down in that

you might call rural farmers. Mine owners came in there and developed very
large properties, and their employees and their interests are much the largest
interests in the county, and when the acute difference arises between the
employer and employee in a county of that sort there is very little of what you
might call independent public sentiment to, in a sense, weigh the contest and
decide between them.
I rather suspect that is one of the reasons they have had so much trouble in
both Logan and Mingo Counties.
The CHAIRMAN. Well, the fundamental proposition down there in your view-
point is in this contest between unionizing these mines and the stand against
unionization?
Mr. OGDEN. Yes; I don't think there is any question about that.

Not exactly that, but the trade unionists are very strong there, and they might

of the labor leaders but what they have very vivid stories about the operation of
mine guards in those counties and the abuses which organizers have been sub-
mitted to. I have heard of many of those stories and two or three I know a
little something about, but I can not say that I know personally about many of
them with any degree of accuracy.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you think there have been abuses of that system?
Mr. OGDEN. I do not think there is any question about it.
The CHAIRMAN. The Republican Party in their platform declared against it

Mr. OGDEN. Yes, sir. At the convention held in Wheeling in 1920, there was

correct, I believe, the abuses of the mine system.
The CHAIRMAN. Did the Democratic Party do the same?
Mr. OGDEN. I think not. I think, to my memory, they adopted a resolution, but

The CHAIRMAN. Then, the legislature, which was Republican, did nothing, or

wards recommitted.
The CHAIRMAN. And never came up for action?
Mr. OGDEN. I am stating that from my recollection.

Mr. WILEY. A great many.
