===== [扫描序号 963] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
949
Mr. WILEY. The operation of the union, sir, is very serious and seems to be
very different in different parts of the country. The mines that have been union-
ized for some time, understanding the contract and the principles which the
leaders of the union inculcate in their men, get along comparatively easily.
When a mine is newly unionized the men seem to think that a great many
things that are economically impossible are going to happen and a great many
things for which the union leaders do not stand will happen.
When my mines were newly organized they gave me, all of them, a vast
amount of trouble, and a constant going to the State board at Charleston before
they learned the limitation of the benefit that the union would be to them. I
suppose there was one month there when these mines were newly organized
that I went up on an average of three times a week to Charleston, which is a
very unpleasant trip. After a while they would learn some of the things they
hoped for could not be done..
The CHAIRMAN. You mean you went up to headquarters to talk things over?
Mr. WILEY. We have a series of courts. To refer to the contract, there runs
through the contract this thread of thought all the way and all the time, that
any differences between the operator and the men shall be heard first by the
foreman and the mine committee. It goes from him to the superintendent, and
from him to the general superintendent, and from him to the general manager,
and then from him to the board in Charleston, formed between a committee of
the operators and a committee of the miners. That is the highest court. If
they disagree it is then left to an arbitrator.
So these men who are unaccustomed to working under a union contract, in
demanding a great many things that could not be given and were not intended
to be given by the union leaders, would go through these various courts, which
wound up in Charleston; and it was in that way I went to Charleston, sir, in
addition to which I was on the grievance committee or scale committee myself,
and I had to attend these meetings for other mines in addition to our own.
The CHAIRMAN. Go ahead now with your grievances and troubles.
Mr. WILEY. I do not know just how to paint this picture to you in the short-
est time. I want to take up just as little time as possible.
The men who expect to get their remuneration by their work to a very large
extent do not attend the union meetings. The men who do attend the union
meetings regularly are to a considerable extent the agitators, men who expect
to rise to high positions in the union ranks; and of these agitators who go to
the meeting, the arch agitator usually takes the lead in his talk.
It is very easy to stir an audience when you tell them that there is some
great wrong to be righted, that there is some great benefit to come from the
doing of certain things. It is extremely difficult to stir an audience when you
talk to them about self-control, self-restraint, and holding themselves in check.
Somehow that lacks the dramatic qualities. So that these men, in trying to
get prominent in their local union, which in turn would give them prominence
with their State organization, when the mine is newly organized always have
a thousand and one different things to suggest that they can get in working
conditions or advantages of one sort and another, and it takes him and them
a long time of education from his own officers before he learns what he can not
have and learns what he can have, and that made a great deal of trouble.
I forgot to say this in that connection: The thread of thought that runs all
through the contract is that there shall be no strikes. The advantage of being
a union mine is that you shall be permitted to conduct your work evenly every
day. And this thread of thought runs all through the contract, that if differences
come up strikes shall not be the way to settle them, but that these various
boards shall settle them-or various courts, as we call them.
The CHAIRMAN. Who signs those contracts in behalf of the union?
Mr. WILEY. They are signed by the officers and board of District 17, in which
district we work, on the side of the miners, and by the officers and board of
the Kanawha Operators' Association on the side of the operators.
Now, as to that, I would like to say that that is a very unfa'r contract in
that we have our property on the table and are responsible for what we do,
and can easily be made so.
When this last condition came up in our field so that we could not operate
in the field under the economic conditions which confronted us, we asked to
have a discuss on and talk over our contract to see if we could not come to
a basis where the union and ourselves would both be advantaged by some
modification, because we were out of business.
The CHAIRMAN. Who did you ask to have that sort of conference?

AGREEMENT BY AND BETWEEN THE OPERATORS OF THE KANAWHA DISTRICT OF
WEST VIRGINIA AND THE UNITED MINE WORKERS OF AMERICA, DISTRICT No. 17.
(Effective Aug. 1, 1920. Expiring Mar. 31, 1922.)
AWARD OF BITUMINOUS COAL COMMISSION.
Following is the award contained in the majority report of the United States
Bituminous Coal Commission to the President:
We hereby award that all the terms, conditions, and provisions, mining
rates, and wage schedules in effect on October 31, 1919, in what is known as the
Washington agreement, dated October 6, 1917, and the agreements preceding the
Washington agreement, to which the Washington agreement is supplemental
and upon which it is predicated, applying to the central competitive field and
the outlying districts, shall be written into the agreement for which these
findings constitute a basis, except as the same may be modified by the awards
and recommendations hereinafter set forth.
As a modification of the terms of the agreements above recited, we award:
A. That the following specific awards shall constitute the basis upon which
wage agreements in all districts shall be predicated. They are not subject to
negotiations, but shall be written into all agreements and schedules of wages.
B. That the 14 per cent average increase in wages fixed by the United States
Fuel Administration shall be eliminated on March 31, 1920, and in lieu thereof
the wage scale of the Washington agreement referred to shall be increased as set
forth herein.
C. That the agreement for which this award constitutes a basis shall take
effect April 1, 1920, and continue in effect up to and including March 31, 1922.
D. That the mining prices for mining mine-run coal, pick and machine, shall
be advanced 24 cents per ton.
E. That in the block-coal field of Indiana and in other localities that are still
on the screened-coal base the usual methods of applying the tonnage rates shall
continue. This also has its application to districts that have a joint understand-
ing in applying wage increases to low coal.
F. That all day labor and monthly men (the advance to monthly men to be
based on an average of the usual number of days he is required to work in a
month), except trappers and other boys, be advanced $1 per day. Trappers
and boys-receiving less than men's wages to be advanced 53 cents per day.
G. That all yardage, dead work, and room turning be advanced 20 per cent:
Provided, however, That nothing shall prevent the representatives of the miners
and operators in any district in joint conference from taking the flat equivalent
of the 20 per cent and applying it to yardage, dead work, and room turning
if by so doing they will make for uniformity and maintain the differentials.
Failing, however, to agree to such application, then the 20 per cent shall be
applied on the existing rates, effective October 31, 1919.
H. That the decisions which hereinbefore appear in the body of this report
and which are hereinafter summarized are to be incorporated, according to the
letter and spirit of the said decisions, in the agreements to be drawn between
the miners and operators; and that the said decisions shall constitute the basis
upon which the wage agreements in all districts shall be predicated. They are

Washington agreement, dated October 6, 1917, and the agreements preceding the
Washington agreement, to which the Washington agreement is supplemental,
applying in the central competitive field and outlying districts, shall be written
into the agreements for which these findings constitute a basis.
3. That the pushing of cars, loaded or empty, by the mine worker is natural
to the industry and is an integral part of the day's work, and that through
the negotiations of 30 years this work, where practiced, has been paid for in
general in the tonnage rates.
4. That pending the joint district agreement between the miners and operators
covering a fair schedule for piecework or tonnage operation of any new de-
vice or machinery shall not be questioned, and his selection of such men as
he may desire to conduct such tests with or operate such device or machinery
shall not be in any way interfered with or obstructed by the miners or their
representatives, provided the wages offered are at least equal to the estab-
lished scale rates for similar labor.
The operator shall be privileged to pay in excess of the established scale rates
of pay without such excess pay being considered as establishing a permanent
condition for the operation of said device or machine.
After the device or machine shall have passed the experimental stage and
is in shape to be introduced as a regular component part of the production of
coal, then for the purpose of determining a permanent scale of rates (such
rates to continue until the joint scale conference above referred to fixes a
scale) for operating such device or machine the mine workers may have a
representative present for a reasonable time to witness its operation, after
which a schedule of rates shall be determined by mutual agreement, which
scale shall be concluded within 60 days after a fair test has been made.
The test will disclose the labor saving in the cost of producing coal, out of
which labor saving the mine worker shall receive the equivalent of the con-
tract rates for the class of work displaced, plus a fair proportion of the labor
saving effected.
In like manner new or untried systems of mining: For instance, long wall,
retreating long wall, or the panel system may be introduced by the operator
for the purpose of conservation, increasing production, the lessening of cost,
or in the interest of safety, without his right to make such change being
abridged: Provided, however, That for this class of work the mine worker
shall in the same manner receive the equivalent of the contract rates for the
class of work displaced, plus a fair proportion of the labor saving effected.
5. That a commission be selected by the scale committee of miners and oper-
ators in the central competitive field, respectively, which shall study the dif-
ferentials hereinafter set forth as to the working conditions, wage earnings,
production costs, and competitive relations, as well as the check-off system
of collecting dues for the United Mine Workers of America, the award of such
commission to become part of the wage agreements in the district affected.
The commission shall consider:
(a) The differential between pick and machine mining rates in Indiana.
(b) The thick and thin vein differential in the Pittsburgh district.
(c) The 7-cent machine differential in Illinois.
(d) The differential in tonnage rates in southern Illinois.
(e) The discontinuance of the check-off system of collecting dues for the
United Mine Workers of America.
We furthermore recommend that this commission shall be composed of eight
members, one mine worker and operator from each district in the central
competitive field; also that the expense of this commission shall be borne by


===== [扫描序号 967] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
953
the mine workers and operators affected, each paying one-half; and that the
commission so constituted shall make a report at the regular joint conference
of the central competitive field, to be held at the expiration of agreements based
upon this award.
6. That if, and when, during the life of the agreement to be drawn by the joint
wage conference (which agreement is to be predicated upon this report), such
boards and tribunals as recommended by the President's industrial conference
are set up, they shall be employed in connection with the investigation of ques-
tions of controversy between miners and operators: Provided, however, That in
the event that no such machinery is created that a board of inquiry and adjust-
ment for the bituminous coal industry shall be created and maintained under
the said joint agreement-this board to consist of a chairman and two other
representatives appointed by the President, two representatives of the mine
workers selected by the mine workers, and two representatives of the mine
operators selected by the mine operators-and that matters in controversy be-
tween the bituminous coal miners and operators be submitted thereto; that the
expense of such board be borne by the mine workers and operators equally; and
that such tribunal, board, or commission shall immediately undertake the inves-
tigation of the questions in controversy, and shall publish within 60 days its
findings of fact, and if not unanimous, then in separate reports, and that pend-
ing such report no general strike shall be called: Provided, however, That if no
report is published within the designated period, then a retarding of the strike
shall end.
7. That the price at which house coal shall be furnished the mine workers at
the tipple shall be determined by adding to the price in effect on October 31,
1919, the average percentage allowed as an increase on the wage scale, to wit,
27 per cent, and that when the coal is delivered to the miners' houses by the
operator the actual cost of delivery shall be added.
8. That for the purpose of the new agreement the prices charged the miners
for blacksmithing shall be on the basis of existing contracts: Provided, how-
ever, That the maximum charge shall not exceed three-fourths of 1 per cent of
the miners' gross earnings.
9. That explosives shall be furnished the miners at cost, which is to include
handling, transportation, and insurance.
10. That since the miners and operators have agreed in joint conference to the
establishment of a joint commission for the purpose of making an investigation
within the Kanawha, Paint Creek, and Cabin Creek fields for the possible cor-
rection of inequalities in order to bring about a more uniform condition, but
have had no opportunity to present their report to the joint conference, and as
both the operators and miners have asked that the findings of this commission
be written into the new joint agreement which is to be predicated on this report,
we direct that the mine workers and operators compose their differences in har-
mony with the report of the joint commission referred to, and that the findings of
that commission be written into the agreement.
11. That the mine workers of District No. 12, Illinois, and the Illinois Coal
Operators' Association, respectively, shall each select two members of a joint
commission to study the situation in northern Illinois, Assumption, Ill., and
Decatur, Ill., as to wage earnings, working conditions, production costs, and
competitive relations, which commission shall report its findings to the next regu-
lar joint conference of the Illinois mine workers and operators following the
expiration of the agreement for which this award constitutes a basis. The
expense of this commission shall be borne by the mine workers and operators
affected, each paying one-half.
12. That the United Mine Workers of District No. 10, Washington, and the
Washington Coal Producers' Association, respectively, shall each select two
members of a commission and the four members so selected shall appoint an
experienced mining engineer who shall also be a member of the commission.
This commission shall, within 30 days from appointment, investigate and report
to the joint conference of mine workers and operators of the State of Washing-
ton the effect of the application of the awards herein set forth to the agreements
and wage schedules in that State. In the meantime the awards herein shall
not apply in Washington. The expenses of this commission shall be borne by
the mine workers and operators affected, each paying one half.
I. That the above summary shall in no way modify the decisions and awards
set out in this report.

EIGHT-HOUR DAY.
5.20-6.70
5. 68-7.18
SECTION 1. That an 8-hour day means 8 hours' work in the mine at usual
working places for all classes of inside day labor. This shall be exclusive


===== [扫描序号 970] =====
956
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
of the time required in reaching such working places in the morning and
departing from the same at night.
Regarding drivers, they shall take their mules to and from stables, and the
time required in so doing shall not include any part of the day's labor, their
work beginning when they reach the change at which they receive empty cars,
but in no case shall the driver's time be docked while he is waiting for such
cars at the point named. The prevailing custom for drivers relative to har-
nessing and unharnessing their mules shall continue.
OVERTIME FOR DAY LABOR.
SEC. 2. Any class of day labor may be paid, at the option of the operator,
for the number of hours and fractions thereof actually worked at an hour
rate based on one-eighth of the scale rate per day: Provided, however, That
when the day men go into the mine in the morning they shall be entitled to two
hours' pay, whether the mine runs coal two hours or not, except in the event
that they voluntarily leave their work during this time without the consent
of the operator they shall forfeit their two hours' pay: Provided further,
That overtime by day laborers, when necessary to supply railroad chutes with
coal by night or Sunday, where no regular men therefor are exclusively em-
ployed or when necessary in order not to impede the operation of the mine the
day following, and for work which can not be performed or completed by the
regular shift during regular hours without impeding the operation of the mine,
may be performed and paid for at the same rate per hour.
CHECK OFF.
SEC. 3. We adopt the check-off system as a part of this agreement. Check
off to include all men working in and around the mine eligible for membership
in the United Mine Workers of America, exempting from membership mine
foremen, mine foreman's assistant, weighman, dock boss or trimmer, tipple
boss, stable boss, one head electrician for each mine, night watchman, and em-
ployees of central repair shop when one is maintained for a group of mines.
This pertains to the regular dues and assessments of the United Mine Workers
of America, not to exceed $3 from each employee in any given month. The
initiation fee to be in addition to the above.
In order to be honored the check-off list must be furnished to the company
not later than 24 hours after expiration of each half, and the United Mine
Workers of America of District No. 17 agrees to protect the operators under
this clause.
MACHINE WORK.
SEC. 4. The price paid in machine mining for loading coal in narrow work,
by the ton, shall be the same as in wide work, the excess price now paid for
loading to be on a yardage basis according to the number of tons of coal pro-
duced in each yard of narrow work, at the option of the operator.
SEC. 5. Machine men will be required to cut coal level and close to the bottom,
and all machine men leaving more bottomr than 4 inches, except in case of
pots or extreme variations, will be required to lift same, or it shall be lifted
at their expense.
SEC. 6. In case sprags are left by machine men, they shall be notified by the
loader, and if they refuse to remove same the loader shall do so and be allowed
50 cents for so doing; the said 50 cents shall be charged to the machine men.
SEC. 7. All machine loaders shall be awarded two rooms or equivalent of
three rooms in thin seams for each two men, and they work "buddies," and
in that way load from one room at a time so that it will give them an oppor-
tunity to cut the other room and not lose any time to machine or loaders, and
the operator will provide such rooms for each two men at the earliest possible
moment, but, in the event of territory becoming scarce from a squeeze or
striking a horseback or any other unavoidable obstacle, this shall not be
construed so as to diminish the output of the mine.
CHECK WEIGHMAN.
SEC. 8. Checkweighman, selected as required by law from among the em-
ployees at that mine, may be placed on each tipple at the expense of the
miners, and their duties shall be only those prescribed by the laws of the State


===== [扫描序号 971] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
957
of West Virginia, and all weigh scales may be tested by the miners at any rea-
sonable time. In case a suitable man can not be found at any mine an outsider
may be employed by and with the mutual consent of the operator and his
miners.
TRADE.
SEC. 9. Employees have the right to trade where they please.
RUN-OF-MINE-SCREENED BASIS.
SEC. 10. The mining rate per ton for split or hard coal shall be fixed upon
a run-of-mine basis, but screened lump coal may be mined provided the in-
creased rate paid for screened lump coal shall be according to the percentage
of screenings in producing screened lump as against mine-run coal.
HIRE AND DISCHARGE.
SEC. 11. The operator or his superintendent or mine foreman shall be re-
spected in the management of the mine and the direction of the working force.
The authority to hire and discharge shall be vested in the mine superintendent
or mine foreman, and nothing in this agreement shall be construed to abridge
the right of the employer in either of these respects. Day men must perform
any class of work at the direction of the mine foreman, provided the scale rate
is paid or the individual is not asked to take a reduced rate of wages.
LOADING CARS OR BARGES.
SEC. 12. The operator shall at all times be at liberty to load any railroad
cars or barges whatsoever, regardless of their ownership, with coal and sell
and deliver such coal in any market and to any person, firm, or corporation
that he may desire.
SEMIMONTHLY PAY.
SEC. 13. All labor shall be paid semimonthly. Semimonthly pay means that
the miners shall be paid twice a month, pay days to be determined locally, and
statements shall be available 24 hours prior to pay day.
MINING-WORKMANLIKE METHODS-TIMBERING,
SEC. 14. The miners shall be required to load the coal in every case free
from slate, bone, niggerhead, and other impurities.
SEC. 15. All coal mined, drilled, and blasted by the miners must be done in
a practical and workmanlike manner and in accordance with the State mining
laws of West Virginia.
SEC. 16. In paying for coal before it is screened it is not intended to encour-
age unworkmanlike methods of mining and blasting coal or to decrease the pro-
portion of screened lump and any miner will be subjected to discipline who,
from ignorance, carelessness, or any other cause, fails to properly mine, shoot,
and load the coal.
SEC. 17. The scale of prices agreed to for mining coal shall include the work
required to mine, shoot, and load the coal, and properly timber the working
places in the mines, and the operators shall be required to furnish the neces-
sary props and timber to properly timber all working places. The custom at
each mine relative to scraping working places and the laying of jumpers shall
continue unless changed by mutual agreement.
SEC. 18. If any miner shall fail to properly timber and care for his working
place and such failure shall entail falls of slate rock and the like, or if by im-
proper or reckless shooting of the coal in room or entry the mine props or other
timbers shall be disturbed, or unecessary falls result, the miner whose fault is
the occasion of such damage shall repair the said damage without compensa-
tion, and if such miner fails to repair such damage it shall be considered a
dischargeable offense, and he may be dealt with at the discretion of the super-
intendent.
SEC. 19. In any case where the mine foreman directs the placing of cross-
bars to secure the roadway, then, and in such cases only, the miner shall be
paid prices for such crossbars as may be agreed upon between him and the


===== [扫描序号 972] =====
958
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
mine foreman. In case of miners shooting bottom, should any of the props be
loosened or displaced, thereby endangering the safety of the workmen, the
miner agrees to reset same. The above does not contemplate any change from
the ordinary method of timbering by the miner for his own safety.
DOCKS.
SEC. 20. In case any slate, bone, sulphur, or other impurities are sent out
by the miner, it shall be the duty of the trimmer of the car to call the attention
of the weighman and checkweighman, where one is employed, to the same, so
as to deduct weight of such impurities as estimated by the trimmer or dock
boss from the ascertained weight of such car; for the second offense he may be
suspended for one working day or fined 50 cents; for the third and each subse-
quent offense occurring in any one calendar month he may be suspended, dis-
charged, or fined $1, at the option of the superintendent; that in malicious and
aggravated cases the superintendent shall have the right to suspend or dis-
charge for the first or any subsequent offense.
SEC. 21. Any miner abusing or seeking to embarrass the trimmer for perform-
ing his duties shall be fined $3 or be discharged, at the option of the superin-
tendent.
SEC. 22. It is understood that if the checkweighman leaves his post to investi-
gate the amount of impurities thrown out, or for any other purpose, the run-
ning of coal over the tipple will not be suspended during his absence.
SEC. 23. Splint coal loaded out with gas coal when it is ordered to be sep-
arated shall be considered as impurities and shall be dealt with as such.
SEC. 24. The proceeds of all fines arising under this clause to be paid into
the funeral fund. Under no circumstances shall the fines be remitted or
refunded.
MINE COMMITTEE GRIEVANCES.
SEC. 25. The duties of the mine committee shall be confined to the adjustment
of disputes that the mine boss and miner or miners have tried to but are unable
to adjust.
The mine committee shall have no authority nor exercise any other control,
nor in any way interfere with the operation of the mine, and for violation of this
clause the committee or any member thereof may be discharged.
SEC. 25a. In case of any local trouble arising at any mine the aggrieved party
shall first make an earnest effort to adjust the dispute with the mine foreman.
In case they are unable to agree the matter shall be referred to the mine com-
mittee and the local management of the mine, and if they fail to agree, the
commissioner of the operators' association and the miners' officials, and if they
fail to agree, to the district board of the two organiaztion, and should they
fail to agree, they shall select an umpire or referee, and the decision of the
majority of them shall constitute a final and binding award. In all such cases
all parties involved must continue at work pending the investigation and adjust-
ment as above set forth.
SEC. 25b. If any employee for whom the scale is made refuses to work because
of any grievance which has not been taken up in the manner provided herein,
and such action shall seem likely to impede the operation of the mines, the
employee, or any of them, will subject themselves to dismissal without re-
course at the option of the company, and the mine committee shall immediately
furnish a man or men to take such place or places at the scale rate in order
that the mine shall continue at work, and it shall be the duty of any member
or members of the United Mine Workers who may be called upon by the mine
board or mine committee, to immediately take the place or places assigned him
or them in pursuance thereof.
SEC. 25c. The mine committee shall under no circumstances go around the
mine for any cause whatsoever unless called upon by the mine foreman or by
the miner or day man who may have agrievance that he can not settle with
the mine boss, and then only to investigate that grievance with the parties
involved. Mine committee shall take up all grievances outside of working
hours unless by mutual consent of both parties.
SEC. 25d. Members of the mine committee employed as day men shall not
leave their places of duty during the working hours except with the permission
of the mine foreman or in cases involving the stopping of the mine.
SEC. 25e. All discharge or suspension cases for violation of the contract
shall be taken up and disposed of within five days, and should it be proven


===== [扫描序号 973] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
959
that the party discharged or suspended has been unjustly dealt with, he shall
be reinstated to his former employment and compensated for the time lost
during the hours the mine operated, not to exceed $5.20 per day. In such
cases where he was employed as a day laborer he shall be compensated at
the scale rate provided for in this agreement for his regular employment and
in no cases shall the company be responsible for more than five days' compen-
sation. In all discharge or suspension cases the operator may, at his option,
employ the employees at any other work pending the settlement of the case
without prejudice, which must be disposed of in the time above provided.
Discharge cases shall take precedence over all cases.
DISCIPLINE.
SEC. 25f. No strike or stoppage of work shall occur at any mine until the
question in dispute shall have been considered and finally disposed of, as pro-
vided for in section 25a.
(a) Should any officer or officers of the United Mine Workers of America,
or any member or members thereof employed at any mine, cause the mine
or part of the mine to shut down in violation of this rule, each member of the
United Mine Workers of America employed at such mine, except those who
continue at work, shall have deducted from his earnings the sum of $1 per
day for each day or part of a day they remain idle.
(b) Should any operator or his representative lock the men out for the
purpose of forcing a settlement of any grievance or cause the mine or a part
of the mine to shut down in violation of this rule, he shall be fined $1 per
day for each employee for each day or part of a day the mine is thus thrown
idle.
(c) All money assessed against the employees under this rule shall be col-
lected from the pay for the half month in which the violation of the rule
occurs or from the first money due thereafter. All moneys assessed against
the operator for violation of this rule shall be turned over to District No. 17
of the United Mine Workers of America, and all moneys assessed against the
miners shall be turned over to the Kanawha Coal Operators' Association.
All fines provided for in all agreements shall be automatically collected,
and any operator failing to collect and forward to proper parties such fine
shall pay a penalty of $2 for each employee subject to be fined, the same to be
collected and retained in the miners' district organization. And in no case
shall the fine be refunded except by mutual agreement of the accredited rep-
resentatives of the operators and miners.
It is further agreed that where any employee enters suit in civil courts to
recover any fine collected in accordance herewith the district organization
shall reimburse the operator for expense incurred on account of such suit.
NEGOTIATIONS DURING SUSPENSION.
SEC. 26. Under no circumstances will the operator recognize or treat with
any representatives of the United Mine Workers of America during the sus-
pension of work contrary to this agreement.
WORKING IRREGULARLY.
SEC. 27. When a miner absents himself from duty for two days or more or
persists in working irregularly, except on account of sickness, without giving
advance notice to the mine boss or mine superintendent when possible, he
forfeits his position.
When a machine runner or any employee upon whose work other employees
of the mine are dependent absents himself from duty without giving advance
notice, when possible, to the mine boss, he forfeits his position.
TURN.
SEC. 28. The operator will see that an equal turn is offered each miner, and
that he is given a fair chance to obtain same. The checkweighman, where one
is employed, shall keep a turn bulletin for the turn keeper's guidance. The
drivers shall be subject to whoever the mine boss shall designate as turn
keeper in pursuance hereof. This rule is not applicable and shall not be consid-


===== [扫描序号 974] =====
960
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
ered as preventing the operator from driving entries as rapidly as he may
desire.
SEC. 29. Miners of this district will wait one-half hour for railroad cars to
be placed at the mine when mine management has been informed that cars
are on their way and will be placed. If any mine can furnish work by dumping
coal in coal chutes and furnish work the same as loading railroad cars, miners
shall report for work.
If any company attempts to take advantage of this rule by having men
report for work contrary to its provisions, the rule then may be subject to
change at this mine or mines by the same method as other grievances are
adjusted under the contract.
DOUBLE-SHIFTING ENTRIES.
SEC. 30. Miners shall drive double-shift entries when called upon to do so
by the operator, and 344 cents per yard extra shall be paid for pick entry and
27 cents per yard for machine entry.
BURIAL FUND,
SEC. 31. A burial fund may be established by each mine or local, to which
fund each miner shall contribute 25 to 50 cents per month until a sum of not
less than $250 and not more than $1,000 shall have been created, when collec-
tions shall cease until the fund is reduced by death, when a collection of 25 or
50 cents per man per month shall again be made until the amount reaches the
maximum agreed upon, and so on, and the operator shall contribute in case
of the death of a miner, or any member of his family, an amount agreed upon
by the operator and the burial fund committee. In consideration of this con-
tribution it is agreed and understood that the miners and day men will not
cease work to attend the funeral of either miner or member of the miner's
family, except in case the miner is killed outright while at work in the mine,
in which event the mine way be closed the day of his death, resuming work
the following morning.
This is not to be construed to mean that individual mine workers or relatives
of the deceased shall not attend the funeral if they desire to do so.
There shall be a committee appointed known as the funeral fund committee to
take charge of these funds and make all necessary funeral arrangements in
case of any death, and said committee shall be paid for such duties as may
be agreed upon locally.
ENTRY GOB.
SEC. 32. Where there is not sufficient room to gob ordinary conditions the
loader or miner shall load it in bank cars and the company shall unload it.
SEC. 33. It is understood that in the event of a disagreement between operators
and mine workers, steam and electrical engineers, firemen, and pumpmen are
required to continue to perform such work as is in line with their duties.
DEAD WORK NOT STIPULATED AND LOCAL CONDITIONS.
SEC. 34. For dead work, where unusual conditions exist, the price to be paid
for same shall be a question for local adjustment.
SEC. 35. Under the terms of this contract nothing shall be done or enacted
that shall increase the cost of producing coal to the operator or decrease the
earning power of the miner, except by mutual consent.
EMERGENCY WORK AND ORDINARY REPAIRS.
SEC. 36. The operators shall have the right in cases of emergency work or
ordinary repairs to the plant to employ in connection therewith such men as in
their judgment are best acquainted with and suited to the work to be performed.
except where men are permanently employed for such work. Blacksmiths and
other skilled labor shall make any necessary repairs to machinery and boilers.
CONSTRUCTION AND EXTENSIVE REPAIRS.
The erection of head frames, buildings, scale, machinery, railroad switches,
etc., necessary for the completion of a plant to run coal, all being in the nature

of construction work, are to be excluded from the jurisdiction of the United
Mine Workers of America. Extensive repairs to or rebuilding the same class
of work shall also be included in the same exception, the employees thereon to
be excluded, as above, when employed on such work only.
CONSTRUCION AND REPAIR WORK DURING SUSPENSION.
During any strike or suspension, it is hereby understood that all men on all
kinds of outside construction and repair work, together with all kinds of work
inside the mine that is not producing coal, must continue at work; and it is
further understood that such miners as are necessary are to be permitted to
mine coal for the boilers and domestic consumption on the property, but this
is not to be construed to mean to mine coal for shipment.
SPLINT COAL SEPARATION IN GAS SEAMS.
SEC. 37. Where splint coal is separated and thrown back and stored to meet
exceptional market conditions and afterwards loaded, there shall be paid 12
cents per ton extra. Where splint coal is loaded in separate cars as mined, 5
cents per ton extra shall be paid.
SEC. 38. All local rules in violation of this contract shall be null and void,
and no local union or group of local unions shall pass any rules in vioation,
neither shall any company enforce any rule in violation of this contract. In
addition to local rules this contract takes precedence over the constitution of
the United Mine Workers of America.

Mr. WILEY. I would like to speak just a word about collective bargaining.
We have got in the habit of using terminology which means different things
with different men. The collection of men in one of our mines, in treating
with them, the collection of men in all of our mines would be one thing and
the collection of men in the Kanawha field would be another; the collection of
men in the State of West Virginia would be still another. But all of these are
entirely different from a collection of men in the whole United States controlled
by people who have no knowledge of the conditions of my men, for instance, and
what they want, and what is for their good.
The theory of that is that what is good for the greatest number is best for
the men in my immediate vicinity.
In talking about collective bargaining, it seems to me we ought to name just
what the collection is. No one would have any objection to treating with their
own men as a collection.
Another thing which has grown out of this is the claim on the part of the
miners that they have a right to an adviser, like the Operators Employers'
Council, and that they have the right to select their adviser.
There is still quite a difference in that.
We employ a counsel as an adviser in truth. He has no authority. When
you have a collective bargaining, and the most skilled negotiator on the miners'
side is a man in authority, he is not an adviser; he is the absolute boss of the
situation. And there is a good deal of difference in that.
Now, as to bargaining, in the three years I have been in West Virginia, and
in such investigations as I have been able to make in order to become educated
on the situation, there has never been any bargaining at all in regard to this
contract. It is a curious thing to notice the operators go through motions.
When the time approaches to take up a contract they have a meeting and
imagine themselves appointing a committee which is going to talk about some-
thing, and they amuse themselves by appointing the committee which goes to
meet the miners' committee, who amuse themselves with a conference lasting
three or four days, knowing before the conference starts that there is nothing
determined by the discussion, but the contract here, made by the central com-


===== [扫描序号 976] =====

WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
petitive fields, is submitted to the committee in Charleston for the Kanawha
field, and they know before they begin to talk about it that not a scintilla or
tittle of that can be changed in any particular. They take it or leave it.
So that, as far as the Kanawha field is concerned, on this contract there is no
bargaining.
To go on from that just a little, there is a clause in this contract described
in heavy black letters at the top, "Hire and discharge." It is section 11, on
page 19:
"The operator or superintendent or mine foreman "-I am just going to
skip part of this-" shall be expected in the management of the mine and the
direction of the working places of the working force. The power to hire and
discharge shall be vested in the mine superintendent or mine foreman, and
nothing in this agreement shall be assumed to abridge the right of the em-
ployer in either of these respects."
There is a clause in this contract in another place which says a man shall
not be discharged for union activities, which is perfectly proper. But by twist-
ing every time you want to discharge a man to the position that he is being
discharged for union activities, the net result is that the clause I have read you
is absolutely advocated, and you can not discharge a man.
The CHAIRMAN. Suppose a man is absolutely inefficient and is not doing good
work, can you discharge him?
Mr. WILEY. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Why not?
Mr. WILEY. I am not permitted to.
The CHAIRMAN. What?
Mr. WILEY. I am not permitted to.
The CHAIRMAN. You are not permitted to because it is held he is a union man
and you are discharging him because he is a union man?
Mr. WILEY. No, sir-well, that may be the argument, but the theory is, as
announced to me by the different committees and I think Mr. Walsh an-
nounced it the other day-I forget who the witness was-but didn't he have a
right to his job? That is the theory of it.
Now, the result of that is I have got, we will say, two men at work; one
man goes right up in the collar and does his best; he saves supplies, he gives
me good work, he pays attention to his business, and when I ask him to do
something he listens to you so he gives you good results. The other man is
careless, sits back in the britchen, tries to see how little he can do, throws
his supplies away right and left, does not hear what you say-if he does hear
it, pays no attention to what you say; has no interest in it-lacks interest.
That is the main thing. The good workman earns more than he receives. The
poor workman earns a great deal less. But I can do nothing to encourage the
poor workman to take an interest in his business, nor can I do anything to
reward the good workman for the additional profit he makes for my company.
They must both be the same, and the poor workman takes to himself the benefit
of the profit that the good workman makes.
Further, there is a rule growing out of precedence that any working condi-
tion which obtains must continue.
If my foreman, although he has direct instructions from the officer to see
that certain things are done-if he neglects in any degree to see that those
things are actually done by their men, there grows up a condition which it is
claimed is a condition of the mine, and can not be changed.
For instance, it is very important in some kinds of mining to have the
gob-do you know what the gob is? The waste that does not come out of the
mine to have the gob thrown on one side instead of on both sides. It is a
little more trouble to do that, but not a great deal.
We found by accident once, that that was not being done in one of our mines,
although the rule was very strict that the gob should go on one side. The com-
mittee took it up and we had a very severe fight-I mean fight in the sense
of arguments and meetings and courts, to prevent them from having it con-
cluded, that because the foreman had permitted this by his neglect to have been
done for a reasonable time, it should always be done, and for us to maintain
the position that it was not a working condition of the mine and should always
continue.
We do our business upon the basis in our company that you can not buy men.
They don't want concessions; that men are really red blooded citizens and what
they want is a good, fair, square deal, and an honest, straightforward inter-
pretation of the terms of the agreement. We try to give them that.


===== [扫描序号 977] =====

963
An agitator frequently tries to bring the men in and ask for some concession
which will advance the agitator's position with the men. He always wants
to show that he has won something from the company. If he comes in and
fails, the men seem to be pleased. They want to know the conditions under
which they work. They don't want to have constantly changed conditions
and annoyances, and they are happier when those conditions are clearly defined
and honestly lived up to by them.
Now, the foreman or superintendent frequently, finding it hard to stand the
gaff, make concessions and these concessions make irritation with the men.
And, strange as it may seem, it does not conduce with contentment and
happiness. They want to know they are going along a certain definite line,
and that the line will be maintained.
When these concessions are made it has been understood that the foreman
or superintendent of the business who makes them will be discharged without
any argument at all, because it is by not giving things that we ought not to
give that we continue on good terms with our people.
If a foreman, however, with this strict rule in front of him, surreptitiously,
without the knowledge of the office, increases the pay of any man, or permits
more posts to be put up where the men are paid, or does anything of that sort,
that is immediately fastened on the mind as a condition and they can not
go back and change it.
Personally, I am not a low-pay man. I believe in paying high pay for good
service. But such efficiency as I have been able to get out of business is by
studying the kind of service I get, paying the money necessary to get the best
men, and through them getting the best service. If I can not give the best
man something to reward him, if I can not give the poorest man some kind
of discipline to let not only him-it is all a matter of going to school, this
matter of business, anyway-so that the others can see that he loses by his
lack of interest, I can not get that efficiency.
It is one of my theories in business that the man sells the cheapest thing he has
got for money, and that is his time and labor; that the best thing he has got
to give, his loyalty and interest in the business, has to be earned by the
management; that it is not a voluntary act on his part to give it, but that
the management has to so treat him that they arouse in him and get from
him this loyalty and interest in the business that can not be bought with money.
I can not do that at all. So that, however much brains may be in the
employee of my company to get efficiency, it is all nullified by the fact that
men can not be discharged, that they can not have their conditions improved,
that I can not pay any higher wages to one than to another, and that the
man who does not give that service can not be punished.
Maybe I can make that clear to you in this: The transportation system of
a mine-
Mr. WALSH. Would I interrupt you, Mr. Wiley, by asking you-I have for-
gotten-when did you say you bought in there?
Mr. WILEY. Three years ago.
Mr. WALSH. What was the date-1919, or 1918?
Mr. WILEY. 1918.
The transportation system in a mine is quite an extensive one; you run
quite a railroad in each mine. The operation of that transportation has a
great deal to do with the production of the mine. The locomotives are very
delicate electrical machines, and a great deal depends on their lubrication
and the way in which they are handled.
If a man feels his job is not at stake by his carelessness and inefficiency, he
throws the power on the locomotive and rushes it ahead and spins the wheels
on the track, and he rushes back and throws the power that way and spins
the wheels going back. He does not pay any attention to his lubrication; he does
not do any of the things that will help him to get a production through his
transportation system for the day. He has not any interest in it. He gets just as
much money if there is no production comes out as he does if he gets a good
production. His position is just as secure to him. And human. nature is such
that if his locomotive goes to pieces for lack of lubrication or any of these
other things that happen, he sits down against the wall and waits for the
electrician to come and put it in order, although it might take but a very
little thing to do it; and he says, very naturally, “I get my day's wages, and
if the company wants me to haul this coal they must get me a good locomotive,
and they can't expect me to haul it unless they do get a good locomotive; and
I will make just as much sitting here as I will hauling coal."

My theory of meeting that situation would be this: When the day's work is
over have the locomotive driven spend an hour, for which the company would
pay, in examining his locomotive and checking it up to see that it is in con-
dition for the morrow, with a high-grade electrical expert who knows more
about the inside of a locomotive than he does. It is important that the driver
be there to tell what happened during the day, what weaknesses developed. It
is important for him to be there to see what weaknesses he has to guard
against the next day.
By paying him for the time he spends inspecting that locomotive and getting
it ready for business the next day we would get a big production from our
transportation system, and we would be very glad to pay a bonus to the loco-
motive driver for hauling a certain number of tons without a breakdown or
for making a certain amount of mileage without a breakdown-any way that
is satisfactory--the idea being not to get more work out of him, but to arouse
his interest in the business to such an extent that he has got an interest in
how many tons of coal he can pull with that engine without a breakdown,
Those are the things that cost us inefficiency to such extent-I don't know
just how to get it before you, sir. Maybe this dramatic statement may do it:
All of our mines were down to a pretty low state of efficiency, as much as
we were trying to build them up, and I was told that at one mine there were
two or three radicals who kept production down very badly. It was very much
lower than our other mines. A number of people told me that they should be
discharged. They were doing the things that could-if I had been put on the
stand, I should have had to say, if they were discharged, they were discharged
for their union activities; and as I try to tell the truth I could not go before
the board and have one of the board members say, "Now, Mr. Wiley, are you
discharging this man for his union activities?" I would have to say "Yes."
So they were not discharged, but at the late uprising they became very active
and indictments were brought against them.

If a radical can find some great wrong, he is going to write and say, "Now,

accident grew some argument between the members of the constabulary and the

disarmed the policemen, to prevent people from coming from the State capital,
to prevent the disarming of the constabulary and prevent people from coming
to arrest these men who had fired on the deputy. That continued until the
three deputy sheriffs whom I have employed in my section found the threat
against their lives so great they left. They left me without any pretense of
civil authority in the whole county in which I am established.
Let me go back just a little. These meetings were held in Charleston, and
about the 20th of August the men began to attempt at Marmet, of which I read
in the newspapers a day or two after that-they started to march across to
Danville. You can see it right there on the map, sir, and Gen. Bandholtz was
asked to come down to see us, which he did. He met with Mr. Keeney, the
president of our District No. 17, and Mr. Keeney went to Madison and Dan-
ville-they are practically the same thing, only a mile between them-and made
a talk to the men, and a large number of the men were put on a train and sent
out. Col. Bandholtz never seemed to have heard of the trouble which we had
in our part of the country since the 12th of August, and on that night a train
at Clothier was commandeered and run down the road as far as Willett's
Branch and loaded with people and taken back up to Blair. The number of
people taken up on that train has been variously estimated at from 500 to 800
men. I imagine about 500. The people who expressed it to me said, “All they
could possibly get on the train." That occurred the very night the men were
supposed to have been turned back from Danville.
I forgot to tell you all the wires were cut. They were cut on the night of
August 12, and we could not sell any coal and could not run our business. Our
coal was sold all over the Middle West and a large portion of the East, and we
were just shut off from the world.
The CHAIRMAN. You mean the telephone or the telegraph wires?
Mr. WILEY. Both. We had no communication with the outside world, except
the mail trains would stop, and our mail would come in and go out, and no
police protection and no civil law of any kind or description.

I want to say very emphatically just here in this connection that I was
strongly impressed with the idea that the men working for my company had
no interest with any of this trouble and no wish to be in it. They came to see
me, a committee did, and told me there was no industrial trouble, no differences
of any kind or description between them and us, and that they wanted to do
everything in their power to protect our property and our people and to do
everything for me and the company they could do, and from the start to the
finish of this they did do it. Nothing that I asked of them but what they did
cheerfully and kindly, and the feeling between them and myself was of the
very warmest.
When these men came up to Blair and the mob turned back from
Danville they would not believe, my own committees, would not be-
lieve that the thing had been settled and they sent a man down to
Madison to see somebody to become convinced that the trouble was over, and
they went down and came back and said to me they were ready to go to work
Mondy morning, and we expected to go to work Monday morning. The
night of the 27th, which was Saturday night, I was sitting on my porch
with my general superintendent and my superintendent. We heard that the
deputies and constabulary were marching down Beech Creek. We have two
mines at the head of Beech Creek near Ethel, and other mines on Beech Creek
No. 2 and No. 3, at the lower end of Beech Creek. We did not believe it.
Rumors had been running rife and we would hear all kinds of things, that
usually turned out not to be true, but about, I should say between 8 and 9
o'clock that night, firing began, a bunch of scattered shots, which we would
hear down at No. 2 camp, which was about a mile from where I was sitting.
The detail of this does not interest you, however, after waiting a very consid
erable time and thinking if they were constabulary I would see them march
around the corner of Beech Creek and see them pass by, I still became con-
vinced they were not constabulary, and about 1 o'clock I went down to find out
about it. Of course, all the paths and the roads and everything about the en-
tire camp was guarded.
Mr. VINSON. You mean guarded by constabulary?
Mr. WILEY. No, sir; guarded by the miners, with high-powered rifles, and at
any turn in the dark you were liable to butt into a colored man, who did not
know anything about a rifle, and have him jab one in your stomach. There
was no danger to me, but there was a good deal of having these rifles go off
accidentally and by various ways, or there was a very great danger of having
somebody tell you to halt and you not hear him.
About 1 o'clock I went down, and I met one of the committeemen, who told
me he thought the men had made a mistake and fired on each other and had
killed their own men, the miners. That was the best information he could get.
I went into my office and asked if there was anybody who had been over there
who did know anything about it, and then I learned, for the first time, it was
the constabulary and the deputy sheriff. This committeeman then said to me
that the thing had gotten very serious, and if the troops did not come in that
a great many deaths were going to result, and he asked me-he said to me—
"If you ask for your troops you will not get them; if I ask for troops I will
not get them, because you would ask for one side and I would ask for one
side, but if you and I together go and ask we will get them." Then he said to
me, Will you go around with me"? I said, Yes; there is a train leaves
Clothier at 4.25 in the morning; can we get down and catch that train"? He
said, "We don't dare to drive from here to Clothier in the dark," the danger
being that we might be halted and the car made so much noise that we might
not hear it and stop, and be shot.

The CHAIRMAN. This was a committeeman of the miners?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir. After daylight in the morning we got up very early,

the troops were sent.

I want to say one thing about the terrorism that was there. It is impossible
to describe it. The air was filled with the feeling that if you did not do as
you were told to do that something-and the very greatness of the dread grew
out of the fact that that "something was indefinite-would happen to you.
Men who were in my employ in the office would feel that the first one or two
days they would get out. Some of the men whom you would think as the
most courageous would leave; others of them you thought would be nervous
stayed through the whole time with a smile on their faces without being the
least disturbed. It developed a lying propensity of the men very greatly;
some of the men would go out and say to their families that they would be
back immediately and never come back until the troops; others had a sick child
somewhere, or a sick wife; and you would see the fellow come in the door day
after day and see this terrorism just grow in his face and you could just tell
when it would get the best of him and when he would begin to make excuses
to get out.
The CHAIRMAN. Was that, while this army was coming along there; did that
come through Sharpless past your works?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Was that when this terrorism you speak of existed?
Mr. WILEY. The terrorism began with the guarding of the roads and grew
gradually worse day by day, and the worst was when the army began to
march through. Now, the army did not march through. In 1919 there was a
march like this, similar to this; the labor leaders are the past masters of
publicity. They make the operators look like 30 cents. They know just what
kind of a thing will catch the newspapers' attention; they have studied the
newspaper men so carefully that they know just exactly what kind of thing
to put up to them to get them on the front page, and they do the things
necessary to put themselves there. They have made a scientific study of it,
and the results are perfectly marvelous. They wanted to get on the front
page in 1919, and I think the march was held at that time to put themselves
on the front page, and they got there in great shape. In this last march that
we had, and I want to differentiate for a moment between the march and the
fight, because to my mind they were two different things-in this last march
they had had serious differences with Gov. Morgan. They knew the impor-
tance of getting the public sentiment with them. One of the ways to get the
public sentiment with them was to get on the front pages of the newspapers
and to get there with their story told there, because the operators and the
business men are inarticulate; they can not get things in the newspapers
This aggregation of men and the marching across and the dramatic way in
which it was done would enable them to grab the front page of the papers
and tell their story and get their public sentiment with them. And it was,
in addition to that, a sort of protest, because Gov. Morgan had not acceded
to some demands which they had made in their meeting in Charleston. No-
body seemed to care anything about us orphans, who were up in the corner
of Logan County without any government. The newspapers had not paid
any attention to this shooting up of Embrey's car, or the disarmament of
the constabulary; if the governor knew about it he did not evidence knowl-
edge of it or much interest in it. Gen. Bandholtz evidently had not heard
of it. We were up there, cut off from the whole world, and we thought we
were in a pretty tough row of stumps. This march, which I say was for
publicity reasons, stopped at Danville.
The CHAIRMAN. How far is that from Sharpless?
Mr. WILEY. About 16 miles. The night that the shooting occurred at our No.
2 camp there was a very different attitude put over the whole situation. They
did not then march, in my judgment, for publicity purposes; they marched to
go to Logan, and instead of marching they commandeered all of the automo-
biles in that section of the country; they took all the arms they could find,
either out of stores or houses, and they came in crowds, in automobiles all over
the road at a very considerable rate of speed. They commandeered the rail-
road. May I show you this for just a moment, sir? [Referring to map.]
The CHAIRMAN. Certainly.
Mr. WILEY. If you will notice the railroad from St. Albans up into Big Coal
River and Little Coal River branches at Sproul.
The CHAIRMAN. When you say "up," what do you mean?
Mr. WILEY. Up the creek, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. This is the railroad you speak of? [Indicating.}

Mr. WILEY. No. In regard to all of my stores, sir, to show how nicely my
men behaved, nothing was taken from any of the stores. I asked them, in
order to avail myself of the psychology of maintaining law and order as much
as I could, and respect for everyday rules, I asked the committees if they
wanted anything from our stores to make an order for it and come and get it,
hoping by that means the destruction of store property and the general let-down
of things might be prevented. They agreed to do that. That was strictly
lived up to. Two men from the outside, whom we did not know, came into the
store once and asked to see some red handkerchiefs, and these were shown, and
one fellow started out and said-the storekeeper told him the conditions under
which we were operating, and he was a little ugly, I suppose personally bilious,
and he went on away with the handkerchief, and he was not stopped, sir.
Now, the other stores, at one time-and this may give you the idea of the men
and how they felt they were within their rights and doing what was proper;
it is very interesting as showing the psychology of how they felt they were well
within their rights and that they did not mean to do what they were doing in
any offensive way to the people like myself in our neighborhood. At the No. 4
store some Cabin Creek man came in one night hungry. There was no store
man there available. They broke into the store and got the food necessary to
feed these men and reported it; kept an account of what they took; they did
not think that was thieving or committing burglary; they paid for the goods,
and every dollar that was taken out of any of our stores was paid for by the
men.
The CHAIRMAN. By whom?
Mr. WILEY. By the committees.
The CHAIRMAN. You submitted the bills to the committees?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. And they paid them?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir; kept tab on it and did not give it out without an order.
The CHAIRMAN. Did your men join-most of your men go out at that time
and join this army?
Mr. WILEY. All of them did.
The CHAIRMAN. How long was your plant shut down?
Mr. WILEY. A week.
The CHAIRMAN. Did you ever go over to Blair Mountain or see the actual
hostilities?
Mr. WILEY. No, sir; my policy was to be right where my men could talk to

possible of what they did not want me to know. There was only one time when
I tried to raise the cover a little bit. I did not see why they objected to having
the wires up; it was extremely trying to be up there without any communica-
tion with anybody, and I went to my committees, as the only avenue of ap-
proach I had, to ask them if they could not go to somebody in authority, I did
not know who, and let me talk to him about the advisability of putting the
wires up, it being, as far as I could see, as advantageous to them to have the
wires up as it was to me. But I never got anywheres near anybody in author-
ity; the committee seemed to object to discussing it and seemed to object to put-
ting me in touch with any such person. I heard a lot of wire rumors about
certain men being in authority at certain places, but nothing I attached any
importance to.
The CHAIRMAN. Did you make any investigation to learn who really had
charge of this movement, who was managing this march?
Mr. WILEY. It was on this occasion I tried to find out, and I did not.
The CHAIRMAN. They seemed to be moving according to some plan, did they
not?
Mr. WILEY. Very distinctly, sir; they had commissaries; they had field hos-
pitals; they commandeered the doctors. I was coming down the road one day
and met two carloads, I think, of Red Cross nurses with "N. M. W." on the front
of their caps. They went after the thing very thoroughly and, I thought, very
ably. There was one young Army officer who came in afterwards, and I said
I thought the thing had been pretty well organized and pretty well managed,
and he said he did not think so; but he was the only man who did not think
so. All the rest of us thought it well organized and managed.
The CHAIRMAN. Did he have anything to do with it?
Mr. WILEY. No; he was in the Regular Army-came in with the troops after-
wards.

The CHAIRMAN. Were there any ex-service men?
Mr. WILEY. I heard there was a very large number, sir. I saw a good many
uniforms that led to confirm me in that view. I think quite a large number of
them were.
I should like to cite the trouble about starting and stopping these things. It
is not a matter of any particularly great amount of ability to stir people up
without either real or imaginary wrongs to resentment, but it does require a
great deal of ability to bestir them with your eloquence. Mr. Murray, the vice
president of the United Mine Workers, came to see me in the midst of this
trouble and asked me to tell him the condition, which I did. He turned to me
and said, "Suppose I am asked to do the impossible and go out and stop these
men now; do you think I can do it?" I said, "You might as well try to sweep
up the Atlantic Ocean with a broom." He said: "Don't you believe, Mr. Wiley,
if I did go out and try to stop this I would lose my life?" I said: "Yes, sir;
I do believe it."
The CHAIRMAN. Did Mr. Murray want to stop it?
Mr. WILEY. I thought he very, very much wanted to stop it; he did not say
so in words, but I gathered that in conversation.
The CHAIRMAN. But he thought he could not stop it?
Mr. WILEY. He certainly felt he could not stop it.
The CHAIRMAN. And you felt the same way about it?
Mr. WILEY. I was perfectly satisfied he could not stop it, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. What could have stopped it?
Mr. WILEY. I do not think anything in the world could stop it at that time
but the troops that did stop it.
The CHAIRMAN. What, in your judgment, would have happened if the troops
had not arrived?
Mr. WILEY. My personal opinion is that the men, while they were very large
in quantity, were not sufficiently trained to go up against the much better
trained men of the Logan field. I think they would have been defeated, and
in the event of their defeat the men who came back in our hollow would have
been in such a bad temper that they would have destroyed property and persons,
probably, and we would have had the worst anarchy that we ever have had.
The CHAIRMAN. You heard these men talking, and of course the atmosphere
was charged with the matter. What was their object? What was the object
of this invading army, as you gathered it?
Mr. WILEY. In addition to being the past masters of pubicity, I think that
the labor leaders are the past masters of crowd psychology.
The CHAIRMAN. What kind of psychology?
Mr. WILEY. Crowd psychology. They have what I consider a most admirable
knowledge of the reaction of the crowd to certain things. I think they felt
they had been defeated in the Mingo trouble and they lacked something to fill
up the imagination of the people to induce them to do the things necessary to
be done to unionize Logan. The Logan nonunion fields are very commonly
talked about as being well equipped with an arsenal and with men and with
plans of defense, and it is a very difficult thing, when that talk is around, to
get men to go up against what they believe to be guns. The killing of these
men in our No. 2 camp, that was necessary-that was the thing that they used
to fire the imagination of the men, and gave them the ability to talk it into
them, and so they could say, "Now, we have told you that these deputy sheriffs
are terribly bad men who, if they get over here, will shoot you up and kill
women and children," and that they had just been down on this camp and
killed these women and children right in the camp, because one of the papers
the next day said a woman had been killed there, and that was used to influence
them to the extent of going to the trouble with their feet, that had already been
made in marching to Danville, and ride with their guns to the firing line, on
the edge of the nonunion fields. I think they wanted to unionize those fields
and wanted to use this, a most dramatic incident, as the inflammatory material
necessary to get that done.
The CHAIRMAN. You think they intended to go on to Logan and on to Mingo
County, or did they want to be stopped?
Mr. WILEY. I think they wanted to be stopped at Danville, but I do not think
they wanted to be stopped this second time, after they started to Logan.
The CHAIRMAN. When the troops came in there, they retired?
Mr. WILEY. No, sir; when the troops came in they fired-continued this fire
for about 36 hours afterwards.
The CHAIRMAN. After the troops came in?

"Well, one crowd climbs up on one side of a hill and the other crowd climbs

The CHAIRMAN. You could hear the shooting?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir; and one of the curious things was that there was so
much of it at night. If I had been an officer on either side I should have been

There is very heavy growth of timber, and in the night, with no light coming
through, it would have been extremely dangerous, and I do not see how in the
world they could keep firing at night the way they did if they really were
shooting at somebody, but practically, from my memory of it, they kept it
up almost continuously and shot away wastefully more ammunition than
I believed was possible.
The CHAIRMAN. Was more firing done in the night than in the daytime?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir; I thought so.
The CHAIRMAN. What do you understand as to how many were killed on

Mr. WILEY. Senator, I never could get a reasonable figure on that. They
seem to want to not talk about it. And, as I tell you, the things they do
not want to talk about I just back off from.
The CHAIRMAN. But you think the percentage of the death rate was small in
proportion to the amount of shots fired?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. You did not think all of this shooting was merely to get

The CHAIRMAN. They got on the front page, I suppose?
