said they simply were not there; that he scoured the whole country and could
not find them. Later we learned that they had got between-in the first place
the major had ordered them not to leave the troops; that it was very dangerous,
but they seemed to think they were playing pinochle up in the hills, and they
wanted to get in the front line and hired two men to guide them to a place
where they could get on the front line.
After getting to this place the man had told them they were perfectly safe,
because he had just been there himself, but he carried a gun-they got into
this position and then both sides began firing on them and they were under
cross-fire, and it took a long while to convey the idea that they were unarmed
and did not want to fight. Meanwhile I think the woman reporter had been
nicked on the thumb and a man was shot in the leg and shot a glancing blow
on the head, and somebody else was shot. I think three of them were shot.
The CHAIRMAN. It was a sort of a dangerous thing for a newspaper man to
get fired on by both sides?
Mr. WALSH. They treated him just like they do Congressmen.
The CHAIRMAN. Are there any more questions you want to ask, Mr. Walsh?
Mr. WALSH. I thought I would like to ask him a few. He is going to stay
here and I see it is 25 minutes to.1. I tought I would do so after lunch.
Mr. WILEY. I should like to make a little statement, Senator, if you will hear
me about this. It will only take me about five minutes. Shall I wait until
after luncheon or make it now?
The CHAIRMAN. Let us have it now.
Mr. WILEY. I want to suggest to you, sir, that in my conversation with my
associate operators, and with other people, and even with the newspapers, that
the brains and ability of the labor leaders do not seem to have the recognition
that I feel they are entitled to. That is a sort of a-not that it is ever said in
words but they are acting really with brains and with some definite purpose,
but because it is done by a labor leader the general attitude is to decry it.
Their knowledge of the psychology of crowds, which is very little studied-I
think Le Bon is the only one who has ever written a book on the subject-
they are the masters of it; just how to get a reaction from a crowd, just how
to appeal to them. Their ability to speak, to me, is most remarkable. Where
they learned it I do not know, but they have got the biggest percentage of real
good speakers, who can carry a crowd with them, of any number of people that
I have ever come in contact with. Their knowledge of publicity I have re-
ferred to.
I want to tell you a little story as I saw it, that occurred here in Wash-
ington, that covers both of those points. During Dr. Garfield's administration
of fuel there was trouble grew up, and two scale committees were called here
from the union and from the operators. When they arrived in Washington
they had the publicity on the side of the operators to a degree, and all of the
reporters believed that the operator was on the right side. Public sentiment
was entirely with the operator. The union was whipped to a frazzle. Before


===== [扫描序号 989] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
975
they had been here a week that sentiment had completely changed. The news-
paper men had got an entirely different view of the situation, and public
sentiment had veered from the operator right around to the miner, and it
had been accomplished not by any particular thing that was said, but in the
attitude of Mr. Lewis, who, when he came out of a meeting, having nothing to
say, chewed his cigar and gave the newspaper boys such a talk that they
could get something in the paper and something to fill up the space, and just
reached out and grabbed them and pulled them to him like that and got his
people out of the danger to a degree that was marvelous. The operator was
tongue-tied, inarticulate, gruff, and drove the public, the newspapers, and the
public sentiment right away from him.
On the night we appeared before Dr. Garfield, Dr. Garfield announced that
he had taken 14 per cent away from the operators and given it to the miners.
Now, please note that the operator lost and the miner gained. Immediately
there was the most magnificent bunch of oratory you ever heard started in
protest against this decision, although he got the 14 per cent; and Dr. Garfield
was subjected to the most grilling, deep-reaching cross-examination a man ever
stood up against, and everybody told of it from the miners' side. From the
operators' side there was one voice which said, "If you do this to us, some of
these people who have been in business a long time will be put out," which
had nothing to do with the argument. I never in my life saw a bunch of men
run over by another bunch as occurred that night.
Now, these men, with all of their great ability and far-reaching vision and
knowledge of how to handle the public pulse have announced, as I understand
it, that they are going to get the full social value of their wages.
The CHAIRMAN. What do they mean by that?
Mr. WILEY. As I understand it, as explained in the conference that oc-
curred after this statement, they meant to get so much of it that there would
be nothing left for the man who put his capital in.
The CHAIRMAN. You really think that is the intention of it?
Mr. WILEY. I do believe, and I further believe, the best reading and con-
versation I have had with these men, that they mean to pull down the Ameri-
can Government and put themselves in the place of it.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you believe that?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. You really think that is the intention of the United Mine
Workers of America?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir; I believe the United Mine Workers of America started
a union at a time when it was most tremendously needed, at a time when the
operators were doing most dreadful things; and that there was a union needed,
and they have done a wonderful work, but as the power has grown in them they
seem to have lost a sense of the benefit to the men, the conditions that they
wanted to remedy when there were no more conditions to remedy; and they
are looking now for new worlds to conquer, and there has come this theory
of going in and making themselves the Government; and that is what hurts
me so, because of all things in the world I love my Government, and the most
valuable thing I have got on earth is the liberties, personal, that my ancestors
have left me, and anybody who attacks those, no matter who does, I can
not help but raise my voice against.
Little by little, so little at a time that nobody notices it, every time they come
into contact with an operators' committee they creep up just a little bit. Every
time they come in contact with a group committee of the commissioners they
come up, just a little bit. None of these advances are so great that it arouses
the public to its danger; the Government never seems to see it; Congress never
seems to see it; the legislatures never seem to see it, but there is this gradual
creeping up and education of the public, and the public becomes so educated to
that that they accept it as quite a matter of course to-morrow; following a line
of policy, going to their own objective and never being turned back or hesitated
at any time since they have started, until it is not far from taking charge of the
government in West Virginia and showing that that has failed, to coming to
Washington and showing that this has failed.
I do not believe that the men want this. I do not believe the leaders want it.
I think that they are riding on a wave that is very dangerous, and they know
the danger and they try to hold back the radicals in their organization, and
ask you read between the lines in some of their meetings you see that they do
not want to be pushed into these positions, but that the radical element forces
them into it, and that they are really trying to hold it back and control the radi-


===== [扫描序号 990] =====
976
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
cal element and to keep themselves in the saddle, but they are being forced by
a power that is too strong for them.
The CHAIRMAN. You think the radicals in the organization are driving on
the leaders to become radicals?
Mr. WILEY. I think the leaders are some of the brainiest men in the United
States, sir, and I think they are trying with all the ability they have got to
hold it back, and I think the radicals are doing it in the general movement and
are having their way, or will to a certain extent, against the leaders' wishes,
just as it happens in my local unions, where the men try to hold it back and
be reasonable, but where the radicals, with that magnificent knowledge of what
a vociferous minority can do, constantly dominate. They evoke a system of
terrorism to men who do not belong to their unions to force them to join that
is remarkable. Nothing specific is done, but the man knows it is to his interest
to join. They go to their legislators and rattle the sword. There is nothing
specifically done, but they are made to join. They come to Washington and do
exactly the same thing. They claim to have a vote back of them which is
perfectly enormous, but whenever they have asked to deliver that vote it does
not materialize, but when they rattle the sword and shake the bones the legis
lators are afraid it is going to happen and cater to them.
The CHAIRMAN. Is there anything more?
Mr. WILEY. No, sir, that is all.

For instance, take the crowds in New York. It is perfectly marvelous to me to

Now, we don't do that in our everyday laws. The labor movement has in-
sidiously, and with a great deal of brains, taught the American people that
wrong committed to either life or property in an industrial dispute is to be
condoned. They have been teaching the public that for 30 years until it has

I think this last march-not march, but this last attack-upon the constituted

else in this country, more than the people who live in West Virginia. My judg
ment is they feel that was a serious mistake, and they did not mean to do it,

strongly in their minds that they could do a thing like that.
Now, if we are to have law and order-and by "law and order" I don't mean
the surface of things; I mean that a man has got to have, not the nominal right,
but the real right to belong to the union or not, as he pleases. If he can feel
that if this terrorism is removed, if this force is removed, all these questions
would be settled between the men and the operators without any trouble. I
don't think there is any reason why a man should not belong to a union, why
he should not do as he pleases, and I fully believe that if he does belong to the
union that should not be counted against him. It is his prerogative as an Amer-
ican citizen to do as he pleases, but he should not cower or browbeat his brother
workmen or the operators.
The CHAIRMAN. He should not browbeat his brother workman who does not
belong to the union.


===== [扫描序号 1003] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
989
Mr. WILEY. Or who does. He browbeats the man who belongs to the union.
Mr. WALSH. And he should not be browbeaten for belonging to the union.
Mr. WILEY. Exactly. That is what I tried to say a minute ago.
The men in the Kanawha field, as I understand it, the members of the union,
on this last occasion were browbeaten and threatened and forced into that
attack. I think that 90 per cent of the people in the field did not want to go
and would not have gone had they not been browbeaten into it.
I will go just a step further. I do not know much about the Guvon side of
our field. I have lived next door to it and I have tried to put myself in their
place and see what I would do under certain conditions. If law and order went
no further than superficially, if the organizer could enter into their field and by
terrorism frighten men into belonging to the union that did not want to belong
to it, I would imagine that they would object. I would if I were over there.
But if it were left up to each man to do for himself without coercion, which it
would be if they were American about it, that would be the better way.
So when we produce law and order, Senator, it has got to be more than a
surface policeman. You have got to provide that kind of protection which will
go so far that the men will not surreptitiously threaten and frighten a man out
of his boots by anonymous letters and threats.
With reference to the psychology of this last trouble that we have had, I got
one great lesson there which was very interesting to me. I lived out West a
good many years where men carry guns and are great shots, and they fight.
I have known a good many so-called bad man of the West; but when this crowd
started down there was a peculiar kind of fear that came from the cry of the
pack that was entirely different from the kind of fear or nervousness that
would come from some man telling you he was going to shoot you on sight. On
this occasion it was demonstrated beyond peradventure. The cry of the pack
got in there until they weakened and ran just as fast as they could go.
It is that cry of the pack that frightens men into doing things that they do
not want to do, and it is the kind of thing against which we must have a remedy.
Mr. VINSON. The cry of "scab" has a deterrent and a frightful effect upon
men that want to work in a nonunion plant, has it not, Colonel?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir; and it is not the cry of "scab ' as applied to himself.
He can stand that without any trouble; but when his wife comes in and says,
"I can not live here. They call me a scab wife." And his children come in
crying and saying, "I am miserable because the other fellows will not play with
me. They call me scab." It is more than a man can be expected to stand, and
he takes the easiest way and gives up his principles and does what he is
told to do.
Mr. VINSON. And joins the union?
Mr. WILEY. The pressure is too great to expect a man to stand it. He not
only joins the union but obeys the union, takes his gun in his hand and goes
out and marches when the union tells him to go out and march.
It is the funniest thing-I can not express just what I mean. As far as
I know, in this trouble my local union did not have anything to do with it.
The men told me that they were not called on to vote at all; that some com-
mittee came there who had authority vested in them; that they did not know
where that authority came from or why they exercised it or by what right,
and that when the meeting was over or what was supposed to be the meeting,
these chaps stayed on there and decided what was to be done.
Mr. VINSON. You mean the fellows that came there to the meeting, the out-
siders?
Mr. WILEY. Yes; this committee whom they did not know. I can not explain
any further than that, as having been told me.
Mr. VINSON. But these men that came there and did that, Mr. Wiley, were
representatives of the United Mine Workers?
Mr. WILEY. Well, sir, I suppose so. I took it for granted they were, or rep-
resentatives of the Charlestown board-well, I don't know; that is the truth.
It was a very curious thing to me.
Mr. WALSH. It was not the Law and Order League, was it?
Mr. VINSON. They did meet and confer with the local at your place?
Mr. WILEY. Yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. And your local obeyed what they commanded?
Mr. WILEY. That is what I understand.
Mr. VINSON. Now, Mr. Wiley, you were speaking with Senator Kenyon a few
moments ago about the lack of respect that people have for law, looking upon
it as either unjust or discriminatory. In that connection what is your opinion

You only want to know what happened during that march? You do not want

The CHAIRMAN. Yes.
Mr. RICHARDS. I would have to go back, then, to Labor Day of 1919. A short
time prior to Labor Day, 1919, the miners in our camp notified us that they were
going to have a celebration that day for themselves and their families; that it
would be a local affair. They were going to have an ox roast and there would
be just their local speakers. We contributed to that, believing it was for that
purpose. All went merrily along until about noontime or a little bit later when

the train gets up there. When that train arrived Mr. Mooney and Mr. Keeney
dropped off and they went before those miners and made speeches to them. I
at that time was possibly a thousand feet-something like that—from where
they were, sitting on my front porch. I could hear quite a commotion, but I
could not determine what was being said. I watched the men there for a
little while and I would see them stirring around quite lively. All at once they
seemed to make a break for the camp, scattered here and there through the

iron that they could muster. They formed up and I said to my folks at that

something that I could stop."
I went down there and said, "What is the matter here? Who is here?"
"Oh," they said, “Keeney and Mooney are here." Then I determined quite
quickly that there was nothing for me to do. I saw that line form and the
march started. They went toward Sovereign.

===== [扫描序号 1006] =====
992
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Mr. VINSON. How long has it been, measuring over what period of time?
Mr. RICHARDS. That is, my entire time around the mines?
Mr. VINSON. Yes, sir.
Mr. RICHARDS. Forty-two years.
Our miners were good, loyal workmen. We were organized, I believe, early
in 1914. From that day to this we have had one local strike. That strike was
caused by the men resenting the authority of their officials. The entire body
of men was removed by direction of the officials, and from that day to this
we have never had a local strike. I do not think anybody had a better work-
ing force than I had. Everything was going along peaceably. The mine was
giving us good production. I do not believe those miners wanted to do a
thing against their Government, either State or National, evidenced by the
fact that they stayed at their working places until men from other mines went
there with guns and forced them to pull the switch and ordered them out.
I have been associated in the mining business, I expect, ever since the or-
ganization has been formed, and I have great regard for men in that organiza-
tion, but I believe, in so far as West Virginia is concerned, the leadership has
fallen down.
I am hoping that those in authority in that organization will be able to cor-
rect that situation. I prefer to work on a union basis. I do not know any
other; but I am frank to say to you that if the reign of terror is to continue,
as it has been down there, I am certainly willing to take off my coat and help
to put that institution out of business. I will do that from the standpoint of
an American citizen.
The CHAIRMAN. Just why as an American citizen?
Mr. RICHARDS. Because I believe it would be in the interest of good govern-
ment to stop a move of that kind. I will make this statement to you: I do not
want you to ask me for my authority, but I will say this to you, that the leader
of that army at Blair told me personally that he did not know what to expect
from the men that were being sent in there to him.
The CHAIRMAN. What did he mean by that?
Mr. RICHARDS. The circumstances that caused him to make that statement
to me were that we were having a pay roll come in. I said to him, “I am hav-
ing a pay roll come in here. I believe I could protect that pay roll, but it
might be better if you would assign the protection." I did not want to do
anything that would in any way get me into a controversy with these men.
He said, "I think you are right. I think you ought to have protection, and
I will put some of your own men there, for with the kind of people we are get-
ting in here, God only knows what they will do."
I saw those trains come up there at night. I could not determine who was
on them, because it was dark. A train was stopped below our place, just a
short distance. I could see them from my porch. Those men marched past
my place across to their headquarters, which was a schoolhouse about 500 feet
from where I was sitting.
The CHAIRMAN. How many of them assembled at Blair?
Mr. RICHARDS. We estimated 1,500.
The CHAIRMAN. How far away was this battle of Blair Mountain? How
near Blair was it?
Mr. RICHARDS. I judge a mile and a half.
The CHAIRMAN. Were you out there at all?
Mr. RICHARDS. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. You could hear the shooting?
Mr. RICHARDS. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. How long did it keep up?
Mr. RICHARDS. Several days.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you know anything about how many people there were
killed?
Mr. RICHARDS. I saw two bodies brought out and was told that there were
three taken over the hill. I do not know whether that is true or not.
The CHAIRMAN. You do not know how many were killed?
Mr. RICHARDS. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Did this shooting keep on all the time, continuously, for two
or three days?
Mr. RICHARDS. Oh, no; there were intermissions.
The CHAIRMAN. How was it at night?
Mr. RICHARDS. I believe the heaviest of the shooting was from evening on
to morning.

The CHAIRMAN. And three men were killed?
Mr. ARNOLD. Three men on what we would term-only three men that I
know of being killed.
The CHAIRMAN. Have you any idea how many shots during the war were
estimated to have been fired for every man killed.
Mr. ARNOLD. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. They were either not firing very straight or were not firing
at one another?
Mr. ARNOLD. They were not firing at one another, sir. In the daytime scarce
any one could be seen. There was nothing to fire at. That is, there were no
men to fire at. At night wild reports were coming across, and a constant firing
was kept up as a big bluff, chiefly.
The CHAIRMAN. How far apart were the two forces?
Mr. ARNOLD. From three-quarters of a mile to 1 mile.
The CHAIRMAN. Were they both on the same mountain, on different sides
of the mountain?
Mr. ARNOLD. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. With a valley between?
Mr. ARNOLD. Partly a valley between, and then around at intervening ravines.
The CHAIRMAN. Were you ever back there after the thing was all over?
Mr. ARNOLD. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Did they have trenches and forts, or anything of that kind?
Mr. ARNOLD. No, sir; none on the defending side, sir. I never saw any,
myself.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you know how many men were massed along that line
for 25 miles to protect Logan?
Mr. ARNOLD. There were about 1,500 men armed to protect Logan County,
but there would not be any more than half that number-I would say five or
six hundred up there was the highest number that was ever up there at any
one time.
The CHAIRMAN. How long did that condition continue?
Mr. ARNOLD. It continued two and a half days after I came there, and I
understood about three days before that.
The CHAIRMAN. You left when the Federal troops came there?
Mr. ARNOLD. The next day after, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Was there any firing after the Federal troops came there?
Mr. ARNOLD. Yes. I might say yes and no. The Federal troops came in on
Saturday. The officers came up and looked over the situation and talked
around awhile and said they would go back down and sleep all night and come
up next morning, which they did; and there was firing after they arrived in
Logan County.
The CHAIRMAN. It stopped soon after?
Mr. ARNOLD. It stopped practically at the time they went up and took up
their positions.
The CHAIRMAN. Are there any questions you desire to ask, Mr. Walsh?
Mr. WALSH. No, thank you, Mr. Chairman.
The CHAIRMAN. Col. Vinson?
Mr. VINSON. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Is there anything else you desire to say, Captain?
Mr. ARNOLD. Not very much, Senator. I believe there are one or two things.
One witness brought up the question if there could not be some law whereby
the sheriff could better function. In West Virginia we have 55 sheriffs, and
they have a sheriffs' association. This association has been trying for some
time to get a law enacted to create a county treasurer and then let the sheriff
be a true sheriff and more of a law-enforc`ng officer.
Mr. VINSON. Under the law now the sheriff himself is county treasurer?
Mr. ARNOLD. The sheriff himself is county treasurer, and some of those sherffs
have given a bond of five hundred to a million dollars.
The CHAIRMAN. How much?

Mr. ARNOLD. Five hundred thousand to a million dollars. They seem to be

The sheriff of Kanawha County, where most of the trouble has been, I

think any one familiar with the legislature of our State would know that it
is not very easy for one man to cause a law to be enacted. The governor can,
of course, veto a bill, but not enact law.
Another point comes up: A great many of the big operators of West Virginia
have expressed a willingness that such time as the State police could be
organized with sufficient force to be relieved of this work of enforcing martial
law in Mingo County and that they would volunteer and gladly do away with
the mine-guard system. In fact, that has already taken place in three or four
instances.
But Gov. Morgan is not to be blamed in this question. I think he is working
hard and sincerely so.
One other question, Senator, if you will pardon me for taking up the time:
In West Virginia a man has to procure a license, giving his name, age, address,
etc., in order to hunt squirrels, but he can go and hunt men with impunity. I
think there should be a law covering high-powered rifles.
The CHAIRMAN. There are too many firearms down there?
Mr. ARNOLD. Yes, sir; too many firearms down there. It is so easy for
anyone to get a license to carry a revolver. They simply go to the judge of
the court and obtain a license, and immediately walk across the street to a
bonding company and give a $3,500 bond for carrying the revolver. Probably
next door is the hardware store, and they go in and purchase a revolver, and
the next day they are out shooting some man. I presume in West Virginia
they have given out five or ten thousand licenses to carry revolvers.
nearly every case of trouble we find the man has a license to carry a revolver.
Mr. WALSH. What are the provisions of that bond? Does it run in favor of
anyone that might be shot?
Mr. ARNOLD. You are required to give a bond of $3,500 to carry a revolver.
Mr. WALSH. To do what? What are the provisions of the bond?
In
Mr. ARNOLD. It is to protect the State-to protect anyone who receives an
injury from that gun; so that the man can be sued upon it.

(On the chairman's return, the hearing proceeded as follows:)
Mr. LANE. You have just asked me what the fundemental issue is. At
bottom the issue in my opinion is a clash between two fundamental and oppos-
ing desires; the desire on the one hand of men in the unorganized fields of
West Virginia who want to join a labor organization, and of the men in the
organization who want to induce them to join the labor organization, and
the desire of the coal operators in the unorganized fields who want to keep
their men out of the labor organization and keep the labor organization away
from their fields. It is a clash of two fundamental conceptions of industrial
relations, two different philosophies.
Stated in a question form, it might be put in this way; shall the miners
in the unorganized fields of West Virginia be allowed to join a labor organiza-
tion and shall the agents and representatives of the United Mine Workers of
America be allowed to carry on proselytization among them?
The CHAIRMAN. Do you hear much complaint of the deputy sheriff or guard
system there?
Mr. LANE. Yes, sir; a great deal; in substance, the complaints that have
been made by other witnesses here before you.
The CHAIRMAN. Can you add anything to the general picture that we have
had, Mr. Lane?
Mr. LANE. I don't think I can tell you very much in the way of actual
facts that you do not already know-that you have not already been told.
There is one point that has struck me that I do not know has been dwelt upon
here as a person looking at it from the outside, and that is that every step
in the direction of settlement of the controversy or conflict-or whatever you
call it seems to be a step in the direction in the use of force. In the last
year and a half since the strike was called in Mingo County Mingo has been
under military control twice and under martial law once. Federal troops
have been called into the State three times; a crowd of armed miners has
congregated and has threatened to invade one county; the State constabulary
has been on duty in Mingo County almost continuously; the National Guard
is at present being reorganized.
The location of the various units of that National Guard shows, it seems
to me, one of the purposes for which it is being organized. The ultimate
strength, as I understand it, is that the West Virginia National Guards will
be 6,400. The number to be permitted to be recruited this year is 1,500, to
be divided up into about 15 companies. Two of those companies are to be
in Williamson; one of them in Logan; two in Welch, the county seat of
McDowell County; two in Bluefield in Mercer County; three in Huntington,
which, by reason of its geographical location, commands quick and easy access
to the various nonunion fields-that is, to Mingo, Logan, Mercer, and McDowell
Counties-two in Charleston, which is perhaps 30 miles from Logan County;
one in St. Albans, which is slightly nearer to Logan County than Charleston;
and one in Weston. The one in Weston is the only one which is at all removed
from the nonunion fields. The others are constituted in the southern and
western part of the State, about one-fourth of the whole State, and this loca-
tion has been made in spite of what has been stated to me by Maj. Davis of
the adjutant general's staff that requests have come from counties in every
side of the State. In other words, the organization is going ahead with the


===== [扫描序号 1014] =====
1000
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
idea of concentrating the men in and around the nonunion field, so as to be
ready for mobilization in case of further industrial trouble.
Now, each of those measures may have been entirely justified in the emer-
gency that called it forth. I am not disputing that justification. That seems
to me, as far as I can learn, to be entirely divorced from any general
or peaceable plan of settlement of the controversy. The acme of statesman-
ship seems to lie in suppressing disorder.
Now, if the conflict there is as I have stated it, if it is a fundamental con-
flict between two opposing desires, two conceptions of industrial relations, the
mere building up of instruments of force, quite apart from any peaceful, or
any attempt at peaceful settlement, will, not, it seems to me, help in bringing
about such a settlement.
I should suppose that anyone who studied the history of the West Virginia
conflict, which dates back 30 years or more, will admit that it has thriven
upon force; that force indulged in by both sides has inflamed the people and
has augmented the violence and bloodshed; such fiends as Staniford in 1902,
when men were killed in battle between mine guards and miners, or the
battle of Paint Creek in 1912, when miniature civil war raged for awhile,
as Matewan in 1920, are the most spectacular manifestations of the conflict.
Now, I do not believe that a continuance in the reliance upon force will
settle the West Virginia conflict.
The CHAIRMAN. Well, what would be your idea of a peaceful settlement
or the means of settlement?
Mr. LANE. Well, it is possible to imagine several methods or processes of
settlement. One would be that the nonunion operators in West Virginia should
decide to accept the union. I mean intellectually that is conceivable. The like-
lihood of it is, of course, apparent to anyone who has heard the testimony
given here. That would be a settlement.
Another possible settlement would be the decision of the union to accept
the status quo and the decision of the union miners in West Virginia to accept
the status quo and the decision of the nonunion miners to go without the
union.
Anyone who has talked to the union leaders and nroved around in those
fields and knows the intensity of the feeling of many of the miners in both the
union and nonunion fields-the intensity of the feeling of those people in the
Mingo tent colonies, for example-knows the likelihood of such a settlement.
Another possible settlement would be-
Mr. WALSH. Knows the liklihood of the unlikelihood.
Mr. LANE. Well, I said likelihood. I mean, of course, that there is no like-
lihood. Another possible settlement would be for all of the parties involved
in this controversy to accept the fact that this is an issue between two oppos-
ing conceptions of industrial relations and to decide to let the issue be deter-
mined without any artificial or forciful or discriminatory methods being em-
ployed; for the operators to state frankly, “We don't want the union; we
shall attempt to make conditions in our mines so favorable that our ren
wont' want the union; but if, nevertheless, they do want it, if you agents of
the United Mine Workers of America can convince them that the union is
better for them, we shall withdraw any opposition based upon any form of
restraint or coercion, and for the union on its part to pursue only per-
fectly legitimate, peaceful methods of persuasion." Ultimately, that would
bring about a settlement, I suppose. Whether it would bring about the unioni-
zation of the nonunion mines is a matter of the future. The decision would
rest in the hands of the nonunion miners themselves.
Now, I realize, of course, that that is painting a chimerical pocture, how-
ever.
I have no ready-made plan of settlement. I do think this, however, that very
little would be gained by a mere finding of facts and publishing of a report
by this committee. I think the situation is too intense to be affected in that
way.
One nonunion operator said to me, "You can tell the union that if it comes
in here, I'll get an army," and his mine superintendent spoke up and said,
"And I'll eat it."
Mr. Keeney, president of District 17 of the union, said to me, "West Virginia
will be organized and it will be organized completely. If Frank Keeney can't
do it, someone else will."
I don't believe that the mere publishing of a report, however cogent and con-
vincing it might be, will affect the situation.

WEST VIRGINIA.
THE CIVIL WAR IN ITS COAL FIELDS.
By WINTHROP D. LANE.
The leaves are just beginning to turn on the steep hills which overlook the
winding, narrow valleys of western West Virginia. Here lie some of the
richest seams of bituminous coal in the world. Nature, as if to conceal her
treasure, has covered all with a thick verdure of trees, impenetrable to the
eye. But man has found his way into her recesses and has tunneled and
bored her mountains until she has yielded her bounty. To do this an army
of workmen has been employed, whose occupations have taken them under-
ground, where day is turned into night. For 30 years many of these men
have been engaged in a conflict with their employers over their right to belong
to the Mine Workers' Union.
I have just visited the latest scenes of this conflict. Ten months ago I had
spent several weeks there at a time when the huge mouths of black mines
gasped in snow-clad hills. During the interval one county has been placed
under martial law, violence has been rampant in a part of the State, Federal
troops have been called in and are still there, thousands of miners have joined
in a cross-country march in protest against what they regarded as a violation
of the rights of their fellows; engagements have been fought with airplanes
and machine-guns. The conflict is farther from settlement than ever. Ani-
mosities have become keener; the atmosphere of the struggle has grown more
intense. There are more arms in the troubled regions of West Virginia to-
day, I think, than ever before.
Force is the weapon chiefly relied upon to settle the dispute. When it is not
force of a direct kind, it is indirect force or repression. Jails stand crowded.
Arrests are made on a wholesale scale. Grand juries vie with each other in
returning indictments. The State is reorganizing her National Guard. These
measures are wholly divorced from any general or peaceful plan of adjustment.
The acme of statesmanship seems to lie in suppressing disorder. As one goes
about the State he finds a sinister and corroding cynicism in the minds of many
people. Weary of the long struggle, they no longer expect an immediate or
friendly settlement. The causes of the conflict grow and fester, while only
the surface manifestations are given attention. Every step in the direction of
settlement is a step toward the use of force, and it is force that has brought
the struggle to its present proportions.
There is a tragic interest in some of the features of the conflict. Miners
who joined the union and were refused recognition by the operators went on
strike. They were compelled to leave their company-owned houses and are
still living with their families in tent colonies along the Tug River and on the
hillsides of Mingo County. It was a surprise to see, after the lapse of 10 months,
the same faces peering out of the same tents that were exposed to the cold
and wet last winter. For more than a year now many of these men, women,
and children have been living in their slight and flapping shelters; they have
withstood every argument of weather and unemployment to return to work.
Women held up their babies and asked the visitor to see how they had grown
during the interval. Men explained that they had not been entirely idle, and
pointed to new floors in their tents and to other improvements.
Senator W. S. Kenyon and Senator S. M. Shortridge who visited the tent
colonies last month found determination still strong among them.
"Hello, Senator Kenyon," said a Negro, as the senatorial party came up.
"How are you?"

The strike in Mingo County, which has been the center of the conflict in
the public mind, is, I think, lost. The operators claim that they have had their
full number of employees since the first of the year, and that production has
not suffered from the strike since that time. They have brought in several
hundred strike breakers, and have conducted a wide and costly campaign of
advertising in the newspapers, partly to bring their own men back to work,
and partly to lay the case of the nonunion employees before the public. The
exact measure of their success is, of course, difficult of independent verification,
but despite the 1,300 or 1,400 people who are sticking it out in the tent
colonies and the others living elsewhere, the mines would be seem to be
capable of running at nearly normal capacity if the demand for coal required
it. Yet, the loss of this particular strike will be only an incident in the long
struggle. We may expect to see the union bide its time and strike again when
the occasion is ripe.
Who are the miners who are thus at odds with their employers? Native
white Americans predominate among them. To one who has heard much talk
of their "bolshevism" and "socialistic tendencies" this may come as a sur-
prise. According to the annual report of the State department of mines in
1919, the latest available statistics, there are 91,366 men working "in and
around the mines" of the State. Of these 31,404 are American whites, 10,341
are negroes, and 23,821 are of foreign nationality. Ital ans, Hungarians, Aus-
trians, and Poles are the chief groups of foreigners. Except for a slightly
higher percentage of negroes, the ratios do not vary much in the five counties
comprising the bulk of the nonunion territory, where 16,808 are American
whites, 9,375 negroes, and 7,934 of foreign nationality.
Do these miners who now lack the union desire it? The owners and man-
agers of nonunion mines answer "No" to this question without fail.
"Our
men are satisfied as they are," they say, and such owners and managers have
done all they can to make satisfaction certain by intelligently planned and ex-
pensive welfare work. But as one goes around, he doubts the authority of
their mandate to speak finally for their men on this point. Why the men who
happen to be working in the mines of five particular counties 'n West Virginia
should be so different from their fellows throughout the country is not easy
to see. Moreover, there are indications that the operators do not see all the
facts. When several thousand men joined the union within a few months in
Mingo County a year and a half ago the success was due in part at least to
spontaneous request from the men for admission. Organizers have gone into
Logan County. Desp'te the difficulties of talking unionism in that field, where
deputy sheriffs paid by the operators keep a sharp lookout for "agitators,"
petitions have been signed there by miners requesting the union to organize
them. One such pet'tion, frayel and worn, is in the files of the union in
Charleston brought out by an organizer who tramped over the hills and who
concealed the petition in his shoe in order to prevent its discovery.
Throughout the country to-day the bituminous coal fields are largely organ-
ized. Soft coal is produced in some 20 States. Such large coal-producing areas
as Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, and western Pennsylvania have almost solidly accepted
the union. The United Mine Workers of America is a relatively advanced ele-
ment of the American labor movement. Its national body has demanded the
nationalization of the coal mines, and certain districts have begun to demand a
share in the maintenance and control of production. Among the most important
nonunion fields are the Connellsville section in Pennsylvania, another strip
along the Allegheny River, the Alabama fields, Utah, and these nonunion areas
of West Virginia. But by bit the union has succeedel in wresting one section
after another of West Virginia. Bloody scenes have marked this progress at
intervals. To-day approximately half of the 95,000 miners in the State are
members of the union. The unorganized portions are concentrated, for the most
part, in the five counties of Logan, Wyoming, Mercer, McDowell, and Mingo.
Who are the operators in this district that are so hostile to unionism? Not
as much is known about the ownership of coal lands in West Virginia as might
be. Some clue to the forces back of the struggle is gained. however, from the
fact that the United States Steel Corporation is one of the largest owners of
nonunion coal land. Subs diary companies of the corporation own 50,736 acres
of coking coal land and 32,648 acres of surface coal land in Logan and Mingo
counties combined, according to its annual report for 1919. In the Pocahontas
field-chiefly McDowell, Mercer and Wyoming counties-the corporation leases

1007
through subsidiaries 63,766 acres of the best coking and fuel property. The
Norfolk and Western Railway Company, which traverses the Pocahontas field,
is also heavily interested in coal lands in these parts. It owns nearly every
share of the Pocahontas Coal & Coke Company, a leasing company, on whose
lands upward of 25 mining companies operate. The Norfolk and Western Rail-
way Company is commonly understood to be controlled by the Pennsylvania
Railroad. There are, of course, other large owners and many smaller ones. The
resident owner is not scarce, but a great deal of the land in these regions is
owned by absentee holders, living in other states and the large cities. None
the less, the West Virginia operators allege that a conspiracy exists, and has
existed for years, between the United Mine Workers of America and the union
operators of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, and Western Pennsylvania to organize the
nonunion mines of their State. The purpose of this conspiracy, they say, is to
compel them to accept competition on an equal basis with the union fields in
spite of their own geographical isolation, surrounded on nearly all sides as they
are by mines nearer the large industrial markets.
The West Virginia employers, moreover, back up their stand by saying that
the public interest demands that a portion of the coal of the country remain
nonunion, so that in the event of a national strike of miners there may be some
source of coal to keep the nation from freezing to death.
The fight is not, therefore, a local struggle merely. It is a fight between huge
combinations of capital and resources on the one hand, and one of the largest
and most aggressive of labor unions on the other. It is a fight between two
different industrial philosophies, for the steel trade is the stronghold of anti-
unionism in American industry, and the Pennsylvania Railroad has taken at
times a belligerent attitude toward railroad labor organizations.
The operators have sought the courts in their efforts to stem the union's
activities in West Virginia. To-day injunctions protect nearly the whole of
Mercer and McDowell counties against encroachment by the union; no union
organizer or representative can enter those counties with the message of union-
ism on his lips without danger of arrest. Individual contracts with their em-
ployees have also been resorted to by the operators-the "yellow dog" contracts
of union phraseology-whereby the men bind themselves not to "join or belong
to" any mine labor organization "so long as the relation of employer and em-
ployee exists.", These contracts have been used especially in Mercer and
McDowell counties.
A further means of relief at the hands of the law has been sought by the
operators, to be used in the event that some of their men should actually join
the union. They have set up the contention that the relation, between the em-
ployer and the employee, in regard to the house which the miner rents from the
coal company, is not that of landlord and tenant, but that of master and serv-
ant. The object of this is to permit them not only to discharge a man who joins
the union, but to put him out of his house as well. A large number of evictions
have occurred under this interpretation of relationships, and their effect has
been to render all of the miners and their families, comprising about one-fourth
of the State's population, insecure in their right to domicile. The miners have
no shelter that is not subject to immediate confiscation. The houses owned by
the coal companies are the only ones there are to live in.
Other methods to oppose the union have been used. That deputy sheriffs are
paid by the operators is both admitted and defended by the employers them-
selves. No less an authority than the attorney general of the State, E. T. Eng-
land, says that "everyone knows that one of the duties of these deputies is to
keep the union out." The use of agents of the Baldwin-Felts Detective Agency
and "under-cover" men is now well established.
Precisely what resort it had to "armed guards," men who are employed
privately by the operators, and equipped with guns on the understanding that
they are to keep away all agents of the union, is not clear. That this has been
the practice in the past in a few, at least, of the nonunion districts, was the
unequivocal statement to me of T. L. Lewis, now secretary of the New River
Coal Operators' Association and formerly an official of the union. Many of
the deputy sheriffs are, of course, no other than armed guards in effect. Ex-
travagant statements are sometimes made by the union in regard to the number
of such persons employed by the operators but it is clear that here is a kind or
opposition that keeps men in constant fear for their personal safety and that
the union will never cease agitating for the riddance of what it regards as a
direct threat to the physical welfare of its representatives. /

The acts of such armed men are not easy to control. The operators may
say, of course, that they have never planned or ordered assaults on union or-
ganizers or men who “talked unionism,” but such assaults have been committed
none the less. A commission appointed by former Gov. Cornwell two years ago
to inquire into conditions in Logan County secured ample evidence that union
agents and sympathizers had been beaten up and injured by deputy sheriffs
in that county. Affidavits have been given to the Senate Committee on Edu-
cation and Labor, charging that a union bricklayer from Huntington was shot
in cold blood in the jail in Logan County on September 1 by two deputy sheriffs,
one of the witnesses alleging that the act was committed not 3 feet from his
cell.
Union miners have resorted to violence in their turn. There have ben car-
fully planned attacks on the property of nonunion coal compaies and on persons
idntified with hostility to the union. Mingo County has been the scene of much
violence of this sort. Guerilla warfare, made comparatively safe by the to-
pography of the country, which is marked by wooded hills overlooking open,
hollow valleys, has raged intermittently for over a year. In this warfare shots
have been fired by both sides.
The possession of arms is no secret. "We had some bad luck," I overheard a
person identified with the side of the miners say. "Some guns that were meant
for our fellows at
were put off at the wrong station and the other side
got 'em." In Logan County an operator showed me his "arsenal." The county
authorities throughout the nonunion district are, in a sense, commanders of
small garrisons. They can mobilize and equip scores, if not hundreds, of men
on short notice.
What, meanwhile, has the State government been doing to bring peace and
order to a situation so intense as this? For four months it has been main-
taining martial law in Mingo County for one thing. This is the third time
within a year that some form of military control has been proclamed in that
strike-swept area; on the other two occasions Federal troops were called in.
To-day the State is using its own force-rifle company of the National Guard,
which is now being reorganized. When a "three days' battle" occurred along
a 10-mile front in Mingo County on May 12, 13, and 14, during which shots
were exchanged by union and nonunion elements, the tent colonies were fired
into and damage was done to the property of coal companies, local authorities
appealed to Gov. E. F. Morgan to assist them. Gov. Morgan accordingly pro-
claimed that a state of "war, insurrection, and riot" existed in Mingo County,
and directed Maj. Thomas B. Davis, acting adjutant general, to proceed there,
and, with the aid of the State constabulary and deputy sheriffs, to place the
region under martial law.
The legality of this procedure was assailed by the United Mine Workers of
America when its members were arrested under the martial-law proclamation.
The State supreme court of appeals held the edict invalid. The reason given
by the court was that the proclamation could only be enforced by the occupancy
of the zone covered by a military force, and that the State constabulary and
deputy sheriffs were not a military force.
Thereupon Gov. Morgan, to provide such a force, issued a new proclamation
ordering the enrollment of the "unorganized militia" of the county. This, it
is said, was done under an old statute. Every person liable to military duty in
the county became subject to draft in this new militia. Two companies of
65 men each were formed and these citizens and residents of the county
shouldered guns and proceeded to give effectiveness to the governor's proclama-
tion of martial law. Two months later the first company of the reorganized
National Guard took their place.
Both military and civil authorities are clothed with the power to make
arrests in Mingo County, but only the civil courts are trying persons for
offenses. For some time the jail has had over 100 men, some of whom, accord-
ing to the jailer, have no charges against them of which he is aware. C. F.
Keeney, president of District 17 of the United Mine Workers of America, and
Fred Mooney, secretary, are in the Mingo jail, charged with complicity in the
murder several months ago of two men. Both officials say that they were
attending a convention of the State Federation of Labor in Huntington at the
time and know nothing of the killing. Mr. Keeney and Mr. Mooney are also
under indictment in Logan County for having taken part in the recent "armed
march," and Mr. Keeney is under a third indictment in Boone County, charged
with carrying a pistol. Neither is anxious to secure bail, the reason being that

when released they would be liable to further arrest and incarceration in Logan
County, where their lives might not be safe.
The State has also called in a thousand United States troops to suppress dis-
order in connection with the "armed march" in last August of union miners
through Boone County toward Logan. These troops were still there October
14. Without doubt this march was a formidable affair. There is reason to
believe, however, that it would have ended more quitely than it did, and that
the 5,000 or so miners in it would have disbanded without serious rupture of
the peace, if a group of State constabulary who were opposing their advance
had not made an apparently uncalled-for attack upon a little town named
Sharpless, near the place where the miners were assembled. This fanned their
expiring purpose to new energy.
One
The object of the demonstration seems to be shrouded in uncertainty.
account has it that the miners intended to march to Mingo County, crossing
Logan County in their path, and protest against the enforcement of martial
law there and the abuses that they understood were being committed against
their fellows. According to this version, what they really hoped for was to
get Federal troops called into Mingo County as a better alternative than the
régime then in force. Another story, credited to the operators and some
residents of Logan County, is that they intended to seize the mines in Logan
and compel the employers to recognize the union. A third is that theirs was a
vague, leaderless uprising without deliberate purpose or objective. Whatever
its motive, there is no doubt that it spread considerable terror among the
inhabitants in its path, especially those in Logan County who were fearful
of an attack.
The miners succeeded in advancing to a point part way up the slope of
Blair Mountain, the high ridge that separates Boone and Logan Counties.
Here they formed a line some 15 miles in length, with the crest of the ridge
before them. One end of the line was at Madison, in Boone County, and
the other at Blair, in Logan. Meanwhile, a large force of hastily recruited
citizens, deputy sheriffs, nonunion miners, and others from Logan and Mingo
Counties were waiting on the other side of the ridge under the leadership of
Don Chafin, Logan County sheriff. A small number of the State constabulary
as well, held part of the defending line. Shots were exchanged in large
numbers and several union miners, the exact number unknown, were killed.
Three persons in the Logan County forces were killed. A small airplaine was
used by the Logan County defenders and a number of bombs were dropped on
territory held by the invading miners. No damage was done in this way.
The Federal troops came upon the scene by two routes. One command entered
behind the Logan, or defending forces, and the other slipped in between the
opposing lines themselves. The Logan forces were thus sandwiched between
two lines of United States soldiers, and the miners, on the other hand, were
effectually barred from further advance. No fighting took place after the
arrival of Uncle Sam's men. The miners disbanded and went home, many of
them being disarmed by the soldiers on their way. The extent of depredations
seems to have been small, and in several instances members or officials of the
union reimbursed storekeepers whose goods had been taken. The "army'
of marchers seems to have imitated military tactics sufficiently to commandeer
railroad stock and some automobiles.
19
The aftermath of this march has been a crop of indictments. A special
Boone County grand jury has indicted 301 persons, 189 of these being charged
with "insurrection" and most of the others with carrying pistols. Everyone
arrested, according to the prosecuting attorney, will be held under heavy bond
or in jail to await the November term of the Circuit Court. But Boone County
has been restrained in comparison with Logan, where 900 people are wanted
in connection with the demonstration. The miners, however, who took part in
or witnessed the march are taking this matter into their own hands. Over
a thousand of them, according to Col. C. S. Martin, who is in charge of the
Federal troops there, have already left the scene of the disturbance. Many
of them are taking their families with them and leaving no addresses behind.
The reorganization of the State's National Guard is proceeding under au-
thority granted by the legislature last spring. This is another public measure
directed at the conflict over unionism. West Virginia's former National Guard
had ceased to exist when its members were mustered out of the United States
Army at the end of the war. To-day the reorganization is being speeded up.
One company is already in active service and is giving effect to the proclama-
tion of martial law in Mingo County.


===== [扫描序号 1024] =====

Fifteen companies will be formed this year, although the ultimate strength
of the guard will be much larger. The distribution of these companies
is significant. Fourteen of the whole number are being concentrated in or near
the nonunion coal fields. One more will be recruited in Mingo County, one
in Logan County, two at Welch, county seat of McDowell County; two at
Bluefield, in Mercer County; three at Huntington, which commands quick and
easy entrance to the nonunion fields; three at Charleston, only 30 miles from
Logan County; one at St. Albans, near Charleston, and one at Weston. Only
the last is not in position to be of immediate service in protecting the non-
union territory. Meanwhile, three-fourths of the State, the eastern and
northern sections, are, in spite of applications for them, going without any
companies of the National Guard.
A disagreement evidently exists in regard to the admission of members of
labor unions. Maj. T. C. Davis, of the adjutant general's staff (not the Maj.
Davis who is in charge of martial law in Mingo County), said that no member
of a union would be admitted. "It is a rule of the National Guard," he said,
"not to take in union men. They don't make good members. At any rate,
that is the policy we are adopting here." This was later denied by Adjt. Gen.
J. H. Charnock, in charge of the reorganization. "We want the best men
we can get," said the adjutant general. "If a member of a union is a good
citizen we have no objection to him. We do aim to exclude radicals and
undesirables. Our support is coming from business and professional classes
for the most part." The two officers agreed that the guard was to act as
"a strictly neutral organization."
We have now seen the elements that compose West Virginia's industrial strug-
gle. What is to be the outcome? Two groups, each with roots reaching outside
the State, are engaged in what is little different from civil war. From time to
time the strong arms of the State and Federal Governments are interposed to
separate the combatants. Many of the instruments of modern warfare have
been used; airplanes have hovered over the State, bombs have been dropped,
machine guns have rattled, tear gas and Big Berthas remain to be used. But
does public reliance solely on such methods of suppression get anywhere in the
long run? Col. Martin, in command of the United States soldiers who came to
check the recent march, sees the situation clearly. "We have quieted the dis-
order for the moment," he said. "The fundamental causes remain. Whatever
produced this disturbance may give rise to another."

and blowing up of tipples and houses and things of that sort?
Mr. LANE. I do not think Mr. Shear did.
Mr. VINSON. Have you asked any operators or counsel for the operators to
give you a detailed statement of that?
Mr. LANE. I have heard detailed statements of a great many individual
instances of them.
Mr. VINSON. I am asking you about-do you come to the other side and ask
of anyone-
Mr. LANE. I mean I have asked it of operators; yes, sir.
Mr. VINSON. Of who, for instance?
Mr. LANE. Well, I have had testimony of that sort from Mrs. Joseph G.
Bradley.
Mr. VINSON. About the detail of the striking down there in Mingo?
Mr. LANE. Did your question include Mingo?
Mr. VINSON. Yes; I included Mingo; yes.
Mr. LANE. I got information of that sort in Mingo County from Mr. Bause-
wine, secretary of the Williamson Coal Operators' Association.
Mr. VINSON. He gave you a detailed statement of it, did he?
Mr. LANE. I do not know what you mean by a detailed statement of it.
Mr. VINSON. I mean how the attacks were made and what the result was of
that attack, and who made it, and how many people were killed, if any; that is
what I mean by that.
Mr. LANE. I think Mr. Bausewine gave me information of that sort.
Mr. VINSON. Did you believe him?
Mr. LANE. Well, I did not pass judgment on his statements.
Mr. VINSON. Do you believe it now or do you not? You do one or the other.
Mr. LANE. I neither believe nor disbelieve Mr. Bausewine's statements on
that point. I do believe statements that were made to Senator Kenyon and
Senator Shortridge by superintendents of coal companies in Mingo County-one
the White Star Mining Co., at Merrimac; one the Borderland Coal Co., I think-
in regard to shooting up their plants.
Mr. VINSON. You heard those statements, did you?
Mr. LANE. I heard them, and I have published them.
Mr. VINSON. In what paper?
Mr. LANE. In the Survey and in the New York Evening Post.
Mr. VINSON. Did you publish Mr. Perkins's statement of the White Star and
the shooting up the woman, and that she had to run with her baby?
Mr. LANE. Yes.
Mr. VINSON. And had to get behind a car, and they shot at her there for a
while, and then she had to run across the street into her house, and they kept
on shooting at her?


===== [扫描序号 1032] =====
1018
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Mr. LANE. I published the incident about the woman.
Mr. VINSON. You did not publish the details of it? You did not publish Mr.
Perkins's testimony?
Mr. LANE. I gave enough of it to show just what had happened. Of course,
nobody could publish in any publication all the testimony that was given to the
Senators on the trip.
Mr. VINSON. But you thought that was a very horrible thing, did you not?
Mr. LANE. I did; yes.
Mr. VINSON. Did you think that was as horrible as the fact of Sid Hatfield
becoming a detective and getting into the union organization for that purpose?
Mr. LANE. Mr. Lively, you mean.
Mr. VINSON. Lively, I mean. Which did you think was the more horrible of
the two?
66
Mr. LANE. Well, I suppose you would have to define the word horrible."
Mr. VINSON. I mean the thing that would shock people, shock the very con-
science of men; that is what I mean by horrible.
Mr. LANE. My conscience, in view of the whole history of the West Virginia
conflict-my conscience, I think, is shocked more by the practices, continued,
deliberate practices, of undercover men or labor spies, than there will be by a
single instance of the exercise of violence.
Mr. VINSON. As I understand, your answer to that question is that your con-
science has received a greater shock at the conduct of men like Lively, seeking to
ferret out crimes, becoming members of the United Mine Workers for that pur-
pose, than men hiding away in a hill shooting a woman, or trying to shoot her,
and when she is trying to escape, and hiding behind cars and behind houses,
and keeping on shooting at her until she finally disappeared, carrying her baby
in her arms. As I understand, your answer is that the shock to your conscience
is greater in the Lively instance than it is in the other?
Mr. LANE. No; that is not the answer, because your question assumes that
the purpose of Mr. Lively was solely to detect the commission of crimes. My
statement used the words "undercover men and labor spies," which means a
very different thing.
Mr. VINSON. Well, now, then, putting your own interpretation upon Mr.
Lively's conduct, and then will you answer my first question, which strikes
your conscience as being the most horrible?
Mr. LANE. My interpretation of Mr. Lively's conduct, as revealed by him
on testimony, is that he joined the United Mine Workers of America, acted as
an official of one or more of its locals, assisted in the organization-
Mr. VINSON. That is all in evidence, every bit of it.
Mr. WALSH. I object to the interruption.
The CHAIRMAN. Go ahead.
Mr. LANE. Assisted in the organization of locals in Mingo County, adminis-
tered the obligation or oath to the new members of at least one local, and
that he did this posing to the members of the union simply as a union man
while he was actually in the employ of the Baldwin-Felts Detective Agency,
serving as a secret operative of that agency and supplying information to that
agency, presumably for the use of the coal operators in regard to the efforts of
their men and the plans of their men to form labor organizations. That is my
interpretation of Mr. Lively's conduct. My answer is that my conscience is
shocked more by the continued, deliberate practice of that kind of espionage
and spying than it is by a single instance of violence in a strike field in which
violence is a daily occurrence.
Mr. VINSON. I see. Then, if I understand you, you do not think that Mr.
Lively was very ethical in his methods to run down criminals?
Mr. LANE. Well, again you have used the phrase "run down criminals."
Mr. VINSON. Let us put it on that score. This question assumes that Mr.
Lively was sent there, as the testimony shows he was, to get evidence to punish
men who stood indicted for murder. Now, that is the evidence in this case.
Mr. LANE. I beg pardon; the evidence shows more than that.
Mr. WALSH. I was going to say, Mr. Chairman.
Mr. VINSON. Let us assume that the evidence is true for the sake of the
question I am going to ask you. Now, then, in order to get that evidence, in
order to bring these people to justice, do you think that Mr. Lively's method of
joining the union there in order to get the evidence was unethical or improper?
Mr. LANE. No; I am not sure that it was at all. If that were his purpose,
if he had solely the purpose that you have assumed.

Mr. VINSON. Now, just one other question: Did you belong to the pacifist
organizations during the late war in New York?
Mr. LANE. I did not; no.
Mr. VINSON. Were you not in a pacifist parade there?
Mr. LANE. I was not; no.
Mr. VINSON. You are quite sure of that?
Mr. LANE. I am.

(The exhibits offered in evidence October 27, 1921, are as follows:)
INVESTIGATION OF LOGAN COUNTY.
Due to the stand taken by the citizens of Logan County for law and order
and the successful turning back of the armed march of rebellious union miners,
Logan County is being investigated by the Committee on Education and Labor
of the United States Senate.
This investigation, and others preceding it in other counties, tend to arrive
at the living and working conditions of the miners. It has followed this course
in the investigation of Logan County. It has also inquired of the operators
the cause of the armed rebellion. We insist that the United Mine Workers of
America are not coming into Logan County, or trying to come in, for the pur-
pose of bettering living conditions, improving working conditions, or to in-
crease the wages of the miners in this field. The living and working conditions
in the Logan district of West Virginia surpass those in any union field in the
United States. As to wages, the records speak for themselves. They are not
coming in to give their members more steady work. The Logan field provides
its men with more work than any other field (union) in the country.
records of production will attest to this. Note that in spite of market condi-
tions the Logan field expects to break its high record of 1918, when over
10,000,000 tons of coal were shipped.
The
The United Mine Workers desire the unionization of the Logan field for two
reasons-first, to live up to their understanding with the operators in the
central competitive field; second, to dominate the coal industry of the United
States. No strike instituted by the United Mine Workers can be successful as
long as those fields working on the open-shop plan remain free from organi-
zation.
We suggest to the honorable committee that after it has satisfied itself in
regard to living and working conditions that it proceed in an investigation of
the United Mine Workers of America, especially as to its connection with the
recent armed insurrection. They have admitted their guilt by the payments
made for trains; by their defense in court of their members indicated on vari-
ous counts for participation in this march; and by the giving of orders for
commandeered food obtained on Coal River.
It is suggested that the committee obtain answers to the following:
1. Who organized and directed this march?
2. Who paid for the arms and ammunition?
3. Who supplied the arms and ammunition?
4. Who commanded and directed the work of their commissary?
5. Why, if Mr. Keeney was merely obeying the Government's order in turn-
ing his men back at Madison, were representatives of the press and others
barred from the park where the speech was made?
6. Did Mr. Keeney tell them to go back, and, if so, how far?
That the march was well organized and directed there is no doubt. That
they had an abundance of arms and ammunition there is no doubt. That they
had a well-organized commissary there is no doubt. The members of your
committee who have visited this country know that thousands of men could not
live on the country. If Mr. Keeney was obeying the law, there seems no
reason to make a secret of it. There is doubt that the instructions given by him
were plain.
The committee has at its disposal the secret service, the special agents of
the Department of Justice, the Post Office inspectors, and the Army intelligence


===== [扫描序号 1034] =====
1020

office, and we believe that the answers to these questions could be obtained
without delay.
LAW AND ORDER.
So much has been printed about lawlessness; labor disturbances; illicit dis-
tilling of liquor, etc., in southern West Virginia that we believe an authentic
statement in regard to law and order in Logan County should be made.
Logan County is peaceful; its citizens are law abiding.
To bring out this point a table showing area, population, number of police
officers, and the number of arrests made over a given period is given. The
table covers the city of Huntington and the whole of Logan County.

In connection with law and order an article appearing in the Huntington Dis-
patch quotes one of the State prohibition officers as stating that Logan County
is the dryest county in the State. Considering the topography of the county this
speaks well for the sheriff of Logan County and his deputies.
There have been no labor disturbances in Logan district during its existence,
or from 1905 to date.

Assessment per ton.
It will be seen from the totals that the assessment for this purpose was in 1920
less than one-half cent per ton, while in 1921, to and including September,
1921, it was slightly more than one-half cent per ton.
A statement made before this committee by Attorney England, of the State
of West Virginia, to the effect that assessments for this purpose amounted to
10 cents per ton is absolutely untrue.
In connection with the policing of Logan County it should be noted that the
real and personal property valuations as set by the assessor amount to
$23,356,676, and the cost of policing and protecting Logan County's property
is negligible.
The increase in the amount paid is due to the necessary increase in men to
handle the illicit distilling of liquor. That this work has been pushed and
that the results have been satisfactory there can be no doubt. The following
from the Huntington Dispatch attests to this:

LOGAN IS DRYEST COUNTY IS REPORT OF FEDERAL AGENT.
"Federal Prohibiion Agent James R. Gillette returned to the city yesterday
from Logan County, where he has been assisting Sheriff Don Chafil in the
suppression of liquor traffic.
"Mr. Gillette stated yesterday that a thorough campaign of the county
failed to reveal any evidences of liquor and declared that Logan County was
absolutely clean and probably the dryest spot in the entire State."
It was suggested by Senator Kenyon that the police power of the county
should not be paid for by the operators. Free schools and adequate schools
are also a duty of the State, yet no criticism is leveled at the operators for
their contributions to this cause, and it is thought that as much harm can
be done in the schools as in the use of police power.

2. Housing conditions in the Logan district are excellent. In building the
operator has had to take advantage of every available inch of flat ground, and
to our minds has done a good job. When you consider that in some places
the creek and railroad take up all flat ground it is remarkable that towns have
been built. In building the operator has taken advantage of every modern im-
provement and has built with the idea of both comfort and durability.
3. In giving you costs of lighting it should be remembered that electrical de-
vices to save the housewife have come into vogue and the prices of lighting
also covers the use of cleaners, washing machines, etc.

It will be noted that the company stores sell their merchandise at prices com-

class of stores in Huntington. In connection with the comparison of prices at
company stores with stores in Logan and Huntington, freight rates should be
considered. There are no through freight rates to Logan, a differential being
paid with Barboursville, W. Va., as the junction point. First-class rates per
100 pounds from Barboursville to Logan are 494 cents, while the mine that pur-
chases from a wholesaler in Logan pays an additional charge based on distance
from Logan.
THRIFT OF LOGAN'S LABOR.
That the men employed in the mines in the Logan district are thrifty and
therefore dependable, there can be no doubt. Men not satisfied with their work
or their surroundings, their living conditions, or who are being "worked on " by
agitators, have no incentive to save for that which is bigger and better.

ACTIVITY OF THE LOGAN DISTRICT.
Notwithstanding market conditions this year the Logan district has, to
October 15, produced 8,169,319 tons, and fully expects to break its 1918 record
of 10,228,690 tons.
In comparison to this it is interesting to note that in the fields where union
agreements are in effect the mines are practically shut down, its labor unem-
ployed, and therefore restless. Great stress has been laid recently about the
need for providing employment for the millions now out of work, but no steps
have been taken, nor will there be, by the United Mine Workers to bring their
scales into line with present-day business, and thus permit their members to
return to work.
During the great strike of 1919 the United States Geological Survey reported
that the Pocahontas, Tug River, Williamson, Logan, Hazard, southwest Vir-
ginia, sections of Winding Gulf, Somerset County (Pa.), and Alabama were
not affected by the strike order. This means that during that time these
fields stood between the public and freezing. The Logan district during that
period shipped 1,210,565 tons of coal, a weekly average of 242,113. Since that
time development has advanced and Logan could be depended upon to supply
more coal than it did in 1919.

SCHOOLS IN LOGAN COUNTY.
The Logan district high school was organized 10 years ago as a third-class
school. Six years ago it was made a first-class school. It now has an enroll-
ment of 317 pupils and employs 12 college-trained teachers. Courses are of-


===== [扫描序号 1042] =====
1028
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
fered in the following subjects: English, Latin, history, physics, chemistry,
biology, general science, sanitation, hygiene, cooking, sewing, home making,
typewriting, stenography, bookkeeping, commercial arithmetic, business Eng-
lish, manual training, mechanical drawing, algebra, plane solic geometry,
French, and Spanish.
Three years ago junior high schools were established at Omar, Holden,
Ethel, and Aracoma, the first three named being for white children, the one at
Aracoma for colored children. Two years of high-school work is offered in
each of these schools.
At present there are 49 enrolled at Ethel, 29 at Omar, 14 at Holden, and
20 at Aracoma; 64.7 per cent of these enrolled at Logan come from the mining
towns in the Logan district.
THE COAL OPERATOR AND THE SCHOOLS.
One company completed a schoolhouse where the county board was unable
to do so, at a cost of $12,500; another completed a school at the cost of $3,000;
another, at the cost of $1,200. Total, $16,700.
In no instance has this money been paid back to either coal company, and it
is uncertain just when it will be.
Teachers' salaries have been supplemented this year by different companies
to the amount of $6,000.
Teacherages have been furnished and equipped at a cost of $2,000.
Playgrounds apparatus has been installed at a cost of $5,000.
Schoolhouses have been painted and fenced free of cost to the board, $3,000.
Twenty-five buildings have been furnished for colored schools, with no cost
to the board, $2,500.
The above items are carried each year by the coal companies.
It would be conservative to say that the coal companies of Logan County,
in addition to having paid their proportion of school taxes, have contributed in
one way or another to the benefit of the public schools within the last four
years $100,000.
WHAT DOES THE UNION HOLD OUT TO THE MINERS OF THE LOGAN DISTRICT?
The union can not hold out improved living conditions, because such condi-
tions in the Logan field are unsurpassed by any union field.
The union can not hold out improved working conditions unless it is to put
the inefficient on the same basis with the efficient.
The union can not hold out increased wages, because of fees, monthly dues,
and special assessments, not to mention the smaller pay on account of occa-
sional strikes and disturbances.
The miner joining the union is called for $10 initiation fee and $2.25 monthly
dues (average); total. $12.25.
There are at least 8,000 men in the Logan field, which would mean $98,000
for the union to begin with. Then, there is a monthly income of $18,000 from
the usual monthly dues. To this could be added special assessments, which are
usually laid for the use of organizers and agitators working in the nonunion
fields. If the Logan field should become organized, the United Mine Workers
would increase their already enormous income by $216,000 per year. Is it
any wonder, aside from their desire to dominate the coal industry, that they
desire the organization of the Logan field? It might also be mentioned that
the union further enriches itself at the expense of the miner by the levying of
fines for infractions of working rules.
It is estimated, and conservatively, that the first year of unionism would cost
the miners of the Logan district at least $1,380,000, or $172.50 per man.
Have you ever realized that every man working in the Logan district, unless
he is a native, has had to pass through a union coal field in order to get to
Logan? The only exception to this statement covers men from the Pocahontas,
Tug River, and Williamson fields, but to those alone.
Why, then, we ask, if the unions hold out so much to their members, do these
men pass them by and come to an open-shop field?
