The CHAIRMAN. The committee will come to order. Are you ready to proceed?
Mr. VINSON. Mr. Chairman, I would like to hand to the stenographer at this
time the article submitted to the committee the other day, entitled "The curse
of unionism is evil leadership." At the time of its submission the committee
took under advisement the question of whether it should be admitted or not,
and I understand the committee has now decided that it shall go in the record,
and I ask that it be inserted in the record at this point.
The CHAIRMAN. Very well. It may go in the record at this point.
(The document referred to is here printed in the record in full, as follows:)
THE CURSE OF UNIONISM IS EVIL LEADERSHIP,
So long as the labor unions of the country are willing to tolerate the vicious
activities of men like Van Bittner, international representative of the United
Mine Workers of America, and others of his stripe, just so long will industrial
disputes be accompanied by the most bitter strife and disorder, ending ultimately
in the destruction of property and the loss of life. The part which this utterly
unworthy representative of the better elements in union labor played during
the recent coal-miners' strike in Alabama, and before he was finally compelled
by an outraged public sentiment to leave that State, resulted in a damage to
his own cause, to the cause of the coal mining and other industries in the State,
and to the cause of decency and respect for law and properly vested authority,
that is certain to take many months and even years to eradicate. The Birming-
ham News said at the time:
"Mr. Bittner's utterances at Blocton have done incalculable damage to the
cause of union labor in the Birmingham district. Many persons who had
been won to sympathy in recent months have changed their minds in view of
that speech. The News is informed that more than one representative labor
leader in Birmingham has expressed privately the keenest regret that the
speech was made. The News believes that one speech has done more harm
to labor probably than any single thing that has happened here in years. It
will take right living and right speaking a long time to live it down."
The outstanding feature of the situation existing in Alabama for the past
year and more is the unspeakable injustice in the settled practice of the
United Mine Workers and other labor unions of sending paid agitators to call
strikes in States where the industrial relations have been entirely satisfactory
74020-21-VOL 2-28
1029


===== [扫描序号 1044] =====
1030
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
to both employer and employee. Differences which arise as to hours and wages
between the employer and the workmen can be adjusted with much greater
satisfaction to all concerned when the situation is not clouded and intentionally
befogged by the utterly vicious activities of the agitator from without, the man
who is paid to foment this particular kind of strife.
In a recent issue of the Manufacturers Record we reviewed some of the
causes leading up to this strike, showing how it had been called in May, 1920, in
the coal fields of Alabama to enforce recognition of the union, and how, when
this failed, the national officers of the miners' union, located in Indianapolis,
called a general strike to take effect on September 7, 1920. As stated by Gov.
Kilby, the strike was ordered without just cause or for the purpose of adjusting
any grievance, but in deliberate violation of an agreement already existing
between the mine owners and the miners of Alabama, and thus it was both
illegal and immoral.
In a speech at Wylan, Ala., on March 27, Van Bittner said among other
things:
“The main thing to-day is to rid the mines and camps of the scabs who have
come in and taken your jobs and homes, and if you can not get them out one way,
try another. I want every man to apply for his old job at once. If you are
refused work I am not telling you what to do, but I know what I would do.
Don't expect anyone to give you anything, but take it."
Note also the following blasphemous remarks which Van Bittner made at
Blocton, Ala., on March 30:
"They may have a right to work, but by the eternal gods they haven't any
right to your jobs. It has been entirely too healthy for scabs around Blocton;
that has been the trouble with you. What would you do with a rattlesnake if
one of them would start crawling into this meeting now?"
A VOICE. "Kill him."
BITTNER. “A rattlesnake never did you half as much harm as a scab did. I
have not said that the scabs should be driven out. But you know what Christ
did with those money lenders in the temple at Jerusalem. Remember the story?
He picked them by the seat of their pants and threw them into the middle of
the street. That is what Christ did with the money lenders in the temple at
Jerusalem. I guess you are allowed to carry out Christ's laws, laws laid down
by Christ. I have always felt that you were just as safe under Christ's guid-
ance as you were under any of these coal operators or even the governor of
the State, and I would not except even Gen. Steiner.
"That is what Christ did with these fellows that were not any good; these
money lenders were saints compared with these scabs who are around in these
mines. There you have Christ's law. God's law, rather, laid down through our
Savior, as an example to go by here in Alabama. I like to see men who are
Christians be Christians through and through, practical Christians, men who are
willing to put Christianity into their every day life. Do that here and you
won't have any trouble getting your jobs back. You have every God-given right
to do that, my friends.

The United Mine Workers of America will be in Alabama long after
Charlie De Bardeleben, Gov. Kilby, Walter Moore, and Charlie Oakley are in
hell. This little two-by-four governor that you have here in Alabama ren-
dered some kind of a decision. This is not Gov. Kilby's decision, but Charlie De
Bardeleben, Frank Nelson, Walter Moore, and this dirty crowd that has been
running Alabama wrote that decision and they told him that they would
expose him and show the people of Alabama just what kind of a governor they
had, and Gov. Kilby, like the poor weakling that he is, decided that he would
sign his name to this decision that the coal operators wrote for him. There
has not been any strike yet. We are just going to start."
Officially the strike was called off by Van Bittner and the other union rep-
resentatives on the 22d of February of this year, in accord with the agreement
submitting the whole controversy to the governor, and between that date and
the time of Van Bittner's speech at Blocton there were no outbreaks in the
district. But immediately following this speech violence was resumed and
a number of deaths resulted during the following week. When Van Bittner
saw in cold type extracts from his Blocton address, he immediately issued a
statement to members of the unions of Alabama, urging them "to abstain
from violence and to violate no laws." He attempted to take the ground that
he had not advocated force. The record, however, is clear, and the press and
the people of Alabama united in insisting that Van Bittner leave "the infernal
State," as he called it. But the evil which he and other leaders of his type
have done and are doing lives after them, and, as everybody knows, the real
sufferers are the families of the laborers themselves, both union and nonunion.
They must bear the burden of unemployment and stoppage of wages, while
leaders of the Bittner type transfer their activities to greener fields. And now
several thousand of these union-mine strikers are living in tents and they and
their families are on the verge of starvation. Appeals are being made for help
for them, but many who are asked to contribute are replying that they are to
their utmost ability contributing to other causes and why should they now
succor men who refused to work and brought this poverty upon themselves and
their families? The miners' union has stopped the strike benefits to these men
and the coal operators do not need them in their mines, for they have an
abundant supply of labor to mine all the coal they can sell.
Until the labor unions of the country are willing and anxious to rid them-
selves of men of Van Bittner's stripe they need not feel any surprise that the
men over whom they exercise control are dominated largely by fear; fear of
that the labor organizers will or can do to them if they fail to obey their
commands. There can be no surprise anywhere that while such men direct
them, the labor unions continue to be un-American in principle, a menace to
the industrial peace and welfare of the Nation, and a curse to the workers
themselves.
The labor unions have far better types of men than these radicals among
their membership. Why is this better type not brought forth to guide these
organizations?

Col. FORD. The second occasion was on the 1st of September, remaining

The CHAIRMAN. When was the order made for the sending of Federal troops
into West Virginia?
Col. FORD. The request was made by Gen. Bandholtz, under the instructions

Col. FORD. We were not informed as to the exact time of the issuance of the

The CHAIRMAN. That request came the 1st of September?

The CHAIRMAN. You had charge of the actual work of getting the regiments

The CHAIRMAN. What regiment did you put in there?

The CHAIRMAN. How many men?
Col. FORD. Approximately 1,000 men.
There were also portions of the
Fortieth, Tenth, and a recruit detachment from Fifth Corps Area. Those latter
detachments came from Columbus Barracks.
The CHAIRMAN. How many troops altogether did you have there?

The CHAIRMAN. Have any of those troops been withdrawn?
Col. FORD. Yes. All troops have been withdrawn except what now constitutes

The CHAIRMAN. Where are they located now?
Col. FORD. The last report we had was that they were located at Charleston
and St. Albans.
The CHAIRMAN. Have any orders been made public as to the time the troops
will be removed from West Virginia?
Col. FORD. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. When you were there on the 26th of August, you remained,
I believe you said, a couple of days?
Col. FORD. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Where did you go and what did you find out about that

Col. FORD. Gen. Bandholtz and I arrived in Charleston about 3 a. m. August
26 and went direct to the statehouse. We were met there by Maj. Thompson,
a representative of the commanding general of the Fifth Corps Area, and Maj.
Thompson oriented us on the situation. At the conclusion of the conference
with him Gen. Bandholtz notified the governor of our presence and asked him
if he would come to his office for a conference. He appeared about 4 a. m.
and repeated to us substantially what had been included in a telegram to the
Secretary of War concerning the situation in West Virginia.
The CHAIRMAN. Had that march commenced at that time, the march at
Marmet?
Col. FORD. That concerned particularly the march from Marmet. The governor
was finally interrogated as to whether in his opinion he had exhausted all
the means at his disposal for quieting the disturbance. He stated in no uncertain
terms that he had done so, and therefore requested that the United States
troops be dispatched to the scene of the trouble. He was then asked if he


===== [扫描序号 1047] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
1033
desired to be present when Gen. Bandholtz interrogated Mr. Keeney, Mr.
Mooney, and Mr. Houston, the president, secretary-treasurer, and attorney,
respectively, of District No. 17 of the United Mine Workers of America. The
governor expressed himself as not desiring to be present, thinking perhaps it
would be better for him to be absent.
At 4.55, as I recall, the three gentlemen of the United Mine Workers of
America appeared before Gen. Bandholtz, and Gen. Bandholtz interrogated
them at length concerning the situation, their relations with the situation, and
their influence upon it. Concluding the conference, Mr. Keeney was asked if
he thought that he could stop the march at that time. He stated that he could
do so, he thought. Then on the suggestion of Gen. Bandholtz Mr. Keeney,
accompanied by Mr. Mooney, left in an automobile about 5.30 in the morning
of the 26th for the scene of the trouble. They were furnished with a brief
memorandum signed by Gen. Bandholtz stating their mission. They were re-
quested to inform Gen. Bandholtz of the situation as they found it, and the
disposition on the part of the marching miners to return to their homes as
requested.
As I recall, about 11.30 the same morning, August 26th, the first message
was received. It was from the vicinity of Racine, stating that the miners had
then stopped there, and word had been sent to other places informing the march-
ing miners that Mr. Keeney and Mr. Mooney were on their way, and to dis
continue the march until their arrival. From that time on various reports were
received during the rest of the day, indicating that the miners were returning.
The concluding report was that they had voted to return and would do so,
and requested the assistance of the authorities to provide rail transportation
for miners coming out of the Coal River district. That request was called
to the attention of the State authorities. Later on a similar request was
received, stating that the cars had not arrived, and details of that character.
Gen. Bandholtz made the plan that night to visit the various places along the
line of march early the next morning, to verify for himself the accuracy of
the reports sent in by the officers of the United Mine Workers of America.
Gen. Bandholtz, accompanied by myself and Maj. Thompson, left early in the
morning of the 27th of August, going as far as Marmet together, where we
separated, sending Maj. Thompson in one direction and Gen. Bandholtz and I
going in the direction of Racine. All along the road as far as Marmet and
beyond we saw returning miners coming back in small groups. Upon arrival at
Racine there were perhaps 150 armed miners there awaiting rail transportation.
Before we left the train equipment sufficient for taking them out arrived and
they were transported back.
All the indications were that the miners, so far as that particular march was
concerned, were disposed to return, and every evidence was given that they had
returned during the course of the day. Gen. Bandholtz then made his final report
to the War Department, stating that in his opinion the troops that were being
held in readiness-that is, the Federal troops-would not be required im-
mediately, but they should be earmarked for the purpose, in case emergency
arose. We left Charleston the night of the 27th.
The CHAIRMAN. For Washington?
Col. FORD. For Washington.
The CHAIRMAN. What happened after that?
Col. FORD. On the 29th of August word came to us officially that there was a
recurrence of the trouble in West Virginia, and Gen. Bandholtz and I were
directed to make our preparations to go at once. The governor of West
Virginia had sent a telegram to the Secretary of War again requesting that
Federal troops be sent to West Virginia. In addition to Gen. Bandholtz and
myself there was designated for the detail an officer of the Judge Advocate
General's Department, and an officer of the Militia Bureau to act as assistants.
We selected the means that would take us or effect our arrival in Charleston
at the earliest possible date.
The President had issued a proclamation requesting the armed miners in
West Virginia to disperse and repair peaceably to their homes. Following that
proclamation Gen. Bandholtz received instructions to go to the scene of the
trouble in West Virginia, examine into and report upon the extent to which
the offending persons were complying with the President's request. In case
compliance was not apparent, Gen. Bandholtz had instructions to report the
extent to which noncompliance was evident, the number of offending persons,


===== [扫描序号 1048] =====
1034
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
and the number of troops that should be sent to West Virginia to quiet the
trouble.
In accordance with those instructions, Gen. Bandholtz and his staff arrived
at Charleston, W. Va., at 11.30, September 1, 1921, one-half hour before the
expiration of the time given in the proclamation of the President. The time
limit therein given was stated at 12 o'clock noon, September 1. An immediate
conference was requested with Gov. Morgan, and such conference was held.
Also a conference was held with those officers of the United Mine Workers of
America that we were able to return. As I recall, Mr. Philip Murray, the
international vice president of the association, came before Gen. Bandholtz.
The conditions in West Virginia at that time could not be fully determined
at Charleston, so Gen. Bandholtz directed me to visit the scene of the trouble
and later make a report. I did so, accompanied on that trip by Maj. Thompson,
and repaired by way of St. Albans to the Coal River district, visiting Madison,
Clothier, Jefferys, Sharpless, and a number of towns that were reported to
be occupied by armed miners. I was informed that Mr. Murray had gone down
there to use his influence in stopping the march of the miners. I finally met him
somewhere along the road and had a conference with him. The result of my
trip in the Coal River Valley convinced me that the offending miners had not
obeyed the President's proclamation, nor did they intend to do so. Accordingly
I returned to Charleston and so reported to Gen. Bandholtz, who immediately
dispatched a telegram to the War Department requesting that Federal troops
be sent without delay.
Acting upon that request, Federal troops began to arrive on the evening of
September 3. Upon arrival the troops were met by staff officers designated
for the purpose to give information to the commanding officers as to their loca-
tions in West Virginia and duties that would be required of them. The dis-
position of the troops-that is to say, their actual location-had been arranged
beforehand, and as fast as troops arrived they were placed and instructions
given to take the necessary preventive measures against further disorder and
to quiet any existing disorders.
Briefly, the troops were located in two districts-the district of the vicinity
of Logan and the Coal River district. The troops in both of those districts
worked in conjunction with each other and cooperated with each other to the
extent that the patrols sent from either side met and exchanged information.
From the time of arrival of the Federal troops it became apparent that the
disorder would cease and quiet would again be restored. There were some
1,300, as I recall, armed miners that were passed through the United States
troops in the Coal River district. The other armed miners apparently, upon
arrival of the United States troops, or upon information reaching them that
they had arrived, repaired to their homes by way of various routes and trails
through the mountains.
Inspection by staff officers, as well as by Gen. Bandholtz, and the reports from
various commanding officers in the area, indicated that the miners were repair-
ing to their homes as fast as was physically possible to do so.
On the 7th of September quiet had been restored to such an extent that a
normal condition obtained, so that Gen. Bandholtz felt it proper to advise the
War Department of his recommendation that the Twenty-sixth Infantry be
returned to its station at Camp Dix. The War Department acted upon that
advice, and accordingly orders were issued for the relief of the Twenty-sixth In-
fantry, as well as certain Air Service units and chemical war service units.
Upon the departure of the Twenty-sixth Infantry the plan for the distribution
of the remaining troops was made. This plan involved the withdrawal of
troops from Logan, the redistribution of them in the Coal River district, a small
detachment at Charleston, and one farther east. The number of troops re-
maining for that purpose in the plan was about 400. No further relief has been
effected, except those due to the discharge of men whose expiration of term of
enlistment has arrived.
The CHAIRMAN. Colonel, did you make any estimate, or can you give the
committee any estimate, of the number of men in what has been termed here this
invading army?
Col. FORD. Yes, sir. That was required by the instructions given by the War
Department. I might say that it was only an estimate. It was humanly impos-
sible to arrive at accurate figures. The various reports indicated the number to
be from 7.000 to 10,000. In the War Department telegrams that were sent by
Gen. Bandholtz the estimate was placed conservatively at 5,000.

West Virginia which is unionized and with that which is not.
The CHAIRMAN. Yes.
Col. FORD. It was also reported that efforts made on the part of union men
to unionize certain nonunion mines in Mingo were met with resistance. This
information was conveyed to the union miners in other parts of West Virginia,
and as a remonstrance to the declaration of martial law by the governor in
Mingo County, and the fact that the union men had been imprisoned there, the
union miners armed themselves for the purpose of marching into Mingo County
and releasing the miners that were imprisoned.
The CHAIRMAN. You think that was the prime object of the march?
Col. FORD. Briefly, that is as it was reported to us.
The CHAIRMAN. Are there any questions, Mr. Walsh?
Mr. WALSH. Colonel, I saw quoted in some paper, and I have had a general

Col. FORD. I recall there was a telegram in substance that.

TESTIMONY OF MR. W. JETT LAUCK.
'The witness, having been first duly sworn by the chairman, testified as
follows:
The CHAIRMAN. I believe Mr. Lauck is the last witness, gentlemen.
Have you given your name to the reporter?
Mr. LAUCK. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. What is your business, Mr. Lauck?
Mr. LAUCK. I am an economist by profession.
The CHAIRMAN. Are you connected with the United Mine Workers' associa-
tion?
Mr. LAUCK. Not permanently, but I ain from time to time in the case of
wage disputes or wage arbitrations.
The CHAIRMAN. Were you connected with the War Labor Board in some
capacity?
Mr. LAUCK. I was secretary of the War Labor Board.
The CHAIRMAN. You are not familiar, except as the evidence has disclosed
here, with the various things that happened in West Virginia, I assume, and
do not care to go into that?
Mr. LAUCK. Not at all. I have not been at the so-called scene of conflict
there, and I do not know anything at first hand.
The CHAIRMAN. Can you furnish us any evidence as to the ownership of
lands there? Have you gone into that?
Mr. LAUCK. I have gone into that from the official reports of the Steel Corpo-
ration and from the reports of the Norfolk & Western Railroad and other
sources of that kind, and the exhibit submitted by Mr. Murray represents
the results of the investigation that I have made.
The CHAIRMAN. You have nothing to add to that?
Mr. LAUCK. Nothing additional; no, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Have you given a good deal of thought and consideration to
this industrial situation there, Mr. Lauck?
Mr. LAUCK. I have, sir. That is the main point of interest that I have in
the present discussion.
The CHAIRMAN. Now, in your own way, I would like to have your views
about it, the causes of the trouble, and, if you have any suggestions as to
remedies for not only this, but general industrial difficulties, I would like to
have them.
Mr. WALSH. First, the cause of the trouble?
The CHAIRMAN. Yes.
Mr. LAUCK. I think that one case that stands out clear as a pikestaff, you
might say, is the discrimination against men for belonging to trade-unions. That
is the fundamental and primary cause. In approaching the subject with the
idea of any remedy, that is the one factor that has to be met.
I was very much impressed with what Mr. Wiley said yesterday. In his
concluding statement, when you asked him for a solution of the matter, in
one of the solutions that he put forward-I think it was the last-he said that
if in Logan and Mingo Counties there would be no discrimination against a
man for membership in the union, or the United Mine Workers of America,
and that, on the other hand, if the union men would agree not to discriminate
or to coerce or intimidate a nonunion man, or would not attempt to intimidate or
coerce the operator into recognizing the union, the whole matter would be settled.
I think that is the fundamental cause and that is the fundamental basis of
settlement. I think that violence and disorder, from what I have gathered
from the evidence and what I knew before, have arisen primarily from that
situation.
As to what should be done about it, it seems to me that the Federal Government
should intervene in Mingo County and in Logan County. They have already
intervened, of course, in the form of armed forces, in an effort to maintain order,
but that will really not be effective; that is, the situation may require that
the Federal Government intervene again in order that order may be main-
tained, or West Virginia may be able to maintain order. But the situation
will never be settled until the Federal Government intervenes with a code
or series of principles that enlightened public opinion has sanctioned, such
as the right to organize free from discrimination and to belong to trade-unions,
and the equal safeguards from the standpoint of the operators, that a man
belonging to a union will not attempt to coerce or intimidate a nonunion
man or induce or coerce the operators to recognize his union. Or, in other


===== [扫描序号 1051] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
1037
words, the fundamental principle of the War Labor Board, which was agreed
upon during the period of hostilities, in a joint conference of employers and
employees, should be the fundamental principles that should become operative
in Mingo and Logan Counties and which would compose the situation.
The CHAIRMAN. Have you that declaration of the War Labor Board of
fundamentals?
Mr. LAUCK. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Could you put it into the record or furnish us a copy?
Mr. LAUCK. I have the principles, and also the docket of the War Labor
Board, which I would like to submit for the records of the committee.
The CHAIRMAN. The docket?
Mr. LAUCK. The docket of cases; that is, as to how these principles were
applied. I probably should not have said "docket." I should have said
"record of cases," and the application of the principles.
It is my idea, Mr. Chairman, that the Federal Government should use its
efforts to compose this matter by requiring both parties to enter into an
arrangement under which they would subscribe to these fundamental princi-
ples of the right of organization and protection against discrimination-and
if they would not do that, as a coercive measure to enact legislation creating
a board or agency of adjustment which would have as its guiding force these
principles of the War Labor Board.
You understand that would not imply union recognition on the one hand and
would be a protection to the operators against union intimidation or coercion
on the other hand.
I may say that in making this suggestion I am speaking personally and not for
the United Mine Workers of America, although Mr. Murray set forth as his
basis of composing the situation an agreement based upon these fundamental
principles in which he added the principles of freedom of speech and freedom
of assembly which are constitutional guaranties, of course; and he also wished
as a condition to an arrangement the returning of the men to work in Mingo
County who had been on strike or who had been locked out.
The CHAIRMAN. Your idea of a permanent solution is a board or a court of
some kind based on certain well-defined fundamental propositions?
Mr. LAUCK. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Such as the propositions of the War Labor Board?
Mr. LAUCK. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you think they cover every disputed question?
Mr. LAUCK. I think from the public standpoint they are sufficient to compose
the situation. From a union standpoint, of course, the union leader or the union
representative would advocate union recognition probably as a basis of settle-
ment, although they might be willing, as Mr. Murray indicated, to accept an
agreement based upon purely the right to organize.
On the other hand, while perhaps the operators are evidently well within
their constitutional rights, technically speaking, it seems to me that their atti-
túde from the standpoint of enlightened public opinion and from the real devel-
opment of public thinking upon these questions is decidedly backward, and
while constitutionally proper, morally you might say it is improper.
I have here the principles of the War Labor Board and its method of pro-
cedure as proclaimed by the President during the war.
The CHAIRMAN. Those principles we would like to have in the record, Mr.
Lauck.
Mr. VINSON. I would suggest his simply giving them to the stenographer, with-
out taking time to read them.
The CHAIRMAN. I am familiar with them, and I want them in the record.
(The statement of principles referred to will be found at the end of Mr.
Lauck's testimony.)
The CHAIRMAN. Mr. Taft was a member of the board, and Mr. Walsh was also

out in the evidence. I heard the statement; yes. The conclusion I got from that
statement was that he refused to sign a closed-shop agreement and from that
time on he was a constant target of rifles and disorder and violence, etc.
Mr. VINSON. And the utter destruction of his property?
Mr. LAUCK. And I consider there were other factors the committee was not
advised about. It is perfectly obvious there were.
Mr. VINSON. Have you or not stated to this committee, Mr. Lauck-I have
forgotten-that this committee and the Congress has not constitutional power
to pass the legislation that would coerce the nonunion mine workers to recog-
nize the union and to employ union men who were active in trying to establish
the union in the nonunion mines?
Mr. LAUCK. I think that is correct-operators, you mean?
Mr. VINSON. Yes.
Mr. LAUCK. I have been very much interested in your constitutional attitude.
It seems to me that your attitude constitutionally is something like the con-
stitutional question at the time of the Civil War. Take, for instance, at the
time of the Civil War, those of us who are from the South may say that there
was no doubt that the constitutional right, technically speaking, of seceding
from the Union, based upon the original interpretation and the debates on it,
was unquestionable, but since the formation of the Constitution up to the Civil
War there had been developments, men's minds had changed, conditions had
changed, social usages had changed, and it was a wrong thing to do, as we look
back on it. Now, perhaps, every southerner would agree it was a wrong thing
to do, although it was constitutionally right to do.
Now, it seems to me that is peculiarly your situation here. That is, you are
standing on constitutional arbitraries, technicalities, when, as a matter of
fact, the development of public opinion has changed the original situation-of
course, we all know that law is a crystallization of public opinion, and that the
Constitution in its interpretation is applied to existing conditions. For in-
stance, you have the Supreme Court deciding in the Adamson eight-hour law
case, that it was for the public welfare and similar cases the Brandies Oregon
case.
I think you are in identically the same situation that developed in the war-
for instance, in the case of the War Labor Board, in the Hichman case, that Mr.
Coolidge has referred to-the legalization of the constitutional right of indi-
vidual contracts. It was decided in the War Labor Board by eminent jurists-
we were taught there that the Hichman decision was constitutionally right, but
morally wrong.
I think you are constitutionally right, but from the standpoint of industrial
usages, industrial precedence, public opinion, and every other consideration
that has grown up in the last 30 years, that you are morally wrong. I think
the public opinion will crystallize into law as soon as the safeguards you are
relying on the Constitution to protect you against-
Mr. COOLIDGE. You think the individual rights-
Mr. WALSH. I think these interruptions should cease at least to this extent,
that we ought to stick to one counsel.
Mr. COOLIDGE. If Mr. Vinson does not object, you need not object.
Mr. WALSH. I do object.

Mr. LAUCK. I would like to answer Mr. Coolidge's question.
Mr. VINSON. Just one question, then I wish you would go back to Mr.
Coolidge's question. Your idea, then, Mr. Lauck-

PRINCIPLES AND POLICIES TO GOVERN RELATIONS BETWEEN WORKERS AND EMPLOYERS
IN WAR INDUSTRIES FOR THE DURATION OF THE WAR.
There should be no strikes or lockouts during the war.
Right to organize.--The right of workers to organize in trade-unions and to
bargain collectively through chosen representatives is recognized and affirmed.
This right shall not be denied, abridged, or interfered with by the employers in
any manner whatsoever.
The right of employers to organize in associations or groups and to bargain
collectively through chosen representatives is recognized and affirmed. This
right shall not be denied, abridged, or interfered with by the workers in any
manner whatsoever.
Employers should not discharge workers for membership in trade-unions
nor for legitimate trade-union activities.
The workers, in the exercise of their right to organize, should not use
coercive measures of any kind to induce persons to join their organizations
nor to induce employers to bargain or deal therewith.
Existing conditions.—In establishments where the union shop exists the same
shall continue, and the union standards as to wages, hours of labor, and other
conditions of employment shall be maintained.
In establishments where union and nonunion men and women now work
together and the employer meets only with employees or representatives en-
gaged in said establishments, the continuance of such conditions shall not be
deemed a grievance. This declaration, however, is not intended in any manner
to deny the right or discourage the practice of the formation of labor unions
or the joining of the same by the workers in said establishments, as guaran-
teed in the preceding section, nor to prevent the War Labor Board from urging
or any umpire from granting, under the machinery herein provided, improve-
ment of their situation in the matter of wages, hours of labor, or other con-
ditions as shall be found desirable from time to time.


===== [扫描序号 1062] =====
1048
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
Established safeguards and regulations for the protection of the health and
safety of workers shall not be relaxed.
Women in industry.-If it shall become necessary to employ women on work
ordinarily performed by men, they must be allowed equal pay for equal work,
and must not be allotted tasks disproportionate to their strength.
Hours of labor.-The basic eight-hour day is recognized as applying in all
cases in which existing law requires it. In all other cases the question of hours
of labor shall be settled with due regard to governmental necessities and the
welfare, health, and proper comfort of the workers.
Maximum production.—The maximum production of all war industries should
be maintained, and methods of work and operation on the part of employees or
workers which operate to delay or limit production, or which have a tendency
to artificially increase the cost thereof, should be discouraged.
Mobilization of labor.-For the purpose of mobilizing the labor supply with
a view to its rapid and effective distribution, a permanent list of the numbers
of skilled and other workers available in different parts of the country shall be
kept on file by the Department of Labor, the information to be constantly fur-
nished-
1. By the trade-unions.
2. By State employment bureaus and Federal agencies of like character.
3. By the managers and operators of industrial establishments throughout
the country.
These agences shall be given opportunity to aid in the distribution of labor
as necessity demands.
Custom of localities.—In fixing wages hours, and conditions of labor, regard
should always be had to the labor standards, wage scales, and other conditions
prevailing in the localities affected.
The living wage.-1. The right of all workers, including common laborers, to
a living wage, is hereby declared.
2. In fixing wages, minimum rates of pay shall be established which will
insure the subsistence of the worker and his family in health and reasonable
comfort.
PROPOSED AGREEMENT.
1. At the request of the Senate Committee on Education and Labor, acting
through its chairman, Hon. William S. Kenyon, of Iowa, the representatives of
the coal operators of the counties of Mingo, Logan, Mercer, and McDowell of
the State of West Virginia, and the representatives of the mine workers from
the same counties, in order to avoid industrial warfare, to promote general tran-
quility, to prevent stoppages of work, and to accelerate the production of coal,
hereby subscribe to the following principles as mandatory upon working rela-
tions and conditions in the coal mining operations of the aforementioned coun-
ties, and pledge their complete and unreserved support to the establishment and
maintenance of these principles:
(a) The maintenance of the constitutional guarantees of freedom of speech,
freedom of assemblage, and freedom of movement.
(b) Armed guards, with the exception of ordinary watchmen for the usual
protection of property, shall not be employed by the operators.
(c) Neither the miners or operators shall employ detectives or contribute
either directly or indirectly to the maintenance of sheriffs or constables.
(d) The right of the miners to organize in trade-unions and to bargain col-
lectively through their chosen representatives is recognized and affirmed. This
right shall not be denied, abridged, or interfered with by the operators in any
manner whatsoever.
(e) The right of the operators to organize in associations or groups and to
bargain collectively through their chosen representatives is recognized and
affirmed. This right shall not be denied, abridged, or interfered with by the
miners in any manner whatsoever.
(f) The operators shall not discharge miners for membership in trade-
unions, nor for the legitimate trade-union activities.
(g) The miners, in the exercise of their right to organize, shall not use
coercive measures of any kind to induce persons to join their unions.
(h) No miner shall be evicted from a company house or domicile, save and
except in compliance with the provisions of the landlord and tenant laws of
the State, so long as he is willing and able or continues to work for the
company pending the determination of any differences or controversy that
may arise between the miners and operators.


===== [扫描序号 1063] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
1049
(i) Men now on strike be given an opportunity to return to work.
2. There shall be established in each of the aforesaid counties a board of
conciliation composed of six members, three to be selected by and to repre-
sent the miners, and three to be selected by and to represent the operators.
3. The Senate Committee on Education and Labor, through its chairman,
Hon. William S. Kenyon, shall request the Chief Justice of the United States
to appoint an impartial administrator of this agreement.
4. The salaries and expenses of the members of the boards of conciliation
shall be paid by the miners and operators, respectively, each fixing and paying
the amount of compensation of their representatives.
5. The compensation of the impartial administrator shall be $10,000 per
annum, and the compensation together with all necessary expenses of the im-
partial administrator shall be paid one-half by the miners and one-half by the
operators.
6. All differences which may arise as to the interpretation and application
of this agreement, as well as all grievances which may be brought forward in
the future by either the operators or the miners, shall be referred to the
aforementioned county boards of conciliation for adjustment.
7. In the event that the county boards of conciliation, after an interval of
30 days from the date on which the dispute or grievance is submitted to the
board of conciliation, are unable to reach a decision, the matters in dispute
shall be referred to the impartial administrator.
8. The decision of the impartial administrator shall be final and must be
rendered within 30 days from the date on which the case is referred to him.
9. Pending the final decision of the impartial administrator, and for 30 days
thereafter, there shall be no strike on the part of the miners or lockout on the
part of the operators.
10. In case of a strike the county boards of conciliation and the impartial
administrator shall not take jurisdiction in the case until the strikers have
returned to work under the conditions prevailing at the time of the strike.
11. In case of a lockout the county boards of conciliation and the impartial
administrator shall not take jurisdiction in the case until the operators have
restored to the miners the opportunity to continue at work under the conditions
prevailing at the time of the lockout.
12. Decisions and determinations of the county boards of conciliation shall
be by a majority vote.
13. The county boards of conciliation in conference with the impartial admin-
istrator shall establish their own rules and procedure on a uniform basis.
14. The term "miner" in this agreement is used to designate and include all
workers in and about the mines.
15. This agreement shall be operative immediately upon its signature by
the parties concerned, and shall continue in effect for a period of two years
thereafter, or until modified by mutual agreement.

NATIONAL LABOR BOARD.
Whereas in the period through which we are now passing of adjustment of war-
time conditions of business and industry to normal conditions there exists no
general national agency for the settlement of industrial disputes, or for the
determination of a general labor policy; and
Whereas no general arrangement has as yet been worked out by representatives
of employers and employees as to the fundamental principles which should
obtain in the adjustment of industrial relations and conditions, or the labor
standards which should be observed; and
Whereas the general public has suffered much from this state of affairs and
will suffer further loss and inconvenience if the present situation is allowed
to continue; and
Whereas, unless some national machinery, based on well-defined principles, for
the peaceable adjustment of industrial disputes is established, not only the


===== [扫描序号 1064] =====
1050
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
continuity of production can not be maintained but also the acceleration of
production to maximum proportions, of which our country and the world are
in so grievous need, can not be hoped for: Therefore be it
Resolved by the Senate (the House of Representatives concurring), That the
following principles shall be made mandatory upon industrial relations and con-
ditions throughout the United States in all adjustment of labor disputes:
Right to organize.-The right of workers to organize in trade-unions and
to bargain collectively through chosen representatives is recognized and affirmed.
This right shall not be denied, abridged, or interfered with by the employers in
any manner whatsoever.
The employers shall not discharge workers for membership in trade-union
activities.
The workers in the exercise of their right to organize, shall not use coercive
measures of any kind to induce persons to join their organizations (nor to
induce employers to bargain or deal therewith).
Women in industry.-When women are employed on work ordinarily per-
formed by men, they must be allowed equal pay for equal work, and must not be
allotted tasks disproportionate to their strength.
The living wage.-1. The right of all workers, including common laborers, to
a living wage is hereby declared.
2. In fixing wages, minimum wage rates of pay shall be established which will
insure the subsistence of the worker and his family in health and reasonable
comfort.
To interpret and apply the principles enumerated above and to determine and
settle any differences or controversies that may arise between wage earners
and employers, a board to be known as the national labor board is to be created
consisting of three representatives of employees, three representatives of the
employers, and two joint chairmen, representative of the public, all members of
the board to be appointed or designated by the President of the United States.
The representatives of the employees shall be selected from a list of six
nominations made by the American Federation of Labor, the representatives
of the employers shall be selected from a list of six nominations made by the
national industrial conference board, one joint chairman shall be designated from
a list of three nominations made by the labor representatives of the board, and
one joint chairman from a list of three nominations made by the three
representatives of the employers. The expenses of the board shall be paid,
one-half by the employees and one-half by the employers.
In case of refusal or failure of either the American Federation of Labor or
national industrial conference to submit nominations within 30 days after the
approval of this resolution, the President shall select his own appointees without
nominations.
In case of a strike, the board shall not take jurisdiction in the case until
the strikers have returned to work under the conditions prevailing at the time
of the strike.
In case of a lockout, the board shall not take jurisdiction in case until the
employer has restored to the wage earners the opportunity to continue at work
under the conditions prevailing at the time of the lockout.
Decisions and determinations of the board shall be effective as of the date
of its taking jurisdiction in a case, except as otherwise provided in a joint sub-
mission agreement.
Decisions and determinations of the board shall be by a majority vote. In
event the board shall be unable to reach a decision or determination in any
cause brought before it, the case shall be referred to an umpire to be chosen
by lot from a list of 10 nominations made by the President of the United States,
the decision or determination of the umpire to be final and binding.
The board shall establish its rules and procedure, taking as a basis therefor
the rules and procedure of the National War Labor Board.
The National Labor Board shall receive for adjudication either ex parte com-
plaints or jo'nt-submissions from employers and employees, or, it may institute
proceedings in any controversy on its own motion or on the recommendation of
the President or the Congress.
It shall establish in the leading industries and trades joint boards of em-
ployers and employees for the adjustment of labor disputes and for such other
purposes as it may deem proper for the advancement of industrial peace and
the public welfare.
Decisions shall be rendered by the board within a period of 30 days from the
date of the submission of the complaint or joint submission, and decisions of


===== [扫描序号 1065] =====
WEST VIRGINIA COAL FIELDS.
1051
umpires shall be made within a period of 15 days from the date on which
matters in dispute are referred to them by the board.
Pending a final decision by the board or an umpire there shall be no strikes
or lockouts.
For the official administration of the functions vested in the Labor Board,
any member thereof may require, by subpoena issued and signed by himself,
the attendance of any witness and the production of any book, paper, docu-
ment, or other evidence from any place in the United States at any designated
place of hearing, and the taking of a deposition before any designated person
having power to administer oaths. In the case of a deposition the testimony
shall be reduced to writing by the person taking the deposition or under his
direction, and shall then be subscribed to by the deponent. Any member of the
Labor Board may administer oaths and examine any witness. Any witness
summoned before the board and any witness whose deposition is taken shall be
paid the same fees and mileage as are witnesses in the courts of the United
States.
In case of failure to comply with any subpoena or in case of the contumacy
of any witness appearing before the Labor Board, the board may invoke the
aid of any United States district court. Such court may thereupon order the
witness to comply with the requirements of such subpoena, or to give evidence
touching the matter in question, as the case may be. Any failure to obey such
order may be punished by such court as a contempt thereof.
(The following letter is a reply in behalf of the Iron League of New York
regarding published statements of Samuel Untermyer before the Committee on
Education and Labor.)
(Thereupon at 11.45 a. m., the committee adjourned sine die.)
IRON LEAGUE OF NEW YORK,
New York, October 26, 1921.
To the COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION AND LABOR,
United States Senate.
GENTLEMEN: In behalf of the Iron League of New York I desire to reply
to published statements of Samuel Untermyer before your committee regarding
the structural-iron situation in New York City.
Mr. Untermyer's charges regarding improper or unlawful control of steel in
New York were fully investigated in the present year by a special Federal
grand jury, special assistants to the Attorney General, and a corps of investi
gators. In addition to the minutes of the Lockwood committee and the evidence
secured by the Federal investigators, the books and records of both the National
Erectors' Association and the Iron League were voluntarily submitted and ex-
haustively examined. Members of the league voluntarily appeared as witnesses
and waived immunity. Upon this full and complete investigation the grand
jury refused to take action upon the charges.
The erection of structural iron and steel has been conducted upon an open-
shop basis in New York continuously since 1905. The Iron League was not
organized by the National Erectors, but was in existence many years before the
national association was formed. Only four of the members of the Iron League
are members of the National Erectors' Association. Neither the Bethlehem Co.
nor the Steel Corporation, nor any of their subsidiaries, are members of the
Iron League, and neither of these companies has ever dominated or controlled
the league in any way, either directly or indirectly.
The Iron League comprises the one group of employers in the building indus-
try of New York City which is not a party to the so-called Brindell combination.
and the fight against the league in 1919 and 1920 was due to an effort to force
the league to become a party to the Brindell combine. Under the laws of New
York such a combination to control material, as charged by Mr. Untermyer,
would be lawful. Combinations more vicious in character than anything charged
against the iron contractors have long existed in the building industry, yet Mr.
Untermyer, as counsel for the Lockwood committee, has taken no steps to secure
legislation making such combinations unlawful.
Any charge of discrimination in the employment of workmen is untrue, and
two-thirds of the employees of the members of the league are union men.
May I ask that in justice to the Iron League this statement be made a part
of the record of your committee?
Respectfully,
WALTER DREW, Counsel.
